I must say I really enjoy this title. I have over 100 hours in the original version of this game and then 40 in their enhanced edition. They made a huge amount of improvements upon the base game as well as added a lot of new features and skills.
When the enhanced version dropped, a friend (that I played the original with) and myself immediately started a game without really reading what all the new features were. As we play I am the one who will usually hoard potions, scrolls and bombs since my friend plays the caster type, making most these items useless to him. We get to this one part early one that we are fighting a large group of undead that during the fight decide to group up, in chat I tell my friend, "Oh! Don't worry, I got this." I go to use a grenade, thinking about how epic this will be, but there is a new feature that we did not read. They added a skill called Grenadier and without it thrown items have a random trajectory. So instead of blowing up this nicely huddled group of skeletons in a blaze of glory, I fumble the grenade, throwing it straight behind me and into my friends face... killing him instantly.
10/10 wouldn't take Grenadier again!
Love the game so far.

If you're a fan of any of the Ultimas of old - you'll see all the potential that the pre-alpha of Shroud of the Avatar has of being the "spiritual successor to Ultima" as Richard Garriott once said.
With each monthly release the world continues to expand as the sounds become richer, the graphics and lighting improve and the conversations and characters become more believable.
The story, of course, is a closely guarded secret and will be until the game is near completion.. but rumor has it that it will be among the best tales that any rpg has ever told.
Combat is the only real controversy. Instead of the traditional fixed skill hotbar, your skills are randomized. It's been coined "card combat" because it's like your cards have been shuffled and are being dealt out to you as if Fate himself was the dealer. You can control the speed at which your skills are dealt, you can even fix some skills in a locked position if you prefer the classic mmo hotbar. Any locked skill can't be combined with other skills for combos.. so you have a reason to steer clear from locking skills. The system still needs fleshed out and you'll either love it or hate it.
So, if you're ready for some old school game mechanics (free-flow chat where you type what you want to say to npcs instead of click on pre-written sentences, no quest markers or arrows, etc) with some new school designs (card combat) mixed with immersion and a very active and helpful player community - then Shroud of the Avatar may be what you've been dreaming of in a game.

update 1/13/2017
many bits of this review will stay the same. the one glaring change was the lack of a use-based skill system. they did replace the traditional leveling system with one that was use-based. they included skill decay, and that really does help keep the player engaged.
I've had my pledge in for this game since the end of october 2014.
Since then, i've:
Forced my guild to go multi-game, so I wouldn't have to disband the guild and start a new one.
Gotten many of my guildies to pledge.
Gotten several of my coworkers to pledge.
Made many MANY new friends within the community.
Heavily participated in their official forums.
Realized that developers are people too, and these in particular really enjoy working with, and playing with, us gamers. they ARE gamers..
Decided to play this game for the next 6 years at least.
speaking on the "they're just people too..." aspect,
on my third day in game, i met richard garriot again. first time here. we were chatting about brewing for almost half an hour, while i served him mead at the bar i was keeping, on the houseboot we were throwing a party at.. we, being the community.
then i told the devs during one of their hangouts (starr long, specifically) that i was in silent protest for not having kilts in game (yet), by wearing a skirt the whole time..still haven't taken it off (i like the breeze!) - for a while a couple of them checked up on me to make sure i still had it on. i mean seriously..which other dev team would do something like that, these days?
from my perspective, coming from a very long history of gaming as well as working QA for many games over the years.. at this stage in development, 95% of the games i've been a part of had zero finish/polish on them, and the quality of code was truly horrible. this is simply not the case here.
I consider this game to have more polish on it than many AAA games have when they've gone gold. yeah, some of the systems are in place but not complete. but in pre-alpha that is to be expected.
______________edit_________
old text:
with an upcoming release that will include unity5 support, it will get even better, there is no doubt. i hope they add speedtrees too. what a wonderful asset that is.
new text:
well it did just that. the unity upgrades they've done since the origional review have helped pretty drastically with quality of lighting, godrays, darker darks, lighter lights, and framerates.  and they added speedtrees too! i saw a pretty heavy rise in framerates and lowering of memory footprint when they did that.
_____________/edit____________
this isn't saying that there are no issues or problem with the game, but the sheer awesomeness overcomes almost all of them for me.
for example, the new and innovative combat deck system, is pretty neat once you get used to it. there is a learning curve, but once you start down that hill, its gravy from then on and can enhance your gaming experiences tenfold.
______edit________
old text:
my one true gripe is their decision to NOT go with a use-skill system, and focus more on a traditional leveling system. beyond that single item, i have no other complaints..and in pre-alpha, that is truly remarkable in and of itself.
new text:
seems they replaced the leveling system entirely with a use-based system. it has been in place a while now, and it is really neat.
_________/edit__________
i wish these folks many years of good times, and i fully expect to be there with them.

20 years from now, someone will ask you if you played Shroud of the Avatar. If you say no, you'll wish you had.
Shroud of the Avatar is being created by a small but dedicated team of highly experienced developers. In conjuction with the fans, this development team has created innovative new ideas that large publishers will someday copy and market without remorse.
The game has three core systems:
1. A truly player driven economy.  The players make everything!  Trade is regional and localized.  Even in-game currency is intended to be made by the players.  This is a crafters dream!
2. Limited and meaningful housing.  Players can decorate their housing in more unique and creative ways than in any other game.  Housing, like all items in Shroud of the Avatar, are both functional and interactive.  Doors open and close, store valuables, and provide a base of operations to build your reputation and socialize with your friends and acquaintances.  Housing is truly finite and unique, giving active players the ability to feel like the game world is alive.
3. Combat and PVP.  Combat battles are more than just repetitive key presses, and players are encouraged to THINK about what they're doing.  PVP is designed to be both consensual AND meaningful.  Which means that the goal is not only to make a competitive playing field, but to also have accomplished something when it's performed.  Risk will be Rewarded and True Accomplishments will be Remembered!
Still in Pre-Alpha, I have followed this game's development since the beginning, and I remain strongly passionate about its direction and spirit.  But I do have concerns.
1. The current implementation of PVP is currently built on a Damage Per Second (DPS) model.  There is no way to block or counter attacks. This creates a very poor base to build more meaningful pvp that focuses on player’s skill and not "best builds".  The community is currently giving feedback to push this in the right direction.
2. Magic has no ritual component to it.  Everything is a damage spell.  Which makes the use of magic more casual and common.  Currently in Pre-Alpha Release 14, magic is used by almost all characters because it is cheap, powerful, and requires no discipline or knowledge to use.  From a roleplaying standpoint, this reduces magic to the lowest common denominator and encourages all players to be a hybrid.  This too is an area that needs improvement.
3. The current AI for summoned creatures and PVE monsters is very poor.  Shroud of the Avatar is extremely fun to play in PVE, but it's currently easy and typical MMO tactics like kiting reduce all AI to an almost childlike behavior.  I'm looking forward to future releases where this is not the case.
In closing, I want to stress that I believe Shroud of the Avatar will overcome my concerns.  The development team and the community are champions of collaborative feedback and each release the game gets better and better.
If you want to be involved in what I believe will be the best roleplaying game of our time. Do yourself a favor and join us now.  Years later you'll remember making this choice and you’ll be glad you did.

I love this game. Thats what I need to say first.
Few game tips at the very end.
Pros:

In depth review:
Okay so this game is really worth buying but I feel like $20 is expensive a bit, so I recommend you to buy this game when its on sale. It is worth a buy! It is totally worth a buy, because you will enjoy the thrill the game gives you. Anyways, I'm gonna go through few of the pros and cons I've listed.
First, good team balance. I say it's balanced because the sharks can kill divers really quick (depends on how fast the player thrashes, but you can still kill the divers easily unless you do not thrash at all). This does not mean the sharks are super OP hands down. The diver who has been caught is really helpless, so it depends on the other three divers. If two sharks caught two divers, then there are the other two that can help them out. Then wouldn't that mean the sharks busy eating would also be helpless? Well this matters on how you play as a shark. Yes, you are hopeless when you're in middle of divers with guns doing nothing but eating. No, you're not completely helpless if you hit and run. After biting, sharks need to run or else they can die. Now, the divers can choose to watch his mate helplessly die or to chase after the shark to help the diver out or at least avenge for the gonner. This game can be played without team work, but it will be definitely fun to have your friends to get some team work.
In case if you are wondering with the highlighting and heart beat system, read this next two paragraph. If not, don't read it. I want to save your time.
As a diver you have this heart beat system. As you can already guess, when the sharks comes closer your heart beat increases to warn you. But you do not know the sharks exact location. They can be right by the corner, they be on the opposite side of the wall, they can be right above you. You do actually get to know their exact location if they bite one of the divers, be detected by flares, or by being detected by sonar buoys.
As a shark, if you come closer to the divers you can see them highlighted through walls or even without walls. This helps the shark side so much because if there wasn't any system like this, I tell you, the divers immediately becomes a stealth squad and you would ask yourself a question which is suppose to be the hunter and prey.
Okay next. The team balance is excellent, but matchmaking is HORRIBLE. I had to make that in caps for these reasons. One, maybe because there aren't enough people playing this game, but man it can take more than 3 - 5 minutes to find a match. It could be possible that this is due to the game being underrated, poor servers, or whatever the reasons. Although, sometimes you can find a match ultra super hyper excellently fast. Sometimes, even you chose to be a shark or diver you get on the oppsite team of what you wished. This is probably because the game couldnt find enough players on one side. Secondly and lastly, you do not get to play with the player on your skill level. So yes you do meet with level 80's and 100's sometimes even though you're like level 1, 2, 20, doesn't matter. However think like this, the level does not actually tell how good they are. Skilled players are skilled and non-skilled are non-skilled, level does not matter. Some level 100s can be weaker than a 20, 30, whatever level. Seriously though, in this game level does not really matter it all depends on your skills. You can level up quickly in the beginning so you can unlock skills and items real quick. After you go through the learning curves its all about your skills. But yeah higher levels are more experienced so they are usually stronger. But think about it. This was probably a sacrifice the devs had to make due to the lack of population.
If you feel like buying this game here are few tips for beginners:
STICK TO S.T.E.V.E. DIVERS (its a robot where divers put all their treasures in)
Sharks: Don't think about breaking S.T.E.V.E. because its just impossible unless your opponent is all clueless about the game.
Don't leave the game just because your opponent is ultra fantasticoly super hyper nova strong.
Don't leave because the seals dodge you in the perfect timing.
Don't leave because you're gonna get a bot take over your place.
Don't underestimate the bots because they are really smart. They've got aim hacks, wall hacks, and insta (not really) kill hacks.
Here are some reasons why I nominated this game for awards: this game, first of all, does not have much attention even though its really great. Second, the price is not bad for what it provides. Now, you even have cool skins to play around with. Third, for a pvp game this is great. No toxic community, no salt, intense, fun to play solo and with friends, not super competetive, and fairly balanced pvp.

Depth is a game that will get your blood pumping.
Whether you're playing as a shark or as a diver, Depth's gameplay isn't shallow.
TLDR: Depth is a fun game.
Divers escort a loot-hungry robot through the Depth™s of the ocean and win by reducing the sharks' lives to 0 or safely returning the satiated robot to the starting area.
The sharks' goal is to eat the aforementioned divers.
Sharks can regularly see the locations of divers to make locating them possible, and divers' heartbeats will grow louder/faster relative to the proximity of a shark.
Queue times are usually pretty good especially if you are queue as "Either" instead of choosing specifically Shark or Diver. The game allows easily grouping with up to 5 friends for matchmaking or private matches.
There are twelve different maps in the default game mode and if for some reason you don't like one (I like them all) you can choose which maps you're willing to play on, though I assume doing so could result in longer queue times.
There is also a game mode called Megalodon Hunt which has all players (except one) as divers and whoever kills the Megalodon gets to become it until they in turn are killed.
As a heads up, the main method of dealing damage as shark comes from "thrashing" which is done by wilding thrashing your mouse left and right while a diver is in your jaws. This can be a bit taxing on your hands, I would imagine moreso if you suffer from joint pains or anything like that. I would say that for most people this shouldn't be an issue, and it does feel satisfying to shred your foes.
If you want to know some more information, feel free to read the next section. It's a bit long but it has some information about customisation of divers as well as the different sharks which are available to play.
--------------------------------------------------
A normal game in Blood And Gold matchmaking will have four divers playing against two sharks.
Divers have access to a large number of weapons to suit your playstyle.
Divers will start with a Knife, two empty weapon slots and one empty consumable slot.
The weapon list: two pistols, two automatic rifles, two harpoon guns, one pistol-harpoon hybrid, and a shotgun. There are also four interesting utility weapons: the Sensor, the Bang Stick, the DPV and the Net Gun.
These four utility weapons allow the user to support their team in different ways.
The Sensor can be used to send a sonar pulse in the direction fired which will highlight 'hit' sharks and can be used an unlimited number of times with just a short cooldown in between shots. It will also highlight loot for you, making it easier to collect and giving your team of divers an cash advantage.
The Bang Stick is more of a novelty item but is extremely satisfying when used successfully. Your foes will think you to be a fool when you dart through the water towards their open jaws but when they get a mouthful of your stick they'll be in need of more than a dentist.
The DPV (Diver Propulsion Vehicle) can be used to move at greater speeds through the water and assist the diver in dodging lunging sharks as well as collect all of the loots. It can be upgraded to show the location of loot as well as give greater bursts of speed and even pick up nearby loot automatically.
Lastly, the Net Gun can be used to trap sharks in tiny nets. A tiny net is a death sentence, it's a net and it's tiny! The net can be upgraded to either do damage to the captured shark, or attach a tracking device which will reveal the shark to you and your fellow divers, which usually results in some good sashimi.
The other guns have different upgrades but some common ones include: adding a bleed effect to your bullets which do more damage to a shark if it moves, a tranquilizing efect which drains the stamina of the shark, limiting its mobility, and tagging which will reveal the shark to all divers for a short while.
Consumables are another tool available to divers which a good team will usually utilize.
Flares can make it easier to see in the dark ocean,
sonar buoys reveal nearby sharks until destroyed,
sea mines are like land mines but in the sea,
medkits and supply kits are scattered around the ocean by default but can be purchased and placed in safer locations,
shark shields can be used to severly limit the senses of enemy sharks for their short duration,
and the relatively new P.A.T. (Portable Aquatic Turret) can be set up to alarm divers of nearby sharks shortly before raining bullets down upon them.
Now, enough of the divers - let's talk about the sharks.
Instead of cash, the sharks use an "Evolution Point" currency to make their sharks stronger and deadlier. The main way to gain evolution points is by dealing a killing blow to a diver. A wounded shark may choose to tactically retreat and feed on delicious, innocent seals to restore lost health.
When you join a game as a shark you'll be able to choose from one of six sharks which I will detail below. Note that some of these descriptions will be copied from the "Learn" section of the game.
Great White: "The Great White is as large as he is dangerous. Being both slow moving and hard hitting the Great White will continue his onslaught as bullets and spears sail his way."
The Great White's active ability allows it to reduce damage taken and when upgraded will ignore nets and slows for its duration.
Mako: "The Mako may be a smaller shark, but don't let that trick you; he's fast as hell and twice as mean. With a sleek but fragile frame the Mako is built for speed and agility."
The Mako's active ability allows it to mark a diver, allowing (I believe) both sharks to see the diver much more clearly and constantly and if the diver dies before the mark ends, the Mako will recieve bonus Evolution Points.
Tiger: "The Tiger is a real man eater, and his striped hide makes him hard to spot. With a solid build and powerful muscles, the Tiger is adaptable to a wide variety of strategies ranging from hit-and-run to all out aggression."
The Tiger's active ability is Adaptive Hide which allows it to remain undetectable by tracking devices for its duration. I believe the ability also makes the Tiger harder for divers to see.
Hammerhead: "The Great Hammerhead fights tooth and nail as he thrashes and bashes prey to a crimson pulp. Unique to the Hammerhead is the ability to passively crush enemies, fast and direct hits into any solid object will cause prey in his jaws to take damage proportional to the force."
The Hammerhead's active ability allows it to regain stamina, and health at Level 3, when impacting any solid object.
Thresher: "The Thresher doesn't look notably dangerous with its unassuming jaws, however its true weapon is a long, blade-like tail capable of lacerating and disorienting multiple prey at once."
With probably the most interesting ability, the Thresher is able to tailwhip nearby divers to disable flashlights, break walls and consumables (at levels 2 and 3 respectively), and deal damage to the divers it affects. A tailwhip can quickly finish a wounded diver or allow the Thresher's companion to take advantage of the confusion.
Bull: "The Bull shark is a medium threat with an anger problem, making it an aggressive and unpredictable foe. Though it lacks immediate force, the Bull's true strength lies in its ability to Enrage, temporarily becoming one of the strongest beasts in the sea."
The Bull is the newest addition to Depth and as mentioned in its description its ability allows it to become much stronger for short bursts of time. It gains rage while within 'close' proximity of divers and this rage can be transformed into bonus health, stamina and damage for 4 to 6 seconds.
That's it from me, if you decide to burchase Depth I look forward to eating you in game!

I like Plants vs Zombies a lot, but Bloons is probably my favorite tower defense game of all times. This charmingly cute game with cartoony graphics carries surprising depth and difficulty. I have in less than a week played more hours than I ever imagined. If you are considering buying this game, you can even try the flash version for free on
The developers, from what I've seen, are very active and helpful on the forums and other communication platforms should you experience any issues. I haven't so far though.
The game, being a freemium game on the browser and with micro transactions on the mobile version, has everything available for in-game currency (and only in-game currency) on Steam. Any benefits that you may purchase can be deactivated, meaning that those that are more insane, such as the Double Cash Mode, can be disabled at any time to avoid the game being too easy while still being available in case you are struggling with a daily challenge or want to let your younger siblings or kids play.
Content-wise, there are over total 50 levels over five difficulties; Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced, Expert and Exteme. Each level can in turn be played in four different difficulties, all available both in normal and reverse paths. This should offer a challenge for both those new to tower defense games and the more experienced players.
There is also a simple coop mode, which simply splits the map and money in half, and allows you to hand money to the other player. You can play both with steam friends and a random quick match. While this doesn't offer that much new, it is very fun to be able to play with friends.
There are ten special missions available that make you think creatively, as well as 250 random missions with varying themes and difficulties. The special missions at least, are replayable at a lower rewards, in case you want to complete them differently, maybe with some perks disabled.
Along with all this content, there are also weekly odysseys, which are 3-5 levels(depending on difficulty) that you must complete in a row, rewarding great treasure, and daily challenges(which is to complete a level with only four available towers) at all four difficulties so you can earn some extra cash.
In short, there is no shortage of content and always a reason to return.
The downsides are that the levels are fairly repetitive - all difficulties have a set order of bloons incoming in the rounds. The option menu is also somewhat lacking, the only options being cloud upload/download, mute/unmute music, mute/unmute sound effects and windowed mode, as well as a language options and the ability to change controls between click and drop and drag and drop.
All in all, I would recommend the game to anyone, and at the current price it's basically a steal!

Ok, so, once upon a time there was this guy named Matt, and he decided "I'll make an RPG cause why not."
So then Epic Battle Fantasy was made, and it was cool.
A few months later, Matt talked to this girl who went by Phyrnna, and was like "You wanna help me out with this?" and she was like "k"
So then EBF 2 was made, and it was great.
So the, Matt was on his throne of loot, and he was like "this isn't working" and so he gave EBF open world mechanics, side quests, and loads of other♥♥♥♥♥♥
And so, EBF 3 was made, and it was AWESOME.
2 spinoffs later, Matt decided to then just go "eh screw it" and made another, this time with more length, sidequests, enemies, equipment, skills, strategy, and of course, amazing goddamn music.
And so EBF 4 was made.
And it was concluded that the game was ♥♥♥♥ing amazing.
Ok, so, actual review:
STORYTIME
The story isn't much to ride home about, but it's enough to keep the game moving along, so it sorta works. It is still moderately engaging, and doesn't just devolve to "go here because we aren't gonna say". At least I can still remember what happened in the game.
6/10? 6/10.
The Graphics
Very colorful, slightly animu style graphics that are all in all nice to look at. Also, goddamn, some of those abilities are amazing visually (mostly the limit breaks).
8/10 m8
The Gameplay
My first runthrough was on normal mode, cause I'm a ♥♥♥♥♥. But I'm currently trying to get through the game on Hard and later on Epic, so yeah.
Basically, this game doesn't fall into the common RPG problem of being able to just spam normal attack to win except on bosses or something, and actually requires a large amount of strategy to get through it. You actually need to be able to adapt to situations, and exploit certain weaknesses to be able to defeat certain enemies (ex. That Goddamn Cosmic Monolith)
Exploration is also awarded well in this game too. There are several points in the game where backtracking and exploration can be very useful to you, mostly after you get key items. As well, this game has two optional areas, one small and pretty easy, with the other being basically a super dungeon where the enemies scale to your level and you fight some really powerful bosses. (Again, ♥♥♥♥ cosmic monoliths.)
Also, there are a metric ton of deifferent pieces of equipment to customize your character with, allowing you to find a way to fit almost any situation by the time you begin the New Game+ runthroughs.
Also, the two NG+ runthroughs cause the enemies to level up with you. That's pretty damn awesome.
10/10 Am playing again
Music
You ever heard of Phyrnna? No? well you should listen to her songs. The EBF 4 soundtrack, along with the soundtrakcs for EBF 3 and 2 provide some of the best songs I have heard in a video game ever. Weshdoor Concert? Amazing. Derelict Factory of Twisted Metal? Amazing. Outside the Battlements? Amazing. The Rim of Battle Mountain? Amazing. Fallen Blood? Best final boss theme ever. Every single track here is amazing, and you should listen to all of it.

I've never written a review for a game on steam before but I thought that I just had to write something about it after finishing it. I got this game as a gift, I started it with zero expectations and it just blew my mind. Everything about it, from the stunning visuals to the amazing sound track, to the fluid animation and controls. In an era dominated by first person shooters and online mobas, we barely ever get good flushed out 2D platforming, exploration games. If you're a classic gamer who grew up playing Super Mario, Super Metroid, Heart of Darkness or any sidescrolling platformer, you're going to LOVE this game. It's worth every penny in my opinion so please support this studio so they can make more masterpieces like this one.
The game starts off with some beautiful cinematics and music. It introduces the story/characters and you start playing shortly after. You start off with basic movement and controls and the pacing of the game is quite excellent (I had no trouble with the controls whatsoever). The game progressively gets harder as you play but luckily you're given a skill tree to equip yourself with upgrades to keep pushing forward. The game combines platforming, level-design and puzzles in such a charming way that I haven't seen since Odd World and Heart of Darkness.
If I had any negative feedback, it would be just two small things. The game can use a mini-map. I saw myself flipping back and forth between the game and the map quite often. That could have easily been avoided with a toggable minimap at the top right corner of the screen. My last little complaint about the game is that it's quite difficult or nearly impossible to beat it 100% unless you know what's coming. There are areas in the game that become impossible to access later on in the game and if you hadn't found a way to explore them fully before, you can't clear the game and get all the items 100%.
These are just nitpicks from my end but otherwise the game is a masterpiece! Buy it and play it NOW!

The concept of Reus, like other have stated, is very good and would make for a great game to have in your library when you want to partake in some casual god-like desire. You have these giants who possess the power to terraform the planet, to control the environment, and that is awesome.  The game has a nice art style and it's visually pleasant to look at.
So you played through the tutorial and you're ready to take on your first game. You start out nice and slow doing everything you learned,  you're doing fine so far until you start to realize that you are not so much in control of the world that you yourself help create, because it turns out you are there to fulfill the needs of the people. It starts getting frustrating, you end up pausing the game constantly to think about every single thing you want to do, because there is yet more stuff that you haven't learned. Your patience is running thin as the game before you unfolds as being more of a chore than a fun experience.
I tried multiple times to get into the gameplay, but the core of the game is just dull. When you have to learn so much about how to actually play a game, by checking its own Wiki page (which you can bring up during the game btw) you can't help but quickly lose interest.

Reus is a solid and entertaining game. You control four giants who help form a brand new planet as you see fit. It takes some strategy to combine the right resources so that you villages may flourish. And that makes it really addictive, because the better your villages do, the more powers your giants get to add new and more powerful resources. The game also makes good use of developments/achievements, which in itself is quite rewarding when you finish a game.
When starting out playing this game it might take a while to figure out how to combine resources and how to make your giants stronger, but don't let this get you down. You learn a lot by just trying stuff and the in-game explanations make combining resources easier. I would definitely recommend this game for anyone who likes a perfect mix of good artwork and intelligent gameplay. It's one of the best ones I've ever played!

After giving it multiple goes after reinstalling it, and finally just sticking with it, I just still can't really recommend it for multiple reasons.
It is obvious that much of this game was made to simply just try to jump onto the success of more modern shooters like Call of Duty, even though the series originated from much of the opposite. Almost every gun except for the shotgun has Aim Down Sights, no more collecting and using med-kits because your health regenerates, only two weapons max, and instead of leaning left and right you press a button to glue yourself to nearby chest-high-walls.
There are so many things wrong with this game not only from the point of an original F.E.A.R. fan, but even when stood on its own.
-Annoying and unrealistic Bloody Screen when wounded, accompanied with fast acting health regeneration.
Completely slows down gameplay, makes certain areas extremely easy due to being near invincible, and makes some areas extremely hard due to not being able to heal instantaneously via med-kit and having to find a spot not being hitscanned into oblivion.
-Kung-fu moves have been chopped out. No punches, just a knife. No bicycle kicks, just one dinky kick. These simple animations made the last games so much more fun, even if the new moves do exactly the same purpose. The aesthetic just isn't the same.
-The first 2 or 3 level designs are ripped straight out of Modern Warfare. "Escape the Prison!" "Escape the South American Favela!" Truly takes you out of the F.E.A.R. universe, and it's a shame that they thought opening with such unfitting levels would be a good idea when it only helps make an even worse first impression.
-No more finding health and slowmo upgrades throughout the environment. To improve your health and slowmo, you have to rank up with the new score and challenge system. You can still find hidden dolls and certain bodies that give instant extra "score" (XP really), but it's such a strange decision to add a rank and score system into a game that was basically the opposite of an arcade/points based game...
-The horror aspect of this game was weaker than ever before, even though it was never my favorite part of the games before these. There are a lot less times where the game tries to jump scare you, and even when they do you don't get caught off gaurd because they try to pull one off in the middle of a warzone.
-They gave Point-man a face. A boring, bearded, scowling face. Yet he still never talks... As if it wasn't enough that he couldn't do badass psychic kung-fu anymore.
-The enemies are just not intimidating anymore. The AI is still OK, but it just does not seem as good as the AI in the first game. The voices for them don't have the badass radio static that the first game had, and they spend 90% of their time completely behind cover.
-The new cover system is ok, but having the ability to lean like we used to is much more handy as it gives the player to make useful cover out of anything, whereas now you can only lean out from very certain few pieces of scenery. Half of your head seems to be poking out of cover most of the time as you can still get torn to shreds, enemies are able to hide in cover better than you.
The game overall is OK, but as a F.E.A.R. game, or as an olds-chool shooter, it is just so underwhelming and hard to enjoy. Even if I was a completely blank slate on the series, I would still feel very unfavorably for this game, as it seems to attempt to merge the newer Modern Warfare type shooter with older Doom (3) type shooters, and it just becomes such a clunky mess. There are an annoying amount of out-of-character cutscenes, there are an annoying amount of context actions like going through doors, or turnstiles, or over chest-high-walls...
It's just a shame that the series that helped make PC gaming PC Gaming was obviously developed for more of the younger console crowd involved, but only managed to sort of make an experience not very enjoyable for either type of gamer, PC or console. All I can really hope for is for some sort of spiritual successor to F.E.A.R. that incorporates super psychic kung-fu soldiers in a more modern engine and graphics set, because this game just leaves me itching for more of the classics.

I went into this game with low expectations. I was pleasantly surprised. I was told that there was no horror in this one, that's not true. The atmosphere and sound engineering are top notch in this game. The three things that divided fans most were that Alma takes a back seat role, the horror is minimized and the levels are too straightforward.
Let's address those one by one. First, I personally like that Alma took a back seat role. After a Fear 1 and Fear 2 marathon I was getting really tired of seeing a naked girl or a little kid in a red dress run across my screen. It's nice to see the other creatures take over more. Second, the horror is minimized. No, it's not, not at all. There's just as much as Fear 2. And that's from someone who played all 3 over a weekend. Rather than use the same boring jump scares (although they're still there) this game aims more for atmosphere and sound tension. The dread of something jumping out actually makes the game pretty tense. Third, the levels are too straight-forward. I 100% agree. There is almost no collecting, it's all done by achievements this time around. Rather than finding a needle to get more slo-mo, you just kill X amount of enemies with X or something. And even then there is no curiosity about it, just go down the tunnel and kill everything.
Another complaint is the “COD-ification” of Fear. Again, I agree, in this game you can only carry two weapons off the bat and barely any ammo. This also works in the games' favor as the action mechanics in this game are far and away the best. Gunplay is tight, and solid. Seriously, the shooting in this game is easily the best in the series. All the weapons are absolutely lethal and splatter enemies. Sadly, the health regen (which I personally hate) from COD is in this game as well. Also, because there is health regen, there are some seriously cheap deaths.
+
Best shooting mechanics in the series
Fluid gameplay (smooth FPS throughout)
Great atmosphere
All the guns are useful again
Two playable characters give the levels some replayability (You can play as either Paxton Fettel or Point Man)
-
The scares themselves are a bit minimized
No collection, just overused achievements
Lazy level layout
No medkits
Overall 8/10, it's not perfect, but I really enjoyed it

I've played the old 2150 series (Escape from the Blue Planet, Moon Project & Lost Souls) and I really wanted to like this new part of the earth series ... Sadly that's not really possible.
Maybe I'm overly nostalgic from what earth 2150 has and 2160 hasn't but even as a fan of RTS games this game feels very halfhearted.
1) The Unit Editor
This is why the Earth series felt so unique: Build your own army, by picking a chassis, add weapons & shields and voila. Earth 2160 even added a few extra features. Now you can add engines, armour as well as gimmicks such as auto repair drones.
In the old Earth games, shields kept you alive deflecting plasma or electro canon fire. Now armour is way more important than shields as most weapons simply bypass shields. What sounds like a great feature simply turns the game into a game of rock, paper, sicssors, lizard, spock. Either your army wipes the floor with your enemies or they get crushed within seconds. Reload, build units using other armour and try again.
Once you get to the enemy base, the game really starts showing you the middle finger. Almost all weapons have reduced damage against buildings and if you don't want to get shreaded by basic defense turrets you'll need artillery units to slowly tear the base down bit by bit. Remember how much more fun it was to have your army charge in and blow up buildings? I do -.-
2) No Mainbase / Veteran units
Remember when you could do research between missions at your mainbase? Now you'll have to do all your research during missions. It helps that each research center you build no longer gives a timebonus, but instead allows simultanious research yet in the end you're just waiting for new chassis to unlock. Very boring.
Veteran units you can take from mission to mission can no longer be picked by you, instead the game apparently randomly chooses units from previous missions as starting units. Granted, each unit now has a pilot who earns the XP and can be placed in another vehicle, but it's just not the same.
3) Hero Units
I loved "Fang" from the previous games, so I was curious how this one would play out. Fang was pretty OP, but not as OP as the new hero units in earth, that can take out armies without breaking a sweat. Not to mention the horrible dialogues and voice acting. No idea why the games doesn't pause during dialogues *or* why I can't control units during this blah blah *or* why everyone wants to talk during attacks.
4) Bugs bugs bugs
I was stuck on a mission because I've taken a different path to my objective, not triggering a dialogue. Still not as fun as  watching my units drive right next to the enemy before opening fire or simply not attacking at all despite "follow enemy" settings and being under heavy fire. Also why does my hero move in slow motion sometimes? No idea.

Earth 2160 is a great game but might not appeal to everyone.
The game seems a bit outdated by today standards, especially graphics wise. Furthermore it's a somewhat slow paced game that requires time and thought put into it.
It's a science-fiction based RTS game featuring advanced base building, ressource gathering and combat. The economic aspect of the game is quite basic. Gather ressources to fund your base and units, base building is pretty extensive depending on the factions. The combat is quite good but challenging. One of the most important mechanics is the unit customization, through research you can design your own units with various strengths and weaknesses. This allows for some major tactical planning and you really need to think what type of unit is effective against another type of unit. Overall this mechanic is very rewarding but can be frustrating. Sometimes your units will just be annihilated and you won't have the time or patience to find a new design that suits your needs.
Two aspects of this game that I find very appealing are the factions and the campaigns. The factions are completely different and feel distinct. Each faction has a unique way of playing and focus, some have completely different structures and designs that opt for different playstyles. The mission campaigns are extremely well done, especially for an rts game. You have dialogues and cutscenes, some rpg elements as well and a decent storyline. Furthermore you will have several campaigns at your disposal to play.
The multiplayer is seviceable and works quite well. So are the graphics and soundtrack. Nothing to complain about.

Shroud of the Avatar is simply the best game I've played in the last five years. It has so many layers of interaction to choose from, whether you want to spend the day adventuring out in the field, or gather resources and craft items for personal use or to sell to other players, or if you just want to stay in town and strike up a conversation with fellow players over a pint of mead, Shroud delivers. If you want to enter an arena or PvP-enabled area and test your mettle against anyone else who might be there, you can also do that.
Currently in Pre-Alpha, most of the storyline has been hidden away for launch. Ok, so, once upon a time there was this guy named Matt, and he decided "I'll make an RPG cause why not."
So then Epic Battle Fantasy was made, and it was cool.
A few months later, Matt talked to this girl who went by Phyrnna, and was like "You wanna help me out with this?" and she was like "k"
So then EBF 2 was made, and it was great.
So the, Matt was on his throne of loot, and he was like "this isn't working" and so he gave EBF open world mechanics, side quests, and loads of other♥♥♥♥♥♥
And so, EBF 3 was made, and it was AWESOME.
2 spinoffs later, Matt decided to then just go "eh screw it" and made another, this time with more length, sidequests, enemies, equipment, skills, strategy, and of course, amazing goddamn music.
And so EBF 4 was made.
And it was concluded that the game was ♥♥♥♥ing amazing.
Ok, so, actual review:
STORYTIME
The story isn't much to ride home about, but it's enough to keep the game moving along, so it sorta works. It is still moderately engaging, and doesn't just devolve to "go here because we aren't gonna say". At least I can still remember what happened in the game.
6/10? 6/10.
The Graphics
Very colorful, slightly animu style graphics that are all in all nice to look at. Also, goddamn, some of those abilities are amazing visually (mostly the limit breaks).
8/10 m8
The Gameplay
My first runthrough was on normal mode, cause I'm a ♥♥♥♥♥. But I'm currently trying to get through the game on Hard and later on Epic, so yeah.
Basically, this game doesn't fall into the common RPG problem of being able to just spam normal attack to win except on bosses or something, and actually requires a large amount of strategy to get through it. You actually need to be able to adapt to situations, and exploit certain weaknesses to be able to defeat certain enemies (ex. That Goddamn Cosmic Monolith)
Exploration is also awarded well in this game too. There are several points in the game where backtracking and exploration can be very useful to you, mostly after you get key items. As well, this game has two optional areas, one small and pretty easy, with the other being basically a super dungeon where the enemies scale to your level and you fight some really powerful bosses. (Again, ♥♥♥♥ cosmic monoliths.)
Also, there are a metric ton of deifferent pieces of equipment to customize your character with, allowing you to find a way to fit almost any situation by the time you begin the New Game+ runthroughs.
Also, the two NG+ runthroughs cause the enemies to level up with you. That's pretty damn awesome.
10/10 Am playing again
Music
You ever heard of Phyrnna? No? well you should listen to her songs. The EBF 4 soundtrack, along with the soundtrakcs for EBF 3 and 2 provide some of the best songs I have heard in a video game ever. Weshdoor Concert? Amazing. Derelict Factory of Twisted Metal? Amazing. Outside the Battlements? Amazing. The Rim of Battle Mountain? Amazing. Fallen Blood? Best final boss theme ever. Every single track here is amazing, and you should listen to all of it.

Epic Battle Fantasy 4 - The first thing that popped into my head when I heard of this game was, "what kind of name is that?" Going by the title alone, you almost expect this to be the most cliche RPG ever, and it is - in a good way.
EBF4 is a bit of a parody of RPGs. You have turn based combat, level ups, and gear, just like in all your normal RPGs. You've also got characters that crack jokes at their own game, and much like the little indie game EvoLand, it likes to make reference to other games fairly often as you bash enemies over the head with oversized weapons.
At first glance, this game looks like the kind of flash game you'd play in your internet browser when you were little - the art is colorful but looks primitive and the controls aren't complex. Yet this is the kind of 'flash game' that someone poured hours and hours into, and it shows; the art style may very well be simple, but that's before considering how much you can customize your characters. Each and every helm in the game gives the characters a different hairstyle, for one - heck, I spent more time than I'd like to admit mixing and matching outfits to see what was both stylish and combat practical.
The game is very lax in terms of its rules. It could almost be said that it got rid of all the little bits that make RPGs frustrating - encounters are not random, running away is penalty free, all gear is useable once upgraded, grinding is not necessary (except maybe for Epic mode) and upgrade ingredients are plentiful. The game doesn't have you trecking an hour to get a single ingredient - everything progresses at a quick and painless pace.
Make no mistake, the game is challenging on Hard and Epic modes. One's ability to arm characters with the right attacks and gear is mandatory for taking on the game's big bosses, even if said big bosses look too comical to take seriously.
Overall, a very pleasant game, and there's no way I can't recommend it. It's not the kind of gripping story about trust and betrayal that will move you to tears, but it's a fun little title that does everything right, and should be recognized for it.

Review:
I'm going to be completely honest, this game is pretty short which I will get around to but I have put more hours into this game than I expected. I played it a lot after I beat it just to see how fast I could beat it, which makes up for the lack of replay value. With that, I will go further in depth.
Ori and the Blind Forest is a single-player platformer with great looking scenerey and an interesting story to go along with it. In the game you play as the protagonist named Ori, who is on a mission to restore light to the forest after the raven whom which I forgot the name of, tried to destroy it. The game itself looks already really good without even going into the game yet. For the game play, I honestly really enjoyed this one. The feel of the game was really fun and it felt like you were really mobile. Also, you were given lots of cool abilities throughout the game such as the dash ability which was by far my favorite. Honestly, through the initial playthrough till then end, there isn't much for me to say without spoiling it other than the game looks great and the gameplay is fun.
I don't really have much bad to say about this game except for one thing, lack of replay value. Although you come to expect this after you beat the game, I really wish they had made something like maybe a hard mode or something like that. Although I did play it several times after to see how fast I could beat it, you could see how that would get frustrating and boring after a while (my fastest time so far is 2 hours and 30 minutes by the way). Also, I felt like there were not enough extras for me to go after as I played along the game which I can understand that it was a story built game, but come on. In my opinion, this game is a little on the pricey end for the amount of time you get to put into the game. I would say the average playthrough for this game is about 5-7 hours and the price for the game without sales is $20. I put in about 17 hours, but other players might not if they don't find speed-running very fun.
To conclude this, the game was really fun initially and looks great all around, just the lack of replay value and extras is a bit dissapointing. Although yes the replay value is lacking, I would still say this game is probably worth the amount of money you put into it. If you think that it is a little too pricey for you though, then I would wait for a sale.

Note: I received a copy of To The Moon for my birthday!
First off I would like to start by stating that you don't actually have to use your mouse (some people get annoyed), you can use your arrow keys and your space bar (interaction key) and just use your mouse as a guide. Also, this game's graphics isn't the best (pixel art) but I promise it actually grows on you and you will start to like it. Especially because there are some sick illustrations later on.
Positives:
+ Deep storyline (very well thought out, kudos to the Developer's efforts) - you don't actually know what to expect when you first start playing this game; it's much more than you think it is
+ Relatively nice graphics (Pixel Art)
+ Beautiful and fitting music (Situational)
+ Extra minisodes (DLCS)
+ Character development is simply wonderful, and very well done
+ Good excuse to go grab some ice cream as soon as you get to 'Act 3' (I cried a little)
+ Maps aren't too large, but large enough to explore thoroughly and enjoyably especially with the little dialogues or things you pick up
+ Relatively easy puzzles, but not too easy - it also displays the lowest amount of moves needed to complete the puzzle which makes you visualise the outcomes and how to complete it with the least amount of moves. Tip:
+ Saving options are very well thought out - automatic saves for important actions and you can also use manual saving
+ There are nice little extras in the game menu where it shows you the items you have and specific 'notes' or interesting things you have found out - this is updated quite frequently and worth your time to check out
Negatives:
- Although I loved the character development and thought it was very well done, I definitely would have liked it more if there was more background information about Johnny's mother. We only know a little about her but I feel like she plays a bigger role than that.
- Puzzles that can get repetitive (it's not too bad)
- Walking speed is quite slow and can get annoying waiting for them to hurry up
- Some larger maps can get tedious - walking around and finding things
Overall:
The main focus of the actual game (storyline) is very beautiful, relatable and enjoyable. It made me cry after 'Act 3' at various scenes (those who have played know what I mean). The way the story is set out seems a bit odd at first, but as you continue on it makes a lot of sense and I feel is the perfect way to lay it out. The ending was simply beautiful and you don't really see it coming - in fact, you don't see many events (plot twists people) happening until it does. There is a little bit of humour, especially with the protagonists and it's a very deep, heartfelt story. Despite the negatives, I would like to say that the postitives definitely outweigh the negatives.
I love stories like these because you don't have to make any serious choices, yet the choices the protagonists make, makes you think about
morals and what
would do in such a situation. I've spent some time considering the many options and the options the protagonists made plus the repurcussions and their situations, and I finally came to the conclusion of what was morally correct. I'm fully content with the ending. I think this game is a lot about the morality of how these people help the man, as well as others. The DLCs do explore the concept of morality and how some people think what they do is immoral.
It's not perfect but it's close enough. Definitely worth the full price (and if you like the music, get the soundtracks too) and you get free minisodes (DLCS).
I could go on and on and on... But let me say this: Just play the game, you won't regret it.

-combat - probably the best factor of the game, really makes you think about combining elements, i.e. if you freeze someone then another party member fireballs them it will undo that. Unfortunately this game is a crowd control fest, far too many debilitating abilties to lock out enemies or yourself, stuns, freezes, slows, fears, knockdowns, charms, etc.  If you don't use them the enemy will.
-classes - there isn't set "classes" so you get play however you want. obviously you are going to be building a character towards a specific warrior/mage/rogue type archetype and putting your points in specific areas, like if you are a going for a warrior plastyle you'll be going investing in strength/master of arms/two handed weapons skills etc.  Range classes are much better in this game than melee till probably the end when they start to catch up.
neutral -
story is ok, standard rpg stuff of beating the greater evil, some funny dialogue parts. It has certain charm/intimidate dialogue checks like most rpg's except they then force you to play rock/paper scissors to win or not. There are 4 story companions available to journey with and you can also hire more. With a total party size of 4 though, and 2 of those are your created characters then that leaves just 2 slots left so you will have limited party interaction with them and their stories are largely forgetable
cons
- loot,  this game LOVES putting heaps of barrels/baskets all over the place. You kind of feel obligated to check everything as you can find gear and scrolls /potions in them. But you end up with massive inventory bloat of junk though as you don't know what is valuable or not. Probably the worst rpg game for trash items i've played, I spend longer sorting through my inventory than any other rpg i've played. Overall loot is poorly optimized because of no set classes resulting in random unhelpful stats like a item with sneaking bonus on a strength item
-quests, incredibly vague quests that often can not be completed till much later in the game, no quest markers or help means you will be looking up guides on the internet unless you like experimenting for hours. By the end of the game I still had about 20 uncompleted active quests in my log I couldn't seem to finish because they had reached a dead end. I've never had to look up walkthrough guides so much for any other game.
-puzzles, This has some of the most annoying rpg puzzles you will ever find in a game, lots of "find the hidden swtich" puzzles that leaves you staring at the screen playing "hunt the pixel".
- camera angle is a top down view at an angle, did not like it alot, also this game is slow,  the characters move slow and combat can't be sped up or automated making every battle tedious. Even out of combat you have cooldowns on spells, probably about 1/3 of this game "played" hours is just waiting for things, or standing around trying to figure out switch puzzles, the actual play time is illusionanry.
I feel there is alot of unecessary frustration in this game to warrant it a thumbs up and have a love/hate relationship with it.  it's still an ok game and I will maybe get D:OS 2 when it's on sale to see if they've improved on anything. A good rpg is one that wants you to play through a second time but I have no interest in going through all that again, one play through was enough to slog through and there is essentially no ending difference in regards to your choices

If you're up for a quickie, this is the exploration game for you.
The vanilla adventure takes a promising 2-3 hours. The content can be extended/changed with some workshop mods that make the game significantly easier or head-bangingly more difficult; it's something to keep in mind if you're looking for a game that can fit your needs.
The main question is,
The lack of any map at all will certainly frustrate some, even if it's done in one comfortable sitting. Thankfully, the game is not confusing and having to remember where to go next won't/shouldn't be an issue.
It's unfortunately backed with some backtracking and some animals that will attempt to ruin your work or outright kill you. You can kill them using the environment, but it will take some effort.
The environment can trap you if you're not careful. This is in combination with auto-save, so restarts might be a possibility.
The sound and level designs are fantastic. You will feel an urge to explore them, run through the trees as you desire, looking for secrets and such, it's well deserving of exploration. There were no noticeable glitches.
There are a few, side-track things you can do to occupy your time such as hatching animals for your own benefit or killing the rowdier animals. Also, runes and deciphering.
The ending will leave your opinions going... "back and forth" I should say.
If you like being thrust into worlds and having to figure out the story for yourself, then absolutely. Otherwise, if you're not much for exploration games, games with little/no text, have a phobia of birds, or don't like puzzles, this isn't for you.
Three stars out of five.

Secrets of Rætikon is as gorgeous and ethereal as it is tedious and poorly designed.
It’s a game about exploration and discovery, hampered by convoluted level designs and the inexcusable absence of any sort of map. It’s a game of peaceful puzzle solving and nonlinear exploration disrupted by annoyingly persistent enemies, and no means of attack to ward them off. More than anything though it’s a game of false allegations of an overarching mystery, that in the end is nothing more than a horrendously incomprehensible and random moment, preceded by an unnecessarily grotesque event that quite frankly made me sick.
At it’s core, Rætikon is constructed like a large fetch quest collectathon, requiring you to explore levels in order to collect scattered shards which can then be used to power up ancient machinery. These machines exist both in opening new pathways for you, and in presenting you with larger shards which must then be brought back to a sort of hub and deposited into the sockets of yet another large machine.
Though it had the potential to be an enjoyably open experience, allowing you to freely traverse the world as you hunt for these shards and machines, Rætikon idiotically forces you to spend an aggravating amount of time back tracking through levels in order to return to the hub. This could have been avoided with a better connected world, but with only two paths into the hub, you’re required to haul your luggage through numerous screens over and over again. This is made even more frustrating do to the inevitable games of keep away you get into with other animals, which can sometimes make the simple act of getting from one side of the screen to the other almost painful in how aggressive the other creatures are.
This all adds up to make Secrets of Rætikon an absolute chore to get through. It’s a gorgeous game, with some incredible origami-like artwork, a fantastically ambient soundtrack and great sense of atmosphere, but it’s all brought down by some horrible design decisions that sour the entire experience. When you finally get to the end it only makes matters worse, with a disturbing and baffling turn of events that sells home the point that the designers seemed to have little idea where they were going with their game, nor a clue how to get there.

This game is a suprise delight. Someone bought it for me, and i wasn't expecting to really get much out of it, but now it's quickly become one of my favourites. I've purchased the game 3 times now (once on xbox, and twice for other people), as well as some merch.
The characters may not seem like much upon first impression, and there isn't a huge roster to choose from (There are still a good few choices), but you'll grow to like them a lot. Each character is unique, and you can tell that the developers really put their heart into giving each character a distinct playstyle, as well as an interesting personality. There's something for everyone. The game itself just feels very smooth and comfortable, and the art style, and animations are GREAT. I've never seen a game that looks as nice as this one.
This is also a great game for beginners to the genre. I am one myself (And by god was i bad when i first started.), only just getting into them recently, and the tutorials in this game were very clear and in depth, and will teach you enough to get started. Of course if you want to be decent at the game you will need to put in more time, and really learn the game. Veterans will love it too. There is plenty of depth, and it doesnt cut corners.
The developers really put a lot of love into this game too, with frequent updates, often featuring new content, and even more characters are on the way. Also, each new character DLC is free for a few months, to thank those that chose to support the game early, so if you buy it now it will pay off.
This is the kind of game that if you put some time into it, you will really grow to love it. If you think you will enjoy this game, you probably will and even if you don't expect to get too much out of it, it might suprise you. In short, if you think you may enjoy it, then buy it. It's well worth the price.

Epic Battle Fantasy 4 looks like a shallow game you would find on a smartphone at first glance. While it isn't that complex once you actually dig beneath the surface and start playing you quickly find a well crafted turn based RPG with a lot of good mechanics and customization. A lot of the character's abilities are as comedic and far fetched as the story and it turns out to be a lot of fun. Advised for any Turn Based RPG Fan.

I honestly could not stress how much I recommend this game to RPG enthusiasts. I played the Epic Battle Fantasy series when it was just an evolving flash series (with a really fun bullet hell offshoot) on Kongregate. I loved each and every iteration, and I loved EBF4 to the point I sat down and went full nerd-out on it with writing things down, calculating, minmaxing, the whole nerd-works. I loved it enough I actually put money towards the microtransaction it had. When I heard it was coming to Steam, I was super hype for it, but I never was able to get around to snatching it. Now that I have it, i've revisited it and am having just as much fun - if not more! - than I was on Kongregate.
The game itself is what I would call a tribute parody. The entire thing is self-aware of its genre, but also faithful to what it's parodying. Classic turn based combat with a rock-paper-scissors elemental / buff / debuff system, many items to equip to this end, a buttload of spells and abilities both natural to each character AND others that can be passed between each. Saving on the fly, resuming on the fly, overworld monster encounters instead of the random encounters we all are used to from classic RPGs, and those monsters tend to disappear permanently if they areb locking your main path. The scanbot allows you quick reference mid-battle to what an enemy is capable of, while also giving you a permanent bestiary entry for later reference. There are plenty of other features that really speak that an RPG enthusiast is behind the development, who has gone through the caveats and annoying nuances that many RPGs over the years have tossed at us that plenty a gamer have thrown their hands up at in rage. There is an abundance of humor, including puns, references, tropes and similar things that make fun of itself and its genre, and also referring to other games, series, memes, etc. without being overbearing and causing you to roll your eyes.
tl;dr: This is an RPG made by, and for, RPG lovers, and I could honestly say you're missing out if you pass this up and are an avid player of RPGs.

Having never played a previous Gauntlet title, I approached this as a standalone experience with no obligatory features in mind. With that considered, Gauntlet is one of my top games of the year.
On easier difficulty levels, when starting out, the competitive nature of gold collection mechanics make the game hilarious to play with friends. As the challenge isn't too great, using this time to mess around while also levelling up your chosen characters is extremely enjoyable.
Once you've mastered the basics, entering into unfair difficulty offers a substantial challenge. Although the mechanics for each individual player are fairly simplistic and straight forward, when combined, the depth of the combat in a 4 player party astounded me. Reliably progressing through areas requires individual skill with ones character, as well as great teamwork when combining abilities into formidable combinations.
Negative points are few, but include:
- Lack of content
Clearing the game on a lesser difficulty, and then again on Unfair (which is an entirely new experience) will take about 15-20 hours in a 4 player party.
- Uneven Character Responsibility
Following in Magika's footsteps, the Wizard has a wide array of abilities, all of which are important for tackling challenges. The other characters do not have as much diversity though, and some can seem kind of useless at times.

Alright, I have finally completed this game and have seen mixed reviews. What I have seen in the negative reviews is "the game is too short, I finished in 3 hours." or, "It is really repetitive and boring." The first statement is false, and the second is an uninformed opinion. The game is not short at all.  I have over 20 hours of time on it and finished around the 24 hour mark. Bear in mind, I spent some time grinding and replaying some levels with friends. Which leads me to the second statement. To say a Dungeon Crawler is repetitive is like saying a Bugatti Veyron is too fast. While it may be true, that is the whole reason behind it. Dungeon Crawlers are supposed to be repetitive. That, in my opinion, is where the fun is. Grinding through waves of enemies to level up and finally beat that unstoppable boss. And trust me, the bosses in this game do not mess around.    So to answer the two main questions. "Is the game short?" That depends on you. But you should be able to get at least 10 hours of playtime. "Is it repetitive?" Yes, yes it is. Its a Dungeon Crawler, if you were not expecting that, the game is probably not for you.
Now, the story of the game is as follows. A Wizard named Morak summoned an immense magical dungeon known by heroes and common people as "the Gauntlet". Inside is the usual treasure, traps and evil creatures. And of course, no one has ever made it out. So Morak calls on the four protagonists promising them wealth and all sorts of goodies and of course, a sword slashing, fire blasting good time.
The heroes you can pick from are the Warrior, Valkyrie, Wizard, and Elf. The Warrior is my personal favorite. He has plenty of health, and can easily cut down waves of enemies. The Valkyrie has a short sword that can swing incredibly fast at the cost of short range. A shield that can block all means of damage, and she can throw her shield to have a sort of chain lighting effect. The wizard is the most complex. In order to cast his spells (with the default controls) You have to push the "Shift", "Space", or "RMB" keys to conjure the spell.  What makes him more complex is that pressing "Shift" first and "Space" second may make a fire spell. While pressing "Space" first and "Shift" second may create an ice spell. It requires some getting used to. And then finally we have the the Elf. He has a dodge ability, a bomb that can be attached to his arrows or be placed, and can fire arrows incredibly fast.
The gameplay, as mentioned before, can be repetitive. But this is a game you need to grind in. The "levels" in the game are called masteries. You level them up by completing certain tasks. For example. The "Mummy Slayer" mastery may require 5000 mummy kills to reach the Bronze rank. After doing that, you get increased damage against mummies and the towers that spawn them. Each enemy type has a mastery to go with it. Making the grinding worth while in the long run.
The actual levels themselves are divided up as follows. There are 3 sets of 4 doors each. The first door in each set consists of three basic levels. The second door has a procedurally  generated level and tons of places requiring keys. And the third door contains a level that requires performing a specified task to open the exit. And the fourth door in each set contains the boss. To make up for what may seem like a repetitive formula. Each set of doors has a different atmosphere and enemy types. The first set takes place in a sand buried crypt containing Mummies and skeleton warriors. The second set is themed in dark caves that are sometimes, literally pitch black. Here you fight orcs, grunts and the occasional Spider queen. The final set appears to be placed in a volcano or Hell itself. Here you will find fanatic cultists, and many types of demonized creatures.
Now, I won't say anything about the bosses. The first two are just challenging enough to make the victory worth it all. While the final boss and ending seem just hastily thrown together. I won't spoil anything of course, but the final boss was, in my opinion, more annoying then fun, and the ending did not have any closure. It left me wondering, and to honest, very dissappointed. But the game in its entirety made up for it.
Gauntlet is a fantastic Dungeon Crawler in my opinion and a nice addition to the series. If you have the spare change like I did, pick it up for some friends and play a marathon or two. Good times can be found in every nook and cranny in the depths of this particular dungeon.

I was very intrigued when I first saw this game. I thought it would be some sort of space exploration game, so I bought it. I was not prepared for the amazing roller coaster ride that is To The Moon.
First of all, the soundtrack is absolutely gorgeous. I'm a fan of Laura Shigihara and I flipped when I found out she was involved with the game's music. The music has a very sweet and calming feel to it, and it really gets you into the mood of the game.
Secondly, I fell in love the characters, especially River since we share the same condition. They made me laugh, they made me cry, and they made me scream furiously at the screen (much to the chagrin of my siblings and parents).
Thirdly, the story, though a tad complex, kept me hooked and made me excited for what would come next. The concept was unique and well-thought out, and as far as I could tell, there weren't any plotholes.
Lastly, the artwork for this game was absolutely incredible. 100% awesomeness.
The only thing that I didn't really like about this game was the puzzles, but then again, I suck at puzzles in general :P
I give this game a 10/10. It is worth every cent that I paid.
