Exceptional promise backed by the best Development team and MMO community in the history of the genre.  Lots of room for growth and improvement but the core game is exceptional.   Get in on the ground floor on what will very likely revolutionize the MMO and RPG genres.
When Ultima Online released the game revolutionized the gaming industry. I remember playing on a very new technology called a cable modem at an amazing 10 Mbps and outrunning fireballs. I would invite friends over and explain to them the other characters in game were other people playing online. Almost twenty years later lets pull off our glasses.
Ultima Online at release had so many game breaking issues. A complete lack of MOBS, literally almost no MOBS people would swarm any spawns. Poor quality graphics, remember Everquest would release approximately a year after and 3D was the rage in gaming. Lag was tremendous. Disconnects frequent. No quests. Limited features. Player griefing to an extreme. Lack of content. Hacks, cheats, macro leveling. Just to name a handful of the issues.
Ultima Online gave us players a game where we could do what we wanted, when we wanted, and how we envisioned. Few games since have provided the open environment of the original Ultima. Most games have been boring theme park rides with flashy lights and very restricted player interaction. Many have complained about the lack of variety in the stale MMO genre.
Shroud of the Avatar isn't perfect. Lots of issues present in the current R26. Yet I think back to even R13 and see amazing progress. Look at some of the screenshots and functionality of the earlier releases and consider the progress. Sure people can complain something isn't in the game. People in general tend to be negative. Negativity gets attention.
Shroud of the Avatar won't release in a perfect state. In fact the game will never be in a perfect state. The goal is to release and build. Just as Ultima Online built. Except this time there is no publisher dictating the build. The team is very qualified and focused on building a long term successful game. 8 Million dollars currently pledged is nothing. Long term a successful Shroud can make hundreds of millions.
The point of my review isn't to cheer lead. My point is to remind of the past, because history does repeat. The foundation is in place. Hold on and let the magic unfold. Enjoy the journey.   No other game has the opportunity to really revolutionize the stale, repetitive MMO genre.
Join the revolution early or miss out on the fun.   Each release gets closer to the promise.  You can buy the base game and grind your way into housing or pay rent for a house if this matters.   The game is as far from pay to win as you can get.   I believe WoW is more pay to win except you have to deal with gold resellers for the payment.
Change isn't always perceived as positive.   The big Publishers have a lot to lose when the masses fail to consume their content.    Games like Shroud of the Avatar and Star Citizen receive a lot of negativity.  I suspect some is driven by the big Publishers.   Stop being a lemming.

For most, an enjoyable combat system is of primary importance when choosing an mmo to call home.  In its current stage of alpha development and even with its staggering alpha purchase price, SotA fails to deliver.
Before buying, take a look at a few videos from GW2, Tera or upcoming Everquest Next to see how modern interfaces should feel.  Then take a vid look at combat in SotA -- what a huge let down.
SotA offers three combat UI's.  First, you will find a rather novel but likely never to be copied random card based system.  While in combat, cards of different types (e.g., thrust, bash, etc.) randomly slide into key slot positions within your deck hand.  Once in slot, these random cards can be activated in a traditional way via selection (keyboard) or clicking (mouse).  If left too long without selection, the cards slide off the screen awaiting random card repopulation of that empty slot.  In other words, imagine any other mmo's UI's (user interfaces) wherein combat functions (or cards) are placed in fixed positions.  Then, randomly shuffle everything in a vegas pull the slots handle sort of way and you'll catch the drift.  This interfaces forces a player to look at a key to determine what will happen when the press a keyboard button to activate.
Further forcing this eyes on the UI playstyle, cards of certain types can be combined by dragging and dropping of a particular card type onto another particular card type.  This requires not only eyes on, but dedicated user interface interaction to carry out.  It ends up being so engaging (and somewhat fun) that a player loses track of the gaming action going on.  If instead, you focus on the actual combat, no combining will be available and worse, a player will not know what will happen when pressing a "1" or other button will end up causing.  In pvp and other combat focus requiring situations, this can lead to just spam pressing a bunch of 1's, 2's, 3's, etc. in rapid sequence hoping to activate some card, any random card, that happens to slide in place.
This random deck interface seems only viable to enhance otherwise very boring, non-moving combat such as is found here in SotA's solo pve grind.  If there is any combat movement or eyes on your opponent type interaction required, the random deck proves annoying at best.  To make sure this doesn't happen, SotA has designed normal pve mobs and associated AI to be as simplistic as possible and thus not requiring one's eyes to leave the random button bar mini-game.  Mobs approach and stand still like you will likely do and a slug fest will continue without your seeing it happen as you drag and drop cards atop each other and wait for needed card slide ins and outs so you can maximize your character's unseen performance.
But such simplistic interaction is not available in pvp.  There, players expect to retreat, chase and circle their opponents, one trying to counter and overcome the other through position and movement.  Eyes on an opponent here is most often required.  Devs recognized that random deck functionality fails hard for such game play, so they also offer a fixed deck option.  Such option involves a long traditional approach of placing a combat function (card) into a slot and it stays there for you to activate without looking by pressing a number key.  Press a "1" and you "slash" for example.
Over the decades, fixed decks have been the go to, eyes off user interfaces for mmo combat.  But they have evolved to offer many interesting features such as combo'g, procs, buff and debuff interactions, enhanced motion moves and so on.  SotA's is a throw back, and without any enhancements at all.  It looks merely like a quick afterthought to quell complaints regarding eyes-off random deck failures.  The third option offers a mix and match of the fixed deck and random deck, where some key slots are fixed and others random which adds little to the mix in terms of solving anything.
Many players expect a new mmo to offer advanced mob AI (i.e., acts much like a pvp opponent), twitch play interactions, and motion integrated gameplay.  Most modern mmo's deliver this in spades.  Jump and double jump moves, charges, roots, breaks, fire trails, jump-landing explosions and knockdowns, blinks, dodge left-right-back, reactive moves (parrying, blocking and ripostes), quick withdraws, escapes, teleport backward or behind another player, etc., seem always part of now current UI combat kits.  And all of these features being carried out via fixed, eyes-off interfaces.  Don't expect any of this in SotA.
To recap, for pve, here is what you'll get if you buy this game today.  Mobs run at you, stand there and periodically attack without moving an inch until falling over dead.  Likely you won't notice any of this though because you will be nearly fully engaged in a random deck mini-game without moving an inch till your target falls over dead, or you do because you couldn't even afford the time to check your health or you run out of energy (focus).  In dismay, you may then switch to an overly simplistic fixed deck (with absolutely zero bells or whistles) and watch the lacking mob AI and twitchless, motionless and stationary combat play out.  This fixed deck will also be your pvp go to, unfortunately.  You will still move here and there if you have any hope against a hopper, but your motion will be no more than what you might have found 20 years ago -- get in range, press a key or two, circle and so on all manually through normal mouse and direction key interactions.
Beyond combat, the game seems to have a pretty solid infrastructure, but to gain access to much of developers product playgrounds you have to keep opening your wallet to pay more and more.  So don't be fooled.  You will soon realize that this is quite the expensive game to try at this point in development.  And you, like me, will likely get bored and move on wishing you had spent your moneys elsewhere.
Even so, if you are seeking a way-laid back pve grinding play style where killing ordinary mobs normally always bores you, this may be your game.  If you also detest pvp and adrenaline pumped smart pve mob and boss encounters, this IS your game.
Some may claim that the current UI and mob AI are just early placeholders or skeletons for something better to come.   They may be right, BUT this alpha is priced higher than nearly all released games.  Yikes!
I also always thought that combat was one of the first things to get straight before fluffing out content.  Sadly, this leads me to believe that the current SotA combat UI offerings are here to stay.

F.E.A.R. 3 gets something of a bad rap from fans of the series, and as someone who's played the whole trilogy, I can see why. The third full F.E.A.R. title lacks a lot of the impending doom and powerlessness that made the first two games so great, abandoned in favor of more and bigger gunfights, as well as further exploring the abilities of Point Man, the first game's supersoldier protagonist, and his ghost bro, Paxton Fettel. These are both fun in their own right, but feel like they don't live up to the F.E.A.R. legacy.
Another issue with the game is its mission structure. Narrative takes a back seat to repeatable missions and rewards for different tasks on those missions, as well as ranking built into the game's competitive co-op feature. These additions feel like an attempt to milk replayability more than anything else, and don't add much, if anything. to the game as a whole.
Those issues aside, F.E.A.R. 3 is still pretty good, if less F.E.A.R.-y. Co-op play is often recommended, but even single player is worth a try as both Point Man and Paxton, as both play completely differently. Point Man strikes a nice balance between returning home to his original F.E.A.R. play style and feeling like even more of a badass, while Paxton rellies more on deception and possession, offering a more indirect and strategic feel to his progress. Also, the bullet wound that ended Paxton's life remains prominent on his non-corporeal forehead, a constant reminder of how he went out.
F.E.A.R. 3's story feels like a reasonable wrap to the plot from the first two games as well, and does a lot of exploration of what turned Point Man and Paxton into the living (or not-so-living) wonders they are today. It clarifies both their connections to Alma, and while it doesn't tie things up with the neatest little bow, it's clear they tried. If anything, I would have liked fewer closed-circuit camera shots of their room as children; that got tired really fast.
Despite the grief some have given F.E.A.R. 3, it's definitely okay, even if you're a F.E.A.R. die-hard. You at least owe it to yourself to wrap up the story, and the gunplay and/or ghostplay is fun enough to warrant the time you'll put into it.

This is a complicated game.
When I heard about this game coming out, I was completely psyched and ready for it, but it was years before it was planned to be released.
They later gave a release date and I was excited for it alllll over again.
They announced the game on steam and put it up for early purchase, and I purchased it.
The game was released while I wasn't home, and I kept hearing about all sorts of people were crashing or couldn't play the game, but I found out it was because their rigs couldn't handle it, which mine could. I got home, and began playing the game.
The tutorial had me scared out of my mind, stranded on the planet running out of life support and struggling with radioactivity. I didn't wanna go anywhere that I wouldn't be able to see my ship in fear of being eaten by a giant space worm or being attacked by a giant robot or something, but I got my ship into the air. I've now been to tons of planets, tons of galaxies and have a bit over 1 million credits, and I still use the beta ship.
To be completely honest: I enjoyed this game, I enjoy this game, and I will continue to enjoy this game. I played it a ton when it was first released, and I started playing it again about a month ago because of the new release.
True, it would be much better and I would enjoy it a lot more if I could have my friend flying through space with me,  but that doesn't make it so I stop playing.
True, I felt like I was running out of ideas, doing the same thing over and over again, but the new update changed everything.
I now have a new purpose for playing this game, a reason to keep going. Sure, there's always the end goal of reaching the center (and the goal of avoiding spoilers for those who actually TRIED reaching it, instead of following the atlas storyline like I have been. Before the update, there was always the goal of collecting all the resources I needed from a planet by landing on it once at a random station, and items marked as "rare" were found everywhere, such as plutonium, so I could waste whatever I wanted on whatever I wanted to do because I could just land at any planet and collect 200 plutonium in about 12 seconds. After that, I would craft a few warp thingies and started off towards the next atlas objective.
Now, after playing the new update for a bit, I still haven't chosen a planet for a house. I now have the goal of finding the perfect planet with all the materials that I want in the right galaxy that has no atmospheric issues, other than life support dropping but that happens anyway.
I've also been collecting more money, as I've found the type of ship that I want that usually has the same specific price. Every now and then when I think I have enough money I'll wait at a station for a bit, but realize I either don't have enough for the perfect ship or that I'm in an empty galaxy with not too much commotion, which is perfectly fine with me because it means less pirates.
There's also the endgoal of getting a frigate. That is going to come much later for me and once I get my perfect ship and find a home, I can start grinding for money for a frigate, which I will take with me to the center of the galaxy (assuming I ever finish the atlas storyline).
After all this ranting and my story, if you're still here, well, yes. I would recommend this game.
The game was released as a sort of "pre-release", almost enough to the point where it could have been an early access game and no one would hate on it constantly, but there is more coming. I almost gave up on it but eventually went back when the new update came because I knew it meant they were still going, still working on it.
Sure, maybe they'll even make a way for multiplayer to work.
TL:DR = If you're fine with grinding for stuff, then you'll have fun. The way you have to look at this game though, is a game about exploration. Sure, grinding is a big part of it, but if you look at it in the sense that you're looking for some cool, new planets and cool new creatures (although a lot of them look like demented kangoroos), you won't really run out of excitement. Most of the planets before the update were just either deserts or snowstorms, but I believe the update contained something about terrain reformations, and there seem to be different types of planets now.
Anyway, I enjoyed the game but don't have very many hours into it because I've been busy a lot, but making this review made me remember what I enjoyed about this game.
If you do purchase it, congratulations, there's more to come and you could really enjoy it. If you don't decide to purchase it, maybe check back on it in a while, they might've added another update.

This game is an awesome bundle of fun.
It has a lot of the charming qualities that old turn-based RPGs had and it also has some decent writing to boot. There's a large equipment pool and a good variety of enemies. It's technical enough to be fun without dubming too much down. Proper preparation prior to battle can mean the difference between a 20-second battle and a 1-minute battle.
As far as difficulty goes, the game is not very hard. The endless battles, monster marathons, and boss rush modes can provide a mild challenge if you play on Epic difficulty.
Achievement-wise, there are some very simple achievements along with your standard beat-the-game achievements. There's also ones designed for hilarity (click on Natz' bewbs and touch the chicken)! You can tell the person who designed the game has a good sense of humor. The only thing I didn't like is how tedious the game felt while going through the 3rd playthrough. Since I am an achievement hunter, I felt compelled to 100% the game and trek on through playthrough #3 in order to get one of my last few achievements. One thing that I felt could have been done better is some variety when it comes to consequent playthroughs. I found myself picking up chests which served no purpose because it gave equipment I already had. If anything, those chests you've opened on older playthroughs should have something else.
I recommend this game to turn-based RPG fans. It's a good deal and provides 10-15 hours of fun on each playthrough if you casually go through the content.

I hesitate to select "no" on this, but I guess I wasn't sure what to expect before I began playing it. Needless to say, I approached with optimism.
I played the hell out of Gauntlet Legends way back on my N64 with my brother and sister, as well as some of Dark Legacy. Although this game has upgrades you can buy ("relics", kind of like constant passives) and a small amount of persistence, there's a lot that doesn't work in this iteration of a classic.
-This game is short.
-The bosses are easy.
-Teamwork is non-existent in most PUG scenarios (and anti-team actions are even actively encouraged).
-The latter fire/hell-themed dungeons are depressingly boring and empty; devoid of even minor details.
-There's literally nothing to unlock as you progress except for ugly skull-obsessed cosmetics and minor passives: no new hero classes (jester?) or full reskins (like the minotaur from Legends, for instance)... not even the ability to change your colour. Maybe a skull helm though; well done, hero.
-DID I MENTION THE SKULLS-ON-CLOTHES THING??
My biggest gripe though: there is literally no reason this game had to strip out the numerous advancements of the formula established in Dark Legacy and Legends. Those were damned good games (but nostalgia may be strong with this one), and in their place we get a shallow experience wearing the skin and spinning the axe of Gauntlets of yesteryear. It had some potential but feels like the ball was dropped.
EDIT: You can get new characters... in DLC! Frabjous day!
EDIT 2: I should note that some dude got mad about my review, saying "it was supposed to be like the first Gauntlet", as if that somehow excuses it from being boring or feeling barebones. If it could be better, then it could be rated down, period. I'll use this as an example: a bunch of my friends own it, and I have the most time in the game, by at least a dozen hours. This should probably be something a game tries to avoid.
Great game, but is far more fun when you have 2 or 3 friends with you.

The solid and engaging game mechanics of Gauntlet are undermined by its terrible merchant system. Few relics are truly useful and the loadout gear is simply cosmetic. The value and usefulness of gold degrades far too rapidly, dampening the rewards of prolonged play. However, the competitive nature of the cooperative multiplayer sets the stage for some hilariously enjoyable trolling moments. Bring a buddy and put your friendship to the test! In the end, Gauntlet is a bright star that burns fast and is best enjoyed with friends. 8/10

As of the date of this review, PreAlpha Release 14 has been open to the majority of backers for just over 24 hours.  Many details will change and I'll try to use the review to convey more about the tone and gameplay convention being aimed for than the present limitations.
That said, here's the cut and dry history.  Shroud of the Avatar is a game being developed by Richard Gariott, famous for the Ultima series of games (which helped pioneer the MMORPG genre with Ultima Online), as well as a team of authors and artists he knows both in industry and elsewhere.  It's loosely based on a tabletop campaign Gariott played long ago, and went onto Kickstarter a while back on the premise that the development will open to scrutiny for backers who help make the game happen.  In the vein of it's lineage, you can thematically expect a very vanilla fantasy setting with knights, elves, magic, traditional midieval weaponry, and perhaps some magitek.  It is heavily influenced by the world of Ultima, even borrowing names (Britannia in Ultima becomes New Britannia in SOTA) to try and increase the 'this could be the same universe' suspension of disbelief.  Onward to mechanical.

- in fact it pulls apart a lot of the MMORPG model and will even be playable offline, or with friends only, only release.  It can also be played in a public online space with other players, but uses copies of maps and friendslist wizardry to prevent overcrowding in areas and prioritize whether you're in the same copy of a zone as your friend, all zones separated by a worldmap you travel between locations with random encounter combat.  Is this as strange as it sounds?  Absolutely.  You get used to it though.  Any zone is referred to as a 'scene' and in terms of the meta hierarchy of the game, you might think of this as a combination between a Diablo style
(offline/online play and friend lobbies),
(seamless overflow servers in crowded locations), and any older RPG with a worldmap that features encounters (
being the more obvious title to pull to mind).
How about questing and dialogue?  This is supposed to be a shining feature of the game.  Unlike your now commonplace theme park RPG experience, SOTA embraces the older sandbox MMO approach of using a dialogue system in which you actually converse with Non Playable Characters.  NPCs parse keywords in your conversation in order to continue speaking, and you can use both highlighted keywords and secret keywords to recieve quests or progress in them.  Right now, this system is admittedly kind of clumsy, but has incredible potential as a system given how long it's been sitting out the RPG scene.  Even using a clunky version of this system is refreshing, and you feel rewarded for making a clever connection and mentioning some NPC's name to another for new dialogue.  It lends every character a distinct sense of identity in the game world when it works, and hopefully as development progresses those working on NPC dialogue will create general dialogue tree rules for zones, or general questions, to make a conversation feel more fluid, if occasionally broken.  This seems to just be a matter of anticipating a player's questions better and filling in the dialogue gaps.  To truly stand out, I'm really hoping for some kind of persuasion or charisma system that hooks into the dialogue.  It would be really nice to see NPCs react to your reputation, or to you sweet talking them, and offer specific minor questlines, or better deals on what they sell.  The quests that emerge from this system are more varied than a theme park MMO and often involve discovering another NPC and continuing a string of conversations with decisions and multiple possible outcomes.  Chatbox dialogue is unquestionably the lifeblood of the game at this early stage in its development, and sets this up to be a prime game for players who want to roleplay, as well as any players who are just sick of ignoring dialogue in a speech bubble and then going to kill 10 of some animal.
While we're talking about one of the most roleplay friendly features in the game, it's worth mentioning the other major feature this game brags about- persistant player housing.  Here's how the system works- there are a limited number of lots in most towns, and you can purchase and use an equivalent level property deed to purchase them.  Then you can purchase a house and set it up in the town or city.  Some limitations on this: if you're not a backer at a certain level, you will have to pay property taxes each month on your player housing, and the property in general.  Otherwise, all of it gets rolled up and dumped into the bank (presumably with its configuration intact) and the lot itself reverts to being for sale.  It will also revert to sale if you haven't logged in within a certain amount of time, regardless of whether your property is tax free. Houses are very customizable, lots of objects to buy and place, and basements.  RPers will be very happy.
Combat is interesting to say the least.  The present combat system in the game is partially inspired by card games- you build a deck of skills you want to use, and you don't have full control over which skills are available to you at which time.  You do have control of the pool of skills, and where you distribute your skill points- and there are a lot of skill points- right now you gain 8 with each new level.  You can level many skills up which determine both passive stats and active abilities, combine multiple skills for certain outcomes, and more.  More work needs to be done on this system- while PvP has now been ingame for a few releases, it's still too early to pick apart the finer points of combat, and a lot of it is likely to be retuned many times.  I can't speak to whether a majority of players will like combat, but I appreciate it so far for what it is- a bold attempt to be different.  It kind of reminds me of the original Guild Wars, which offered a myriad of skills and limited you to 8 skills at a time when adventuring, leading to a high level of customization and dynamic character builds that changed over the life of the game with each patch.
Visually the game feels...basic right now.  It's in pre alpha, that's to be expected.  That said, it's unlikely this will change all that much.  The team has been outspoken about their enthusiasm for the Unity engine, using it for the game and many early assets were the type one could purchase from the unity store.  They will be developing their own visual assets and releasing them to developers for free use in other games, only asking for credit attribution in return for use.  That's a cool idea, but it further seems to push the game toward a visual identity that looks homogenous and unrealized.
That's not to say that nothing about the game looks distinctive.  The layout of certain environments so far have a flourish to them, emphasized when certain areas are rendered in distinct building materials or setpieces (Ardoris features 2 massive palaces, a large shrine to a character called The Oracle, and a large statue in the middle that all help it stand out significantly in this regard, in addition to its less common skybox colors and seagulls flying around the water.)  The look of the game has improved a lot since the first prerelease, but what will keep it ultimately from feeling boring is going to be how distinct each area is from others, how the game develops a visual aesthetic that sets it apart from its contemporaries, and how it follows through on working that into things like UI or map lighting.
As for crafting or sound, there's much too little to comment on right now.
Final analysis: Definitely consider this game.  It does many things differently, shows a lot of promise, and we should get enough people ingame encourage developer Portalarium to deliver on as much of it as possible.

Oct 2016 Edit: I'm seeing some negative responses and "did you actually play the game" type of comments. Folks should note that I posted this review in Jan 2015. It's now Oct 2016, and the game has changed. A lot. The crafting system, for example, has been revamped like twice from scratch, and even the spell system was revamped completely once. Both of those systems have improved from their original form. I will say this: as much as this team asks for money or pushes the telethons or the selling of stuff on their store, you can see where your money is going. Updates and improvements are happening all the time... these devs are not sitting on their♥♥♥♥♥with your money. The game still looks beautiful, and keeps looking better and better with every update. It's also expanding, in terms of the world's size.
I still think it's a good successor to Ultima, but I couldn't tell you much about pvp, since I don't really participate in it these days. It's still grindy, it still doesn't hold your hand. I stand by my original assessment in that if you don't want an "easy" game, this one is that and still enjoyable.
By this point in the game's life and with an advanced community that's been with it since the kickstarter, it is a fact that if you don't come into the game now with some money in hand, and purchase house lots and deeds, then you will be pretty far behind. But starting any game two years later means you're going to be pretty far behind. If what you're looking for is player housing, know that you will be very hard pressed to get any without dropping real money into it.
Original Review, Jan 2015:
I love this freaking game so hard.
HOWEVER... I recommend it with a caveat. The reason I love this game is because my first video game AND RPG ever was Ultima 7. I played every Ultima after that, inculding Ultima Online, and went back and played older Ultima as well. Shroud of the Avatar is the spiritual successor to Ultima. It's Ultima in everything but name, and almost in that too.
It's an old school RPG with a bit more of a hardcore, almost grindy, feel to it. This game won't appeal to folks who want a World of Warcraft style RPG. I don't mean that negatively, it's just that I grew up on totally different RPGs then the folks who started their gaming careers with WoW. WoW holds you by the hand and gives you pretty explicit direction on where to go, who to talk to, etc.
Shroud won't do that. You gotta talk to everyone in town to find quests, there's no markings on a map to tell you where to go (figure it out from your journal and talking to folks), your weapons and armor deteriorate fast and also weigh you down depending on your strength stat... and if you are active in PVP, you can and will lose your gear to people who kill you.
There's non-instanced player housing, the crafting system is wonderfully complex, and combat isn't static... it shifts and changes and you have to be an active participant in it.
I love Shroud, but it's a very different type of RPG from the modern stuff out there right now. You've been warned.

Note: This game is Early Acces, it is not complete and some of the negative comments given relate to issues yet to be ironed out or related to parts of the game that are unfinished - you are buying an incomplete game at this stage and there will be character wipes to come before release. Bear all this in mind before you purchase but do not let that scare you off as there is still much enjoyment to be gained from spending time in the game even at this stage.
SOTA is very playable and polished for an early access title despite there being many elements of the game that are either missing or are a work in progress, what is there works well and there are some interesting mechanics and systems that move away from the MMO norm - there is definitely a lot of enjoyment to get out of this game even at this stage.
Learning curve can be a little steep at first and this game does not hold your hand like many other modern MMOs such as WoW. Currently there are limitations playing as a mage or archer and it is easier right now to play as a melee character, the combat system i think works well and the potential is there for some very varied character builds. I am playing a mage style build using death and fire magic and swinging a sword who is now in the mid-30s level wise and it is getting easier but being a pure cloth wearing caster it is easy to get overwhelmed and killed while out hunting.
Housing system is very advanced for an MMO, when the crafting skills fully come into play this game should have that feeling that UO did where you could be a skilled crafter working in the community and proud of your virtual home and its contents. Player owned vendors will be making a comeback as well. It will even be possible eventually to rent out rooms in your house to those players not fortunate enough to own their own home.
There are PvP options in the game including open PvP areas but this is not a fully open PvP world as UO was pre-trammel. In a way thats a good thing as the modern MMO community does not behave in the same way as the initial UO players did and it would just boil down to a lot of griefing and killing just for the 'lulz' (its a shame really that players have changed so much). Average game, horrible sequel. The gameplay is reasonably fun and does have some qualities, same for some environments. As mentioned in the key features of the game : "F.E.A.R. 3 delivers all the hallmarks that define the F.E.A.R. brand". Indeed, it's all about the “coolness” and the “attitude” of what F.E.A.R is supposed to be rather than what made it great in the first place, because the marketing derpartement always know what is good for us.
Long gone is the atmospheric shooter with tense combat, welcome to a shootfest with generic AI and the usual corridor missions. You'll get the shallow experience you've probably seen somewhere else, not terrible not great either, good fun for an afternoon perhaps. On the other hand, the second character is quite interesting due to his unconventional “ghostly” gameplay, making it worth replaying the game or convincing/fighting your coop partner to get a chance to play as him. Its just a shame you cannot use him right from the start in single player.
When I said it is a bad sequel, I'm mostly mentioning its worst offence to the spirit of the series made manifest into the achievement system popping up every five seconds to tell you how great you are, increasing your level but more importantly, your score. Why ? Because the game's design is centred around competitive coop, who gets the best score, gets the ending associated to his character. While it isn't a bad idea on the paper, having the scoring in mind and constant pop-ups definitely breaks the atmosphere that used to be a hallmark of the series. This is even worse if you play in single player since the competition becomes irrelevant as you get the ending of the character you are playing.
This competitive idea, also serve a purpose in the story, since both involved characters are competing
. The two main protagonists writing is also incredibly weak. If they were supposed to be unfortunate companions hating each other, it never shows, as one is completely silent and never seems to not care, making all the snaky comments of the other guy who is bent on trying to be edgy and dark even more pointless and annoying. The ending is definitely puts the last nail in the coffin to the F.E.A.R franchise, because F.E.A.R online never existed.

F.E.A.R. 3 is a decent game on its own, but unfortunately I can't recommend it to anyone because the experience alone doesn't quite cut it like the first installment.
The core gameplay design is based around cooperative play with a partner, however due to non-existent player base, it's almost impossible to play this game online. The campaign is very short and can be finished in less than 4 hours. Unlike the first installment, this game is not worth buying just for solo experience.
Even if you do manage to find someone to play with, you would probably experience a lot of problems (like lag and desync) which stem from bad netcode and unoptimized load management.
The only good thing about this game is its sophisticated A.I. which honestly, is one of the best I've played against. But again, it was the same case with F.E.A.R. 1 as well.
Other than that, level design is uninspiring and story is boring. If you're looking for about 4 hours of solo content, go ahead and buy it. Otherwise, buy the first installment. F.E.A.R. 1 is one of the best games ever made.

Economy? Static.
Spacefights? Tedious.
Spaceship flights? Claustrophobic and with a lot of limitations.
Animals? Sometimes cute or funny, but mostly liveless.
Planets? One biome per Planet and after 20h und 7+ Galaxies there was only one Planet I enjoyed being on (cute plant monsters) - everything else was empty or felt empty.
Navigation? ... None. Thats probably the main reason I dislike this game. Makes it claustrophobic but not for the right reasons.

RNG dependent Fetchquests, which is the prime cause for my time spent playing this.

I liked this game right from the start...... but then, I hadn't read any of the speculation of what the game was supposed to be before I played it, so had no preconceived ideas about it.  This was a gift from my son, so I just jumped in and started playing.  I was excited to be playing a game that was procedurally generated, not having played one of those before.  My impressions after playing 200+ hrs has been multifold.....  repeative npc's, animals, plants, and planets.... you run out of things to do really quickly if you're looking for quest driven stuff... trying to get to the center of the universe seems like something only the most dedicated could accomplish (I never made it there)....... Thoughts since the latest update:  base building, etc. has offered more to do, along with quest driven things.  Love the portal from the space station idea.  That solved so much (trying to get back to base after jumping to other star systems, for example)....  Great update.  I look forward to more in the future, hopefully adding yet more to do in the game.  It still tends to get rather repetitive, but this last update seems to indicate more coming in the future.
The price is STILL too high for this game, however.......... so unless and until it comes down, I would not recommend the game.  If/when it does come down, either via sale or price, I would recommend it.... it'll be fun for awhile.

Disclaimers: I got this on sale, and I've only ever played the Survival mode. I agree with some other reviews that the price is probably too high for what this game delivers, but with some reservations I'm recommending it anyway. Try to get it on sale.
Pros:
+Exploring various planets and star systems is fun for at least the first 10 hours
+Survival mode offers enough challenge that it really feels like an accomplishment when you get that next upgrade or make it to safety just in time
+The sights and sounds can be very relaxing and beautiful
+Harvesting resources has a satisfying feel
Cons:
-The aliens are all clearly just dudes in costumes and talking to them feels like talking to a vending machine
-In survival mode you spend a ton of time just waiting around in caves for conditions to improve so you can travel. This would be fine if the caves had anything interesting in them, but they don't
-There isn't a story, so if you're looking for something like Mass Effect with infinite worlds to visit, keep looking
-Combat is: stand in one spot, point, shoot, wait for enemy to die while hoping you don't die first
-You can't look around when you're sitting on the ground in your ship... wtf.

If you know you really wanted to get this game, but are still undecided because of the initial bad publicity, I would suggest watching recent gameplay videos or look at some of the more positive reviews. The people that love this game will tell you what they love about it and maybe it's what you will love as well.
It's been a great experience!  It's absolutely what I wanted it to be.  Explore, survival, mine, farm, and space battle.  I hope they never bring in Multiplayer.  I want my own universe to play with and that's what I got right now.  I don't want someone coming in and messing it up.
There is lots to do, but you really only figure that out after a while of playing.  You will see some amazing terrains, creatures, ships, aliens, ect.  It will take a while to figure out how to upgrade and max out your suit, multitool, ships, base, and freighter.
Look into the Mods available for the game as well.  There are a lot out there surprisingly.  I use a mod that makes space darker and a mod that improves flight.
The game is not perfect and I'm sure it will improve.  Again, look into the mods.  They can really improve certain areas of the game.  I really wanted to play it at release, but decided to wait to see what updates came after all of the bad publicity it had.  I did wait until the game was discounted before I bought it.  Knowing what I know now, I would have paid full price after the Foundation update if a discount wasn't available.

Though if you want to go all Farmville, there's a large number of quests, achievements and a huge sense of satisfaction just seeing your gold and honor rising steadily.

- The ability to play the game on almost every platform, including iOS and Android is a great bonus. The PC version of the game is more baked, while the mobile versions (newly released) still have some way to go in my opinion, Just having it available on all these platforms is a rarity.
- The number of hours I've played is evidence to one of the downsides to SHK. It has a tendency to take a hold of players lives, at least of those that get very involved in it. SHK can be hard to leave alone. If it does take a hold of you, when your not playing the game, you'll find yourself thinking about it, when you perhaps should be focused on something more productive. This is only exacerbated by the persistent nature of SHK.
- There's also a pay to win aspect to SHK, as you might have noticed by the other reviews.  Some benefits are only available to those who invest not only time but money. Hiding features behind a paywall is never popular and it's something I can't defend. Automated trading and scouting along with the ability to queue research and village buildings under construction are just some of the features hidden behind a pay wall.
- Requiring the purchase of Crowns (the in game currency) to increase the number of free strategy cards  your receive each day, is another tactic used by Firefly that I don't look kindly on .  You have to remember though, the game has to be supported and without money the developers can’t do this, I just wish Firefly could find a way to support the development, while making all of it's features available  to free to play players (perhaps with a little extra grinding), as well as those willing to open their wallets.

However as long as you can find a balance when you weigh up the pros and cons, before going into the game, you shouldn’t be disappointed. It may take you longer to achieve your goals in Stronghold Kingdoms if you play it entirely Free To Play, you may also have a hard time going up against people who play it Pay To Win (and know what they’re doing) but there’s no reason why you still can’t have a lot of fun playing this game and meat a lot of cool and interesting people along the way.

Let me start with saying I am a huge fan of the earth series,
-Earth 2160 continues the story of its predecessors through 4 campaigns of around average length that will most likely keep you busy for a while.
-The game features 4 very unique races which vary greatly in terms of playstyle.
-Lets you modify your units as you see fit to execute their job perfectly.
-It comes with a skirmish mode and supports up to 8 players for lan and i-net multiplayer. Has a bunch of extra maps added to it, some of which I recall seeing in fan patches.
-The game natviely supports most modern resolutions up to 1920x1080.
-Despite its age the graphics are still very neat to look at and features like its day and night cycle make the game quite pretty.
-Note: You will have to register the game ingame via its product code allocated by steam to unlock its full content, which might scare some people off but I dont exactly see any harm in it. (not like most modern games dont require you to make accounts :p)
Gameplay:
Eurasian Dynasty (ED)
The ED originated from Russia and while they may not be the fastest, they certainly have some of the toughest units in the game featuring heavy tanks, artillery and bombers. They weaponry ranges from conventional weapons to heat rays.
Their basebuilding consists of placing a main 'core' at the center of your base from which you build pipes to connect a variety of structures and generators to power your network of buildings. They can also build walls and a variety of other defenses.
Their ressource gathering is done by mobile refineries which can hover from depot to depot and process all ressources gathered on the spot for a steady income.
Strength: Very tough units, able to turtle quite well using a ring of walls around the mainframe, simple ressource gathering
Weakness: Slow units, buildings are vulnerable to get disconnected from the frame and can get disabled due to lack of power, basebuilding takes up a lot of time and needs to be planned ahead a bit in order to make room for future buildings.
United Civilized States (UCS)
The UCS originated from the United states of america, they have a variety of mechs and jets at their disposal and use a lot of energy based weaponry as well as ballistic missiles.
Their basebuilding is probably the most 'normal' and executed by flying drones that place structures which then build themselves as they drain the ressources needed. Their bases have the unique feature to use add-ons to enhance buildings in a specific way, such as making generators create more power or making refineries generate more income.
Their ressource gathering is rather traditional and has flying harvesters land on top of the ressources, gathering them and returning back to the nearest refinery for dropoff.
Strength: Fairly easy to master, strong missiles backed up by laser weapons, simple basebuilding which doesnt need babysitting. Can place turrets and walls to some extend to provide decent defense. Can teleport freshly trained units.
Weakness: Their structures while efficient can get costy to replace with a bunch of add-ons added to them and expanding to get more ressources does require you to set up additional outposts. Their laser weaponry is prone to get tackled by shields early on which renders them inefficient.
Lunar Corporation (LC)
The LC created orbital colonies and initially settled down on the Moon. They were able to study alien technology and feature the most advanced weaponry out of all the races. Their vehicles are hovertanks, infantry has jetpacks and aircraft are speedy.
Basebuilding for the LC means placing a basic module on the ground and stacking other modules on top to create a tower which depending on modules you places can fill in a variety of roles from research and unit training to combat modules to turn them into tough fortresses. They can also place external turrets and laser walls and all structures can be placed anywhere as they are dropped in from the sky. (you can only call in a limited number of buildings at a time though)
Their ressource gathering is as simple as dropping a mining base next to a ressource field. They will harvest and process it automatically.
Strength: Some of the fastest units in the game, very strong weaponry that is specialized to usually fit a single purpose, probably have the ability to expand in terms of ressources easier than any other race, can build foward or hidden bases anytime, anywhere.
Weakness: Due to their 'stacking' mechanic of modules their structural integrity is often at risk and they are prone to have their buildings get sniped which are even more expensive to replace than fully modded ucs building, their early game units while fast are fairly weak in terms of hp.
Aliens
The aliens are a new addition in Earth 2160 and feature the most unique playstyle using cloning and evolution to create their units and having no ressource gathering in the traditional way.
They can morph strong defensive structures which are able to provide heavy cover for units while they clone and evolve or block off ressource points from your enemies.
Instead of ressource gathering their units absorb a small amount of ressources to evolve into different species, starting with a basic unit that has no way of attacking and a basic mothership you have to clone them to create more and evolve those into different strands to create the perfect army.
Note: It is advised that you keep at the very least one basic unit to replicate as you might be unable to reproduce if you dont!
Strength: Strong structures, heaviest aircraft in the game, fast and lethal units, can easily poke at hostile bases and harass them.
Weakness: Beyond static turrets no way to defend yourself, take great amounts of planning and macro management to keep track of your units and their evolutions, easy to get harassed and crippled if cloning units are exposed.
Virtual Agents:
Virtual Agents are 'Hero units' which will offer their services for the highest bidder. As Aliens have no means to store ressources they are unable to obtain any.
Agents pop up every now and then , initially after a few minutes three random ones will pop up and ask if the player wants to hire them. You have to be quick and go for whichever suits you best or simply bid on them all if you feel generous with your ressources. Your enemies also have the chance to obtain them and can make them a better offer. In the end they will join whichever side is willing to spend the most money on them.
Once hired you can spawn the VA anywhere you like and they will remain in your service for a limited amount of time till their contract expires, after which you have to pay them again. If they get killed their contract is also terminated.
Those Virtual agents offer a variety of bonuses for certain playstyles, such as reducing the cost of flying units by 25% or having your ground units start as veterans. The VA's also come in a variety of shapes and often are a powerful unit on their own that if used right can pack quite a punch.
You can have up to 3 agents at a time which will most likely start to chat with one another at some point. This usually leads to quite some hilarious conversations which might entertain you if you like bad puns and sarcastic comments.
Note: Virtual Agents can be disabled during game setup if you dont want to have them around.
Thats about all I can tell ya, if youd like to know more you should just take the game for a spin, especially since its currently on offer for a laughable price. The rts genre usually doesnt bring forth as many games as other genres do currently which is why many of us still play 'older' games to pass the time.
This one is a little gem, sure has its flaws but it can be a bunch of fun, especially if you're looking to get it to play with some friends of yours who are also willing to spend a single dollar or euro to get it.

Very linear compared to other titles in the Gauntlet franchise, this game is not recommended for solo play. I grew up playing the original Gauntlet, Gauntlet 2 and Legends, but this game falls very short compared to those.
This game
+Good co=op
+Nice graphics
+Throw backs ("Elf shot the food!")
+Each character plays differently
-Poor choice for solo play
-Short campaign
-Characters feel very sluggish
-Way to linear
-All enemies are variants on a few with cosmetic changes
-A good 15% of the game is in pitch blackness
The original titles
+Non-linear -- Both on a single floor and the ability to skip floors
+Power-ups -- Shots bounce, invisibility, etc
+Shot potions still help
+Death isn't an instant KO, and it's possible to kill Death
+Different characters walked at different speeds, something missing from the new Gauntlet game
+Mini boss dragon that, upon killing, gave upgrades that lasts through a playthrough
+Still fun as a solo experience
+Legends had a pretty good story and had a lot to keep a gamer engaged too -- diversity, power ups, level aesthetics
These games had their down sides too of course.
-The NES didn't have a battery, so no saves...and it was a LONG game.
-The 3D games were a little clunky as most every game in the N64/PS1 era was.
-Graphics were a little touch and go depending on what you like.
-Possible to trap yourself until all the walls turn to exits (which is also a pro in some regards too)
-Only a few enemy types. They didn't cover it up though, and used that to their advantage. I'd rather beat 1000 ghosts than see a green, yellow, and purple one that look different but they really only take more hits.
I've only reviewed one other game, but I felt this one needed another voice. I don't hate it, far from it. I played through the entire game on normal, and played the first level on unfair. Unfair is the proper term for it too. Probably near impossible without co-op. I also really like Arrowhead as a studio, but there are a lot of things missing from this game and feels like a grab for money at gamers with nostalgia. I thought I'd read that there would be some procedurally generated levels, but that appears not the be the case. I had to play through a few levels once because I fell through a wall (wouldn't have happend on NES!) and nothing was different.
+Add temporary power-ups (maybe only on unfair?)
+Add a room after completing the game that will procedurally generate levels using all the assets in the game
+Speed up the game a bit. At 7.6 hours, I feel like this overstayed it's welcome.
+Add Gauntlet from the NES as an easter egg if possible. Arrowhead likes easter eggs, this would be awesome!
+Add mini-bosses with slight persistent power-ups. Doesn't have to be much!
+Less darkness. Seriously, I don't care if it's a level's gimmick, no one likes not being able to see the game. That just boils down to "let's follow my blue/green/yellow/red dot through a tunnel, turning when I hit a wall."
Hopefully the developers are still looking at the comments and feedback. Good job on this title, but I'm afraid with as little content that this title has and as linear as it is, I'm afraid I have to recommend a pass at this time.

8/10 - BEAUTIFUL, MYSTERIOUS AND SURPRISING!
This was an impulse buy for me and it did not disappoint. The game involves playing as a small birdman, and you flap around an open 2D world trying to find golden shards and bring them back to a "machine". Along the way there are plenty of physics puzzles and even the combat is physics based. Predator birds will try to knock you out of the sky but you can defeat them with the environment by either grabbing and throwing them into a thorny bush, grabbing a thorny vine and swinging it into them, or dropping a boulder on their head. It really lets you use your brain to figure out a good tactic and experiment.
As far as exploration goes the game doesn't disappoint. There are hidden caves everywhere and a few secrets to find that aren't required to complete the game. Along the way you'll find hidden "runes" which will allow you to decipher engraved stones. The messages tend to not be that important and are quite cryptic, but finding al the runes will land you with an achievement anyway. The game clocks in at around 2-3 hours so the world isn't huge by any means, but they've managed to pack quite a lot to explore into it. I would have liked the game to be longer but i reckon the gameplay would have become quite stale eventually.
The visuals are stunning and the soundtrack works well. This is a very solid game that drives the player with it's sense of mystery and discovery. Unfortunately while the message at the end of the game was one i enjoyed seeing, it wasn't that well written and left a lot of people confused and feelign unfulfilled, myself included. Only after Googling it i understood what was going on. Despite that though the journey itself is a lot of fun and i urge you to grab a copy .
If you are looking for a memorable, but quick, game this is a great choice. The style fits well and the game delivers enjoyable exploration with a unique-yet familiar- feel.

Its hard to find a role-playing game that matches the experience of sitting down with your friends to play a session of AD&D.
A lot of times, single-player RPGs have rich lore, a great amount of depth to the world, and a large amount of tools to expand your character and create your own content - you might be able to customize your appearance, forge your own weapons and armor, form relationships, and build your own house. But they become depressing when you realize you can't share the world with your friends; that you're essentially doing all of that only for yourself and by yourself.
Multi-player RPGs allow you to play with friends, but often have very shallow game world that doesn't feel alive. They might be restricted so much to feel like a theme park, where you as a player have no influence on the world, are just put on a track through the story quests, and are given boring raids to do with parties. Or, on the other hand, they might be so empty of a feeling of a shared lore and shared community, that it never gets past the sense of being just an empty sandbox for people to repetitively grind monsters, farm gold, and do PvP. Groups and guilds might form in the game, but theyre essentially about those things: grinding monsters, farming gold, and doing PvP.
Shroud of the Avatar tries to bring the best aspects of single-player and multi-player RPGs together to bring the play experience much closer to that of a pen-and-paper game session.
The way it does this is through instancing; which although used by a handful of reviewers here as a perjorative, is found in almost all games, and solves a lot of problems. Instancing is why when you go down into a dungeon to defeat some dragon, you won't find the dragon missing, with a group of other players camping the area and waiting for it to respawn. Instancing is why when you go to talk to a king about an important quest, you won't find dozens of other players around him, recieving the exact same quest. Instancing is why, when you go out into the wilderness, you'll be more likely to run into your friends than strangers, or more likely to run into people the game thinks will create an interesting adventure for you, than a boring one.
What it simply means is that the game can control, for each place in the game, which players you see and which you don't. In some places - like cities - this might be a huge number people, which is appropriate to make them feel bustling and alive. In other places - like in the wilderness - you might only run into a small number people, likely to include your friends. In other places, specific to plot-sensitive quests you're going on, it might be restricted to you and your party. And in a few, only you alone might be allowed.
Housing is not instanced. When you go into a city, you see everybody's houses, and you'll see everybody's vendors, when the vendor system comes online. You can also see into the windows of the houses, and look outside the window of your own house. There's a system in the game that allows new towns to be easy placed on the game map, and to also expand with time, and many will be entirely player owned and administrated. A home might be a simple building, or a wizard's tower, or a castle with a large courtyard, and might have no basement, or one that goes down many stories and hosts secret meetings.
The world itself will not be level-gated: you'll be free to travel anywhere you want and at any time, and not specifically only into zones fitted for your character level, and monsters in the wild will also not scale to your level. As should be expected, the further you go away from safe areas, like towns, and the deeper you go into dark forests, mountain passes, and oceans, the more challenges you'll find. The world will also be a lot more dangerous at night, with creatures coming out that wouldn't come out in daylight. You'll have to learn the environment, and among the things you'll have to learn is how to stay safe, if you're not planning on a danger-filled adventure.
Combat is moving away from the common gameplay of mindless button-mashing. There are a lot of different types of armor, weapons, and spells, all of which have strengths and weaknesses; what use will need to be carefully chosen. Wearing light armor might give you vulnerabilities that plate doesn't and make combat harder at first blush, but it also allows a lot of flexibility to actively dodge, escape, riposte, handle multiple attacks. A mage specialized in Fire Magic spells might have to watch out for a mage specialized in Water Magic. And all of these skills will have synergies with eachother, and also with the environment. A rogue might use Air Magic to enhance his agility and Moon Magic to become invisible, and a mage might have his Air and Water magic enhanced during a lightning storm.
Weather, moon cycles, and other events will play a great role in the game, not just for combat. Certain herbs that can be used for magic might be more plentiful or more potent during certain weather or under a certain moon - some might be even more plentiful in areas where there's a lot of death, their magic grown from the blood of slain adventurers. Lunar rifts will open at different times and a player will have to watch the stars to figure out to use them.
Banking is local, which means that if you leave an item in a town, you'll have to go back there to pick it up. This makes the economy regional, requiring travel to certain areas to find a better chance of buying something at a good price. It'll also open up chances for player trade routes and caravans. Besides vendors, there'll also be other opportunities to sell like market squares, and consignment. Players will also be able to create coins, and the devs are discussing bringing in multiple currencies to the game, including ones controlled by guilds.
Players, in fact, are contributing in large part to the lore and the feel of the world. A player guild called the College of Arms is helping people get set up with coats of arms, which will display in game, on player shields and tabards, and banners outside their houses. One called the Council of Scribes is helping people write books, collect them, and will be essential to disseminating them into in-game libraries. One called the Bards of Poets' Circle is helping create music and put it in the game, and will be essential to helping build a system by which players will be able to use instruments and sheet music. The developers are also hashing out ways for players to create all sorts of other content, like their own dungeons and quests.
There's a core story in the game written by the developers, though it'll open up into a large number of separate player experiences, which is what will allow players to bring in their own stories to enrich the game lore. It centers around a classic Ultima theme: choices and ethical dilemmas. There'll be different paths that your player will be able to take - and often there will be moral consequences to either choice you make. So you, as a player, need to think wisely what path you want to go down.
Right now, the game is in a very early stage of development. It's in pre-alpha, which will then become alpha, and then beta, before the game is finally published. So, if you start up the game now, you'll see it in an unfinished state. The developers will ever few weeks put out a new release for players, and with every release you can see the game coming together. Some things right now aren't as good as they could be, like loading times and graphics, though its better in every release.
It's a lot of fun even in pre-alpha, though, because of all of the player created content and events. People set up shops, create hedge mazes, hold arena duels, and play out human chess matches. There have been birthday celebrations, complete with cakes and dancing. The developers also participate in the community forums and play alongside everyone else.
Join us!

There are 3 short tutorials that outline the basics and then you progress from early eras to later ones, each giving you more time to complete the goals. These goals are called unlocks and are basically achievements, which then level you up.
The game has the correct pacing; the games last 30+ minutes, each task inside a game gives you 10/15 to complete, though they don't take that long... and yet there's always something more to do and a higher score to reach.
The graphics are 'cute', very cartoony but quaint and adhering and gives the game a non too serious approach.
I got it on daily deal at £1.50 and after 2 hours I've already had my enjoyment's worth out of it, and yet I've unlocked 7 from about 60 unlocks/in game achievements.
Now I'm not a very good gamer, so at some point I won't be able to do more of these challenges. No worries, there's also a freeplay mode, where you can just build up your planet however you want with no worries to over arching objectives for the unlocks... though you cannot progress either. It's more like a skirmish in an RTS game for eg. But this mode by itself is something I'd come back to for a few hours at a time to chill out and watch the world grow.
Overall a unique styled game, lots of fun, right level of challenge; increasing as you progress, and for a couple of quid it's a real valuable game to own.

I cannot find words for proper introduction...What I will say is, that you know when you are playing something unique if even something as trivial as in-game menus are embodiment or art...
Music and art direction are Ori's most amazing and impressive draw. Everything blinks, glows in multitude of colors and makes an incredible, hand-drawn impression of game's world. Locations are distinctive, varied and memorable. Animation is buttery smooth eye joy and the music sells the package with the seal of awesome orchestral mastery. All of those elements are at its peak in few climaxes throughout the game. Those sections, while very spiking in difficulty in comparison to the whole game, are designed and directed FLAWLESSLY. Those moments sell the game! Music pumps you up, world crumbles and spins around and all you are trying to do is to win a gamble for your life... The payoff after those sections? Cathartic.
While story wasn't a tearjerker for me in comparison to experience of others, but I definitely got invested in the game's world. Highest point of the narrative for me? The main antagonist. This isn't your standard videogames fare so this is very impressive on this fact alone. It's more an spiritual adversary in comparison to very direct, down-to-earth ones we are familiar with. Eerie, dark majesty of Kuro is always present and used to the full extent in many points of the game.
Those are the high points. Where are the flaws? The main problem with Ori is that it is "just good" in other deparments, like gameplay. Don't get me wrong, you won't be dissapointed with this Metroidvania's mechanics and the flow and controls will enterntain you for sure. The only gripe is that not many implemented power-ups, ideas for gameplay and combat are new and innovative. There are some, like projectile bashing and a manual save-spot creating, but others are "just" competent. Not oustanding, just good enough. Combat really could use some spicing up, since it isn't as engaging as it could be. It's downplayed and judging by design of other parts of the game, it was an informed decision. That's why exploration aspects, controls and physics of jumps/dashes are more than enough to fill the gap.
But, that I'm talking about. Right now I'm in the middle of "I just finished incredible game and I just cannot take on another after the impression of the last one" hangover. And I'm not kidding you, I have Alien Isolation, Dark Souls and Talos Principle on my backlog right now, I just cannot make myself iup to push an "install" button. I'm still thinking about this little game. I think that speaks for itself. It's up there with: Aquaria, Transitor, The Swapper, Bastion, Cave Story and Freedom Planet, in SSS indie tier.

There is a 8000/200 good to bad review ratio of this game for a reason.  (As of mine on this day)
Ori is one of those titles you can tell everyone gave it all to make the best possible game they could and for the most part it does work.
Our little hero is tasked to bring the world back to the light after a Evil bird like creature name Kuro turns it to darkness and near death. Many trials await you as you fullfill this job. From the enviroment itself to enemies who are warped from despair and anger. With your ally Sein you'll have means to defend yourself and gain more as time goes on.
This is a game full of stunning artistic detail and yet behind it this tale is full of grim and dark natured tones. While to some that might be a turn off, its presentation spurred me on to complete this. The world is never light and dark with a whole lot of grey. Ori is no different here.
This would fall under the "Metroidvania" class of games. But this is probably one of the more difficult ones ever I've touched.  Others have complained about this and one other factor. You will die and you will die often first go around. If you don't like this then, yeah stay away from this one. There is a reason a no death run is the hardest achievement on here. Ori isn't a tank, and has to finesse his way through this game.  Which brings me to the second point. Controls. They suggest beforehand to use a controller and I DON'T argue with that. Keyboard controls are very rough indeed. If you completed this with a one it should be an achievement.  To me controls are very precise and in areas I had to let go of the stick to make sure I stick the jump or landing. Your hand tends to overcorrect.  Control does help to the difficulty as areas because of the precision needed.  However, instead of getting frustrated I was more feeling accomplished when I cleared sections.
And I won't get into the music. It comes in exactly when its needed and makes the moments and game more powerful in its presentation.
So between the feels of the story (and there is quite a few) and the challenge...I can fully recommend this. Still on the fence about Ori, then wait until a sale to lessen the blow if you end up not liking it.

I started in my garage, no one believed I could do it. Just me against the world. "Blam this", "terrible game", "Worse than Call of Duty"..I heard it all. The wife was even being thrasehed with insults at work. My skills were on par with pacman, if he got cancer and later a tumor in his brain. My imaginary wife left me with all our made up kids..I was on edge. Just a string away from madness. Finally..I released the game of the century. Super Makio Mateys. Kids loved it, Adults lived it, and those in between rithed with joy becuase of it. My god, I was literally nothing...but I becaame something. After it's release I spent months researching a way to top it. I followed contracts to get money. I thought about my imaginary wife, but I knew I had to forget about her..literally. It had to be original and it had to be me. I tasted glory and wanted MORE. Finally, I sent out Super Makio Mateys 2! It smashed sales and destroyed the under garments of all my foes! "This was what I was made for", I thought to myself, "this is my time to shine!". Oh, and it was. Until I released the 3rd edition..the reviews came back mediocre at best. I was washed up. Same old same old with new graphics. I had to change it. I HAD to get out of my garage! SO..Horror! A total 360! it was a spin to the realm of chance and death...I survived. Reborn a new, I came out with code slinging like some sort of crazy priest! Hunters, Shooters, Racers, Musicals, Zombies, Dancers...YOU NAME IT! We made it all...All the latest fads. Some landed hits like Baka: The Weaboo Adventures. Some did not..Like: Call Of Shooty: Modern Toxic Online. However we managed to make it to a big time office. My team was known for many of the greatest titles ever known. it was time to venture deep. The fad was coming, we knew it was, however, we never knew it would be so strong.
MMOs were the thing and people wanted them bad. We produced one that took longer than it should have. Debt was all I could see. It was getting the the point where money was no longer the issue, if we failed I was completely prepared to cry. My tears and heart was on the line. It was just that important.
Release day: The Amnesia Night Online Went live. Players knew the name so of course the servers filled well. However, all I could think was.."Will they love it. Will they Stay and play for hours and hours and call out of work sick?". That worry washed over with an awesome wave. Players across the world dropped out of school, left their jobs, and even invested money they would never have..just to play ANO. It was and still is the greatest game of our age. Updates are weekly, every saturday. New content that was so balenced that forums were made just in dedication to appreciate it. With Free DLC, our competitors all gave up and started working for fast food...in the game, that is. We concentrated solely on the content of this game alone, and hardware to run it and the updates of course
30 years passed..time to celebrate everything we accomplished. Looking back, It feels like a dream. I hope I never wake up..

Scribblenauts Unlimited is a strange game, functioning best as a sandbox to play with creativity and absurdity. Focusing on completing the game tasks can become boring, and a fair amount of objectives feel like padding. Completionists will be annoyed by the amount of chores needed to 100% the game.
This may sound like the game is bad, and that could be argued. Approached as a series of tasks to save Lily, the game can feel a bit slow. However, sometimes you need to forget the quests and just mess around. Arm shotguns with shotguns, then hand them to a musical afro. Build a tower of dirty jesters, riding a hated jester on the bottom. Give a dog-fearing man a dog whistle and watch him panic. Play around, and you can really see the pure fun of this game. I've spent at least an hour catching my breath after hilarious events, most of which I didn't expect or plan. That alone is worth the time and money, in this era of pretentious art games and multiplayer communities that make you hate humanity.
Do you want to laugh, preferably without vulgarity? Can you come up with some silly ideas to see what happens? I'd recommend Scribblenauts Unlimited.

Short version:
Don't buy, bad game, waste of money.
Longer version:
Earth 2140 was solid RTS game, Earth 2150 (TMP/LS) was very good one. Earth 2160 is awful. I'm big fan of the series, but honestly, I can't say many good things about Earth 2160.
pros:
+ graphics
+ return of infantry units
+ experience is gained by pilots rather than vehicles
cons:
- balance (Morphid air fleet is virtually indestructible)
- cliched story (in E2140/E2150 story didn't actually matter, in E2160 we get mix of all sci-fi movie themes you can imagine)
- pitiful voice acting (actors don't even pretend to try)
- missions ("good old" objectives like "get from point A to point B" or "gather resources and wipe enemy base(s)")
- "improvments" to good ideas from E2150 (research tree now fits into one screen, too bad it looks as if someone barfed on the screen, different armour types introduce mess and confusion rather than diversity)
- soundtrack (it isn't bad actually, but there are very few tracks that are faction exclusive, it's huge step backwards compared to Earth 2150)
- activation (it kind of made sense when game was released, but now it's just ridiculous, on the other hand - LC campaign is broken and, as far as I remember, multiplayer servers are down, so going through activation process is pointless)
- AI (I was playing last mission in ED campaign on hardest difficulty and I was surprised how AI was "sending small groups of units to certain death", in the same mission AI ground units were getting stuck over and over in narrow valley)

This is game has the potential to be great. From what I've heard, this is the first of 3 planned chapters, so I do hope that they're successful enough to release the next 2. The flying is perfect, the physics are functional, the art style is beautiful, and the minimalist story is intruiging.
However, there are some issues. Firstly is the lack of map. For such complex and somewhat confusing level design, the lack of a  Metroid-style map is absurd. Secondly is the lack of combat options and the surprisingly unforgiving nature of the game. Why is there a healthbar? Why is there death? It can be exceedingly frustrating to be mobbed by a band of mockingbirds 5 or 6 screens in while you're carrying a crystal, only to find yourself restarting at the very first screen. I personally recommend a certain mod, Gentle Raetikon, which you can find on the workshop. It goes a long way to addressing that issue in particular.
The third and final problem is the ending. I don't want to spoil anything, but it sucks big time. I can understand it if it's part of a larger set of games, but
.
TL;DR it's a game I recommend playing, but it needs Gentle Raetikon installed, and it can be very frustrating due to its lack of map and terrible ending

A surprisingly emotional, psychologically intense game. Yes, it's one of those games that people will say, "that's not a 'game'!"  It's  about discovery and story, rather than puzzle solving or world exploration. There aren't any branching story lines or real choices. But don't let that or the simple graphics fool you - the characters are far more real than many HD characters in other games, the soundtrack is absolutely lovely, and it's the kind of story that makes you think. About society and yourself - your assumptions about yourself,  others, your choices, and what choices you think you might make. Even a few weeks after I finished the game, I'm still thinking about it. As a matter of fact I'm saving the two extra DLC/epilogue bits as a treat for later, to extend the experience.
I can't say I necessarily agree with what I think the message was, or agree that it was 100% a happy ending. But I honestly feel like this game is an enriching experience as much as an enjoyable one.  I would even tell someone to put a book down and play this game. There aren't many games I would say that about.
Pretty sure that everyone who has any interest in these sorts of games has already played this. But if by any chance you haven't - please do!
