I am a Kickstarter backer.  The vision for SotA has changed quite a bit since it's Kickstarter days, but all for the better.  Current build is stable and highly playable.
I'll start with the bad.  Keep in mind this game is pre-Alpha and most of what I have an issue with will most likely not exist in final build.
-Avatar creation very limited and not very appealing.
-Limitations of Unity (guessing here) make game world multiple zones.  There is a lot of instancing going on in SotA.
-Combat is wonky and needs a lot of work.
The Good:
-Game world looks very good for such a low budget, crowd funded game.  I expect this will only get better, but nothing wrong with way it looks now
-Crafting system is excellent.  Maker's mark appears on everything made.  Crafted gear is best in game
-Magic system is a work in progress but looks to be deep and complex
-The Ultima Community is alive and well in SotA
Community may actually be the biggest draw to SotA right now.  Many people who have issues with some of the game dynamics continue to p[ay because the Community is one of the best in gaming.  If you are an Ultima fan, SotA is a must buy in my opinion.  If you are an RPer, you will find a home here.  I'm pretty impressed with the progress made over 2014 on the game.  I suspect the game will improve to an even higher dregree over 2015.
If you are on the fence then sit and watch how the game takes shape.  The only drawback to not getting involved now is that land is finite (like Archeage) and if you want to own property you 'may' not have the opportunity, at least right away.
This is a great version of Ultima. If your a fan, you should get this one.

The first time I saw this game was in the Unity 5 demo reel.  Among all the games, this one stood out.  I figured it would be worth looking into, and I searched up a few trailers, and watched the first 20 minutes, to see what this game was about.  I was hooked, and I bought the game, hoping the rest was just as great.
I was blown away.  This game is great, not just from the perspective of a gamer, but a game designer.  From what I've seen, they did everthing right.  The graphics are (obviously) beautiful, and fit perfectly.  The soundtrack itself tells the amazing story this game offers.  I've listened to it countless times, and I've never grown tired of it.  I'm even listening to it as I write this.
My only downside is that there are parts where my computer is too slow to handle the complexity.  I have to play at the lowest resolution and it will still run slowly at times.  I'm sure it will run great on most computers built within a few years, but beauty does come at a price.
I've been trying to think of one reason for you to play this game.  I could tell you about the beautiful story, but I'd be ranting at that point. Was kinda sorta maybe fun? Still trying to decide as I only played the free weekend. I really feel if this game was more on the tactical side and was linear it could have been a dang darn good game. I get a tactical feel for many reasons. One obvious reason is that it was co-developed by Red Storm. It definitly has that Ghost Recon/Rainbow Six HUD going on and I liked that alot. It was cool to see amount of space in the characters bag and amount of aid items I had all without having to switch between gameplay and going to an inventory menu. Probably one of the most comfortably designed HUDs for a third person game. The other bit of what makes this game tactical is the cover system. I enjoyed that once I was in cover I was capable of moving to other places in the enviroment for cover that were highlighted by holding down the cover button. The really distressed looking urban atmosphere though is what really got my chub going. What didn't get my chub going was the story. The whole sleeper agent idea that made up The Division just did not feel plausible at all. I just wanted to skip every scene I was forced to watch. I saw somebody die before I got on a helicopter, right? That happened didn't it? I don't really know who it was, didn't care though. What killed the chub most of all was the RPG system. Never have I cared sssooooo little in a game that had skill system. I didn't feel compelled at all to look what skills were available, nor spending any points I had available. It just didn't seem like it mattered. Though it probably matters later in the game as this is a level based game. I only got excited when I finally got a rifle with a scope. The idea of having a loot-based RPG that is also trying to be tactical just doesn't go well together. At best they make strange bedfellows. In short, this game had potential. Rather than looking to games like Borderland, Diablo, WoW or for that matter any always online MMO RPG where you find random generated weapons and gear that give perks it really should have looked to a game like S.T.A.L.K.E.R.; a game that plays tactically with minor RPG mechanics that has weapons and armor you get excited to find.

Being a HUGE fan of the Bloons TD flash and app games, I was more than a bit skeptical of how much "worth" I'd find from a Steam version of this game. I did jump on Greenlighting this game, but upon release I held off on the purchase. And even now, it was my wife whom bought this game for me since it was on sale and extremely high on my Wishlist. So, after playing a fair share of this game, how do I feel it's holding up?
AWESOMELY!
I couldn't have asked for a better version of this game. The microtransactions from the app version have been beautifully incorporated into the game using in-game cash instead. The menus are extremely easy to use and glitch free (which is the usual issue with app-to-Steam games.) And the graphics are wonderful, no matter if I play full screen or, my preference, windowed. And some features, like using Special Agents, are now easier to use.
My one (and only) complaint... when you have a unit selected, it covers over the Round number with the unit's info which can be a little annoying when you're planning ahead or just wanting to quickly know if you're almost to Freeplay.
TL;DR = This is the best casual tower defense game. <<<Period!!!

Let me preface this by saying that Skullgirls isn't for everyone. If you don't like arcade fighting games, well, you probably won't like Skullgirls.
That being said, if you do like the arcade fighting genre in the slightest this is a must-buy game.  Mechanically the game is among the best as far as fighters go but it's the memorable characters, beautiful artstyle and the imaginitive world on top of the extremely polished gameplay that take this game from being 'great' to being 'absolutely amazing.'
Skullgirls is great for beginners looking to get into the genre as well, offering an extensive tutorial mode that covers the basics all the way up to mechanically-demanding mixups. (Combos that are unpredictable) Sure, tutorials are common in fighting games, however, the sheer depth of Skullgirls' tutorial is what makes it deserving of praise.
Mechanically each of the characters are as diverse as their personalities. Through the tutorial you'll learn each character's role and weaknesses and as new characters are added they're given lessons in the tutorial as well, giving all the more reason to endlessly praise Skullgirls' tutorial.
The roster, although seemingly tiny, is being rounded out by additionally characters being added in future patches. At the time of writing this, three of those characters have been released with the remaining two being actively developed which round out the diverse roster of characters beautifully.
That being said, the game is constantly being updated and patched with no sign of the developer stopping any time soon.
The game is fanservice-y, yes. Is it tasteful? Honestly, yes, it's appropriate in the context of the game and the characters
within it. If you can't handle female characters in sexualized outfits/poses then I don't know how you've played any other fighting game to be honest. The problem isn't that the characters are designed this way, it's that you have overly selective eyes and an extremely closed mind.
So here’s where we’re at when all is said and done: we have a fighting game set in a gloriously original world, racked out with unique characters whose hand drawn animations are stunningly detailed. The soundtrack of the game is – at least for jazz fans – beautiful enough to warrant an OST purchase all on its own. The graphical presentation is phenomenal, the story mode is entertaining, the characters are unique and engaging as a whole. For fans of this genre do yourself a favor and purchase this game. At the $14.99 price point it's a steal as it's worth double that at the very least.

I’ve been looking for a good Dungeon Crawler after putting several hundred hours into Diablo 3 & starting to get a little bored. I watched MrTHagger on YouTube playing some Gauntlet & thought it looked like the type of game I would enjoy. How right I was.
Now I want to start this little review off by stating that this is not a full priced game as we know it. What do I mean by that? Well I mean it’s not a £40 title. Which we are so used to nowadays. This is a £15 game. So when I first started the game up my expectations were low shall we say.
Graphics:
So was I right to have such low expectations. No I wasn’t. This is a fantastic Dungeon Crawler. Granted the graphics (which contrary to general belief is not the most important part of a game) are not mind blowing. That’s ok though. At the end of the day it is a over head hack ‘n’ slash. Your not expecting top quality graphics in this genre. You want a fast paced all action adventure. That’s not to say that this game is ugly. Oh no. This is actually a very nice looking game. If you stop for a second to admire the attention to detail you’ll be surprised at the amount there is. Granted the dynamic backgrounds aren’t quite up to par with such games as Diablo 3 but then again your not paying Diablo 3 money.
Gameplay:
Now for the important part. Gameplay. This has it in spades. It’s very easy to pick up the basics and get involved but will take you a little time to fully master the mechanics. There’s a short tutorial at the beginning which is mandatory but is worth having it in there. Once your into your first dungeon you’ll be gripped by the amount of mobs heading your way all trying to dismember you. The general gameplay is very smooth. It’s not clunky unlike some other games in this genre. Everything seems to just work as it should. Each of the 4 classes feels different. The Warrior feels heavier than say the Elf. Which he should as he’s basically a tank in a loin cloth.
Combat:
Combat is one of the main aspects of this genre. It should feel almost free flowing. Gauntlet has pulled this off great. Again each class feels completely different. I’ve spent most of my time as a Warrior which feels heavy as you wade into a crowded room of mobs swinging your axe around like a mad man. Spinning and slicing your way through trying to grab the crown that a recently deceased mob has dropped. It feels great. You get knocked back by certain mobs and others you spend half your time dodging their fiery balls of death they’re firing at you. All in all the combat feels just right. So many times games have been let down with this aspect of combat. The developers of Gauntlet have obviously spent a long time working on combat & this is very apparent while your playing.
Character Levelling:
Levelling up is always an important part of a Dungeon Crawler. Well gauntlet has done it differently. I’m not 100% sure this was the right way to go but at the same time it does work. You don’t have a level system like other games. Instead you have a Mastery level which comes from completing certain objectives in game. Such as smashing 80 props or killing 2000 of a certain mob. This will then give your character a buff like 10% damage to a certain type of mob etc. So this is different from your normal level 1 to 50 your so used to. The other part of levelling is Relics. You earn gold in the Dungeon. It’s lying around everywhere to be fair. You then use the gold to buy Relics. You can have 2 equipped at a time. These are basically like perks. They use potions which you’ll find in the Dungeons. Relics include faster movement for X amount of time. Fast attack. Have a Gargoyle fight with you. Things which you may need when your in a tight squeeze. You can then level these Relics up by upgrading them in the shop. It’s not cheap but worth doing. You also get items for completing the game on normal, hard & unfair difficulties. Like weapons & armour.
Leaderboards:
One thing I really like is at the end of each Dungeon your given your total money stats & time it took you. Then you are given the top 3 players in the world stats. So it gives you something to aim towards. I’ve been lucky enough to get a couple of No1 positions & always try to aim for the top. A little competition never hurts does it. You can also compete against your friends & show who’s truly the Dungeon Master.

Minigames, like racing vehicles.

I came across this title when it was around a dollar, and even at the normal five bucks it's more than worth it.
Let's get the cons out of the way first: the game explains almost nothing, and has tooltips that simply describe what a building or unit or upgrade is within the universe rather than WHAT IT ACTUALLY DOES in game  For example, there are base upgrades for the UCS that use random technobabble instead of describing it as "provides more power to the UCS power plants" and such.  It gets confusing, and you mostly have to learn by trial and error.  I imagine the campaign may help and serve as a sort of tutorial, but I never made it past the first mission.
The tech tree for each race is also fairly overwhelming at first glance, and you basically need to sit alone with the aliens for a match or two to slowly figure out how they work.  Again, trial and error.

Also, the AI is extremely hard.  Even on the easiest difficulty, my friend and I who are fairly new at the game have to go two against one, and often barely scrape by with wins.  Granted, we are new, but the easy AI should not be anywhere NEAR this hard.  It's fairly ludicrous.
Also, the factions don't appear to be very well balanced, at least in the vanilla (un modded) game.  Late game, aliens are invincible in most cases.
And now to the pros!
The factions in this game are my favorite I have ever seen in an RTS, and I am not exaggerating.  They all feel COMPLETELY different, unlike most games where the factions are basically reskins of each other, build slightly differently, etc.. It is quite fun learning how to play each of them, and figuring out which one best suits your style.  The three non-alien races have their own different tech trees, and you can also construct custom units to make the perfect army.
Another thing: the battles are epic in every sense of the word.  Just in the last match I was playing, my friend and I were fighting with the computer over the middle ground of the map.  My buddy was the alien faction and moved in with large cruisers, while I supported him from the ground with anti-AA tanks (in this game, you can build custom units with different weapons equipped: in this case I outfitted tanks with anti-rocket flares, which protect your air from AA rockets).  The computer mobbed at us with endless anti-air units and large mechs, which my flare tanks mostly took care of, while both sides were being bombared with long-range artillery from each player.  Random other ground-on-ground tanks battled in the middle.  Lasers and flares and rockets all exploded overhead, and explosions were everyhwere.
Battles like this happen all the time in Earth 2160.  It's extremely fascinating to watch, and the game gets incredibly intense in pitched fights.
This is probably the longest review on the game, so I will shorten it up and conclude with this:
Yes, it has flaws, some of which are fairly aggravating, but when the game shines it truly shines.  It's a grind to learn the factions at first, but if you have some friends to play with, you'll find few RTS titles with more intense battles or more interesting factions.  Worth five bucks, easy.

This game is in Alpha and there will be some changes. That being said, the release date is getting closer. Being a huge Ultima Online fan, running 2 UO servers in 98-2002 - I figured i'd give this a go if not for pure nostalgia. The game is literally nothing like Ultima Online used to be, aside from player housing and some basic concepts. If you are looking for an MMO / Ultima Online clone, this is not it. I didn't get into the game thinking it was going to be the next greatest thing but I did expect some decent gameplay.
The game is instanced, meaning you have to load each area before going in. You also get to run around on a larger map (much like final fantasy) and select places to go. That in itself is cool, for a single player game... not an mmo. The maps you load into are also fairly small and have no real substance to them. Player towns are dull and boring, with a lot of common themes throughout. One day I decided to play all the FEAR games front to back, I started with FEAR 1, still as goo as I remembered it and the graphics are still decent for its age. I then played the DLC which I learned are non canon. They felt like singleplayer mods for the base game but a large part is just as good as the original game. FEAR 2 felt like a more streamlined version of the original which is a comon strategy in the gaming world. If a new IP does well the second game will be more streamlined, even if it didn't need to be.
I then played FEAR 3, I immediatly noticed the weak gun sounds, the aweful movement and the damage feedback on you, there is no damage feedback. While in the previous games when you get hit you would at least get a camera shake or a noise indicating you're taking damage in this game you can take damage without noticing it. Sure there's a damage indicator near your crosshair and your screen slowly turns red but you take such a huge amount of damage often times you just stand there taking damage shooting at the enemy right in front of you who also takes quite a bit of damage.
Compare  this to FEAR 1 in which the gunplay was excellent, the gunsounds felt like they packed a punch, the dust and debris flying off walls and decoration made a firefight feel genuine and while enemies in the original did take a lot of damage firefights were fun. You had to take cover and the slow motion was a helpful feature. In FEAR 3 it's not really needed as you don't have to take cover that much.
FEAR 1 was a semi tactical shooter in which you couldn't just attack the enemy without thinking, you had to take cover, fall back and use the slow motion.
Also somehow FEAR 3 looks worse than any of the previous games, sure the textures might be higher but there doesn't seem to be a lot of dynamic lighting and everything looks brown.
The movement feels weird, it might be the little momentum or the lack of movement feedback but it was much better in the previous games.
The bottom line is, the game feels like a budget title, the entire character of the FEAR games was stripped away and replaced with a generic budget shooter with slow motion tacked on. I won't play this game again and will not finish it.

This game is, in a word, frustrating.
This is a game that can't quite decide what it wants to be. On one hand, its an exploratory world with puzzles and secrets to uncover.  On the other hand, it's an RPG with fetch quests, trials, obstacles and things trying to kill you.   These two halves do not mesh as well as they should and the mechanics that would be forgivable in a pure exploration game do not hold up for a battle-less RPG.
Boiled down to it's core, the game play is find the glowing bits, collect them all, feed them to a machine and then activate the machine which either gives you a different glowy bit to bring back the big machine in the middle, or helps you open a door to go through to continue the cycle.   This on it's own, isn't bad. Standard RPG/puzzle quest.  But the controls do not have the proper fine tune to allow the player to actually accomplish these goals easily.   After activating one machine by a door, it dropped down a battering ram that it took me a good 15 minutes to get to actually hit the door in a way that actually broke it down.
Another section involved a maze of thorns that you had to fly against the wind to navigate.  Flap wrong and you're thrown into the waiting thorns much like a ping pong ball and it's near impossible to recover without being thrown into another bed of thorns.    In another, after successfully activating a machine, I was presented with another challenge, having to get a glowing bit from a running stag.  Due to the limitations of the controls and the flaky flapping mechanic, I eventually just gave up as I was never able to get my character to do anything that got it even close to the runner.
The visuals of the game are pretty impressive. Stylized, but not in a way that comes off as pretentious.  If it weren't for the aggressive birds, excessive thorns and fighting against the controls to try and get from place to place, it would be a very nice, laid back exploratory game, which the ambient sounds and lack of any narrative present it as.  But at it's heart, this game more comes off as a frustrating, non linear puzzle platformer who's mechanics just can't hold up to what the player needs to do.  Perhaps with a game pad or under windows, it would work better, but I have neither of those things to test it with, and the graphics and atmosphere alone are not enough to make up for the high level of frustration this brings.

Secondly, you will cry. I don't cry at films, I normally find the kind of pacing that requires just missing. I watched Everest 2015 and sure it was moving but it didn't bring me to tears. This game does look at issues around Autism and Aspergers but it is never the big reason any scene particularly gets you. It adds a strange sense of weight to the troubles and helps to show how normal decisions can be taxing in a very understanding way.
Now it is a semi point and click/ d pad and space bar adventure game but for the most part this is about story not puzzle solving. There is no way you could solve the puzzles unless you had a P.hD in neuroscience memory systems; luckily you play as two doctors who do so that solves that. You are here for the ride, to see the story progress and feel for the characters. There were two moments I needed to use a wiki but in the game's defense I was being dense and a little impatient.
This game is undoubtably worth your time even if you are a robot and want to see if you can feel those weird organic things called emotions. This game will certainly make you malfunction if that is the case.

Let me preface this by saying that Skullgirls isn't for everyone. If you don't like arcade fighting games, well, you probably won't like Skullgirls.
That being said, if you do like the arcade fighting genre in the slightest this is a must-buy game.  Mechanically the game is among the best as far as fighters go but it's the memorable characters, beautiful artstyle and the imaginitive world on top of the extremely polished gameplay that take this game from being 'great' to being 'absolutely amazing.'
Skullgirls is great for beginners looking to get into the genre as well, offering an extensive tutorial mode that covers the basics all the way up to mechanically-demanding mixups. (Combos that are unpredictable) Sure, tutorials are common in fighting games, however, the sheer depth of Skullgirls' tutorial is what makes it deserving of praise.
Mechanically each of the characters are as diverse as their personalities. Through the tutorial you'll learn each character's role and weaknesses and as new characters are added they're given lessons in the tutorial as well, giving all the more reason to endlessly praise Skullgirls' tutorial.
The roster, although seemingly tiny, is being rounded out by additionally characters being added in future patches. At the time of writing this, three of those characters have been released with the remaining two being actively developed which round out the diverse roster of characters beautifully.
That being said, the game is constantly being updated and patched with no sign of the developer stopping any time soon.
The game is fanservice-y, yes. Is it tasteful? Honestly, yes, it's appropriate in the context of the game and the characters
within it. If you can't handle female characters in sexualized outfits/poses then I don't know how you've played any other fighting game to be honest. The problem isn't that the characters are designed this way, it's that you have overly selective eyes and an extremely closed mind.
So here’s where we’re at when all is said and done: we have a fighting game set in a gloriously original world, racked out with unique characters whose hand drawn animations are stunningly detailed. The soundtrack of the game is – at least for jazz fans – beautiful enough to warrant an OST purchase all on its own. The graphical presentation is phenomenal, the story mode is entertaining, the characters are unique and engaging as a whole. For fans of this genre do yourself a favor and purchase this game. At the $14.99 price point it's a steal as it's worth double that at the very least.

After playing it for around 15 hours and completing it 100% (except for three achievements), I can say it has been a great adventure. I've heard a lot about Ori and the Blind Forest prior, but it's only now that I pulled the trigger. And I think it's safe to say people didn't lie or exaggerated. This truly is a great game. It doesn't only look and sound beautiful, it also plays very well thanks to its tight Metroid-like level design. Don't let the "cute" appearance fool you though, because underneath hides a pretty hard game that will challenge you, but in a fair way that usually doesn't cause frustration. If you die, it's usually on you.
There are a few things I didn't particularly liked though. The escape sequences for example smelled a little too much like trial and error, whereas the main game was (as I mentioned earlier) challenging but fair. Also, I think it's pretty odd that the developers chose to permanently close certain areas after you're done with them. If you didn't find the secrets and whatnot in those three dungeons before you exit them, they're locked forever and you can kiss your 100% run farewell (unless you use certain scripts to return to those areas, see the community pages). A shame, because that's the whole charm of a Metroid-like game: being able to venture back all powered up and collect items you didn't get the first time around.
Anyway, despite the one small and one big gripe I have with Ori and the Blind Forest, it's still a great game worthy of your time, especially if you enjoy playing Metroid-like games. Summarised:
+ Visually stunning, every area breathes something unique.
+ Good music, some songs are breathtakingly beautiful.
+ Atmosphere is hauntingly beautiful.
+ Metroid gameplay works excellent with high pacing and varied, great power ups.
+ Going for 100% is challenging, hard. But the best part is it feels fair.
- The escape sequences felt a little uncharacteristic with some trial and error.
- Several areas (the three dungeons) are permanently locked afterwards, which may prevent you from 100% completing it and finding all power ups and items.

Minigames, like racing vehicles.

Checked back after a few months, and there has been some progress. Not everything for the better, unfortunately. At this point, I'm not sure if this is going in a good direction.
- some content has been added and missing game mechanics integrated, so far so good. still not a whole lot to actually do in the game, but it is still pre-alpha afterall
- day/night cycle appears to be working now
- travel map got a lot more beautiful, unfortunately also a lot less useful in the process. the new perspective does not allow you to really see where you are going, you cannot properly zoom to get an overview, all in all it feels quite off and the old version, even if it was ugly, was better from a gameplay perspective (as I understand, the awkward camera perspective and inability to properly zoom has technical reasons, partially due to the fact that you need to be able to also look at the sky/moons due to game mechanics)
- combat mechanics improved very slightly, but it is still far from where I'd say it has a decent combat system, still very static. animations in combat are very jerky, this was also a lot better in earlier versions. the whole combat system probably needs to be scrapped and redone from scratch.
- enemy AI appears to have disappeared completely, mobs just stand where they are and do not move, only attacking you if you deliberately get into striking distance, and leave you alone as soon as you move back a couple meters. this was working in previous versions, they'd get close and atack by themselves, and even hunt you down when you were fleeing
- no real visual improvement apart from the travel map mentioned above, in general I'm even inclined to say visuals degraded compared to previous versions, especially character animations have gotten a lot worse, jumping looks rather grotesque, and the transitions for example from walking to standing are nonexistant
- performance has improved, with a decent rig you can actually crank it up to maximum settings now, and there seem to be no severe performance degradation anymore when playing a while
I'd not say that this project has failed already, but I'm getting the feeling that they somewhat lost their direction and it didn't get much closer to transition from pre-alpha to alpha or even beta stage in the past months.

(old review of release build 202 below, shortened because TLDR)
Given the track record of the producers, I believe this will be a fantastic game someday, but not in the near future. Keep in mind it is pre-Alpha, but since you are about to spend $45 on it, here is why I dont recommend it yet:
- first and foremost, the current state of the game could best be described as a tech demo, obviously this is what early access is for, and the tech demo is working and you can play, but there is a host of stuff still missing, you can see a vision of what the game is supposed to be, but it is not ready to play for a general audience.
- balance issues, as a starter character it is pretty hard to get to explore some content, as pretty much every place you find, or random encounter you have will be filled with mobs way above your skill level
- somewhat lackluster combat and skill system design in my opinion, you can decide between the usual 'skills in hotbar', which gives a skill usage penalty, and a variant where you randomly get your skills switched into your hotbar. with the second variant, you can combo if you have two fitting skills, kinda unique idea to it but too much micromanagement, and very static combat. also needs some basic skilling first, not easily accessible for starter character
- lack of atmosphere in cities, and utter chaos due to immense amount of player owned housing. makes it hard to impossible to find the npc you are looking for, gives a deserted feeling in cities, and also some of the player houses are seriously grotesque, which can be a serious immersion breaker.
- poorly implemented npc conversation system. while the idea itself is definitely brilliant and appealing to ultima fans, it is a horrible player experience. what you do is write in a chatbox to talk to the npc, and he will recognize a few keywords he has responses for. for example "can i help you" will ask him for any quests he can give. as a long time ultima fan, I can somewhat appreciate the idea, but it ends up being a huge hassle
- instance systems for points of interest, and the instances are rather smallish. you do travelling on a worldmap, and can enter cities or combat instances where you can really walk around and do stuff with your character. not a bad thing in itself, but it gives a bit of an 'empty world' feeling, even with the occasional random encounter that will force-load a combat instance. there is no opportunity to stray from the beaten path, which in my opinion severly limits the adventure feeling.
- weird day/night cycles when changing maps. you'll be in the worldmap in bright sunlight, enter an instance where it is midnight, leave instance seconds later, and are back in sunlight. add to that the lack of orientation points, making it very hard to actually know where you are going in darkness. even with a torch, it is hard to move. some moonlight at least in the outside areas would not hurt.
- UI needs a lot of work and has conceptual flaws imho, it is popup windows cluttering the screen, while they will certainly improve a lot visually (they are currently very text-heavy with some ugly, barely recognizable icons mixed in), I feel that the concept itself is not a good design. while you could say it is flexible, all it does for me is interrupting the game flow with unwanted window management way too often. ymmv here though, some may like it.
- if you are a gfx kinda person, which I'm not really, you'll probably feel that the visuals have a somewhat dated feeling to them, not what you'll expect in 2015. it is not horrible and works, and in fact many MMOs have that issue, but for my taste there are too many squares, rectangles, cubes, cones and the like, and it is lacking a bit of 'flow' if that makes sense.
Certainly worth keeping this on your watchlist given the developer team they have, they certainly have the expertise to turn it into an awesome game. At this point though, you'll not get your moneys worth if you just want to play a game imho, consider buying if you want to support the project.

The original text was published on Kanobu on 17.04.2016.
Triangular sun floats above the straight geometrical line of the horizon. You can “jump” above it, but the gravity will pull you back shortly. A vulture floating in an airflow carries its prey. Somewhere below spruces swing in the wind, bobcats hunt the jays, mysterious altars await their time, giant foxes sleep in their lair, and cryptic runestones emit blue light. And everything is made out of triangles. Previous game of Broken Rules studio celebrated torn paper aesthetic; Secrets of Rætikon echoes it trying hard to look like an origami composition.
This is Ecco the Dolphin which has been drained, but preserved the iconic arc jump when you try to go up above the skyline. As a bird which literally felt from the sky will have to find a way yourself through the mountains, lakes and underground temples. A short tutorial will familiarize you with basics of controls and key items — yellow glowing shards. Flapping the wings and finding beneficial airflows is a pure joy. An ability to clutch anything is a surprisingly powerful way to interact with the world. You can pick up a stone or a running rabbit with the same ease (if you’re agile enough to catch it). A torn out sprout will regenerate your health, a rock falling from above will crush anything it falls on. If you’re observant enough you’ll find more complex interactions on your way. Bringing an egg laying on the ground back to the nest will make it hatch, and the nestling will throw about blue spheres. What do you need them for? Oh, that’s another small secret which are numerous in the game. Hidden passages, runic writings, ciphers and keys — the world is compact but bursting with content.
No help will come from anywhere, nothing to rely on besides yourself, your memory and attention to detail. The majority of obstacles only seem hard. Take a pause, wait and observe and a solution will come. Lure a lynx to the moose which has a key item stuck in his horns, pick up a stone to dive deeper on the pond — right actions are logical and evident, like the game world itself. Below the surface though there is another layer, not physical, but mythological in nature.
The tales or rets, an ancient tribe inhabited Alps long time ago isn’t exactly a key to what’s happening on the screen. It’s an optional vignette, a reward for the patient player. You can finish the game paying no attention to the messages on the runestones, and then the giant foxes will remain just an exercise in design. The statues that you’ll assemble from the broken pieces will stay nothing but a method to open a new path. But aren’t you curious about what they actually mean?
Forest inhabitants live their own lives paying little to no attention to the player who in their eyes is just another harmless and insignificant part of the world.
Secrets of Rætikon doesn’t follow the path of usual expansiveness of metroidvanias. Instead the game sticks to the bare minimum that would be sufficient for a compact, tight and intense adventure. The number of shards in the game’s world is the exact amount that you need to activate all the altars. Seven resulting fragments will be used to start the mechanism at the center of the labyrinth. The world will collapse and transform into an unbreakable circle leaving you dumbfounded. Initially developers planned to make a trilogy out of the concept, but the concept was scrapped. So it’s an open finale which you can interpret freely.

All in all… WHAT THE POINT?!?

Epic Battle Fantasy 4 is the latest game in the series of flash driven, turn based RPGs by Kupo Games. Its tiny development team, headed by Matt Roszak (Whom is credited for design, art, story and programming).
This is a game which should be praised, for the amount of effort put in. The result is a well realised and full RPG experience full of character and heart.
The game retains enough nostalgia from old school RPGs but still manages to feel fresh and new. If you’ve ever played any Final Fantasy title pre FFXI you’ll be familiar with this format.
It gives a master class in how a turn based system should play along with all the usual elements you’d expect, being able to cast magic, summon other creatures, use items and attack and it does this as well as any JRPG does. Its appeal for me was that this is a finely tuned machine of a game. Usually with turn-based RPGs you eventually become so powerful that nothing is really a challenge, except maybe some bosses but with a combination of a difficulty slider that makes a difference and some well paced scaling of foes, Epic Battle Fantasy 4 keeps you on your toes and makes you think a little bit.
I’ve always loved turn based RPGs when done well and RPGs in general, but turn based more so than Action. The reason being it brings an element of strategy with out reliance on quick time events [which i hate]. Epic Battle Fantasy 4 makes full use of the strategic element of the genre.
It does this through its use of equipment and skills. The majority of weapons have an elemental effect which will assist you in tearing through enemies that are weak to that element and each piece of equipment has a use, without the collect and discard method used in most games. Weapons can be swapped out in combat also but this will take up a valuable turn to do so. Not only that, you won’t be receiving that free ride through an area.
The skill and specials pool is a very well implemented way of customising your characters and their skillset. Skills can only be learned by that specific character and specials can be learned by all, but only one character may have it at any one time. Once again, brings some difficult decisions forward. You can also equip the characters with items that will provide passive bonuses or abilities within battle, another little customisable option for balancing your team some buffing characters and some casting abilities at dice-rolled intervals. Gone, in this game, is any idea of an “Ultimate” weapon. For me, that’s refreshing. Each weapon can be upgraded as you collect items from combat or treasure.
The characters are well written and interact nicely. The personalities feel genuine and It seems like they are inspired by or based in some way on friends of the developer. At times they do act like close friends who have a lot of fun in each other’s company. This game is no doubt a labour of love and the small team at Kupo Games must have poured a lot of time into this game. It is increasingly rare to see triple-A games give this creative warmth, probably due to the size of the teams but Steam lets this flourish.
There are a lot of small gestures and references that experienced RPG fans will appreciate showing a good dose of humour. From the snow covered Djinn from Golden Sun in Whitefall Town to the name of some of the achievements you can gain for using new items they flow through the whole game well.
Epic Battle Fantasy’s achievement/medal system is well implemented. Some are very difficult to obtain, some pretty much laughing in the face at how ridiculous achievement systems are. When combined with the bestiary gives you that feeling of collection that a lot of games look past. It makes you want to collect them, this is important.
A game by a turn-based RPG fan, for turn-based RPG fans, this will likely not appeal to those who only play Shooters or Wii Fit games but give it a chance and it may well draw you in.
To wrap up, Epic Battle Fantasy 4 is an absolutely fantastic game, made even more impressive by the huge contribution by Matt Roszak.
It is a game i’ve played over the Christmas holidays and will likely play again soon. With a Newgame+ option it is set up well for this. The art is soft and friendly, the enemies range from menacing to adorable. The mechanics are solid, the story is well written, the characters engaging and the experience is enjoyable.
It can also be bought for next to nothing because ‘Steam’.

Epic Battle Fantasy 4 is by far the best parody games I have ever played.  It pokes fun at a lot of classic console RPGs, but the real heat of the game is the way they combined what made so many other games so memorable.
The game is a simplistic true turn based RPG on the outside, but stesses a depth of strategy with a wide variety of equipment and monsters that have elemental strengths and weaknesses.  There isn't a single weapon or piece of armor in the game that is optimal for each and every battle (there are some that come close to defying this though).  You strenthen your weapons and armor through a basic crafting system that requires a hunt of scarce materials, but offers an item shop near the end of the game where you can buy the materials you might need at a hefty cash price.  There is even a achievement for poking...  Uh...  Nevermind.  The storyline and plot is pretty flimsy, but on the flip side, there isn't a need to grind to complete the game.
I strongly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys console RPGs of the 90s, even if they didn't grow up in the 90s.  There isn't any need to play the earlier iterations of the games to keep up with the jokes.

Greatest of all TD.  I love this game.  This is the gold standard.  If you like TD, this is where you should be.
Played the IOS version for abut 100+ hours, unlocking most abilities, beating most of the levels up to Unpoppable.  I'm buying this version now because the lag is too insane when playing the later difficulties.  This game might set a record for "most explosions at once" as it's not unusual to pop 100s (if not 1000s) of incoming bloons in one go, especially later with abilities, which makes my smartphone & gameboy glitch out.  It's a good game on the phone & java, but this game is too good for those platforms & fully desereves a space on your computer if you are serious about winning the later levels.  The lag spikes are pushing your hardware to its limits as "Bloons" pushes it's own pop-p-ping possibilities.  After all of this, I am willing to buy it on a 3rd device.  I *want* to win!
The RPG like aspects of alternate advancement paired with penalties make the classes brilliant, each specialty helping to solve levels in unique & creative ways.  The grind is fun and sensible, feeling naturally progressive with challenges.  What begins as a normal TD game turns into semi-real-time gaming with abilities needing to be qued up at the right times.   The further you go, the faster their cast time may be reduced, resulting in what essentially turns into an action / quick turn-based game of sorts.  For example, one must collect bananas as quickly as possible.  Like it?  Tap away!  Don't like it?  Level up the Bloon Shredder to do it automatically for you!  This is brilliant thinking for those of us who would like a choice in our play style.
The tactical placement of towers allows for lots of creative control.  There is no wrong way to build things if your monkeys are skilled.  Some levels require very unique strategies.  With radar, some units can be used for recon, allowing for submarines to destroy bloons from afar.  The Monkey Hut especially allows for grand strategy, as all buffed monkeys must be within it's range.  Having 3 huts specializing in say, ability timers, money, & power mean that 3 stations will be doing separate tasks and then have multiple monkeys (even of the same class) doing different jobs.  This is pertinent to aim, which completes the formula, allowing monkeys to target the first, last, closest, or strongest bloons, plus a few more specialty shots for other classes.  The combinations seem endless.
This is a TD game we're talking about here!  It sounds more like a TBRPG or war game.  Popping bloons may seem silly, but it's progressive casual play grows over time to seriously difficult insanity.
This is Bloons.  It's the most fun I've ever had playing a TD & one of my favorite games of all time.  I can go to it to relax.  I can go to it for a real challenge.  It's good ol' family gaming fun.  I can't recommend 'Bloons' enough.

This is like the Warcraft/Starcraft Funmaps where each player owns a base and has to send units to destroy the enemy base. The twist is that the minions/spells/buildings are actually cards from a deck you build and you need mana to summon them like in any Collectible Card Game.

There is a good playerbase. You can find a good match in 1-2 minutes.
The game gets weekly updates with balance fixes, new cards and even new gamemodes. The devs are really on top with the balance fixes and respond very quickly if anything is off.
The game is going to be free to play once it releases. The free to play model of the game is very fair. The free cards you start with are very strong. And if you log in every day and do your dailes you get a decent card collection pretty fast.
Within 70 hours i got to the second highest league without spending a single cent.
I really recommend trying this game. Especially if you like quick (each match is 3-5 minutes long) strategic games.

As far as possibilities goes, the game certainly answer well, you have tons of bricks, you can unlock things, you can use npc etc...
The possibilities seems really endless, as expected, and the character movement are very complete (scaling up trees etc) and cutely animated
On to the bad points:
No options. I mean, none of the important options that gamer use all the time, as if the developers thought they could tell us how to play our game?
- No windowed mode (though I looked around and apparently they intend to add one)
- No first person. In a game like this, first person is an amazing thing, it allow better immersion and better control of what the player do

For now I find the game extremely hard to play because the camera is never pointing correctly, even if I turn it. It would be ten time easier if the camera stuck to the back of your character, so you could actually see where you're going. -Destroy anything I bump into. This derivate from the camera problem, but being unable to see where I'm going, I keep bumping into things and destroying them. Earth 2160 is a somewhat unappreciated RTS with a number of nice features mixed in with a truckload of bland. It will provide some decent entertainment in the here and now but it will never be remembered for anything.
Earth 2160 sets you in the future, corporations fight for control over the Solar System's dwindling resources as a new discovery rocks the power structure and sets the game's events in motion. As you start out you get to play as either a generic male dominated corporation or the curiously female dominated Mars corporation. They both, not surprisingly, turn out to be evil rather quickly into the campaign and you eventually get to play as the "good" faction, a generic robot corporation that really has no personality and eventually, a menacing alien horde.
The storyline really isn't anything to write home about, it's all pretty standard stuff, good guys works for the bad corporation but eventually rebels against them. The dialog and cut scenes are of a particularly low quality that will often make you cringe at just how awful it really is.
Where Earth 2160 gains a points is in the gameplay however, each faction has a unique set of units and a unique way of base construction, the Mars women for example focusing on individual strong point structures that can have additional modules added on top for research, defense or unit production whereas the alien horde have no real base construction instead focusing entirely on cloning and evolving their units.
And as if this uniqueness to each faction wasn't enough each faction come with a complete research tree and the ability to customize each unit with various types of weapons, shields and engines allowing you to really make the faction your own. This customization does have it's flaws however, particularly where single-player is concerned as the AI does not adapt to your unit builds it is fairly trivial to make an exact counter to what the AI is building and just stomp them using rock-paper-scissors.
The slight RPG elements wherein you occasionally have a hero unit or two that can pick up items feels somewhat misplaced and rarely add anything beyond something to worry about as losing a hero often leads to a game over.
Earth 2160 is not a bad game and it's a game you can get a lot of fun out of especially if you skip past the cut scenes. it is however not a game that will stand the test of time and as such it's not really something I'd recommend anyone buys any longer.

At long last, after 15 years, this is the game I have been waiting for. Lord British once proves trhat he is still the kingof RPGs. This time, he and his talented team bring us this love letter to us Ultima fans clamoring for more.
It is a completely modular and innovative game; do you prefer single-player epic RPGs? You can play it as one. Do you prefer the MMORPG, with thousands of other players, using the best bits of Ultima Online, but not having to pay a monthly fee? You can do that, too. Familiar faces are here, the crafting system is better than any game I've ever seen, and combat has been re-invented for a refreshing new experience (unless you'd rather just stick with classic MMO-style fighting, which you can also do).
This will be a game which appeal to everyone, from PVP-obsessed guild folk, to solo storytelling and dungeon crawlers, to those who want to just decorate their house and sell homemade potions. Players can tackle a dragon with only their friends if they so wish.
Even in pre-alpha, this game is gorgeous and the music is top-notch. The player-made towns and events are a bonus plus, and I cannot emphasize enough how this game is worth every single penny I paid.

I'm not normally someone that like fighting games, but I can see when a game is polished and balanced. This is again something that is present here.
The online multiplayer is constant without lag, only problem, it is really for pro player, don't go online before clearing arcade mode or story mode at hard, the community is clearly professionnal even if the graphic style and the general atmosphere seems childish.
If you want to actually put hours in this game, but want to learn the basics to the most difficult moves each character possess, there is an extensive tutorial plus an extensive training ground.
all and all, for an independant release, it's unreal how much work and passion for fighting games went in this.

So, basically, you are rewarded for teasing a busty girl, running away with her intimate clothing and leaving her dead in the end. Just like real life. 10/10
But here's the real review.
Originating from a browser game, the fourth installment of Epic Battle Fantasy is on Steam, and for a very good reason. I haven't seen a lot of turn-based fighting RPGs like this one, but it really hits the spot.
It has excellent humor, and I often find myself laughing uncontrollably as I press space to advance through the chatting/cutscenes, seeing hilarious lines being announced by the characters, either in the arguing present everywhere in the game (because Natalie's boobs/Matt being a disgrace/Anna living in a tree/Lance having microcameras stored in his armor to "look" at Natalie's boobs), or in the battling of hundreds of enemies (because they are too weak/strong/disgusting/cool/tasty/scary, or because they resemble Pok*mon too much).
The characters are beautifully designed, and their personalities are constantly clashing with each other due to their differences, creating a constantly interesting atmosphere to get your mind off the battling and strategy if you're playing on Epic. There's things to like in all of them (and if you look at my profile you MIGHT find out which one is my favourite), and the soundtrack is amazing as well.
All in all, it sounds like I'm reviewing a GOTY title. And I can't say I don't love Epic Battle Fantasy the Fourth. Thank you Matt Roszak for making this game.

Some shard-obtaining methods and items that can be spawned in are clever references to pop culture such as the shard obtained upon riding a yacht, "I'm on a boat!" and the items 'Ceiling Cat,' 'Monorail Cat,' and of course, 'Nyan Cat.' I thought to get this game because I loved minecraft and Lego being sort of the irl, original minecraft, it could only be better right?
As far as possibilities goes, the game certainly answer well, you have tons of bricks, you can unlock things, you can use npc etc...
The possibilities seems really endless, as expected, and the character movement are very complete (scaling up trees etc) and cutely animated
On to the bad points:
No options. I mean, none of the important options that gamer use all the time, as if the developers thought they could tell us how to play our game?
- No windowed mode (though I looked around and apparently they intend to add one)
- No first person. In a game like this, first person is an amazing thing, it allow better immersion and better control of what the player do
- No "stick camera to character". If first person isn't introduced, this is the other option. For now I find the game extremely hard to play because the camera is never pointing correctly, even if I turn it. It would be ten time easier if the camera stuck to the back of your character, so you could actually see where you're going. A simple checkbox "camera follow" to switch between free camera mode and sticky, that would be amazing
-Destroy anything I bump into. This derivate from the camera problem, but being unable to see where I'm going, I keep bumping into things and destroying them. If I want to destroy stuff, I can hit it, why make it so everything is so frail and explode on touch? It's useful to pick up coins? Nope, sorry, to me that's too weak an argument.
-Having to find things THEN buy them before using them. That is (with the camera) the biggest flaw of a game based on building whatever we want.
Finding all the items scattered around is a nightmare, and then we also have to buy them... I think the dev' mixed two system here, which make a stupid result.
To make it better they should make it so we unlock object for free by finding them, or we buy them if we can't find them.
- Less cutscene when we find a character or an item? They get boring after the first dozen.
In the end, yes I do recommend the game, for its possibilities and because since it's early access, we can only hope the dev's will listen to us, and make improvement as needed.

I am quite addicted to the game. This is the kind of game with such a beautiful, immersive world that you find yourself thinking about it even after you’ve stopped playing. I remember laying in bed trying to fall asleep, thinking about where the last shard could be because I had seemed to overlook one somewhere in my exploration. The skills you get as a bird are easy enough to master and the true challenge lies in interacting with the environment and wildlife. The challenge is just hard enough to keep you grasping and trying again when you fail, but not so hard that you get discouraged. This is a fine line to walk and Secrets of Raetikon walks it well.
Here's a more long-winded version of my review:

Secrets Of Rætikon is a beautifully rendered game, it's all very colorful. It's hard to explain it gameplay wise. But you're a bird and you have to find artifacts that are scattered all over the world. You might say that it's a Metroidvania game but it's not. You won't gain any skills or abilities and all places are freely accessible. The goal is mainly to survive, while finding these artifacts. There are several types of 'enemies' and not all of them will attack you on the spot. Some of them will try to grab you or your artifact and others will just leave you alone because they're lower on the food chain. You can go faster by flapping your wings and you can even dive to increase your speed. The controls are unusual but work very good.
There's no map system in the game so you have to find everything by scouting the areas carefully. This can be hard, but fortunately the game is only a few hours (3-4) long so the world isn't
big.
I really enjoyed playing the game, but one thing that bothered me was the fact that you can't continue the game once you finish it. So make sure you do everything before dropping that last artifact, unless you want to play through it again, of course.
There's always room for improvement and Secrets Of Rætikon is no different. But despite its shortcomings I had a great time playing in this magical and very stylish world.
[Rating: 84/100]

Beautiful piece of art. Secrets of Rætikon can be both relaxing and frustrating (in a good way). The music is very unique and calming. One of my favourite aspects is that they nailed being a bird; the flight motion is perfect, the prey/predator interaction is amazing, and not being constrained by walking (in fact, you can't walk) is refreshing.
This game is well worth the money, even at regular price. Works best with a controller, as the flight is meant to be smooth and circular.

Starbound + Elite 3 + Noctis (whatever version was the last version) == No Man's Sky.  If you want more than that then you will be disappointed.  This, however, was exactly what I wanted it to be.
This is not a space battle sim, it's more like an intergalatic walking sim; you're dropped randomly into the universe on a planet and just told to fix your ship and then go see what's out there.  The planets are all fairly similiar out of necessity (otherwise only about 1/10000 start points would allow you to get off world), the plants and animals all do seem to run together, but dispite that it's still a wonderful game.
It's the only surface-to-sky space sim I've seen that actually works.  Many attempts at this have been made and all of them have failed in some vital way.  This succeeds.
The hatred seems to mostly come from early adopters, backers, and others whose expectations could never, ever have been met any ways.  Maybe that's the fault of the developer, I don't care at all about that.  It's fun, thoughtful, immersive, huge, stunning, lonely, all the things it should be.  It's also sort of over priced.
If you go into it knowing what you're getting you'll enjoy it.  If you go into it thinking you're getting the last game you'll ever want to play, you won't.
Get it on sale if you can, but certainly get it.

Alright, many people tend to become expert after a 'mere' 300 ours of gaming. I am approaching the 5,000 hours, so I have been around. And this is a game to pay to win, some people say? Not true. It's possible to buy cards that give advantages. But spending many hours online does get you free cards as well as a bonus. And when fighting a player, using cards does not give an overwhelming advantage. Attacking skills do, and building strong castles helps too.
Lastly, some commentator says starting players are being attacked for they are very weak. Yes, starting players are weak, but for an experienced player to attack a starting player, there is a severe penalty for the experienced player. So starting players are not going to be attacked by the stronger players.
So does paying help? A bit. But it can be countered by staying online a lot like I do. In fact to be online a lot has a greater effect than to pay your way. Paying players will receive some small advantages, but not enough to change the odds when they are stacked against them. Please, if you want to give your opinion, stay with the game long enough to give a good advice.

There are so many things to say here. I've been a backer since the Kickstarter, and before when it was mysteriously named "Ultimate RPG."
Describing the broad spectrum of capabilities that I prefer would be commonplace, however I would like to express how deeply satisfied I am with how SotA (Shroud of the Avatar) has become so far in this pre-alpha release 12. Patienty awaiting the next release 2 days away.
Community:
One thing that stands out over all the things anyone could possibly say about this game is that the community that comes with it is simply AMAZING. So many helpful souls combined in one place. Don't get me wrong, there are still PKs out there :P. But everyone is always bringing up great ideas and squashing some, welcoming newcommers, starting events, answering questions, etc.
Game Experience:
Take all the basic skills you gained from playing all those years of UO and bottle them up, look inside and what do you see? Not SotA. This game's skill system is 'currently' level and skill-tree based, along with card combat and two types of draw/deck systems. The combat feels very deliberate, as if every hit is meant to be the way you thought it would isntead of just button mashing. PvP is intense, the possibility of there being hardcore pvp/full loot as an option is something i hope is going to make it's way into the game.
SotA isn't even close to being done yet and they have nearly perfected the combat system to work in such a smooth and synergetic way, it feels great. I have actually been against the card combat idea before, but it the skill system ties very nicely into a unique combat/armor/weapon/skill relationship/synergy.
My sub-par laptop can run this game with 2-20 fps.
Great game and alpha development experience thus far! Being a part of this game's development, growing with the game, is another experience entirely that humbles me to think of being given the opportunity. Support this game! :)

So many fond memories of Ultima online I had to support this game from the get go. Don't be confused, this isn't UO 2.0, this is something entirely different but along the same vein. The developers have put their heart and soul into this game and really are listening to the player base. This game will become a great success because of the staff behind it's creation and the amazing community that has joined them.

I didn't think there would ever be a game that might outdo Ultima Online, but from what I've played so far, this is doing a really, really good job of it.
A lot of the great things from the single player Ultima games are here (NPC conversation, quests that aren't WoW-style). An ingame journal replaces the typical quest log, and it's done in a way that makes you want to read the backstory. No "go kill 10 murlocs" garbage here.
Combat isn't yet balanced, and isn't a matter of combat mode on/off, and isn't like your usual MMO combat where you have your abilities and use what you want - there is a knack to using it that I haven't worked out yet. It's deck-based combat, but there are ways to "lock" abilities in your bar.
Housing is in. In UO, you could purchase a house outside of town, set up a vendor, put chests in it, and that's about it. Here, you purchase a house within towns, you can have group ownership or you can rent rooms to people. I've seen chess sets, baths with seats, grandstands, theatre stages and probably more I can't remember.
Crafting works like this: each "skill" has a specific crafting table. You have your ingredients, go to the table, put each item on the table, and if there's a recipe for it, you now have that item, and the recipe is in your book. Each subsequent time you craft it, you just go to your book and make it automatically. You can also find or buy or trade recipes throughout the game so you never need to guess or wiki them if you don't want to. Skills for crafting aren't in yet, so this might be a little more restricted later, I don't know.
The community is what really makes the game. While you can play solo, this game has a lot more to do with getting and giving help to and from other people than it is about completing quests and levelling up. I really don't know how they did it.

Let me start off by saying: this game is not for everyone.
However, that being said, I am thoroughly enjoying this game as of right now.  I picked it up for $2 and I have no regrets.  I do not usually play games like this, so I was a little bit hesitant as to whether or not I would enjoy it, but I can say with absolute certaintity that this game is fun for the right audience.
It plays like an RTS, you have 4 elemental godlike giants that control and shape the planet so that the humans can develop there villages.  You need to manage resources and make sure that the villages do not get too greedy otherwise wars will break out (these wars usually don't take too long anyways).  Each giant has the ability to create it's own biome, as well as their own resources.  It's the little things that matter, but I enjoyed that even though you would use the same giant to create plants or animals, it would spawn different plants or animals depending on what biome you are using (e.g. with the same giant you could place chickens in the forest biome and kangaroo rats in the desert biome).
As an incentive to keep playing, there is a levelling up system.  The more you level up the more resources you unlock in terms of plants and animals, which is a good way to keep the player motivated.  One thing that I disagreed with is that you also have to level up to unlock different play times; for example, you start out with 30 minute trials and once you reach level 2 you're allowed to use 60 minute games, etc.  I would have preferred if you could unlock every game time from the beginning.  However, Freeplay mode is unlocked at the beginning, which is a nice addition.  In Freeplay you don't have to worry about helping the humans build a certain amount of projects in the allotted time period, but you also don't level up or unlock anything in Freeplay.
TL;DR if you're looking for a fun, godlike RTS game to pass the time with then this is a great game to pick up, especially if it is on sale.  If you're looking for an RTS with a little bit more depth to it, you may want to pass on this one.
8/10

Story:
There is a theme, but not really a story, which is fine for this game. You are the planet, and you control four sentient giants that place resources to develop villages and unlock new resources. Presumably after your giants fall asleep, the world keep developing and at some point annihilate each other through thermonuclear war, which is why you wake up to a wasteland each time.
Gameplay:
I think Reus' mechanics stand out as the reason why I would come back to this game. There is a race against time to get as much prosperity as you can, but grow a village too fast and it will get greedy. On top of that, random developments means there is never one cookie cutter "best" option, and the ambassador system gives you the hard choice of picking which upgrades you want (and which ones you forsake).
Having said that, I dislike the progression system, where you have to get achievements to unlock higher level resources. Playing two hours to unlock one achievement so you can use the resource that it unlocks to play another two hours to unlock another achievement is not fun. It is possible to get all of the achievements with a minimal number of well-planned playthroughs, but a casual player will not accomplish this.
UI/Controls:
The controls work fine, but the camera can be a pain to manage at times, and it would be a lot better if there was an option to queue up commands. One pain point for me is that the game doesn't tell me which high level natural resources I have access to and what they do until I actually transmute into them, so I often found myself alt-tabbing between the game and the online wiki (which has quite a few errors) when planning what to build.
Graphics/Audio:
Not much to say here. There's some pleasant background music to listen to as you play, and the animal sprites can be fun to watch if you zoom in enough.
Replayability:
I have mixed feelings on this. On the one hand, the game mechanics around developments means that each playthrough will be different, and you can make it even more different if you choose different ambassador setups. Also, the one-hour challenges that appear after you unlock all of the achievements are a reason to keep at the game. However, after playing through the 2-hour era a couple of times, I felt that the minor variations in each playthrough were not enough of an interesting new experience to keep me playing.
Summary:
I would cautiously recommend this game to people who like god games. People who like optimization in games will enjoy the mechanics of this game, but otherwise the slow progression system will likely cause players to burn out.

A unique, well-thought-out RPG featuring a classic battle systesm. With 4 difficulty options that can be swapped at any time, the game has appeal to all fans of the genre, whether you're a hardcore power leveler or just rushing through the mandatory battles, the combat is simple and with many skills to level at your command, battles become more reliant on your own decisions. The dialog both in combat and in the field is witty and surprisingly well written, though some dialogues can be misplaced if missed in an earlier fight. The art in the game is fantastic - the character and enemy models are well-drawn and all have a distinct EBF artstyle. Each piece of equipment modifies the character models enabling the player to decide what their character stats will be and cool or cute they look. The story mode is fairly lengthy, taking anywhere from 15-25 hours on a normal difficulty run depending on completion and grind and features several optional challenges, with massive replayability including New Game + and Battle Island. Last but not least the music, by HalcyonicFalconX is not only great, but each piece fits amazingly with the nature of the battle or field, making the entire RPG experience phenomenal.

A beautiful, gorgeous exploration game. You fly around as a little bird in a world full of dangers: the ferocious lynx, charging hawks, buzzards that will snatch you up and thrust you into deadly thistles. And the meat and potatoes of the game is - exploring. Pulling aside boulders to find out what is behind, collecting mysterious glowing artifacts, and finding out how to avoid or destroy your enemies. Because you don't really have an 'attack' per se, you have to use more creative options to bypass foes. You can utilize thermals (air currents) to pick up incredible speed, suddenly dive mid-air to escape the talons of a foe, or out-wit your opponent and carry him to his doom beneath a rolling rock. Everything in the game reeks of mystery and intrigue, not to mention being /beautifully/ designed in fascinating designs of geometrical components.
Best things in the game: interesting twist on combat, visuals, absorbing mini-puzzles (none very difficult so far), visuals, wonderful sense of atmosphere and believable ecology, great motivation for exploring, and -- did I mention visuals?
Drawbacks: Some of the pursuits can get frustrating (e.g. when a 'magpie' bird steals something important you have to chase it around, the fact that it seems to be faster than you can get annoying). One of the resource/collectible tracks seems very disappointing (I won't explain - it's kind of a spoiler). I'm struggling to find negative things to say!

I tried The Division out in free weekend; I only got it because my friends like it. I think they might be dazzled by playing their first cover shooter. I'm not.
You would expect Tom Clancy's name to mean a realistic, tactical shooter. And the game plays the part. We have muted colors. Characters pull their weapons out of holsters, not hyperspace. Weapon customization and character abilities are bland - no force fields, no biotic charge. It's a tactical cover-based shooter.
Except that only applies to you. Even low level enemies take a whole assault rifle magazine - or two - to go down. Uncommon enemies have ungodly amounts of health and if they ever figure out to charge right at you, you're in trouble. Look at the reviews, everybody complains about the bullet sponges. The people defending it point out that The Division is part RPG.
You need to grind good enough weapons to do enough damage to enemies. Which means I hardly ever found a balanced encounter - either we were getting rushed by bullet sponges or there was a pile of dead enemies right by the door where they came in. This is made worse by the fact that level - normally a good measure of difficulty in RPGs - doesn't matter as much as gear.
The Division doesn't even do RPG that well. I think they could have been onto something, with instead of tank-heal-damage roles you could have suppression-heal-damage roles. In theory, one player could equip a machine gun with tons of bullets and spray them at enemies to keep them in cover while you flank around. Or one person suppresses the big bad guy while the rest of us fight the little ones. In practice, it's hard to trigger the "suppressed" effect, and hard to keep it up because you're outnumbered by bullet sponges. Maybe tank-heal-damage can work, but then I might as well play Overwatch or an actual RPG.
The story is typical Tom Clancy - plausible sci-fi melodrama, boring characters. I can't even remember their names, but half of them are really annoying - e.g. chakra guy.
I do really like the Cleaners faction. They're trying to do the same thing you are - stop the plague, save the world! Except they think they can accomplish it by burning everything and everyone. Kinda cool that half the mooks you're shooting have the same motivation your character does.
If you're ready to give up cool character abilities, fantastic enemy diversity, and colors for a realistic shooter, be disappointed by the bullet sponges. To enjoy the game, I had to ignore the dissonance between the atmosphere and the gameplay, to remember that I'm playing an RPG. With my friends. I would never play this game on my own.

This review comes from 11 hours of single player experience, base game bought at 70% discount:
I first tried the open beta on uplay on 2016, it barely kept me interested for 45 mins, graphics were monstrously washed and i just felt like passenger on another crashed hype train.
This time instead of trying the free weekend i just took a dive because of the offer, to play with a friend who doesnt play fps anymore. I'm glad i took the leap of faith. My friend hasn't joined yet so i went alone not even sharing an emote with other players, to play at my pace and trying to get immersed. I'm happy to report this is probably one of the best graphical engine i have experienced and a strange but overall succesful mix of genres.
-GRAPHICS: There is no texture quality slider, with fat RAM and VRAM you will only see high definition everywhere without any pops, lighting is amazing and fidelity is relaxing with some of the best post process filters like supersampling temporal AA, the only options i didn't max out are nvidia PCSS shadows, and HBAO+, both are too heavy on my RX 580, the first isn't noticeable and the second is too aggressive, maybe the HBAO+ would enhance contrast on screens with TN panels. I play on a 144Hz VA and without those custom nvidia options i stay 100 fps on full HD, otherwise i lose around 20-25 fps with both on, and again regular ambient occlusion on ultra is a cheap performance hit but a game changer on quality.
The sharpen filter is very well tuned and selective, and has a slider but even close to the max wont tire your sight.
The world is very dense and filled with objects or debris, weather effects or fog, the misc objects are very detailed and well placed. The only thing i regret is how fast the time of day is, you can see shadows changing at unnatural speed which is a shame because every time of the day looks great. Being an open world plus multiplayer with perfect detail streaming this would be a solid 10/10.
-SOUND: Won't describe much here but the quality and variety of sounds feels great, placement is spot on, i have an asus xonar dx with 2.0 monitors and i can clearly identify direction without confusion.
-CONTROLS: I had no issues here, navigation is solid and responsive, had 1 or 2 frustrating deaths when the character refused to go beyond a damn step that was too low for climbing and too high for running over, but gladly those were isolated events, the cover system feels nice specially the cover to cover holding space, the character will do the movement combinations to minimize exposure like jumping over or sliding to reach faster, so you can focus other things, it really helps on critical situations.
-GAMEPLAY: Again i have only did singleplayer so far, the MMO ingredients worked better than i thought, since you still have your FPS aim and strat/tact you like, so any kind of fps skill or style you bring you exploit it somehow. For example you dont have range limits other than the weapon spread or range, had no problems stretching the limits with a sniper rifle. The shoot from cover (over your head just exposing the weapon) felt nice and was fun having lucky headshots once in a while, but mostly a great way to finish almost dead mobs. Working your gear is entertaining, i only felt annoyed when you have an item of higher level than your character, wish they tried another way instead of just preventing use.
-STORY: So far at 6% progression and enjoying my time, no hurries and since you can mix progression with messing around you can play without feeling linearity. Lip sync is slightly rigid and a little distracting on cutscenes but no issues on regular gameplay. So far good.
