I've waited a long time to give a review. I knew of this game fom the first major announcment years ago, Pre-Ordered It and was caught up in the hype along with everybody else. And in hindsight those expectations we all set were ridiculous. But we do have high expectations for games nowadays, we've had such great games over the past decade If we try and compare it to the 90's and early 2000's, at least in terms of size/scale, depth of stories and graphics quality. The rate of growth has been incredibly fast, and with stuff like VR a complete possibility now which we dreamed of as kids, it seems like anything should be possible...
And this is where No Man's Sky comes in. I know that I have always wanted a game like this, planet and space exploration, traveling farther than anyone else, seeing what no one else has ever seen before, surviving in unknown hostile environments, finding aliens and lost technology, dinosaurs and sky sharks, space wars between factions... The list could go on. We thought we finally had the ultimate game, we all over-hyped each other thinking we might be able find the "Space Whale" in the never-ending black abyss of this procedurally generated universe.
Right before the game finally launched, amidst all the videos and game predictions/possibilities, I heard something inspiring. Someone said that we are all going to end up hating this game because the hype we built up for it. That it could never live up to the expectations we have. And the best way to calm down the expectations for this game and all games that get over-hyped before release. Is to imagine the game to have come out 10 years ago or even 20. What would people have thought of the game then... 10 years ago this Game would have been in to the top 5 for sure. But 20 years ago, when one of the best games that everyone knew and talked about was let's say Super Mario 64. If we could've had No Man's Sky launch back then, It would've been the best thing ever.
So I put myself in this mindset. Ignored what everyone else was saying about it, good or bad. I calmed down, and waited for the game to release. And of course downloaded it within seconds of it finally coming out. I had days scheduled off work and everything, I was ready to devote as much time as I could to this new universe. NMS was and still is a huge revolution for the game industry in my opinion. I like to think of it as the blueprint or "foundation" to what could be... I believe that with time this game has the opportunity to become what we all wanted it to be, it has gotten better and will get better, either from the dev's or the modding community. Well, let's start with the good and the bad:
The Good:
The game is fun.  It's bright, colorful and charming.  The puzzles aren't too hard, but they're not too easy, either -- they require a bit of brain-stretching.
The dictionary is every bit as extensive as reviews have indicated (and contains quite a few words that I'd never heard before); the dictionary and relatively-challenging puzzles, however, are part of the next section...
The Bad:
The puzzles, in many cases, are simplistic.  Very rarely have I been truly 'stumped' by this game; anyone who does crosswords regularly, or writes in any professional capacity, will quickly solve any given challenge.
In addition. the available -valid- dictionary options for solving any given puzzle are very limited -- in several puzzles, I've created an item that seems quite logical (or at least plausible), only to find that the puzzle won't accept it.
The Conclusion:
This game is wonderful fun for messing about -- creating giant ten-foot-tall Cthulus wearing clown wigs or making cannibalistic deck chairs.  It'll be especially enjoyable for children and younger teens, who are still young enough that the solution might not be obvious.
It's even fun for a 33-year-old (like me), but only in the way that 'Goat Simulator' is fun: it's good for a laugh, but it's not a particularly challenging game.
Do I recommend it? Yes -- as I said, it's charming and fun, and occasionally hilarious.  Show it to your kids -- they'll have a blast, increase their vocabulary, and may even learn to type while they're at it.

Rating 7/10
Overview: FPS with the ability to go into slow-mo
The Good
+ The game features 2 main characters you can play as. You first have to complete the game as 'point man'. This character allows you to slow down time while you blast away your enemies. The other character is Paxton Fettel who has the ability to possess almost any enemy in the game.
+ A cover based system in a first person shooter never seems to work out, yet this game handles the feature nicely. With a single press of a button  you can hide behind cover and easily pop out and shoot your enemies.
+ By completing challenges you acquire experience which is then used to level up your character. Challenges include killing a certain amount of enemies with a weapon, getting headshots, staying in slow-mo for a certain amount of time etc. It's a nice addition and it helps you change up your play style so you're not constantly relying on the same tricks over and over again.
+ I feel the AI has improved (yet still lacking to the first FEAR), enemies flank, hide, take cover and feel like a genuine threat when facing them.
+Variety of different weapons and grenades
+The shooting mechanics feel good, going into slow-mo and shooting enemies is always fun. The game also introduces sections where you ride a mech to change up the gameplay.
The Average:
On a technical level the graphics are decent. Textures are solid, lighting and shadows look decent however artistically the game feels bland and uninspired. Poor color usage and levels that feel and look the same despite being in different environments doesn't help either.
The story is decent but it really is starting to feel convoluted at this point.
Game will provide around 5-7 hours for one playthrough. Multiplayer and playing through the campaign as the second character can extend playtime for a bit.
The game features some multiplayer modes that can be played in single player and extend your game time. The problem is that multiplayer is dead which is sad given that some of these modes looks really fun to play.
The Bad
- multiplayer is dead which also means getting certain achievements is now impossible
- no local co-op
Conclusion
The more FEAR games we get the farther we move away from what made the original so great. This game lacks even less horror elements and tactical shooting from the previous entries and is essentially a straight up first person shooter with the slow-mo ability. I don't consider this a bad game but compared to the last 2 entries it feels like it took 2 steps back and 1 step forward.

If you played and loved Gaunlet on GameCube, do not expect the same type of game here. This game is much more challenging and expect failure at first on higher difficulties.  This game is designed with team coordination in mind.  At Normal or Easy difficulties, the game is easy once you get the hang of it.  But at Hard and Unfair, it becomes very challenging to play solo or with an uncoordinated team members since you have limited lives.  This game is best played with friends or other people.  Though it is doable even on Unfair difficulty, I would not recommend playing this game solo.
There seems to be some imbalance amongst the classes.  Archer and Wizard are arguable the most reliable classes on Hard or Unfair difficulty due to their ability to kite.  Valkyrie would be a close third with his overpowered spammable lance thrust and shield block.  And Warrior is definitely the runt of the liter due to damage and survivability issues.
Warrior offers the least overall damage and the most difficulty avoiding damage while in combat.  His weak attack is appalling and his strong attack is comparable to the Valkyrie's while being slower and having a smaller area of effect.  The only redeemable quality about the Warrior is he unlocks a low-hp regeneration perk and he has the simplest control design.
Wizard has the most complex kit design requiring 2 button combinations between 3 buttons to determine your spell cast.  (XX, XY, XA, YY, YX, YA, AA, AX, AY).  They offer a lot of utility, have comparable sustained damage and a decent kit to kite once you get used to switching spells on the fly, and unlock a shield that blocks damage after 16-20 seconds of being untouched.  Wizard has essentially no burst but plenty of ways to dish out damage over time.
Archer is in my opinion the easiest to use with high burst damage from his bombs, low sustained damage, and a nice roll dodge; just imagine playing a MMO and mobbing monsters.
Valkyrie like I mentioned earlier has a ridiculously power strong attack which offers high amounts of sustained damage; the tradeoff is he's vulnerable to getting hit if he just spams the attack.  The Valkyrie unlocks a powerful perk which makes him very durable at low health.
The leveling and gold system definitely seems a bit bland.  You can buy relics which are temporary perks you can use with potions and new gear but the gear is purely aesthetic.  I do find it interesting that you "level up" by unlocking achievements (eg. killing 10,000 monsters, breaking 500 props, etc) which will give you various benefits.  It seems kind of silly that you unlock some perks for dying.  Some perks have 3 tiers, Bronze Silver and Gold.  Each is just a slight upgrade over the previous perk.  The time it takes max out all the perks is at least 30 hours on a single class.
I would estimate the average playtime will be around 20-40 hours for a person who enjoys this game.  After 40 hours of personal gametime, I would say the game is definitely better played with friends.  Though public rooms are available, the experience is nowhere as fun.  My biggest concern is that the game will lose replayability once you become better at it and master every level on Unfair difficulty since there is a limited amount of actual content (you can speed run through everything on Easy in probably 2 to 4 hours).
Overall, I would give this game a 7 out of 10.  I would say the game's good, but not great, and very fun while chatting with friends over voip.

PLEASE READ IN ITS ENTIRETY, THIS REVIEW IS LENGTHY BUT CONCISE:
This is a really nice fighting game. Despite my meager sum of hours at this point (7.4) and my limited experience with fighting games in general, this game really helped me learn the general meta of fighting games through its insanely well put together tutorial. Any beginner should really pick this as their first fighting game if they can, and if they've been having trouble getting into fighting games, this game should put them right in there. The only catch is that if you want to get into it, you HAVE to play the tutorial. That said, my assumption is that this game has enough depth for any experienced player to hop right in and enjoy (of course utilizing the tutorial and training mode to get comfortable with each character).
In terms of the playability, I am pleased. It has liquid smooth gameplay (as far as I'm concerned) and runs at a rock solid 60 on my Lenovo ThinkPad Yoga. I personally play with the keyboard, since my options involve a 360 controller and said keyboard (and trust me, the controller doesn't do this game any favors - the keyboard is DEFINITELY the better choice). That being said, if you don't have a fight stick, don't feel like you can't play this game and if you have a controller, don't use it. One character I've run into that gives me issue with not having a fight stick is Cerebella, because one of her blockbusters involves a 360 motion, and that is difficult to replicate with wasd. Another character that gave me trouble was Peacock, because one of her blockbusters involved cancelling a grab into said blockbuster, and I was having trouble because my keyboard is bluetooth, and the latency is too slow (so basically this one is negligible, since I did manage to pull off the blockbuster in the end).
RECOMMENDED KEYBOARD BINDINGS:
W-UP
S-DOWN
A-LEFT
D-RIGHT
J-LK
K-MK
L-HK
U-LP
I-MP
O-HP
SPACE-Pause
ENTER-Select
If desired (for team play):
;-Macro 1
P-Macro 2
Leave all other commands unbound.
The character cast is pretty small, two of which (Squigly and Big Band) I do not have, so that leaves me with 8 playable characters: Double, Filia, Ms. Fortune, Peacock, Cerebella, Valentine, Parasoul and Painwheel. However, each character comes with an amount of depth that shows each of them has been crafted with utmost care. Unfortunately, the amount of play time I have does not allow me to discuss the balancing of each of the characters, so I'll leave that to someone with more time in the game.
This game is for one to two players. The gameplay is pretty good, and this I CAN talk about in terms of balance, because there are three ways to play, and each player doesn't necessarily need to choose the same one. The three ways are: one character, two characters and three characters. To balance it out, the damage and health of each character is divided by the amount of characters on a team. When a player has more than one character, the player can use assists, even during blockbusters, and you can also switch between characters, which CAN deal damage.
I have not used the ranked internet play, though I hear the netcode is solid. I HAVE done two person local play, and this works very well, as I was using my keyboard and the other person was using my controller.
Some extra good points involve the simplest key binding process I have ever seen in a fighting game and also a phenomenal jazzy soundtrack that I bought and consequently listen to in order to relax or do work.
In terms of the poor points in this game - I personally can only think of one, and that's the fact that I'm not proficient enough with fighting games to find any flaws.
Hope this review was helpful,

Shroud of the Avatar is a somewhat reimagining of the Classic MMO Ultima Online, a game of which I played for the majority of my life, SOTA feels oldschool and doesn't try to adhere to modern preconceptions, it's not affraid to mix things up and give modern gamers a taste of the good ole' days and I admire the developers for doing so.
I backed the project because I was loyal to Richard Garriott, the man whom started my love for MMOs and the medieval era. That being said, sadly, for the following reasons, I cannot recommend this game;
-The combat is boring, a simple 1 through 0 button press without having to think.
-The lore of the game feels off, having defined plots of land for player housing and rather crazy house designs, it just doesn't feel right in my opinion.
-The game is visually dated, it would be nice in 2007, but for 2014, I expect a higher standard. It feels and looks like a kickstarter game, a budget attempt to recreate something lost to time.
-The controls feel off, a bit clumbsy, and again, dated.
-The animations of characters and monsters are dull and lifeless, monsters don't/hardly react to being hit.
-The UI works, but could be better, I'm a fan of simplism and choice; having a cluttered screen is a huge pet peeve, I hoped it would follow in UO's footsteps in that regard.
-The graphics are too on the cartoony side for my taste.
Many of these reasons are me being picky, people may be able to overlook these issues or not find them one at all, but I expected so much more. I wanted a 3D Ultima Online and while I acknowledge this isn't and wasn't ever supposed to be that, it's what I had in my mind. The feel of oldschool is there, but it's just not enough, I blame Kickstarter for this because the developers had to create rewards for backing the project and thus ruined the lore of the game, segregating player housing, making the world feel patchy and unrealistic. Not even I, who is one of the biggest Garriott fans can play or recommend SOTA, to those whom play and enjoy it, I salute you, but this game is just not for me or those seeking the next best thing Garriott put his hands on. It'll be gone in a few years and forgotton.

Firstly, this is unlike any early access game I've played. It's actually playable!
The basic premise behind this game is the following: you're a bird. You're looking for singing rocks that, when you do find one, everything (read: EVERYTHING) wants to mess you up.
That is, as far as I can tell, the point of the game. But the funny thing is, this unexplained goal is something I
to achieve when playing. Everything about this game makes me want to play, even when I don't know why.
The very well done flying mechanics feel intuitive and, even on the keyboard, I found myself soaring around relatively quickly.
The entire atmosphere and art style feel like a children's book mixed with cave paintings mixed with origami. If that doesn't sound awesome, then stop reading right now.
The music (note: I am a composer, so my music opinion is much more in depth) is a happier sounding minimalism. Basically expect lots of repetition, constant looping ostinatos and continuous percussion that tend to stick out of the mix. Initially, I was put off by the music to be honest. Minimalism isn't really my thing and hearing the same 4 second melody over and over and over? Well, I was beginning to consider switching off the sound after a while...
But it gradually grew on me, especially when I got further into the world. It starts to really come into its own when you meet the more interesting animals. So, I'm passing the music, but would much prefer something more than what's currently available.
Speaking of audio, I did notice repetitive sound effects, so I'm hoping the creators decide to invest in more than the handful of rock cracking sounds they have! I also dislike the wind sound that accompanies a dash. That would work a lot better as a speed activation, rather than a button activated sound effect.
So, the
version:
Beautiful artstyle
Wonderful atmosphere
Very polished controls and engine
World is intriguing
Music can get repetitive and dull over time. Did grow on me though.
Sound effects are obviously few and far between/need to be changed in places
Now, the big question is:
I would definitely say yes. There's a decent amount to go with already, and it's still early access. If the creators keep it updated and improve upon it, then the answer will be:
OH GOD YES!

As you can see, I recommend this game, but it comes with a few caveats.
If you're wanting an experience similar to the classic Gauntlet games, or even like the newer 3D versions like Dark Legacy, this is probably not the game you're looking for. You want to go look at Hammerwatch instead. Trust me.
That's not to say this is a bad game, but it has a lot of short comings, and many gameplay elements of Gauntlet have been dropped, some new ones added, and it just doesn't really feel like the Gauntlet I grew up with. Which to be fair, is one of my favorite games of all time. Both the classic versions and the 3D ones.
Dungeon floors aren't randomized, and while I know this wasn't a feature in the other games in this series, in the current game market this just feels lazy. I'm already getting sick of running the same (very few) levels over and over with the only change being which character I play as. Secrets and the like are also mysteriously lacking.
We might as well talk about those characters, actually. Each one plays differently, and not just in regard to how they attack or what skills they use. They fundamentally control different from each other. The Wizard, for instance, mixes two elements together to create one of a number of spells. The Elf plays similar to a twin stick shooter character, akin to Smash TV or Beat Hazard. The Warrior and Valkyrie are kind of similar, but the Valkyrie has the ability to tank, and defend the party with her shield.
She's also very overpowered compared to the other characters (in my opinion at least) once you learn to use her effectively. A lot of people don't even play her as a tank, and instead spear rush nonstop, which does a lot of damage very quickly. This makes it easy to lead a game in points from having a really high kill score compared to the other players. This is especially true if they haven't learned how to use their character yet.
Each character also has a set of challenges that come with them, which unlock little passive buffs when you complete them. Kill 2000 mummies, get +10% damage against them. Things like this. Progress is not shared across characters, so if you have been mainly playing as one class, then join a multiplayer game where that class is already taken, you'll be missing all the unlocked bonuses for that character, as well as any relics they have bought.
There are a couple minor bugs and AI quirks (enemies can't walk under bridges that are on a higher level than them?), but nothing that is a huge issue. I've only had one instance of the game bugging out and putting me in a state where I could not progress because of a gate not opening as it should have.
It's a co-op game, but not really. What I mean is that it is in your best interest (even if it's not the parties best interest) to hog everything for yourself, let other people die so you can steal the gold they drop, and generally act like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to people you don't know.  While I really don't have a problem with the game allowing that, it has never been how I played Gauntlet with my friends. You always do a lot better if you work as a damn team, even if your score won't be as high from being selfish.
Joining online games is a real chore, and it usually takes me upwards of ten attempts before it finally joins a game without either giving me a timeout error or saying the game is already full.
There's no way to communicate with the other players, outside of four nearly useless emotes that are mapped to the D-pad.  Maybe this was the intent, but when I can just shift+tab to talk to the people via Steam's built in chat, this just feels like an oversight and creates an extra step (and one that takes me out of the game) to offer advice. The biggest problem with not being able to communicate, to me at least, is that it is really bothersome to try to figure out which level everyone wants to do when starting a multiplayer game.
Again, this isn't a bad game, but if you really want something like Gauntlet, go pick up Hammerwatch instead. Otherwise, I'd really wait for a sale for this one.

Arrowhead has adopted the franchise from Midway Games and has decided to reboot it.
Not re-iterate the story, not make a sequel, but to reboot it. In order to do so, they decided to go back to the original arcade games from the 1980's and take a few pointer tips for their inspiration of level design.
However, instead of endless dungeons that the originals produced, this game focuses on more of a linear storyline.
Three worlds - One Boss per world
Four levels each -Three stages per level (Explore, Race, Challenge Arena)
Four difficulties - Easy, Normal, Hard, Unfair
Four characters to select, five with DLC - Warrior, Knight, Wizard, Elf, & Necromancer
*Online and Local Co-op with up to three other players!
Different Masteries per character to unlock
Gone are the days of treasure chests and a variety of potions to unleash upon the hordes.
Nowadays we are prone to smashing pots and boxes for gold. You do collect a potion throughout the entire game, you use these to display your special ability in combat. Special abilties can be bought at the in-game store and you can have up to two at once.
Different skins for your weapon and character are buyable as well, but they are just for looks.
Many complain this game is bland, but it is really just inspired by the "bland-ness" of 1980's retro arcade games. The look and feel is all intentional. If you enjoy that nostalgia, then the price is worth it.
It is a retro rpg - hack and slash - dungeon crawler.
You either love it or you shame it.

No Man’s Sky, at it’s core, just wants you to walk around it’s planets, say “oooh” and head off. It wants to simulate the feeling of finding something unknown, something mysterious and understanding it a tiny bit. It wants to let you jump into a sci-fi novel’s cover and not come back.
What it doesn’t want you to do is become the most badass space-hulk, flying around in order to turn into “ULTIMATE MAN: MAN OF ULTIMATE POWER”. Instead, No Man’s Sky’s curve is so gentle, so obviously pushing you in the direction of “existing slightly better than you did before” instead of “upgrading until you can’t upgrade no-more, congratulations you rule over man, sky, and weird little crab creatures, you have won the game.”
I mean, sure, you can try doing that, and it is possible to get a Very Good Ship™, but this is not the way No Mans Sky wants you to play, despite the triple-A nature of the marketing.
No Man’s Sky, just wants you to walk.

F.E.A.R. 3 is a linear shooter that could be summerized as a bunch of arena like rooms filled with enemies and bound by empty corridors. Scripting is minimal, story is disjuncted, but the environments are well made and interesting to wander through. The game isn't an horror game, but it is spooky in places. The real meat of the experience is combat: great enemy AI, sections with mechas you can control, conventional but efficient weaponry, and most of all a great coop campaign. With the addition of a new playable character that has rather original ways to kill or assist the first player, this coop mode is more than just singleplayer campaign with two players. As both characters complete each other or compete for the highest score, one is more like a grunt shooting in traditional fashion his way through the enemies while the second is more like a tactician able to seize control of an enemy of his choice and thus creating a mess in enemies' ranks, but also able to single enemies out for the first player to kill swiftly. There are other tricks you can use in tandem, but possessing enemies of various kinds never gets old.
All in all this coop mode makes an otherwise conventional game extremely worthwhile for coop afficionados. Be advised that the game is rather short though (5-6 hours long).

I rate the game F.E.A.R. 3 4/5. Good.
This is a fairly impressive FPS game which is designed to be played either as a single player game or entirely as a co-operative game. The plot supports the co-op mode very, very well. While it has some detractors, there is far more to like about this action game than to dislike if you don't mind incredibly violent, occasionally creepy, generally dark games which focus on the family histories of psychotic telepaths.
+Wraps up the previous two FEAR games (and the add-ons for each) very, very well with nearly no loose ends while still leaving the way open for yet another sequel if anyone cares to bother to create one without feeling like it has a cliff-hanger ending.
+While generally this is not a very creepy game (just bloody and horrific) the game does have its moments (particularly picking your way through the haunted houses in the suburbia section of the game).
+The sound and the use of the sound, from the ambient sounds of creaking wood or running feet in another room to the loud gunshots are almost uniformly outstanding. Only the grenades and explosions seemed a little muffled.
+Good voice acting though enemies often did end up saying fairly repetitive things during combat and one soldier often sounded like another.
+Great between level movie scenes.
+Interesting (though often disjointed feeling) plot.
+Outstanding and shockingly impressive graphics (the bullet time mode and effects is very well done) Great lighting effects and use of shadows as well.
+The two playable characters have interesting and different abilities (but playing as the Ghostly Fettel is much, much easier than playing as the flesh and blood Point Man).
+Interesting and varied environments.
+This game's plot causes all of the add-on packs to become canonical.
+Highly replayable game with two different endings (depending on which character you use and/or if playing in cooperative multiplayer mode, who did better on all of the previous missions. FEAR 3 is Possibly one of the best cooperative FPS gaming experiences ever designed.
+Excellent enemy AI and enemy variety.
+Outstanding Mech battle sequences.
+Your character can only pick up two guns at a time and 3 grenades of each of the 3 types causing for much more intense combat situations and requiring you to make more complex tactical choices.
+Excellent controls which support five-button gaming mice.
+/- Incredibly violent (and playing one of the character's this violence will often be seen in slow bullet-time motion in painfully exquisite detail. Definitely not a good game for the weak minded or easily influenced or previously disturbed. This game contains particularly disturbing situations and images throughout.
-Not extremely creepy throughout. Mostly just bloody and horrific.
-This game could have used longer between level cutscenes to flesh out the plot further.
-Uneven difficulty. The game is fairly difficult for the point man character but much, much easier for the ghostly Fettel character.
-In single player mode the other character vanishes (which, in terms of the plot, makes some sense if you are playing the flesh and blood character but not so well if you are playing the ghost). The game should have included an AI controlled character to assist you when in the playing single player mode to stand-in for an actual person particularly as the game's design and difficulty seems to occasionally forget that you might be playing the game by yourself causing some battle situations to be extremely difficult and possibly even frustrating even on the easier (recruit) difficulty.
-The plot will be difficult for newcomers to understand. This game's plot does a very poor job of standing on its own and is clearly intended for those who had played not just the first two games but possibly all of the add-on packs as well.
-Relatively short game with only 2 endings.
-Fairly linear gameplay and level design. The mech battle sequences, while well done and very atmospheric are particularly linear.
-This game has irritating HUD indicators. Text telling you to reload if your clip is not totally full. Stupid on-screen crosshairs that you cannot turn off.
-Mediocre music throughout which succeeds only in setting the right tone but fails to be truly catchy or very interesting.

Beautiful game, with a simple touching story and enjoyable yet challenging gameplay.
This has easily been one of my favourite games this year. The art style and graphics look superb. Ori is a minuscule little creature but darts and jumps across the screen very gracefully and once you get your hands on some of the later game skills it becomes a real pleasure to race through parts of the world that you've visited before.
The save system is also really great, once you start reminding yourself to place save points before tackling a difficult section, it really makes dying a few times a little less frustrating, knowing you mostly have control over where you respawn and how far you have to travel again.
I found the game difficulty just right. Most of the standard playthrough is challenging but it never really took me more than a couple of respawns to get past an area. The puzzle platforming is good too, especially a section which changes the gravity mechanics, really making you think about it. The games does get fairly tricky in the few levels which occur at the end of major story points which you have to escape from collapsing levels and such. The first of these I struggled with and had to leave the game overnight and try the following day to beat, and these are the only sections where I found the game get a little frustrating, but the sense of accomplishment after completing these was well worth it.
The story starts off quite sad but is altogether heart-warming in the end. Even though none of the characters speak, and the narration is in some form of fictional language, the actions of the various characters tell everything.
The biggest enjoyment I got from the game was the gameplay mechanics. Jumping, dodging, climbing walls, launching and stomping enemies and using you spirit flame, all felt so fluid and smooth. As the game progresses you learn new skills which help you traverse the world even quicker and more easily, I found this kept me playing, the more you played through the story, the more enjoyable the movement became.
Even if you don't regularly look for platformers to play, as I usually don't, please play this! I was pleasantly surprised and would find it difficult to imagine anyone else not enjoying this game. A truly great, simple, yet truly enjoyable game and one of my personal unexpected favourites of 2015.

To the Moon is all about its story, so therefore I will not summarize the plot apart from this: the story is about two doctors trying to fulfill a dying man's last wish of getting him to the moon.
As mentioned, the focus with this game and its greatest selling point is the story. The plot is pretty good; it has a few twists and the way the doctors try to help their client is interesting and well written. Also, the characters have real depth, which is the more impressive as To the Moon lasts but a few hours.
However, the story is also completely linear, the player is never presented with a meaningful choice and the levels are really small. Furthermore, the game tries to deliver an emotional experience but as you - due to plot reasons I cannot explain - are an outsider for the majority of the game the things happening on screen sometimes fail to deliver said experience; there is too much detachment.
Gameplay is threadbare and consists for the most part of walking to location/person X and clicking through (sometimes quite a lot of) text. These grant orbs that you need to combine with an item you need to find, after which you need to solve a very simple puzzle to continue the game. Repeat the above for almost every level. As mentioned, the levels are very small so you spend the majority of the time reading the dialogue. The gameplay fits in with the story, though.
What's worse, gameplay is bugged. The characters sometimes don't respond (well) to clicks and sometimes get stuck. Moreover, the mouse is rather imprecise during the puzzles and that is annoying as it leads to more missclicks.
In conclusion, I feel this game has nice characters and at its core a good plot but it lacks choice for the player and the story is completely linear. On top of that, it has bugged, threadbare gameplay that gets really repetitive a few levels in. Due to this, I cannot recommend To the Moon.

Instead you play in "small areas" which you can leave on the borders to the overland map.
For me overland maps in rpg games are a pain. They destroy immersion, gameplay possibilities and the fun travel though a foreign land, not knowing what to see after the next hill/rocks/whatever, completely destroying the raoming and discovery gameplay, but without having any equivalent value. Its like in other games where you cant advance without quitting the game to check forums or guides. The overland map changes the meta level and you are forced to kind of "leave" your character to play it like another genre.
This really is a setback for me, after i was quite sure that this game will please me in all ways.
Dont get me wrong, i dont mislike the areas with natural borders. I can live with the loading screens. But i would connect several areas to build one complete world which feels consistent, instead of some areas which are connected via a not so beautiful map. Encounters arent exciting or fascinating, they are just an annoyance, which needs to be there because of some kind of syntax, a rule. :(
So in my point of view, the overland map was a bad descision. Anyone, devs and players, are welcome to tell me what the value of this feature is for them, or just what you like about it. I will gladly modify my opinion when there are good reasons.
(at this point its is important to clarify that this is just my personal opinion, which depends highly on my playstyle).

PROS:
*Impressive dictionary with unique images for many terms
*Good variety of environments
*Pleasing art
*Unlockable avatars
*Object editor and Steam Workshop integration
CONS:
*Minimal, yet tedious gameplay
*Dictionary gaps and re-used images stand out, though the object editor can alleviate this if the player is willing to do the work
*Story is unnecessary, boring, and not spread throughout the game
GAME LENGTH:
For achievement hunters, this game should take around 10 hours at most.  Those who just want to finish the game can expect to be done in around 7 hours, perhaps even less.
SCORE:
4.5 out of 10
Even though I got this game for only $1, I regret the purchase.
The greatest disappointment for me was that there really isn't much
here:  the player moves from one environment to the next, solving very simple problems by typing an appropriate noun or adjective.  The challenge does not increase, creativity is not demanded, and 95% of the problems to solve feel identical in concept.  In short:  the game was tedious and I never felt challenged.
The game certainly boasts an impressive dictionary with unique images for many terms, including a decent variety of dog breeds.  However, without anything interesting to
with the objects that the player can create, it becomes substantially less impressive.  Moreover, since the dictionary is the star of the game instead of actual gameplay, terms that aren't recognized or given unique images (for example:  two kinds of trees might look identical) stand out.  I understand that it would be impossible to include an exhaustive dictionary with a unique image for each term, but that is why the gameplay needs to pick up the inevitable slack of this category.  Fortunately, the player does have the option of using the object editor to add new terms to the dictionary with custom images or download others' work from the Steam Workshop.  The option wasn't stressed in the game and it seemed like more work than it was worth to me, but other players might enjoy it.
Finally, though this is a very minor point, the story is lackluster.  (Spoilers ahead.)  The player character and his sister play a mostly harmless prank on an old man, who responds quite unfairly by cursing the sister to turn to stone.  The only way to save her is to collect magical "Starites" by helping people around the world, which also unlocks new areas to visit.  In the end, the curse is lifted and the old man who cast it is revealed to be the father.  (What a great guy.)  This is the entirety of the story and it is told entirely at the beginning and the end, rather than weaved throughout the game.  The only reason to even visit the sister is because the game requires it to unlock new areas, but the only aspect of the story that is advanced is how much of her is stone.  As I said, however, this is a minor point; clearly the game is not about the story.
I could perhaps recommend this game for children, but it's just not enough for teenagers or adults.  If I graded games solely according to what developers intended to accomplish, I would give this a 9.5 out of 10, subtracting half a point only for the dictionary's incompleteness and re-used art.  But I grade games in large part according to my enjoyment of them, so, despite the game's art, dictionary, and polish, the tedious nature of what little gameplay there is compels me to give it a 4.5 out of 10.

The following is copied from my review on
, and is a preview for an "as yet unreleased Early Access title"
[Disclosure: Game copy purchased with own money]
Lego Worlds is developed by TT games (better known as Traveller’s Tales pre-merger) and published by Warner Brothers Interactive. Outside of their work on the Lego franchise, TT also have a rich history including titles such as; Crash Bandicoot: The Wrath of Cortex, A Bug’s Life, Sonic R & 3D Blast and of course Toy Story 1 & 2 to name but a few.
Lego Worlds is a procedurally generated sandbox exploration/adventure game. As such the only story is the one you create. The game is reminiscent of all the other Lego titles in the franchise, whereby destruction of objects will allow you to place an object in the world and also generate a certain amount of “studs” which we all know Lego uses as currency, you can then use this currency to unlock various different things to place in the world once unlocked you’re free to place as many as you like.
The game has been compared a lot to Minecraft and Terraria, I personally feel this is really unfair. My experience with Lego Worlds has very much been “this is a digital version of Lego” . To me, It’s a little bit like comparing Borderlands to Call of Duty. Don’t get me wrong what I’m basically trying to say is yes there are similarities but they are completely different games.
The game can be controlled with either keyboard and mouse, or controller as it has full controller support although I would mildly disagree with that, as certain features don’t really work well with the use of a gamepad, which is going to be a major problem if they port it to consoles. The developer has said that they will explore it when the PC version is complete, I would say it is highly likely.
The picture seen above is my attempt to use the in game “block builder” to build myself a house. Many of the options are disabled if you choose to use a gamepad and even using keyboard and mouse, whilst a lot of the wireframes and various different features of the block builder are quite handy, building this structure was rather tedious.
The structure pictured here was imported using the “brick builds” feature, I shudder to think the amount of time and effort required to build a structure this detailed.
The game is chock full of customisation options for characters with more unlockable parts as you meet the various characters in the game. However, one thing I did notice is some characters have a special ability and if you customise your character rather than play as that character, you don’t inherit the special ability as you would in say Lego Marvel Super Heroes which would be nice.
The game also features a basic land and air vehicle system which works really well, the only thing I noticed which was kind of funny was a biplane been able to hover. One thing of note that I thought was really cool is being able to fly a Dragon which also shoots fire balls. One thing I did feel was missing, was the ability to make your own (custom) vehicle that you could drive/fly around. This may be added in later but is difficult to tell if this is on the cards.
Graphically the game looks like all the rest of the Lego games, which is a nice aesthetic and there is a limit to how smooth you can make a block look. The soundtrack is suitably “adventurous” with the sound assets changing to suit the various biomes. However there were a few things I did notice with some of the graphical settings/assets...
Overall the game is still in my opinion very early in development and “works” but is missing a vast amount of features, most notably multiplayer, but I can understand wanting to get the base game working before adding in multiplayer. I would also like to see some NPC interaction perhaps although I don’t know how that would quite fit in. One thing I did want to mention is the game does have a frame rate detector and if it feels as though the game is struggling it will warn you and suggest you lower the graphics settings which is nice to see. This is a very good start but a lot more work is required.
My final thoughts are because it’s so early in development I can’t give it a score but what I will say is if you like Lego and really like the idea of adventure and exploration then it’s a definite recommendation. However if you would like a little bit more, you may want to hold off for a while. Under no circumstances think this is “just like Minecraft, with no survival (creative mode) only in Lego” it isn’t there is no mining (only terrain modification) or crafting.
So basicaly this is a tentative recommendation at this stage of development

I have very mixed reviews about this game. First off, I have heard a lot of the Gauntlet series and the only one I've ever played was Dark Legacy on Gamecube. It had crappy graphics, lame gameplay, nothing complicated but it had something that this Gauntlet did not have..The charm to make me laugh.
Gauntlet, a dungeon crawler I have not played for a long time is a fairly decent game. Comparing it with Diablo would be unfair, since Diablo was a very unbalanced game.
Gauntlet is a very well balanced game with no over-powered character and completely very different play styles between the 4 classes with Wizard being the most complicated but most rewardingly exciting character to wield. Good graphics and pretty much zero story is normal for a game like this. It is straight-forward and simple to get used to.
But Gauntlet's greatest strength for balanced gameplay and better graphics is its very own downfall. It kept the basic skeleton of what Gauntlet is, but it lacked the charm and uniqueness to stand apart from any other dungeon crawler game, let alone apart from Dark Legacy. It was straightforward, but that's all it is, straightforward with a spice of linear and a topping of repetition
What made Dark Legacy truly great is how wacky it was with stupid skills, range attacks for all classes and melee when your character was dealing face-to-face against an enemy. Of course, some excel in one thing while others excel in theirs. Death was also wacky as heck, chasing us like mad while leeching our lives. It had a load of flaws...but those flaws (like Halo1) was it's biggest asset and uniqueness that made me and my friends laugh through the night.
This Gauntlet has stripped away all that charm and replaced it with standard issued factory produced games that can be found anywhere at their bare skeleton. Sure the game requires some skill to play, esspecially with the wizard, but it's not enough to compensate for the lack of fun factor. It's a serious dungeon crawler...and very little levels and character classes. Leveling should have been the better option to keep me playing since there are so few classes. But if there were a ton more kinds of classes, it's current balanced style would have complimented it. Much to experience and much to experiment.
With so little dungeons, unworthy winnings barely worth gaining, very little items to buy...Gauntlet is a decent game, and that's all it is. Decent. I haven't even laughed once since I started playing this game online. It truly made me believe that Dark Legacy was truly better than this Gauntlet.
5 out of 10 is all I can give it. It's a little fun and has it's moments of intensity which I enjoyed. But I'm not laughing and going gaga over this game. I'm already bored of it.
The developers should have taken risks, and did something stupid yet playable rather than trying so hard to make this game perfect and flawless. It's flaws and improvements are both professionally unfun to endure compared to Dark Legacy. It's genericly fun for few hours. That's the most you'd get out of it.

I grew up with Gauntlet, but alas.... this version has sadly mucked with the formula a bit and made it a bit more like Diablo and other grinders, as to be nearly unrecognisable. In fact, it's probably closer to the classic "Smash TV" in gameplay - which is not bad, per se, but it doesn't resemble Gauntlet much.
Most of the classic gameplay elements are there, but some have been meddled with while others are  notorious by their absence. The characters play far differently now - to be completely different from the arcade original. The warror and valkyrie can't shoot, and the wizard has a bunch of spells which can be selected by confusing street-fighter-like button combinations. Also the way magic works in game is not like the original, owing to a  relic system that lets you buy types of magic for in-game gold. The enemy generators are fewer but now take excessive hits to damage. Death is more of a nuisance than he ever was, and now ALL the food is vulnerable to being shot.
As for level design, the rooms are rather too large and you can avoid most of the nasties by running in circles. It's not very claustrophobic and Gauntlet-like at all. Also granted that the game likes to lock you in arena battles is where this game borrows more closely from Smash TV than Gauntlet.
The inclusion of the crown is a welcome addition (like classic Gauntlet II's "it" creature), as are the exploding barrels. Some of the other room elements (moving blocks, lava cranks) don't add much to the game at all and just get in the way of the fun.
I understand the desire to update an old game, but sometimes going crazy and introducing a bunch of cool new things that don't really work together can really imbalance the fundamental gameplay, and that's what's happened here. As it stands as a game in it's own right, it's certainly fun during multiplayer -- if you can bear being the slow old wizard while everyone grabs the gold before you do. Also the boss fights are a bit of a let down... I had to figure out how to kill the first one, and having to solve room puzzles isn't really what Gauntlet is supposed to be about. Just let me hack'n'slash them, thanks.
My fear is that the game will not have much lasting appeal - save for those who love grinders. There are not so many levels and there are no infinitely generated ones like the arcade game. It's just going to become a grindfest for masteries, new character clothes and relics pretty quickly. To top it off, the character speech in-game gets really REALLY repetitive, and the score leaderboards have been plauged by cheats.
It's not a bad game,... in fact it's fun for a while, and will grow on you if you give it a chance .... but it's just not a great game.

Let's say you want to attack an enemy with yout ranged unit. You click on it, nothing happens. You click again, whoops! The monster's animation has just moved the hitbox a couple of pixels and you have now clicked on the ground. Your ranger will run 10 metres through a poisonous cloud into the middle of the melee action and get clobbered.
Then there is the incredibly shoddy writing with no regard to even the most basic principles of storytelling. The pacing of the story makes no sense, and the characters you meet are lazy parodies of fantasy tropes. This disregard of pacing carries over to the quests. It's impossible to finish any one quest at a time either because the next step is either waiting for a completely counter-intuitive action, or requires you to go to an area of the game that is way too difficult for your characters yet. The result is that you run around like a headless chicken and talk to every lazy parody NPC in the game in the hope of fulfilling one step for one of the gazillion open quests in your questbook at random.
Did I mention that you will hardly see anything of the amazing combat system for the first two hours or so? You'll just try to complete pointless quests until you finally reach a level that allows you to leave the first town.
Oh, that's also more or less the only area you'll see for at least the first 10 hours of the game, barring some dungeons. The game simply doesn't take you places, it lets you run around in circles for what is basically one middle-sized map.
So much potential, such a frustrating execution.

The characters have a lot of options and the game allows you to just explore and get to where you're going at your pace.
Ignore many of the negative reviews for this game. They either played less than a few hours or sound like they were looking for easy mode with loot pinatas.
For people looking for a modern hold-your-hand RPG, this isn't it. You have to think. You have to plan. You must consider your actions. You need to reference words in your journal. There are no floating quest markers on the map. You're given directions where to go next, but it's not like Skyrim or something with a super simple quest marking system. It has great NPC's and a quirky storyline. There are bits of humor sprinkled throughout.
Combat can be punishingly hard at times if you don't have a well-rounded group. I found that as time went on the fights got easier. Not because the enemies were less challenging. If anything, they got much more difficult as time went on, but I became used to capitalizing on the synergy of certain characters and using terrain or material features to tip the scales in my favor.
I'm looking forward to playing this co-op sometime. The single player campaign is excellent thus far.
I must admit the first couple times I played I felt like I had no idea what I was doing. I'm happy I persisted though. This will be on my all-time top 5 CRPG's list for sure. I had waited for something to rival the old Baldur's Gate 2 I'd played back in the day and this feel like it.
The only part of the end of this game I am looking forward to is so I can play Divinity Original Sin 2.

No Mans Sky is an over-promised and under-delivered game. We must never forget that and always acknowledge it.
But it's also fun and I've clocked up quite a few hours and haven't lost interest yet.
Let me say first that the procedurally generated galaxy is amazing, but alone would not have been enough to keep me interested - it's very clever what they've done, but things really do start to look the same after a while - after a couple of galaxies you've seen probably 98% of what there is to offer. That, and the  modding community have really brought to light the shortcomings of the vanilla game, if you care to look into it.
Having said that I am still finding surprises as I play on (not big surprises, but surprises nonetheless). Like last night I was attacked by a man-eating gopher with headlights.
But the thing that really draws me back is the gameplay - there's a lot of fun challenges in making it to the center of the galaxy, searching for resources, managing inventories, finding/upgrading tech etc. So really (for me) that is the saving grace, even though IMO it would probably been second to the procedural universe development in Sean Murray's eyes.
And lets admin it - Hello Games have really set somewhat of a bar here. Space games can only get (procedurally) better from this point.
So, GG Hello Games. Let's hope you keep fulfilling your promises.
And yes I can recommend the game as it is now, It's fun, and I do have faith HG will finish what they've started. You should probably wait for a sale though :)

With the limited experience I have with this game I can say with confidence this:
-If you are coming here looking for a multiplayer experience, you will be disappointed.
-If you are coming here looking for a cohesive story line or enriching campaign, you will be disappointed.
-If you are coming here looking for a game that will make you say "Woah, how the f*ck did they make something of this    scale and with these graphics", you will be VERY VERY HAPPY.
This game does have some downfalls, such as repetitive gameplay, tough progression, constantly gathering resources to fuel your ship, etc. However, this game is much more playable than I originally anticipated. I purchased this game over the winter sale, simply because I thought it looked amazing, even with the poor reviews. I can happily tell you that I am not at all upset about my purchase. This game has given me several moments where I fly out of the vast planet that I was gathering resources from into space, look around, and just say "Holy sh*t. This place is huge." This feeling is exactly what Hello Games wanted each and every buyer to feel, and so, in this way, I feel they accomplished their goal.
For those of you looking for an analogy, this game feels as if you are put in first person perspective in the space stage of Spore. I'm pretty sure I even recognize some sounds (not really but you can imagine some). Establishing multiple bases, buying freighters to ship goods to other systems to get the best price, etc. all have parallels to Spore, but this game goes one step further, allowing the player to hop out of their spaceship at any time in order to actually explore the planets they visit.
In conclusion, if you purchase this game with the intent of it filling your certain niche of games and providing you with everything you've ever wanted, you will be sorely disappointed and will miss out on an opportunity to enjoy a fantastic game. With that in mind, my advice to everyone that purchases this game is to throw away your pre-conceived notions about the game and just simply sit down and try it out. If you enter this game throwing away all of the negative reviews you have read and all the criticisms that you will subconciously be looking for throughout playing, you are left with what the developers truly wanted: A game that makes you sit back, look at all of the stars around you, and say, "Holy sh*t. Where do I start."
tl/dr : This game is comparable to Spore if you were put in first person on the Space Stage. While it has flaws, drop the negative reviews you have read, buy this on sale, and try it for yourself. It is truly an awe inspiring game.

This game is what I would like to call the perfect platformer experience, and this isn't without a reason. I think this game has done everything right. The graphics, the music, the story and the gameplay, all of it just goes perfectly hand in hand.
When I first started up the game, it was the graphics that I first noticed. This game is what I consider to be pure art, the graphics and the art style is just gorgeous to look at, and it has so many different areas that you get to explore and experience.
The background scenery, the characters, the monsters, the effects, the abilities, the cutscenes and the the list goes on.... but all of it just seem very fitting and true to the universe.
This game is probably one of the most beautiful games that I have ever played
The music is also one of the reasons that this game is so great, and I could simply sit and listen to the soundtrack all day. The music is just wonderful and it fits very well with the game.
I very much enjoyed the story, and considering this is "just" a platformer, I think they did a perfect job with the story telling. The game is set in a nice little universe, which I really think the graphic and the music helped convey. The story is experienced through the gameplay and multiple cutscenes, and honestly I won't say much more, as I think you should go and experience this by yourself.
The game is a platformer, and to give you a perspective, I would also I like to mention that I am by no means a expert at these kind of games. I am actually quite bad lol.
The game might start out a bit easy, but it progressively gets harder and harder, and trust me when I say this. You will DIE, and you will die A LOT! The game is by no means a easy platformer, and can be very challenging and at certain stages it will also require some fast reaction time.
You however shouldn't worry if you are bad at plaformers like me, as the game offers you almost unlimited save stages. The game developers were nice enough to give us the ability to spend some of our energy on making a save stage, the same energy that is otherwised used for one the more powerful abilities.
One thing I especially enjoyed about this game, was the progression system. I like how you don't start out with all the abilities unlocked, but you have to unlock them as you play through the game.  The timing that you unlock your abilities also felt very nice and rewarding, and I like how the game allows you to back to previous stages and use these new abilirties to obtain items that you previously wasn't obtainable.

Memorable and enjoyable soundtracks are something I love in games.
Extremely well worth the money. This gives you so much more than watching a great movie, while costing a fraction of the price. Characters are well developed and each have their own personality that are enjoyable to watch. I'm pre-emptively trying to find the sequel that has just been announced so I can wishlist it.
There's an overarching storyline that connects the two main scientists to the next game, as they work on multiple "patients", this game covers a single patient's story. So in future sequels, we'll get to see a continuation of the development of these characters. I just love that! You don't see direct connections like that often.
Only gripes are that the sprite grid is a bit too large, like your position is very here-or-there, you can't always position yourself exactly where you want to be easily. Also, in a couple of places I have to switch from using a controller to a mouse because the controller wasn't able to do what I was required to do. Should support all control schemes (especially in simple setups.)
Definitely recommended. A character-focused adventure that just about anyone can relate to and enjoy.

This a game is all about adjacency bonuses. There are two basic kinds of plants/minerals/animals per biome and 5 biomes. Then all of those can be evolved a couple of times with various aspects... and each stage of evolution has different bonuses, usually pertaining to what it is near. At the end of the era, you unlock new plants and animals and minerals to use in future plays.

Reus is a simple game.
What it lacks in depth it makes up for with gameplay that keeps you involved with what’s happening in the various areas of your world. Balance out the demands in all of your established biomes and the people will be happy. Fail to do so and you’ll see wholesale revolt by your populations.
It is quick and easy to get into this game: learn the four biomes and what role the associated giant performs and you’re good to go. The game helps you out by giving you progressively more difficult challenges to meet before advancing to the next level.
Is it re-playable? Most definitely, and I would make it part of the gameplay. By this I mean that you have a countdown timer in the “Era” mode which is like a ‘campaign’ mode (I use the term loosely) where you have to successfully complete all the challenges before unlocking the next level (longer countdown, different challenges). Endless re-playability, but some might say endless repetitiveness.
Unfortunately that’s all there is to Reus and while there is no defined end game (besides dying), you can certainly achieve everything there is to achieve in the “Freeplay” mode (no countdown timer). While I do recommend playing this game (positive Steam rating), I cannot call it a good game; it is mediocre at best because of how limited the gameplay is.

Reus is probably my favorite god-game of the past decade.
At its core, the game is something of a 2D (or really, technically 1D) Sim City RTS. You cannot directly control humanity, but you create and arrange resources in order to help them thrive. Villages need Food, Wealth, and Tech, which can be gained in various combinations from Animal, Plant, and Mineral resources.
It may not be obvious from the screenshots, but the planet is divided up into individual tiles. Each tile can only be occupied by one resource or building at a time, though you can usually "overwrite" a tile's contents.
You direct your four giants (Ocean, Rock, Forest, Swamp) to terraform the world's surface and to place resources on specific tiles. Eventually humans will settle near a resource, reserving several contiguous tiles as a town square, and setting up borders a certain distance from the square. As a village develops, the borders will be pushed back, opening up additional tiles for the village to use.
Most of the game's progression is context-sensitive.
Giants have vague powers, such as "Create Exotic Animal," but the TYPE of animal is determined by which biome (Forest, Swamp, Desert, Mountain, Ocean) the power is cast upon.
Individual resources may grant bonuses depending on what occupies the adjacent tiles (Salt is more useful if there is a different mineral right next to it).
Giants are able to upgrade the attributes of certain resources. For example, the Swamp Giant is able to increase the amount of Tech provided by any plant tile. Improving aspects in this way unlocks the ability to upgrade the resource to a more valuable/effective (but often more specialized) resource. By manipulating aspects, you can develop Blueberries into either Strawberries or an Apple Tree. Each of those choices also has branching upgrades with different bonuses. In order to keep the choices from getting overwhelming, certain upgrades must be unlocked with achievements.
There are two separate classifications of animals, two of minerals, and two of plants. With all the valid combinations of resource-types and biomes, there are 25 possible entry-level resources, each with various upgrade paths.
A village's "type" is determined by whether the town square is planted on Forest, Swamp, or Desert tiles. This will determine what sort of civic projects the villagers will want to build (Forest emphasizes agriculture, Desert emphasizes wealth, and Swamp emphasizes technology).
Villages will occasionally decide to construct specialty buildings. In order to successfully complete these projects, the village must reach a certain quota of Food, Wealth, and Tech (or other factors) within a predetermined length of time. It's worth it to help villages reach these goals, because they unlock achievements and award you a village ambassador. Each ambassador can be assigned to one of your giants, who will as a result unlock (or strengthen) a creation or aspect power. The type of power affected is determined by what type of village provided the ambassador.
Each village has a Greed meter. When a village acquires resources too rapidly, the Greed meter will fill, encouraging that village to attack neighbors (or the giants!). This is disruptive to your ability to efficiently and effectively develop these communities within the time limit (Once time runs out, your accomplishments are judged and you are allowed to continue playing, but some achievements must be reached while the clock is still ticking).
The real meat of this game comes from trying to shuffle your resources around within a village's borders in order to maximize context-specific bonuses, because the project the village wants to build just requires SO MUCH of a given resource (or several!) that it needs to be your singular goal. Except it's your multiple goal, because your other villages are also trying to build their own projects, and you can't upgrade this mineral over here until that giant walks over there and casts that aspect upgrade on it (Did I mention the giants have to walk to the tiles where you want them to take action? They're not fast). Since different projects have different dependencies, it's often necessary to maintain at least one of each type of village (Forest, Desert, and Swamp) to ensure a variety of ambassadors (and, by extension, upgrades).
Reus has vibrant art assets and a pleasant soundtrack. The game is fairly easy to pick up but the depth of it might catch you off-guard. You can also choose from a variety of modifiers (such as planet's size or a speed boost for your giants) when starting a new game. Some of these modifiers prevent you from unlocking high-level achievements, but they are a nice way to get a head start in what can easily turn into a several-hour session.
If you like Populous, Sim City, or Black & White, I would recommend giving this game a try.

Oh, Divinity: Original Sin. I really want to love this game, but I just can't. I've given this game numerous tries, and every time I just end up frustrated with it.
Let's start with the good:
Combat: From what little I've played of the combat, it seems to be pretty damn solid. Many different spells and items and such can be used to give certain status effects to enemies, which can lead to some pretty devastating attack combos. For example, you can throw oil at a group of enemies and cast a fireball spell to make the whole group burst into flames. This creates a pretty in depth combat system, with many variables and strategic options to take into account. I'm sure a lot of fun can be had with this, especially much later in the game. Shame it takes about 5 hours to get to combat again after the tutorial.
Great Co-op/The Partner System: The co-op in this game is very well implemented. In single-player, the game focuses on two characters, who are both source hunters. Both of these characters can be freely customised, and one of them can be given an AI Personality. This is important because there are many times during the game where you can interact with your partner, which can lead to casual discussions as well deciding what to do in important situations. With co-op, you can invite a friend on the character selection screen and they drop right in, immediately taking control of character number 2. They are then free to customise the character as they wish. Instead of interacting with an AI personality, you are instead opening in-game conversations with your friend. This can lead to fun role-play moments, such as having to argue over what to do with a fish thief, whether you should take a new companion, etc. Arguments like these are solved with a rock, paper, scissors minigame. It can be a bit frustrating for whoever is on the losing end though, because you'll have to do whatever the winner wants.
The visuals are pretty, as well.
And now we get to the bad, where the game becomes a bit of a disappointment for me, unfortunately.
Story: This is a big one. One of the main reasons I play crpgs is for the writing, and the many directions I can take my character in. The writing in this game, for as far as I can tell, is a huge disappointment to say the least. The setting is generic Fantasy McFantasyville, full of uninteresting characters with tons of boring exposition who have tons of boring errands to send you on. The whole first part of the game is running around the town of Cyseal investigating a mysterious murder. You run into many similarly voice acted NPCs with boring dialogue which gives you little to no worthwhile information that you didn't already know. If they aren't boring, they really just want to make your life hell by getting in the way of accomplishing a quest objective.
When you do eventually start making progress in the main quest, the game starts to get a little less generic and a little more batshit insane as you go to some temple in space. Unfortunately, this is just as boring as the rest of the game, because in this temple they tell you all about the generic fantasy world you just left, and how you are the chosen one and must gather some stones or some garbage. This drags on for far too long, and drops way too much exposition on you way too fast.
After 2 hours of talking about how the stars sometimes twinkle when the lords of time take a dump, you are deposited right back to Cyseal and are back to the grind of talking to more uninteresting people and doing more uninteresting errands for another 7 hours. Rinse, wash, repeat.
And remember the partner system? Well, it's not all that I made it out to be. Sure, it offers some great roleplaying elements, but it's very limited, with choices being pretty much binary. Let's take the fish thief scenario. In Cyseal, you encounter a poor man who is trying to steal a fish to feed himself. This presents the group with a dilemma. Will you turn away while the thief steals the fish or will you stop him? When me and my friend got to this point, we both asked, "Why can't we just buy the fish for him?" Instead we are forced to pick between 2 options, and while I understand it is hard to implement many different decisions for these scenarios, it still feels cheap to be forced down one of two paths when neither makes much sense to us. From what I've encountered, every decision in the game has a binary choice like this, with pretty much no middle ground whatsoever.
Odd Quest Design: The quests in this game have frustrated me and my friend to no end. Many of them are boring, and many of them are given to you without a way to complete them yet. While this isn't a big problem in theory, these quests clutter your log, and keeping what you have to do organized becomes a bit of a challenge. It's a similar problem that The Witcher had in chapter 2, so if you had problems with that game, you'll definitely have them here too.
Sometimes it's also hard to tell what exactly these quests want you to do, and actively punish you for your playstyle. For example, there's a quest in the game where an elf is planning to kill an orc librarian. You can turn him in, but if you aren't a class that can pickpocket, that's not happening. You can get the amulet from the orc with a speech check to prove to the elf she's dead, but then you wouldn't be able to bring the elf to justice. So if you're roleplaying a character who is wanting to bring the elf to justice, you either have to pickpocket him or kill him, there is no other way.
Pretty much every quest in the game is like this. A lot of them emphasize breaking and entering and stealing things. The feeling I've felt throughout all of the times I've tried this is that if you aren't wanting to break into homes and take everything not nailed down, this game isn't really for you.
Bugs: And this is the kicker. I can deal with odd quest design and even a mediocre story as long as the rpg elements and combat are solid, but holy christ. Me and my friend tried playing earlier and ran into many game breaking bugs in the first 20 minutes. We load into the game, and my friend can't talk to anyone or interact with anything. Great. We reload. That's fixed. We begin doing the talking head quest. One of us takes the head to the cellar and talks to it. The other tries to listen in. They can't. We think it's a bug. Reload again. It's not a bug, it's exactly how it's intended. Great. We go through it, and I tell my friend exactly what the head wants us to do. Exclamation points appear over our characters indicating that a conversation can be initiated. We can't interact with each other now. Great. Reload, go through the thing again, still can't initiate the conversation. We finally just gave up trying.
Okay, is this a solid game? Sure, it can be pretty enjoyable for the right person going in with the right expectations. It seems like it can be a pretty great co-op rpg experience for those interested. Is it a bad game? Definitely not. Why am I not recommending it, then? Quite frankly, I didn't enjoy it, and if you're looking for a great crpg, I don't think this is what you want. Instead, I recommend you go with a more classic title, such as Planescape Torment, Fallout 1 and 2, or Baldur's Gate 1 and 2. There are a few more modern rpg games I'd recommend over this as well, such as Fallout: New Vegas, Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines, and both Knights of the Old Republic games. All of these games are cheaper than this title, as well. You can also check out the sequel to this. While I have not played it, I've heard it's a better game.
If you're a die hard rpg fan and have played the big titles and are dying for more, then I'd say this can be worth it. Be aware, however, that this game has many annoying roleplaying limitations, uninspired characters, and a story that will probably put you to sleep before you get to any combat.

.  The Foundation Update made me realize that building a base or buying a freighter to build rooms adds very little to existing gameplay loops, adds nothing to lore, and requires fetch quests.  The game's core is exploration for the sake of exploration, and now there's building for the sake of building.  The content is a small step forward.  I cannot deny the ~75 hours I played that I enjoyed more than my lack thereof before the Foundation Update .  Likewise, I cannot deny the 10 hours I played after the update which left me disappointed that there wasn't more added to gameplay loops or lore.  The game needs more than a Foundation for me to come back to it.
So I can only recommend this game on sale to anyone who truly loves exploration for the sake of exploration, is excited by building a base & owning a freighter, wants this experience with a retro sci-fi feel, doesn't have a low or mid end rig, AND leaves all hopes & expectations at the door.  Performance wise, my GTX680 & i5 3470 drops as low as 40 FPS when rotating quickly or on a planet with tons of flora & fauna.  Dips to sub 30 happen sometimes when flying on a planet, especially at low speeds.  All this is with medium-to-low graphics settings that I've tweaked a ton.  Its not a dealbreaker for me, but I know that might be for some people.

"Mine resources, so you can build upgrades so you can mine resources faster!"

With the introduction of bases, you now have something to invest in, and with a variety of rare resources which actually take exploration to get and feel satisfying when you succeed, it's got some gameplay. Add to that later game goals with the ability to buy freighters, and it's just about at the stage where it's more of a game and less of a HD remake of Proteus.
