Ori is a game that's easily finished in just a handful of sittings, or even a single one if you're into speedrunning. In terms of graphics and sound, this game is incredible and really immersive. You have this cutesy, almost Disney-like art style coupled with a very melancholic soundtrack. It really fits. Story is really about preference and I'm not going to spoil it, but personally I liked it. To give you an idea, I was getting some pretty intense Studio Ghibli vibes.
In terms of gameplay, it's essentially a platformer. For the most part enemies are pushovers and you have an amazing number of tools to deal with whatever enemies you come across. You can bounce back projectiles, slam enemies dash through them, or even just scale the walls and avoid them alltogether if you happen to be low on health.
All in all I heartily recommend it to anyone who enjoys platformers to some extent. Ori was very refreshing and one of a few platformers I've ever really enjoyed. That being said, Ori will probably last you about 6-7 amazing hours for a single, slow paced playthrough.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a fantastic game. Having finished with 99% completion I can say that it is one of the few games that made me want to go out and get collectibles. Normally I am not a completionist at all, and this game can be done without the extra health and energy pickups. But with each new ability gained, moving around the world gets more and more fun. I don't play too many platformers-the last one I did play was Braid, years ago- but this one hooked me from the start.
Pros:
-Visuals, absolutely gorgeous. The level of detail put into this world is meticulous.
-Music: Engrossing. Part of it has to do with the gameplay, because it's sometimes quite fast paced and unforgiving. The music really draws you into the moment and enhances the tension you're feeling.
-Smooth controls. I played on a keyboard/mouse setup, but I believe a controller would be just as intuitive.
-Challenging, to the right amount. Satisfying when you get past an area you died on dozens of times.
-Storyline is somewhat tried and true, but the emotions felt and connection created between the limited characters are strong.
Cons:
-Can be EXTREMELY frustrating. Cheap deaths, for sure, but in the end it makes the game what it is.
I don't write many reviews, so I'm not very good at them. But if you're on the fence about Ori, I recommend it. If you like platformers, then it's a no-brainer. The soundtrack alone is fantastic.

What do I have to say about this game... pretty much stuff that's already been said. This is the most beautiful game I've ever played in terms of visual appeal. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥even the menu screen put a stupid grin on my face.
In terms of gameplay, the first halfish of the game had really spot on platforming. It allowed a high degree of skill and just felt good, nailing perfect jumps and all. The problem begins about halfway through when you get Kuro's feather, which is an item/ability that lets you glide. Cool right? ... well in a way yes, but adding the shift key into the mix of WASD, space, and left and right mouse clicking gets the controls cluttered. Because you have to press and unpress shift constantly while moving with WASD, jumping, double jumping, triple jumping, timing your clicks and trying really hard not to pres S midair and stomping yourself into spikes.
It got absolutely ridiculous at some points, then guess what, you get the climb ability which overdefines shift to work on walls differently than mid jump. Then you get charged jumps that charge with W and... well yeah.
Could you remap the controls, Yes, but after you get used to the initial controls it's hard to change them mid-game.
Then there was the chase scenes. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥those were frustrating. Normally if you do really well when running from something you get a bit a buffer as you put distance between you so that maybe you can miss a jump towards the end. Not in this game. The timing gives you maybe a 2 second buffer between success and failure which was intended no doubt to make them thrilling but just made them horribly frustrating since if you missed a single step you pretty much had to redo the whole thing.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a side-scrolling adventure game with very little dialogue (I like that) and a skill tree; there will be some dialogue to fill you in on the story but you won't be watching cut scenes or reading pages of text and the skill tree is something you'll use throughout the game that makes your life a bit easier.
Early in the game you may need some patience. I found that I had to get used to the controls while navigating some difficult areas, but rest assured that you will eventually gain abilities that make navigation easier. There is a progression in this game that will allow you to reach certain areas, so there will be some back-tracking, but like I said, it will be much easier to backtrack when you've gained your new skills.
There may be some frustrating moments in this game, but I found that when I was feeling really frustrated, I was often at the end of the frustrating area so I never was entirely♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at the game. Also, don't forget to use the abilities that you're given and take into consideration what objects you can use to help navigate difficult areas. I enjoyed the gameplay mechanics because, while it is basically a platformer, it did require a some brainpower to complete.
As for the visuals, it's a side-scroller, but it appears to be mostly rendered in "3D" (not just flat 2D objects) so it does require a decent GPU to run. I thought that the graphics were done extremely well and for some reason the art reminded me a bit of Odin Sphere.

For very litte, To the Moon is a fantastic game! Don't let the slow first hour turn you off, because this game contains within it a very heart-warming story that will make you tear up in some parts (they're really powerful). This is all thanks to the game's heavy focus on the characters of the game. By playing the game, you'll eventually grow to love and care for the character's presented to you, as you walk through the tough times in the story with them. They are a delightful little cast of characters that I love and I'm sure you'll love them too. Another thing to mention is the game's soundtrack; It's lovely. With a focus on piano's and, at times, violins too, To the Moon's soundtrack is great! I just wish there was more of it, as the same song can sometimes get annoying if you're stuck in the same spot of the game for too long (some song's also play frequently, which could annoy some people). That being said, keep in mind that this is a story heavy game with very little focus on gameplay. You simply walk around as a cute pixel character in a beautiful pixel environment, with the occasional puzzle to solve. It's a very straight-forward game, so don't expect to get lost too often if you pay attention to the story. If you're looking for a gameplay heavy game with a good story; this game only provides a good story. Please don't let that stop you from picking this game up, because after the first hour, To the Moon will keep you engaged until the very end.
P.S This game is about 4-5 hours long and it's best if you play it in one or two sittings. :)

I've been having this game for so long and yet I didn't manage to have a run that is worth of its name until recently. What a mistake! It's everything that a computer RPG needs: highly customizable characters, freedom of movement and action -- you can seriously go anywhere, talk to anyone, kill anyone. The story is engrossing and, despite it being serious, it manages to blend in a lot of humour which is refreshing to see in a sea of dark and sinister fantasy games and lores.
There's a lot of crafting and a lot of the fun consists of finding the right combinations for ingredients to produce items to use and sell -- you will have to think laterally a lot of the time when doing this, as the aformentioned humour pervades also this aspect of the game: for example, if you want to make tomato sauce, you will have to combine a tomato with a hammer.
Graphics are good, not ultra-realistic but realistic enough to be believable. The vivid colour palette adds to the fairly lighthearted ambiance; my only gripe is that there's no day/night cycle, but it is only a minor issue, all considering.
Concluding, I think this is a game that is worthy of your attention if you are anything close to being a fan of classic computer roleplaying games. I'm personally looking forward to the sequel as soon as I complete this episode.
My vote: 9.5 / 10

I feel like I've just finished 10 epic seasons of a fantasy TV show, by which I mean this is a long game! If I keep the analogy going, the first season started promisingly, but got a bit slow and confusing owards the end, but season two onwards kept ramping up the tension until you began to care about the crazy characters and story for the final series of epic showdowns in the final season.
Ok, let's stop that nonsense. This is a really good RPG, up there with the best. It's played in real-time but with turn-based combat, and unlike a lot of RPGs it doesn't get bogged down with endless combat either, there's quite a bit of variety in the types of quests and encounters you'll face. It's perhaps the closest a computer RPG has come to feeling like a Dungeons and Dragons campaign, a real sense of exploration, smart puzzles to overcome, and fun combat encounters with monsters where you have to prepare and think about each situation. The combat system is excellent; it doesn't degenerate into firing off the same spells and the same melee moves, rather you need to assess your enemies, figure out their weaknesses, and use your characters as a team to set up killer damage combos. It really encourages you to think about different loadouts, reconfiguring your characters etc towards the latter half of the game. The physical interaction between elements on the battlefield is also great to manipulate; oil and fire goes boom, water and electricity goes crackle, that kind of thing. At first it can feel overwhelming, burning oil everywhere, poison clouds limiting mobility, but you'll quickly learn how to take advantage of it all.
The game's main weakness is its beginning. There's the obligatory tutorial dungeon which is actually very enjoyable, whetting the appetite for more. And then... the game throws you into a large town with very little idea of what to do next. Trouble is, at this stage I just wanted to keep throwing fireballs around, not wander around chatting with the villagers. It's worth persevering though because there's a lot more in that town than first appears, and it's not too many hours before you'll be venturing out of the gates again and facing pretty stiff combat... especially if you go the wrong way! Throughout this enormous game there are areas that feel right for your level, and areas that are well beyond you. When you first leave the starting town, it isn't at all obvious where you should be going, other than the fact you're going to die. But it does get easier, and then the game really takes off. I wonder how many never make it out of that starting town (including me, for a whole year after I shelved the game).
What else? Well, the story is quite interesting, but it takes a long time to get there. The world has rules, and some curious lore, but you don't really appreciate this until much later on. There's plenty of dialog to read if you wish, or you can listen to the voice acting. It's not that the voice acting is necessarily bad, but everyone.... talks.... so... damn... slowly... and... dramatically.... that... I... just couldn't take it! I quickly turned the voice volume to zero and read the dialog instead.
But in the end, I just couldn't put this game down once it grabbed me. I've not been so addicted to an RPG since... hmmm... well, Divinity 2 in fact. Whatever magic sauce Larian used in the Dragon Knight Saga is present and accounted for here as well. It says a lot that even after 130 hours, I now want to go and play the sequel.

The game has been making significant improvements in both performance as well as the amount of new content added in the past few months. They've recently hired a lot of new developers including programmers and world builders they are doing a great job expanding the world. Recipes are now teachable. They added roving encounters on the overland map.
Crashes seem to be pretty much fixed now at least I haven't experienced one since probably two or three patches ago. The few patches have also improved load times between scenes quite a bit. Still waiting on the upgrade to Unity 5.4 to get further optimization.
Final wipe is here and I'm glad. The good we can finally play without fear of our characters being wiped each month. The bad the game is still heavily in development and has occasional crashes from bugs caused by the Unity graphics engine. Crashes are significantly less now and hopefully they'll be fixed very soon.
This release they added in significant much needed improvements the first one is you can now use E (or whatever key you map it to) to interact with things so double tap it to quick loot a corpse! Second one I'm happy about is you can now use locked cursor mode on the overland using the interact key to enter scenes. Most of the annoying popup hints have been replaced with much more useful hover text although some of it needs improvement still. The tutorial scene for the love quest line (which you start with a bow) is significantly better and more polished while the other quest line tutorials are being worked on and hopefully updated next release.
I've actually been going out and questing and found it's pretty enjoyable although some of the older areas in the game such as Necropolis could use some more polish and I'm sure they'll revisit those later. Right now the "land rush" is happening and I'm waiting to place my lot.
Performance is getting better but still lacking in some areas with frame drops and stuttering occasionally. They are going to try and update to Unity 5.4 in the next month which should hopefully improve things quite a bit.
Crashing and the higher learning curve aside I think most players will have a pretty enjoyable experience with the game in it's current state but like I've stated before it's not 100% done and very much in development so expect bugs and hickups. Be a good citizen and report them on the forums!
This release they added in an auto setting for the graphics that is supposed to help keep a constant frame rate at 30 FPS it's not quite there yet but it's a significant improvement. Currently because of how Unity works a lot of the game is using CPU instead of GPU but after they update to Unity 5.4 a lot of these problems will hopefully be fixed. The targeting system is a ton better and works really good now my main complaint is the actual target symbol but I've already been told that's going to be replaced next release most likely. I love Brittany Fields it's a great new area be sure to check it out. They are making great progress with clothing and armor updates as well as polish on the player avatars.

Well first let me tell you that I have followed the series on Kongregate while it had only released Epic Battle Fantasy 1 and to be honest the first and second game wasn't that great but then the third instalment came to the series and it changed everything becouse it had absolutely everything an JRPG could offer for a flash game.
I played Epic Battle Fantasy 3 about 5 to 10 times and when beating the game it gets a bit repetative so I usually came back for it every other month or so. Even when I had played it 9 times it was still as fun as it was the first time I started the game. But years passed and one day in 2013 just before I was about to turn off my computer I just wanted to check my Kongregate and there it was, Epic Battle Fantasy 4.
I played the game 2 times or so on Kongregate but never really took the time to beat it but then a half year later when it got to steam I instantly bought it and played it through. I'm currently at my second playthrough and it has been some time since I bought it now.
Lets get into the game shall we
Art and Graphics: (10/10 absoultely love the art style)
I personally love the cute anime based art style that the game has and the effects are well animated aswell as the world and items and don't forget all the monsters and characters all have high detail. You may wonder why I say that they are detailed while their not having that mush details like shadows and particles but that is becouse it has a perfect balance between being cartoonish and detailed so i would say that this is a kind of masterpiece.
Sound and Music: (11/10 its my favorite game music and I listen to it all the time)
I think that the sound effects in this game fits perfectly with only some few improvements coming into my mind sometimes but thats just if I'm picky.
The music which is written by HalcyonicFalconX is absolutely stunning and as it changes from every region you visit it also changes the games atmosphere. From relaxing in the forest to intense in the factory aswell as epic while in the volcano. All I can say is that without the music the game wouldn't have such an impact on me as it had.
Gameplay (combat): (8/10 the combat is great but can sometimes get a bit repetative)
The combat system is that of any JRPG just that it is simple, highly detailed and fun but it does get repetative when going through an older region or before you unlock multi target skills. Anyhow the combat can make you quite impressed sometimes as some skills/attacks is simply epic.
Gameplay (exploration): (9/10 the world and exploration is so relaxing)
With a bunch of puzzles, easter eggs and a large variety of biomes to explore the exploration gets quite relaxing and at the same time interesting as you never know what you will find before uncovering the map.
Content: (8/10 very mush content for having one developer)
There is a large variety of quests, skills, items and monster but its not as mush content as you will find in an AAA game but thats obviouse that it would not have as mush content. I'm not saying that the game is low on content of items etc. but when you reach high levels for example you might have acctually leveled all skills to max and uppgraded every piece of equipment to the max. There is still enough of content to satisfy any player but I'm just saying that you might end up with nothing more to level up other than the characters levels but you wont reach the "no more upgrades" untill your in New Game+ or New Game++.
Story: (7/10 even without any focus on the story I still like it)
The game focuses on exploration, upgrading and combat but still offers a small story and its quite lighthearted and ammusing but still every time the game reveales a new part of the story you really feel like you are there in that offten wierd situation.
Final Score: (9.8/10 this game is a must buy)
Why such a high score well here is some ups and downs:
+++ : The music is absolutely amazing
++ : The sound fits very well with almost everything within the game
++ : Exploration and puzzleing is very fun and can get you obsessed to clear everything to a 100%
++ : The combat system is very strategic and interesting but its still simple enough to be played by a child
++ : The sudden notices from the characters can get quite hilleriouse
++ : The games easter eggs makes the game quite fun if you try to notice them all that is
+ : The game offers New Game+ aswell as a large variety of items to use
+ : Some skills/attacks can only be described with one word only: EPIC
- : There is a large variety of Skills and Equipment but after starting New Game+ it feels like you found everything
- : Going back to an older region does not provide with any supported combat untill you reach the next New Game+
This is a must buy for all RPG fans aswell as to all Fantasy and Comedy fans so I hope this review helped and that you might buy this game.

Haters gonna hate. A lot of people are still holding a huge grudge against this game for reasons that, in my opinion, have very little to do with the game at hand and lot more to do with all of Hello Games' pre-release tomfoolery. People are also expressing a lot of dissapointment with the game's lack of adherence to rigidly defined categories, which I actually see as a big plus. If you're going to break new ground and blur old categories together, you have to expect that there's going to be some misses with the hits. That's just the downside of taking risks, something that I think the makers have done admirably.
With over 100 hours played, and a huge resurgence of interest since the game-changing foundation update, here are what I see as some key pros/cons:
CONS:
- god awful navigation of your ship near planet surfaces, still - it floats, speeds up, and slows down based on unclear obstacles and/or altitude factors
- massive, but meaningless space stations - you spend far more time walking around than doing anything in these, and all traders have more or less the exact same thing - the teleporter has added some use to these, but IMo the expereince still needs to be tightened up a lot
- clunky interstellar navigation - again, it feels very floaty - I feel like they sacrificed perofrmance for a sense of vastness
PROS:
- a truly brutal surival mode (post-foundation) with vicious enemies both on- and off-world, constant resource management, cruel planets, and just lots of general carnage. I've died 30+ times in 20 hours, compared to 7 in 80 pre-foundation.
- multi-system resource gathering - If you want to build up a base, you're going to have to travel far and wide looking for the elements you need. Even when you find a planet with the resource you need, you may have to do a lot of hunting.
- a promising, nascent mission system - as you hire underlings for your base, they send you on wild goose chases to upgrade technologies and base components. I find these fun, and providing a bit of structure that the earlier versions of the game lacked, when I want it
- a very slow upgrade system - I don't want to be murdering everything in two hours. I like that things take a while.
- related to the last point, the opportunity to ramp up personal challenges over time - I tried attacking a fugutive ship on survival mode early on, and promptly had my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me. That was a 1-star enemy, labelled "mostly harmless." I don't know how high they go, but I'm looking forward to finding out.

There are obviously a ton of other things people comment on, such as the tediousness of resource gathering (con) or the game's general beauty (pro). I just wanted to comment on a few things that have kept me interested in the game. All I would say if you're considering buying it, is disregard the extracurricular hype, and see if the features of the game itself are appealing to you (it's only going to get better with future patches).

Truly one of the most poignant games I've ever had the pleasure of playing, partly in thanks to the spectacular soundtrack and a mesmerizing art style. I'm normally predisposed to disliking platformers as the genre has become stale and bloated with too much mediocrity, but Ori and the Blind Forest breathes new life for me, not so much through groundbreaking innovation, but just perfection in the tried and true formulas of the Metroidvania games that precede it. The complaint that there is too much glow sometimes is well founded and a legitimate criticism to consider, but the problem seldom surfaced for me and presented trouble only on a number of occasions I could count with one hand.
: 10/10
The story isn't anything too complex, or great, even, but good enough in its own right and good enough to be carried through with soaring highs and heartbreaking lows by a powerful soundtrack that seamlessly accompanies the gameplay and does not linger. Many people have shared their qualms about a certain part later in the story that robs the story of its impact, and whilst I can agree that the cutscene cheapened some of the emotions built up from earlier, it did not devolve into cheesiness and no groans nor eye-rolling occured. Perhaps some explanation regarding
would have been nice.
: 8/10
Gameplay is smooth and responsive and a joy to experience. Difficulty wise, the game suddenly becomes wildly difficult at the first escape sequence; though there was much fun to be had in the twenty hefty minutes it took for me to complete it, I can see that being a complaint when the hours preceding it was practically a walk in the park. As for me, the difficulty was a welcome change from the handholding many games these days are predilected to doing, which I find borderline patronizing sometimes. As always, YMMV, however. The transitions for the other escape sequences were much smoother and handled better.
: 9/10
Conclusively, with a personal aggregate rating of 9.5/10, I would most definitely recommend this game to anybody at its current price (even better on sale for sure) unless they dislike platformers more than I do, or have a lower tolerance threshold on the Cheese-O-Meter, or just really hate being emotionally manipulated by some of the cutest, cuddliest characters the gaming industry has ever seen. If you don't fit into any of those categories, then I strongly suggest you pick up this game and treat yourself to this spectacle of a game.
I wish I could go back and experience this all for the first time again.

I'm pretty easy to please with FPS's, but this together with Perfect Dark Zero and Red Faction 2, is one of the worst sequels I've ever played. I first tried this on the 360 and then got it for pennies on a Steam sale or something apparently, well I want those pennies back. I am a huge fan of the first two games because of the amazing combat, cool atmosphere, and fantastic level design. This fails on all accounts plus more, even the new engine somehow feels chunkier and like a backstep from FEAR 2. The levels are small, the game just spams you with enemies with no time to take in any atmosphere whatsoever, the story and music is dryer than sand, and this game simply does nothing good. Surely there is another FPS you could be playing instead of this. Gotta love those ninja zombies who throw rapid firing silent knives or something at you.

FEAR 3 is a good FPS, but the story pales when compared to the first two games in the series. For starters, it's very short. Granted, I played it on easy as I have too many games to play and kind of rushed it, but it was still very short. The story is also extremely simple in plot and I could describe the entire plot of the game in a few sentences.
The plot involves Point Man, the player character from FEAR (the first game). Set nine months after the events of the first two games, Point Man is currently a prisoner in a favela in Brazil and escapes after a psychic connection with his brother, Paxton, the villain from the first game. After escaping the prison, the two of you travel back to Fairport (basically Seattle), to try and reach Alma, the psychic horror inducing woman/girl from the first two games. If you played the first two games, you'd recall that she♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Beckett, the player character from FEAR 2. Well, you and Paxton crash land in a suburb and have to make your way to the city, teaming up with Jin, the FEAR team member from the first game, and eventually finding Beckett who is being held captive by Armacham, the evil corporation that did the experiments on Alma and you and your brother. I don't wanna spoil the game, but there really isn't that much else to say on the plot. You just fight your way through the city, an airport, the tower, etc, until you reach the endgame.
Being a horror/FPS, I found this to be much less terrifying than the first two games and whenever I saw Alma, I wasn't even phased. It was just kind of like, "Oh, there's Alma. She'll disappear anyway, nothing to worry about. Unlike that one time in FEAR where you actually had to shoot her before she reaches you."
This isn't even a bad game as there actually are elements in this one that aren't in the others. Such as the cover system. At least I'm pretty sure the cover system wasn't in the first two, it's been a while since I played them on the 360. But the cover system in this one was probably the best cover system in an FPS I've played, as you actually stay in first person and can stick to the cover while leaning out.
I guess I can say I was satisfied with this game as it concludes the story of Point Man and Alma, but it could have been a lot more interesting than just fighting your way to the city. There are cutscenes that do explain the story, but, again, it could have been more involved.
Good game though. Shooting elements were, of course, the best bits.

Even though Shroud of the Avatar is only in pre-alpha currently (as of Nov 2014), it is still worth the price of Early Access.  Despite being so early in its development cycle, a lot of features are being rapidly iterated on and getting into a playable and most importantly, fun, state.  Granted, being in Early Access comes with all its bugs and incomplete features and it still requires a ton of balancing, but the world they've created is something to behold, deeply rich in story and lore.  Additionally, the Community is involved in creating content for the game and frequently holds many fun in-game events.
You can see it shaping up to be the true spiritual successor to both the single player Ultimas as well as Ultima Online, yet maintaining its own identiy and unique take on certain gameplay elements, such as selective multiplayer, deck-based combat, persistent housing, free form conversation, and entirely player-driven economy, where even that phat loot dropped by the mobs was created by players (and you'll even know who created it via its maker's mark!).  And it dares to throw away the many tired tropes of handholding MMOs such as quest markers, radar mini-maps, forced/limited dialog trees, global chat, global auction houses, and even quest journals.
Be a part of this ground breaking game and get it now in Early Access!  Highly Recommended.

I have been following this game for ten months now and I have played it since Pre-Alpha Release 10. I have already recommended this game to all my friends and I would recommend it to anyone who likes the RPG, MMO or SandBox genre. Dedicated to make this game right we have Richard Garriott (Yes, Lord British himself!) along with other committed professionals.
The core elements of this game, for me, lies around Community interactions, an impressive housing system, a deep storyline, immersive environments like dungeons, cities and swamps, Crafting and PvP. It's classless system is a real bonus to its combat and crafting mechanics.
In my opinion the only problem of this game right now is it's learning curve. I would say that it will take you 10 to 20 hours of play to understand enough of the combat & crafting mechanics to play the game properly (It's not that much. But you shouldn't expect to master the game in the first few minutes of play like you probably did in some new RPGs and MMOs.). The good news is that you won't need to know it all. For example, if you plan to play as a Blacksmith you won't need to learn the complexity behind the Cooking System. Yes, Cooking is complex here! All this complexity keeps the game interesting for everyone (even cookers!) at the expense of an increased learning curve.
About crafting, I would call any fan of Ultima Online out there to try this game. It will be perfectly possible to play as a Crafter (Blacksmith, Carpenter, Miner, Farmer, etc) with minimal combat interactions.
For PvPers, there will be areas of the game where you are automatically flagged for PvP, you may also duel almost anywhere, you will be able to do a quest that flags you for PvP (almost) anywhere (until you do another quest that takes the PvP flag away) and we will have Guild Wars!
The scenes (Zones/Instances) are awesome. Dungeons are really dark with lots of secret passages that really rewards exploration. Swamp and Snowy scenes are also really immersive.
The housing here is the most awesome idea that I have ever seen. Player housing lies inside the cities of the game. Let's take the NPC town of Owl's Head for a quick example. Owl's Head have about 12 NPC buildings and something around 70 player houses (from simple cabanas to mighty castles!). The city really feels alive. Not to mention Player Owned Towns!
Community Interaction and Role-playing is the best this game have to offer. Player run events like town meetings, guild meetings, PvP Tournaments and much, much more.
Disclaimer: This game is months away from its final release, so you may expect BUGs (and are also welcome to report them), WIPEs and unfinished or unpolished areas/mechanics. With that in mind, I would like to say that this will probably be the game that I will be playing for the next years. (Again) I would recommend it anyone who likes RPG games, Pen & Paper RPGs, RP interactions or MMORPGs.
I hope to see you in-game.

In short:
A definite recommend for any fan of turn-based RPGs. The intricacies of the fighting system in this game are in my opinion the best there are (but I haven't played DoS 2 yet). Fighting feels extremely rewarding once you get what combines with what,
You will enjoy the story if you value choices and possibilities to handle quests in more than one way, and which paints a picture of whom your characters really are (e.g. materialistic, romantic, vindictive or living saints, etc). Other than that the story is rather mediocre, definitely on the cheesy spectrum,  but not bad when they balance the pompous and the cheesy out.
Music is okay, nicely accompanies the game's fantasy settings, but doesn't stay with you once you're done playing.
Took me around 80 hours to complete my playthrough and I must say that at times it felt too long, but overall a pleasurable experience.
Also - it is both couch and online co-op, which means you can get through the entire story with another person, question and argue the decisions they're making and shape the story how you see fit (either by agreeing or disagreeing and then winning a rock/paper/scissors minigame, literally).
--------------Detailed review --------------------
Story - 6.5/10
It's mostly cheesy. Sometimes the comedy was not to my liking, other times it was spot on and very good.
The plot twists moved the story to very pompous hights but I didn't roll my eyes that much.
Thanks to how the game allowed you to reflect your morality (be that your own as a person, or the one you have invented for your characters) I did immerse myself in it,
I even went ahead and made a few choices which went against my personal beliefs, but in accordance with how my characters were shaping up to be, and I really enjoyed the fact that the game made me go out of my moral comfort zone.
Nevertheless, I was rarely going through the story with anticipation of what will happen next.
---
Gameplay: 10/10
This is where the game shines. The combat is turn-based and strategic, allowing you to move around while fighting, sacrificing attack points for movement. Positioning plays some role as well as the environment you're fighting on.
The fights are mainly about setting up the environment and enemies for combos and then reaping the rewards when you execute.
Enemies, weapons,  spells, arrows and granades have different effects or elements and, together with other elements, either create environmental hazards, like burning grounds, slippery ice or electrified water, or cancel each other out (like freezing a burning enemy will take off the damage over time effect that burning does and will never freeze the target, as they were on fire).
Setting up the combos requires you to know which effect goes with what, what resistances the enemies have, etc.
|This knowledge also allow you to react against statuses which are affecting your party members.
The combinations are limited, but for me they were always fun to setup and watch.
Apart from that there is a lot of puzzles of varied difficulty, where you will need to do something or find something before you will be able to move to a next level.
Majority of those puzzles can be completed in more than one way, but not all of them.
I really enjoyed the gameplay aspects of this game, although sometimes the puzzles and fights felt difficult for the sake of having them difficult, or overly complicated to make sure you won't think it's too easy.
That led to some frustration, but nothing a break and clear mind couldn't handle. Though, unfortunately, sometimes the clues given by the game are awfuly vague to the point that some puzzles I have beaten with pure luck rather than understanding of what was required of me to do.
I still give it 10 out of 10 points as I don't remember such a fun combat system in any game I have played.
-------
Graphics:
7/10
The game looks good. The environments are detailed and insteresting, the monsters varied and creative.
My biggest beef with the graphics where locations which clearly reused assets from the previous ones (like, every forest in the game).
This similiarity between zones could have been justified storyise,but after I have seen so many fancy locations in the game, the ones with reused assets hurt twice as badly.
It is nowhere near Dragon AGe 2 bad, but it is clearly visible when assets were reused.
The character creation allows for some customization and a degree of personal preferences, although it is nothing fancy.
----
Music:
6/10
The music is okay. I really don't know how to describe it better.
It fits the fantasy story, sometimes is too much on the happy platformer for a 3 year old side, but most times it accompanies the locations and story nicely.
I didn't mind it, sometimes I loved it, but nothing really stuck with me. I am not sure if I'd be able to recognize if a piece was from this game if someone played to me out of context of the game.

I found Divinity: Original Sin to be an enjoyable game but not without it's flaws.
Generally, I prefer more "serious" RPGs and the storyline of this game was fairly silly at times.  In addition, the battles in the game varied from very well designed to situations where you could easily be one shot killed if an enemy chose to use a particular attack (one boss in particular intiiates combat by mass fireballing your group, which is generally not survivable - you have to know to send one guy in with massive resistances or use specific strategies ahead of time or you won't survive the first round).  In fact, the point at which I stopped playing was during a 2nd playthrough when a particular boss (different from the one already mentioned) used such an attack and took my entire party from full HP to dead in that attack.
There is also a certain area of the game where there are monsters that if aggroed will immediately initiate combat, almost always go first as they have high intiative and charge your party and explode, doing enough damage to kill anyone except a high HP character.  The way to counteract them is to attack them at range out of combat, but as there is no way to initiate turn based mode with a keypress, you have to be able to right click (and then select attack in a drop-down) to attack them while they are on the move between when they move into bow range, before they move close enough to start combat.  I do not enjoy those sort of twitch clicking mechanics in what is supposed to be a turn based game.
All of that said, I found the RPG levelling mechanics and overall gameplay enjoyable.  The spells and abilities in this game are fairly well designed and the crafting system is well thought out and fairly powerful.
I'd recommend Divinity: Original Sin if you enjoy turn based RPGs, perhaps not as highly as other reviews, but it's definitely worth playing.

Reus is a pure optimization game - build a village, give them what they want (but no more) with the limited land available, repeat ad nauseum. The various tech trees of plants/animals/minerals hides its information away and it quickly becomes apparent that the most optimal way to play is with an Excel Spreadsheet and the Wiki next to it. Your reward for optimizing and completing a project is ambassadors and buildings you can use to do more optimizing, all while staring at the same planet you set up at the very start of the game. Want to go exploring the tech tree? Too bad, you've just ruined all the bonuses from your old plants and need to set up new ones, all while dealing with obnoxious cooldown timers.
Reus isn't bad at what it does, but it lacks purpose beyond optimization for its own sake.

There are two schools of game design. The first, puts emphasis on how things “feel”. The second, tries to make all the numbers add up on a spreadsheet. The first may not be all that balanced, but the second tends to be no fun at all. Reus leans too much towards the second.
A session of Reus goes like this: you pick how long you want to play, 30, 60 or 120 minutes. There is a non-time limited Freeplay, but you won’t unlock any new technologies in that mode. As the game starts, you’re presented with a flat, formless planet and four Giants. Each Giant represents a sort-of element: Water, Swamp, Forest and Rock. Each can terraform the landscape in their own way, and manipulate the ecosystem by creating creatures or plants. Casting these “spells” costs nothing, and often you’ll have to overwrite previously placed elements as the situation changes.
Spells don’t have any real logical match-up to their Giant, which can be very confusing until you have it all mapped out via rote memorization. After a terrain type has been made, such as forest, settlers will move in and set up a little camp. The way the Giants move around, the circular cut-away view of the planet, and all the little people doing their thing, is very charming. But underneath that charm is a very cold, soulless spreadsheet that governs how the game plays out.
Reus is more of a puzzle game than a god sim. Settlers will construct a “project”, mostly at random, and you need to manage the landscape within a town’s boundaries to meet the project’s completion criteria. These range from having enough Food, Tech, or more difficult ones, like going to war with another settlement. Fauna and flora have “synergies”, which unlock additional resources when things are placed a certain way. It’s a house-of-cards balancing act, placing things next to other things in the most optimal way. When a project completes, you gain an Ambassador which - when paired with a specific Giant - unlocks more powers for that Giant. New projects start, and you need to rearrange things to meet the new criteria.
The foil to the system comes from Greed. If a town grows too fast, or lacks sufficient Threat from nearby Predators, they’ll stop fearing the Giants and may even start to attack them with arrows. Which is possibly the only real humanising moment to be found in the game, watching the Giants cower. When the time limit runs out, the Giants go to sleep, and you unlock new technologies to use in the next session, depending on how well you did.
I kept asking myself, “is Reus badly designed, or am I just bad at it?” It’s a difficult question, made all the more vexing when you’re aware of the Dunning–Kruger effect. Reus is a badly designed game. But that doesn’t mean it’s a bad game. There just isn’t much to it.

Reus is a simulation strategy game that allows you to control four giants to create a whole world. You can choose between swamps, deserts, mountains, oceans and forests. As you create your world humans will build cities, will you help the humans achieve a utopia... or you can smash them... they probably reserved it.

Has anyone seen this ever watched the old cartoon "The Iron Giant"? (Warner bros, 1999) This game is nothing like that movie. I just wanted to see if there's anyone else that remembers that film. Actually all that's similar is the giant aspect.
I don't think there is a single word spoken throughout the game, the game starts out by teaching you how to use the various giants. and explains how to shape the world around you. When I started I felt very overwhelmed about how much I had to learn, don't worry about learning it all right away, you'll have plenty of time to slowly get used to the concepts in the game as you progress.
As you play you unlock new animals/fruit/plants and longer world lengths. As you progress you need to accomplish various different goals, this give the game a sense of direction to keep trying to get better, and experience different things.
You only control 4 giants, you select various abilities and tell them where to build and what to build. When the humans show up you try to help them and keep their development very balanced so that they don't have more than their neighbors and try to prevent wars... unless you want wars, then go ahead and give one city all the things and watch the humans become greedier then Ebenezer Scrooge.
the game controls are simple, you can play the game with just clicking, but I try to get used to the hot keys for faster response time. the giant also need to move to the selected location before it can build or destroy anything, this does limit how fast you can create on your world.

The achievements in Reus are tied directly with achievements in game, and these achievements, when earned, unlock various new animals/fruit/plants to add to your world. This makes getting achievements actually mean something, other then aesthetics and a good pat on the back.
Reus costs $9.99, I've put in 11 hours so far, this game is by far worth it's price. I did buy the game over the steam summer sale, but even at full price that's pretty good quality.

I strongly recommend the game to anyone who likes strategy games, again the game has some fun things to unlock, and various ways to play through it to unlock more the controls are simple, the strategy is engaging, and I just enjoyed playing this game, and will continue playing because I still haven't played through without getting at least one new thing unlocked.

The divers are playing a first-person-shooter style gameplay, where they look for gold, protect their robotic companion S.T.E.V.E and try to survive the oncoming shark attacks with a variety of different weapons ranging from SPP-1 pistols, past automatics to flares, sonar buoys mines, aka consumables. Join the Division, become part of the largest LARP event in history.
You're an elite Agent, equipped with the best Airsoft BB arsenal your local Toys'R'us has to offer.
But beware! The bad kids don't play by the rules, teach them a lesson, 300 or so BBs to the face will overwhelm them with PAIN, and victory will be yours!
Dress in the tackiest of fashions, pretend like the world is ending, make sure not to hop fences you're not supposed to get behind. Do the same asinine sh*t over and over.
All jokes aside, this game might be one of the worst executions of a great concept in Ubisoft history.
Forcing a tactical squad shooter into the mould of a very average MMORPG is a very painful thing to watch.
There is absolutely no immersion to be found in the Division. It's just not possible. And a shame too, since the world they created looks simply stunning, and the attention to detail is astonishing.
Add to that the slew of technical problems, broken cutscenes, glitchy animations, rubberbanding enemies...
And the worst movement system of any modern Ubisoft game. Considering they clearly know how it's done, you'd think someone from the Watch_Dogs or Assassin's Creed team would have helped out on that front a tiny bit.
The game provides no challange, all missions are pretty much the same, the story is completely forgettable. Fighting "bosses" is always a question of endurance, never skill. Enemy AI is easy to exploit and glitch out, rendering any fight completely pointless and turning the game into a grind.
This bullet-sponge system worked for Borderlands, a game Ubisoft tried very hard to emulate here, when fighting giant mutant dinosaurs, but it all falls apart when you need three times his bodyweight in lead to put down one angry teenager with a shotgun.
Clearly a passion project of a very skilled and talented art team, completely abolished by an incompetent, rookie team of coders and designers.
I opted out of buying this game at launch, after I heared what ubisoft had done through the first reviews, I was hoping the Free Weekend would provide me with some closure, getting to experience the atrocity for myself. That did not turn out so well.
One cannot stop to see an amazing game that could have been.
Years of wasted potential.

This game is a severe letdown for fans of the Gauntlet series. However, if you've never played any of the previous games, this is a decent hack and slash game for playing with friends.
The developers seemingly removed all RPG elements from the former games. No more leveling up or any of the perks that go with it. Speaking of perks, each character's action skill is only a one shot attack now. In previous games, it was a tiered attack that allowed players to build it up all the way by killing enemies and unleash a massive room clearing attack or choose to fire it off early(but less powerful) in dicey situations.
As of this writing, all elements of player customization are gone as well. The Warrior is locked to red; the Valkyrie is locked to blue, etc. Parties cannot have duplicates of characters. In the past games, two players could both join a party as the same character but have different colors. The only customization options left are the mastery levels, which are basically in-game achievements that then give your character passive ability boosts.You can also buy different items to change your character's loadout, although these items are purely cosmetic. Not quite the same as hoarding gold to directly bulk up your character's abilities at the shop.
The levels are exactly what you'd expect for a hack and slash game, though every 2nd level in the 1st world is a run level from Death whereas in previous games Death spawned randomly in any level. Every 2nd level in the 2nd world is a dark cave where you can't see anything, etc. There are 3 worlds each with 3 "chapters" and a boss battle. Each chapter has 3 levels (floors in the game text) Very formulaic.
Bottom line: If you want a decent hack and slash game that's fun with 4 friends (and with friends only) then pick this up when it's on sale. If you're a fan of the old Gauntlet games, my previous statement still stands, just prepare for a massive let down.

Alright here goes nothing.
Before I say anything else, I gotta clarify I got this game in a giveaway (and from what i can tell you did a lot of those to get people into the game).
This game? It's pretty fun. Basically, imagine clash royale with better graphics, rotated sideways, and with no p2w levelling system. (also gratuitous amounts of blood because every game needs that)

There's also a ton of different cards which opens up many different playstyles, from heavier decks to spammier decks to building-based decks to staller decks. Plus the hero system adds a bit more variety to the mix, giving opportunities for synergies between your hero's skills and your decks. There's at least that.
Now the problem is, obtaining the cards themselves is based on a random sort of lootcrate/roulette system. You buy tokens to spin that with in-game gold, which you get from daily challenges, achievements and (possibly) a single daily resource spin. Don't let the rather drab, brown screenshots put you off; this is a game that is both dripping with personality and that is remarkably true to the original arcade experience while simultaneously bringing it bang up to date for a modern audience.
It's not trying to be something it's not. It's not trying to be Diablo or any kind of RPG; it's trying to be a modern-day Gauntlet. And it's doing so remarkably well. The four characters all play in a distinctly unique fashion -- far more so than in the original game -- and in local co-op in particular it's just a joy to crawl some dungeons together, battling over the loot, the crown and the inevitable arguments over "who is the best" on the end-level summary screen.
I couldn't say if it would be quite so fun in single-player as I haven't tried it as of the writing of this review, but if you have at least one friend willing to fight alongside you, I can happily give this a solid recommendation.

The original Gauntlet was perhaps the pre-eminent arcade hack-and-slash quarter eating game. The 2014 remake follows in the tradition of the original game, but changes the formula somewhat; rather than having four identical classes with the levels being what really defines how you fight, instead there are four different classes where the emphasis is on your powers and teamwork.
Overall, the gameplay experience was decent enough, but there wasn’t all that much of it; for $20, only about 4-5 hours of gameplay feels a bit limited, but the limited nature of the gameplay meant that stretching the game out any longer would have been a mistake as well, as there just isn’t enough meat to the game for such. While there are challenges to complete which grant the player permanent minor buffs, and a number of relics which the player can unlock, in the end none of them really felt interesting or exciting enough that I had to play the game over and over again, grinding through the levels to unlock them. At $5, it would be a pretty good value; at $10, it might be something to do with your friends. At $20, though, I have to say that you can get more bang for your buck elsewhere.

Truly one of the most poignant games I've ever had the pleasure of playing, partly in thanks to the spectacular soundtrack and a mesmerizing art style. I'm normally predisposed to disliking platformers as the genre has become stale and bloated with too much mediocrity, but Ori and the Blind Forest breathes new life for me, not so much through groundbreaking innovation, but just perfection in the tried and true formulas of the Metroidvania games that precede it. The complaint that there is too much glow sometimes is well founded and a legitimate criticism to consider, but the problem seldom surfaced for me and presented trouble only on a number of occasions I could count with one hand.
: 10/10
The story isn't anything too complex, or great, even, but good enough in its own right and good enough to be carried through with soaring highs and heartbreaking lows by a powerful soundtrack that seamlessly accompanies the gameplay and does not linger. Many people have shared their qualms about a certain part later in the story that robs the story of its impact, and whilst I can agree that the cutscene cheapened some of the emotions built up from earlier, it did not devolve into cheesiness and no groans nor eye-rolling occured. Perhaps some explanation regarding
would have been nice.
: 8/10
Gameplay is smooth and responsive and a joy to experience. Difficulty wise, the game suddenly becomes wildly difficult at the first escape sequence; though there was much fun to be had in the twenty hefty minutes it took for me to complete it, I can see that being a complaint when the hours preceding it was practically a walk in the park. As for me, the difficulty was a welcome change from the handholding many games these days are predilected to doing, which I find borderline patronizing sometimes. As always, YMMV, however. The transitions for the other escape sequences were much smoother and handled better.
: 9/10
Conclusively, with a personal aggregate rating of 9.5/10, I would most definitely recommend this game to anybody at its current price (even better on sale for sure) unless they dislike platformers more than I do, or have a lower tolerance threshold on the Cheese-O-Meter, or just really hate being emotionally manipulated by some of the cutest, cuddliest characters the gaming industry has ever seen. If you don't fit into any of those categories, then I strongly suggest you pick up this game and treat yourself to this spectacle of a game.
I wish I could go back and experience this all for the first time again.

Just finished the game... Wow, what an incredible gaming experience. The animation combined with the fluid controls produce such a joy of movement. All of this is on top of incredibly beautiful backdrops and accompanied by incredible music that is at times stirring and at times melancholy. And this music in turn is the perfect complement to the story, which is one of the most emotionally engaging of any game I have ever played despite there being no dialog. You don't have to be a platform gamer to enjoy this, though if you aren't accustomed to platform games it might be quite a challenge; this game is classic Nintendo-hard. Get this game.

Imagine taking a supermodel to bed, but then they just jab you in the ribs with a stick for awhile. That's kind of what Ori and the Blind Forest felt like. It's gorgeous on the surface, but when you get down to business you start having second thoughts. It took me 7 hours to complete and I died 261 times. I can't give it a negative review, because it's a very lovingly crafted game and the world is truly something to behold. However, I can warn you about the bad stuff and let you decide for yourself if any of these are dealbreakers:
1: "Nice forest you've got there! It'd be a shame if someone covered fricking everything with spikes, wouldn't it?" I wasn't expecting this game to have death coated death with death filling. I sure hope you like jumping puzzle gauntlets of spikes and one shot death rays that you're forced to repeat over and over with floaty controls, because that's what's on the menu. Nothing takes the majestic out of something like being forced to repeat it until you're ready to throw your controller through the monitor because a random rock hiding behind blinding particle effects just one shot you at the end of a gauntlet while the screen was shaking so hard you couldn't even see what was going on.
2: The combat is terrible. Fighting enemies just isn't fun. You spam an auto-aim attack while trying not to get hit by blinding bright orb thingies hiding behind other blindingly bright thingies. You can't tell which thingies are which, because everything you do or encounter involves blinding bright thingies.
3: Your movement starts out very gimped and you can't reach most areas until the end of the game. Just when running and jumping around finally becomes fluid, it's over. I understand that upgrading abilities is part of progression and has its place, but I think the curve was a bit off here. There's a constant feeling of being held back until the last couple hours.
All in all, I still have to give it a positive review because it's a serviceable platformer with an exceptionally beautiful world. If you're looking for great gameplay though, I'd much sooner recommend Rayman Origins, Rayman Legends, or Battleblock Theater for platforming fun. Ori is largely style over substance and rings a bit hollow because of it.

Once you've done this and located the memento you break a barrier around the memento with the orbs and finish things off with a tile flipping puzzle. You then move on to the next area and repeat the whole process.
I enjoy the humor in this game quite a bit. It's a good mix of cornball, referential, and just plain odd.
The game doesn't seem to support multiple resolutions or even the steam overlay. Screenshots don't work well because of this. I'm used to taking an excess of screenshots during gameplay and constantly found myself missing the ability to do so easily.
I experienced an odd glitch during the course of my playthrough in which I became capable of walking on any surface of the current screen. I was forced to reload due to inability to interact with anything at that point though.
The controls feel a bit loose an imprecise on a wireless xbox 360 controller. The D-pad cannot even be used in an attempt to counter this frustration. You are limited to the left analog joystick. It's necessary to utilize the mouse for the tile flipping puzzle sections. Near the end of the game there's some different gameplay mechanics that I just switched entirely to keyboard in order to better aid in progression.
All told I rather enjoyed this game despite any issues I had with it.

I feel as though I have played this game a reasonable enough amount of time to have a grasp of the various things there are to do in it, and unfortunately not only do not recommend it, I recommend -against- it. The fact of the matter is that since Stronghold Kingdoms is free to play, they need to make their money through microtransactions, else they would not make money. Unless you want ads interrupting your gameplay every so often, that is pretty much the only option.
That being said, because of the model and scope that this game has with the player interaction, it comes down to who has the fattest wallet IRL to shell out tens if not hundreds of dollars on cards, units, and so on in order to overwhelm their enemies. That removes the aspect of earning something through gameplay, and really cheapens the experience as a whole.
Now, there -is- something to be said about being able to engage in politics and utilize diplomacy, subterfuge, spying and so forth to get what you want. I became rather powerful in my time in the game, and was commanding -other- players to attack things for me. That is not boasting, but simply stating how if you can communicate you can better win. Unfortunately it simply does not matter if the enemy is shelling out more IRL money.
Pay-to-win is a common buzzword, and although I love the city-building in this game, almost every facet of it is marred by this unfortunate reminder. Even the time it takes to construct buildings. I hope that some day this franchize is resurrected to its former glory.

I first bought this game quite a few years ago, long before the Enhanced Edition came out. At that time I completed the first act of the game and started slogging through the second before realizing I wasn't having a ton of fun. I then stopped playing. Fast forward to now and I decided to give the Enhanced Edition a go, as I knew the game had potential and was hoping the EE realized it. That was a pretty great decision.
The EE fixes so many issues from the original, and for those of you who are just thinking about buying it today, I would fully recommend it. There are some parts of the game that aren't awesome (mines and traps fricken' every where), but by and large this is an excellent RPG. Combat is a ton of fun (just make sure you are careful when clicking, because enemies jump around or sway and this can lead to some frustrating misclicks), and can be challenging (or not if you play on an easier difficulty). The beginning of the game is a bit rough, you have a bit of combat followed by hours of running around Cyseal talking to everyone. The biggest problem at this point is XP, fighting enemies even 1 level higher than you can be almost impossible, so you need to gather every scrap of XP in Cyseal to make sure you can keep up with the enemies. But after that the game continues along with a great mixture of dungeon crawling, puzzles, story, and combat encounters.
If you are a fan of western style RPGs (Dragon Age, Pillars of Eternity, Baldur's Gate, Knights of the Old Republic, Fallout 1/2, etc) then this could very well be what will occupy you and entertain for the next few weeks! Give it a shot!

SKULLGIRLS
Developed by:
Reverge Labs
Lab Zero Games
Review by:
Aaron Matthew Holmes
Skullgirls, a 2D fighter game developed by Reverge Labs, Lab Zero Games, and published by: Autumn Games, Konami, Marvelous AQL (PC), and CyberFront (Japan), was originally released in April 2012 for the Playstation Network and Xbox Live. The game has recently rereleased on Windows and STEAM systems this year.
The game, in a fantasy setting, takes place in the 1940’s post-war America.
Skullgirls features 14 characters, one non-playable (Marie), and 5 DLC characters.
Skullgirls allows the player to experience single-player and multiplayer battles, however, single player allows the player to view each characters story as they progress through battle after battle.
For the review of Skullgirls, I’ve played through the game with one of the most iconic characters in the game, or at least, one that I’ve seen cosplayed numerous times at conventions; Ms. Fortune.
I can’t necessarily avoid spoilers as the game has been out at least a year at this point, so feel free to continue reading past this point, or skip to the end for my overall review/rating of the game.
Skull-Girls-2
Playing through Skullgirls, and selecting one the character Ms. Fortune, it’s immediately seen just how quickly this game is violent, yet comedic at the same time (see above image). Ms. Fortune attempts to intervene with a creepy guy hitting on an innocent waitress, only to be beheaded, however, there is some fort of magic that allows her to control both her body and head even while detached to then attack and beat the crap out of the man.
Skull-Girls-3
As the storyline continues, Ms. Fortune finds a strong opponent, known as a “Skullgirl” who possesses strong powers, strong enough that they could grant wishes (at least from my first playthrough and understanding).
Skull-Girls-4
After the battle, Ms. Fortune is presented the opportunity to take control of the same power as the Skullgirl to grant her any wish, but decidedly doesn’t use the, obviously evil, power for that. She decides to continue life as she has.
Skull-Girls-5
I’ll definitely be playing this game, in single player only, with the other characters to see how the other stories turn out and to see what kind of twists there are within each. The developers of this game have found a good balance of storytelling and comedy with this fighting game, and it’s definitely changed my thoughts, positively, on fighting games, if only for this game.
Audio:  4/5
Well used audio, several variations for attacks, hitting, and being hit.
Soundtrack is lively and fits with the battles and story scenes.
Only thing that’s missing is well-done voice acting to finish this off for a perfect 5.
Story: 4/5
The stories vary from character to character, and are humorous throughout the game.
The game does, however, throw you into matches with different characters without explaining why you’re fighting them, or how you encountered them. The game does this with specific battles only it seems.
Controls: 3.5 -> 4.5
My rating on the controls is based off the fact that I’m not a master at fighting games, in fact, I’m a “button masher” who just gets lucky when playing these types of games. The game does offer a tutorial system for battling, but when you need to memorize what key on your keyboard or gamepad matches the in-game ‘key terminology’, it becomes confusing and a game of “let’s see what this button does!”.
The controls are much more suited for those who are familiar with the fighter genre and can master combos, skills, and moves with the different characters.
Graphics: 5/5
The graphics in this game are beautiful and well designed, especially when it comes down to the characters themselves. The cutscene artwork, level artwork, and overall graphic design of the game is not inconsistent in any way shape or form, and a great use of the talents of the artists who worked tirelessly on this game.
Overall Score: 4.5/5
This game, while definitely suited toward the Fighter-Game audience, can be played by those with little or no experience, so long as the difficulty is set low enough, and provides a humorous yet enjoyable experience for those who give it a try.

There is so much to love in this utterly gorgeous indie fighter.
1. There's an excellent tutorial, which the more famous (possibly elitist?) fighters seem to neglect. And it's not just "press a button to punch" type shrill, it actually teaches you proper fighting game techniques such as mix-ups and cancelling. So Skullgirls has a far better learning curve than many other fighters.
2. The visuals are stunning. I may be misquoting here but I'm told that the frame rate of the character animations is twice that of other fighters. In addition, a 3D lighting engine is used that looks absolutely sublime, and the game's style - a mix of "dark deco" and anime influences - is just utterly fantastic.
3. The characters (of which there are admittedly few, but more are coming via DLC) are pretty damn cool. How many other games let you play as a madcap cartoon-obsessed cyborg, fighting an eldritch shapeshifting monstrosity?
Of course, some may dismiss the game due to its admittedly heavy use of fanservice, but personally I don't think such a problem exists. Yes, some of the character costumes are somewhat revealing, but other fighters have done far worse, and the fanservice here is never used to define character - It's just a minor detail, which you'll probably wind up paying no attention to because the rest of the game is just
.

IT'S SKULLGIRLS BABEH!
In all seriousness, if you're new to fighting games and want to get into it, this game really is for you. It has an amazing tutorial, teaching you about movement, motions, how to combo, supers and many things more. While some stuff is only used in Skullgirls, others like how to use assists, pushblocking, how to use supers and more are also used in games like marvel vs capcom, street fighter, king of fighters and other 2D fighting games.
While people might get distracted by the almost-all-female cast with a variety of... lets say... unachievable body proportions, the artstyle itself is amazing. It really looks like a cartoon/anime and not just like a fightgame.
While it is easy to learn, it is hard to master. The relatively small cast of characters plays extremely different to each other - not a single character is the same. Even the april-fools "clone" character plays very different to the original character.
VERY BIG BONUS POINTS:
+ The online is absolutely perfect. I don't know a single fighting game (maybe Killer Instinct, I never played it tho) that has such an amazing netcode. Most of the time you can even fight enemies from different continents and it will be fine!
+ The DLC policy. New characters are free for the first 3 months of their release.
+ You get access to the endless beta, where you can play new characters in their early stage and help the game grow.
The only gripe I have with the game is the story mode for some characters. For others it's pretty fun, but some characters have maybe one textbox and it is called a "story". It's still leagues above other storymodes in Fighting games, but let's be real - you only play story modes ONCE. This isn't why you're here.
All in all, I can highly recommend this game. You might think that it is just material to wank to, but believe me - it is far from that. Just because some characters are sexy doesn't mean it just wants you to drop your pants. If you want to do that, you might get a kick out of the DoA Xtreme Beach Volleyball franchise, I guess.

I've only played this one and the original Scribblenauts, so it's possible that this is what all the current games are like, but ...
The basic idea of Scribblenauts is that you are let loose in a series of levels, each of which contains a "Starite." As Max, your goal is to obtain the Starite by any means necessary. Fortunately, you are armed with a magic notebook; when Max writes nouns the game understands in the notebook, whatever he's written is summoned into reality. With Scribblenauts Unlimited he gains the ability to use adjectives, as well, even adding them to existing objects.
In the first Scribblenauts game, getting the Starite usually (but not always) required solving a physics puzzle. In Scribblenauts Unlimited, though, you generally just end up walking up to an NPC, being told the NPC wants something, and then writing down examples of whatever is requested.
For instance, an NPC might be described as a "Hungry Vegetarian." Write down "apple" "pancake" "carrot" get Starite. (That was off the top of my head, but it might actually be in the game. That's the level of sophistication.) It's less a video game and more a vocabulary test. Oh, and since a LOT of puzzles require knowledge of English-language culture, don't even expect to be able to use it to help learn the language.
It doesn't help that in the first game Max would often find himself in danger and need to find a way to protect himself. Here, the first thing you do in each level is click on Max and add adjectives like "Immortal Flying Fireproof" to yourself and then roam with impunity.
Basically ... if the first Scribblenauts was easy, Scribblenauts Ultimate barely qualifies as an activity book. An expensive, overproduced activity book.

If you like the first three Final Fantasy games, you'll like this. It is originally a Flash game, but evolved to become what I think a great classic. It's combat in particular is what I think a high point in the game, the graphics and especially those auto cast skills that appear at random to bombard your enemies will always make you smile. You can have a hat that randomly calls in a tank to blast an enemy with its cannon, or a shirt that calls another tank to rain down machine gun fire to enemies. There's even an attachment that randomly calls a cat to charge at enemies, or radio in airdrop to give a medpack to someone, or cast some random element skills like poison gas, or even an airstrike that drops random stuffs, like a nuclear bomb.
Of course, many boss units have some OP skills as well, like an orbital particle cannon, or some insane defensive skill that switch profile whenever hit by a skill. It is much more variable and over the top than the early FF games, yet maintains the same light heart atmosphere. Your characters will even chatter whenever something interesting or over the top happens. What's more, nobody will disapprove of the ability to summon a blackhole that can suck everyone, good or bad, in.
Light hearted RPG doesn't get much better than this. If you like this type of game, this is a must have.

Epic Battle Fantasy 4 has the best turn-based combat system I have ever played. That, by itself, is enough to warrant playing it. That it contains copious secrets, varied dungeons, good music and a great sense of humor is a bonus.
There's a wide variety of skills and items for every party member, including skills you can only give one person and permanent percentage stat boosts to help "customize" your team. Your equipment and skill selection have a profound impact in battle, but they're all balanced against each other. Every one is useful in different situations, so you'll still be using some stuff from the beginning of the game by the end. Status effects are powerful and varied, and vital to many fights. The "swap in the fourth party member at any time" mechanic is odd at first but actually comes off really well. And if you crank up the difficulty to Epic, the game provides a mighty challenge indeed--even by the end of the first level.
As for whether you should play the free version or the paid one? Well, aside from rewarding creativity, the bonus area is everything you could hope for. You unlock it piece by piece as you progress, and it offers lots of brutal fights and unique items and skills (including rematches against alternate versions of each boss, some entirely new bosses and waves of tough enemies). But best of all, it scales to your level so you can tackle each part whenever you want to and cannot beat it by grinding.
Either way, free version or paid: If you've ever had fun playing any RPG at any point in your life, you should play this game.

All in all, I recommend this game on a deep-discount, or better yet, for free.
