Reus
Since the glorious days of Black & White and the departure of its creator to a more RPG-centered Development there hasn't much news in the god game. Only a few entries were made in the last couple years with no real successor to the genres prime example. Reus is one of these entries. It doesn't try to overthrow the king, but it captures the spirit of Black & White very well. With quite a few changes.
Story
Instead of playing a powerful god that controls cities and mighty creatures alike, and being constantly annoyed by your conscience, you are instead the very planet itself which wakes from its billion years long slumber to fill the surface with life once again. Since you are just a giant rock sorrounding a burning gas ball you receive the aid of four giants to help you fill the surface with all kind of life and protect it, if necessary. I think we had that part somewhere before, didn't end well for the giants. Anyway, your Giants are equipped with very different kinds of powers for that job.
Gameplay
The four Giants are called after the four Biomes they can create. Ocean, Forest, Mountain, and Swamp. They can create Land, setting up Recourses, and even enhance them with different skills, but that later. The first important thing to use is the Terrain Generation. You have five Biomes at your Disposal. While all Giants can only create the Lands they are named after and forest and swamp need to be placed next to an ocean, deserts can only be created when raise a mountain and there is no ocean in its sorounding.
After designing the landscape you are ready for the next step: Resources and Settlements. The main feature of this game is to let small villages settle somewhere and provide them with food and gold and everything they could need. While Black & White lets you decide where to put new villages and what structures they build, you are here to waitfor the game to decide which building they want. And on that comparison, the Villages in Reus are just one single structures you can't interact that much. But that's not that much of a problem since Reus uses a new, almost puzzle-like aproach on how to interact with villages. You create Resources (Animals, Plants, Minerals) and your villagers will start to use them (and give them Food, Wealth, and Tech). Since that alone would be pretty boring, the Resources have special abilities attached to them, which grant additional bonuses if you meet certain requirements. So can a Plant almost double its food output if you place it next to a mineral. And on top of that, the different Resource types behave completely different. While Animal can make your Village more aggresive, while Plants have an effect to counter that. Minerals dont have such a system on that scale like the other two, uses some unique features. Animals and Plants have a range on where they give out their bonuses and form different kinds of Animals and Plants, depending on in which Biome you put them. Minerals on the other hand don't use such fancy techniques. You will create the same Minerals whereever you go (with a few exceptions here and there). And instead of a range system they just throw out all bonus on the place they are standing on. To differentiate them even more you need to overcome a special obstacle (called symbiosis), to to make abilities usable. For this your villages need to already use a certain amount of food, wealt, or tech. Stupid rocks.
Speaking of Villages, these things have, too, some special features worth mentioning. First, Sttlements have Borders. Everything inside these borders will be counted, everything outside ignored. Don't worry, the Borders will expand once the Settlement reached a certain size. The second thing are structures. These are special building outside of the village, which grant certain additional bonuses, depending on what they are. You can have which grants a tech bonus for each Plant within the borders, or fishing docks gives out a food bonus for each fish around it. And completing it will give you the key to victory, an ambassador.
Those little people will then sit on your Giants and unlock new powers. These powers, called Aspects, can increase the output of the recourse a little, or activate the last grand feature in the game, Transmutation. You know, that cool thing where you can transorm something in something completely different. It's fun, just don't try to resurrect your dead mother with it, okay? It works like placing a new resource, the first transmutes are not necessarily more powerful, but more you go down on the transmutation road, the better your outcome will be. Of course, if you don't activate the abilities you won't get much farther with it. So plan ahead and draw yourself a map of all the transmutations (I do and will eventually post it here). It will even help to understand certain structures of the transmutations, like the conjunction between ocean animals, you can jump from both animal a1 and b1 to a2 or b2, while the desert animals a1 and b1 only share c2, a2 and b2 are only reachable from the same letter. So keep that in mind. An interesting addition to this is that in the beginning only very few transmutations are available to you. To unlock additional ones you need to unlock steam achievements, which will be tracked ingame. These things are finally useful for something.
Conclusion
Pretty solid, beautiful drawn, 2-D god game, which can lead to some tedious puzzle work if you want to come far. There are some critic points, like when settlements go and try to beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your Giants. Reus is one of the best examples of the creativity of indie games. If you like slower paced simulations, where you can watch and devolop the towns under your watchful eye, without any pressure, timed or otherwise, you can't do anything wrong with this game. Buy it, enjoy it, and see for yourself.

Bloons TD 5 was my first encounter with the series and it's quite possibly the best tower defense game I've ever played - and I've played quite a few indeed. They've got an excellent gameplay formula. The tower diversity as well as upgrades to both the player as well as towers add a lot of flavor to tactical approach, and overall replayability is excellent.
That said, there are a couple fundamental flaws to watch out for:
-The first and perhaps most crippling is the random crashing that will occur if you're the sort of player that likes to squeese towers into tight spaces at the very border of the 'placeable areas'.
(Note to developers: I feel this likely has something to do with the coordinates arrays and warrants some looking in to.)
-The second is the net code. In many cases this isn't a very big problem, but on some poor connections to the other player, the client has trouble keeping up with game cash balance updates. There have been times I've had to wait as long as 5-10 minutes on the harder difficulties / longer games while the other player's balance was updated on my screen.
Both of these issues can be avoided however, so they should not necessarily sway your decision to get this game.
All in all, worth every penny of the $9.99 USD I paid for it.

This game comes up with a pretty wild idea: A game where all that you do becomes a part of the song. Then you might think "hey, Bastion had this idea long ago!" and similar thoughts... But let me clear one detail: What changes is the song on the background. It might seem such a simple detail, but it actually creates a very impressive atmosphere. And the gameplay itself is that classic, good ol' 2D platformer we all know and love. There is a good deal of exploration to this game, and the items make the gameplay very interesting. Of course, there are a few parts where there's simply nothing much to sing, but that is actually better than if they decided to go full on looping the same parts that you've already heard. For now, this game unfortunatelly does not have an English version, meaning that only those who undestand Brazilian Portuguese would be able to play for now... However, there apparently are plans for an English release later on, so I recommend, yes, for those who already understand Portuguese and for those who don't, look forward for the (possible) English release later on and I guarantee: You won't regret. It's not too long, but the difficulty might keep you playing for a while.

On the first day of summer, dim-witted but charming Ed (Kel Mitchell) experiences a nightmare featuring talking burgers. Troubled by it, he shows up late to work at Good Burger. On the same morning, Dexter (Kenan Thompson), a high school student, steals his mother's car after she leaves for a business trip. He accidentally crashes into that of his teacher, Mr. Wheat (Sinbad). With no driver's license or insurance, he is in danger of going to jail. Mr. Wheat agrees to allow him to pay for a total of $1,900 in car damage, which later becomes $2,500, instead of calling the police. He must find a summer job to pay for the expenses. He first finds employment at Mondo Burger, but after a clash with the strict manager, Kurt Bozwell (Jan Schweiterman), he is fired and has to find employment at another place, and manages to do so at Good Burger. There, he meets and reluctantly befriends Ed (who helps him find a job position) and a slew of colorful employees. Little does he know Ed inadvertently caused the car accident; he was rushing to make a delivery on rollerblades, and skated in front of Dexter, causing him to swerve and hit Mr. Wheat's car.
Dexter finds much success at Good Burger, but his success takes a turn for the worse. Across the street, the Mondo Burger where he previously worked opens to the public. It produces oversized burgers, much bigger than the Good Burgers, and threatens to put them out of business. Fortunately, with the invention of Ed's "secret sauce," they are saved. After Dexter realizes that Ed caused his car accident, he takes part of Ed's bonus paychecks earned from the sauce to pay off his debt to Mr. Wheat.
Good Burger continues to be popular because of Ed's sauce, causing Kurt to attempt to steal it. First, he entices Ed with a higher hourly wage at Mondo Burger. Dedicated to Good Burger, he denies it. He buys Dexter a similar yo-yo that his dad bought him as a kid. It was at this moment that he not only begins to truly care about Ed, but he is also overcome with guilt for taking most of Ed's bonus money. Kurt then sends in an attractive employee named Roxanne (Carmen Electra) who fails to seduce Ed into divulging his "secret sauce" recipe, ending up badly injured.
Meanwhile, Dexter takes a shine to coworker Monique (Shar Jackson), and she eventually agrees to a double date with him along with Ed and Roxanne. The next day, however, she tells him off and breaks up with him after she discovers his attempts to cheat Ed out of most of his money.
Later on, Ed and Dexter encounter a dog on the street and attempt to feed him a Good Burger and a Mondo Burger. It eats the former, but refuses to even look at the latter, apparently sensing something wrong with the meat. Suspicious, Ed and Dexter disguise themselves as old women and enter Mondo Burger to find out what is wrong with their meat. They discover that they chemically induced their burgers with an illegal food additive called "Triampathol," which makes them oversized. Kurt is not fooled by Ed and Dexter's disguises and kidnaps them by sending them to Demented Hills Mental Hospital (run by his friend) to prevent the public from learning Mondo Burger's secret.
After sending Ed and Dexter to Demented Hills, Kurt and his employees break into Good Burger after closing hours and spike Ed's "secret sauce" with shark poison. When Ed and Dexter's coworker, Otis (Abe Vigoda), attempts to call the police on them, Kurt takes him captive and sends him to Demented Hills as well. There, he tells Ed and Dexter about Kurt's scheme to poison the "secret sauce." They devise a plan to escape. Ed begins to dance and sing, encouraging the other patients to join in. After the entire mental hospital breaks out in dance, the trio escapes. They steal an ice cream truck to leave, but are pursued by a Demented Hills van; cleverly, Ed and Dexter throw ice cream treats at it, causing it to crash. Upon arriving at Good Burger, Ed stops a lady from eating a Good Burger with the poison-laced sauce just in time. Dexter then informs the staff that the sauce has been poisoned by Kurt and convinces them not to let anyone consume it. Ed and Dexter then break into Mondo Burger so they could expose the chemically-induced burgers to the police. While Dexter provides a distraction, Ed tries to take a can of Triampathol, but accidentally knocks one into the meat grinder. Ed then decides to pours the rest of it into there. On the roof, Kurt catches Ed and Dexter and confiscates the empty can that Ed is holding. Just then, the building begins to blow up, caused by the Triampathol-overdosed burgers exploding. After it destructs and the patrons flee, the police arrest Kurt for illegal substance use. Ed then explains to Dexter that he did that on purpose to prevent Kurt from manipulating the legal system and escaping conviction, ironically responding to Dexter's questions by saying, "I'm not stupid." With the destruction of Mondo Burger, Mr. Wheat's car is destroyed once again (much to Dexter's amusement as he hands him the first half of the money owed for the damage).
Dexter apologizes to Ed for taking advantage of the latter's salary from the sauce and both end up on friendly terms. They then walk back to Good Burger, where the employees praise them, especially Ed, as Good Burger heroes. The film ends as Ed proudly says "Welcome to Good Burger, home of the Good Burger. Can I take your order?"

Epic Battle Fantasy as a series is, in my opinion, the one of (if not) the best indie RPGs that I've played in... quite possibly ever.
The game is well done and there are countless different ways to build your characters early on, though this drops off a bit due to being able to get everything later (bar a few spells/abilities that are 1-person only). The combat system, while basic, works great with very little errors outside ones made by the player.The maps are also well designed and often have more secrets in them than meets the eye, in many cases either requiring a return trip or waiting for something to flash upon the screen (though block puzzles, in my eyes, are unforgivable!).
The 'many ways to build a character' is even more evident because of the inclusion of the 4th character (fitting that you get the 4th member in the 4th game), meaning that someone is back in the sidelines ready for action should you need to swap one of your (three) party members out.
Cleverness and hilarity is also abundant in EBF with countless (sometimes censored due to copyright) references and/or memes.
As I write the review, I have not actually gotten to any of the 'Premium' (Read: Pay for) part of the game, as I'm doing an Epic difficulty playthrough and have not started the Battle Mountain or Survival battles.
If you're looking to try the game, go to some place like Kongregate and play it there to see if it's to your liking.
If you're looking to get the game (and support the amazing developer), buy it.
Don't anger the cats by the way; they tend to bring about the apocalypse in the form of elder gods when you do so.
November 2015 Edit: Still amazing, though I forgot to mention (long ago in the original review) that this takes an obscene amount of comp usage for no real reason, so don't be surprised with large amounts of slowdown!

Epic Battle Fantasy has always been one of my favorite parody series, which is itself one of my favorite genres. But unlike your average "take that, Final Fantasy!" mimicry affair, EBF stands on its own in every regard:
Colorful art design, imaginative enemies, and I can't think of an adjective for the writing that quite encapsulates the unique blend of self-depriciative humor. The protagonists have a "band of idiots" shtick that in any other parody would just come off as mean, but EBF manages to convey a genuine sense of chemistry, that these idiots have been working with and through each others' eccentricities. The humor really comes alive when EBF satirizes not just the genre but also its players, with Anna playing straight man to a trio of 4th-wall-breaking powergamers.
It wouldn't be a Japanese-style RPG without a story, and where the first three EBF games went for the "here is a villain go fight him" excuse to skip to the action, the fourth instalment has tried its hand at some actual worldbuilding this time, though at the cost of assuming players are familiar with the events of the third game. Returning party members Matt, Natz, and Lance are quickly discovering that the various save-the-world plots aren't as standalone and isolated as they assumed, and larger forces have been resetting their little pawns whie they were busy level grinding the Pickpocket skill.
As for gameplay, EBF is quickly recognizable to anyone who has ever touched a Square Enix RPG, and at the same time found its own way to keep the turn-based combat fresh. Not content with just elemental rock-paper-scisors, EBF ensures stats buffs and status effects/ailments are incredibly critical during the late game, but thankfully the player is slowly eased into it all. There's a great deal of customization, especially if you want to eek out every precious damage point from your foes, but if you feel that you're stopping too often to fiddle with menus the game leaves open the possibility of overleveling yourself (to a point). If you know what you're doing the game will be happy to throw you enough curveballs to keep yourself from feeling overpowered but never tries to make you entirely helpless either.
The only real thing to watch out for is possible slowdown. Might wanna check how your computer handles Flash, since that's what this game was originally built in, and large numbers of vector images, since that's what the original Flash engine rendered in. My other main complaint is that late-game bosses can be a bit of a slog if you aren't an absolute min-maxer, but in a way that's sort of the point.
Overall, EBF4 is a happy, charming little affair from start to finish. Matt Roszak has stated that he made the series so he can see a game with everything he likes in it, and the level of love put into the product from start to finish really shows through. If you like swords, sorcery, slimes, and squishing the latter with the former, I recommend giving Epic Battle Fantasy a look; chances are there will be a lot you will like as well.

The gameplay is mostly decent, although I'd wish for some more environmental interactivity in combat locations, and more streamlined crafting and inventory management. Some quality of life features. There really is no point having to spend 20 mins to sort out all the brick-a-brack you pick up on your travels. Much of it is just junk. And the crafting system is too complicated and not appropriately introduced, which is a shame, but no deal-braker.
One *major* gripe I have with this game is its broken auto save system. Everything is going well, you go kill a boss, go back to town, do your shopping trips, craft some nice gear, and are ready to move on. You teleport out of town, and suddenly the game decides to kill you for a stupid reason, like people running into hazardous terrain over and over again, and you can't heal all affected at the same time. Or you run into a trap you forgot to clear out, and that starts a chain reaction that ends up killing your 2 mains. Or something, does not matter really. Important thing is you can die at any time for any stupid reason. Not only when you know that danger is ahead. Once misclick is enough to be fatal. Have fun reloading and replaying that 1-2h shopping trip, crafting gear, swapping out party members etc. No thanks.
If you have an auto-save system with multiple slots, as this game does, pretty please, use it appropriately. The game does not save when you teleport (it should), it does not save when you enter combat (it should).
The devs designed an experience where you're supposed to save-scum manually all the time, because any stupid thing can kill you (digging a hole with your shovel, you may be insta-killed, better save). Once the game succeeds in being good enough in terms of immersion and engagement, that you forget to press f5 because you're engrossed in the narrative and don't deem yourself in danger, it punishes you hard. It's stupid to happen on a first run, and it is a reason for uninstalling on subsequent runs. I've not completed tactician mode because of that nonsense.
Regarding tactician mode (hard mode). First of all it is too hard in early-game and and too easy from mid-game on. You level pretty fast because you gain more xp, and once you settle for an informed party setup and build, you won't likely die in combat except for some 'interesting' encounters where the game chooses to be unfair.
All in all it's a decent tactical combat RPG. Companions are bland, story is meh, but the possibilities in combat are a fresh take on things. Worth it for that alone.

I try to finish games on 100%, meaning I try to complete every quest, do every activity and seek all the hidden secrets to fully enjoy it and get the best experience. This review does not serve as a guide or tips and tricks, etc.
First things first, you need to create two main characters. The character creation allows you to customize they way your characters look to a certain degree and you can choose portrait. But the most important and amazing thing with the creation is that you can COMPLETELY customize your skill points, traits and abilities.
You can pick from one of starting classes but you can rescpec all the points if you desire, that leaves you with a huge pool of choises right from the start. The only thing that class determine is the starting gear. However I wouldn’t recommend making your character from the scratch because you might end up unbalanced and that could possibly lead to defeat in every battle and need of rerolling your game.
Now the beauty of the game is exploration. You will have to figure out almost all the mechanics and quests by yourself, the game won’t tell you a single thing and it’s not gonna hold your hand in any way. That being said this is where, for me the biggest flaws lies. In first few hours of the game you will probably feel lost. You won’t know how to craft, how to repair your items and where the game limits lies. Most of the things the game has to offer is up to you, go and figure basically and I can see alot of frustration in a first 10 hours or so. But it’s worth knowing that enduring painfull start will reward you with great rewards.
Once you figured out basic mechanics it’s time to continue with your first quest. You will get to a real battles somewhere around level 3-4, that took me about 10 hours into a game. 10 hours and no real battle?! What were you doing I hear you ask. Well here is one of the game strongest element. The story and it’s storytelling.
There is a lot and I mean ALOT of reading through out the game. Dialogs are long, fun and very witty. It is a blast reading through them. All of the lines in the game are fully dubbed. The voice actors did an amazing job for the majority of the game, sure a few voices will sound familiar, but that doesn’t break immersion in any way. Choises in dialogues can and will vary depending on your actions. Most of the choises you make in dialogue will have permanent effect and have a consequences. You can avoid many battles that way, or engage them. You can learn about hidden treasures, quest, etc.
Game has a paper, rock scissor mechanic in the dialogues, basically RNG arguement ( depending on your trais ) Traits are, intimidate, charm and reason. I am not a big fan of RNG in dialogues that could possible lead to a very different outcome than you would expect.
So once you are set to journey out to seek the danger and enemies the combat kicks in. Now I will admit I am not a huge fan of turn based combat. But the combat in Divinity feels very hard, demanding and complex, yet so easy to pick up after a few fights. You will never feel as if the enemies are cheating on you. In fact as you progress the game you will notice how better you are getting, and how once great threads to you are now a mere bother.
You will have to take advantage of the battleground as well and it’s a key to a victory. You will have to focus on every little detail and turn most of the things to your advantage. You will simply have to think in a fight otherwise you won’t succede.
The loot itself is okey at best. Finding more powerfull gear is great and exciting, however that feeling is crushed down once you found out that the new bow you just found looks exactly the same as the one you have currently equiped. It’s not a big deal considering you will spent all of your time above your characters, however more significant changes of appearance would be nice.
Divinity Original Sin has become on of my most favourite RPG ever. It’s unique, original and rich world stading side by side with it’s amazingly delivered story and greatly stylized graphics makes a perfect combination for a perfect game. There are a few flaws as I mentioned above, but all of them are outshined by all the pros that outweight them. For RPG lovers this is a absolute must buy matter. Beating the game on 100% took me about 93 hours.
•	Amazing and original story
•	Complex, rich world
•	Masterfully hard and engaging combat
•	Freedom of choise and consequences of your actions
•	Excellent dialogues
•	Great humour
•	Lenght of the game
•	Very unfriendly first few hours
•	RNG dialogue mini game
•	Small variety of unique gear and weapons

I'm just going to start off by saying that I absolutely love this game, in fact, it's my second favourite fighting game (Only being beaten by the excellent Blazblue series). So, don't expect too many negatives on this review as I'm probably more biased to this game then I'd like to admit.
To start, the game has a great tutorial that (unlike most fighting games) actually teaches you the moves and inputs, requesting that you perform the moves multiple times in order to learn the features of the game as well as the special moves of each character, whereas most fighting games would only ask you to do it once and for inexperienced fighting game players this usually means stumbling onto the correct input. The game has 11 stories (at the time of this review, Elizabeth has still yet to be released) to play through, with about 5-6 fights per story which is not bad considering most fighting games ignore story mode altogether *Cough, cough* Street Fighter *Cough, cough*.
The characters are suprisingly well balanced (Despite my frustration against fighting Fuuka), which is difficult to do in a fighting game since players have a tendency of discovering infinites and exploits, luckily the game features "Infinity breakers" requiring the victim of an infinite combo to press ANY button to burst out of it. Although I have heard some stories of griefers using that feature to lock opponents into a different infinite, so I can't give much of an explanation on that. I'd also like to state that my online play has been a bit short, with fighting against one friend taking a majority of that game time.
The game plays similar to the Marvel vs Capcom series, with three characters on each side fighting it out. You have the ability to swap between the three during combat either to keep an ally alive or to dish out some serious damage, especially with the "Blockbuster" moves being chainable. Here's a good team for that sort of thing: Cerebella, Ms. Fortune, and Peacock, since all of their Blockbusters have the same input, although using Peacock to start this combo is not  advised as she'll end up pushing the opponent away from you, and the other two teammates have shorter range Blockbusters.
The stages are beautifully done with multiple background characters changing every time that you visit these locations, so you're not seeing the exact same guy cheering in the background, you might see a robot or Eldtrich abonimation cheering you on instead. The music in this game is great, its more classy and uses a variety of instruments from brass, to string, to piano. My personal favourite background music is the one in Little Innsmouth (Yes, THAT Innsmouth), not sure why it just sounds a so cheery for a battle between a cyborg built of brass instruments and a neko woman who can easily remove her own head and bowl it at you.
As for negatives? Well, besides hating on Fuuka, I suppose the game has a bit of a short roster, however Lab Zero is currently implementing a few extra characters. Plus there are a few moves that are easy to abuse, such as Big Band's "Brass Knuckles" which have armour and deal quite a bit of damage if it connects (I'm looking at you, only friend who owns this game).

Epic Battle Fantasy 4 Pays homage to the classics of JRPG genre while making fun them at the same time. with its old school turn based gameplay and great humor it's diffently a must play for fans of the genre.

First off, Yes, you can play this game on Kongregate or Newgrounds (or possibly Matt's DA), however the version you play will not be this one.
In other words, No, this isn't the same game you can play on the sites I previously mentioned.
What you'll play is indeed an RPG akin to the old days of Final Fantasy, when Combat wasn't real-time combat with before-use cooldowns.
To those unfamiliar with the Epic Battle Fantasy series (namely the ones with actual story elements) This is an RPG game with tons of funny things here and there, self-referencing humor, and things that reference alot of other things.
So basically the story so far is there's 3 heroes.
One is Matt, who jsut wants food, like swords and piracy... He's also a pirate.. Did I mention he has a guitar and likes Death Metal? I jsut did, you're welcome, reason 1 to buy this game.
There's Natalie, whose powers are in her awe-inspiring magical powers, witty remarks, different mindset of the others, and her boobs. No seriously she's kinda the "Big boobed girl cliche" of the series, though she's hilariously not jsut eye candy,  dishing out the sage advice and owning remarks. But even more seriously she's literally the only one who can decently heal and revive party members. She's kinda the most important character combat-wise.
There's Lance who is a military guy.
In a world filled with big demons (like the last villain you kill in #3), sapient cats with no limbs able to wield weapons via unexplained telepathy powers, elementals, magic, Lance is the one who kills things with overwhelming firepower. Seriously though, he melts those who are weak to bomb-type attacks and even has decent fire and electric attacks.
There's a 4th character, a huntress druid girl for Natalie to relate to.
This game also has achievements alongside the medals of the game, giving you elevated bragging rights.
Your progress on this version won't be wiped by clearing your cache or cookies.
There's what I call a Shamievement, an achievement that's more or less a badge of shame like Duke Nukem Forever's Turd Burglar. You'll be rewarded for being a perv by this, though it really could be worse, so in terms of them, it's really not bad.
Here's the part you care about though... The exclusive content.
This version has more weapons, and more items in general, save for crafting materials (i think) and this game has an entire area called Challenge Mountain. This area is literally filled with enemy encounters which all have 8 enemy encounters each and stronger versions of the bosses in the game which are WAY harder to kill.
Every enemy in thise area scales with level, which means you can get past all enemies at level 1, though you do need quest items like the axe or battery to get past some bits.
How does this game fare? Well for someone who played the first half 3 times on Kongregate, I can say the game fares really awesomely. I mean... never did I once say "Oh god not this part again" or the infamous "Why can't I just skip this" and I'm one of many who found Diablo 2 monotonous after Normal difficulty.
This game is very fun, has some funny elements and even gets challenging properly without feeling unfair. This game doesn't have any difficulty spikes... until the final area, but around then you're ready for it. This game is simply a blast, the only thing stopping me from playing it is just the simple fact I'm feeling a bit bored of RPGs in general.
Alongside such big titles like Final Fantasy, Diablo, Torchlight, and even anything else you could really think of, this game holds it's own ground. The game is honestly fairly unique in my opinion.
This game in my books gets a 7/10. It's pretty good honestly, and I'd easily recommend it to anyone who likes Turn-Based games and RPGs, Despite the fact you can play the game on Kongregate with 30% less content for free.

EBF4 is a solidly built RPG with turn based combat reminiscent of Final Fantasy with a dash of self referencial/ 4th wall breaking humor thrown in for good measure.
The story is simple enough that you don't need to play the previous three installments. But if you wish to they're easily found online for free.
The combat largely revolves around equipping your characters with the proper equipment prior to the fight so as to exploit the enemies weaknesses and bolster your own defenses against their attacks.
It's not overly long, and maybe not worth the full $11.99 price tag, but it's definitely worth picking up when it goes on sale.

If you love old school Japanese RPGs I strongly recommend that you play this game. If the price tag isn't wroth it you can find the free to play version of the game on Newgrounds and Kongregate. The steam version to my knowledge has a few extra features like more equipment and the new optional area. All in all it's an okay game to at least play through once if you're not into the idea of paying for extra features then I suggest you play the free to play version.

An excellent PvP game you should really check out. There are very good reviews already, but seeing as the game is rated as "mostly positive", I felt like adding my 2 cents, because it deserves much more.
Pros:
- Very quick battles, often over in under 5 minutes.
- Good card variety (95 cards as of the writing of this review) allowing for different strategies.
- Your deck consists of 10 cards, and your hand of 4. This means you can quickly cycle your deck, and the game revolves a lot more around skill than luck of the draw, like other card games.
- Next to no RNG. Some cards are pure RNG, but they're a gamble you chose to take. The only RNG that's forced on you is the initial hand and draw. Some decks rely on a single card that you buff / heal, if you don't draw this card first, this can be a problem. However, this is also a risk you chose to take. You can make a versatile deck that has an answer for almost everything, so any draw can be useful with those.
- Looks great, and sounds nice.
- Draft mode and 2v2 if 1v1 isn't your thing, this means you can play with a buddy.
- You can customize your arena, and master skins are coming.
-
, this is a very important point. Many reviews claim that this game is pay-to-win, but top tier players can reach top 1-5 with almost only basic cards.
Cons:
- You need a good computer to be able to run it on max settings.
- Small playerbase, this means you will see the same people very often. This is a bad thing for some people, a good thing for others.
- 95 different cards can also be a con for a new player, since you can feel overwhelmed until you know which card does what.

To the Moon is an RPGMaker interactive movie that is… is…
Just… just play it. Just buy it and play it. There should be nothing else said about. Just… play it.
Don’t let the appearance fool you: To the Moon may have been created with RPG Maker XP, but it is an interactive movie through and through. Player input is minimal and it is restricted to walking around, examining things, and two minigames.
The main theme of the story is memories. Memories of a lifetime, to be exact: you play as two scientists, whose job is to create an artificial set of memories for a dying old man, so he can reach happiness in his final moments.
The memory exploration is twofold: on one hand, we are witnesses to key moments of the man’s life going backwards in time, slowly learning what choices and events led to his final decision.
But the journey is also quite symbolic, even allegoric. All memories are tied to small mementos, and as the journey progresses, we learn how much importance a seemingly insignificant object can hold for someone… Something I’m sure all of us are familiar in our own lives.
There are two minor problem with the game. Two smudges on this perfect gem. One is the overabundance of slapstick; its purpose is to have small emotional pauses in this story, but sometimes it is misused. The other is the obstacle-passing minigame towards the end that just feels completely out of place and nonsensical.
Still, even with these, To the Moon is still probably the best indie game available on Steam. So… just buy it and play it.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a big gem of 2015. It's powerful soundtrack, it's goregous art and atmosphere, it's simply the best looking game I've played all year. But is it as good as it looks?
The Short Review - If you love video games with great atmosphere or hell, love video games, this is it. This is what you need to play.
The game's story isn't as great as you'd wish for it to be, but it's emotional, moving, and heartfelt. Ori's journey carries him across the land of Nibel on the objective of restoring the lands and preventing the disastors caused by the game's main antagonist, Kuro. I won't spoil much from here, but the game's ending is probably the best part of the story.
Ori and the Blind Forest isn't a super-long game, and that's fine. The overall level design and flow feels akin to your typical Metroidvania (Go through "dungeons", Collect new moves/abilities, find hidden power-ups/upgrade stuff), but it still feels refined and unique. Unlike your Simons and Samuses, Ori is very vulnerable. and his/her moveset (According to the developers Ori's gender is whatever you think it is. I guess.) reflects that. You don't have charge shots, or missles (Although you technichally do get a charge attack later). Ori's moves allow for fast traversal, solving platforming puzzles, and discovering hidden secrets. The game's combat isn't interesting nor is it horrible but it could be better. Fighting enemies can be a bit annoying sometimes but you'll be able to use your other moves to dispatch them quicker.
I should note that I came in this game expecting it to be hard, which it is. However, it's not super brutal or anything. You'll get frustrated at a few moments in the game, and you'll probably die a lot. If you are very casual to video games, this one will seriously beat you up in every way possible (Toughen up them skills hmm).
The game has light RPG elements as well. You can earn experience and get ability points for a skill tree. It's entirely optional although a few of the upgrades do make things a bit easier.
Traversing through the game can few a bit like backtracking since you'll be going to areas you've been to before constantly, but it's not frustrating or annoying, thanks to the abilities given to make traversal fast and allow for you to reach secrets you couldn't reach before.
Is there anything I don't like about the game? Well, the game doesn't allow you to continue playing after finishing it. Once you enter the final dungeon, there's no going back. This sucks because there are tons of collectables for players to achieve and in order to go back and get them, well you have to replay the entire game. That's pretty much all I have going against it. I'm also not a fan of the way you save in the game. You save in any safe spot, but it'll cost energy. That's fine, but this limit makes it really aggrevating because there is no auto-saving. If you die in a room and your last checkpoint was the start of the room, too bad. It's more of a nitpick then anything, since it's not that bad. You just need to be careful on when you save.
Ori and the Blind Forest is a fantastic gem of a game that you have to play. It's a powerful game with fantastic music and visuals. The game mechanics are solid (Although very, very familiar) and Ori's moveset is a perfect fit for the character and the game's platforming.

I wasn't certain what to rate this title. This is one of those cases where a neutral vote would really be useful, because even though I've chosen to go with the down vote, it's not because it's a bad game. It's because it doesn't feel like the Gauntlet I remember.
Rewind back to the late 80's, when I was a late adopter NES and Gauntlet was maybe my third or fourth game. I played through that game many times: trial and error, writing things down, mapping on paper, reaching level 99 and being unable to proceed because I didn't have the vault password. I remember missing clues before and not taking Morak's "You will never be able to reach the orb. Ha ha ha"" seriously. Played through it again, numerous times, getting the clues I could, writing down passwords so I could make up for old mistakes, eventually getting past level 99 into level 00...err, 100. Then getting crushed by the dragon which I thought was unbeatable -- it had so much health.
In the end I never did finish that game. I believe it fell prey to a house hazard but I must have spent dozens of hours playing it nonetheless. It still holds a fond place in my memories.
Fast forward to now. I've finished Gauntlet 2014, and yet, it feels rather empty. It's a solid dungeon crawler, but like many modern games are being rightfully criticized for, it's a hallway. Gone are the convoluted routes and exploration of the original Gauntlet. Yes you can find a few secret walls here and there but there seems to be no true exploration in this game. There's nothing for me to find now that I've beaten it once, and the road there had no intersections.
The length can be a bit deceiving. The game has effectively nine standard levels, nine procedurally generated levels, nine mob rush miniboss levels, and three bosses. At first I was hoping from more when I saw the twelve doorways in the lobby room. It's a pretty short game, but in its defense it only had a release price of 1/3 the typical release price of AAA titles.
The pacing of battles have also slowed significantly. Granted, the original Gauntlet had to move quickly because you'd often be put in a position where you could never beat the game, but this one can be downright tedious at times. Going through as Questor on Normal, who is undeniably the easiest character for your first play through, all the levels seemed the same: Kiting and herding crowds of mooks, blowing them up with bombs, destroying generators whose health are considerably higher than in the original version. Use chaos crystal (arguably the best item for any character) to get mobs off you and tumble away when you get overwhelmed. Somehow the second chapter was easier than the first, though the final chapter added direct target enemies that you need to prioritize above all others.
One of the fundamental things that made the series unique also changed -- in the original, instead of lives, you have huge pool of health and could mow through enemies without even swinging your sword or firing your bow, albeit at a health cost. You also had a slow health drain which added urgency to your quest. One life, game over -- but it was fair, and it was a staple of Gauntlet for some time. Now they've gone to a multiple lives system. You continue where you left off, but all the characters are paper, and that seems to take a bit from the enjoyment.
It also creates a huge character imbalance. While Gauntlet had always favored the Elf and the Wizard to some degree, now it's like they're demigods and the Valkyrie and especially the Warrior are mere mortals. With everyone being paper as I mentioned earlier, it behooves you to avoid melee range altogether -- but the Warrior doesn't have a choice, and his health pool hardly makes up for the enormous power difference. Playing as Thor the Warrior is just downright frustrating, but playing as Questor the Elf is just tedious.
Thor's usefulness may be greater in multiplayer, and perhaps the designers only had multiplayer in mind with him, but good luck finding a group of people who will support the tank, who requires a lot of food to continue filling that role effectively. He is easily the worst resource grabber because of his slow speed.
What has been added are modern overused tropes such as leveling up mini-achievements to make your characters more powerful. It must be done individually for each character. You'll either like it or despise it, and I for one am a bit cynical about leveling up in an action game. Compulsion-based gameplay stops working once you overdo it -- and the whole industry has been overdoing it for the last 7 or 8 years now. (mobile, especially)
In the end, I'm giving this game a weak thumb's down. The presentation is solid, the music is solid, and the ending reminds me of early NES endings, in a bad way. I might occasionally do a couple campaigns but I'm otherwise disappointed in this reboot. I've seen much more truer-to-the-original reboots and some are even on Steam.

If you want a good PC fighter with amazing artwork, fast gameplay, and constant updates, this is the game for you.

I'm just going to start off by saying that I absolutely love this game, in fact, it's my second favourite fighting game (Only being beaten by the excellent Blazblue series). So, don't expect too many negatives on this review as I'm probably more biased to this game then I'd like to admit.
To start, the game has a great tutorial that (unlike most fighting games) actually teaches you the moves and inputs, requesting that you perform the moves multiple times in order to learn the features of the game as well as the special moves of each character, whereas most fighting games would only ask you to do it once and for inexperienced fighting game players this usually means stumbling onto the correct input. The game has 11 stories (at the time of this review, Elizabeth has still yet to be released) to play through, with about 5-6 fights per story which is not bad considering most fighting games ignore story mode altogether *Cough, cough* Street Fighter *Cough, cough*.
The characters are suprisingly well balanced (Despite my frustration against fighting Fuuka), which is difficult to do in a fighting game since players have a tendency of discovering infinites and exploits, luckily the game features "Infinity breakers" requiring the victim of an infinite combo to press ANY button to burst out of it. Although I have heard some stories of griefers using that feature to lock opponents into a different infinite, so I can't give much of an explanation on that. I'd also like to state that my online play has been a bit short, with fighting against one friend taking a majority of that game time.
The game plays similar to the Marvel vs Capcom series, with three characters on each side fighting it out. You have the ability to swap between the three during combat either to keep an ally alive or to dish out some serious damage, especially with the "Blockbuster" moves being chainable. Here's a good team for that sort of thing: Cerebella, Ms. Fortune, and Peacock, since all of their Blockbusters have the same input, although using Peacock to start this combo is not  advised as she'll end up pushing the opponent away from you, and the other two teammates have shorter range Blockbusters.
The stages are beautifully done with multiple background characters changing every time that you visit these locations, so you're not seeing the exact same guy cheering in the background, you might see a robot or Eldtrich abonimation cheering you on instead. The music in this game is great, its more classy and uses a variety of instruments from brass, to string, to piano. My personal favourite background music is the one in Little Innsmouth (Yes, THAT Innsmouth), not sure why it just sounds a so cheery for a battle between a cyborg built of brass instruments and a neko woman who can easily remove her own head and bowl it at you.
As for negatives? Well, besides hating on Fuuka, I suppose the game has a bit of a short roster, however Lab Zero is currently implementing a few extra characters. Plus there are a few moves that are easy to abuse, such as Big Band's "Brass Knuckles" which have armour and deal quite a bit of damage if it connects (I'm looking at you, only friend who owns this game).

I would recommend this to anyone even remotely interested in fighting games. 10/10 Good Job to Lab Zero and Autumn, keep up the good work and Good Luck to you in your future endeavors.

Honestly one of the best games I've ever played. The items are great, the gameplay is easy to understand, and the character interaction is hilarious.
Each weapon/attack/item has it's pluses and minuses. What may be great for one battle may be awful for another. This is nice because you actually need to pay attention to equips, not just get "the one armor set." You actually have to use your brain a little bit to play, but not so much that it's exahausting (for example, you wouldn't go into a battle with light creatures wearing only darkness armor, you'd be screwed).
In terms of gameplay, you can switch between using your mouse or your keyboard, an option that other games lack. Also, in terms of battles, you have plenty of time to think and do what you need. While some may like time-constraints, Epic Battle Fantasy 4 provides for a more stress-free type gameplay. All your abilities and options are easy to navigate to, and thus far I have not run into a single glitch.
The characters are great. That's something that could be said about this entire franchise, but especially this and EBF3. There is so much interaction between the characters, enemies, and the environment. Battle after battle can get boring, but the witty dialogue balances this out nicely.
All-in-all, this game is perfect for those looking for a relaxed RPG experience: no time-constraints or reflex-speed battles, vibrant colors that don't strain your eyes, and lots of easter eggs from Minecraft, Pokémon, and more just in case the fantastic characters didn't already have you hooked.

I usually skip over all types of round-bases-battle-RPGs but I'm glad I made an exception here. EBF4 is a tongue-in-cheek RPG with hilarious characters who dress as stereotypical pirates, rangers or red mages. On the over-world map you collect hidden goodies, explore branching ways and follow the farce of a storyline. If you choose to bump into an enemy the fighting starts, no tedious random encounters after any x steps. Also heroes slowly heal after battle for convenience and most creatures respawn.
The battle system isn't boring but really fun with lots of different skills, weapons, equipment, usable items.
Skills are unlocked and upgraded with skill points. Levels are gained by experience. Weapons and Armor are found or bought in shops and upgraded with items. There are also summons usable by anyone, limit breaks and "specials" which are skills you can assign to complement a characters skill set like a fire attack or a heal spell.
You may try out the EBF game series on some websites for free to understand how the game works.
Epic Battle Fantasy 4 is one of the best rpg games around.

First of all, this is my first review. I am not pretty good at it, English is not my first language but I'll give it a try because I think that this game needs its reviews.
There are multiple things that really need to change.
The camera is in 3rd person - this is horrible. Moving is already pretty hard, but the 3rd person perspective makes moving harder than drinking tea while riding a dragon upside down. It's awful.
Building - if you wan't to build, please don't buy it. Play Minecraft or another building game instead. I know that there are a lot of people who love to play with Lego again but now on a PC, but this game is simply not ready to be able to handle the building. The mechanics are bad, the camera is bad, and it will be pretty hard to build a decent house.
Even though there are a lot of things that are great and makes this game wonderful.
You have the discovering mechanism. Whenever you discover something, for example a horse, and you ride it or interact with it someway, it becomes yours. You can unlock it in the spawn-menu and you can call this horse whenever you want to.
So, you see a new animal/vehicle, you interact with it, you go to this spawn menu, you buy it and you can always get it. You only have to buy it once, with in-game money (which is earned extremely fast, so don't bother yourself with that).
This is one of the greatest things I've seen, and exploring is really rewarding.
The same goes with props, small objects that you can find all over the world. I have had more fun with that than building a village in Minecraft.
For example: there is a dark forest biome where some kind of cannibals live. I unlocked their props, which include tents and bonfires, and placed them somewhere, acting that those cannibals are uniting themselves. I built a castle, used my warlock (you can swith characters as well, same story as with the animals/vehicles) to change it into ruins and acted as if those cannibals defeated the people living within these walls. It was great, I felt like a child again.
These wonderful experiences - flying with a dragon looking for chests, riding my horse through enormous hills, building a cannibal's camp - they are all great, and I know that this game shows a lot of potential.
Don't expect a lot of content yet - after a couple of hours, you have seen everything, but it is definitely worth buying or at least keeping your eye on.

I'm not really sure where to start with this. I started playing RPGs with KOTOR and Jade Empire, until those games I had never even tried RPGs. I have played and enjoyed Pillars of Eternity, yet found myself unable to even get halfway through Tyranny so far. This was an interesting experience, I was very much frustrated and annoyed through several areas of this game. I also had lots of enjoyable and entertaining experiences. I have to admit, I hated this games quest format, or maybe lack of format may suit it better. You're given like one sentence of text vaugely talking about a problem, and nothing else to go off of. That may be enjoyable, and indeed preferable to people who consider themselves more "hardcore" or "old school" or what have you, but I found this irritating the entire game. Likewise, the game took a ridiculous jump in difficulty with Braccus Rex, in a way I simply felt was bad. 4 bosses at once, 3 of them you've already killed previously? Come on, Ornstein and Smough is more forgiving. The only way I got past that quest was by spending 2 hours cheeseing it by moving Vases around.
The Sandstorm Area in Luculla Forest was one of the most ridiculous areas in the entire game. You are penalized with a party wide Slow debuff, which reduces Action Points and Action Point refill, meanwhile, the Spider enemies are utterly immune to this, can teleport around the entire battlefield at will, utterly ignoring your hardier frontline fighters. You get at best 1 attack per turn in this area, while the enemies get several due to them not being affected. Likewise there is almost no way to midigate this effect on your party. Later on, in the Phantom Forest, in order to get into the Source Temple you have to get through this absolutely outrageous Maze full of locked doors, all of which having maximum magical protections and loaded with mines and insta death traps and no keys to be found outside. It took me literally almost 8 hours to get through this damn Maze, if I hadn't found the 1 video on the internet about how to do it, this Maze would have made me quit the game and never come back. To me, personally, that was just not fun. Which to me, is the point of a game. Lastly, the entire Crafting system felt entirely pointless, I basically never used it, and even if I wanted to, I didn't really understand how it works.
With all that said, you're probably wondering why on earth I have given this game a thumbs up. Well allow me to inform you why. For starters, the combat systems in this game are simply revolutionary for turn based RPGs. I've never seen so many possible combos from usage of enviroment. Using blood of dead enemies to electrocute the others and stunning them? Who thinks of that? I never would have. This game incorporates the enviroment into the game in ways no other game ever has, and it consistently amazed me through the entire experience. In fact I am so not use to such depth from RPG combat, I often forgot about such combos. The list of abilities, and the way you can use abilities and teleportation to bypass many hazards, as well as in combat, simply put was mind blowing for me as someone whos spent thousands upon thousands of hours playing RPGs in my life.
Lastly, the writing felt very solid in most aspects, the primary storyline personally had me curious, and wondering what would happen and what discoveries would be made next. Jahan was by far the most compelling Companion in my opinion, and his arc was very nicely constructed. I obviously can't speak about writing in as nearly as much depth as the rest of the game, due to spoilers.
The pinnacle of RPG play experiences

There are many great games that are along the cusp of perfection, holding themselves back by flaws too minor to ruin the experience yet too numerous to ignore. Divinity: Original Sin is a prime example of this outcome. Even as much as I love the game, there are as many great things to praise as well as admonish that will dissuade players from completion.
Years ago I had tried many times to get into CRPGS; I had thought a modern interpretation like DOS would be easier to get into than ‘90s games like Baldur’s Gate. However, it’s DOS’s “interesting” difficulty, the technical and UI issues on AMD cards as well as the overabundance of humor that had prevented me from playing far for some time. Eventually, the game won me over on a different computer, and it is thanks to the release of its sequel that compelled me to discover the greater game that lies underneath that manages to shine through the muck that the sequel manages to polish to its perfection.

This statement is said not because my preferences are to play RPGs alone nor that I find the comedic value of the game to be grating. Comedy is subjective, yes; however, moderation of something good is always an ideal as buddy comedies last only an hour and a half to two hours at most. Even the Earthbound-inspired games manage different tones to keep their gags from overstaying their welcome. The second issue is the buddy system itself, which is not as broken but feels jarring for solo-players who must either auto-resolve an AI with a strict personality or argue with themselves as two players. The cooperation elements feel sparse with RNG based decisions to create more freeform consequences, and the dialogue system often simplifies into binary “For/Against” quips.
Cooperation, outside of combat, is perhaps the most underutilized feature in a game that promotes it so heavily. The narrative and the RPG mechanics themselves work against one another as there might be one outcome to result in progress like recruiting an NPC where you have to control the other player to agree with you. In contrast, DOS2 manages to prove that you can write a RPG smartly for both coop and solo play if the premise is centered around cooperation with your party members as well as the dialogue system. Instead of quips, the sequel uses second-person decisions to allow more freedom with the writing and choices, which also saves the budget for full voice-acting.
Even though both games have a linear main plot, there is a greater sense of freedom in the sequel because the cooperation (and comedy) elements work together with the combat system’s promotion of ingenuity to create a greater sense of freedom.
However, with more freedom to handle situations violently or nonviolently, there is an indescribable difficulty with DOS to explain why it is harder/easier for others. As an iron-man veteran of classic/commander of Firaxis’ XCOM games and Core Rules of Baldur’s Gate, DOS has one of the most perplexing difficulty systems I have ever encountered. This is largely the result of the combat system itself, the battle environments, the elemental damage system, and the AI behaviors tied to different difficulty settings.
The first three stem from the combat system itself and how it is more based on mastering the battleground than beating the enemies. Encounters are turn-based, Fallout 1+2 style battles where action-points are used and refunded every turn. Environments create unique encounters either due to line-of-sight and/or environmental surfaces, which can create opportunities/hazards if an elemental attack is used (ex. electric attacks on water/blood surfaces.) Unlike the Infinity Engine games where battlegrounds are ubiquitous, where you are fighting and on what surface matters as you can create power-keg situations in your (or the enemy’s) favor. Moments where you can throw an oil-barrel on a group of enemies and set them ablaze is one of many moments that is the foundation of DOS’s combat.
However, the issue with this game and having a fair sense of challenge, is the AI itself and how it can appear randomized. On Explorer, enemies don’t pose as great of a threat as they have lower HP and their attack patterns are more lenient. On Classic and above, aside from HP bonuses to all enemies, all bosses have new AI as well as additional obstacles that would make them more rewarding if they were predictable. What should be a more rewarding experience can quickly become irritating because either the AI is too demanding, the environment isn’t working as you planned, or your tactics simply aren’t working as intended due to the order of turns (initiative). This is also ignoring the moments where due to a model’s animation, players can miss their attacks because of the cursor, making the player spend an action point on movement as well as get the player hurt if an enemy can strike back with Opportunist. (The safest solution is always to target a portrait, and if not, then zoom in to exploit the free-aim.)
These sorts of issues do not crop up until later sections of the game where the player is heavily dependent on following a set path of gaining XP to stand a chance at certain enemies, which is why the Explorer mode feels more proper of an experience. It’s a shame that the added AI behaviors are not included because Classic Mode forces you to use the full extent of the game’s numerous consumables (potions, elemental arrows, scrolls, etc.) that makes combat have as much punch as rhythm to the experience.

Having torn apart DOS with my main gripes, the game remains as charming as ever and it does offer a greater sense of reward for its journey, especially with the Six Man Party mod that better balances out the difficulty to be more casual on Classic. (There are still other issues like the end-game temple filler that would be enjoyable if it didn’t have insta-kill death-traps from those Sentinel enemies and the final boss battle that is almost ruined because of an idiotic NPC that can be killed within a single-turn at not fault of your own.) It’s also praiseworthy that the Enhanced Edition not only adds new story elements, full voice-acting, new gameplay features and dozens of other changes like more difficulty options all free for previous owners of the standard game.
The happy ending to this review is that, if you can look past all these glaring faults, there is still a great game to enjoy for RPG veterans, young and old, single or couples, that is the cornerstone of an even greater RPG that follows, Divinity Original Sin 2.

It's a pretty good game overall, but large parts of the game seem like a complete waste of time. It has many of the same let's-do-everything problems Neverwinter Nights had.
- Blacksmithing seems like a waste of time.
- Crafting seems like a waste of time.
- Weight limits are always stupid, but it's never really a problem in this game because most items have very low carry weights.
- Since crafting is useless, that means most items in the game are useless. Bones, feathers, teeth, mushrooms, etc. It's all vendor trash.
- Giving NPCs a money limit is just stupid. I should be able to sell my garbage in one shot. Going through my stuff 20 times for 20 different NPCs breaks the immersion of the game and makes it boring.
- The story and side plots are not interesting at all. it's exactly like Neverwinter Nights. Everyone has some long, drawn-out story, and I can't get into it because I don't care about any of these characters.
- The combat is extremely unbalanced and wonky. Due to long cooldown times, one cannot make a party that has a dedicated healer. You get 1 healing cast every 4 turns or so, but half of your party can be killed in 1-2 turns, so the healing spells are completely useless during combat. Potions are useless as well because they don't heal very much. A potion heals 20%, but 1 shot from a boss does 40%, and he hits twice per turn.
- Melee characters are completely useless. It seems like they take the same damage per hit, and they do the same damage per hit, but they get hit 10x as often.My first party had a cleric with a shield, and the cleric would get destroyed all the time. I made another party that was just 2 mages, and they steamrolled everything; most fights would take no damage at all.
It just seems like the game is trying to do too many things at once, but none of them are done particularly well. It needs to be a bit more structured and simplified

Let me first say that I love many of the moves, the stories, character designs (well, most of them...) and (most of) the concepts.  This game is EXCELLENTLY drawn and animated, as the physics seem to be the most realistic for any 2D fighting game I have ever seen.  And the tutorials are just SOOOOO AMAZING. :D  Do the tutorials before you get playing!
Now onto my UNrecommendation...
The gameplay ITSELF is a big issue.  I will be frank... it is MOST DEFINITELY not noob friendly.  Online versus matches are practically CRAWLING with pro players with movesets LEAGUES beyond the hardest CPU difficulty, Nightmare.
The ONE THING that contributes to this... the very heart of this problem... resides in the game's INFINITE COMBO SYSTEM.  This allows for move combos to be excecuted again and again and again and AGAIN, as the final move in such combos can "cancel", or transition without delay, into the first move of the combo, resulting in an endless loop.
Once one excecutes an infinite combo, it's pretty much GAME OVER.
The infinite combo is difficult to prevent, difficult to learn, difficult to execute (especially if you use a PC keyboard, like me), keeps the victim's character stunned long enough to excecute the rest of the moves in perfect and rapid succession, and before you know it, you've lost well over 50% of your health before they come back to trim your health bar to 0.  This defeats the purpose of the awesome heavier-hitting moves (especially many of the "Blockbuster" attacks, Skullgirls' version of ultra moves).  Aesthetically, it just looks plain unrealistic... I would think that games like these would portray an all-out brawl, rather than having one character beat the snot out of the other.
The store page states that one of the key features is "A Robust Anti-Infinite Combo system keeps competitive play free of abusive tactics," but I have yet to see any tutorial or guide for said "Anti-Infinite Combo system."  So far, there is this mechanism (I think it's called "Drama") which allows one to break free of an attack chain and repulse the enemy for about one second (before attempting a total reversal, if you're a pro or getting creamed again by an infinite combo).
If you are a PC gamer, I think this game might be easier to play if an arcade controller was used... but that would mean an additional cost.  Also, if you use 2GB of RAM on your computer, the game will start lagging when someone initiates a blockbuster (which will stop if you switch in/out of fullscreen or windowed mode using "Alt + Enter", but this gets very annoying).
I've been playing about 86 hours up to this point, but I've practically given up.  I've tried many different combinations of fighters to see if there was some way that I can stop the infinite combo, but so far, I have totally failed.
I sincerely hope that the programmers find this review to be helpful, and take it into consideration, hopefully adjust the game mechanics accordingly (specifically, slowing some moves in a chain in order to prevent infinite combos and/or a MUCH HIGHER Drama meter charge rate...).
Overall, this does NOT mean that I will stop playing the game altogether... the game is still amazing, and has great promise... the mechanics just need a little adjustment, that's all.  I hope future players find my review helpful. :)

Pros:
Looks great
Sounds great in terms of music and voice acting
Nostalgic sense of humor and references
Challenging
Relics are a very cool addition to the game and offer a lot of variety, especially with upgrades
Unique playstyles for each class, and it is rewarding to master one when playing multiplayer
No microtransactions: the way the relic upgrades and gold system works in the game, I could very easily see that being an option, and it would have been terrible had they done it
Cons:
Very short game: 12 levels, 3 of which are boss fights, and not really levels even.
Very little (if any) challenge in the "traps" or "secrets"
"Hmm, this crumbly wall sure if awfully close to this explosive barrel spawner... I wonder if maybe..., nah that'd be too easy." and you'll probably die to the very first spike trap, and then never again for the remainder of the time you play this game.
Difficulty settings don't actually change very much, because by the time you move up, you've already mastered not getting hit in the first place. So creeps doing more damage is not really noticable. Not much else changes.
No real sense of exploration. Very linear game, even in (if not especially in) the randomly generated levels. Run down a hallway, run into a room and fight a couple spawners, run into a room with treasure and food, run down another hallways, etc, etc. There's no branching paths, no secret rooms outside of the blatantly obvious bomb rooms that are always RIGHT beside the explosive barrels, and those only contain a couple potions or turkeys usually. Keys are damn near unneccessary in this game, because you only ever get exactly the number of them that you need to move down the linear map.
Very few potions spread throughout maps. Especially noticable when playing multiplayer. Potions and keys do not carry over between levels either.
No chat options for playing with strangers means you have very little room for strategizing, picking classes optimally, or conversing in any way. The average skill level of random people online is very, very low, and if you don't have friends to play the game with, you're going to be stuck in singleplayer for the most part, and that's just not how Gauntlet was supposed to be played. Kind of seems like a moneygrab for the 4-packs honestly.
Holding out for updates in the future to address some of the complaints, the chief one being lack of content. Custom maps and community sharing of those maps would be incredible. An endless horde mode would also be a nice addition. If they added those things, it would add a lot of replay value to the game, and it wouldn't get stale so quickly.
Overall, it's well worth buying and playing, multiplayer or singleplayer. Challenging and innovative in a lot of ways, while remaining true to the "Gauntlet" feel.
But it does seem like an unfinished game despite this. Only 4 or 5 hours worth of gameplay before you're just grinding the same levels over again. Regardless, $20 is pretty cheap, and you get your money's worth out of it.
7.5/10, would be 8.5 with map editor for sure.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Amazing game, must play. Simple to pick up, hard to master. You can seriously compete without spending any money. Many great strong decks that do not include legendary or even supreme cards. Really great community as well. The game is not perfect needs some more balance updates. They are making new content and modes which is nice, but just have to make sure they don't ignore current issues. You wouldn't think this game was in EA, it feels 100% completed..
You gotta ignore a lot of these negative reviews. I have personally read many of them and most of them are from people who simply do not understand how the game works or they are just insanely impatient. You can easily obtain a collection for free without any real issues. You get on overage 2k+ gold per quest which is enough to purchase 2 cards and you get 1 quest per day. In 1 week time of playing about 1 or 2 hours a day you will have 14+ cards from quest and another 3/4+ or so from playing, it will depend on how much you win for the ones you get from playing.
I've ranked up pretty high (Master / Grandmaster) with only using the most basic cards. No supreme, no legendary, 1 or 2 rares and that's it. I'm not really that wild about the legendary cards for the most part, they are kind of specific and good for certain things, but not really all around type cards.
The only negative would be the masters could take a little while to unlock. 2 are on a weekly rotation and fairly soon you will earn enough to purchase 1 more. Just like any other f2p game if you don't want to spend ANY money at all then you better damn well expect to spend a fair amount of time to earn them. Why does everyone always want everything for free all the time instantly as if we live in a fairytale world?
If you want things unlocked sooner then spend 20$ and get a MASSIVE jump start to the game. You can legit spend only 20$ and have a ton of stuff unlocked in a short amount of time. You get 2500 rubies which can purchase SEVERAL masters plus double gold and xp for 1 year. This game is note even remotely close to being considered p2w because of the extremely low amount of money you would need to spend to instantly unlock everything. I'm talking about unlocking basically everything from day 1 without even playing the game, it wouldn't cost that much at all. You can definitely just spend 20$ and with a reasonable amount of time have most of the cards you want with almost all the masters.
The development team is really impressive and active. This is the first game i've seen where the devlopers are constantly active in the streams and not just the ones with the most people. I was starting off streaming and nobody is there except 1 of the developers. They are active on forums and take lots of input to balance changes and ideas. I've also met lots of friendly players who I play with regularly.
This is really nice, especially with how a lot of games have greedy developers putting games behind unrealistic paywalls or cancerous communites. I've only seen about 2 or 3 people who are pure cancer and 10 times that of good friendly players. You can also get this game for free just from watching streams, they give out steam keys often.

I'd like to start out saying that this is a solid game regardless, but I encountered too many bugs and problems with the design of the UI to the point that combat and inventory management became increasingly frustrating.
In combat my rogue could be trying to walk around an enemy for a backstab and get hit by an opportunity attack because the area of the model of a fence glitched between my rogue and the skeleton they were attacking. It didn't matter that my character was right beside the skeleton the entire time they were moving around it. Sometimes this would happen even if there was no object glitching between my rogue and the enemy. I've restarted saves because my characters have died to this and I didn't want them to lose out on EXP.
There are Waypoints, but they aren't placed well and I still end up having to walk a long way to get where I need to go at points. If I want to go to a destination between two Waypoints, I can either walk, or take the Waypoint and walk back half the way. I end up walking regardless.
If I try to craft using the experimental crafting screen, sometimes the items will continue to drag after I've clicked to enter them in one of the two ingredient boxes, and because they drag, when I go to click "combine" the item that dragged removes itself, nothing gets made, and I have to re-add it again. That can lead to more frustration if I double-click it because it can end up replacing the other item and then I have to put that item back in as well.
I enjoyed the game better after I turned the sound off. Although I get this is supposed to be a whimsical game, the theatrical voice acting was too much for me, and when I go into a dungeon, I don't want to hear a woman going "la dee da doo deee" like I'm hopping away merrily into the sunset instead of fighting in a cave.
I like that some of the gear is random and some of it is placed, but I don't like finding a really good item, going to go get gold for it, only to come back to find that the NPC's inventory has already changed and the item is no longer there. I didn't have a problem with money, so missing out on good gear (it was immunity gear) because I left to another area really grated on me.
