I purchased this game with the fond memories of Gauntlet Legacy, my all-time favorite arcade game that would suck away my quarters to no end. The game I got has the bare bones of the old Gauntlet Legacy game, there are indeed spawning structures that must be destroyed and and endless spawning of minions until they are destroyed... but something is lost in this reiteration of the game. There are a couple of things different that change the game drastically that I think one should know before purcashing this game.
1. The levels are rather small and lacking in the same grandour that the levels in GL used to produce. In addition after playing for a couple of hours all the levels start to blend together until it's more like having 3 stages your run through repeatedly. Even though each stage has 3 areas they all follow a similar kind of routine. The areas you run through go in this order- you run around a smallish map,  you run through a narrow map that has similarish rooms, you fight in one big room an annoyingly large amount of monsters; honestly it gets boring after a while.
2. Killing the spawning buildings. These buildings are massive tanks that can tank dozens of hits from any class. In GL the buildings weren't absolute tanks and the monsters weakened the futher the buildings were destroyed. This is NOT the case in this one, this leads to monsters becoming a huge annoyance. As I found myself playing wizard in unfair mode I found it a simple matter of flame jumping onto the building, using forceshield, icebeam in a rinse and repeat measure was a simple way of taking down buildings in the hardest difficulty!!! This means to me that the way they have buildings is just a way to inflate the amount of time spent trying to clear a level to make up for a lack of map size.
3. The next thing I miss from GL is the boss fights. The boss fights in this current rendition of the game are long, tedious,  and relatively easy. The final boss is a little tricky but even then isn't that hard to a new player as long as they know how to control their characters by doing the basic tutorial where the game does an excellent job of explaining some of the more complex aspects.
As I see it, this game is just the newest rendition of the games that use the title of Gauntlet, however I shalls till miss seeing the gold coins and pile of bones when I complete a level, of being able to go super size, or to tri-shot with archer. Honestly this game is okay with the little nuances they have added, but for it to truely be the Gauntlet I yearn for then

A charming game that expresses the innocent sense of curiosity and imagination of a young child in a way I have rarely seen.
If you're not familiar with the Scribblenauts series, they are platformer sandbox puzzle games where you can summon just about any object from the dictionary (with some reasonable exceptions such as copyrighted things, alcohol, and proper nouns) and expect them to interact in a believable way. If you can think of any food, animal, household item, weapon, mythological creature, or vehicle, chances are you can make it appear. We're talking tens of thousands of possibilities. A few surprises can also be summoned, such as a variety of internet memes and special objects, if you can think of them.
You can summon objects, or add adjectives to existing objects, to solve puzzles and make all the townspeople happy. Or, you could just screw around for hours summoning gods and beasts and riding them across the world as your epic mounts, or watching them run loose and terrorize the villagers.
The puzzles are all ridiculously easy, but difficulty is obviously not the point. Personally, my favorite way to play this game is to think of the most obnoxiously ridiculous solutions to every puzzle. Most puzzles will have a bluntly obvious solution, but you can make hilarity ensue if you can think of something creative. For instance, a guy wanted something to help carve his ice sculpture. I gave him a toenail clipper. Hansel and Gretel needed something to make a trail with through the forest. I gave them thumbtacks. A buzzard wanted something to eat. I gave it a dead baby. A tracking dog needed something that smelled like Santa so he could search for Santa. I summoned Santa.
It's an excellent game packed with great humor and content, and it's miles ahead of the Nintendo DS games it was based on. My only complaint is that it got a bit boring after the first few hours, but I fixed that just by taking some breaks and not playing it all on one sitting. But I never once stopped appreciating how wonderful the game is. Highly recommended for anyone who wants to rediscover their inner child, complete with borderline politically incorrect humor, in a way that very few games can provide.
(Achievement hunters: getting 100% is very tedious, as you will need to solve over a hundred riddles to acquire the remaining bonus pieces. Usually you will solve some of them on accident throughout normal gameplay if you try to use creative solutions. However, if you ever get bored, you can just look at a FAQ to fully complete the game effortlessly.)

Allow me to start by saying that I adore story-heavy games. Love them to death.
After reading rave reviews about this game's amazing, tear-inducing plotline, I decided to give it a try.
It failed to suck me in at first, but I nonetheless stuck with it through the slow, horrendous gameplay, and several exceedingly weird scenes (that one zombie scene comes to mind...), in hopes of eventually getting overwheled by an astounding twist or reveal in the story, one way or another.
But no such thing happened.
Instead, I was smacked in the face by the game's excuse of a plotline, tear-inducing in all its right, but not at all through emotional depth or significance, but from its sheer incompetency in being able to make sense, much less entertain.
Perhaps I'm too critical, seeing to how my opinion is vastly different from many of the others who've played this game and fell in love with it, but the way I see it, "To The Moon" is a complete waste of time.
The game's storyline is convoluted, shallow, and nonsensical at best, and the "plot twist" (if it even merits that title), sorry to say, consists of nothing more than sheer STUPIDITY. Paired with it's lazy gameplay mechanics, this game did nothing but frustrate and annoy me the whole way through.
Although I got it on sale for only a dollar or so, I still feel cheated. I'm never getting those hours of my life back.
Do yourself a favor, and don't bother with this game. Just don't.

I loved this deeply emotional and philosophical game. The themes are very accessible in terms of the common human experience they explore, yet they are presented with very interesting nuance and complexity. The Memento-like mechanic of moving backwards through time in vignettes works really well to create a solid narrative suspense.
The minisodes are not as good. They explore the social implications of the technology that is at the base of the game as well as some mystery about the main characters, which is interesting, but the gameplay is weak, involving a lot of back and forth between screens.
Controlling with the mouse was a bit clunky at times for me, but this is a wonderful game with a touching story. I highly recommend it!

This is, by far, one of the most moving stories I have ever had the pleasure of experiencing in a video game. The gameplay is somewhat non-existent. A few taps, some puzzles, and you've figured out this game. The meat of this game comes from the intense story, the moving music, and the twist ending. Sure, this is more of an interactive movie than it is a video game, and to some it MAY not be worth the $9.99 price tag, but it is certainly something that everyone who cares about artistry and story in video games, as well as an amazing soundtrack, should have the pleasure of experiencing. I'm glad to have this as an addition to my library, and as an avid space lover myself, it is certainly ranked as one of the greatest Steam games I've ever played.

I'm reviewing OS:EE & OS:2 after playing about 400 hours of OS:Classic, OS:EE, OS:2 at the time of writing this and I'm still not done.
I'm comparing the two OSEE & OS2 to each other.  Don't play Classic... EE is way better.
OS:Classic 70 - Can be frustrating
OS:EE        85 - Only minor gripes on Audio and Dialog
OS:2           90 - Polished beautifully, however, it is missing some features from OS:EE
The purpose of this review is to recommend both games.  But not OS:Classic
1.  Turn-based combat (OS:EE & OS2):
*Classic Mode*  I can sometimes see ways for the enemy to beat me and it does not.  I dont like that.
*Tactition Mode* I sometimes find myself frustrated that it is too difficult but most times it is pretty fun.
2.  Story
(OS:EE)  I like it.
(OS:2)  A bit better than OS:EE
3.  Crafting
(OS:EE)  Very good.  Lots of stuff to make and putting points in crafting/blacksmithing improves quality.
(OS:2)  Not so good compared to OS:EE.  I didn't even craft in OS:2 because it didn't seem to be worth it.  Maybe I wasn't understanding it but I was very disappointed.
4.  Graphics
(OS:EE)  Somewhat more stylised then OS:2 and less attractive then OS:2
(OS:2)  Spot on.
5.  Audio Music & Ambiance
(OS:EE)  Annoying at times.  Loops and cycles of sounds get very tedious.
(OS:2)  Way better than OS:EE but still sometimes repetitive.

6.  Writing / Dialog / Story
(OS:EE)  Not nearly as good as OS:2
(OS:2)  Best writing I have ever experienced in a game.
7.  Character Development.
(OS:EE)  Really good.  I wish that OS:2 had exactly the same method for defining your character's personality.
(OS:2)  Limited compared to EE
8.  Replayability:
(OS:EE) I played classic for about 60 hours and then played EE for about 100 at the time of writing this.  I'm still not done.
(OS:2)  Way more replayable with undead as an extra challenge.
9.  Maturity level
(OS:EE)  Has some real-world references that I found humorous but after playing OS:2  and thne playing EE again I felt like they didn't need to be in the game.
(OS:2)  Love the mood and humor of the game.  Its perfect.
Conclusion:  I recommend Divinity as the best turn-based RPG out of my experience as a gamer for over 20 years.  The only game I would consider as good was Final Fantasy 7 when it was first released.   It's way better than XCOM and way deeper then Chaos.  However, I felt that Chaos has a little better AI when it comes to battles.  I played Baulder's Gate but I don't remember it so I can't really compare it.
Its kinda hard to compare to Witcher III, Fallout 4, and Skyrim but in its own way it is just as good.
Really looking forward to more of Larian's productions.  Thanks to Larian Studios for making such great games.

At first I wasn't a big fan of turn based RPG's, and mostly played "Hack & Slash" type of RPG games. But that changed when I tried Divinity: Original Sin. I loved the freedom at what you could do in the game.
How every conversation or action could turn into unexpected side quest or reveal a hidden branch of quest. How crafting system worked with incredible amounts of different ingredients and their combinations. How game didn't hold your hand before every corner but instead let you rush straight into things. How skills and talents were limited but vast in variety and functionality, so you had to truly invest into right ones to aid you in the right moment. How you could pass judgment on anything and everything (to an extent), for example, I once lured an angry horde of orcs into the city and let them slaughter everyone just so I could see what happens. Turns out if you murder the whole city, you have a lot of loot but no one to sell it to, haha.
Anyways, the game has come long way since the initial Kickstarter release and even got a "facelift" recently with insane amount of modifications. Game has pretty much a bit of everything, some serious parts, some sad parts, some funny parts and amazing parts that you will enjoy. Story is unique and engaging with a lot of information and dialogues, hidden clues and plot twists. And then there's side quests, secrets and easter eggs all around for you to find.
Did I mention the world is rich in detail and beautiful? And there are many different regions, with different weather and environments. Game is not taxing on the hardware and it looks great, runs great so it's awesome experience all around.
I jumped right into the Enhanced Edition, which comes free of charge if you own the base game, and I'm already 60+ hours in, earned over 600 000 gold, because I vacuum everything that is not nailed to floor and even then I take the nails and grab the stuff anyways.
This game was made by AWESOME developer team, which was fueled by AWESOME community support and in the end it turned into an AWESOME turn based, fantasy RPG!
In other words: AAA

My characters are Source Hunters, stooping to grave digging seems rather beneath them (pardon the pun), but I'm so desperate for xp and money that now anything goes.
These items are a general annoyance for me in any RPG game, not just Divinity, so no points lost there, just a feeling of opportunities missed by designers
I am enjoying the combat, it's not just power gaming so far, but the bosses that I've encountered have all had some serious AOE death bombs that have made them impossible for me so far (party wipe even when at full health), and I'm feeling a little bit blocked at the moment.
Still recommending this game though.

This game...... it's one of a kind. For some reason, I always expect these kind of platformers to be the same, jump around in a side-scrolling world, and kill enemies... basically a Mario game. But when I read on their offical website that they took the bases of Zelda and other retro games, and used them to inspire the creation of Ori, I knew had to play this game. Not because of my crazy love of Zelda, but because of the way they wrote about how it inspired them. That is something I completely understand. When I loaded up the game, I found not just another platformer, but a game with the most gorgeous artwork for texturing, and a beautifully orchestrated soundtrack. When a player sees and hears that, just from the start menu, you know an enormous amount of effort went into the creation of this game. And once you play this game... well, its an experience like no other. At first the game mechanics confused me, like the abilty to save only when you had enough resources, but after a very well thought out gameplay introduction, it began to make a lot more sense. What is even more lovely about this game, is that you don't have to learn everything all at once; the farther you progress into the game, the more you master your abilities, and then a new ability is presented to you. This is great because you can be sure by the time you reach the end of the game, you will know how to use Ori's powers inside and out.
Now, for those who are skeptical about buying this game, I understand. $20 is a lot of money to spend on Steam, especially on just one game. To you I say, please, watch this playthrough that I recorded of me playing though Ori. It doesn't reveal too much, only the intro and a few other cut scenes, but trust me you will want to watch those again yourself anyways. And after watching, if you still don't want to pay that much, at least put this game into your wishlist, for it will inevitably will go on sale sometime.
And lastly, I say many thanks to the creators of this game, who put more effort than I could imagine into its' creation.

This game is pretty entertaining for the first 15 levels or so. You can complete all the PvE challenges and reach the Silver PvP rankings relatively quickly. However, once you reach the Silver level, you will go back and forth between Silver and Bronze for quite awhile. The reasons for this are systemic. The cards you recieve as a reward are random and the difference in power level, mana cost, and usefulness vary wildly between rarity levels (common, regular, rare, legendary, and supreme). For this reason, those who subscribe to the pay to win game style (at the cost of other players' fun) or those who have been playing the game enough to accumulate a quality card collection quickly begin to dominate the game, countered only by bad luck in their randomized draws during individual matches. This turns the game into yet another one of those skinner box games that eschews interesting gameplay as it's primary mechanism for engaging and retaining its player base.
Tl;dr
This is skinner box game that is fun for a day, so long as you bought it on sale, but beware of getting sucked into grinding just to be competitive.

Epic Battle Fantasy is a story set in a fantasy land that encapsulates total humour. It's powerful role playing essentials prove that an RPG does not have to be made with great graphics or new complicated battle mechanics - it just needs a firm storyline such as this.
The story unfolds with four heroes that find each other along the journey, fight monsters, and as usual, attempt to claim world peace from this unseemingly harmless boss - the Godcat. Throughout the way, dry R16 humour develops throughout the story, and even when you are engaging in difficult battles, somewhat the characters randomly crack jokes in a light hearted manner. Hmm...
The system is brilliant. Brilliant in the sense that the forging and money systems go hand-in-hand nicely unlike many other games that introduce poverty into the heroes. Summons actually help a lot, and battle statuses are not just those nice symbols floating on your heads - they actually kill you. Simple but effective.
Music is fine, although the tunes are reminiscent of popular music. Canon in D - main theme. Enjoyable but I didn't love it as much and it somewhat did not match the situations.
Overall, a must try for fantasy fans. Also has a very high replay value.

Fallout 3
I first played this game when it came out on Xbox 360 in 2009. Back then, this game blew my mind and has since been my favorite game to date. This game set the standard for Open World games and their DLC's since my original playthrough of it, and subsequent ones as the DLC's were released, then the GOTY later on.
After playing the Original games, Fallout 1-4 including Tactics and New Vegas (Excl. BOS), I still believe that Fallout 3 has my favorite storyline, and gameplay. I wasn't too fond of NV's Aim system or Fallout 4's Run and Gun FPS gameplay.
The add-ons were solid, and actually all of them added a fair amount of content, some valuable (and possibly overpowered) loot, and various experiences, people, and stories for your charactor to explore.
Honestly, making this long story and review short, Fallout 3 will always be my favorite game of all time, and I highly recommend this game to anyone looking to play Fallout.

Started playing after Foundation update and on 40% sale. I wouldn't pay $60 for any game let alone this one, but it was tempting on sale so I jumped on it. I gotta say this game doesn't deserve half of the nerd rage that it gets. If you're checking this game out to buy it, look at reviews (both neg and pos) that give reasons rather than mere insults. And I tried Spore first because of all of the afore mentioned nerd rage. After 200 some hours in this game, I gotta say it is worlds better than Spore and while it borrows many ideas from that game's space stage, it is a completely different and more updated game than Spore.
Pros:
first person exploration (space and planetary)
planets are diverse. desert moons, frozen mountainous wastes, radioactive jungles with lakes, hot volcanic environments with trees like bat wings.
Alien animal life
The funky soundtrack
The colorful creative screenshot candy
Spaceship designs and upgrading
Love the cars for tearing around extreme weather planets.
As of Atlas Rises, update 1.35, lots of crashes are fixed. I don't notice any tech problems except an occassional fps drop on planets, but I don't have a very modern machine. Even with most settings turned down, it still looks great.
Cons:
The Star Map looks great but is exceedingly frustrating. It used to be impossible just to retrace my steps back one jump to the system I had visited just before, but thankfully this past "Path Finder" update fixed that problem (you can mark visited systems with waypoints in the discoveries menu).
Sometimes the nebula colors (space is never black in NMS) make it hard to see things.
Repetitive: Alien creatures sometimes begin to look all alike but you're "discovering" them as new.
and difficult learning curve since almost nothing is explained:
The beginning of the game starts with a white screen and the word "Initialise..." and what looked like a logo shaped like an E. I took this to be a loading screen. Did an End Task twice before looking at the forums and finding that it was, in fact, up to me to press the letter E. That was frustrating because the anti-hype had me expecting the game to crash from the start but it was actually part of the learning curve. E is the activate key for everything.
Final thought: If you like the idea of a unique fantasy space exploration game and it's on sale, get it. But don't expect much from the Atlas or center of the universe plots, rather just do your own thing. I read the spoilers because of the negative reactions to that part and it seems justified. Oh, and don't bother with survival mode for long. Fuel costs for taking off once will drain your fuel tank, essentially keeping you on whatever planet you find so that you can surive long enough to get more fuel. It's fun the first time, but not every time you land.
UPDATE 1.3: The Atlas update broke the universe. If you had a saved game, now there's a whole lot wrong with it and unless there's a pretty hefty hotfix on the way, it's looking like Hello Games expected us to wipe our own saves without announcing it. The first two updates didn't mess with our saves, but this one does, so just buyer beware.
Edit: the hotfixes were indeed hefty and after five patches, my old save game runs well again. I love the new features and the new Artemis quests. Weird, unbelievable story line, but it's a trippy game, so I go with it.

So here's the deal. I like this game, but it's not the game I expected to play.  Going in, I was hoping for a great story with some halfway decent platforming elements, but instead I received a great platformer with some halfway decent story elements.  That doesn't mean it's not a great game.  I really loved it, and the difficulty was spot on, getting slightly more difficult with every new objective, and always staying just out of the realm of easy.  However, I felt as though the story was merely slapped onto the start and finish with an extended fetch quest as filler in between.  What story there was in the middle felt like dry exposition, and didn't really have the emotional depth of the start and finish.  (The opening two minutes had me crying, but nothing after that made me feel anything whatsoever, except for a bit of confusion here and there, until the finale which gave a really nice, happy feeling)  That being said, the art design was breathtaking, the music was phenomenal, the platforming was fluid and intuitive, and the mechanics were simple, fun, and increasingly clever.
Final verdict/TLDR:
Definitely worth playing, but not as focused on storytelling as you may be led to believe.  Still, I highly recommend it, if for nothing else but the gameplay and artistic design.

I've had a lot of fun with this game so far. The characters each have their own advantages and disadvantages to complement their unique play styles. The game also proved somewhat challenging to beat on unfair difficulty. My only complaints are that it's currently a bit too grindy, requiring you to get over 200,000 kills to complete all of the class's mastery pages. Additionally, the devs have yet to implement random level generation akin to the old arcade-style Gauntlet. Instead, there are only three sections of the game, each is broken into 4 chapters. Three chapters in every set of four contain 3 levels each, the fourth containing the boss fight. Each set of 3 levels is mostly the same: the first always a challenge level with keys, locked doors, and monster summoners, the second always an "escape level" of sorts with a constantly respawning threat (Death, spiders, demons), and the third an arena-style level with monster summoners that takes place in one room. Furthermore, all of the bossfights have the very simplified mechanic of avoiding the boss for a set amount of time until they become vulnerable, then attacking them for about 5 seconds before they become invincible again. Rinse and repeat. Despite these complaints, the game is still a lot of fun to play with friends provided two or more of you didn't want to play the same class. This game is worth it if you can spit the cost of the four pack, but I'd wait for it to go on sale to buy it just for yourself unless you already have people to play it with.

I'm old enough to have played the original Gauntlet arcade game, back in ~1985. This new steam version, is based on that, rather than the newer versions that came out in the 1990's.
I never liked the original arcade game. The repetition of spamming the fire button, while you fed the machine quarters, to increase your slowly, yet inevitably draining life, never appealed to me. I loved the music and digitized speech though.
Arrowhead, the developers of this new game also created the game, Majicka. I found the demo of Majicka mediocre.
I do love this new version of Gauntlet. Let me start with the negatives:
- There is no lobby chat, in-game chat or world chat. There's no chat period. It is strange, noticeable and frustrating.
- The game is not properly integrated into Steam, so there's no way to add players that you played with. Social networking is a pain and something that is done in the community hub.
- The game will randomly disconnect you from a game, due to some kind of flaw in the networking code. The game does have a "rushed-out-the-door" feeling to it.
- Some people who played the game on easy or normal complain at the "lack of content", since they finished the game in 3 - 7 hours. I have only only ever played the game on Hard and Unfair.
- A couple of days ago, I saw my first hacker. The game had high score hacks, on day zero. That did not matter to me. However, I recently played with a warrior, with no cooldown on his abilities, which is a huge cheat! A friend also saw a valkyrie using an infinite health hack. I'm seeing more people talking about hackers in the community forum and I think that eventually, this game might end up the same way that Max Payne 3 multiplayer did ( overrun by hackers ). I don't think that developers care about hackers, to be honest ( they got their money ). Somebody mentioned on the forum, that saves are client side, therefore hacks were inevitable:
- The population is rapidly dropping to less than 3,000 players, from a peak of 12,669:
The positives:
- I love the challenging combat and AI on Hard and Unfair. The melee characters are fairly basic. Warrior has a heavy cleave attack, a 360 degree spin attack and dash, which knocks over enemies. Valkyrie has: a spear thrust; a shield defence, that renders her immune to attacks; a shield throw, where she uses her shield as a killer frisbee ( like in the 1980's movie, Krull ). Elf is a dynamic bowman that can tumble, drop bombs and snipe at long ranges. He can also attach bombs to his arrows, which is an excellent game mechanic. Wizard, my favourite character, has to juggle 9 spells: light fireball, heavy fireball, teleportation, spherical shield, ice freeze, area effect ice slow, short range electric shotgun arc, long range electric shock. Wizard alone, makes having an XBOX controller for PC, a must.
- I love the orchestral music, which seems to change depending on what is going on in the environment.
- I really enjoy the level design. I think that a lot of thought was put into the aesthetics. There's a stereotypical temple setting, a scary, cavernous, spider crypt and a fiery, lava realm.
Value:
Using a level 49 Wizard, I have solod the harder realms, on the hardest difficulty level. There are about 10 levels per realm, for a total of roughly 30 levels. The developers could have added another 3 - 6 realms but at the same time, the game was available for $20 and through trading, I actually paid $10. It's hard to say how much value you will get out of the game because it depends on what difficulty level you play and which, ( if any ) characters appeal to you. I enjoy playing the valkyrie, elf and wizard. I find the warrior painfully boring but will play him occasionally.

A fantastic Action RPG, Fallout 3 combines all the best elements from first person shooter games with all the RPG from a game such as Oblivion. (Both games run on the Gamebryo engine which is highly moddable.) The base game was fantastic alone, but with the DLC's, the level cap and ending are both enhanced. I won't go into detail, because this review is about 7 years late.
Guide:

Third canonical entry of the beloved classical RPG franchise Fallout. First one ever produced in a decade, if you discount the spin-off Brotherhood of Steel tactical RPG and the action game released on Playstation. Also the first title since Bethesda took over. This one generate quite a bit of controversy within the Fallout community, largely due to the fact it plays different than previous titles, as Bethesda decides to use the Elder Scrolls' engine based on GameBryo, which obviously is what they excel at.
Contrast to previous titles' isometric CRPG aspect, Fallout 3 is recommended by the developer to play in First Person perspective, even though a third person is present in the game. Some may mistake this game as an FPS on first glance, but rest assured this is still a pretty heavy CRPG, where character development, stats, skills and perks play the most important role in terms of gameplay, rather than the player's aiming skill.
Suffice to say, Beth created this Fallout title with love and homage to the original titles produced by Interplay, who sold the license and rights to them. This curiously gathered a lot of hate within the community towards them, even though in my opinion it was Interplay's fault to mismanage itself and go bankrupt. Other than the perspective, this game plays and feels like a true Fallout title, all the concepts and aesthetics were nicely adapted into the familiar Elder Scrolls-like gameplay, which personally is quite a happy mix due to my loyalty to that series.
Needless to say, the gameplay leans more toward Elder Scrolls titles rather than the old Fallout games in the 90's. Some may see as a problem, but I don't. Especially if you live in 2015, you can literally find spiritual successers to every classic RPGs: Wasteland 2 to Fallout (and of course the original Wasteland, which Fallout is loosely based on), Pillars of Eternity to Baldur's Gate, Torment: Tides of Numenera to Planescape, Divinity: Original Sin to Ultima, and a bunch of excellent tile-based dungeon crawlers to the classics like Eyes of the Beholder in early 90s. So you see, Fallout 3 being different than before isn't a problem for me personally, and it surely wasn't a problem for the original Fallout crew, of which a large proportion of developers work for Obsidian to strike a deal with Beth to work on a title truer to the original spirit of Fallout to based on Fallout 3's base game. See New Vegas.
One benefit of Beth's taking over that no one can deny is obviously the production value. Fallout 3 is a step up in almost every direction up from Oblivion, which FO3 is built upon. Some folks jokingly name the new Fallout as "Oblivion with guns", which indeed tells some truth. Gone is the old turn based tactical combat, in with the new hectic real-time action with pausible VATS system which allows you to plan and spend your action points. I wouldn't favor one system over the other,  but FO3 does bring some fresh air to this aged franchise.
Worldcrafting wise, Beth does what it does best. Exploration is rewarding as ever. This time around, the game is set in DC and has an east coast vide, as opposed to the West Coast settings in Fallout 1 and 2. You can definitely tell this is due to Bethesda locating in Maryland. The gameworld itself is slightly smaller than that of Oblivion. This doesn't mean it has less details. If anything, the world in this game is even more vibrant. Beth clearly learnt their mistake with the generic tones of the Radiant system in Oblivion and improved upon it. This also paved the road for future titles like Skyrim and Fallout 4 to progressively become more and more organic and polished. The excellent sequal New Vegas developed by part of the original Fallout crew also take advantage of Fallout 3's engine and many of the existing gameworld assets. which is a nod to Beth's skill and will to inherit this franchise.
Final verdict: 9/10. A true Fallout fan's must have. Niche audience of open world and CRPG genre will also find quite a bang for your buck. Although avid fans only waiting for Van Buren project should be advised to find nostalgia elsewhere in titles like Wasteland 2. You may reserve your opinion towards many of the new aspects of this new title, yet nobody can deny this is hell of a game and a truly a rewarding RPG experience.

I've been playing this game for the past 2 weeks and absolutely love it. At first I thought it might be one of those parody/homage to old RPGs but while this game doesn't do anything revolutionary with the turn based formula it does present an interesting challenge without any of the annoyances of past well known games.
First thing you should know that it does contain a lot of references from old school games like Final Fantasy to Pokemon to some less obvious. That doesn't mean this game isn't original. It's got a light hearted story and a charming cast of characters. There are a few references of previous Epic Battle Fantasy games that might be lost on you but they happen more so for comedic effect and doesn't hinder understanding the story whatsoever.
I think what really makes this game enjoyable is the battle system. There's a few notable improvements on the old turn based formula that make fighting more strategic and less of a chore:
1. You are able to change equipment and characters on the fly - In the middle of a battle you aren't bound to the 3 characters and if you're not quite properly equipped to handle the foes you're battling you can easily swap out equipment during your turn. Characters in reserve also recover HP/MP each turn so it makes things slightly easier.
2. Elements and status effects play a prominent role in fights - This adds a bit of challenge. Generally there's 10 elemental resistances and another dozen status effects. Instead of always equipping the stronger weapon / armor you'll find yourself adjusting to weapons of different elements for maximum damage and defense. I find this particularly nice and adds a bit of strategy because depending on the foes you're going to be changing equipment a lot.
3. Limits / Summons - Will do wonders if you know when to use them. You could opt for a blind challenge in which you don't know any of your enemies' weaknesses but, if you're not into blindly hitting anything that moves you'll end up scanning foes a lot to learn what makes them tick. Unlike most RPGs the scan feature in this game is super useful. It also helps that the scanned information is readily available after you scan each foe. It doesn't just disappear for it to be forgotten and spam attacks anyway.
4. Upgrades - You keep all your equipment so it helps that you can use various items to improve weapon resistance and deal added damage.
While I do enjoy playing most games with a controller I found using my mouse extremely simple to move, access menus  and fight. Also the environments are vibrant and fresh so you don't get bored too quickly. The side quest Battle Mountain and varying difficulty levels are available for those who love a challenge. There's also 100+ achievements for the would be hunters to come back and 100% this game. I've only been on my first playthrough but I don't think replayability is high but for the price you have a decent 20hr minimum game on your hands. I would suggest if you're a fan of RPGs to get this. It's a bit light on story but it's done a couple of fun things with the battle system that will keep you entertained for a while.

If you like Final Fantasy and silly humour this game is pure win.
EDIT:  After finishing the whole game on normal, I'm still very impressed and have penciled in a second playthrough on hard difficulty at some point.  Here's a more in depth analysis.
First up, I love the inventory.  You can hold every item in the game but there is no problems with clutter.  You never have to worry about a full inventory or wonder if you should sell an item you may need later on.  Huge time saver, I hate managing inventory.
Abilities are chosen with experience points.  There are skills and specials.  Skills are character specific, like the fighter gets sword skills, the ranger gets bow skills.  Specials can potentially be learned by 2-4 characters but only one of them can actually learn it.  For example the skill "power metal" can be learned by either of the guys but not both of the guys.  Limit breaks (yes there are limit breaks) fall into one of these two categories as well.  So there's some careful balancing to make sure your party functions well.
Equipment is easy to manage and you will be needing to switch weapons/armor/trinkets from time to time to deal with various types of enemies.  Your mage wont be needing that fire damage staff against fire elementals, for example.  Equipment can be changed during combat at the cost of a turn in case you get caught by something unexpected.  Certain fights you'll be changing gear more then once as different enemies appear.
Equipment can all be upgraded through crafting.  Not the sort of annoying crafting where you have to sort through tons of crap and figure out just how much rough stone you need to make enough widgets to make 20 springs.  Basically you open the upgrade menu, things that can be upgraded with your current mats are highlighted, things that can't are not.  It cuts the crap and simply boils it down to the desicion of, is this where you'd like to spend these materials?  Most of the items I was using were maxed by the end of the game with no particular effort to farm or buy materials.  2-3 weapons per char, 1-2 armors, 1-2 helmets, and a whole whack of trinkets.
The real meat of the combat boils down to resistances and damage types.  8 types of elemental damage and 8 debuffs, all with their own counterpart resist stat.  Fortunatley you don't have to memorize 16 stats for every enemy type.  When an enemy typs is scanned with your scanbot, you can hover over them to check their stats at any time for the rest of the game.
There are also summons, as you'd expect from a final fantasy game, however they are not spammable in this.  You get summoning points for each kill depending on monster strength and use the summoning points to ... summon.
One thing that always bothered me about Final fantasy and Chrono Trigger was how end game tended to revolve around spamming your biggest AoE, a lot.  It looked like this game was heading that direction in the mid game, but toward the end that was just not possible.  Mixed immunities ensures you aren't just spamming a single AoE forever.  This game really took all the good out of final fantasy and boiled away a lot of the crap.  8.5/10

Epic Battle Fantasy 4 is an interesting game.  It's an "old-school inspired", JRPG-esque game but it's also heavily Western in styling...I know that's a strange sentance but this is a strange game.  The characters and dialogue are cheeky, fun, and likable, and the animations are well done and seem powerful.  The music is pretty good (although repetitive) and there are almost too many collectable and upgradable weapons, skills, and summons to digest at once.
Even with all that said, while playing this game I strangely felt like there wasn't all that much compelling me to keep going.  I got a few hours enjoyment out of it so I don't necessarily regret the purchase but it just wasn't a gripping title by any means.  It's really a glorified web/flash game with a few perks that it picked up when it moved to Steam.
Epic Battle Fantasy 4 isn't bad per se, but I don't think I would recommend it to other gamers.  That said, if it looks interesting, I'd recommend playing it for free in its original medium - a web flash game:
If you like it and/or want to purchase it to support the developer please go ahead, the game works flawlessly as a desktop title and the port from web to client went very smoothly.
All in all I'd give it a 6/10 - and I would recommend once again that interested parties check out the web version before purchasing.  The game shows potential, but really it seems to be trying to pull off what Cthulhu Saves the World and Breath of Death VII achieve much more gracefully.  However, the production value and syling of Epic Battle Fantasy seems of higher quality than the other two titles I listed, so if the author can make a few tweaks I see bright things for the future of this series.

Since there is no established genre which Reus would fit in and it’s not easy to intuitively understand what the deal with the game is, I’ll explain the core gameplay loop in detail.
At first you’re presented with your barren 2D planet and you’re given control of Reus’ four trademark giants. With them you create your planet’s biomes and resource nodes, which in turn leads to establishment of human settlements. Each settlement’s most important attribute is its resource count, split into three categories: food, wealth, technology. Resource count will gradually rise from nothing at founding to some maximum amount dynamically determined by composition of resource nodes within settlements’ borders. Resources don’t have any traditional functions (i.e. food isn’t used to feed the population), they are simply gathered for two purposes: they count towards overall score and are used to complete so-called ‘projects’.
Projects are the core gameplay concept in Reus. They are buildings, such as a granary or an observatory, which spontaneously appear as construction sites within settlements’ borders and they are completed once settlement gathers certain amount of resources. Each project provides a unique passive bonus to its settlement, so players are usually forced to adjust their resource composition once a new project pops up. Completing projects is rewarded with ‘ambassadors’ each of whom is assigned to a giant thus upgrading it. Upgrades allow giants to create more advanced resource nodes which in turn makes it possible to complete increasingly demanding projects.
I’d recommend Reus to anyone who is going to enjoy getting familiar with characteristics of a large number of resource types, combining them in a manner that will extract the most value from each land patch, tinkering with secondary resources to power up their settlements’ growth, analyze what upgrade path will best suit their current situation, etc.
As far as presentation goes Reus is pretty strong. Graphics are simple but stylish. Music is calm and pleasant even if it becomes slightly repetitive after a while. Interface is tidy and responsive, although some of the tooltips are not informative enough (luckily there’s a wiki website which describes everything in detail).
This is not a god game, so if anyone is looking for that particular fix - look elsewhere. Humans of Reus have extremely limited autonomy and the game requires lots of micromanagement.
There is no form of time compression so sporadically players will have to sit through a period of nothing to do. Generally pace of the game is rather slow with plenty of waiting for cooldowns or for giants to move between settlements. Players with little patience might want to think twice before plunging in.
And completionists beware – top tier projects require some serious analysis and calculations and on top of that there are tons of unlocks available. Generally, you won’t be able to just breeze through the content.

I love this game. But--full disclosure--the strategy genre is almost exclusively where I spend my gaming hours. The remaining time is usually allocated to sandbox games, and Reus sort of falls into both these categories.
While definitely not an
game by any stretch of the imagination [the world is literally a closed ring], Reus follows the sandbox/god game pattern of affecting the world in a way similar to an artist painting a portrait. Using the proper tools (the Giants and their abilities), you masterfully paint your world on the blank canvas that is the earth. Unlike the artist, however, your creations are living beings!
For the most part, you play the game by ordering your four Giants to either place resources, augment existing resources, terraform/terramorph the planet, or attack an area. This basic premise is compelling, and the art style is rather charming. However, once you start to really dig in to Reus, its weaknesses start to come to the surface.
At a macro level, the only real issue with the game is its repetitiveness; a trait which is no stranger to the genre, and Reus certainly doesn't aim to change that. You're literally starting from the same place every time you play [an empty planet], with little deviation in your opening choices from game to game. This weakness is something of a non-issue to genre fans, of course. Just be aware that if you struggle to enjoy city/empire-building strategy games like Civilization V, for instance, you're not likely to be won over by Reus.
More specific to the gameplay: the aspect of Reus that makes it compelling happens to also be its biggest drawback. Reus retains replay value in two major ways: randomness/chance and unlocks [achievements]. The random aspect is the aforementioned double-edged sword: your villages grow by completing projects, which are chosen from a pool of potential projects (depending on terrain, etc.), which each have a randomly-chosen resource perk, which in turn dictates how you should build moving forward.
This RNG is obviously intended to keep the game fresh, however it is often at odds with the direction your unlocks want you to follow (especially once you're down to your last handful). The game requires a lot of pre-planning (
), but then forces you to rely very heavily on what are essentially a series of dice rolls to line up perfectly. If you're averse to save scumming, you're gonna have a bad time.
The game engine also has minor goofs from time to time [no surprise, it's an indie game!]. Such as: a village spiking from 1 greed [high levels of greed are obtained by growing too fast and determine how aggressive villagers are] to attacking their neighbors just by loading savegame. These events seem to be rare, however.
If you enjoy the planning aspect of strategy games, and don't mind a lot of waiting [as resources build and for projects to start/finish], Reus is will reward you with hours upon hours of relaxing cognition.
Seriously. Reus can give Civilization a run for its money with all the pausing and tabbing out you do in a 120-minute game.

In the beginning, it's pretty simple. You build a world for civilization to survive, they grow a bit and you gain more ways to help them. Repeat this over and over. Eventually the game requires you to help the people grow larger and larger by giving the cities near exact conditions for certain feats.
So while the game starts off simple, it quickly becomes a puzzle of the best ways to achieve your goals. Efficiency is you friend.

Reus seems relatively simple at first, but becomes more and more complex. As space becomes more limited (with population increase), the task of balancing resources requires ever more clever ways of combining them. With the building threat of villages going to war with each other, it can become quite a challenge.
This is a strategy game with an indie feel and no real fighting, so it's not for everyone, but if that's your jam then Reus is worth checking out. The concentration required in solving these environmental problems certainly had me immersed.

Bloond TD5 SE is the fifth installment to the Bloons Tower Defense series and the last one to date. It's almost the perfect tower defence game in my opinion and features different gamemodes and hundreds of tracks(maps). It has everything and unlike the mobile version, everything is unlockable by ingame currency and there is no way to purchase this currency, which makes this game completely Play to Win.
I've been playing Bloons since Bloons 3 was the newest one, and it's my abselute favorite tower defense game, so I might be a little patriotic writing this.
Bloond TD5 is a game between you and the bloons. You start of as a rank 1 with only one option of "weapons" to chose from. It's the ever loved Dart Monkey. You see, all the "weapons" in this game are monkeys with different superpowers or even "real" weapons. Every rank you unlock a new monkey until you hace all of them. This is easily done by playing only one game on the first track on easy mode till level 50. After that you need to unlock all the upgrades for all the monkeys, and that's when the real fun starts.
You can start a new game every time and the experience will be different. You try and try to find the overall best strategy to be able to get the furthest you can and to the highest wave possible. Every time you eventually lose is a bigg loss in the head, but you always learn something new that's gonna help you the next time you play.
A big thing about BTD5 is the co-op mode where you can either play with strangers, or even better, your friends. There are seperate co-op maps to chose from and they all bring a challenge to the table. This is one of the parts of the game that in my opinion makes it superior to other TD games.
The graphics are also really fresh, and contain many strong colors. This is a good thing for this sort of game with the characters it has and all. I often find tower defense games to be very dark and boring, so this is a new fresh look I like.
There are frequent big updates to this game and I can't wait to see what the developers has in mind next. I also really hope for a BTD6 in the near future, but that's just me.

I'd been monitoring Skullgirls' progress for years. Even back then, when it looked like something that would run on a PlayStation 1, I knew it had potential. Something about the art style and design really interested me, and I'm always up for a new fighting game - even amongst the really terrible ones, there's only a few I actually hate.
I kept tabs on it for a while, but for a couple of years, there wasn't really a lot of progress. Then, about late 2010/early 2011, I came across the revamped SG, which was the beginning of its shaping up to the current model. I was marveled at how much the graphics had improved. Having a composer and voice actors whose work I enjoyed, also continued to pique my curiosity, and having Mike Z, whose name I recognized from fighting game websites, working on the game's mechanics only served to tell me that this was going to be a major labor of love.
As news continued to come out for the game, I only kept getting more and more excited. I worried that I was getting hyped for nothing, and that it wouldn't live up to my expectations. And sadly, I wasn't even able to play it when it first released - I ended up moving only days before it dropped, and couldn't afford it. Thankfully, though, I had come into some Microsoft Points about a month later, and was able to get it on Xbox Live.
I was pretty much floored. It was everything I had hoped for and more. The graphics, the humor, the story, the voice acting, the mechanics, the music... it's all just this perfect little package of awesomeness. I played it for longer in one sitting than I've probably played any other game except maybe Brawl. Many months later, after I'd been more or less forced to move my 360 into the other room and my PS3 became more prominent, I went ahead and bought it on that system, too. There have been very few times when I've purchased a game on more than one platform without them being radically different, but Skullgirls was worth every penny.
Then the PC version was announced. I'm not a huge PC gamer guy anymore (never really was, but I had at least played as much as I did my consoles once upon a time), but once the Indiegogo rolled around, I knew I had to help these guys out. I also saw a chance to cross-promote one of my own characters, but there was no way I could afford $1000, even if I had just gotten my income tax check. But I made a few deals and I was able to get Patron Saint status, mostly to give back to these guys who had given me so much enjoyment.
Since I wasn't a big PC gamer, I never even got Steam until the release of Bad Bots (which I just had to buy, for various reasons). So I had Steam for only a short while before Skullgirls released. I figured there was no way that I could run something this powerful on my old laptop, but lo and behold, after just one patch of the beta it ran smoothly. If more fighters come to Steam and are this fluid, I'm gonna eventually go broke.
So while Skullgirls isn't for everyone, it certainly is for me.

I will start out with my conclusion - I love this game! I just purchased it with a Steam card I received for Christmas from my son. (Yes, I am a boomer.) This game reminds me of the old PC DOS game called Starflight. I have read the reviews over the last few months and I totally get the frustration a lot of people have with the way the game was promoted and released. In my opinion it was clearly released before the developers had reached their desired initial  goals for the game. I won't speculate on who was at fault. Since I have only actually played the game with the "Foundation update" my view of the game comes from that perspective. So far I have put in about 35 hours so I think I have some reasonable feel for it. For background, I do not like FPS's and I am not a fan of most multiplayer online games because frankly, there are too many um, less than desirable people messing around with the game and the players. I do a lot of table top wargaming at the local game/comic book shops so I know the type. But on-line it is very hard to avoid the hyper-aggressive and the trolls.
I really enjoy the planet and space exploration that I can do at my own pace without worrying about anything except the occassional planet-side predator or space pirate. The graphics and ai are very good (although I clearly need a newer video card),I have no interest in building a permanent base right now. I like the free roaming exploration and occassional adventure. Maybe I will build a base when I tire of roaming. I actually like the "sentinel" drones. They provide a small amount of amusement, and also a 'familiar friend' as I cruise around. I also have no interest in following the meta-game objective of getting to the center of the universe. I am aware from reviews that it doesn't amount to much. So I am content to experience the "journey" and take a pass on the "destination." At least until they come up with a more compelling story.  I have not experienced any significant glitches in game play. The game only crashed once on my PC, but the game recovered in exactly the same place. It has been steady as rock otherwise with no surprises while playing the game. Everything seems to work and interact as it should.
Pros:
- Beautiful environment
- Go at my own pace
- No PvP
- Exploring, naming, and upgrading are fun when I have no particular goal I want to reach
- A nice alternative to the zillions of "Medal of Duty: Halo Fall XIV" games
- Game has been stable (especially for a PC game)
Cons:
- They definitely need to add a greater variety of creatures, plants, planet environments, and "local objectives" other than the overall objective of getting to the center of the universe.
-  Please add at least a few more more "specimen" graphics!
- Even though the artwork and environments are good, there is still a lot of room to enhance the graphics quality.
- Need a deeper storyline with "regional/local" objectives for people that like more structure in their games
- I want to be able to name my ships! (Maybe I am missing an option somewhere?)
This is definitely not a game for goal-oriented, multiplayer team, tightly plot-driven game play. This is a game for people that like open exploration, a huge sandbox to roam around in, and just enough challenges to overcome and have the curiousity to see what is just around the next corner (or planet). They evidently made some good prograss with the Foundation update. (It looks to me like they are probably catching up on features that were originally planned and hit the cutting room floor to make a deadline. There is no way everything that came out in the update could have been done from scratch in four months IMO.) There is a great "foundation" here for vastly expanded gameplay and even multi-player support once they create a little deeper universe. Right now the universe is wide, but not so deep. I just hope they keep the single player mode as an option. Otherwise I will have to "explore" elsewhere.
And let me name my own ship!
Pathfinder update:
I can name my ship! They listened. They really listened!  ;)
Hello Games really made significant progress with this update IMO. The graphics are improved and much faster. The game loads for me much faster, and I was able to bump my graphics settings up a bit. Being able to increase texture detail from "medium" to "high" has made a big difference visual quality, but more important, I can see important items and bases on the ground much more clearly from the air.
Game variety has also increased nicely. I like the classes of starships, and the addition of nanites that are required to get blueprints instead of just being handed blueprints. Adding "merchants" to the space stations is a big upgrade to me. I don't build bases or stick around on a home planet so I can't comment on the additional building options. For now the ground transport is also of no use to me. I hope they enable ground vehicles on more than just the home planet in future releases.One part that I think went backwards was interaction with the alien races at depots, etc. Instead of giving them carbon we now have to give them expensive artifacts. That wouldn't be so bad if the information we recieved was useful, but in fact we get much less from the alien interactions that we did before. No blueprints, no healing, no new words. Mostly just "your reputation with the "insert race here" has increased." There is not nearly as much reason to interact with aliens now IMO. I hope they revisit that part of the game for future updates.
I have played with the photo tool a bit. It seems like a very flexible and creative tool. One thing it highlights is just how beautiful the environment and artwork is in this game.
More variety, more music, better graphics. All in the right direction IMO. I just hope they never add multiplayer. Ugh. Cooperative gameplay would be okay. But PvP would ruin the game for me.
Atlas Rises Update:
This game has come a long way. All of the "cons" in my original review have been addressed and then some. I am 400 hours into the game now and I am still enjoying it immensely. I now have a nice base that is farming for revenue. I regularly use the exocraft to explore and mine on planets, and I am following the new storyline adventure while still taking time to just explore as I go. The side quests tied to guilds are a bit simplistic, but it is an improvement.  The game and setting certainly feels fully fleshed out to me. As stated above, I have no interest in multi-player and would prefer not to see that happen, so I think the game has reached a reasonable "completion" state. But I am looking forward to the developers adding more storyline into the game. I love the universe and I think additional structured game play and exploration options is icing on the cake at this point. There is plenty that can be added, but the game feels "whole" to me now.

Greetings Everyone!  Game Developer Tycoon is a simple game, perhaps too simple for a Tycoon style game and especially on a PC.  You build games through a series of menus and adjustable bars but never really go beyond this, it seems to drown in its own simplicity quickly; your only goal being to build another game to sell for a profit and use those profits to build another game…
Why am I playing this:  I felt this game would be better suited for a SMART Phone or as a browser based game, not an installed PC game; overall it just didn’t grab me for more than 20 minutes at a time.  This seems to be the point; turn it on for a few minutes while waiting for a friend or dinner.  But, again, you are stuck with the thought:  why not a smart phone?
Eh, why not:  The game isn’t white knuckle but there is some enjoyment to be had if you play it in short bursts and the game is controlled and executed simply enough to add value to this model, not sure if the price tag is worth it however.  But as an Indy game’s first attempt, I happily support it, even if I didn’t enjoy it beyond the first 20 minutes.
Overall, I really don’t feel this game is worth the money or time you’d put into it.  For that reason I can’t recommend it on that basis alone, though I do want you all to support this company, just understand that as a standalone game…just isn’t worth it for me.  Enjoy!

The foundation update was a step in the right direction. Looking forward to future updates. Really hoping to see freighter/starship construction soon. However, even that would not be enough, at the very least there needs to be conflict.
I would recommend randomly spawning "strategic points" that signal players within a reasonable distance, causing a "capture-the-flag/base" style combat with a hefty reward or prestige for the victors. Preferrably with faction vs faction ad infinitum, or species vs species vs species with all players proportionally assigned to each species.
Another idea is to have the sentinels play a more fundamental role. Instead of simply throwing drones around to keep tourists from picking all the flowers, try turning them into a full blown existential threat. Give them bases, home-planets, give them bigger, badder drones. Set them out to conquer the galaxy, let player's reconquer systems from the sentinels.
All in all, I've found sentinel hunting and pirating to be the funnest part of the game, as they are the only real challenges to the game so far. However, I will admit the outpost puzzles can be fun too. Now, I've gotten to the point where I can take down sentinel starships incredibly easily. The game gets rather boring at that point.
Sentinel starships need better flight patterns, their turns are unnecessarily wide. Also, please remove the speed limit zones during space battles and around space stations, I would rather die a hundred times learning not to fly into objects rather than wait two minutes trying to dock at a space station, or four minutes trying to save a freighter from pirates on the other side of the system.
The speed limits within a planet's atmosphere are understandable. However, I have noticed a few bugs after the update, when entering a planet at max speed (when the atmosphere around the hull ionizes) and upon getting as close as possible to the ground, my starship begins moving incredibly slow, almost coming to a stop with no ability to turn due to the ionization-effect continuing longer than it should. Essentially, it looks like I'm a meteor hanging above the ground not moving. Also, there have been times when I have landed my starship and I have been thrown out of it rather than placed on the ground in front of it.
All in all, this game still has great potential. I recently saw the inside of an Atlas Pass v3 locked room and was sorely disappointed to see nothing of import. However, recongizing in-game structures, I saw the capacity to add more rooms, keeping my fingers crossed for now.

One of the best tycoon games out there, Game Dev Tycoon is a game with rather simple mechanics that slowly through time become more complex. As the game says, you are a Game Dev working hard to create the greatest video game development company. This game starts in the 80s with the Commodore64 all the way to New Gen PlayStation/Xbox, giving you a throwdown of gaming history. Now game mechanics, the first and most important mechanic, Game Developing. Game developing in Game Dev Tycoon is simple you choose a name, topic, genre, console, and engine, then you are greeted with 3 Development stages. In the all the stages you adjust sliders representing Game Ingredients (Gameplay, Graphics, Story, Engine, A.I, Level Design, etc.) you have to adjust the sliders based on your topic and genre this get slightly more complex later on. You can also hire staff once you move to a new office, this is when the game becomes more challanging and where the real test starts, whether or not you can become a successfull video game company.

Very solid game.  Really makes work for success.
On occasion, there are some frustrating moments.  For instance, if you only have a couple million left in the bank and you are a larger company, it seems impossible to make a succesful game to dig yourself out of danger.  Almost every time I was in that situation, I would make sure to create a type/genre that is typically succesful.  I assign people proportionately to the design sliders, finish the game, and watch the reviews come in.  4/10 across the board.  The success and failure of a game can seem a little too arbitrary.
Now that we are past my major gripe, here are my pros and cons.
Pros:
-Detailed management:  You need to hire the right people and train them to ensure success in the future.  You really do feel like you have a lot of control.
-The "Harvest Moon" effect:  This game just keeps you going on a routine.  You never want to stop.  You always have a new idea you want to try.
-Options:  If you are a smaller company with fewer fans, you can get your name out there by working with publishers.  Or, you can make smaller games without a publisher and make a name for yourself.  You can also invest in creating new engines and researching new tools to add to your engines.
Cons:
-Arbitrary Outcomes:  Sometimes it seems a little random whether or not a game will succeed.  I get that you don't want the game to be predictable, but jesus I have almost chucked my mouse a couple of times.
-Design sliders:  The sliders for each stage and game element determine how much time is spent on a particular part (sound, level design, AI, etc.).  There is one slider named "Gameplay" and I'm not really sure what exactly it includes.  Mechanics, perhaps?  You can unlock guidance on where you should set sliders for each genre by generating a report for each game.  The problem is, I have generated a report many times for the same genre, but certain sliders will absolutely never provide hints, it seems.
Overall:  Enjoyable and worth it.

I'm always a fan of Final Fantasy style games, the ones where you take turns doing damage to your enemies, and them to you. What I especially like about the Epic Battle Fantasy games however, is the differences it has that make it stand out as a game. For instance, at the highest levels, your weapons that you've had since the beginning are still options to use for battle, instead of other games where your starter weapon was probably sold at the first shop for some extra cash. For the final bosses as well, unlike the FF games, where simple grinding could make anything easy, this game relies on intelligent strategy to beat a boss.
You can't simply use brute force to take down an enemy here, it requires actual thinking. You have to consider:
-What weapons do I use?
-What's their weakness?
-What armour do I wear to compensate for their skills and mine?
-What skills do I use, and which special abilities (Only one person gets it, but you choose) gets which skills.
All of this, a decent storyline, great music, good characters with unique personalities, and a vast world are all reasons why Epic Battle Fantasy 4 should be considered a great buy.

Epic Battle Fantasy 4...truly a wonderful nod to the RPG's of old, and filled to the brim with personality, humor, and references everywhere. The game plays like a traditional RPG, where you walk around the world, find items in chests, complete a few quests for NPC's (and by 'quest', I mean go and find them some junk and bring it back), and fight enemies.
Of course, there is a deeper play to it. Anyone who has played the prior Epic Battle Fantasy games on Flash game sites such as Armorgames or Kongregate will know that equipping the right stuff is key to the game, and even armor and items you find early on may play key roles later on, especially if you upgrade them. No weapon or armor is useless in this game, and it allows for a good amount of customization. Plus, the proper armor and weapons show up on the character as you switch them, which is a fine little bonus~
And for those who are skeptical of buying this knowing that there is indeed a Free-to-Play version out there, the money is well worth the spending, because you're not only supporting the creator of this fine series (kudos to you, Matt Rozak), but you get some extra content in the form of new weapons/armor, new summons, and a tough optional area that will test your skills in more ways than one. Plus you get the soundtrack to boot~
Overall, it's a very good game, especially for one made in Flash. If you're looking for a light-hearted RPG, this may just be the one for you.~

Now to the actual review. Fallout 3 is an open world rpg from the makers of the elder scrolls series. In this, you're a person who was stuck in a vault for god knows how long, but now you're out and enjoying the sights. Not that the wasteland is a pretty thing to look at.
Pros:
Good storyline. So far, the story line has been enjoyable. The main story line has drawn me in to the point where I get upset in points just through seeing certian objects together (curse you skeleton with a teddy bear). The side quests are also well done, adding more to the plot itself without having to be done in order to understand everything.
Likeable characters. When you meet a character, after a bit of talking I've found that I know whether or not I like them or not. Sure it sounds lame, but a lot of games have missed having good npcs in favor of god knows what. Fallout delivers on good characters.
Good atmosphere. The atmosphere of the game is never interuppted or shattered through bad design, or weird music in the wrong place.
Hilarious bugs. I believe it was once said better than I could ever hope to. Person: Is this a bug or a feature? // Bethesda: Yes. All in all so long as bugs arent game breaking, they can be hilarious. At one point, I chainsawed a person to death only to watch their corpse jiggle all over the place and expand like a slenderman.
Cons:
Bugs. Its a Bethesda game though so this is always to be expected. Of course, the only cons are game breaking bugs. Like getting stuck in a bookcase because you jumped in to look for books. Of course, most bugs can be fixed easily on PC.
Hacking. I'm honestly too stupid for the hacking game, and it wasnt explained very well when I first encountered it.
Character customization. While yes, it does have character customization, I do believe the customization you
do was very limited. However I believe this was a limitation of the time, and so isnt too big of a deal.
All in all it is very much a game I would recommend, as you will find yourself in love with everything.

Do you like to follow rules? This is a game for you. One of the great things about simulations is that it gives you a playground to experiment and create "what if" scenarios. This game, unfortunately, strips away a lot of that freedom.
Throughout the tutorial, I tried to experiment and push the limits of the trains. Consistently, the tutorial pushed back with various rude responses such as "terminating" the scenario and taking away my control of the train for my own good.
I thought this might get better, but then many of the scenarios had the same kind of limits on speed, etc. unless you started a pure sandbox mode where there is literally nothing else to do but drive around. In many scenarios, you don't even have control of where to go, as all switching is handled automatically. Some of the scenario descriptions even read a lot like "10 hours of obeying speed limits and minding signals." Ugh. Not to mention that a lot of the scenarios cost additional money, which I absolutely was not willing to put up given my experience to this point.
I tried to at least enjoy the sandbox mode, and found that I could indeed drive there without nanny interference, but with nothing else like a need to haul cargo to occupy me, I found myself sightseeing, looking at the landscape. It was then that I started noticing that everything looked the same - the same 5 or 6 trees everywhere, the same buildings repeated in each town, symmetry everywhere.
I drove to the end of the line, and my locomotive just mysteriously vanished. At that point, so did my interest in this game/simulator.

For a more in depth acknowledgement of Divinity, this game is truly an RPG experience that AAA companies have all but forgotten about today. This game is hard, the questlines sometimes feel like a detective game instead of giving you goals to go for, the game can't always decide when it wants to be really easy or really difficult, and you almost have to 100% it to have a chance at defeating it. It's extremely easy to be doing really well with your party then get utterly demolished by some new enemy, forcing you to spend another hour or two either looking up strategies online (if you're lazy) or figuring them out yourself.
I mean really, particularly in the final ending area this game was on the verge of giving me an aneruism with the constant "haha TAKE THAT" it kept throwing at you, but I was too deep, I was too far. I had to finish it.
Luckily it was worth finishing, but it's just hard to recommend this. If you don't play any other games, or have ample time available to juggle a bunch of games, then Divinity will suit you if you want a lasting RPG of old-style fashion in a modern design. The world sucks you in, and you'll be remembering and probably wanting to find someone to talk about all the stories for weeks to come, and that's not something I've been able to say about a game for an extremely long time. I just wish there weren't so many hoops to jump through to get to it all.

This game looked and sounded super cool.
What I liked about it:
I love upgrade-tree games like Element Tower Defense, the WC3 custom map. During the tutorial, it felt like this game was going to be like that. You plop down a plot of animals/plants/minerals, which has different attributes based on what kind of land you plop it down on. Then, you influence that plot of whatever with an "aspect", pushing it towards its next level where it gets different attributes. Then you can do it agan (and maybe again). Pretty sweet, right?
What I didn't like:
The upgrades don't make sense. I'm not saying they SHOULD make sense, but if they don't make sense, they should feel good in some other way. Every upgrade is a gamble. You hope that it will keep being symbiotic with the things around it, or keep providing the same kind of resource. For example you might upgrade a plant that gives food and money, and its next level will only give technology.
This might not sound like a big problem. Sure, it's a "strategy" game; if you want to play it "right" you have to learn it. But you play in 60 minute sessions, and what progress you made in that session determines what is available for you in the next session, in a rogue-light way. But if you lose towards the end of that session, you just lose everything.
It's a cool idea, cool visual style, but in the end the execution makes it one of the few games I would advise people not to bother with.

This is a great addition to the Scribblenauts series, but it's the best and not the best at the same time for different reasons.
Puzzle-wise, it's a tad too simplistic and easy.  If you want a bit more brain-work, try Super Scribblenauts for the DS.  Unlimited's puzzles are ok and funny at times, but don't require as much effort as the first two DS titles'.
There is also reason that Unliminted should specifically be purchased, though, and that is the object editor.  The previous games allowed you to create "anything", but you couldn't create Darth Vader, or a car with cookies for wheels, or medusa with spoons for hair instead of snakes, or alcohol, or yourself.  Now, you can add a... well, UNLIMITED level of creativity to the game by making anything to put it in the game.  Then, the Steam workshop allows you to gaze in wonder or even use the creations of others.
Looking at Scribblenauts as a whole, it's a seriously fun series.  One can spend hours just messing around with different items and discovering what is present in the game and what it can do.  A great lighthearted romp.
Scoring:
Story Mode: 7/10
Object Editor: 9/10
Scribblenauts Gameplay: 8.5/10
Whole experience wrapped into one: 8.2/10
