This game has undergone so many changes, it astounds me. The first review i made for this game was way back in 2015, and I have had the game ever since Day 1 EA. I also cannot wait to tell you how wrong the majority of reviews are.
{TL;DR at the bottom}
The LEGO Worlds that I know today is an
Game. Nothing about it is "Misrepresented".
I made sure to get to the end of the game, obtain all the gold bricks, and collect a vast majority of achievements and collectables before reviewing the game fairly. When I first started, I was suprised to see that the game had gotten a MASSIVE UI overhaul, same with a graphics revamp and really great optimization. I can run this game at 60 FPS most of the time (Obviously excluding new chunk loads) and at full graphics. (AMD FX 6300 Six-core and a AMD Radeon R9 380 4gb graphics card). In a lot of earlier EA builds there was enough content to easily 100% collect. Now, after 20 hours of constant collecting, I've surpassed 700 discoveries and I find more every time I play.
There have been a lot of complaints about the game that are really contradictory, leading me to believe a lot of reviewers did not even bother to finish the game. A lot just assumed that it was an entirely different game, and were let down when the quite small dev team working on the game actually delivered. I've seen a few people say that "devs lied!", or "devs misrepresented!"; None of this is true. The devs did more than deliver. I cannot stand to see people say that they didn't listen to the community, because they did more than that. A massive proportion of the game right now is ALL player requested features. Randomly generated towns and cities with people in it,
, Quests, even having to find the bricks you use to build was a requested feature. (<- if you are too impatient to try and collect all the bricks, just use the code to unlock them all in the extras menu)
TL;DR :
Basically the game is exactly what it says it is, you explore giant worlds, discover litterally thousands of people, animals, vehicles, props, structures, etc. and there is nothing stopping you from building whatever you want. I'm absolutely sick and tired of people playing the game for less than an hour calling the game a waste of time when they don't spend the time to play the game to it's full potential.
11/10 would participate in one of the most interactive early access communities I've ever seen for a LEGO game with this much potential again (Game still accepts suggestions btw, check it out)

Very solid game.  Really makes work for success.
On occasion, there are some frustrating moments.  For instance, if you only have a couple million left in the bank and you are a larger company, it seems impossible to make a succesful game to dig yourself out of danger.  Almost every time I was in that situation, I would make sure to create a type/genre that is typically succesful.  I assign people proportionately to the design sliders, finish the game, and watch the reviews come in.  4/10 across the board.  The success and failure of a game can seem a little too arbitrary.
Now that we are past my major gripe, here are my pros and cons.
Pros:
-Detailed management:  You need to hire the right people and train them to ensure success in the future.  You really do feel like you have a lot of control.
-The "Harvest Moon" effect:  This game just keeps you going on a routine.  You never want to stop.  You always have a new idea you want to try.
-Options:  If you are a smaller company with fewer fans, you can get your name out there by working with publishers.  Or, you can make smaller games without a publisher and make a name for yourself.  You can also invest in creating new engines and researching new tools to add to your engines.
Cons:
-Arbitrary Outcomes:  Sometimes it seems a little random whether or not a game will succeed.  I get that you don't want the game to be predictable, but jesus I have almost chucked my mouse a couple of times.
-Design sliders:  The sliders for each stage and game element determine how much time is spent on a particular part (sound, level design, AI, etc.).  There is one slider named "Gameplay" and I'm not really sure what exactly it includes.  Mechanics, perhaps?  You can unlock guidance on where you should set sliders for each genre by generating a report for each game.  The problem is, I have generated a report many times for the same genre, but certain sliders will absolutely never provide hints, it seems.
Overall:  Enjoyable and worth it.

Very creative, and gives the player good insights (mostly) regarding what goes into video games and how the industry developed.
You start as a guy with a few bucks in a garage, trying to come up with a decent game, with the 2D graphics of the original Donkey Kong Era; eventually, if you play your cards right, you can end up in charge of a mega video game company with billions in the bank, and selling consoles of your own.
This game does a good job at showing how hard and how long it takes to make a good game. The game is highly sympathetic with game development, hence the name, and it has a number of jokes, puns, and poking light fun at major video game companies (Ninvento or Mbox, anyone?), as well as providing a few moral decisions (such as whether or not to sabotage other companies or to sue peopel who mod previous games you made).
Overall, glad I got this.

This is a lot closer to being a Visual Novel / Hidden Item Hunt than other games western audiences would expect to find on Steam. I personally wouldn't put it in any 'adventure' genre as that implies there are enemies or mechanics or choices to make, which are not features in this game.
Most of the 'gameplay' is basically 'find the next doodad' and there is no agency afforded to the player, nor will you find faceless/voiceless characters for the player to self-insert with. This is strictly a story of the characters within the game. You will spend the entire game clicking items and reading what the characters have to say about those items. Also, unlike a stereotypical VN there are no routes, bad ends, or alternate ends of any sort.
That said, it isn't necessarily a bad thing. I bought this game on sale and I came away believing I had a decent experience with it. I did like the story and the little sequels that it came with. There are also some hints at a meta-story if you are into that sort of thing.
And to the Japanophiles out there: This is decent entry level. If you are looking for your next fulfilling VN, you should probably take a rain check on this one despite your friends' rave reviews.

Downloadable content (DLC) is additional content created for a released video game. It is distributed through the Internet by the game's official publisher. Downloadable content can be of several types, ranging from aesthetic outfit changes to a new, extensive storyline, similar to an expansion pack. As such, DLC may add new game modes, objects, levels, challenges or other features to a complete, already released game. It is a form of video game monetization, enabling a publisher to gain additional revenue from a title after it has been purchased by offering DLC at low costs, frequently using a type of microtransaction system for payment.

This game is more of a model railroad builder than a simulator, although it does get quite a few aspects of simulation right. If you want hardcore simulation I do not recommend this, on the other hand if you like building routes or driving trains in third person (although a first-person view is possible) then this is the sim for you.
Trainz: A New Era is running a very old graphics engine and the whole setup in general is quite aged, but the gameplay and content you get from it is satisfactory. What you make is where it really counts. I've not tried the multiplayer, but the concept is quite intreguing and I will say it is unique to this sim vs. others such as DoveTail Games' Train Simulator 2018.
Pros:
-Tons of content is available on steam, TrainzPortal, DownloadStations, etc. to expand your experience. (Most of it is paid.)
-The audio is usually very satisfying and blows other games such as Train Sim 2018 out of the water.
-Multiplayer
-Seasonal changes (the season may change the texture on your locomotive or the trees, etc.)
-Freedom: you can build a route the way you want it, and do what you want to do on it.
Cons:
-Graphics are not terrible if you stick with T:ANE content and not the included content from past Trainz versions, but they certainly aren't top of the line.
-Simulation: as I said previously this game is not a great simulator, at least not when it comes to interacting with buttons and levers in the cab. (only a few are modelled) On the other hand, driving physics seem quite good.
-Framerate is not on-par with modern standards. (Turning the quality of shadows down will greatly improve framerate.)

Reus is a good combination of a light and cheerful art direction, a low-pressure game pace, and a set of simple starting concepts that begin to interact and interconnect in a combinatorial explosion.
Reus delivers on the sense of shaping a world. Beginning from player-directed general biome placement (small islands? long mountain ranges? Endless swamps?) to placing animals, plants and minerals around the villages that spring up to live off of them. From there, managing symbiotic effects gives a sense of juggling the welfare of a planet while still encouraging experimentation. The scoring system is crystal clear and provides helpful goals without fussing over every last point of wealth or food. Finally, as cities develop, trying to control the people within them indirectly either by managing dangerous environments or building respectful awe with your creation adds yet another dynamic to the game.
The weakness of Reus is probably its overwhelming complexity: beyond having to balance many systems, there is an almost endless amount of minutae (transmutation paths and required essences, which ambassador boosts what, the symbiosis effect for each resource) the wiki, or cheat-sheets of your own creation, are almost necessary.

Gauntlet does a lot of things right and Arrowhead (the developer) has raised the bar for this type of experience in a lot of ways. Items of note:
No game I've played does a better job of making you feel like you're fighting against unending hordes of enemies. The Dead Rising series comes close, but Gauntlet's core combat mechanics are built around it. Every combat move that a character has is designed with careful consideration to how you would use it in a horde of bad guys, with pros and cons. This isn't always balanced well between the character classes. Let's segue to that:
Gauntlet, unlike its predecessors, only allows you to pick one of each character class. This means there's no Red Wizard and Blue Wizard. There's just Wizard. I understand the purpose of this, and in a lot of ways, it's better for the game. Each class is very different. Unlike previous entries in the series, the classes all play very differently. The control schemes are different, and your primary tactics are different. Forcing players to choose different characters means there are a lot more interesting and varied things happening in the game, and that is undoubtedly cooler. It also prevents exploits that would be plentiful... I can only imagine what 4 of any one class could do if they strategized to take advantage of their strengths. If the game had balanced around the need for that, the characters would have lost some of their most fun and defining abilities in the interest of balance.
However, it means matchmaking online, or even with your friends, can be a bit of a pain because you will undoubtedly have a favorite class. There's also a 75% chance that nobody you're playing with will want to be the Warrior. I beat the game with the Valkyrie (the game tracks progression separately for each character class), but I put in significant time with each class. I can say with some confidence that the Warrior is underpowered and difficult to play. The Valkyrie and the Warrior are the two characters with the most similar control schemes, but the Valkyrie's moves are often more practical and easier to use than the Warrior's. I won't go into depth, but I'll simply recommend that the game is better with 3 players than with 4, assuming nobody plays the Warrior.
The lighting and art style are perfect for the content of the game. The story is forgettable and pointless, but the characters have fun personalities and they spew Left 4 Dead-style quips at each other. The dungeon's master Morak (more like Genorak amirite?) has a sadistic GLaDOS quality, especially when he mocks you for destroying food, and the game is genuinely fun to listen to. They did an excellent job with effects and sound design for giving the player tons of feedback, despite a hugely crowded play-space once the hordes get going.
I would be very happy to recommend Gauntlet, especially for co-op play.

It’s difficult for me to review this game, as ever since playing the public beta it instantly grabbed me as being one of the best games I’ve ever played, despite it being a combination of games I’m not really the biggest fan of, such as WoW and Borderlands being a few examples. But this mixture of gameplay, visuals, story, is simply put nothing but amazing. There’s a reason this game isn’t ‘dead’ as many keep saying it falsely is over and over. There is simply nothing else like it. It’s not yet another CoD clone, WoW clone, or copying any other game. It is incredibly unique and fresh, and deservers to be continued.
However I’m not one to be blinded by fanboyism, there are things wrong with this game that does need to be fixed and rectified. While recent updates have shown great promise of keeping this game going for awhile yet and solving several issues, there still isn’t a solid anti-hack/cheat system in place. The ‘light zone’ as you’ll come to know it as should have been utilized better (thankfully patch 1.8 gives promise to fixing that in the future). Many features that were promised have been added in new updates, but not all of them.
The TLDR; this game is astonishing and truly is worth a try. Nab it on sale or give the first 6 hours free a try! A note, a lot of good ‘end game’ content comes after reaching level 30, which sadly can’t be used that much until you reach it. So don’t give up so soon, there’s a ton of great stuff at the end of the tunnel waiting!

The question is: do you like MMOs?
It's an MMO. It's not The Witcher 3, it's not Ghost Recon, it's an MMO built around a cover shooter. I don't know if its worth full price, but on sale it certainly is. If you don't like MMOs, you probably will hate this game. Leveling up, quests, gear, player interaction, and currency ALL function like an MMO. If you find yourself thinking this game is repetitive and bland, or grindy, thats the MMO formula at work. Here's how this works out:
You explore the city completing quests to level up, this is basically a trial, where you learn the skills to succeed. When you hit level 30, which is the cap, you are represented by a gear score instead of a level. This also unlocks the 'endgame' where a ton of new game modes and mission types open up, and the story proceeds. There's queues, instances, token currency...the works.
I repeat, it's an MMO.

The best Yakumo Yukari simulator ever. :P
But seriously, this game is such a gem. I for one highly disliked the original Scribblenauts, it had many issues and was extremely repetitive and limited. So I was very pleased to find that this game fixes pretty much all the flaws the original had. It features a semi-sandbox-ish design, which makes it very fun to explore the areas and mess around with all the things.
It really gives you an amazing sensation of sheer power(like turning the angry cop who is chasing you into a coward who will run away), as well as providing many amusing situations that are not exactly challenging, but will push your imagination while you try to solve rather mundane tasks in the most absurd and awesome ways possible! It really feels great to give a funny raptor to a bored guy and have it work! :D
That said though, after the initial power boom dies, the game gets a little more restrictive with it's solutions. Sometimes the obvious solution seems to be the only one that works, and the only way to make it amusing is to make the hammer into a giant golden shiny holy hammer... Which is cool, but doesn't really change much of anything. Still, it does have it's moments every now and then, and you can always just forget the missions and do whatever you want, too!
Possibly the greatest strenght of this game is the Steam workshop. Obviously, you cannot summon copyrighted material from the vanilla game, but the workshop allows that, letting you create the most awesome scenarios ever! Ever wanted to see Megaman X, Kamina and Jesus in a battle? Perhaps Link vs. The Dragonborn? Or Charizard vs. Greymon? Or maybe just ride on the head of a giant Sukuna Shinmyoumaru? You can do that! However, I gotta say that when it comes to creating your own objects, it can be pretty annoying, since the in-game editor can be very strange at times, and it doesn't really give you anything ressembling a tutorial. I think it could use some serious improvements, because as I said, it is quite possibly the strongest point of this game.
But overall, this game is lots of fun. I definitly recommend it to anyone who's looking for some nice, lighthearted(or not! >:3) fun times!

I only got into the Fallout franchise a couple of months back, with my purchase of Fallout Shelter. I decided to purchase Fallout 3 since it was cheap and seemed a little more interesting than its turn-based predecessors.
Best choice of my life.
F3 has rapidly become one of my favorite games, with its huge open world, spectrum of dialogue, array of weapons, and spot-on application of everything in it—if that even makes any sense. In the two months that I've had it, I've already played it for 95 hours and played through the campaign three times. I have yet to run out of things to do in it, and I'm discovering new things in it every day.
On to the actual review, Fallout 3 simply nails the abandoned, lonely atmosphere of a nuclear wasteland. With the exception of the civilizations on the game, F3 does really feel like you're your only ally in the harsh, deserted world. What I find even more interesting is that the feeling of the game can change dpending on where and when you're playing the game. What I mean is—and many agree—when I wander the subways at noontime in real life, for example, it's similar to the rest of the game: Lonely, with enemies sprinkled here and there. But when I do it at night, I'm turning white every time I hear the scream of a Feral Ghoul. The game can actually be very scary.
What else I like about this game is its simple open world. You can walk around, do what you like, and in this game, even change the way people view you and have stories told about your character. It's such a brilliant game that lets you carve your own story in nearly any way possible. From small changes like upping your Charisma to bigger ones like altering your Karma and doing deeds to be broadcasted by good ol' Three Dog, every player has a diferent story.
On to the gameplay, it's great. It's not too hard, not too easy, and filled with nifty little machanics that always spice everything up, like hacking and speech or skill checks. The function that your weapons and armor lose condition makes sure you can't just go willy-nilly with your new T-51b Power Armor and keeps a healthy dose of re-earning everything to keep them alert.
There's nothing much more I can say about this game, aside from the graphics, which I never care about. Overrall, Fallout 3 an amazing game, and one that I am sad to not see become timeless game. At least the franchise is certain to be.

This game's as special as you've heard.
It is story-driven in a way that few games are, meaning that the story feels like it _matters_ pretty much from the get-go (despite dialogue that has strong ideas behind it, but is sometimes a little bit hammy).
The music and evocation of scenes/emotions is wonderful; it's moving, at several points.
It grapples with "issues" (memory; choice; autism) in an unforced, graceful way.
Couple cons: "play" is obviously not its strong suit, BUT it didn't to ME feel as "on rails" as it may have to some.
A little more substantively, a thing happens towards the end which drives the last act of the plot which didn't have, for me, the revelatory necessity of the rest of the story. Because the rest of the story felt so grounded in real-ness, even if it's a science fictive setup.
But this is all really... to be even complaining at that level about a game means it's a very special game. This is a very special game, and really really worth 4-5 hours of your time.

This game left me both disappointed and satisfied. Its art and music are astounding. They are both breathtaking and varied enough to keep you mesmerized for the whole game. Everything good that has been said about the art direction and the music is true.
The gameplay is lack luster. Unless the level design forces you to use the various abilities they are easily forgotten. The Bash ability is essentially all you need. You'll be using it in most puzzle, escape sequences and it will be the only way to kill certain enemies or to simply skip them. The best option to move around at high speed is also the Bash ability.
The game design is on par with the gameplay. Sometimes during the play sessions its becomes plainly clear that the game is linear. There's no point in actually exploring the world. While you could wander around the world for power ups, there are enough littered around the golden path that its actually superfluous. The golden path is always indicated and thus the next area to be explored is obvious. This leads the player to pursue the objectives quickly in order to acquire the abilities required to get the hidden power ups. The most serious flaw is discovered at this point. One could argue that its either the fact that the game's autosave overwrites the user's save data or that the final state of the game does not let the player acquire all of the power ups. Of the two possible fixes, making the autosave use a hidden slot that is loaded when the player uses the "continue" button would not only have been simple but expected of games of this millenium.
I recommend it simply because its a beautiful experience. It will be remembered for its art and music... and not much else.

I read the reviews before playing this game and have played 'free-to-play' games, before.  I just got done sinking 6 months of intensive time into this game; and then left it like so many others. Turns out that player turnaround is high - is it any wonder why? Firefly certainly doesn't seem to care as long as buckets of money are pouring in.
In a nutshell, it is a very addictive game and it 'can' be fun - but veteran players can be very 'clickie'. Also, many people end up in a fat cloud of disappointment for a few different reasons despite their best efforts.
For example: If you manage to be lucky enough to start fresh in a new world that has just opened (I got to participate in 2 of them; I found the already-established worlds to be - well, established); don't expect to be anything other than a farmer or a merchant unless you are a heavy 'carder' - someone who sinks lots of money into cards for the game.
No, you don't need to sink a bunch of money into the game, yourself - but other players who are on power trips and apparently have nothing better to do with hundreds of dollars; can really put a kink into your game experience. Unless you are kissing their butts, of course. And in that case, you are often just a tool for them to use.
And don't expect to be able to come into the game with new perspectives and ideas... You will promptly be put in your place real fast.
Also, don't even bother trying out the PvE 'wolf world' until they get it out of Beta. They make you pay for that game and it is so out of balance, it is ridiculous - although the game moves faster and is the most fun world to play, in my opinion (if/when they get it reasonably playable -I may return to check it out if they ever do).
For instance, in the PvE world; AI castles can move in and immediately land as a large castle with several hundred soldiers that can immediately be used against you. Wheras, YOU can only have an army of 500 - and only 400 of those can be on your castle at a time to defend it. Add multiple captain attacks coming at your villa at once, and you DEFINITELY need cards. You CANNOT play in the wolf world without them - and even then, don't expect to get very far very fast. Even with lots of help from other players.
If you don't have a lot of money to sink into this game, but you have some... Do buy the 2 sets of crowns that they want you to buy to progress for about $5 each. That will bump you up to getting 14 cards a week to use or turn in for other cards that you need. You can stop there and not spend any more - you will also win extra cards & prizes, at times. Also, foraging will bring you lots of wheel spins in the PvE world if you really want to try that one out using as little money as possible.
Do I recommend Stronghold Kingdoms? Only if you are a hardcore gamer who likes to be on a ts (teamspeak) team.

This game is decent. Nothing super spectacular but also not bad. First off, I am a Fear fan and I am not a major FPS player.
So, Fear 3 is the latest chapter in the events dealing with Alma. In the first game, you were an agent sent to find a psychic commander and subdue him. Well things went crazy, this girl named Alma was trying to kill you will demonic powers, The guy you were hunting has an army of soldiers he is controlling hunting you down, and the security group holding Alma wants to cover all tracks and is hunting everyone not officially working in the building. Basically you have a horror FPS that was light on the FPS and heavy with story and horror.
Fast forward to the third game. You are in a prison and the ghost of the psychic commander (Paxton Fettel) comes to you and says you have to escape and go to mother (Alma) because she is pregnant. So now the two of you break out and travel to her. The game changes its style and becomes more FPS than horror.
You play as both brothers. First you must complete the current mission with Point Man which unlocks Paxton Fettel to play. Throughout the game you work your way through several different environments destroyed from the events of the first game to find Alma who is ready to give birth. Demonic creatures, soldiers, mech’s, and demented people roam the streets trying to prevent you from your family reunion.
The graphics are great. The lighting in each area varies considerably depending on where you are and at what time it is during the day. When traveling through the suburbs it is all bright and peaceful looking. The houses that have not been destroyed or overrun look like a picture perfect place a family would like to live. As you hop fences and go through the wreckage, mech’s and soldiers break down walls and fences. Leave this area and go into the grocery market and the lighting turns to the florescent lighting found in these locations. The windows are all boarded up, the TV’s are all on, and most of the lighting is burnt out. The place looks mysterious and evil. Each different location adds its little bits to make it stand out and not be overly repetitive as many FPS’s can be.
With all that said, the game looks great. However, the main feature about Fear is the horror. Unfortunately they dropped that for a faster paced game. There are far too little instances of demonic craziness found in previous versions. Additionally the story is highly lacking. Alma has nothing to do with this game except as a pretext for making this game. Fattel coming back and enlisting the aid of the one who killed him and Point Man just sitting in a cell being interrogated all comes off way to cheap.
Overall, if you want a decent FPS this is a good short game. If you are looking for the Horror that was in the first game however, you are going to be highly disappointed. Overall a good game to buy on sale to finish the storyline.

Gauntlet was an underwhelming experience. Here are some more points that should reinforce my statement:
1. The game is around 5 hours long.
2. There are approximately 4 mobs that you fight that look slightly different every level or so. Combat boils down to destroying summoning stones. You'll be doing this for every single level. Have fun!
3. Relics are utterly useless. Gold doesn't really matter. It doesn't matter if you die either. In fact, you get rewarded for dying. The game is very forgiving.
4. The last boss just sucked. Besides having to wait until you can actually kill him, you get to fight all those fun and varied mobs that you fought all game. The only thing that was missing was even more summoning stones.
5. For me, the game has absolutely no replayability. Once you've done it all, what else is there to do?
6. The ending is a slideshow of 3 pictures with some guy talking in the background. No, really.
7. The characters talk way too much. You'll be hearing the same lines over and over. Enjoy.

Do you love slaughtering monsters by the thousands?
Do you love feeling like an epic badass?
Do you love working as a team?
Do you love backstabbing people on your team?
Do you hate dealing with mountains of items and sheets of numbers and just want to fight through dungeons?
If the answer to all these questions is Yes, Gauntlet is the game for you.

The game really lives up to its expectations and appeal for Gauntlet fans without over complicating things.  I'll keep my review short and objective.  The pros and cons I've found below:
Pros:
- No level grinding trying to find better gear if you just want to jump in a game and not wonder if you are the right level and geared up.  Those games are great but sometimes we just want a quick session of fun!
- Game sticks to its roots with all four original classes.  I've found the Elf the easiest to use and stay alive.  Merlin is cool too but my reflexes are not fast enough to dish out those nice spells.  So whatever your playstyle is whether it be magic, ranged combat, or melee it's all here!
- Level design is neatly layed out so you don't get lost.
- Graphics are surprisingly great.
- Plenty of achievements to invest in mastery of each of the four classes.
- Nice spells with the potions.  You can carry max of 5 potions so you can equip two pieces of gear before entering dungeons.
- Great local co-op fun too.  My mom and I connected two conrollers and had a blast.  She is new to games so she fought melee while I covered her with my Elf.  It is quite a blast if you have other local players to with.  Brings back memories of 4 player co-op at the arcade!
Cons:
- Tried quick match for multiplayer and was unable to join a match.  I also opened my game to public but during entire session no one joined my game.  This might be a glitch.  I'm sure this will be fixed soon.  This is really my only con so far.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

As near-future apocalypse simulators go, this one is far and away the best.
Pros:
plenty of content for the kind of player I am (dad with precious little time to play games)
interesting mystery behind the Dollar Flu cataclysm grounded in a bit more reality than other apocalypse games
the single player content is excellent and the multiplayer content is easy enough to get in to if you feel like it
lots of interesting variety in terms of gear and ability options
very nice graphics
Cons:
bullet sponge opponents are the main "immersion breaker" on a game otherwise grounded in reality
getting in to the multiplayer dark zones is fascinating but the leveling mechanics discourage slow/casual players like me
I can see how the game might get tedious if you are a faster player with lots of free time
This review only reflects my particular experience, but if you're looking for something to play slowly over a long period of time, this is a good choice. I've sunk about 120+ hours combined on both the PC and Xbox versions leveling up four characters so far, and expect I'll be playing this game for another year or two at least. It's very fun to jump in, engage with it for a few hours, then put it aside and not feel like you're missing out....all except for the dark zones, where unfortunately your points acquired degrade over time. But I wasn't looking for something to obsess over daily, as I can at best find time to play a couple times a month, and this game is great for that pace.

If you enjoy playing highly goal-oriented strategy games in short bursts, planning out and thinking about the game alot before your even start, and accept ingame randomness that you have no control over, then this game can bring you hours of enjoyment. Reus has problems, but the core gameplay is in my opinion worth the irritation of the programming and design shortcomings. It's casual friendly and it can be played without having to dedicate huge stretches of time. You can put in 30 minutes or down for a 6 hour session and accomplish something either way.
Reus is the very definition of an achievement hunter game, where your game mode choices are a set timed level or the free play option.
It's very important to understand this, because your enjoyment depends on your approach to the game. In Reus you play either a 30-, 60- or 120-minute round with a gameplan decided before you even start for unlocking predetermined achievements, then you end that round and start anew. There's no grand strategy per se, you don't build anything to last. If you can accept this and adjust, you can have some really enjoyable times with Reus and I would highly recommend it to you.
This point needs to be reiterated: you will have to be going for achievements. There's no choice, really. You unlock the stuff you build through clearing them, meaning if you don't bother with them then you *will not* progress in the game. It's designed around that concept, of doing one or a set of achievements per run.
Some achievements are really tricky, and if you're partial to that kind of stuff you will definately find some of these challenges to your liking!
If you're looking for a Civilization-, Sim City- or Paradox Interactive-style game, this is not it. Unless you do a "free play" run, your upgrade limit to your four giants, your builders, means you *have* to specialize in one or two areas. You will not be able to min-max your towns, but with time running out fast you wouldn't be able to anyway. Decide what you want out of that run and specialize your giants to achieve that goal.
Once you've unlocked everything, however, there's a "free play" option that allows you to get every upgrade to your giants. You could easily spend 15-20 hours min-maxing a huge world that way, and absolutely love it! Problem is, the people who don't give a damn about achievements are forced to sit through hours upon hours of achievement hunting to get there, and the people who only care about achievements are done by that point.
Additionally, a large part of the game has been randomized for some reason, from the quality of upgrades to your buildings (applying aspects to natural resources) to where your peoples build their towns and what projects they undertake. Having them place a town one, two or three spaces wrong can be a huge source of irritation, and it will lead to "save-load-load-load"-situations for the OCD crowd of gamers. Also, town projects give bonuses, sometimes really good and sometimes really useless depending on what kind of run you're going for. So if you've upgraded your giants for the plant and/or mineral tech tree and your towns insist on making animal projects, then you can either destroy the town and hope the next one will build in the same spot as well as hope they make another project, or you can just say "screw it" and make the project to just not waste even more time.
If someone tells you that the game encourages adjustment to your peoples' randomness, they're lying. There's no adjusting in the game, because once you've upgraded a giant, it's not going to change. You get four upgrades per giant, and to get the best buildings available for each game mode time frame, you need to know beforehand what to go for.
Runs get very messy very quick, and if you see the randomness as ruining your plans, you should stay away. If you look at it as just another layer of added difficulty, it's surmountable.
When it comes to some of the more technical problems with the game, know that windowed mode tends to crash the game eventually. The game also has weird crashing problems when trying to move the window from one screen to the other. Also, the ingame text does not scale well and can become hard to read. The game can also stop working from too much happening at once, or sometimes just from having been running for too long, so make sure to have auto save active and frequently save manually.
You will also notice ingame bugs happening once in a while, like your giants getting stuck and become unresponsive after trying to do an action. Just save and reload and they'll start working again. Also, sometimes your giants attacks against angry mobs or armies won't work, and that can have dire consequences for your runs, but I've found no way of rectifying this other than reloading an older save and hoping the town won't send out that army or angry mob again.
In conclusion:
I mostly enjoyed playing Reus, partly because I'm a huge fan of strategy games where you build and develop your surroundings. It's a flawed game, however, with bugs, randomness and imbalances that can bog down an otherwise great run. However, for me, the upsides and the good times outweighed the bad.

First and foremost, this game is not pay to win. Obviously, if you do pay then you can get things quicker, but it doesn't really have any major influence on winning or not. I have been using a combination of cards that is mostly made up of the ones that I started the game with and have won more than I have lost. With regular playing and completing the challenges, you can build up a good deck and save shards and rubies to open up new characters and arenas. Obvously, if you are impatient and want to get everything immediately, then paying for the premium upgrade will help you to unlock all the main masters and some arenas. Some grinding will always be present in games where there are unlockables.
A lot of people have made the comment that the game is dependent on luck, which I don't think is entirely true - tactics can win the game. Spamming low cost cards will sometimes work, but carefully using the deck will get around this. If you don't invest time in the game, then it will feel superficial. Give it some time, try out new masters and card combinations until you find soemthng that works and then go with that.
The graphics are great, the animation is smooth and the community isn't full of people shouting obscenitites at each other. Gameplay is well paced and balanced - but it does take time to master.
An excellent game that I look forward to seeing grow. Highly recommended.

As much as I like this game, I just can't recommend it. It's kind of a let-down. We were promised a new train simulator built from the ground up, but we just got the same thing we've been getting for years now with some little extra scripts that just add minor visual appeal.

Now there are some things about this game that I really like, but it's mainly in the UI. It's got a very user-friendly interface. Routes are incredibly easy to build. And the content available for the game is massive.
Now you may notice my play time in this and wonder why I give such a negative review. Well, most of that time has been spent trying to download stuff with their content manager. In conclusion, if you've never bought a game from these guys before, heavily consider your purchase. If you have bought from these people before, then don't bother buying this one since it's pretty much the same as the one you already have.
I'll be waiting for when they actually build a new engine and everything from scratch instead of rehashing a program from 2004 before I consider buying another one of their train sims.

This is one of the best metroidlike games money can buy. It has by far the best story/characters out of all of them. The game looks absolutely gorgeous, the progression system is well thought out and the skill tree actually has a sizable impact on the game. It would be THE best metroidlike game if not for the following gripes.
Ori moves a tad too sluggish for my taste. Just a tad. To make Ori move really smooth and acrobatic, the developers favoured style over substance a little bit too much. It's just a minor gripe, the game controls really well, it' a long way removed from Rayman, but it's not quite Super Meat Boy either.
By far my biggest beef is that there are multiple areas in the game that become inaccessible once you passed through them once. They also host important items that are gone forever when you finish that area. Now it's my understanding that metroidlike games are supposed to present you items along the way that you simply can't reach without progressing further so you have to come back later to pick them up. Backtracking is an integral part of this type of game and this one has plenty of those instances. So at first you walk around, inaccessible items left and right, no big deal, you can come back later and pick them up, ocd is kept in check. Suddenly the last area vanishes off the face of the earth and you know you didn't collect everything because you thought you could get back there to clean up. Suddenly your ocd kicks in to maximum overdrive and you have to collect everything right now, even though there are plenty of legitimate unreachable items scattered around the map. It's kinda like a bait and switch and left me a little bit disappointed.
The game also has a lot of trial and error passages where you have to make live-or-die-decisions on the fly (literally, mid-air) while being chased by OHK entities. It's satisfying when you finally get through but also very frustrating as you inch closer to the end, with every death respawning you at the very beginning of the passage.
I put a lot of emphasis on the things I didn't like in this review so it might come across as very negative, but when you read this just think of the perfect (metroid)game and subtract the negatives from it. The game is still very good and the current Metacritic average of 88% is pretty much exactly where I would place the game.
TL;DR: It's the best Metroidlike game you can buy on Steam by a landslide.

77 hours and still haven't got through this game. I bought the non-enhanced edition on release and never completed it, then with the arrival of Original Sin 2, that got me interested again and a promise I made to myself to complete this game. Whatever they added to the enhanced version isn't obvious to me, I got this free for buying the non-enhanced version so it's not a problem.
Divinity Original Sin feels like a modern title, but plays like a RPG from 20 years ago. That's to say it's very hard, even the combat in normal difficulty is punishing. Dieing and reloading for encounters is a constant grind. The enemy don't follow patterns, are well armed, tactical and won't die easily. Even the the most basic of encounters will often batter you a few times before you work out how to get the advantage or get a lucky break. Think of Dark Souls in pure RPG form. Much of my playtime has been spent mearly on keeping up with the constant arms race of having the latest levelled weapons and armour; selling and buying gear from vendors, and crafting.
Between the tough combat theirs a brilliant twisting story, professionally voice acted scripts, charming characters and varied and well drawn locations with decent puzzles, along with a half-decent crafting system. In all it's a truly exceptional title.
If you crave a challenging RPG, look no further. Where most modern RPG's have a difficulty level set in your favour so to play out the story in an orderly pace and win, Original Sin wants you to fail, you'll always feel everything is stacked against you. It can be frustrating, but you'll be driven to overcome the constant adversity to follow the excellent story. And I promise you this, I'm going to finish this game!

Before I start my review I would like to point out that I've played a multitude of RPG's ranging from the old legends like Arcanum, Lionheart, Neverwinter Nights and Baldur's Gate all the way through to Diablo 3, Grim Dawn and the like.
And I would have to say that Divinity: Original Sin is among the best. As a friend of mine stated: "Its the best RPG I've played in the last 10 years, second only to Arcanum" - Kerghan, and I wholeheartedly agree!
The game is jam packed with everything ranging from humour, little Easter eggs (like finding needles in haystacks) to incredibly well thought out dialogs, breath-taking music and a million ways to play your party, not forgetting the amount of hidden secrets, brain teasing puzzles and a landscape of pure visual delight.
It's your game to play, and you have no limits on how you want to achieve your goal.
I was captivated from the start and refused to leave the game unfinished, even though it meant having a few late nights too many!! Worth every waking moment!
I would highly, highly, HIGHLY recommend this game to anybody that has a love for RPG's as this game captivates it all.
I give it a 9/10!

This game wasn't actually made by Monolith; it was developed by Day One Studios, the studio that was previously only responsible for making the console ports of FEAR 1 and its expansions. It shows, in a lot of ways. The levels are much more linear, you're limited to two weapons, and the graphics are arguably worse than FEAR 2's and maybe even FEAR 1's. The story is barely coherent at best (which isn't helped by the fact that despite FEAR 3 having actual cutscenes, Pointman is still a silent protagonist who only communicates through furiously scrunching his eyebrows), and you don't even get a clear goal or an idea of where you're actually going until around halfway through the game's 4 hour campaign. The only aspect of the game that's anything interesting is the co-op system, in which the two players are cooperating but still loosely competing against each other to decide which ending they get, which works a lot better than it does in games that somehow manage to be even worse than this one like Call of Juarez: The Cartel. And that's a good thing, because the only way I can recommend even considering playing this game is if you have a friend to play it with, though even then it's only a loose recommendation since this game is really only that fun under the "any game is fun with a friend" rule. This game barely has enough content to be a hard sell if it were priced at $10 or $15 like the first two games are, but at $20 it's absolutely not worth picking up unless you just really want to suffer through an evening with a friend and have expended all other available options.

I just recently downloaded this game because of the free weekend, and took it as an opportunity to see if the over 40,000 reviews (an overall of mixed) on STEAM were truly justified. I don't think they are for the most part.
Of course we have the issue of hating a game that has things like survival mode as a DLC, and sure, that's money grubbing and we all hate it. But of course if no one bought it, these things would stop happening. And yet they keep occurring or get worse for some odd reason......hmmmm, wonder why. I don't feel the DLC being available detracts from the game and its ability to be fun and enjoyable though.
At the time of me writing this review the community hub shows 26,500 people currently in game.  And yet many comments reference that finding people to play with is tough.  Due to the free weekend, the numbers are obviously quite massive. And according to the STEAM charts, user log time shows close to 2,500 to 5,000 people normally. So finding people to play with in some areas may be tough, and others not as much.  But unfortunately, across the internet and multiplayer games the world over, playing with random people instead of people you know in team based games is difficult, if not impossible at times. Especially when people tend to just rush enemies recklessly, which they so often do in this game. A very unwise choice as time goes on.
I would say my biggest issue with this game is that I am constantly finding myself in matches where people don't speak the same language; and this is a key issue from UBIsoft due to their lack of desire to offer area based servers. Instead, anyone and everyone can join a game, so finding people you can communicate with can be tough.  If you play well with a random group of people, I would highly recommend you friend list them for future games.
Overall players speaking different languages makes the game an annoyance more than anything else, and the mute button can be employed with fervor as a solution.  And yet at the end of the day, not everyone uses their microphones for much of anything, so it is not necessarily a deal breaker, but communication and coordination and teamwork are what make this game a blast, and it is the sole reason that I played it for almost 9 straight hours after downloading. I ended up joing random games, and eventually found myself with someone like minded who spoke my language. We then leveled up, joined up with another person by pure chance, and our three man squad was rushing the dark zone at level 8, calling out flanks, coordinating our attacks instead of recklessly charging five to ten enemies at once, healing and effectively using cover, and working towards objectives to become stronger and better.
Essentially, here are my reasons to get the game, and reasons why you might not want to get the game:
Reasons to get the game:
1.  You already play with other people regularly and are looking for a game that will reward your teamwork and has a lot of options; PVE, PVP, crafting, base building, tons of side quests and missions, and a good story overall.
2.  You like guns. The gun design is spot on, and the sound effects are fantastic.  Notice I did not say realistic, I said fantastic.
3.  Level cap is around 30 I believe, and will take quite some time to achieve.
4.  Enemies are generally your level, or the higher level in the group. So don't expect level 5 enemies everywhere. But that doesn't mean you won't randomly find some wandering around.
5.  The game is on sale right now., and UBIsoft wants people to play it and buy in to it, and they are making improvements.
Reason to not get the game:
1.  You want to play it on your own. I am not saying this isn't doable, but it will be agonizing, and it is tough, and the game will try to break you if you don't break your screen first. The game is meant for teamwork, so worst case, you will be involved in matchmaking a bit, and hopefully you will find people you mesh well with for future games. Sometimes this can just be a pain to do though, but is not necessarily a deal breaker.
2.  Wierd bugs in game.  There are still bugs in game that have existed since product release; doors not opening and requiring a restart, videos/cinematics not playing any volume.....
3.  DLC.  However, you don't have to buy it. But many users agree that it expands the game and makes it fun. Other scream it should have been in the base game. Some will say you need a team of four to really get the most out of it, others will not.  I advise you research the comments and gameplay yourself before purchasing if you plan on doing so. There is also the Season Pass option....
4.  NPC's literally do nothing.  They just stand around in their army fatigues.  I watched them get shot by enemies until death and they just stood there. Useless NPC characters are the worst in these types of games. If you aren't going to be useful, why are you here.
5.  You can't do anything you want.  For example, you cannot shoot random people.  This may sound sick, but it is GTA style fun. Obviously this would not mesh well with the story and the character, but it would add a touch of realism if civilans were in the middle of a firefight or gunfure, and bullets did something more than magically never hurt them.  But I can give them candy bars and soda all day if they are in need.
Overall:
I would recommend giving it a try if you have not. It's a fun game, and it has lots of potential, which I think it is living up to these days based on my research of user comments and how the game has progressed. There was clearly a lot of work and effort put in to the game from a design standpoint, and a balance standpoint.  As such, you essentially get a well crafted world that plays as a modern MMO. But you don't necessarily feel like you are doing MMO style tasks.

I first played this because I thought it looked cute and sounded like a good time.  I spent a few days 100%ing it and enjoyed it a lot.
At some point, I mentioned the premise to my girlfriend and she wanted to try it out.  She spent a few days 100%ing it.  She said her daughter (5yo) might like it, but we weren't sure how she would do with having to type words into the notepad.  We decided to wait a little since she was just learning to sound words out at school at the time.
6 months later and this is my girlfriend's daughter's favourite game.  She's sounding out and spelling words like "violinist", "firetruck", "invincible" (she seriously got it on her own except for an s in place of the c, and that's an easy mistake to make really).
Quick warning for parents: we unexpectedly had to explain what cannibalism was.  She spent a few days talking about "the guy who wouldn't eat hamburgers and mommy gave him a person and he ate him."  It was awkward.  She didn't seem terribly marked by it (she just says eating people is gross) but it may not be suitable for all children her age; control the media your child consumes and try to supervise so you can find talking points (for instance, "is it ok to eat your neighbors?")

is an adventure puzzle game. As Maxwell, save your sister Lily from a curse by creating happiness around the world with the use of your magical notepad that can create anything you can write.
: The game has an astonishing amount of potential content. Almost any word and adjective you can think of, you can create by typing it. There is a lot of different method to resolve any situation, and the fun comes in finding new and unexpected ways to do so. You will find yourself attempting different solutions again and again even after you already succeeded just to see if you can find an easter egg or game secret. Usable created objects also add game elements to work with, and combining people or objects with one or more adjectives increases the possibilities tenfold.
: The game is short, you can breeze through it, getting the Starites you need to win the game within a few hours. Many of the puzzles are easy, half of which can usually be resolved with the same few objects. There are multiple passageways to move around a level, but they are often useless as it won't take time for you to always make sure you have a jet-pack or pair of wings to move around. Unless you want to explore the possibilities, you won't find much replayability as resolving a puzzle in different ways still ends up with the exact same result.
: ★★★★☆ - Next on your list!
If you're looking for an exciting story, grand adventure or mind-bending puzzles, turn away. But if you're looking for an entertaining time trying to push the limit of the game, and exploring just how far you can go, it's a great one. The Steam Workshop makes it easier than ever to add dozens, if not hundreds of new objects and options, assuming you don't use the object creator to add your own. Furthermore, the game is great for all ages, maybe even more so for younger gamers. Of course, if you didn't like previous Scribblenauts games, you're unlikely to enjoy this one. But if you did,
will go where previous ones never went before!

I normally don't like any civilization-building or strategy type games, but I really liked this. I was drawn to it because of the art, it just looked so pretty and it was on sale!
I love games where there are a huge number of achievements and possibilities. This game is great. Visually, it is very nice and calming, though simple. You control 4 giants that control different aspects of life on the planet; for example, the Rock Giant can create mountains and deserts, ore mines, can give upgrades to a few different parts of the game, and can destroy villages with earthquakes. (Other giants are swamp, forest, and ocean)
You have to create a balance...two of the giants can give different types of animals, two can give different plants, and one can give ores/minerals. Each land type (swamp, forest, ocean, desert, and mountain) creates different options for what resource can be placed, and each resource gives off a different reward (wealth, food, technology, danger, etc.) (Example - you can use the Ocean Giant's animal resource in the forest and get a chicken or swamp for a frog (each area has a different outcome.)) Placing certain things beside each other will, also, give special rewards. You can use the upgrades from each giant to transform the resource into a better and different one that may give off different rewards.
As you build up your planet, humans will settle and begin building villages. As they become more prosperous, they start trying to build shrines, churches, trade markets, schools, etc. Each one requires a certain amount of wealth, food, etc so you have to carefully plan out where to place everything for the most reward in a small space. There is a time limit, you can open longer times as you play. You can also unlock new animals, plants, ores, achievements, etc.
If you don't get the balance right, the village may not thrive. If the village becomes to prosperous, it may cause wars against each other, or even against the giants themselves.
This game can be maddening and overwhelming, especially when you are still a low level, but it really fun and rewarding when you accomplish your goals. I enjoy playing it when I just need to relax or, maybe, take out some villages with some swamp slime.

Stronghold kingdoms is a difficult game to explain at the outset, so I'll just go over the basics without going past a few paragraphs. It's a good game, though it requires a lot of patience, for reasons you can read below if you want. In sum, it's for a patient, deliberate type of gamer, and is certainly a rewarding experience. Onto the real meat:
You'll see pretty much every negative review on this game say it's "pay to win", which shows that they took one look at the game, saw that they had to pay, and then quit. It's essentially a subscription-based model, where you pay for premium either by the week or the month, which makes progressing through the game much faster than if you were a free player. It rounds out to about $8 a month, plus some spare change left over to buy card packs. At the cost of a Netflix subscription (or a large case of soda), it's worth the money to spend just for the benefits that you get as a premium member. The only way for money to become a serious problem is if you're spending thousands of dollars on the game to progress at ludicrously fast speeds, at which point the player is a bigger problem that the game can handle.
So now onto the review. The game is a medieval, strategy-based, simulation MMO where you build a kingdom, interact with other kingdoms, and do your best to balance the two without going overboard. It doesn't sum up the tense and thoughtful experience that you get with the game, nor will most of the promotional materials. It's a game about tactics, waiting, thinking, and looking into the future to see what you best actions will be a day or two from now. It's an accurate simulation of the politics and world-building of the middle ages all bottled up into a deliberately paced experience, one that's definitely worth trying out just to feel the experience.
Naturally, time is an important factor in this game. To get anything done, you need to produce raw materials with your buildings. This includes resources, weapons, and gold - all of which you have to wait a while to get in large amounts. By "a while", it's more like hours until you have the opportunity to expand on a larger scale - waiting for your village to populate, your buildings to produce, and your merchants to trade with others. Much like an idle game, it's best to wait a long time between play sessions to get the most out of your game. Otherwise you'll be checking it all the time, obsessed over when you have the opportunity to start developing. Unlike an idle game, it's not just a matter of upgrading the most expensive thing you can afford and waiting for another day. Indeed, you spend a long time looking over all the options you have at your disposal until you realise you don't have anything left to do at the time.
There is a level of depth and strategy in this game that is completely unique from most games that I've played. The game is simply about optimisation - you have to optimise your buildings, your research, your village placement, your military, and the production of materials to create all these. You also have to optimise the timeframe of when you create these events. This means you have to decide what to create, when to create it, how it will affect your village, your military, and your production, and you have to know if it'll create any difference in the short term to realise your long-term plans. It is a deep experience to go into, with the possibilities rolling in your mind the entire time you're looking at your village statistics. It's like upgrading your character in an RPG, feeling the same amount of pride you do in yourself as you do with your kingdom.
Also, you don't need to worry too much about the community. Pretty much all of the players are friendly, looking out for their best interests instead of trying to ruin your day. Most battles are petty, with a small-time raider taking the resources of another village far away - even then only if they're an incredibly weak and defenseless target. If you're at the point where you can let anybody walk in and take your resources, then you let that happen to yourself. The only way for a decent player to have all their villages destroyed is to♥♥♥♥♥♥off a large vassal without making any diplomacy, which is how all my villages were destroyed two years ago.
In essence, it's a good game, whether or not you can pay the subscription fee. It gets much better and much faster if you can pay for it, and it is an investment I recommend. It isn't at all a distilled experience like you get with almost every other kingdom-building game on the market, and is a worthy video game in it's own right. It's a unique and engrossing game for sure, and it's one you can download in a few minutes and try out. You do get a two-day subscription to see if you like it, which is a nice feature, if a bit like bait. I really do like this game, even if all my playtime is off the Steam client.

Last time I looked at it, was a while ago. So I don't know what has changed / improved. But one of things I really disliked was use of very old assets to promote a "next generation" game / graphics engine. Really, assets that would have looked OK in 2001. Perhaps in  2004. But not in 2015 or later!
And not just one or two minor assets, but a lot of assets. Important assets. Like major stations. Prime locomotives coming with a route.
OK - the routes were older. But if you sell them along your new shiny "next-generation" train sim, upgrade those assets, please!
What else do I dislike about it? Well, every train drives like it's a US diesel-electric! All have the same (HUD) controls. Really. It is absolutely awful. This is why for me it's a digital model railway, not a sim.
And the steam engine simulation, well in 2006 I was happy with it. It was a bit better than MSTS and gave you a 3D cab.
Then RailSimulator came along and improved the graphics, the simulation of steam trains, everything.
Trainz got  stuck in that area and at least when it comes to simulation, it feels that it still is stuck in that area in it's "New Era".
Lastly, most routes do not have seasonal textures. This was a new feature for Trainz in 2010. Still most of the T:ANE routes do not have seasonal textures!
Despite this already being a features of MSTS in 2001...
There are good things about T:ANE. The DownloadStation has a lot of assets to choose from, for free, that are uploaded by hobbyists. This gives you a central location from where you can choose and download stuff. That is much more convenient than TS2017, especially since it will also look at dependencies and download updates to content for you.
What else is good? Well, I guess that more areas of the world are covered in Trainz than in TS2017, due to more hobbyists uploading freeware assets to the Download Station. This makes it easier to actually explore places like China and Russia for instance, when compared to having to hunt downloads from local websites.
Last good point, the route editor. This is just so much easier to use than the TS2017 route editor.
The scenario scoring is not as harsh and punishing as in TS2017.
When driving a US diesel, the braking feels more real than on TS2017.
Overall depth of driving experience however, and depth and quality of scenarios however, are just not as good in T:ANE as they are in TS2017.
So, that's about it for my review of T:ANE...
I hoped that T:ANE would be a major improvement over Trainz2012, but unfortunately beyond new capabilities in the engine that are applied to some new assets, this failed to materialize. It is not the radical departure, enhancement, "new era" of train simulation that for instance TSW is compared to anything previous.
It is a major rewrite to facilitate what appear to be minor enhancements.
So overall TS and TSW remain the simulators of choice for me.

I bought this game during weekend deal so it was 80% off. Even with that sale the game is not worth the money. Considering I enjoy playing Train Simulator, I was curious about Trainz: A New Era when it was on a 80% discount sale. The reviews were mixed, just like Train Simulator's reviews. But I couldn't find any review comparing the two. I'll use "T:ANE" to refer to Trainz: A New Era, and "TS" to refer to Train Simulator.
I had a lot more problems getting started in T:ANE than I had in TS. Activating the free DLC Niddertalbahn was a disaster. Apparently you need to register an account with Trainz for it to work. It could be just me, but the interface isn't as clear as TS. But that could also because of the differences in terminology between the two. The tutorials in T:ANE are pretty good, and follow a more logical line than in TS. Downside is that by the time I had done the tutorials, I had my 2 hours of gameplay and blew my chance for a refund.
Both games are roughly within the same price range, and DLC seems to have similar pricing too. Buying T:ANE without any further content gives you 4 routes to drive on. Each route comes with a selection of "sessions", a total of 20. A "session" is what you could consider a "scenario" in TS-terminology. More sessions are available at prices ranging from 5 to 10 dollars per session. The session seem to have a longer duration than TS scenarios though. Downside is that some sessions do not have their estimated duration or difficulty listed. The routes included are an American route, a British route, an Australian route and a fictional American-themed route. They all come with a selection of rolling stock, but the exact selection is still unclear to me. One thing that really surprised me, is that the British route goes all the way from London to Edinburgh, a trip that normally takes more than 4 hours by train. I'm not sure T:ANE did this route on a 1:1 scale. That's considerably longer than TS routes which are 100 miles at best (often shorter though). The free Niddertalbahn is a 30km long route, and includes one Quick Drive session. I was unable to find any German rolling stock to go on the route though.
And the amount of questions and unclear things is what bothers me. Before buying TS you can look up the content included. TS always comes with a bundle of DLC, and every DLC lists the length of the route, the amount of scenarios, and the rolling stock included. The amount of content itself may actually be similar; 3 routes, each one with 5 to 10 scenarios and usually 2 or 3 trains each. But it's so much easier to discover what's inside the TS-package, and so difficult to figure out what's in the T:ANE-package.
Both T:ANE and TS have two ways to operate trains: Simple controls (or DCC) comparable with model railroads and toy trains, and realistic controls. Being used to TS keybind controls, I was struggling with T:ANE controls which differ quite a bit. The trains seem to be less detailed in T:ANE, and the route layout reminded me more of a model railroad. The in-cab experience was less enjoyable too. I soon decided I best enjoy T:ANE with a camera view looking down upon my train, much like you'd do with a model railway. The sessions often included shunting operations; coupling and uncoupling of wagons. One of the biggest advantages over TS is that you can actually load and unload cargo wagons in T:ANE. Unlike TS, which seems to be more focussed on driving trains, and less about the shunting/(un)loading operations.
Driving steam trains was quite a challenge. You can either use simple controls, or the realistic ones. There's no middle way. There's no auto-fireman and auto-watering like TS offers.
I also dearly miss the HUD route display that TS has. The little bar on the bottom of the screen giving a visual indication of upcoming signals, speed limits, siding and stations for the next mile or so. T:ANE uses a panel that lists the distances in numbers, which is perfectly fine, but I'd have prefered a visual indication rather than pure numbers. There's no distance to the next station displayed though, unless it's an objective in a session.
Both games have a Quick Drive option. However, Quick Drive in T:ANE isn't as quick as I hoped it would be. You first need to place your train somewhere on the tracks. Then you also need to place any other rolling stock as well. And if you want them to drive, you also have to give each train a driver and objectives. Plus you'd need to make sure all junctions/switches are set correctly. Basically, in TS-terminology, you'd be making a scenario. In TS these scenarios have already been made, and you only need to select a route, a starting point, a destination, and a train. Off you go, including AI trains which you do not need to set up, and all switches set correctly. TS Quick Drive may have less freedom though, but it's quick. TS offers its freedom in other modes.
T:ANE uses a Trainz account for several features I haven't all discovered yet. But you need it if you want the DLC (including the free Niddertalbahn) activated. When I had questions I naturally ask them at the forums here at Steam. No developer seem to be active at all, and the number of players active on the community seems pretty limited as well. The T:ANE community here on Steam is a lot smaller than the TS community, although both communities seem to be friendly and helpful.
Graphics aren't the most important part of a game, but I was dissapointed by the T:ANE graphic quality. TBH, I think the graphic quality of TS, although dated, is still better.
Now I haven't really delved into this one, but from a first impression T:ANE seem to have better and more user-friendly tools available to create your own routes and content. TS also offers tools, but those seem to be more difficult to understand, and only a small amount of players actually creates routes.
T:ANE is more like a virtual model railway. Shunting and (un)loading wagons, and creating routes.
TS is more like a real railway. Drive from A to B, reading signals and handling safety systems.
I'm not recommending this game because of the trouble I have understand how to install content, what exactly is included and no support on Steam. Gameplay isn't what I expected it to be, but that could be because my expectations were biased. I got this on a 80% discount and still don't think it was worth it.

I don't really write reviews that are serious, let alone reviews at all, but I had to for this game. Especially considering it's apparently the least owned game on my friends list, when both of my housemates own Dino D-day, but not this, then it's a sad day.
Ori and the Blind Forest is probably the best game I have played in the past 5 years, and is without a doubt my new favourite platformer ever, and it's heavily reminiscent of Nintendo tier difficulty from the NES / SNES, I read a mixed review about Ori stating the game is like a piano, it's fun when you're hitting all the right keys, but frustrating and it snaps the mood when you're not, to some this might be a negative, to people like myself it's a positive. Games these days often pander to a more casual audience particularly when it comes to a more niche market, but with Ori they stay true to the formula, the controls are tight and any mistake is your fault, the level design is fantastic and the abilities you pick up in the game aren't original, however they are executed perfectly to meld within the areas, the map arches in all different directions and naturally you unlock certain areas once you've obtained different abilities, there's also a levelling system with three different trees, personally I obtained everything in the tree which gave me any form of mobility as I'm pedantic about map exploration and uncovering secrets, I then levelled the other two trees after, however it doesn't matter how you level yourself, hell there's even an achievement for not using of the levels.
The visuals of the game are something to be commended, the art is fantastic and gorgeous to say the least, every area has the right lighting, and the transition between areas is perfect, but like a lot of art forms music and sound plays its part and the music and sound in Ori is perfect, the music blends with the visuals and creates the perfect atmosphere in every area of the game, particular areas involving Kuro execute the sound perfectly and you can literally feel yourself tense as it sets the scene and creates a sense of panic so well.
The story is sweet and simple, but it's very touching and the first 5 minutes will make you cry like a ♥♥♥♥♥ like you did during UP.
The combat is pretty basic and involves nothing too special besides spamming your mouse click and if you like you can use other abilities to kill enemies, however the game is hardly centred around it, the main aspect is the tight controls and seamless gameplay towards the end you'll find yourself ignoring enemies a lot more. Overall it takes around 10-12 hours to beat the game fully with secrets and map exploration etc., it took me 11 hours on my first playthrough, but I am usually a lot slower than most people as I'm fastidious about exploring every nook and cranny, but if you just play the game through and you're not too serious about that stuff it should take you a lot less.
All up, Ori and the Blind Forest is probably one of the best games I've ever played and it definitely in my top 5, and it's one of few games I've actually paid full price for and not just bought whilst on sale, believe	 all the positive reviews as they're right, this game is incredible and it's well worth $20.
Ori and the Blind Forest is a 10/10.
