The story modes for the characters are all rather short. A couple random fights, a fight with Valentine and Double, and then the fight with the Skullgirl.
If you like other fighting games, I could recommend this to you. However, you most likely will want to use an Xbox controller, or if you have a Dualshock controller and the DS3/ MotioninJoy (that's the actual name) program, you can use one of those. [EDIT 12/3/2015: Fixed some problems with this review to make it more relevant with the current game.]
(Note that this is solely based on playing offline so far with about 30+ hours put into the game. I also suck at 2D fighting games.)
Pros: So far this game is probably one of the best fighting games on Steam. It has by far the best sprites I have ever seen in terms of both art design and frame count, and so far has been consistently at 60 FPS making the game very intense and hectic experience. The game has probably the best tutorial for 2D fighting games I've ever seen, which is surprising since this is an indie game, and the training room is very useful compared to other games. All characters (including the DLC and "joke" characters) all feel very unique and different from one another, with usually the DLC characters having a much larger difficulty curve to use.
Cons: These are minor nitpicks at best. For one, you can still play on a keyboard like I have with little problems; however certain commands with be much harder to do without Macros. These can include double P, double K, throws. However the one issue with a keyboard that can't be fixed using Macros are 360 direction motions, which are near impossible to do on a keyboard. I also feel like the game should allow you to have more optional Macros for said problems. The game has a rather limited roster (8 characters for the vanilla build and 5 DLC characters with 1 free "joke" character. DLC characters are somewhat pricey (though this is justified as they were free for a limited time).
Overall, I'd say definitely get this game. Its made by a small indie group that clearly are fighting game fans, and want to create the perfect 2D fighting game. Plus, the game is only $15, so its fairly cheap.

Bought this game as part of the Winter Sale. I'd been leery, because of all the negative reviews. However, it was on sale, had updated, and I'd really wanted this game before reading the reviews.
It took me awhile to get into the groove. Heck, it took me a half an hour to realize how to even enter the game. Had to read a discussion board to realize what I was doing wrong. But once I was in, oh...
Oh this was what I was looking for.
Maybe not the attack by the ferocious winter weather dinos or the eerie looking brain crab. But walking along, seeing the animals, trying to feed them or scare them off, discovering new plants, rocks, trees, mining for gold and iridium, looting jettisoned drop boxes, investigating abandoned outposts, investigating unabandoned outposts, slowly (oh god, so slowly) learning new words, navigating how to fight pirates (why are they shooting at me?! I got nothing in the hulll... Oh, right, I just mined a lot of asteroids...). And that was just in the one system. Then once I got out there, there was more.
Now, is it perfect? Oh no. I'm terrible at this. I get lost. I get confused in the caves. I manage to bypass the starbases. Personally, I'm glad I got a base way the heck back near the start, because I'm still fumbling through on the way out there. I'll probably move it forward when I have a few more skills under my belt.
Gotta mention, love the bases, the freighters, the added storage. I mean, it's all new to me, but given how much difference it makes to me, a new player, I can only imagine how much it means to those who are old hands at it.
As for mods.... yes, I wish this had more mod features. One of the things I love about steam is how easy it makes to add and delete mods. I love seeing the brilliance of other people. And this game could use people who love making new things, new trees, new plants, new ruins, etc. I mean, there are mods out there and I intend to try them. But for now it's been fun.
I will mention here that this game reminds of a roguelike space merchant game called Prospector. It's got similarities in the option to visit new systems with loads of planets (some of which might kill you) and (except the universe there is randomly generated through seed numbers). It's got differences - and not just in the visuals. But I can see where the inspiration for this game grew from similar games previous to it and it's really kind of awesome.
As for multiplayer? Personally, I can live without it, especially if its the kind of PvP thing that I know some would want. I'm not interested in PvP at all. At all. But I'd love to see the opportunity to build merchant fleets, maybe patrol fleets, or exploratory fleets. Or even just bars and stores and bases where friends could hang out. There is a ton of potential here. I mean, just an amazing amount. But given how antisocial I am, I'd like to be able to toggle the multiplayer off or select the options of how I want to run it for myself. Not that this is in the future per se, but the potential might be there.
I say this because Hello games has apparently been updating like mad and I anticipate we'll continue to see an expansion of what is already a vast universe - either through updates or DLC. I look forward to it. I also look forward to the possible evolutions in gaming this might inspire.
So, down to the nitty gritty, would I recommend this game? Yes. Absollutely. I would recommend it for patient and mature people interested in exploration, soft puzzle solving, alien interactions, base building and sundry other possible experiences. I would not necessarily recommend this for those more interested in super fast paced games with lots of shooting and mayhem.
Though, given the pirates and the wild animals, who knows...
Personally I love this game. I hope others will also enjoy it.

When I first tried this game a couple of years ago, I got bored with it within the first 10-20 minutes inside the tutorial dungeon. I tried again... and failed. But as the story goes, third time is the charm. And what a charm!
I've seldom come across such amazing dialog writing, which unfortuntely sometimes gets a bit butchered by the voice actors. In general it is not enough to get annoying, only in very few characters, and even so, you'll get charmed by the narative.
The enhanced edition is simply put beautiful! The spell effects are indeed awesome and you never get tired of casting the same spell over and over again.
If I ever had some issues with the game one of the things is that you rather often feel stuck and the quest log is so vauge as to hint where, what and when to do the quests. So just remember that if you are stuck; explore the entire map! I'm also fairly often frustrated that my characters are not able to perform actions simultaneously like in the Infinity Engine games. And to this point, I miss my tactical pause, which it seems like there is no good reason for not to be there. The argument against it might be the multiplayer aspect, but it seems like people play with friends anyway, where they can communicate quite well if they need a bathroom break. Besides, why should I, playing solo, be punished by the fact that it is possible to play multiplayer? Also I have clicked behind monsters several times due to it moving suddenly in it's prone state, this would have been averted with a simple pause.
Now last thing, which I think most people agree on, is the crafting system (yes even in the EE) still feels weird and lacking in explanation.
BUT (<- very big but) despite all this I still long to play more and unwravel more of the story, and thus my advice is to play this as soon as you are ready to get sucked into a game that will swallow your attention for weeks!

Okay so I am old enough to played most of the games in the Gauntlet series at their time of release so I pre-ordered this one too.  So what do I think? Well it is a tricky one, I think if you hold it up against the early games in the series this seems the next logical step. Keep to the 4 character format, and make use of co-op (No Diablo players running off like kids on drugs grabbing loot, you are all stuck in the same area!). The 4 characters are varied but only have one primary skill each, I think there should be some options here. There are 3 zones, with 10 levels each. Not a vast amount, but enough until they release some DLC (I guess they plan to, depending on popularity).
You can pay for cosmetic costumes with in-game cash  (why these couldn't add minor stat perks is anyone's guess) and you get relics that act as specials for potions (these can be levelled up and are quite varied). There are also perks you unlock by completing achievements and this is where my main criticism comes in. This is a great idea and would keep you coming back, but their should be more and evenly spaced. You get some for dying once, others for killing thousands of monsters!
I find this game fun, and will play it more in small doses chasing some achievements and harder modes. I completed normal mode in a few hours but then you have hard and unfair to go at, where good teammates are a required (let's hope there are enough active players later on). Plus I should have earned a few more perks by then. I think the price is a bit steep for what you get (I think it should be about 1/3 cheaper). Also as I said at the start it ignores some of the advances made by some of the newer Gauntlet games such as more character choices and a 3D perspective, but for us old boys it mostly ticks the nostalgic box. I give it a thumbs up, but it is a bit of a *shrug* too.

If you're unfamiliar with the Scribblenauts series of games you are in for a treat. You control the perpetual do-gooder Maxwell and his magic notebook which is able to conjure into reality anything written into it. The game itself is staged like a loose adventure where you bump into various people or animals who are in need of help. Your job as the player is to help them out by summoning objects or even changing the properties of existing objects. If a cat is stuck up a tree, you can summon a ladder or a cherry picker to go up and rescue the cat. Or you could apply an adjective to the tree itself: say that it is tiny and bring the cat to you. The possibilities are seemingly endless and as you play you will marvel at the size of the dictionary and the clever ways you can interact with things. The main campaign involves Maxwell helping out in themed stages (pirate theme, city theme, space theme, etc.) but there is also a sizeable list of challenges to summon up objects in response to simple riddles. It's cute and coming up with silly or outlandish solutions to the puzzles becomes quite addictive.
Superficially, Scribblenauts Unlimited is pitched at children. There is a tired framing story for the game where a pair of siblings is punished for playing a cruel trick on an old lady and the game literally ends with "...so remember kids..." which should be relegated back to the 1980s where it belongs. Most of the puzzles will punish you to begin again if you manage to kill anyone needlessly (though you can do it) and the majority of the puzzles aren't overly difficult to dream up a solution to. Though, when you consider the way in which the puzzles can be solved, it's clear that the Scribblenauts developers fully expected adults to be playing as well.
There are probably two main things that I had difficulty with. Mainly it's the menu system. It doesn't take much thinking to predict that designing a UI for a game like this is difficult. You control Maxwell with the arrow keys, you can click on virtually everything on screen and most of the solutions are typed out. I can't say that user interaction is revolutionary, but it does the job. The menus, though, are a drag. While you typically wouldn't use them, the "side quest" of extra puzzles, which number about 200, can only be brought up by going three menus deep and then scrolling to where you're up to. If you're planning to go for 100%, prepare for some clicking frustrations. The second issue I had was to do with the lack of localisation. The dictionary and references will probably be best utilised by players from the USA. As an Australian, I found more than a few times where the terminology I would use would not match the American term for the same thing. (Off the top of my head Poker Machine vs. Slot Machine comes to mind.) It was frustrating to know the definite answer to a puzzle conceptually and thinking that the dictionary didn't contain my object only to find that it did, but I needed to use an American term. But probably more problematic is the inclusion of low level American popular culture references. At a high level I understand the baseball terms, for example, but I have no idea about what a "light bat" is supposed to be. I had to look up online to find out it's part of an advertising campaign that nobody outside the US would have seen. As a humorous side note, I did notice that invoking a cricket bat caused a baseball bat to be created! I'd like to stress, though, that these particular frustrations were not numerous and Scribblenauts Unlimited remains largely accessible to all English speakers.
All in all I really enjoyed this game. I had fun bouncing ideas off my wife while playing and could easily imagine playing alongside children. I was motivated to 100% completion. Would highly recommend.

I don't really write reviews that are serious, let alone reviews at all, but I had to for this game. Especially considering it's apparently the least owned game on my friends list, when both of my housemates own Dino D-day, but not this, then it's a sad day.
Ori and the Blind Forest is probably the best game I have played in the past 5 years, and is without a doubt my new favourite platformer ever, and it's heavily reminiscent of Nintendo tier difficulty from the NES / SNES, I read a mixed review about Ori stating the game is like a piano, it's fun when you're hitting all the right keys, but frustrating and it snaps the mood when you're not, to some this might be a negative, to people like myself it's a positive. Games these days often pander to a more casual audience particularly when it comes to a more niche market, but with Ori they stay true to the formula, the controls are tight and any mistake is your fault, the level design is fantastic and the abilities you pick up in the game aren't original, however they are executed perfectly to meld within the areas, the map arches in all different directions and naturally you unlock certain areas once you've obtained different abilities, there's also a levelling system with three different trees, personally I obtained everything in the tree which gave me any form of mobility as I'm pedantic about map exploration and uncovering secrets, I then levelled the other two trees after, however it doesn't matter how you level yourself, hell there's even an achievement for not using of the levels.
The visuals of the game are something to be commended, the art is fantastic and gorgeous to say the least, every area has the right lighting, and the transition between areas is perfect, but like a lot of art forms music and sound plays its part and the music and sound in Ori is perfect, the music blends with the visuals and creates the perfect atmosphere in every area of the game, particular areas involving Kuro execute the sound perfectly and you can literally feel yourself tense as it sets the scene and creates a sense of panic so well.
The story is sweet and simple, but it's very touching and the first 5 minutes will make you cry like a ♥♥♥♥♥ like you did during UP.
The combat is pretty basic and involves nothing too special besides spamming your mouse click and if you like you can use other abilities to kill enemies, however the game is hardly centred around it, the main aspect is the tight controls and seamless gameplay towards the end you'll find yourself ignoring enemies a lot more. Overall it takes around 10-12 hours to beat the game fully with secrets and map exploration etc., it took me 11 hours on my first playthrough, but I am usually a lot slower than most people as I'm fastidious about exploring every nook and cranny, but if you just play the game through and you're not too serious about that stuff it should take you a lot less.
All up, Ori and the Blind Forest is probably one of the best games I've ever played and it definitely in my top 5, and it's one of few games I've actually paid full price for and not just bought whilst on sale, believe	 all the positive reviews as they're right, this game is incredible and it's well worth $20.

So yeah this game kind of sucked me in. The basic premise is that you start up a software company in your garage in 1980. Back then that was very common, many of the big names started that way.

This game doesn't offer a huge amount of options as you play through, however what's here is done very well. I have played through 2 careers doing slightly different things and still find it fun. WIll this be a game you play a year from now? Maybe for the fond memories of it, but it's not really engaging enough to keep you playing it all the time.
However, the creators did add a couple of nice messages in the game thanking you for the support and for purchasing their game which I thought was kinda nice,

It's easy to judge the crap out of a game called Skullgirls, and for most guys, the odd looking characters and logo tend to repel them away from giving it a try.  However, you shouldn't let those things repel you as this game is truly a hidden gem.  The controls are tight, the combat fun, and the characters, though strange at first are very attachable and full of personality.  The game also bosts some of the best looking sprites in gaming, and a fantastic sound track.  The female eye candy is rather nice too.
On the down sides there's a lot to learn to become good, and sometimes even the tutorials are quite challenging.  Not to mention things can be awfully unfair when players use cheap tactics (which is almost all the time)  or certain character combinations, but the game does it's best to even things out by stopping infinite combos and ones that just go on too long.
Overall, Skullgirls is a fantastic game, and a must have for all fighting fanatics, and really gamers in general. It's good if you want to play casually or hardcore, and personally I'd put it on my list of top 10 all time favorite video games.

TLDR: A truly amazing and groundbreaking combat system, severely let down by wonky pacing, frustrating interfaces, poor writing, and a baffling lack of freedom everywhere else. If you're expecting a Bioware-style roleplaying experience, do not buy.
I imagine my experience with this game is I imagine the same as many: hearing the universally glowing reviews and deciding to pick it up on a Steam sale. Sadly, while I can see the reason it's gotten so much acclaim, I was personally very disappointed. In this review, I will attempt to explain why, in the hopes that others of similar mind to myself can avoid a similar experience.
I'll start out on a positive note: The combat. I love the combat in this game. It's incredible. I've played many videogames, from Dragon Age: Origins to Bioshock to Mass Effect that talk about how you can 'combine the elements to create devastating effects.' It's such a common marketing blurb that I barely even pay attention anymore, since all of them are lying. Sure, in Dragon Age, if you hit an enemy that has the 'Frozen' status effect with a critical hit in melee, it does a little more damage, but that's about it. D:OS is the first videogame I've played that actually delivers on that promise. The sheer amount of ways that all the various elements combine and interact to change the conditions of the battlefield is staggering. And unlike Bioshock, where you could zap puddles or light oil spills on fire, but it was only ever a contextual opportunity set up for you by the game, here it is always entirely under your control with abilities like teleporting barrels of water or oil around so that they break in a desired spot, or the ability to call a rainstorm to soak all combatants and make them more vulnerable to lightning spells, or your allies more resistant to fire. It has a great watercooler quality, creating stories like the time when my archer broke open an oil barrel over a crowd of skeletons, and my warrior immolated them by picking up and dropping a lit candle that happened to be part of the decor. Some of my personal favorite tactics involve my Pyromancer creating a burning line in front of my party, and then having my Hydrosophist create a rainstorm to douse the fire and create a steam cloud to shield us from enemy archers. While it is an intensely rewarding experience to figure out creative uses for these elements (like what I experienced when I discovered that a spell I was using to freeze enemies solid could also be cast on my allies in order to extinguish them when they're on fire), mastering their creative use is essential. I cannot stress enough: the combat is awesome. It's just unfortunate that the entire rest of the game isn't that great.
First of all, the pacing is odd. The combat is the game's great strength, but after an opening section to get familiar with the controls and the mindset of combat, the game locks you into a lengthy, dialogue-heavy investigation setting, with very little instruction as to what you're even supposed to be doing. And you can't skip it, since the monsters outside town will wreck you if you don't do quests inside and level up. So you're forced into a long, confusing section with nothing but the game's writing to carry you. And the writing is... I'm sorry, but it's bad, guys. The game swiftly throws up a the-world-is-ending-and-only-you-can-stop-it scenario, which is both laden with nonsensical exposition and painfully cliche. You could argue that it's part of the joke, and it's true that the game does not take itself very seriously. But I personally fail to see the humor in a game with a cliche plot that says "Hey, this is sure something fantasy games do a lot, ain't it?" I just in general don't see the humor value in this game. What is funny about an otherwise normal unique longsword having a "Made in China" inscription? Why does an undead pirate captain have the name "Pontius Pirate," but otherwise speak and act like a normal pirate captain? Why is my character (who can talk to animals) expressing surprise over a talking seashell supposed to be funny? It's like the game is constantly expecting me to laugh at its jokes that never get as far as an actual punchline. It doesn't help that every line of dialogue is written like a soliloquy worthy of an Amateur Dramatics production of Shakespeare in the Park. There are no characters in this game, just broad charactures, made to be 'quirky' (This guy is deaf and mishears you a lot. This guy has chronic hiccups. This woman is a ♥♥♥♥♥. Ect) rather than dynamic or interesting. And every line in the game is voice-acted. Including the lines of dialogue that the NPCs in town say to each other. On loop. Forever. I finally had to turn the Voice volume all the way down in the options, because if I heard those sailors talking about the captain's indiscretions with the Lizard Councilor's wife one more time, I'd throw my computer out the window.
Another constant annoyance is the interface. I can't make heads or tails of the reasons for the many poor design choices here. Why do I have to open the inventory to activate my stats and skills, but my active abilities have an entirely separate menu? Why do the inventory and container screens both pop up in the same spot on the screen, so I will always have to drag one or the other aside in order to transfer items? Why can't I resize the inventory to take up more of the screen? These constantly niggling annoyances really pile up. In a game with this much emphasis on item combinations and crafting (IE: collecting tons of random crap on assumption it will be useful later), there is no excuse for this.
But even with all of those issues aside, it leaves my most damned criticism for this game: the lack of roleplaying freedom. For a game that touts itself as a return to classic cRPGs, make no mistake: this game wants you to play it /its/ way, and employs several measures to help bash you into line.
It starts immediately, at character creation. In single player, you can customize the name and appears of the two main characters. The options are fairly extensive, with a range of faces, hairstyles, and skintones available. However, the character portraits that you'll be staring at a lot more often are fixed, and don't reflect the in-game character model at all. And unlike Baldur's Gate or Pillars of Eternity, there is no way to add custom portraits without some back-door hacking in the game files. As someone who loves roleplaying games and has a collection of beloved characters I like to play in various games, this is a serious problem. This extends to how you build your characters as well. From the start, you can extensively customize your characters for any role you choose, with some really cool and interesting combinations available. However, this is a largely party-based experienced, and your choices of companions are severely limited. The game only provides four companions: a knight using two-handed weapons, a dual-wielding thief, a ranger, and a wizard specializing in ice and air magic. There is also a collection of "hirelings" you can buy, but you can't choose their stats either, and usually have fairly nonsensical choices to start with. Judging by the poorly written character biographies for most of them, I suspect these are made to represent prominent Kickstarter backers than be a serious addition to the game. So this leaves a very limited selection of skillsets you can bring with you in the field, with (as far as I know) no way to respec. If you want to play a character that has the same role, rather than one of the unclaimed specializations (Pyromancy, Geomancy, Witchcraft, Barter, Shield Expert), then you'll find yourself at a disadvantage.
In its current state, this game has a whole lot of really interesting ideas, but has a hard time realizing most of them. As a proof of concept, it succeeds admirably, and I look forward to its ideas being borrowed and iterated on by others.

A Great Start!
Should you buy this game? Not unless you're REALLY excited. There's quite a bit to explore and see, but not a whole lot to do. It's a really solid foundational experience, but needs a lot before it's a full game. The game seems to be embracing creativity and exploration, without crafting or survival elements.
Pros:
> GORGEOUS world generation. So many awesome biome types, with tons of destructible "prop" objects to discover. The world feels varied and dense.
> The third person controls and animations are very well implemented. Jumping and climbing around the world is not only easy, but lots of fun. Your minifig looks awesome doing it, too.
> Animations and graphics in general. The game looks flashy and funny
> Good controller support. I'm using a 360 controller, and (almost) everything feels tight.
> Lots of stuff to find and unlock. Rideable creatures, vehicles, characters (that you can then turn into), and some equippable weapons and items. These things give you a goal to aim for, and a reason to keep exploring the huge world.
Cons:
> Eventually the stuff runs out. Finding new things is fun, but it doesn't take that long to see most of it at this point. It was a real bummer when I found the last item and realized looking for chests was now pointless.
> Building with bricks. I'm personally not a fan of large-scale brick structures, it's just not that fun for me, so I don't have an opinion on that. The small-scale (brick-by-brick) creation system has a lot of potential but right now feels pretty awkward to use. Especially with a controller, but also mouse/keyboard. Brick selection currently is very small, but will get larger as time goes on. There's no goals or limits to building, which is nice in some ways, but I would prefer some reasons within the world to build things.
> Vehicle controls. You accelerate and reverse with the same left stick. It's super easy to go the wrong way or get stuck. This isn't a huge deal right now, but vehicles with nuanced controls that are fun to race around could be really great when multiplayer hits.
> Not SUPER optimized. It's early access, so this isn't expected, and generally it runs fine, but keep this in mind if your PC is on the edge.
While I definitely recommend this game, if $15 matters a lot to you, I would not spend it here, not right now. It's Early Access in the best possible way, but still Early Access. Others have said the price will go up later, but I'm not sure that's reason enough to spend your money if you're on the fence.

Bought this game as part of the Winter Sale. I'd been leery, because of all the negative reviews. However, it was on sale, had updated, and I'd really wanted this game before reading the reviews.
It took me awhile to get into the groove. Heck, it took me a half an hour to realize how to even enter the game. Had to read a discussion board to realize what I was doing wrong. But once I was in, oh...
Oh this was what I was looking for.
Maybe not the attack by the ferocious winter weather dinos or the eerie looking brain crab. But walking along, seeing the animals, trying to feed them or scare them off, discovering new plants, rocks, trees, mining for gold and iridium, looting jettisoned drop boxes, investigating abandoned outposts, investigating unabandoned outposts, slowly (oh god, so slowly) learning new words, navigating how to fight pirates (why are they shooting at me?! I got nothing in the hulll... Oh, right, I just mined a lot of asteroids...). And that was just in the one system. Then once I got out there, there was more.
Now, is it perfect? Oh no. I'm terrible at this. I get lost. I get confused in the caves. I manage to bypass the starbases. Personally, I'm glad I got a base way the heck back near the start, because I'm still fumbling through on the way out there. I'll probably move it forward when I have a few more skills under my belt.
Gotta mention, love the bases, the freighters, the added storage. I mean, it's all new to me, but given how much difference it makes to me, a new player, I can only imagine how much it means to those who are old hands at it.
As for mods.... yes, I wish this had more mod features. One of the things I love about steam is how easy it makes to add and delete mods. I love seeing the brilliance of other people. And this game could use people who love making new things, new trees, new plants, new ruins, etc. I mean, there are mods out there and I intend to try them. But for now it's been fun.
I will mention here that this game reminds of a roguelike space merchant game called Prospector. It's got similarities in the option to visit new systems with loads of planets (some of which might kill you) and (except the universe there is randomly generated through seed numbers). It's got differences - and not just in the visuals. But I can see where the inspiration for this game grew from similar games previous to it and it's really kind of awesome.
As for multiplayer? Personally, I can live without it, especially if its the kind of PvP thing that I know some would want. I'm not interested in PvP at all. At all. But I'd love to see the opportunity to build merchant fleets, maybe patrol fleets, or exploratory fleets. Or even just bars and stores and bases where friends could hang out. There is a ton of potential here. I mean, just an amazing amount. But given how antisocial I am, I'd like to be able to toggle the multiplayer off or select the options of how I want to run it for myself. Not that this is in the future per se, but the potential might be there.
I say this because Hello games has apparently been updating like mad and I anticipate we'll continue to see an expansion of what is already a vast universe - either through updates or DLC. I look forward to it. I also look forward to the possible evolutions in gaming this might inspire.
So, down to the nitty gritty, would I recommend this game? Yes. Absollutely. I would recommend it for patient and mature people interested in exploration, soft puzzle solving, alien interactions, base building and sundry other possible experiences. I would not necessarily recommend this for those more interested in super fast paced games with lots of shooting and mayhem.
Though, given the pirates and the wild animals, who knows...
Personally I love this game. I hope others will also enjoy it.

BUY THIS GAME
There. Now that's out of the way let's actually get to the revewing part. Just going to say, this is the first time I'm revewing something on Steam.
Now, why should you buy this game? Haven't you seen this game has "Overwhelmingly Positive" reviews? Wait... that's not how you review games, is it? Ok, let me try harder.
This game is beautiful. When I first heard about it I learned it had a sad story and puzzling. I never expected anything else. I was wrong. It has one of the most beautiful and well written stories in a video game I've ever seen, and - to my shame - it made me want to cry many, many times. It's hard to explain without spoiling it, you really have to play to see. Let's put it this way. You play as Dr. Eva Rosalene and Dr. Neil Watts, two scientists working for Sigmund Corp. Their job is changing dying people's memories so that they can fulfil a wish they alwas had, and that's exactly what you're there to do. You were contacted by Johnny, a dying man, who wants to fulfil his wish of going to the moon. Not saying anymore.
As for the art... it's simplistic, but don't let that throw you down.  This game's strong point is truly the story. But art comes in many forms, one of which is music, and BY THE EMPEROR is it beautiful. Go on YouTube right away and search "for river to the moon" and see for yourself. Avoid the comments if you haven't played, though, they might have spoilers.
This game isn't very good when it comes to controls. You can walk in two ways: by clicking on the world with your mouse or by using the arrow keys. Moving with the arrows isn't very precise but neither is moving with the mouse, but it shouldn't be much of a problem. The game-play is looking for "clues" (they aren't exactly "clues" but I don't know how to name them) and finding mementos and you have to use your mouse for this. It's more of a point-and-click adventure so I recommend using the mouse. Once you find a memento and "break it" you have to prepare it for transfer (the game will tell you what I mean once you play it, I know you will) and the way you do this is with a puzzle of filling in the tiles. They aren't particularly good. They aren't bad and they aren't frustrating, but they are pretty easy. If you are looking for a puzzler, this isn't it. You should play it anyway.
The characters are very, VERY, well written. So well, in fact, that I'm not going to spoil their personalities. Once again, PLAY THIS GAME.
Overall, well... it's brilliant. One of the best stories I've seen in a game. It has two 20 minute minisodes that are free and worth playing as well.
Now, TO THE SCORE!
Scores:
1 - Not recommended;
2 - Only if you're a fan of the series;
3 - Recommended.
Therefore, I give this game a 3/3. PLAY IT.
EDIT: Nominated for the "Best Use Of The Wrong Engine For This Type Of Game" award 2017!

Well let me just get this out the way now. The game look gorgeous and playing it is like a visual feast for the eyes. Now with that out of the way, onto the review.
Ori and the Blind Forest is about the Guardian Spirit Ori who is seperated from the Spirit Tree at birth and is raised by Naru. Life was good until the forest start to decay and die. Ori set off on an adventure to find out why and restore life to the forest. Since Ori do not speak, most of the story is told by the narrator and Sein, the light and eyes of the Spirit Tree.  The story is pretty straight forward, but do have a good twist on why the main antagonist is the way they are. The opening is heartwarming only to throw some tragedy into it. Even though the game can look happy and colorful, the story can take some dark turns.
The gameplay is 2D platformer, similar to Metroid. You progress through an area until you find an ability that will allow you to get to new areas. There an upgrade system, that will let you upgrade your abilities and attacks. Along with finding new abilities, as you progress through events new areas will become available to you. You may find yourself doing some backtracking to find powerups and other things to help you upgrade Ori and Sein. One unique thing this game do is have save states, called soul links. You gotta decide when to use it because the meter that determine the number of time you can save state also allow you perform heavier attacks or open doors. So you got to use control saving otherwise you may find yourself at a door you can't open because you no longer have the energy to open it.
This game look like beautiful  picture book. The whole time I'm playing this game, I felt like I was running through a forest painting. Each area force me to use my new techniques in combination with my old to overcome various platforming challenges. I found myself getting more involved in the story than I thought I would. My only negative comment is that it fairly short, you could probably clear it in 4~5 hours first playthrough if you're not going for 100% and backtracking. But don't let that stop you from joining Ori in this beautiful forest.

I also appreciated how this game connects each characters role in the Skullgirls universe in the story. Aside from that the theme of the game looked very difficult to pull off (a dark deco theme with a huge jazz motif) yet they delivered in every way. The dev team made some tough calls so their child would wither to nothing and that struck something with me. While that whole situation was going on I was selling my consoles to build my first gaming pc ( pc master race) and I was actually very happy that out of all the games I lost Skullgirls was still there only this time in pc form. So it was one of the first games I bought on my new computer. At the end of the day Skullgirls has sentimental value as a game and where ever it goes I will too!

I never really got into old school turn-based RPG's like Baldur's Gate or Neverwinter Nights, so I don't know how this game compares to the classics.  I play mostly real-time action RPG's, you know, like Bioware and Bethesda stuff. I was pleasently surprised to find this gem of a game though. I'll probably play more turn-based RPG's because of it.
What I think really makes this game shine is the writing, theatrical voice acting, humor, and thoughtful lore. There's this light-heartedness to Larian games that I'm really starting to like.
I found the gameplay to be fun and challenging. There's nothing quite like beating overwhelming odds with carefully staggered crowd-control, which I imagine to be only possible in turn-based games. (I'm new to this type of game.)
I don't know how the classics compare or if it's typical of this genre, but I have mixed feelings about the puzzles in this game. I'll try to explain as best as I can to give some people a heads up. Ever played classic point-and-click adventure games where there's a ton of pixel-hunting frustration? There's a lot of that in this game. I can't speak for everyone, but I definitely get stuck a lot when questing and it really bogs down the pacing. I can imagine this is a feature for some people, as the questing doesn't feel as formulaic. The trade-off is that the pacing isn't as smooth as the RPG's i'm used to playing.
I guess if you really enjoy freedom, exploration, puzzle and your mood allows for some frustration, then it should be no problem. I think Larian intended the game to be this way.
However, the writing and voice-acting is so good that I really wanted to solve those darn puzzles to be rewarded with more content. Overall the game is a very addicting experience. I haven't stayed up late gaming in a long time.
Divinity: Original Sin is well-worth the money, even for someone like me who normally avoids turn-based games.

I didn't buy it when it released. I rarely purchase a game when it is new. Since I play games on a PC, instead of a console, I get most of my games through online retailers such as Steam. I am glad I waited. The frustration of those who were early "investors" put me on guard.  When I read the reviews and articles about the problems, I was content to wait. So when the winter sales of 2016 arrived, I added No Man's Sky to my collection.
As of today, I am 26 hours into the game. I have started two games with slightly different play styles. The first game was about getting off of the starting planet as quickly as possible and experience multiple planets. The second game was slower paced and I have stuck around on each planet longer to see what it has to offer.
No Man's Sky is not a game that holds your hand and tells you how to play. You are free to go about the storyline. So far, I haven't found much of a plot to the story. There are some threads you can follow. As I explore more, I may find more substance. At this point, though, it is an open ranging experience. For people who like a solid story to carry you through a game, don't start looking here. I like open world experiences, though. I have enjoyed both styles of game play. And spent too many hours at one time playing through the slower paced style.
It is a pretty game. The planets are nicely rendered. The plant and animal life get a little redundant (at the "level" I am playing). There are some hard to achieve objectives. And there is a LOT to see. The planets are huge. And then the galaxy is expansive. The core "goal" of the game is to reach the galactic core. For people who have to reach the finish line, it is possible to do it quickly. At least I have heard of people doing it quickly. But this game is meant to be taken at a slower pace. The universe is meant to be explored.
No Man's Sky is solitary. You character interacts with other species of intelligent life. But there is extremely limited multi-player interaction. This is not a game for the social gamer. If you want to squad up with 3 of your buds and take on space pirates, you need to check out a different game. This is an introverts dream, though. You can explore peacefully without the constant chatter of a chat stream. You can interact with programmed bots that allow you to choose how you will respond. You have little markers that let you know that someone else was here before you. You leave little markers that let others know you have been here. But there is no real social interaction with another living soul.
This is a Trekkers game, not a galaxy far, far away. This is not a game of exciting twists and turns. It plays out slowly. It is more exploration than adventure. This is Star Trek: The Next Generation at its purest (without the need to inject romance/intrigue/action). This is an effort to go where no one has gone before. It is a mind game more than a button mashing game. You cannot experience this game waiting for the next bad guy to pop up. You can experience this game anticipating what is over the horizon or when you break through the atmosphere.
Hello Games took a beating in reviews because they didn't deliver the game that gamers were expecting. I sort of let my expectations go away. I entered the game with a bit of trepidation that it would be a waste of time. But I have enjoyed it. It has turned into one of those "just 10 more minutes" kind of games. My wife is probably a little miffed that it consumed as much time as it did. And I will be backing off of it now that the extraordinary schedule of the holidays are passed. But I will be coming back to it again and again.

Expect a true sequel to the previous two games, and feel disappointment.
Approach it as a, say, side story made by a different team (which it is) and enjoy a solid, fun, action-packed FPS that is great both on your own and with friends.
It's not scary, although it tries to be at times, but atmospheric enough to hide the very much arcady shooting mechanics. That said, these mechanics are fantastic, and as a shooter FEAR 3 is highly enjoyable and, to my surprise, easily replayable.
It's also hands down one of the best linear coop experiences you'll have in an FPS in terms of variety and coordination.
The multiplayer oozes with original and fun ideas which sadly made it into game modes that didn't last long before the community died out, but if you have at least 3 friends who are into this game, get them together and have a blast in the surprisingly innovative multiplayer.
It's been 4 years but FEAR 3 remains a highly enjoyable experience to this day. And if, like me, you were slightly disappointed with how FEAR2 turned out in relation to FEAR1, the third installment won't be MUCH of a disappointment, but rather a great time waster - be it alone or with friends.
Get it. Just remember that it's not what its predecessors were.

A diamond in the ruff.  Most of us can remember the days of the arcades.  And Gauntlet was one of the top pics, at least for me, to dump my hard begged quarters into.  This revamp does it proud.  Classic Gauntlet nostalgia comes to life here as early as the loading screen for me.  Only one major flaw to note.  It's terribly short IMHO but that doesnt mean that DLC couldn't be on the way. Overall, the game is good.
It could use some fine tuning.
The Cons:
Character building could use slightly more depth.  Legends had it on the money, but I suppose relics are the compromise between Classic and Legends.
Multiplayer needs an update.  Specifically, being able to jump directly into a Public game regardless of if they're in a lobby waiting.  I've had way too many people join and quit before entering a dungeon.
Levels are too few.  I've only had the game a few days, playing it only a few hours a day and am almost done on Normal.  At the very least, I'd hope they release some sort of endless challenge dungeon.
Pros:
The game is a nice blend of Classic Gauntlet and the modern hack-n-slash grinder.
Graphical refresh is slick as hell.  Though, the close-up character models could stand for an upgrade.  They look a bit to iOSish, as though they could be planning a port one of these days...
Gameplay is for the most part solid.  There are a couple minor annoyances, but pretty negligible in the end.  Probably the most annoying thing is using a key because your weapon hit a door while attacking.
Multiplayer gameplay-wise is spot on.
For $20, you can't really beat it at all.  If this iteration of the game is any indication of where the franchise is going, I'm really looking forward to expansions and the potential for a sequel.  Good game.  Good price.  Support it.

Completed the game in a four player group.
It's Gauntlet. Monster spawners well... spawn monsters and you kill those monsters while using keys to open doors and collecting treasure. It does that aspect of Gauntlet very well and the game is pleasing visually, although the enemies lack variety in terms of design.
The individual classes themselves are interesting and while it feels a bit odd not allowing more than one person per class, they make the game interesting. Each of the characters has a focus; the warrior has strong single and arched melee damage output and can take a few more hits than the others, the ranger has high mobility and very high single target damage output at range, the wizard has a variety of AoE's and utility spells and the valkyrie is a well rounded class with tanking tendancies.
Aside from the cosmetic costume pieces, the only way to customize your character is through "relics", which require potions found while exploring the level in order to use. However every character gets access to the same relics, which reduces a bit of the impact that your choices make. The variety of effects available is interesting, but with short durations, or low damage output, they don't really have as much weight in gameplay as you might expect. The worst decision as far as I'm concerned in regards to relics is that while it takes a substantial amount of gold to fully upgrade a relic, you do not get potions (the items needed to actually USE the relics) during boss fights, at least not on normal difficulty. That would be one time that you would definetely want to bring out all of your character's potential, only to find them somewhat crippled.
It's not a bad game by any means, and there are far worse titles that you could spend 15-20 dollars on. You just might not find anything that really wow's you.

Game Dev Tycoon is a casual management sim around running your own game company.  The game has a simple but charming asthetic and follows the story of gaming from the early boom of the 80's to the modern day.  Making decisions on  the theme and design of your game and managing your staff are early challenges.  Later you will train staff, market your games and even develop your own console.

The preset combination that determines what reviewers deem "a good game" is often a mystery to you until you fail.  With a lack of detailed information of why your game failed its easy to become frustrated by this core mechanic.  This can be seen by the huge number of guides available on how to win the game, at this point you might as well be playing "spreadsheet the game".

Overall, i'd say the games pro's outweigh its somewhat shallow mechanics.  If you can pick this one up on sale for under a fiver I'd give this one a somewhat half-hearted reccomendation.

An honest, hype/hate free review:
Let me preface this by first saying that A: I got this game at a *steep* discount, and B: I use a whole suite of mods.
That being said, I like this game. A lot. I recommend it, but not for $60. And the mods I use are mostly for graphical performance optimization that don't affect the core game-play experience. That part came later, as you'll see. I didn't get No Man's Sky until after the Foundations update. By then the over-hype, and ensuing backlash had (mostly) passed. I had watched a few Let's Plays, and I felt like I was ready. (read: I had low expectations.)
First, the bad:
The first time I started a new vanilla game, it took nearly 3 minutes to load, and the low FPS made the game nearly unplayable. I have a very good gaming PC, so this was new in my experience. This is where most people would have stopped and got a refund. To be fair, I spent most of the first day testing different mods to see what worked, or broke the game. (I highly recommend looking at
The optimization mods helped keep the game looking good, but brought the load time down from 3 minutes to 38 seconds. Tolerable at least.
My (good) Experience:
Once I got the game running smooth like butter, I did what any good tester would do, and tried my best to break it. You see, I had heard that most of the game-play was grinding. Grinding for money, resources for upgrades, for inventory expansions, etc. So the first thing I did was eliminate all of that to see if there was still a game left. After a bit of hacking, I started a new game with all inventor slots unlocked, all crafting recipes known, and 100 million units (money). Now you might say that it made the game stupid-easy, but I still had to find and collect the resources I needed. This way, I was still forced to explore. And I'm glad I did. You see, I could have just given myself unlimited warp fuel, and high-tailed it for the galactic center (the 'end' of the game) but I had already watched a video of 'the end' of the game and I wasn't in a hurry to reach it.
No. The hidden gem of this game is in the exploring. Once you've gotten the hang of surviving the basic elements of the weather, and the knack of dealing with the odd pirate attack, it's less about the pitched excitement of danger and combat, and more about seeing the sights, making discoveries, meeting aliens, and learning about the alien backstories and language, which is my favorite part. I like the varying pace of the game. Mostly peaceful, with excitement sprinkled in when you least expect it. Like going for a bike ride in the park, and then every so often the bike briefly turns into a bear.
I was able to get to, and focus on this aspect of the game quickly (within a couple hours) by eliminating the busywork of grinding. (And I won't sugarcoat it, the grind is real.) The grind serves to pad gameplay time, but I don't feel it adds to the experience in a meaningful way. BUT! you can still enjoy the game with the grind, just at a slower pace.
I was trying to see how fast I could get to the point where the -core- gameplay stopped being fun. But after over 25 hours (at time of writing) in a couple marathon sessions, I haven't found it. Sure, a lot of the locations have that copy-pasta feel to them, but it never stopped being engaging for me. Even if I started the game with the best ship and weapon, and all the upgrades from the word go, already knowing how the game 'ends', I would still have a blast jet-setting around and meeting people, and seeing things, claiming a home planet and building a base. (The last part, coming with the new update, bringing a whole other new, good, dimension to the game.)
Ultimately, I like the game. A lot! But I had to do a TON of exceptional things to get there, and that shouldn't be required of the average player. Which is a shame. Because at it's heart NMS is a fantastic gem. But it's mired by a lot of rough that you have to get through to see it. I can only hope that with future updates, these core problems may get addressed. As it is, my review is, like it's current rating, Mixed. But I still recommend it because I think it's worth a chance. This game needs more positive reviews to off-set the negative, vocal minority.
TL;DR: Good game at heart. Has (fixable) technical issues. KNOW what kind of game you're getting into. Don't pay full price ($60).

Why should you get this game? In short: It is fun, and unique.
Just 10 minutes into the game and you can see everything that has been inspired from games of old. Turn Based battle system, a fun, laid back skill system, and visual cues that darn well give away hints.
If you're looking for an extremely hardcore RPG, you have come to the wrong place, if however - you are looking for a "comfy" JRPG which focuses more on fun, you have come to the right place. Not to say the game is not challenging - far from it. It's just more relaxing to play than other JRPGs on the market. Hence the term "Comfy JRPG"; it's something you can play all night without realizing the time, which is exactly what happened to me last night.
Even-though I have some of the best JRPGs ever created in my library I choose to play this for hours instead. Now, you're probably wondering why? The answer is simple: Fun. Literally pure fun. With some of the classic JRPGs you get ups and downs, and sometimes just can't be bothered to keep playing - but with this, it's just all ups and I never wanted to put the mouse down. - Would be nice to perhaps Controller support in the future though.
The story/plot is very unique, and the game has some nice light humour, which is very nice to see in a JRPG. This is a game that doesn't take itself too serious. It's less about hardcore grinding, and more about fun. The story up to now has been great, but I won't say much as it would ruin surprises for you.
It's quite funny seeing certain thing's in game and you think to yourself "Wait a minute! That looks familiar!) - There are clear references to Final Fantasy, Zelda, Pokemon, etc. It was funny seeing that Pikachu on the fire, and other stuff which I won't mention it as it could spoil the surprise. There are plenty of different foes, and might I add - the art style is very good too. Would be nice to see 1080p support in the future for those who can make use of it.
The battle system is very relaxing. There is no rushing, no stress. You do stuff in your own time. There are a lot of skills and specials to choose from. Items can also give you permanent boosts, as well as your mandatory heal items, etc you would come to expect from a JRPG.
At first the item collecting seemed weird - but after a bit of time I realized it's another great element to the game, and it reminds me of when I used to be a kid and collected rare items in games. It's nice to have something like that again. Although, it would be nice if there was a few less item quests, and perhaps a few more hunt x monsters quests.
So what are the final thoughts for EBF4? It's almost the ultimate comfy JRPG, and that's not a light thing to say. This game is VERY FUN. So if you want to sit on the couch or desk for hours and hours and forget about time and eventually grow a beard and never wash again because you are so damn addicted, then this game is for you. Seriously. BUY IT NOW. Feel free to look at my reviews for other games, I normally score most games low, but this get's an 8/10 from me.
Also; Did I mention you can make bewbs bounce, and play with♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ :3

Great, game with massive potential but a serious flawed play to win system makes it almost unplayable,
most people leave the game quickly after realising how horribly broken it is.
The churn of players must be truly massive.
The game is run by no more than 5 players on each world.
They spend tonnes of money in some cases thousands of dollars but ruin it for everyone one else.
Players leave, the world get stale and they create a new world.
Pay to win is  how the company makes their money but with no upper limit its an arms race most don't bother with and they drop out.
This is sad as the game has  great mechanics but these are broken by the pay  to win system making it the only game mechanic that matters.
I believe this is a vulnerable business model for several reasons.
1) More and more  pay to win games are coming out firefly are now  competing in a crowded market place.
2) The mobile market is taking more of this type of games market.
3) The game hasn't  evolved at all since it's inception ( no insignificant features like paladin castles  don't count) players will  get bored and leave.
4) Including the  significant "big spenders" not good having  a  significant chunk of your revenue at the whim of a few people. They loose interest  then what?
I believe an alternate option could make the game more profitable, decrease churn and  be more fun.
I suggest a limit to the amount of cards a player can play in a day.
I am sure if you looked at the average churn rate, the average spend of those players before they where burnt, compare it with the average spend of your current
low tier, mid tier and hight tier spenders you could work out a card limit that doesn't break the game and is more profitable then what you have got now.
Do some projection on how long you have to keep players in the game  and/or reduction in churn rate you need  to recoup any loss from the difference between the max spend and the big spenders.
The math wouldn't be that hard,
This still gives the advantage to purchasing cards but does not break the game.
The limit will make card  selection a tactic, what cards to use when.
Heavy spenders would still spend money to get either the "good" cards  or trade in for better cards. But they would have to choose when to use them.
This would be an advantage but not as big as now getting to Prince  in 5 days, or instant spam armies, capture village build full castle, rinse repeat.
They would not be able to bully the entire server which forces everyone to leave, and loss of income for firefly.
It would be a safer more sustainable business model, it would also most likely accumulate over time.
To have many people paying a little is better than a few paying a lot.
Players not willing to even get involved in the Pay to win war would probably spend if they new that they had a chance of  competing and if this bullying was gone.
This change would bring many players back to the game,
I suggest you trial it as a world, just like the wolf world.
It would be a great marketing event to  bring back old players.
I mean seriously there would be approximately 2000 active players looking at the world figures.
You boast 4 Million players signed up,  that means you have a  retention rate of about  0.05%  or about 1 in 2000.

Reus is a simple, yet challenging resource management god-sim. The objective of each era is to help the humans progress as much as possible before the time limit. After each era, if certain criteria are met, additional play modes and resources become unlocked. Be warned, this game can get pretty repetitive. But the unlockable resources mix things up just enough to keep you hooked. The price for the entertainment of this game makes it entirely worth it.

Reus plays almost like a card game. The planet is split into tiny sections were you can place your 'cards' (plants, animals or minerals) and these differ depending on the land type they're placed on (swamp, forest, desert, mountain and sea). These "cards" for my analogies sake, work in combination with those surrounding, either the section next to it, a highlighted range around it or the village's range. Together they give bonuses to one another and give your villages their resources.
You are the planet and you help the villagers using your giant avatars. The villagers will want resources for projects, complete these and your giant can pick them up, unlocking a skill. These skills can be used to transform the 'cards' you've put down into more advanced or specialised 'cards' making the combos etc more complex. You can unlock the advanced and specialised cards by completing achievements in the game. Your villagers will get greedy if you spoil them however and destroy other villages through war. You don't have a faction, you gain skills by having villages of different land types so you want to keep everyone flourishing. To try and keep your greedy villages at bay you have to provide them with dangers that keep them occupied in the form of predators or dangerous mines etc but this is quite difficult and occasionally you may need to intervene with your giants. Villages may turn on you and attack your giants if they are unhappy, not in enough awe of the giants or just greedy but eventually enough pummeling will set them straight.
As well as unlocking more of the advanced/specialised 'cards' to place you will also unlock longer play time as well. So each time you play you start of with a dead planet but have a few more tricks up your sleave allowing you to advance farther quicker and with more time in which to do it. After a few goes it felt like I was playing the same game over and over but depending on your villager's projects depends on what you place, how your planet looks and which skills you can unlock for that particular playthrough. So it always ends up different and the more you achieve the more you unlock. A very addictive game, with a bit of a learning curb as you learn what all the skills the 'cards' have. Its really satisfying get good combos working however. I'd highly recommend the game if you like strategy or card games but won't mind if their aren't actually any cards.

Please note that this is my first ever extensive review for a game. I hope that, in case you find yourself pondering upon the question of whether or not you should buy this game, this review will help you come to an answer to this question. This review is
If you disagree, feel free to do so. There will most most likely be a few aspects of the game that will not be spoken of here.
I just wish to share my thoughts on the game.
Game Dev Tycoon has it's flaws (i.e. exploitation of simple patterns, repetitiveness). It can be a nice little experience, nonetheless. At least for a few hours of playtime. It delivered on what it had to offer, and executed it well. It feels like there could be more, however.
Game Dev Tycoon is about management, as you have to work around your staff, money, hyping your products, knowing the market, etc. if you want to achieve success. You start off from a garage and move up in the world as you develop your own games and follow the history of gaming. You get to see some of the classic consoles from the real world (albeit renamed to avoid issues with claims) get released and develop games for them. Some of the events that also occurred in real life are also referenced in the game very briefly (i.e. the original Playstation's back story), if I am not mistaken.
This is a game development simulator, so it should give you a lot of impact and choice when you design a game. Although, when you design a game, you choose it's name, target audience, platform, genre, type and engine. There are three main phases of development, afterwards, where you can turn three sliders and tune some options on and off. There isn't much choice to be had. To add onto that, these sliders can be set in different patterns for a specific combination for genres and types of games for guaranteed top scores. There's many guides out there that show you how to do this exactly, effectively exploiting the game for an easy way out.
You have to work around the engines that you can never directly upgrade (so instead you just make a new one from scratch), employee's salaries and different working skills (including yours), weekly paychecks, events, and more. These can be a huge dent on your salary if you don't spend your money properly.
A note worth adding is the fact that this game has mod support. This can be quite useful for those who are looking for a new experience or adding some extra utility features to the game... or just screw around. That works too. The mods add some aspect to the game's replay value, which is always a saving grace for a type of game like this that can get boring quite quickly for some.
The game has a clean and straightforward UI with satisfying sound effects to back it up. One of the most memorable things about the gameplay is when you're planning out your next release and those clean, blue and orange bubbles pop up and come through the screen with the most satisfying of noises a human can hear. The art style feels washed up and too monotone, for me, though. Nothing really stands out unless the game goes out of it's way to do so, which is quite rare. It makes sense in an office environment, but makes it look boring and stale.
I recommend you to check it out if it's at a discount, someone gives it to you (if ya' got friends that are so generous to do that), or if you just have money to spend and simply don't care about it. It has it's sweet moments, but is nothing too special in particular. The reason I do not rate this is because I, personally, have a hard time not recommending this game, but find it to be a bit too overpriced for what it offers.

This game has a learning curve, or something like a comfort curve. It was different from the action RPGs, like Path of Exile or Diablo, that I'm used to. One of the first things that really threw me off was the movement speed. The slower movement speed just slowed everything down.
But that just made everything feel more real.
What do I mean by real? Your creativity and imagination matters. How you read and interpret quest logs and conversations matters. Honestly, there are so many ways things can go 'wrong' because the game is so free.
This game doesn't hold my hands as much as other games. It was hard, it was frustrating. Every completed quest felt so much more fulfilling and compelling. You put effort into it, it wasn't a cookie cutter kill x things. Hell, your build might matter, like putting points into pet pal to talk to animals. I loved this game.
But, holy crap, it got frustrating for me at one point. All progression just grinded to halt. My friend and I had no idea what to do. BY THE WAY, THIS GAME IS MEANT TO BE PLAYED CO-OP. LIKE REALLY. We had completed all the story but hadn't used the bloodstone/starstone thing, and had no idea that it was linked to continuing the quest.
And so, what happened is that we completed 90% of the game's main storyline, 'main' because of all the side quests, and we got stuck. We thought there was more quests to do, something we were missing in order to continue. But, after some googling, we figured out the problem and suddenly propelled to the end of the game.
In another game it would be doing and completing all the game's main storylines and quests without receiving them for the quest-giver. Then after completing everything, you meet the guy who's supposed to give you the quest and find out you completed everything.
The game has humour too. I laughed when I met a totem that claimed it could show me the future, and it did.
TLDR Great game. Huge time sink. Difficulty is compelling. Freedom for creative use of skills is refreshing. Freedom backfired on us and got us stuck in storyline. Definitely play it co-op. Personally played for story, will not play again. Recommend 10/10. YMMV. Looking forward to playing Divinity: Original Sin 2.

A turn-based RPG reminiscient of older games like Golden Sun, Sword of Mana, and early Final Fantasy. Aside from a few quirky bits, there isn't really anything here that makes the game stand out - it's standard JRPG fare. The characters and story are decent enough, the combat/leveling seems fine, enemies are reasonable, puzzles are somewhat easy but can have tricky parts here and there, etc. You can adjust the difficulty level at any time if you feel the game is getting too easy.
The art style is questionable, but it looks better in-game than it does in the store page's screenshots. I would prefer a different style but this is acceptable.
Some of the reviews mentioned this game being online, so I checked, and yep you can play for free on Kongregate. The Steam version has additional content and more options though, so it's probably worth a couple of dollars (I picked this up for $3 in the summer sale). I played through about half of the first level online to see if the game was even worth playing, and I'd recommend the same to anyone who might be thinking about buying this.
The first boss is a surprise due to its power level, which is far above anything you've already dealt with. You'd expect that from a boss, but not to this extent. The boss could one-shot the healer, which was slightly annoying. It's still not "hard" to beat the boss, but some grinding will be necessary for a few people (depending on the difficulty mode). The other bosses seem easier in relation to your power level, so it seems the power curve is better-adjusted after this first boss.
Overall this game seems worth some money and time if you like RPGs. It's a bit on the casual side and definitely not perfect, but for $3 there isn't much to complain about. It's worth checking out.

Skulls. Girls. Girls decorated with skulls, parasites, and mutations.
Not much more to ask for, and yet Skullgirls delivers that and further still as the months go by.
The game has an amazing cast of characters; each of them being their own unique monstrosity in some way shape or form and an interesting story following them-- sometimes even an emotional story. The character designs are well-thought-out and very unique, and their voices are very well picked for the personalities they're meant to reflect. It didn't take long for neither myself nor those getting into this game alongside me to get hooked on the game simply out of interest in the characters.
The world and backstory dynamics are also quick to get interested in, albeit they're only touched on briefly in each story. A corrupted area run by a corrupt mafia, and those negatively affected by their actions are looking to fight back-- each through different means and thus pitting against each other by virtue of their conflicting motivations. But is that really all there is behind the story? I heavily suggest playing to find out.
The music is brilliant and captures the atmosphere of each stage incredibly well, though it comes as no surprise given the composer-- Michiru Yamane-- and their past works in larger franchises. The Castlevania vibes in the soundtrack are hard to miss in certain tracks, but it if anything that nostalgic feeling conveyed is praiseworthy.
The main con I can think of is the disappointment that comes from short length of each character's story, but as more characters are released more parts of the story become available, making the game a strong long-term investment and and a great means of mindless  short-term fun in the meantime.

If you want a rich, immersive story-driven experience with amazing soundtrack, this is the game for you.
It's only 4.5 hours and it is best to play it in one sitting to get the most of the immersion, and believe me - once you start it, you will be hooked and you won't want to let it go until the end. The game does a very good job of pulling you in by presenting mysteries and questions early on and keeping the tension up while gradually revealing everything about its plot.
The gameplay is almost non-existent - there is some walking around to get from place to place and some trivial jigsaw puzzles. It chooses to focus on its strong points - the story, the sound, the characters, the dialogue - and that is where it shines.
It has a perfect blend of both lighthearted humor and heartbreaking drama.
A must-play for anyone who enjoys a good story with a very emotional plot.

Well this game was a lot more involved than I was expecting. You have 4 giants, and each one has one main skill (terraforming).  Forest makes forests, Water makes oceans, Rock makes mountains/desert, Swamp makes swampland. Then each one can make plants, animals, or mineral deposits. Each thing you place interacts with other things you can place, to give bonuses. When a town forms in each area (desert, forest, swamp), they start a project objective you have to help them meet by adding more things to get their scores up. If you win, you get an ambassador, which opens new upgrade options. Then each thing previously placed can be upgraded. Those upgrades interact with each thing differently than the original, so you change all of your bonuses each time you change something. As you go along the projects get more difficult. That can make for a lot of different play combinations.
The 30 minute games advance you, but I have not worked through those yet. I wanted to do some free play to figure out how everything worked together first. There is definitely plenty of game play for days, here. It's a good game to fiddle with and then save to come back to. Once you become familiar with the rules, you can then alter things further with game options (e.g., world size, "speed play", and "no pause") to challenge yourself further.
