Okay, I am going to get right into this and say that F.E.A.R. 3 is a BAD game, but it is only a BAD game to people who have played the other games. If you've played the other F.E.A.R. games, you understand why this game is the bane of our existance, but, if not, I shall explain it to you.
Alright, F.E.A.R. and F.E.A.R. 2: Project origin were both made by the same company and in the same style. They had large maps that you could get lost in and unnerving environments. Monolith was NOT afraid to hit you with a scare that comes across as mild, though is nothing compaired to the rest of the game, but it get's you anyway, probably even more than the really big scares. It was the small things that kept people on edge for the duration of your play time. The characters were well thought out and they were in no way scared to be brutal. They slapped you with a psychic canibal clone commander from the start who blew through innocent men and woman to get to the people who tortured and killed his mother who was forced into carrying to children via clone fetus implant. Yeah... Pretty sick stuff.
The Problem with F.E.A.R. 3, however, was, not only the fact that the developer who made it KNOWS NOTHING ABOUT HORROR, but also the fact that it was so pointless and soul-crushing that it totally went in the OPPOSITE DIRECTION of what the original creators wanted. Day 1 RUINED F.E.A.R. by turning it into a light, CHEAP, co-op, FPS hell. They almost entirely removed the horror aspect of the game and handed us one of the biggest loads of trash. The problems are as follows.
1. Going by the story line of the previous games, the ending was anti-climactic and a serious let down.
2. The horror aspect it an attempt to use wierd sounds and over-cooked map textures to scare people as well as cheap jumpscares that would hardly startle a small infant.
3. They changed the characters to a fault. The two biggest examples being the Characters Paxton Fettel and Point Man. Paxton had always been propper and rightfully creepy simply by the way he delivered his lines and their context. He now speaks in partial slang and comes across more annoying with his lines than his former eree. Point Man was originally personality-less, intended to be that way by the company that was implimenting his make-shift powers. They didn't want him to have a personality. This also helped the immersion of the game by allowing the player to impliment themselves onto the character. NOW, Point Man has a very angry and cliche silent-protagonist role, comming across as an overused-"badass" steriotype.
4. CUTSCENES. The other games had little to no cutscenes. What few they had were all in first person and allowed the player some range of head movement. In F.E.A.R. 3, however, the cutscenes are full on thirdperson with no choice, no point, and do little to advance the story. If anything, they just annoy the player. (Paxton's cheesy jokes don't help any.) This also breaks the immersion charm that the F.E.A.R. games were known for.
5. The story is dead. Yes, they continue on from the last game involving Alma's third child, but hardly any of the game is even about that. You play a "must save the princess" sort of game with the Character Jin sun-qwan who can't seem to keep away from trouble, but was a total badass in the other games. She didn't need to be saved and was a good ally. In this game, she even has the gall to be annoyingly bossy, something I quite detest, especially seeing as her voice actor get's very ear-clenching after level two. They also make sure to kill off the Protagonist from F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin in an unessisarily brutal way and give him a voice, though he had none in his own game (Though I wonder HOW IN THE HELL THIS GAME GOT AHOLD OF ROBIN ATKIN DOWNS.)
6. They play Alma as a completely innocent little girl, running from the tyrant that was her father. Alma was, in no way, innocent. She was an evil, demonic spirit who killed many to get what she wanted and even mind♥♥♥♥♥♥♥her youngest son to get it, making HIM kill many people as well at age 10 and again at age 30. Another thing to note is that Harlon Wade did some bad things, but, as it is shown in F.E.A.R. 2, was reluctant to do said things to Alma, but did because he thought they were for the better. He certainly loved Alma, though she did kill him, and was clouded in judgement by those of the Armacham corperation. A spirirt such as his could not have come back as a demon, let a long one with so much power over the surviving family.
7. Inconsistantcy. Paxton's role in this game, on its own, is an inconsistancy. Not only is he a ghost, which he shouldn't be due to him gaining a new body off of a clone in the DLC for F.E.A.R. 2, Reborn, but he seems to like becoming visible and invisible to anyone but Point Man at any given time. What I mean by this is: During the cutscenes, the game shows that Paxton is totally invisible to anyone but his brother, but, in combat and totally BAD times, he is visible to the world and can be harmed by bullets, though in some scenes it is depicted that bullets have no effect on him, which leads no another problem when, in Point Man's ending, he stops Fettel by shooting him. I know what they were trying to do in paying  respect to the first game, but with the way they loused it all up, it just doesn't work.
8. (Finally) The endings. In Point Man's ending, he shoots Paxton in the head, delivers Alma's baby, then leaves with it. (I've already explained the two problems with this ending.) and In Paxton's ending, he possesses his brother, delivers the baby, then eats his own mother, claiming it'll give him the power to take over the world, which, isn't just cliche, but NEVER HIS GOAL IN THE FIRST PLACE. Paxton's goal was always to avenge his mother and serve her. Now he wants world domination. What in the... Never mind... I digress...
ALSO, if you want a bonus: THE FINAL BOSS IS SO EASY THAT YOU'D HAVE TO BE BRAIN DEAD WITH YOUR NON-FUNCTIONAL BRAIN REMOVED NOT TO BEAT IT THE FIRST TIME ON THE HIGHEST DIFFICULTY. I swear, it is as obvious as a five-foot black spider on a white bedroom wall and as liniar as the lines on a road.
It has bad shotguns, too. They are 50% glass. That isn't a safe thing.

For all those who have played the co-op of the original Gauntlet late into the afternoon or evening at a buddy's house, this game isn't going to invoke that feeling of nostalgia; it's just not the same game. It feels shorter than its predecessor and there's just not as much going on. The "floors" or levels of each chapter are very formulaic in their design with nearly identical enemies each time; first there's a classic dungeon crawl, then there's a "race to the finish" and then you have a brawl to kill the enemy spawners. And the final floor is always a boss fight. A lot of the replay value will be from increasing the difficulty and challenging yourself and your friends.
This review may make the game sound unappealing, but it's pretty fantastic for what it is, which is a $20 reboot of a classic game. It has its flaws, but it also has its own charms which shouldn't be overlooked. For those of you who just want a way to spend some time online with friends and have a good time killing monsters, it's a relatively cheap pick-up and worth its price.

A dissapointment compared to the Dark Legacy game, I expected a lot more from Gauntlet 2014. It's really short, containing 3 different areas. Each area includes 4 levels that rehashes the same map per the area you are in. The first area of a level introduces you to a map, the second level makes you play the first map again, the third level of the map is an arena and the last level of any given area is just the boss fight.
There is no longer any character progression in the game. Things like buying new weapons, armor, magic or just upgrading your character at all with money is gone and replaced with an achievement system that gives you extra stats automatically. This really just boils the game down into one long grinding session since the game is so short there really doesn't even need to be an upgrade system.
All weapons and armor are purely cosmetic which is also locked behind an achievement wall.
The game took me about 2 days to finish and the length is about 3-4 hours long. I think the main reason for why I didn't like this game was how short it was. Dark Legacy had much much more content that made upgrading your character a satisfying experience for me. It was fun starting off really weak and then at the end of the game turning into an unstoppable killing machine so when Gauntlet 2014 ended up being a top-down beatem up game, I got dissapointed. Fun gameplay, but it gets repetitive fast.
Your character never gets stronger beyond slight "perks" that all fall along the lines of "+10% damage to spiders", which isn't at all interesting.
The only thing to spend gold on are cosmetic armor/weapons which are expensive and don't even look that great or different, or relics, which you can only use maybe 2 or 3 times per level because they run off of potions, which are rare, accidentally destroyable, and you have to compete for them with the other players.
Fights are mostly easy but unforgiving. You'll find yourself breezing through everything up until you make one little mistake and lose half your health to one attack from one of the weaker monsters. The traps are all the same spick pits, and easily avoidable. Even Death himself is a complete joke that chases you at a snail's pace for a few seconds before despawning. The only way to die to him is to afk.
Class balance is horrible. The wizard is the most dificult, but also most interesting to play, due to his spellcasting mechanic. But no matter how well you play him, the valkyrie spamming left and right click next to you completely outclassing you is quite depressing. The wizard also makes all the other classes looked half-baked. The wizard has 9 unique and interesting spells, while every other class has only 4 attacks.
All in all, it was fun at first, but the terribly repetitive gameplay and total lack of content killed this one for me. It would make sense as maybe a $5 title, but I can't justify the $20 I spent on it.

Post Release Update: With the last few Early Access patches I had become sceptical wether the scope of the project hadn't overwhelmed Tt. Gameplay features were added, but they felt tacked on and not successful at all.
Enter patch 1.0 - what a difference. The game now has a proper setting where you hop from planet to planet in your spaceship. This makes "save" management much less of a chore. You have an objective: Collect gold bricks to upgrade your ship, gain special items and become a master builder. These gold bricks can be gained by helping out friendly NPCs in many different ways, finding treasure, and catching a new type of enemy that just runs away. Some of these NPC quests designate an area where you then are supposed to build a structure, sometimes using specific parts. This gives building a well integrated purpose and jumpstarts your creativity if you don't quite know what to build.
The selection of availiable bricks is much better than before and enough for most of what you would want to do.
The presentation has been upgraded more than a notch for sure: The soundtrack has always been good, but now it features a good amount of variety. It also is a good listen for studying and work. The new spaceship that gets you from planet to planet is plain adorable and the initial player characters work much better than the generic explorers. They are now space girl and an astronaut with the copper visor. A new narrator helps you through the initial learning steps without being annoying. Great voice, and although the intructions are clearly intended to work even with younger kids, they don't get overbearing.
Now, not all is perfectly well for sure. Bugs exist and can be quite annoying, fortunately none of the ones I experienced are gamebreaking and can be fixed by either resetting your position with a skydive or reloading the save.
While there is a lot more to do than initially, the main feature of the game is still building, and if you aren't interested in that for various reasons the game is certainly not for you.
The progression system gates bricks and parts, so you do have to go through the exploration stuff to be able to build what you want - this is only an issue if you want to play 'legit', though, as there are cheatcodes in this game. In 2017!
The building itself can be odd at times. I play with a controller (both X-Box 360 and Steam work well, although the Steam controller isn't supported as well as it could be), so that could be a part of it, but overall it is still much less intuitive than Minecraft. For more on this, look into the old part of this review I made on the initial Early Access version, not much has changed here.
I also heard of some motion-sickness concerns, which haven't affected me, but whom you should be weary of if you have a disposition for it.
The game is as close to the perfect LEGO videogame you can get. Now that it introduced proper objectives and made discovery very fun, it reminds me a lot of the vision the developers of the first LEGO game, LEGO Island, had, but couldn't quite realize with 1998s technology. Some things I'd like to see to bring it to perfection aren't there, like vehicle building akin to earlier LEGO Racers games, since building vehicles is one of the core aspects of what you can do with physical LEGO.
I can recommend this game, as I enjoy it greatly after the release patch. Be aware of bugs, this is not a perfectly polished product and consider that if you don't enjoy building, there isn't that much more to the game to still justify it.
Old stuff starts here, read if you want to see where the game has come from, some of it is still relevant, too:
[Disclaimer: This game is in early access and clearly not finished! It may not even run properly on your machine (AMD CPUs are at this point apearently not supported too well). You should not buy any early access games if that bothers you. It may also lessen the fun you will have when the game finally comes out, as you may be tired of it.
So that out of the I have to say that this game amazes me. This really is the video game that captures the spirit of lego perfectly. It marries the procedually generated worlds that made Minecraft special with the lightheartedness of the worlds favourite toys. The worlds just look fantastic.
It is obvious that this game was heavily inspired by Mojangs smash-hit, but it deviates from the formula in all the right places. There is no survival here. Weapons and other objects are found in structures around the world, so no crafting in that sense either. Instead of first person the game uses the classic Tt lego game third person. Building is done very differently as well. You pretty much switch to an editor view, which is very powerfull, but also no where near as intuitive as Minecrafts building is. You can achieve a lot more, but it is also going to be harder.
Thankfully you also have the ability to put prebuild structures into the game. These have 3 categories: Sets, Brickbuilds, and Props. Props are prebuild small anythings that range from foliage to lamps and a barbeque. Some of them can be interacted with, which results in some good old lego game humor. Sets are actual lego sets that are availiable for purchase. So far there only is one of them, which essentially is a (nice looking) collection of props. Brickbuilds is where it really shines. There are a bit more than 50 buildings already in the game. Most of these are pretty goofy with things like a gingerbread house, the Tt Games logo or some random pixel (bricksel?) art, but there also are two really nice houses. The truly amazing thing about this category however is that you can import your own builds from Lego Digital Designer. This is incredible for building big structures like houses, or things that you will need often, like tables chairs and other pieces of furniture.
There also is a good terrain editor in the game. It is intuitive and produces great results.
The gameplay and combat in particular is pretty much what you know from Tt Games lego games. It is not very deep, but fun and sufficient for this game, where the focus clearly is on building things. (It also definitly is an upgrade over minecrafts cardboard-waving combat.)
There also are some problems. Obviously there still are a lot of features missing. Those include multiplayer, meaningfull interaction with NPCs, a ton of lego bricks (DOORS!) and many other things you could wish for. As this is early access these things will change. The camera can be terrible, especially when building underground or driving a vehicle in small spaces. Building brick by brick is flawed, but you have Digital Designer for that.
In conclusion I say that this game has huge potential. The randomly generated terrain alone is fascinating. Add to that the ability to pretty much build anything you want and you have a true lego experience. Another thing that made a positive impression on me is the balance between male and female characters, which are all pretty likeable. If you just want an infinite box of lego you can buy this game right now and will not have regrets. If you are focussed on game mechanics you should not, as at this point there really is not a lot you can do.
Now if you will excuse me, I have to dig a cave using my bazooka, have a nice day!]

Skulls. Girls. Girls decorated with skulls, parasites, and mutations.
Not much more to ask for, and yet Skullgirls delivers that and further still as the months go by.
The game has an amazing cast of characters; each of them being their own unique monstrosity in some way shape or form and an interesting story following them-- sometimes even an emotional story. The character designs are well-thought-out and very unique, and their voices are very well picked for the personalities they're meant to reflect. It didn't take long for neither myself nor those getting into this game alongside me to get hooked on the game simply out of interest in the characters.
The world and backstory dynamics are also quick to get interested in, albeit they're only touched on briefly in each story. A corrupted area run by a corrupt mafia, and those negatively affected by their actions are looking to fight back-- each through different means and thus pitting against each other by virtue of their conflicting motivations. But is that really all there is behind the story? I heavily suggest playing to find out.
The music is brilliant and captures the atmosphere of each stage incredibly well, though it comes as no surprise given the composer-- Michiru Yamane-- and their past works in larger franchises. The Castlevania vibes in the soundtrack are hard to miss in certain tracks, but it if anything that nostalgic feeling conveyed is praiseworthy.
The main con I can think of is the disappointment that comes from short length of each character's story, but as more characters are released more parts of the story become available, making the game a strong long-term investment and and a great means of mindless  short-term fun in the meantime.

After reading so many negative reviews of this game and finding that I still enjoy it, I would like to add to my comments made earlier.
Do not buy this game if you want a high intensity, "shoot em up," competitive, action game.  You will not like it.  The game plods along as you explore various star systems, planets, and the aliens who inhabit them. I find that once I start the game it is difficult to stop because there is always one more planet to explore or something unknown on the otherside of a mountain.  And, no, I have never encountered any evidence of another human player in all of my hours of exploration.
I work in an Emergency Room and I find the game play an immersing and relaxing break from my work place.  I also enjoy trekking, travel, science, and reading about the same.  The game is not The Voyage of the Beagle, but it has many of the same qualities that would have attracted Darwin to work as he did on that exploration of a world unknow to Europe in the 1800's.
This game obviously caters to a small audience.  I would strongly suggest you try it out on a friend's system before purchasing it.  I would further suggest that you have a robust system to play it with a robust graphics card to handle it.  Based on the reviews, though, this is definitely NOT a game for a very large portion of the gaming population on Steam.

A turn based, tactical, coop RPG with a very old-school feeling to it. There's no handholding, and subsequently you're offered a lot of freedom. While there's surely an 'optimal' path to take, you can generally approach things however you like and do things super out of order. As the game never really tells you "GO HERE!" with a giant objective marker (like in most RPGs nowadays), you must read the dialogue and quest logs to figure out where to go next. It's a refreshing change of pace, actually playing the game for yourself and figuring out things as you go, and it's very rewarding, especially when you finally figure some of the trickier things out.
This freedom extends to your characters as well, where there are no classes and anyone can spec into whatever they want, and even into multiple different skills at once. You can get some really crazy combinations of skills and abilities, that really make the combat a blast to play. There's a huge amount of depth to it all, that will leave you figuring out new stuff even after playing for 100 hours. My only complaint in this is that the respec system is extremely punishing and only comes around very near the end of the game, so if you mis-spec somewhere down the line (and you typically will), you've pretty much wasted those points for good unless you can justify the cost and hasstle of respeccing.
The overarcing story can be a bit difficult to follow at times (and the confusing mess of a quest log certainly doesn't help), but the writing is generally very entertaining, with a nice quirky sense of humour, and the newly added voice overs make sitting through the absolute metric ton of dialogue much more bearable.
If you can find a friend to play this with: do it! Coop is certainly the way this was meant to be played, and it's got to be one of the best damn coop games I've ever played.
I have 160 hours between this enhanced edition and the original version of the game, and even wouldn't mind playing it again. There's a good deal of replayability, not only by trying out new character builds, but also by picking different companion characters and quest options--not to mention the numerous side quests I probably missed, be it by not having the prerequisite skills, by killing some character vital to a quest, or just simply by running along and never finding them.
There are certainly some annoying bugs in this game, but given the scope and level of freedom it gives the player, it's completely understandable and does not detract from the game in any way. Definitely recommend grabbing this one, just be warned of the game's length--a single playthrough took me 80 hours!
Also, can't help but mention this somewhere: The music is awesome! Go look up "battle theme 6" on Youtube, and you'll see what I mean. RIP Kirill Pokrovsky (composer).

Divinity: Original Sin seems impenetrable from an outside perspective; and naturally so. Hotbars, action points, taking turns: these are some of the staples of classical RPGs that the industry has left behind for a more streamlined audience. If you've played a Bioware game (of Mass Effect and Dragon Age fame) in recent years; you've seen the classical RPG stripped down into linear systems that have attracted a new cult fanbase.
Divinity is best played cooperatively with a like-minded friend; who I am extremely lucky enough to have. Quests, dialogue, combat, puzzles, the list goes on; can all be experienced with an ally at hand. This is a game where you are constantly communicating with your partner on what to do, how to proceed, and why they just killed your character for the 15th time with a meteor strike -- it's all there. There are no quest markers telling you where to go, which is a fantastic way of breeding organic conversation between players.
Of course this doesn't come with some heavy faults. The initial quest is a murder mystery; and although this is my personal favorite questline due to the level of freedom it provides; many will find this overwhelming. There isn't too much handholding in this game, so being intimidated by little to no direction is common. Alongside the dense questing system, there are quite a few layers to the user interface. To players new to the genre: adding stats upon levelling up feels like deciphering an archiac language and navigating through menus feels like a chore.
All user-interface and non-handholding aside: this is an incredible game for a good pair of people to play. Every combat encounter feels like you and your partner against the developers. Divinity constantly challenges the two of you to push past punishing and hazardous environments that can swing battles into your favor with the right level of creativity and communication. Find a good friend, and be prepared for a game that you can't find anywhere else these days.

I wanted to love this game.  After playing games like "Brothers," this was suggested to me.  I was ready for the experience.  But in the end, with a ton of games in my stable and decades of gaming, I ended up just dropping it - unable to motivate myself to play any longer.  Here's why.
I love adventure games but I don't get why people love old school graphics. I grew up with Kings Quest, Ultima etc. and despite getting nostalgic for those classics, why would I want to play on sucky looking games?  So really I found the unatractiveness of the presentation a real bore.  Some peole love that stuff and if that's you, get this game and have a cry.  I just don't see the point in this day and age.  By all means give me a game with the meaning and the feelies, but tell me a great story with at least some decent presentation please!
But it's not just the graphics.  It's the gameplay.  Again, as an experienced adventure gamer who even used to play text based adventures like Zork and Wishbringer, I didn't mind it in the 80's but it's not like I want to play them again.  Fetch quests get dull after a while no matter what.  Adventure games need a emotional/psychological pay-off with every completed task to motivate the player.  This one, for me, doesn't have enough.
There are a lot of admirable adventure games old and new.  They might not all have the poignant subject matter of "To the Moon" but I prefer something that not only has a good story but decent graphics and good game mecahnics as well.  So, I just can't finish this one because I find it tedious. Alternatives: The Longest Journey, Grim Fandango, Syberia, Machinarium.

First of all, I never played F.E.A.R 2, but thanks to Google, I knew what happened as far as the plot is concerned. Gameplay wise, I would have to pass.

The scares were freaky at best, with little fright value as compared to the first game. Remember the part where Alma was waiting at the top of the ladder? Yeah, nothing like that here. Although the sense of vulnerability is still present, much thanks to the survival horror themed inventory system. As for the enemies, well, they are fairly challenging, especially those high up in the ranks. Boss fights are straightforward, so nothing big about that.

I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone who's never played any F.E.A.R title just yet. As for those who follow the franchise, well try to keep your expectations low.

Skullgirls is an interestingly designed fighting game that will surely please newcomers to fighters and older experts too. Despite the name "Skullgirls", not every character is female, because that title ties in with the story. An artifact called the Skull Heart grants the wishes of a woman, but often curses them to be a powerful being called a Skullgirl. Right off the bat, Skullgirls has a stylized art deco or 1920-40 movie look evident in the game's menus and UI. The backgrounds are nicely drawn and do fit in with the deco style. The main artistic draw of this game is that each fighter's sprite is hand drawn with many frames, leading to a great looking and well animated feel when playing. There does tend to be lots of shots showcasing some fighters' busts or panties, but putting that aside, it's very easy to appreciate the animation quality with lots of frames and unique character design in Skullgirls. The music for this game tends to be jazz oriented to tie in with the graphical style of the game, although it does veer off to other kinds of genres when the situation arises. The songs in the game sound nice and help cement the art deco style by putting music that somewhat ties in to the early to mid 1900s. Again, not all songs are strictly jazz, as there are some different genre styles that break things up from being too consistent and give more variety.
The core fighting gameplay of Skullgirls is inspired by Marvel vs. Capcom 2, but it can also be likened to Street Fighter or Capcom's Vs. Series. There are 6 buttons of punches and kicks like in Street Fighter, but there is a chain system for normals to automatically combo into each other like in the Vs. Series. There are also super combos that can deal lots of damage and be used to end a combo. Teams can be formed of 1, 2, or 3, characters. Assists are available for 2 or 3 character teams. Special features that expert players will enjoy are the infinite combo prevention system and an anti unblockable move mechanic, which solves some issues that fighting games have.
For new players, Skullgirls has a robust tutorial that teaches the basics of fighting games and some Skullgirls based mechanics. Doing the tutorial is highly recommended as it teaches so many useful things seen in other fighting games along with introducing the gameplay style of Skullgirls. The tutorial is a bit long winded with lots of text and can take a while to do, and there are some fairly tricky combos that new players might have trouble doing. Fortunately, this game's combo system is a bit easier than some other games that require stricter timing.
With a unique style that the game and characters have and a simple yet robust fighting system, Skullgirls will please both new and old fighter players. Some are allured by the game's style while others may be drawn to the gameplay system. Whatever the case, Skullgirls is a solid fighting game that is well designed in its gameplay and style.

When Game Dev Tycoon originally came out, it was probably the first major release of it's type on the PC (in USA at least). It was met with praise and disappointment - it had enough charm, content, challenge and clean interface to get players attention, but didn't provide enough feedback to players into why a game would succeed or fail, making it a long shot for anybody to figure out how to make a good game, outside of memorizing patterns and consulting wiki pages.
Greenheart games has fixed this issue with a Research ability, allowing the player to research why their games recieved the score that they did. This fixed my number one issue with GDT, making it easy to recommend to anybody who has a remote interest in this genre or idea of "a tycoon game about making games".
Unfortunately, this game has one seriously stupid problem - performance. How a game with 2D Flash/HTML 5 graphics at best can slow down even the heartiest machines to sub 60, 50, even 40 FPS is almost beyond me - I only can assume there are tons of calculations slowing the game down when alot of actions are happening (research, hardware development, staff working)
There is also mod support which allows mods that can add more platforms and topics, or the timeframe in which certain consoles release. There are even UI mods. The screen space could be better used and more information could be available from various menus, so mods are very helpful in this regard.
Game Dev Tycoon was a nice game with issues, but is significantly better. I was going to say this game earns the Overwhelmingly Positive reviews, until I had the performance issues. Otherwise,  This is the premier game development tycoon game on PC.

A must have game for any strategy lovers.

Reus is an enjoyable little strategy/puzzle game. You know how the Civilization games let you build improvements on the land around your cities, like irrigation, roads, farms, etc.? Reus takes that mechanic and expands it into a full game. You'll have to weigh the pros and cons of each resource you place in order to make the best use of the limited land available to your villages.
You progress through the game largely by completing achievement-style objectives within the game's time limits. These are well designed for the most part and encourage you to create interesting scenarios in your worlds, like creating a massive harbor town or maintaining a balanced war between villages to power them up without wiping each other out. The art style of the game is definitely visually appealing and it's enjoyable to see how your villages change visually as they grow around your decisions.
If you like god games, city builders, and the like, check out Reus.

Hi.  My name is Amber_Rose, and I am a SHK addict.  (Say "Hi Amber_Rose!")  I've been playing for almost four years.  I do sometimes get irritated with the game, and it often seems like a full-time job, but I've never seriously considered leaving it.  Yes, it has flaws.  Yes, it requires a lot of dedication.  But it has aspects that draw you back to it.  It's highly complex and can take years to master.  It has quirks that you learn to work around.  But it also has a great group of dedicated players from all over the world, and the opportunity to get to know people in a remarkably personal way.
I've read a lot of complaints here about it being 'pay to play'.  But many of the best players I know spend very little (if anything) to play.  It's not a game for people who buy an Xbox game and expect to master it in a week.  It rewards you for sticking with it.
I've experienced great success in the game, and I've experienced monumental failures.  I've made serious enemies who have threatened to find me in real life, and I've made lifelong friends.  I've seen people disappear from the game for years only to suddenly return.  Every day brings  something new.  In some ways it's changed my life.  And my knowledge of the geography of Europe has improved tremendously!
So if you're looking for some amusement on a boring day, don't consider this game.  But if you're someone who has the time and inclination to immerse themselves in a virtual world with like-minded people, by all means try it.

"No Man’s Sky had a controversial launch to say the least.
The game was heavily anticipated by PC and PlayStation 4 gamers alike, with space-sim and survival fans eager to experience more of the supposedly ground-breaking procedurally-generated universe.
However, the game which players received at launch is undeniably different to the version showcased leading up to release, and this has caused furious debate among the game’s passionate fan base.
While some have vigorously defended the title, many gamers have said they feel cheated by the developers. The biggest issue over which all of this conflict has arisen is the game’s multiplayer – or lack thereof.
There is no evidence that No Man’s Sky has any online features beyond the sharing of discoveries such as planets, despite Sean Murray stating during development that players will be able to see and interact with each other.
Amidst all this controversy and arguing, a Reddit user has managed to compile a list of features that were shown in the game’s marketing material but did not appear in the actual game.
The list was reviewed by thousands of people, who all provided evidence in order to verify the missing features.
The original list is very long and has become very specific, so we have collected the biggest confirmed missing features in the game, along with evidence of the features appearing in the game’s marketing material.
Check out the list of features missing from No Man’s Sky below:
Miscellaneous Space Gameplay and Elements
Landing on asteroids – “Yeah, at the moment you can land on asteroids.”
Destroying space stations and fleets – “You take out a space station, or a fleet, or you know, something like that…”
Giant fleets of ships
Large Freighters actually moving
NPC Interaction
Faction affiliations with significance – “Different races have different attributes […] and depending on how I’m playing, I might want to kinda make an allegiance with one or [an]other.”
Trade ships docking with freighters
Large-scale, join-able space battles between factions – “Like here, we’re at the battle between two warring factions. I could join in, I could take sides.”
In-atmosphere freighters
Planets and Stars
Sand Planets
Planets rotating and orbiting
Flying between star systems manually – “Yes, but nobody’s actually done it yet…”
Ships and Flight
Ship Classes and differentiation
Naming Ships – “Ships are actually a discovery just like everything else, and you can name your discoveries”
Natural flight characteristics
Trade and Crafting
Environmental factors affect resources – “Planets that are further from the sun have certain types of resources, planets that are closer have certain types of resources, or planets that have certain environments.”
Complex crafting – “When we release the game, we’re not telling people ‘here are all the formulas,’ we’re just letting players loose, and a little bit like minecraft people can figure out those rules themselves…”
Planetary Surface
Rivers
Crashed freighters
Portals
Sentinels
Sentinels in large packs
Maintaining wanted level indoors
Ambient Walker Sentinels
General gameplay
Seeing and interacting with other players
Beacons marking points of interest
Hacking reinforced doors – “Well normally what you would do is you would hack it, that would be the best way.”
Radio chatter
Transparent glass windshield"

What can I say about F.E.A.R 3? Quite obviously, It's the 3rd game in the F.E.A.R franchise, which, one would expect, would say everything. But in all honesty, it doesn't - in fact, the third installment of the F.E.A.R franchise is much more akin to the generic first person shooter than the trouser-browning horror shooter that the F.E.A.R name is otherwise known for.
The gameplay is, to put it in one word, generic. You have guns, they go bang, there are a LOT of enemies to shoot with them, same old. However, the genericness is tempered slightly with a very nice cover system, the slow-mo mechanic which is a mainstay of the F.E.A.R franchise, and the occasional creepy moment, though undoubtedly nothing as trouser-wetting as the previous games in the series, which I have admittedly not actually played a lot of. There is also some geo-mod, but this is needless and hinders more than it helps. However, the game is still relatively fun despite the genericness and shortcomings.
The story is confusing. Whilst playing through the game I had little idea of what was actually going on, but from what I could gather, Alma, the creepy little F.E.A.R mainstay, has become pregnant for whatever reason, and the main character, the "Point Man" and his brother Paxton Fettel, who was killed in F.E.A.R 1 and who has somehow returned, have to find her and... well, Fettel wants to eat the child and Point Man wants to destroy it. That's as much as I could gather.
The game takes about 6 to 7 hours to beat, though this is somewhat artificially extended by the game's difficulty. I was playing on "Commando" (Normal) difficulty, and some areas of the game were heavily confusing and others were incredibly difficult, particularly one section where I had to defeat a massive mech which could kill me in a few shots and tear any cover you might choose to use to pieces, and also another where I was attacked by TWO of the most annoying enemy in the game, which needless to say was frustrating.
To summarise, F.E.A.R 3 is generic, difficult, short, confusing and has stupidly large numbers of incredibly annoying enemies. FEAR 3 (or "F.3.A.R." if you are so inclined) is an odd game. It's a horror FPS with a coop campaign, that grades you on play time and CoD style challenges. None of those things are exactly helpful when trying to establish a scary atmosphere. However, this doesn't stop the game from being an immensely fun shooter on it's own terms. All the important parts like weapon feel, movement, AI and enemy variety are solidly executed.
If that would have been it, I would probably have played through the game in single player mode once and left it at that. The reason however for why I keep returning to this entry into the series and not the others, is the totally unique, totally awesome Paxton Fettel ghost mode. Using the (un)dead brother's ghost abilities feels just as satisfying as pulling of a really cool slow-motion moment, except with a much higher frequency. Possessing enemies across the map, shooting their squadmates and then bursting out of your unfortunate host practically never gets old. Why none of this gets unlocked for single player before beating the campaign once is beyond me.
As much as FEAR 3 is the sequel, that nobody asked for, it's quite an underrated game. If you don't actually care about the story in FEAR and are looking for an, in many ways, unique shooter, I recommend it.

Excellent independent game! If you're a fan of Final Fantasy, Golden Sun or any other RPG along those lines, you'll find plenty of things to like here.
Its a fairly simple system in terms of skills and weapons. Find the right materials and you can forge your equipment to be better. Higher level equipment requires rarer items. After winning a battle you get ability points which you can spend towards spells and skills. Higher levels need more ability points and so on. This is in addition to a standard leveling system (get exp and level up).
The skill and equipment sets feel very well thought out. No one skill or item is designated as "crap" each feels like its part of one option for strategy, and I can say you will probably use every piece of equipment at one point or another. Another cool touch is that each item shows up on the characters both in battle and outside. It's a nice little touch.
The story is also simple to follow, but its almost like a parody of the traditional RPG plot. It doesn't take itself seriously at many points, yet still keeps you somewhat invested in fighting the big bad guy at the end. There are references galore to other RPG's and internet stuff among other things, and its just a straight up fun ride.
Finally, the music kicks♥♥♥♥♥ That's all I have to say about that.
And this was made by one guy who made flash games in the past.  While the price might be a little off putting to some, buy this to help support the guy. Plus he threw in some extra content exclusive to Steam, so its a pretty good deal.

I am even more impressed now that not only do I have the pleasure of being able to play this game for free as a result of that, since they sent me a steam key for this game, but this version is even better. I was a rank 69 on Deluxe and I already know I'm going to get much higher than that on this game because it wasn't a simple remaster, but there were many other things that were changed as well, and I believe they were all for the better.
First off, right from the beginning, the title screen has been completely redesigned with all the deluxe upgrades being split up into two different categories. They are small percentile bonuses that you can increase as you get more tokens. Tokens are unlocked by playing each track and higher difficulties yield more tokens.
In addition to the redesigned upgrade system, there are new tracks, towers, and even new special agents. There just appears to be something new everywhere. It's really quite surprising. To top it all off, seeing all the remastered tracks after playing the Deluxe version so much is really a treat. They really did a fantastic job on remastering these tracks. I recommend this game completely. 10/10

A lot of wasted potential, but if it's available on sale (I bought it for -75%), it's definitely worth it. Don't even bother to purchase it at full price. It won't be as good as Train Simulator or Train Sim World, but has several strong elements that can make it interesting. Nevertheless I cannot fully recommend it - I will still play it, but would definitely never buy it for the standard price and I will not buy any DLCs as those seem overpriced too. As the week long deal ends in less than 24 hours and the review will be here after that, I don't want anyone to get a wrong impression about this game's price-to-quality ratio which is really poor. For more details, read the full review of what works and what doesn't below:
Note that I only have it for a couple of days and I have no optimization problems. I don't know how it's been in the past but it seems all right now.
1. A lot of different goods and great ability to customize what you're carrying. You can easily set up a route where you can take whatever you want - coal (and A LOT OF different variations of it), cattle, general goods, fruit, vegetables, fertilizers, cement, cars, almost anything you want, and you can even customize how much to take. There are also industries that produce goods or need them which is a very nice touch.
2. Making routes and different sessions is insanely easy and offers a lot of customization.
3. Routes available for the base price are really nice - you get Australian route from the 1910s - I don't recally any TS route from this period which is a shame, a 1950s American one which is great too, and probably the best one - 1970s British route that covers the ENTIRE route from London to Edinburgh - almost 400 miles. I don't think there's any route for TS that even compares to that. Those tend to be a lot too short unfortunately.
4. There are a lot of great routes and assets available online and there is no problem with dependencies - download center checks what you'll need and downloads it. But at the same time, don't expect top notch quality - many of them are pretty dated. What I liked the most are old routes that Train Simulator lacks - England, France and Silesia from the 1930s and 1940s wartime Germany.
5. Performance is really good and there are three performance presets that you can change on the fly to find what works best for you. It worked pretty well for me.
6. Free Internal Camera - it feels almost as if you're walking around the train like in Train Sim World.
1. First class tickets. You will need one to download community made routes (otherwise downloading is capped at 10 kb/s, and most of the time around 9 kb/s) and it costs as much as $7.49 for 30 days or $26.99 for the whole year now. FOR SHAME!
2. Graphics are way worse than TS ones and way way worse than Train Sim World. Even no moving passengers waiting for you at the station. Just static figures. Kinda breaks the immersion for me.
3. There are very few DLCs and those are worse than TS ones.
4. TS has a much better GUI.
5. It lacks quick drive feature of TS - you can't just set time, season, and weather and drive enjoying AI traffic and in the world that feels alive. You have to either set everything manually or download a session, and those are really hard to find. AI schedule for the London-Edinburgh route I downloaded failed to show up in the game's menu.
6. One that was already mentioned a few times - asking price. Train Simulator 2017 is cheaper and at the same time much better than TANE. I'm sorry but this is the main reason why I cannot recommend this game. It's price-to-value ratio is poor to put it midly and DLCs are no different.
7. Steam train physics and handling are worse than TS's.

I had this game for quite a while, sitting quietly in my Steam library, and hadn't played it despite all the good things I'd heard about it.  I had played A Bird Story already, and it was absolutely wonderful, so I thought I'd spend a quiet rainy night with 'To the Moon.'
Five hours later - I've finished the game and -  wow, just wow.  "To the Moon' has instantly moved to the top of my games list.  I've been playing games since I was a small child, and nothing I've ever come across has affected me quite so deeply as the story in To the Moon.
This is an almost entirely story-driven game, so be warned that if you're looking for high end graphics or action, you're barking up the wrong tree.  However, if you can overlook the clunky controls and RPGMaker graphics, you'll find yourself engrossed and entranced by (in my opinion, at least) one of the best video game stories ever written.  To the Moon spans the entire lifetime of a man who, at the end of his life and with the help of a research company, wants to experience travelling to the moon.  Without giving too much away, the story quickly becomes far more complicated, with every new detail leaving you wanting to play more just so you can see how the tale unfolds ... and quite a wonderful and enchanting tale it is.  The dialogue is so well written that you actually feel the characters in the story come to life in your mind, and by the end of the story you truly feel what each is going through, and ultimately understand their motives and ... well ... their reason for being.
Along with the amazing story, the player is also treated to a delightful soundtrack, both enchanting and haunting, that makes this game worth the price of admission on its own merits.  I highly suggest purchasing the soundtrack along with the game - you're going to want to listen to it over and over again.
In conclusion - I can't speak highly enough of 'To the Moon'.  If it's sitting in your Steam library gathering dust you need to brush it off and give it an evening - you're going to love it.  If you don't own it yet, it's worth every penny at full price (and then some), and once you've finished the game, I can almost guarantee that you're going to be recommending it to everyone you know.  Yes ... it's that good.
10/10  This is a must play game for fans of story-driven games. :)

It's a very linear game, with little scope for failing or getting stuck.  If anything, this adds to the charm.  You play as visitors to someone else's life, taking part at arm's length, out of danger.  The lack of peril means that you can concentrate on the story, which is quite spectacular and emotional.  Make sure you don't read about it before playing through; experience it yourself.

I bought this game on steam daily sale after I'd had a few drinks. Not my best purchase. I normally don't play games in this style. To The Moon is a retro, jrpg style indie game that is completely story driven, all three of which (retro, jrpg style, story driven) I usually stay away from, so I was surprised it engaged me so. Even though I couldn't put it down for the 3ish hours it takes to complete, I do feel it's extremely overrated and only ok. Here's my thoughts.
First the easy part to critique, the gameplay. The gameplay sucks. You're viewing your characters in top down jrpg style like an old final fantasy game but you move by clicking the mouse and then you have to click items but the controls are finicky. You'll be clicking an item and sometimes your guy moves there, sometimes he won't. It just doesn't work right. Then a lot of it is repetitive and cumbersome when really you just want to get through to the next part of the story. The gameplay is a hindrance in most cases. Also it's not consistent at all. Some chapters you do a lot of clicking and searching then other ones are full out cutscenes with zero gameplay. I don't understand it.
Second the presentation. The graphics are fine for what it's supposed to be, though I don't get all nostalgic for old school 16 bit graphics. I think this game could've be way better with something new and fresh like hand drawn flash animation or cartoon stylized. But the devs made their choice and it's good within its limits. But my issues with the presentation are this story makes so much more sense as a book or a movie. The story tries to get emotional and make you feel empathy and invested in characters but being a video game it just can't develop. I really appreciate developers trying to push boundaries of gaming and I'm fascinated by the philosophical discussion of narratives and art form in video games, and this one tries very heroically but ultimately fails for me. If it was a book that had more time to flesh out relationships and personalities or a movie that had actors to impress those upon the viewer I think it would work. Reading 16 bit dialogue though leaves something lacking for me.
That's why I don't understand the reviews that say this game is a masterpiece, it's so evocative, it made me cry. I'm like really? So a couple 16 bit characters sharing 30 lines of typed dialogue is enough to establish an emotional connection for you? I think you need to get out into the real world more. The story is kind of like the movie inception where this company can change your memories the moment before you die so you can have the life you've always wanted in your mind and die happy. It follows these two scientist employees who are trying to help this old guy rewrite his memories to go to the moon, his dying wish.
I also had serious issues with the story once I thought about it in depth a bit. The whole point was that his bonds with River were so strong that she remained in his mind even when removed, that he would do anything to be with her. Just like how he wanted to go to the moon in the first place even though he couldn't remember exactly why. And in the end they hold hands as they reach the moon and he dies. Ok, fine, so he loved her a lot and his love conquered all except it really didn't because the whole freakin thing was IN HIS HEAD. River is still dead, she still chose building the house over the treatment and left him. He still had a ton of pain in his life, but it's supposed to be all ok because he doesn't remember it? That's what I don't like at all, how our imposed virtual reality now trumps what actually happened. Although I guess maybe the devs were doing this on purpose to push the question of what is reality and is it only in the mind and memories? I appreciate the question but the story felt more like the point was , aww look how much he loved her and now everything's alright, and I just didn't feel that way. She still chose to build the house and die. They never actually met on the moon.
The music I also had issues with. Not because it's bad, cus it's not, it's quite good. It's beautifully simplistic and I enjoyed it as background video game music. It fits the story and mood well. But reviews rave about it like it's a Beethoven symphony. It's not that great or talented, and the one with lyrics was borderline emo rocker ballad. I feel like this generation doesn't know what great music is anymore. The music fits the game well and is good, but it's still extremely overrated.
Overall overrated game experience. If the game moves you to tears I feel like you should have a serious discussion with yourself over why. Did you relate to a specific part of the game? Did some of what's in it happen to you in real life? Because that I can understand but otherwise I think those with that kind of response are overreaching because the want to feel a connection to something. There's far better, deeper game stories out there with better characters to feel connection to than these.
Graphics: 6/10. They're retro 16 bit style and not supposed to be great but I still rate them poor because I think so much more could've been done here.
Music: 8/10. It is good. Just not groundbreaking as claimed.
Gameplay: 1/10. Clunky. Just there so it can be called a game and not a digital novel/movie. Gets in the way of the story imo.
Story and writing: 6/10. Some of the dialogue is clever and the story is fine but the medium fails to tell it well enough for me and it is predictable. Nothing special.
Overall: 5/10
Still I'm glad I played it because it was an experience, even if not a great one.

So To the Moon is one of those games that seemed to have a pretty unanimously positive customer perspective.  The reviews of this game cumulate at a very high rating, noting that it's "simple...full of heart", "absolutely beautiful", and as put by Eurogamer: "How do I explain why it's brilliant without spoiling what makes it so?"  The conclusion that can be drawn from these reviews is that To the Moon is a touching story game with little actual gameplay (since the actual gameplay isn't mentioned anywhere).  OH BOY.  Regardless, I had played some games like that before and I had actually enjoyed them, so I grabbed this at a low price and decided to complete it.  My conclusion after beating it:
To the Moon is an absolutely awful game that I believe would have been much more interesting had it been made in to a graphic novel or animated film.  The few game elements that exist are very poorly executed.  Movement itself can be frustrating and glitchy when using a mouse (I frequently found my character not responding as I expected when clicking where I wanted him to go, and at one point I had managed to walk in to the clouds and I could not get down), the search quests are horrid, and all of the other 'minigames' are trivial and completely out of place.  So, if the bare-bones gameplay elements are minimal and poorly-executed, why bother making this a game at all?  You spend most of your time clicking through conversations anyway; does that make things any more interesting?  I don't think it does at all, and by the end of the 4th hour I was completely overwhelmed at how tiring To the Moon was.  I can't believe that a GAME reviewed by GAME CRITICS recieved such high ratings for nothing other than its PLOT when the GAMEPLAY was this horrid.
Now I don't think anyone beat To the Moon and said to his or herself: "To the Moon was one of the most invigorating gameplay experience of the past year" or anything close to that, so the game was made great by the story (as shown by other reviewers).  Now I must admit that through most of the game I was very touched by the events that transpired; I will reluctantly admit that I teared up at a few moments.  The journey to the end, in terms of plot, was very respectable and  despite the childish "charm" of all the characters and the "click through the words" cutscenes I managed to actually enjoy that particular element.  I would never have given the game a 10/10, but perhaps a 6/7/8.  That was until I beat the damn thing
(SPOILERS BELOW)
To the Moon's story fails in how it wraps up the tale that it tells. You essentially spend the entire game re-living various aspects of a man's life in order to determine why he wants to go to the moon, seeing all of the experiences he'd had over the years that shaped who he was, suffered through major hardships of his life only to erase those from his memory at the end of the game so you can complete your job.  I practically threw my hands up in the air in disbelief when I realized that's how the game was going to end.  The ONLY REDEEMING ASPECT that To the Moon had going for it was smuthered out in the last minutes of this awful title and I would not recommend it to you unless you are the kind of person that likes to marvel at laughably bad titles.

I preordered this game sometime ago with the brought-in premise that it would be ambitious. Of course, it was. No Man's Sky is by far an excellency of scenic entertainment, and I've collected more than a few hours (and many, many screenshots) from this game.
For many, this game was a let-down. However, in my personal opinion this game is exactly as I thought it to be. While the price may be quite outrageous, I've had lots of fun on this game so far. I think this game brings out many aesthetic possibilities, and as a creative thinker myself, I love to see what a procedural universe can generate -- whether it's limited or unlimited.
Other people seemed to downplay this game. Saying that it's "the biggest letdown in 2016." However, this game gave us exactly what we promised. What many failed to realize was the fact that the game was engineered by a small team of about fifteen people. The fact of it is -- it wasn't going to be this huge amazing universe that Sean Murray promised. Of course, he wanted it to be -- but alas it wasn't. This isn't the first time a let-down like this has happened. Many other games (Spore, for example) was not what we expected it to be.
In conclusion, this game met my realistic standards. I highly recommend it for creative minds like myself. While the gameplay and price isn't quite as we wanted, it's still a great game. For those who buy it, I say "Have fun!"

Skullgirls reigns almost unmatched for its style and graphics.  Every one of the high-definition, hand-drawn characters looks absolutely stunning; the quality is almost unbelievable.  From the opening music to the announcer's "Showtime!' the sound is excellent.  The keyboard works surprisingly well for a fighting game, but the controller still bests it, and beyond that, the arcade pad reigns supreme.
Despite its excellent assets, the story is lackluster: people fighting over a powerful artifact.  The amount of fanservice doesn't mesh well with the fact that the artifact empowers only women.  Similar to how a writer may end with 'it was all a dream,' the ending is lazily tacked on.  As new IP, some consulting would have worked wonders and hopefully developers aren't afraid to retcon the rough edges.
Skullgirls' tutorial is by far the best among all the fighting games, but still not enough to condition new players.  Fighting games in general need to fix this problem or continue to lose popularity: having to slog through a couple hours of practicing the same combo over and over again is not 'fun' and doesn't feel like 'improvement.'
Skullgirls manages to be both a strong introduction for beginners and an intricate game purpose-built for veterans.

It's quite alright. Depending on your tastes in either aesthetics or mechanics this might be a hit or bust to you.
Firstly, the mechanics are very simple and easy to start out with. This game very much resembles Marvel vs Capcom 2 in gameplay without the same amount of brokeness in terms of characters. That said though, this game relies heavily on execution and rememebring your combo-strings rather than focusing on mixups etc. For the majority of the characters you have to string normals (light punch, light kick, medium punch.. etc..) into a launcher and an air combo (wih the same principle), then back onto the ground. You can't start a ground or air combo off of the same normal you've used before (i.e. you can't start the second ground combo with light punch if you've already started a ground combo with light punch before in your combo-string). This can make combos become extremely long-winded, especially in higher level play, and this is how most of the damage will be dealt. It's not as extreme when played casually, but generally you'll find that execution beats tactical play and positioning in this game. The online aspect of the game is superb since it runs on GGPO-netcode. I've played people with 300+ ping and still had an enjoyable game, though you'd generally like someone with better ping. You can also adjust the delay of your button presses to match the lag better if needed (generally I use 1 or 0).
Aesthetically speaking, the game is interesting and original in it's approach. Most (almost all) of the characters of the game are women with a very stilyzed and scant look. Boobs are everywhere. Although the art-style is anime at it's core, it very much resembles the cartoons and characters of the early 30'ies to 60'ies. Broadway-style. This is also apparent in the background settings, clothing and the menu. That is coupled with a somewhat gothic style, especially in character-design (for most characters). There's a bit of a revolting kind of sensibilty in the game, (meat morphing, sound of cutting, blood etc.), be sure f you mind that or not.
All in all, if you like execution-heavy fighting games, and a rather gothic and bloody 50'ies cartoon style game with a heavy emphasis on girls (hence the name Skullgirls) then this is right up your alley. It's very easy and quick to find people online to play against and the netcode is great, altough the battle-pairing system itself could've been better. If you'd rather want a more Technical fighting game without endless combos (i.e. 3rd Strike), you should probably look elsewhere (I suggest Yatagarasu: Attack on Cataclysm when that game releases in the near future).

Felt obligatory to write a proper review for this game.
This is a good game, just not centered to the most common steam users out there.
Couple things to note:
First - You NEED a controller for it. No exceptions.
Second - you need friends, controllers for each of them, preferably a coach and a big TV.
Third - like Gang Beast, chaos is a significant element in this game. Much more fun with 8 players than 3 or 2.
Many reviews diss this game for not suiting their need without justifying it's main audience is couch gaming.
So, here goes the actual review:
Gameplay mechanics are good and simple. The UI could use clearer explanations for sure, but everyone knows the control in a minute.
Map / gamemode variety is just enough or at bare minimum, repetitive yes, but doesn't bother us.
Game pacing is *very* good, where the balance between quick reflexes and tactics are strikingly neat.
One suggestion though - if winning and losing matters more or appears more different to players, this game would be fantastic for friends to get together and just casually battle each other.
Already a very fun game consider the price, just need some more polish here and there.

The soundtracks are beautiful, they are repetitive but not in a nagging annoying kind of way. Personally I was absorbed in the story and the gameplay, so I barely noticed the repetition except for several scenes.
Plot is well made; if you like Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, then you might like this. Never expected the cliffhanger though (especially from  the Sigmund minisodes), thought this was a pretty straightforward game, and I am MISTAKEN!
Puzzles are OK, they had an 'ideal count' counter, but I didn't really care, especially because there were no achievements for it LOL.
Exploring was a bit intimidating at first, since the areas are quite big, but eventually you'll get that there's no such thing as missing a step or a clue (and again, no achievement for the 'right' order) so it's goes pretty smooth once you pass the anxiety.
There was a glitch though at one point, and I actually had to google it. Fortunately it was soon resolved, but it could be much better if the developers fix that minor glitch.
It's a sci-fi romance drama, with some scientific terms but for me I just white-noised them, sad story but bearable (it takes more than this to make me bawling), and most of all, most enjoyable.
Looking forward for the next update (if any) or a sequel (again, if any). Will definitely play!

I wanted to change my review because the old one wasn’t relevant anymore. Since the first review they added Team play and let you play Draft for free once a day (and otherwise at a reduced price of in game currency).
Before the review I want to make one thing clear. I do recommend the game but only if you care to invest some time in it and can play almost daily. I have not paid anything except for the early access prize.
Graphics:
The graphics look good. Everything is really colorful and they got a nice style going. Also all the minions got a good silhouette so they are easily recognized on the playfield. Also there are a lot of visual cues so you can easily tell what’s going in, even in the chaos.
Gameplay:
You collect cards that represent minions and spells and you use those to battle against other players. There are a handful of game modes.
Single player:
This is basically just to prepare for online play. It’s more of a tutorial as the game is very much an online game.
1vs1:
Here you battle against another player and try to destroy their tower.
2v2 Team battle:
Here you team up with another play and take on another team of two. Since they added this game mode I feel there has been a lot more variety in what you can play.
Draft:
Here you get to pick a deck from a number of random selected cards. Every day you get to play it for free one time. Then if you want to play again you have to pay a small amount of in game currency. This mode is really challenging because you can’t always pick what you want. It is also good to try new cards you haven’t had a chance to try out yet.
A small thing I do dislike is the spinner. You can get cards through tokens. A selection of random cards end up on a spinner. The cards spin around and when you click a you get a card. You would think the spinner would actually stop at a card when you click, but actually the card you will get is predetermined. So the spinner is kind of useless.

Game Dev Tycoon has you starting off in your garage, you as a single person abitiously creating video games. When creating your first few games you'll be able to choose a genre and platform, followed by some options for your game.
Once you have your first succesfull game published, the fun truly begins. Eventually you will have enough money for a new studio, and you can also spend it on research to improve your games. You're also able to make game reports of your older games to reseach on what you did right, and what you didn't do right. By doing this, you'll keep expanding and making games.
Game Dev Tycoon does not get boring because the game keeps adding new mechanics (for example creating bigger games, more genres/platforms, events, developing your own console, etc) to keep you entertained.
It's a great simulation and management game that is very easy to learn. It's easy to create decent games in this, but to really thrive you'll have to research your old games for information, which can help you to improve on new games.
Recommended for anyone into business simulators or management games.

Pros: Graphics, Sound, Controls
Cons: Story, Gameplay
Skullgirls reigns almost unmatched for its style and graphics.  Every one of the high-definition, hand-drawn characters looks absolutely stunning; the quality is almost unbelievable.  From the opening music to the announcer's "Showtime!' the sound is excellent.  The keyboard works surprisingly well for a fighting game, but the controller still bests it, and beyond that, the arcade pad reigns supreme.
Despite its excellent assets, the story is lackluster: people fighting over a powerful artifact.  The amount of fanservice doesn't mesh well with the fact that the artifact empowers only women.  Similar to how a writer may end with 'it was all a dream,' the ending is lazily tacked on.  As new IP, some consulting would have worked wonders and hopefully developers aren't afraid to retcon the rough edges.
Skullgirls' tutorial is by far the best among all the fighting games, but still not enough to condition new players.  Fighting games in general need to fix this problem or continue to lose popularity: having to slog through a couple hours of practicing the same combo over and over again is not 'fun' and doesn't feel like 'improvement.'
Skullgirls manages to be both a strong introduction for beginners and an intricate game purpose-built for veterans.

It's quite alright. Depending on your tastes in either aesthetics or mechanics this might be a hit or bust to you.
Firstly, the mechanics are very simple and easy to start out with. This game very much resembles Marvel vs Capcom 2 in gameplay without the same amount of brokeness in terms of characters. That said though, this game relies heavily on execution and rememebring your combo-strings rather than focusing on mixups etc. For the majority of the characters you have to string normals (light punch, light kick, medium punch.. etc..) into a launcher and an air combo (wih the same principle), then back onto the ground. You can't start a ground or air combo off of the same normal you've used before (i.e. you can't start the second ground combo with light punch if you've already started a ground combo with light punch before in your combo-string). This can make combos become extremely long-winded, especially in higher level play, and this is how most of the damage will be dealt. It's not as extreme when played casually, but generally you'll find that execution beats tactical play and positioning in this game. The online aspect of the game is superb since it runs on GGPO-netcode. I've played people with 300+ ping and still had an enjoyable game, though you'd generally like someone with better ping. You can also adjust the delay of your button presses to match the lag better if needed (generally I use 1 or 0).
Aesthetically speaking, the game is interesting and original in it's approach. Most (almost all) of the characters of the game are women with a very stilyzed and scant look. Boobs are everywhere. Although the art-style is anime at it's core, it very much resembles the cartoons and characters of the early 30'ies to 60'ies. Broadway-style. This is also apparent in the background settings, clothing and the menu. That is coupled with a somewhat gothic style, especially in character-design (for most characters). There's a bit of a revolting kind of sensibilty in the game, (meat morphing, sound of cutting, blood etc.), be sure f you mind that or not.
All in all, if you like execution-heavy fighting games, and a rather gothic and bloody 50'ies cartoon style game with a heavy emphasis on girls (hence the name Skullgirls) then this is right up your alley. It's very easy and quick to find people online to play against and the netcode is great, altough the battle-pairing system itself could've been better. If you'd rather want a more Technical fighting game without endless combos (i.e. 3rd Strike), you should probably look elsewhere (I suggest Yatagarasu: Attack on Cataclysm when that game releases in the near future).

First impressions:
Epic Battle Fantasy 4 is a cute turn-based RPG. The art is fantastic, especially for a game of this genre.
The gameplay is simple, similar to what one would expect from a game of the genre. You've got the exploring aspect and the turn-based combat aspect, both of which are reminiscent of classic RPG flash games (Dragon Fable anyone?). It's nothing too special, but it's fun enough to not warrant a complaint from me.
The game's music was fantastic. I really enjoyed it and look forward to getting a copy of the soundtrack for future listening. Oh, and the artstyle, which was also very well done. Just like any other RPG, Epic Battle Fantasy 4 comes packed with a massive (and somewhat complex) skill system. It may have taken a while to get used to it, but it's certainly one of the game's positives.
Epic Battle Fantasy 4 is a great game, earning my recommendation. The artstyle may turn a few people away, but the game itself is fantastic (and besides, that artstyle should be selling more than it already is, right?).

THE LONG
If you are looking for a game where you can travel the a procedurally generated galaxy you have come to the right place, that is assuming that is all you're looking for. There are some great times finding those weirdly named/looking NPCs or cool planets. I feel however that No Man's Sky (NMS) still lacks content at this point in the game (v1.13) for me to recommend this game to anyone. NMS has a very tedious system in place for upgrading your ship/suit/multi-tool, and a extremely shallow quest/missions. With the additional games modes there was a glimmer of some possibilities, but they still need much work. Normal mode with the addition of survival mode might as well be named easy mode. Survival mode feels broke and extra tedious. Plutonium a vital resources required for exploring the planets/galaxy (main point of game?) is extremely rare, seemed like the lazy choice to make game harder. Save managment will be your best friend in survival mode. Creative is not bad to test features out, done/bored in about an hour. I’m talking about everything that can be done from one system, which is everything but getting to the center of the galaxy. With all that said, I am still hopeful that NMS will be morphed into something better through future updates.
Multiplayer is limited to leaving a message behind in a machine (very small sentence) to be discovered or seeing if someone else discovered something before you. No other multiplayer content at time of review (players exist in their on instance of the galaxy)
MY EXPERIENCE
71 hours (decent amount being afk with game running)
Grinded normal (when there was only normal) to max hoping for more at end, only left with trying to get to center. Stop playing do to that grind.
Came back v1.13, played survival, stopped playing after how stupid it was to make your main resource very rare.

Repetative, buggy as hell and STILL a great game! I look forward to further development and fixes, especially when we can share locations with our friends, even if we have to travel for a week to get to them...

I bought into all the hype about how amazing this game was supposed to be on launch. The expectations were set high, the promises were impressive, and the concept was mouth watering. I was very interested in the multiplayer aspect but was excited to find what the game had to offer.
Unfortunately I, like many others, were stunned to find the "multiplayer" aspect wasn't really there. I was discouraged but continued to play on, hoping to find something more to engage myself with in SINGLEPLAYER. I was met with more disappointment, I pushed on past the playtime limit for making a return and reached as far into the game as I could. What I found? A resource gathering game, to upgrade my ship and weapon....to gather more resources. The point? To get to the center of the galaxy just so I can start over.
So now I'm stuck with this unfinished game, I'll never get to experience the multiplayer promised, and the only thing this game has to offer is resource collecting with a few combat events thrown in. I mean sure I'm glad they're adding more like base building and new ships but that doesn't make up for tricking us into buying an unfinished product. I won't trust this developer again.
