Skullgirls is perhaps the prime example of what every modern fighting game should try to be when it comes to gameplay, plot, and overall involvement of the creators. The gameplay is smooth and responsive, feeling just like a fighting game should feel. The game will normally run very smoothly on a standard computer with the exception of a certain fight near the end of the game's story and arcade modes. Fortunately, during the fight, the game is still smooth enough to play without effect upon performance.
While the basics of the game's plot are simple, the intertwined storylines discovered throughout the game's story mode reveal how deep the story of Skullgirls runs, creating a strange and interesting world which is a blast to delve into. The characters are unique and memorable, each having their own personality, appearance, quirks, etc. which set them apart from the others. This much detail was even put into the unplayable side characters seen in the story, making them just as memorable.
The art in the game is unbelievably gorgeous. Every character, stage, and even the menus looks alive. The attention to detail put into everything is admirable. The backgrounds in certain stages will even change, ensuring that you'll never know what you'll see when you go to them.
The gameplay is similar to that of the Street Fighter series and it's similar counterparts, and it implements the common concepts such as the "Hyper Meter" which allows you to pull of your character's strongest attacks. However, Skullgirls uses a rather interesting concept. Like the Marvel vs Capcom series, you can play tag-matches. However, Skullgirls allows you to pick your roster size and strengthens or weakens characters accordingly, which adds a rather unique feel to the fights.
Lab Zero (specifically Skullgirls creators Mike Zaimont and Alex Ahad) is well involved with the community, often listening and researching issues pointed out by players and correcting them in patches. Other than this, they constantly update on upcoming game information and events, and even go as far as to add jokes to the game or even start funding campaigns for additional game conent. Lab Zero truly seems to care about their community and wants to hear their input and be involved with its members.
The game has very few problems. First and formost is the small roster of fighters. At this moment in time, there are only thirteen characters in game (fourteen if the non-canon Fukua is counted). However, Lab Zero is currently in development of three more characters, and perhaps we'll see even more in the future, so hopefully, this is merely a temporary problem. Another issue many critics of the game have is of the heavy fanservice. While I won't deny that it's there, it hasn't really affected the game for me, since I usually overlook this sort of thing. And while it it prevelent troughout the game, it usually isn't that distracting, or , if it is, it's put somewhere that will keep it from stealing attention from the rest of the action.
All and all, other than it's minor problems, Skullgirls is the perfect fighting game. With balanced gameplay, immersive story, and fun, addictive action, this should be in every fighting enthusiast's library.

Imagine: You're a monkey minding your own buisiness in your jungle home when suddenly you are attacked by your most deadliest predator; a herd of baloon shaped creatures called Bloons. They are deadly, terrifying, and worst of all, THEY FLOAT! So you naturally gather your monkey bretheren to defend your homelands using everything at your disposal, such as darts, catapults, bomber planes, battleships, and Terminator M0N-K3Y.
This game, while being a simple tower defense has a nice sense of charm through it's use of arts and resources. It also stands out in that unlike most tower defense games that use the same formula of "Air, Ground, Armor, Etc." units, you instead have bloons that have lives and the only real unique types are "Camo", "Lead", "Bomb/Freeze Resist", and "Regen", all of which have some way to counter them either through creative use of your buildings. Some towers spot nearby Camo bloons to attack, some give other towers the same ability. Some towers remove the camo altogether. All other types are just stronger versions and break down into their weaker counterparts in 1 hit, excluding Ceramics (Which break after a few hits), and MOAB Class, which are in essence bosses.
For those of you who played Bloons TD4 or lower, or played the flash version of this, it is a straight upgrade. Obviously, 5 is greater than 4, and they do a nice job of improving. New towers, refining old ones, adding new strategies. However, if you've played 5 and are still on the fence before actually buying it, realize you are buying everything in the flash version, plus the stuff you would otherwise have to pay extra for, PLUS about 10x the overall content. It is worth the $15.
Pros:
+Great mix of towers and upgrade paths (Where in other TD games you just upgrade, these actually feel as though you are impacting the game instead of just powering up. Some upgrades include faster fire rate, all the way to making a monkey turn into a giant temple of pure Bloon Poppage).
+Upgrades allow for immense strategy (Some are mutually exclusive, some you want to prioritize)
+Map Variation always keeps you entertained (Each map has their own path, and pathing rules (such as 2 starts, 2 exits, splits, loops, Large bodies of water for certain towers, etc.), and you have to plan around how to take advantage of the map (1 tower one 1 map may not work as well on the next).
+Consistency (You play one wave, you can expect that wave again, and it helps you translate from map to map, so you aren't blindsided with a cheap loss)
+Difficulty Matches Skill (If you play for the long run, you are going to find it gets tougher, but if you are good enough at planning ahead it definitely feels as though it pays off (Making it to wave 130 vs to wave 60 feels good)
+MONKEYS
+RAVENOUS BALOONS!
+Challenges (For when you get tired of just playing normally, you can play with special rules in play)
+Strategy outside of maps (Few TD games do this: You can buff certain towers while between maps at the cost of weakened other towers, or get "Agents" who are powerful one map towers with no cost to them besides monkey cash you get from winning.
+Freeplay (You beat the final wave. At this point you can continue on after to see how far you can last without hurting your win. In fact, you get rewarded for making it far enough.)
+Great tutorial. Your first play through it will guide you through how to do certain things, warn you of upcoming waves, etc. And it will do this until you choose to turn it off.
+The payoff for planning ahead (You can be doing amazing one wave, but if you didn't budget for something that can, say, kill Camo Bloons, the next wave will punish you hard).
+Manual Towers (Some towers can/are controlled via Mouse, instead of a behaviour, meaning that you can manually choose how you want your towers to hit. Abilities also do the same thing.
+Progression. Your towers become more powerful the more you use them in that more upgrades are availble to them, and after a certain point of playing long enough and popping enough Bloons you get the powerful tier 4 upgrades, which can range from dropping nukes to turning all units to Super Monkeys.
Cons:
-Multiplayer isn't consistent. Sometimes it works flawlessly, sometimes it won't even connect.
-Waves always appear the same (Wave 65 on Normal is Wave 65 on Hard.)
-Very little change in difficulties (Hard is almost the exact same as Medium, except you need to survive more of the same waves that can be accessed through Medium's freeplay, and you start out with less cash and lives which doesn't really matter later.)
-Challenges don't like new players. If you don't have all upgrades availble, a lot of challenges will not be within a realm of plausibility, so if you don't use a tower a lot (like me and Freeze Towers), it will slap you and say "USE IT!"

An old-school turn based RPG with a shiny modern coat of paint, that sums up Epic Battle Fantasy 4, but also explains very little.  Helpful, aren't I?  Um, anyway.  It's actually a really good time for fans of this sort of game, with game creation software in the hands of anyone who wants it, we have a lot of SNES style RPG games to choose from.  EBF4 really rises above the herd in many ways.
The graphics are pleasing and detailed, which is especially nice since the game has such a wide variety of gear.
There is a good variety of elemental damage and resistance in skills and gear, so that what you  wear can really change the outcome of a battle.  Along with that is the fact that you can always flee from battle and start it over, so you never have to find yourself in the awkward situation of being slaughtered by ice monsters because you wore your fancy fire armor that day.
The humor in EBF4 is self-aware and somewhat silly, without being over-the-top hey hey look at me arrow-knee pie-face lulz.  Well, not too much anyway.
I heartily suggest this game to anyone who likes fantasy, or epic battles, or the numeral four.

This was a nicely crafted tower wars/tug of war game. For something I got for free, I would say it was worth it. Acquiring coins to get better cards is quite the grind, but players can get a few solid hours of gameplay or some fun with their friends.
The
is quite simple and straight forward. Minion Masters is a tug of war/tower game with a few quirks of its own. The players are allowed to choose heroes which have their own special characteristics. For example, the player may choose an archer that can fire anywhere on the field or a mage that uses magic to hit players within a radius. The heroes can be upgraded by controlling a bridge (or two) on the map. To control these bridges, players simply have to have their own units walk across the bridge. Meaning, they have to be the last ones to cross the bridge to claim it for your side.
The player can choose to customize their deck. This means that players are allowed to swap units which work for their playing style. There are many different types of units and many to be unlocked. Some units include archers, gunners, giant knights, ogre rock looking things that like to smash and an outhouse that produces crossbow units. Units can be placed anywhere on the players side of the playing field. It will take a few games to figure out what sort of units work for your playing style. Bigger units will take more "mana" points to deploy. Mana is acquired simply by waiting. It is recommended to have a few "cheap" units to deploy to keep the field and your opponent occupied.
The
suit the game and it's presentation. It is a cartoon-ey feel, but the special effects definitely compliment the game well. The
are good, but I feel they could have been a little better. Every character have their own method of expression (sound). The battle effects could have a little more fine tuning or varied effects to create an immersive environment.
Overall, a decent game. I got it for free and think it should be a free game. If you do want to make a purchase, I would recommend a sale.

This is the first Guantlet Game that I have played. Coming from playing Diablo 3 extensively and Borderlands 2, and other rpg loot based games, this game is on a different class of game. It isn't loot based like most. You can get gold which can go towards different abilities, however it is mostly a classic old-school style hack n' slash game. If you want to relive the glory days of the '80's and '90's style of rpg dungeon crawlers, this is for you.

Plays like the classic Guantlet game with newer graphics and effects.   It can be fun and enjoyable.  I prefer playing as the wizard, because I like the variety.  Some people like the warrior, because he's basically a hack and slash character.  The other two are sort of middle of the road characters.  The game doesn't have that many levels though, and it's lacking a few features that would make it the best Guantlet game ever created.   Here's the bad:
- Screen is shared like in other Guantlet games, and that can be annoying when someone will not move and you can't proceed to the next area.  Some people don't care about this, but I do.  I think it would be a far better game if each player had their own screen.
- No voice or text chat at the time of this review.  You only have emotes, and that can suck since you can't really communicate with other players and meet other people who enjoy the game.
- No browsing for a game, so you'll only be able to join a random game, and sometimes it tells you the game if full, or that you joined a game already in progress and so you must go back and click to find another.  Why can't I just join a game in progress?  Nothing is more annoying than playing with 4 people, one or two quit, and no one can join!  You have to go back to lobby and wait for another random person to come in.  Oh, and there's no lobby chat either.
-  No key rebinding so you have to use the default controls.  The devs have promised they are adding this ability in the near future.  Still, it should have been something that was put into the game by release, but I got to hand it to them that they have responded to this request.  Well, hopefully they will.
-  Steam doesn't appear to be fully integrated.  What I mean by this, is that there is no way to shift tab and look at who you are playing with and easily send a friend request.   At least if they had this fully integrated, you could easily friend people and group chat on steam.
Overall it's a rather short game, but with some replayability.  I like the idea that there are way to level up your character, collect gold and buy upgrades.  But what would be nice is a randomly generated dungeon and perhaps endless dungeon mode, and I have read (but not a 100% sure) that the devs are planning on adding this to the game in a future patch (whenever that will be).
Though it has it's shortcomings, I am enjoying playing it.  So I'd recommend it.  It certainly isn't as complex as Magicka, but then neither was the classic Guantlet game that I was a huge fan of back in the day.  I think that the devs hit the nail on the head when it comes to capturing some of the old Guantlet style of play and sort of adding a modern feel to it of sorts.   The asking price isn't bad for what you get.

I purchased this game (more of a visual novel really) back in march of 2013. It's been two and a half years since then and when I accidentally opened windows media today and saw all the OST tracks that I bought it remined me about this game. Then I realized I never formally wrote a review.
Few things affected me as much as this game, though there are some. There is a certain realm of innocence and simplicity to be tasted and enjoyed in reality. Not enjoyment brought about by shallow desires, the rewards of complicated obligations, and so on. Rather, it is the type of simple joy brought about by life's simple yet greatest gifts: love, care, understanding, compassion, and bonding during difficult times. Though surrounded by complex, scientific methods of changing a person's earliest memories, at its core the story of To the Moon is no more than that: simple, pure, and good. It's a story about a man and his peculiar wife, whom he loves and understands and with whom he endures a great deal. To the Moon is a game about the fullfilment of this man's genuine wish due to his sense of love, loyalty, and unity he feels towards his wife. It's a story that will make you laugh, cry, and ponder life, as it certainly made me do. This game explores life's simple treasures and truly emphasizes what is important in life.
If you're not sure if you should get this game, get it. As simple as that.

First off, let me say this. You WILL NEED A POWERFUL COMPUTER TO RUN THIS. If you're running on a toaster laptop, don't buy this and write a review saying it sucks because it's a lag fest. That is your fault for not doing RESEARCH to learn what hardware is good for a game. Some people even say that the game runs terrible with a top quality machine, so caution is advised before purchasing the game.
As my account would suggest, I am quite the train fan. So much as that I've been playing Trainz since I was a kid, all the way back in 2003 and 2004. I have also purchased most of the major releases up until Trainz: A new Era aswell. However, before you start screaming that I'm a "Trainz fanboy," let me mention that I have in fact left the simulator for a while went to the competitor, Train Simulator aka Railworks. I stayed with the simulator for a while because of the improved graphics and physics but returned due to the horrid process of content creation. I heard about A New Era before and watched it while it was in development. I passed on the Kickstarter and decided to give it a go during the 2015 Christmas sale.
For those of you who are new to Trainz, let me explain the basics of this simulator. The main features of Trainz are Driver and Surveyor. In Driver, you can drive trains and in surveyor, you can create routes, sessions among other things. The game also features a content manager that allows you to manage your content downloaded from the developer's server called the Download Station, or from third party websites through .cdp files.
I for one have never played any of the sessions before, so I honestly cannot say how accurate the Train AI is. I personally just hop in with my models and screw around for a bit and close the game down. If you want to read about sessions, look at a different review.
Those of you who know about Trainz and are wondering if this is a good purchase, let's find out.
What does Trainz A New Era have that previous versions of Trainz do not have?
The main difference right off the bat are the graphics. TANE has real-time shadows that help to lift the look of the simulator, with a bunch of post processing effects to help make it stand out from it's older brothers. These shadows look fantastic (mostly), but they come at a great cost, performance. Currently, I am using a GTX 690 with an i5-2500, and I am barely able to get 30 fps with all settings maxed out except for shadows. These shadows require ALOT of power, almost too much power in fact. If you want this game to run smoothly, do your research to get the best possible combination so the game will run great. Oh, and if you want 60 fps, make sure to set V-Sync to off in the Launcher to enable that. Otherwise, the "half" setting will cap the fps to 30.
The post processing effects range from SSAO to HDR Tonemapping and give you lots of options to play around with. Personally, I can max out the post processing effects to Ultra and have no major performance issues. The effects look nice, but nothing compared to big AAA games such as The Witcher 3, GTA V, Fallout 4, etc.
One feature that I must add is quite fantastic is the ability to add trains while in Driver. This is a feature you wouldn't think is that helpful, but it's a feature that you depend on.
What about third party content Tomix?
Well, this is where it is a mixed bag. Some content may work, while others may require lots of TLC to get running again. This is especially gruesome with content from a previous version of Trainz. You may be there for hours or days fixing content until everything works! Not optimal, but this is not necessarily the simulators fault. Many errors are the user's fault for not fixing in previous versions of the game. Don't understand what I mean? Let me explain.
In Trainz, your content can either have an ERROR or a WARNING. ERRORs will not let the content work in a game, while WARNINGs will let the game run the content. Some WARNINGS that were once fine in previous versions turn into ERRORS in a later version. This is the case with lots of faulty content in TANE.
Remember Content Creator Plus? Yeah, that's gone. As a content creator, this by far is one of the weakest spots of the simulator. Content creator plus saved many hours of painstakingly fixing syntax errors in notepad and had many of the tags you need to make content. How do you do this with TANE? ALL IN NOTEPAD AND THE WIKI. Seriously N3V, why did you remove this? This feature NEEDS to return, otherwise people like myself will have to run back to older versions to make content and then port to TANE.
On the bright side, the new Content manager is quite nice. It's confusing at first, but there is a viewer that allows you to view the model as it would appear in the game, without even starting the game up! It is all around easier to see how the model will work in-game, and as a model maker, I adore this feature.
At the time of this review, Service Pack 1 Hotfix 3 is the latest update. One can assume that more patches will come and make the simulator better and better. I honestly want this simulator to survive and be successful. Unfortunately, N3V need to follow through with more of the stuff that they promised.
Moral of the story, it's the same old Trainz you're used to but with more extra frosting on it. It's your choice whether or not you think it's a good idea. I'd say wait for it to go on sale, or buy it from a third party website.
Keep in mind, there is a bunch of features or bugs that need to be worked on. This is NOT a master piece, but then again, there seems to be no Train Simulator that has everything we all want. This simulator meets my needs, but it may not need yours.
If any of you have further questions or want to make a comment on what I said, comment below.

As much as I don't want to give this game a thumb's down there are so many caveats which with I would need to recommend it that I won't do so in broad strokes. The basic idea and design is good, but the implementation of as many mechanics as not is questionable.
Things that work:
-The core idea of the turn based combat is good, build your own character, cast cool spells, plan out your attacks instead of using reflexes. When you first start out combat feels fun and is what basically draws you to the game.
-The graphics and designs are nice.
-I guess the voice acting isn't bad, some of them are a bit annoying or flat.
-Fast travel avoids the tedium of walking simulators.
Things that just don't work for me:
-Repetitive music and ambience.
-Lack of creatue variety and total enemy encounters.
-Rock paper scissors is terrible, some are unwinnable and there is no tie option so there is no strategy at all but losing can cause you to miss quest exp.
-The dialogue gets really thin after 40% or so, and going back to characters most don't recognize you have resolved a quest they were in.
-Pacing is largely terrible. Early to mid difficulty curve is off if you don't play OP builds. Puzzle difficulty curve is non existent, it's basically hovering everything to find something to click until near the very end where you have to do a fewactual  things, so rather than difficult it's just tedious which is why most people solve them through "cheese" of using scoundrels and teleport instead of actually doing the puzzles. I guess some people praise this for inventiveness but I don't think it's fun to look at a huge temple and beat it in 5 seconds by teleporting past all the mechanics; that doesn't feel creative it just feels poorly planned. It can be easy to go the wrong way and complete quests before finding the precursor hints without even realizing you missed anything.
-Quick saving every 5 minutes is mandatory due to random one shot traps which could be anywhere, I don't know what the point of this is at all except to be frustrating.
-Reloading fights to get a good opening in the early game makes everything take longer than it should. There's some fights where you need your guys standing just so or you take a lot of unncessary damage right off the bat.
-Sometimes I only had an easy time on fights because monsters would bug out and get stupid if they were too far at range.
-Tenebrium is stupid and useless.
-Due to limited engagements and no respawning fights, combat potential opens up too late in the game. By the time you have almost a full build going and can actually do cool stuff, the game is almost over.
-Small details that are supposed to make it a "pay attention we are not holding your hand" kind of game often end up being too pointlessly obscure rather than intuitive.
-Way too much junk items and equipment to pick up.
-Crafting is not fun.
-The story is not engaging.
-The dialogue choices don't feel like impactful or meaningful choices. This partly ties in also with the limited encounters. If you do "bad" things you often miss exp and you can't make that exp up anywhere else. Or you do the bad thing and get the exp anyway and no one outside of that room knows what you did. So I don't agree with people who say the world reacts to your choices. To get full exp you basically also have to kill all the friendly but not "good human" characters, such as goblins, after completing the quests relating to them.
Overall the game just lacks a cohesiveness that other better games have.  Beating it doesn't feel satisfying.
** Thanks for all the hate, just for trying to write a thorough and thoughtful review unlike most of the other negative reviews which are mostly "This game is too hard it sux" or "It doesn't work on my system 0/10 don't buy it" **

Scribblenauts is great. Its even better if you play by your own rules and have an audience.
If you don't know the basic idea is there are people who need the help of your godlike notebook that can create anything you can imagine and write down into it. So this knight needs a weapon to fight off a giant dragon, why not give him a diamond chainsaw? This girl wants to win a race, why not make her a super hero with super speed? Want to ride around on a golden dinosaur or a flying magical cat? Well in Scribblenauts you can.
Its a little easy to get tired of the game though. Its fun and all but the overall difficulty can basically be summed up in "this mouse wants cheese, click notebook write cheese, give cheese to mouse. This football team can't play football without a football.. click on notebook write football, give football to team." ..its absurd how easy the game is. Every once in a while I got totally stuck on something because its a childrens rhyme or a kids logic thing that I am obviously no longer in the loop for but that can be solved with a good audience.
The real fun though comes from messing with the game. So the mouse wants cheese right? Why not give him a cat made out of cheese then watch the hilarity of a mouse eating a live cheese cat. That poor guy needs a doctor, why not give him a zombie doctor? Make it fun and it becomes fun.. let it be boring and it can really tire you out.
Overall its a great game and its easy to 100% (though you'll probably want a walkthrough for the random object challenges). I think it would be great to play with others more than alone and children maybe more than adults.. but its a great game for all ages.

I had to actually change my positive review to a negative one after playing for 2 more hours and realizing that the developers turned this beautiful game into a frustrating platformer after the early stages.
The timing of some of the challenges are insanely tide and it doesn't leave any room for even the slightest of errors. Some of the missions (For example escaping from the water fall) is almost impossible with no checkpoints. You will be spending days trying to jump over things that will kill you while fighting enemy spawns (you need those because you have to bounce off their bullets to jump higher) and escaping from the waterfall which moves faster than light speed.

I've been enjoying this game tremendously. It's a nice break from some of the heavier RPGs I spend a lot of time playing. I've played through 2/3 of the game with the wizard on normal, and 1/3 with the elf on normal by myself. Last night, I had a couple friends over, and we played some three-player local on hard mode. I ran with the wizard. One friend ran with the elf. The other started with the warrior, but that didn't last long. He switched to the valkyrie after 45 minutes and had a MUCH better time.
We found the warrior to be an extreme liability. In any given map, for each Skull Token the wizard and elf used, the warrior would use 3-4. Most of the food went to the warrior as well. I was curious if perhaps it was just my friend being new at this, so I tried a few levels this morning with the warrior...I found the same thing. Here were some thoughts:
1) The warrior's basic attack moves him forward a tiny bit if you aren't careful...this is not good - it leaves him vulnerable after 2-3 swings to enemy hordes which overlap around his attack arc.
2) The warrior's strong attack has a little too much of a delay/wind-up...in the time it takes him to position and wind-up next to a spell caster, the caster can hit him with a bolt and interrupt him.
3) Whirlwind Attack is the saving grace...it's great.
4) Bull rush, again, has timing problems...it takes a bit too long to charge it up. The other three classes "escape" ability is basically instant use - elf press a button, valkyrie hold the stick, and the wizard has TWO-  to press a quick button combo for flame serpents (this does some damage to make up for it,) or protective sphere (which has a persistent knockback and a great duration.) The warrior's takes a charge-up time, and doesn't really do damage...not good.
5) Leaping attack looks great, but isn't terribly effective. It requires good aim, a bull rush (which takes time to charge,) and a timed button press, and does limited damage in terms of multiple targets...not good.
I grant that my experience is limited, but these are my impressions of the warrior.
The other three classes - SO MUCH FUN. Love love love the wizard's mechanics. The elf's agility is fantastic - dodges like no one's business. The valkyrie FEELS like a tank, and I love the art design on her - she looks like someone you would NOT want to tangle with. Overall, I love the game. Red warrior needs rebalance badly.

Do you like Pokemon??
Do you like like Magic the Gathering???
Well....
Until they make 'Monster in my Poke the Gathering' perhaps consider trying Minion Masters!
Minion Masters is an animated collectible cardgame, powering an  RTS-lite battle mode.
The game losely uses traditional rock, scissor, paper, mechanics  with most units having a number of counters but with a twist...
The game features AI battles, friendly battles, 1v1 random and soon group play.
The majority of your time will be spent with your own custom decks, but there is also a draft mode that acts like a mini 3 round tournament with prizes- and a payment to enter to discourage quitters- that provides you with a random selection of cards forcing  you to try new combinations and playstyles.

When learning to play expect defeat, but when it comes try and resist dismissing the game as pay2win.
Instead, think about mixing up your deck and learn when and how to use your cards- optimising your deck with your avatar and unit placement are very important too.
If the deck building intimidates you, copying best builds from the leader board is also an optiion.
Some accuse the game of being pay2win, but with dual methods of payment and the ability to earn all of the ingame currencies, paying only gives you access to the same content as everyone else a bit sooner, it's not an outright advantage.
Crafting  is a much faster method of getting the cards you want than say doing something stupid like openening 37 power tokens.
Essentially, Minion Masters is an addictive, easy to play, hard to master game with plenty or replayability provided by the wide range or avatars, units, spells, and buildings on offer- though not yet finished I'd say it's worth a punt.
The game is currently in early access and features a cheaper early access edition, I'd recommend that over the premium edition as the price is maybe a little bit too high for the premium edition though on sale that argument disappears.
So yeah, try Minion Masters, its not nasty.

I purchased this game (more of a visual novel really) back in march of 2013. It's been two and a half years since then and when I accidentally opened windows media today and saw all the OST tracks that I bought it remined me about this game. Then I realized I never formally wrote a review.
Few things affected me as much as this game, though there are some. There is a certain realm of innocence and simplicity to be tasted and enjoyed in reality. Not enjoyment brought about by shallow desires, the rewards of complicated obligations, and so on. Rather, it is the type of simple joy brought about by life's simple yet greatest gifts: love, care, understanding, compassion, and bonding during difficult times. Though surrounded by complex, scientific methods of changing a person's earliest memories, at its core the story of To the Moon is no more than that: simple, pure, and good. It's a story about a man and his peculiar wife, whom he loves and understands and with whom he endures a great deal. To the Moon is a game about the fullfilment of this man's genuine wish due to his sense of love, loyalty, and unity he feels towards his wife. It's a story that will make you laugh, cry, and ponder life, as it certainly made me do. This game explores life's simple treasures and truly emphasizes what is important in life.
If you're not sure if you should get this game, get it. As simple as that.

This game is simply beautiful! The art is unique and the animation is mind blowing! The music is a mix between symphony and Jazz and fits the mood perfectly. I must also mention the voice acting is extremely good!

As well as being one of the best looking fighting games out there, Skullgirls is a thoroughly enjoyable fighting game with crisp gameplay, diverse character designs and fantastic art/music to boot. Despite lacking abit in specific gamemodes, Skullgirls delivers an experience that is in my opinion, one of the most satisfying and accesible to fighting game players both new and experienced. With a detailed tutorial complementing its refined combat mechanics, Skullgirls has beaten out other fighters like SSF4 and UMVC3 as my personal favorite fighting game. Just a note though, I would recommend playing it with at least a controller if not a fight stick as I find the keyboard controls clunky and lacking, although the game still can be played and learned using them.

As someone who hasn't played 2D fighters for long, I can say that this is a great introduction to the genre. The game comes with an amazing tutorial going over all the basics that help one get started. There is a total of 30 lessons, and each character has a lesson specifically for them, which teaches all their special moves. If you're planning on buying this game, I recommend having a controller or an arcade stick.
There are currently ten characters, or eleven if counting fukua (Fukua is a variant of Filia with a different set of moves). More DLC characters are currently in the works aswell. The current roster is smaller compared to other fighting games. However, The qaulity of each character is worth a small roster. Each character has a unique playstyle. For example Cerebella is a grappler, who specializes in throwing her opponents. There is also a lot of synergy between characters, since one can create a team of multiple characters. Before a match one can choose to roll with a team of one super-powered character, two high-powered characters, or three normal-powered characters.

Another thing cool about the characters are the various palettes. Each character has about 20 unique color palettes. Some are original, but others are based off other fictional characters. For example there are four palettes based of the anime Madoka Magica and a palette of fionna from Adventure Time. The palettes just add a lot more fun to the game, though simple things.
The story mode is pretty short, and like most 2d fighters the focus is the multiplayer. Playing with people can be challenging for begginers, since people who aren't the same skill level will show drastically. When I first joined a quickmatch my opponent was a lot more expirenced than I, and he didn't pull any punches. Luckily there are lobbies for beggingers, and there are tons of people willing to play with somone on their skill level. I'm not sure how many tournaments are hosted for skullgirls, but I did find a group, which holds a newbie night tournament. There was also a side tournament that happened at evo 2014, and I imagine it will be there in the upcoming years as well. I believe there was a $5,000 cash pot, so there definatly is a reward for mastering this game.
This game comes with a variety of ways to play. Singleplayer comes with a story mode, where one can choose any of the characters on the roster and learn their backstory inbetween about three fights and the finally a fight with the skullgirl herself. It also features an arcade mode, which features competent AI bots to fight. When wanting to train, The traing room has a lot of options that can be turned on and off, so you can setup the perfect envimorent to train any skill. Finally the multiplayer has quick matches, lobby play, an a local tournament function. The lobbies in skullgirls can be created to hold a max ammount of 8 people, and you can either spectate or fight someone in the lobby.
Skullgirls is definatly worth the purchase. It's a really stylized 2d fighter that looks and feels great. It's easy to get into for begginers, but hard to master. You'll be having fun playing this for hours upon hours, if you aim to harness you're full potentintal of this game.

Certainly, if you are actually buying the game, i recommend you do buy the deluxe edition. It is just not worth it to buy the one with only four routes, as you will have such limited game time.
The pricing system for DLC is so strange. It's $35 for a brand new 100km Warwick to Wallangara route. It's $35 for a remake of the TS2010 Avery-Drexel route. It's $35 for Bideye Traction Railroad, a route that is so small, I think it probably took one person less than a day to complete it. Why are they all the same price for different amounts of quality and quantity? It is ludicrous!
The locomotives are overpriced. $17 for a regular looking diesel locomotive nearly identical to those available in the base game. $9 for some passenger cars. $9 for some freight cars? Are you kidding? Don't get them.
If they really wanted more people to buy the locomotives and stuff, then why couldn't they just utilize the bundle system and make it genuinely affordable to regular people. (i.e. buy 5 locos for $25 or something.)
I once again want to stress that the game isn't bad, it is just not for everyone including the average gamer joe.

As far as rail simulation goes, I have been involved since 2004. Fiddled with several, and mostly ran out of steam (pun intended) with them. Trainz is detailed, hardcore, full house. The community is great (read: mature) on the forums, and the content is phenominal, free and payware. It's not a game, it's a modelling and simulation system, so I have no idea why gamers and gimme-pigs are rating so low.
Performance is a bit chunky, but TANE is a whole lot easier on resources than T12 was for me. I am maintaining a solid 30-60fps (environment depending) on mid-to-high level settings, which is OK for my GTX760, 16GB, 4790 system. Things are getting better however with every SP and update. If you want full scale gaming experience graphics and arcade fun with action, this is not for you. If you are a rail fan, train lover, railroad modeller (Prototype or not), then it is.

Excellent game overall. Its capable of a lot and has many pros and a few cons.
- A lot of content available. Not all of it is great quality. Some assets are quite old and it shows in game. Others do look superb though. Be aware you may have to pay for some of the superb looking content. But compared to Model Railroad terms its not that bad. I can buy an amazingly detailed loco from JointedRail that looks and sounds great for about $10-$15. Actual model locomotives are much more than this and in Trainz i can duplicate as many of them in my route/session for free!
- You may be limited on content if not a lot of content creators are painting your scheme, fortunately if you're clever you can reskin things yourself.
- Users seem to create most of the content available. This seems to be a double-edged sword. On one had we have tons of content available. Almost anything you'd look for is on the DLS, on the other hand not all of it is the greatest quality.
- Dealing with assets which have missing and broken dependencies can be a pain.
- Its exremely flexible. You can buid just about anything that you can dream up. The session rules and commands available are vast and can be daunting at first but they do provide ultimate flexibility in designing a session and molding gameplay to whatever suits you. Watch the videos on N3V's twitch/youtube channels they're immense help in getting up to speed.
- Visually it looks great. Runs very well on a GTX970. As mentioned some assets and textures are older and some are not the greatest quality so obviously those are not going to look great no matter what.
- DLS is extremely slow (8k/s) unless you have a first class ticket which allows you to pay for quicker downloads. I used to have an issue with this but i've accepted it now. Other games charge for DLC and in this unique case they charge for accessing it at a reasonable pace. I just buy a FCT whenever i need to download a lot of stuff like when route building and/or wait for a sale. Its not the end of the world and helps the dev with a little revenue to keep things going.
- The ability to create model railroad layouts is excellent. There are some greate community created assets which allow you to build your dream layout.
- Some built in assets for such a new game are unusually low quality. It'd be nice to see these updated or removed.
- Ability to bulk replace/move assets in route builder is fantastic.
- Ability to set up custom pick lists so assets you regularly use are readility available. Also fantastic.
- would love to see some abiliy to easily overlay a google map to trace out a real-world line in for building a route. Similarly would be great to automatically shape the terrain based on geographic elevation data.
Overall i've been enjoying it and have only scratched the surface with AI trains, route building, session running. It should provide immense replayability if trains (Model or prototypical) are your thing.

Almost a great sim.  Not quite.
The "almost great" aspects:  serious train-buff attention to details of engines, cab controls, realistic railroad rules and signalling, grades, mass, inertia, acceleration etc.  Decent sized map to start with.  Excellent tutorial introduction.  Terrific sounds -- very convincing and immersive.  Reasonably challenging gameplay once you get into it.  I could definitely enjoy this game for many hours... BUT...
The "not quite" aspects:  graphics are pretty crude/simple by modern standards.  In a gaming world where Dear Esther and Euro Truck Simulator are widely popular (and not super expensive), it's kind of hard to go back to old-school low-res, cartoonish landscapes and objects, bright sun shadows even when it's supposed to be overcast, rain falling inside railroad tunnels, engines that break down into weird isolated shapes if you zoom in too close.  Nevertheless, given the sim's other charms, this "retro" graphical quality could be forgiven.  What can't be forgiven is extreme instability -- on OSX anyway.  I have not been able to play this game for more than 10-15 minutes without a hang or crash.  Another issue is inability to recover from an autosaved position;  if you restart after a crash and try to resume a tutorial (some of the tutorials take 10 or more minutes) you can't.  You have to start over from the beginning.  This gets frustrating fast, especially since the game won't run for long enough to complete the tutorial!  Given the lacklustre graphical quality it seems to be very hard on the gpu, too.  I can run ETS2 at Ultra without much jitter, but Trainz (with its primitive graphics) makes my gpu jitter even at medium settings.  Whatever they're doing is expensive and/or inefficient, but without any surface glitz to show for it.
If the devs can get TANE to run reliably under OSX it will be worth playing if you like trains, even without improved graphics.  If they can get it stable under OSX *and* improve the cosmetics at least to, say, XPLANE 10 standards, they have an attractive sim even for people who aren't train buffs.  If they can get some pretty scenery packs to emulate real railroads (Canadian Rockies anyone?  California's Coast Starlight run?) then they may have a real winner.  Right now I would have to say mixed-to-negative review from me, mostly because of the extreme instability.  Feels like a beta release.

This is a bad shooter that barely belongs in the F.E.A.R. storyline. The second game was tolerable and even good at points but this one makes you wonder why you're not just doing anything else instead. The second mission felt like a bad rip-off of the favela fights in a much better FPS game, and the constant pop-ups for minor achievements are incredibly irritating. For what should theoretically be a relatively slow-paced shooter with bouts of action this one misses the mark completely, and it even throws in regenerating health to hammer the point home. It's like the difference between the Pripyat levels in STALKER and in Modern Warfare - despite having similar themes the feel of them is completely different. This feels barely like the second game and nothing at all like the original. After the favela mission I looked at the "Challenge board" and the "target time" of the mission and decided that it wasn't worth continuing. I bought this a while back on sale and quite enjoyed it, but ultimately I was left dissapointed by the length of the campaign.  F.E.A.R 1 still remains the best of the series (by quite a stretch) but I'd say this is an interesting diversion.
The missions are replayable due to the score/challenge mechanics and the controls are fluid  Most of the campaign missions are enjoyable with very little downtime for exposition and cutscenes, meaning the pace remains fairly solid throughout.  Combat is fast paced, sometimes chaotic, but most of all fun with all the trade mark sillyness that comes from F.E.A.R's melee combat and wonky ragdoll physics.
Both of the main characters have different play styles which does just enough to make each individual playthrough unique.  Although the linier paths through the missions are almost identical for each, they play very differently due to the mechanics.
The multiplayer scene was dead before it even hit the ground.  The netcode is absolutely atrocious and even using direct P2P connections it would only connect on a handful of occasions.  It's a shame because the multiplayer had a chance to be genuinely enjoyable, with both co-operative and competative game modes.
On the plus side you can still play these co-op missions solo via "training", but obviously it's not quite the same.
The reason I'm reviewing this now is because I only recently came back to it and had an absolute blast playing through the campaign.  It's extremely silly, fast paced and mindless and if you can get it for under £5 I'd say it was money well spent.

I would only recommend getting this one if it were on sale for $10 or less, anything more and you're getting the short end of the stick. The most fun I have had from a rpg in recent times. You have a ton of options to approach both combat and your quests allowing for serious role-playing.
Too many games nowadays slap a xp meter and call themselves rpgs. Few games understand choice and consequence which imo was what made older rpgs fun. Divinity gets it.. you approach story and questing the way you want your character to.
And combat, combat is delicious. The enemy is mostly single minded in its hatred and more often that not trips in its single minded goal to kill you. A little strategy is enough to wreck serious havok on it. Its incredibly fun to abuse force enemy units into choke-points while flinging oilbombs and fireballs with a bit of poisoncloud arrows. The interaction between the elements is pure genius. Fire to poison makes a bomb, ice to water makes ground slippery and enemies and allies slip and fall.. and you can play a bit and use fire to convert water to steam and throw lightning at the steam cloud to make a lightning storm. The only drawback is that mages are almost a must. A pure scoundrel/fighter is going to be very difficult to pull off.
Play this game.

This is a particularly interesting game because, while rather simple in concept, it integrates an understanding of gaming development that is not only interesting but also informative.  As you play, you learn the different trends, information on what kinds of games go best with which consoles, and where best to focus your energy to create the best games.  Still, as with the real world, the game can prove quite challenging at moments.
It is the progression of the game, I believe, that makes it so addicting.  Starting in a basement by yourself and working your way up is no easy task;  sometimes you fail before it really feels you begin.  When you get more comfortable with the trends of the game and begin to strategize, only then are you able to succeed long enough to grow your company.  As with any good game, this then raises the stakes and makes failing so much harder.
I have played it through a couple of times now, and I'm trying to wait to pick it up for another round because I know it'll suck me in yet again.  It is interesting to see how every little choice can affect the outcome of the game, from which games to make, to what research should be done, to who to hire.  All in all, if you like games that make you think while giving you a large sense of control and a well-earned sense of accomplishment, I would definitely recommend this game for you.

I adore free roam games where you explore unique landscapes, and LEGO Worlds certainly delivers! The colors are bright and the variety is passable. However, exploration alone does not make a game. There are many areas to improve, such as:
OPTIMIZATION: I'm running this on an Asus ROG laptop. 16 GB ram, Nvidia 860m with 2GB dedicated memory, quad core. Not super high end but it plays any game I've tried at 30fps which is all I need. So why does the game hang whenever I go to build or paint something? It's unbearably laggy. And, being LEGO, I kind of expect to build things.
CAMERA CONTROL: Interesting choice having the camera move uncontrably into 'cinematic' angles whenever you discover something new, which was A LOT in the hour or so I played. There's a reason LOZ has an iconic 'item get' noise instead of an iconic 'item get' camera pan. Even when I can control it the camera moves very slowly.
GENERAL CONTROLS: Again, very slow, aim is dodgy, jumping is unpredictable. When you jump at things you cling to them which could be great, but with poor controls it does more harm than good.
AMBIANCE: This is personal preference and feel free to disregard, but I find the game very quiet. Not in a volume sense, but in an amount-of-things-Im-hearing sense. It could benefit from more animal/npc sound effects.
This game has potential and I can't wait to see it realized! But for now, it leaves much to be desired.

Objectively the best fighter on the market. Objective too strong a word for you fans of fighting game
? Well, Skullgirls has the best training mode, bar none. This means it actually teaches important fundamentals like high/low game, blockstrings, and teching throws. Flexible combat system that allows for easy to learn, difficult to master combos, custom assist moves for partners, or even forgo partners altogether to proportionately increase the health and power of your character(s).
But the best thing is that this is a fighter that is constantly being worked on and supported with a large amount of help and input from the community. Skullgirls is already finishing up their 3rd DLC character and the door's still ajar for a 4th or even 5th. Do you want a fighter with indefinite support? Skullgirls is it.

A great fighting game made specifically for the fighting game community. Not to hard to get into either, with really good tutorials, and if all you can do is mash buttons, you'll still look like you're doing something right.

I love this game... and I hate it.
There seems to be a few things I noticed as time went by as I played fighting games. People tend to favor the much more flashy moves and lengthy combos. Skullgirls does that, moreso I feel, along with some of the newer fighting games. I liked playing Street Fighter 3 and 4 along with Tekken while competing with friends.
While I do love this game, there are things I don't necessarily agree with. Sure, the pokes, punishes, supers, specials and overall gameplay is satisfying. I don't agree with the lengthy and exploitable combos and the IPS system is a bit skippy and sometimes buggy. Sometimes it would activate against me even if I landed my first hit and when a player spammed the same combo it never seemed to kick in. There are plenty of combos that are actually based around burst baiting requires you to burst or end up dying anyway (if you burst you get thrown into another combo). A lot of players suggest anticipating the resets if a combo seems too lengthy and the truth is I've never been able to counter a combo string during a reset (probably due to lag but who knows).
I'll say it once and I'll say it again. I do not agree with the two bar health system for solo vs. solo games. In any fighting game, like Injustice or Killer Instinct. Before they implemented this, me and a couple of sparring partners were able to analyze each other's fighting techniques and bad habits during first and second round with the third and final round having both players mix up our playstyles or lose. I don't know why people seem to dislike this sytem and many say it's based on luck (untrue). Through this sytem I was able to make incredible comebacks even if I didn't know a great combo (I would stick to a combo that did some great damage but it was never too lengthy). The way it is now is with people making their way to deal the most damage with the lengthiest combos, instead of analyzing an opponent and catching them offguard with a well hit super or special. Yes, because a game like Injustice is a great example, especially during the pro tournament where all the 'professional players' just used superman and spammed ice breath and lazer beams.
I just don't agree with the two bars, it's why I left a lot of solo games or if I did stick around to play I would allow the player of the losing round to bring the rest of my bar down so the last round is much more fair. Getting that off of my chest I like the anime type artstyle and the animations. The animations are smooth and the moves are quick, I kind of understand why the game favors lengthy combos, mainly because it is supposed to be very fast paced. While I agree with it being fast paced, lengthy combos actually make the game feel dragged out. I did get a hang of the moves and right now I have a few solid combos but overall I don't like doing lengthy combos because it feels like I'm more or less exploiting the game.
Not much to say other than it is a solid well done game. Although I like it, the game is changing away from my tastes, it seems. With the addition of a two bar system, the lengthy combos, and the exploitable burst system it can still be fun and there are more characters to be added onto it. It was well worth the money, though.

Though there aren't as many characters as many big-name fighting games, Skullgirls makes up for in quantity with a strong foundation of quality. Almost everything about the game is top-notch- art direction, animation, game mechanics, unique characters with distinct playstyles, and sound design are superb and complement each other nicely. Pulling off basic combos is simple and intuitive, and most of the special moves are easy to pull off for a casual fighting game fan. However, Skullgirls still has lots of depth for the hardcore player to experience, and helps ease in new players with its comprehensive in-game tutorial. I honestly can't think of any major flaws that haven't already been adressed by patches and upates.
Skullgirls probably isn't a game that will get you into fighters, but i'f you're already a fan of the genre it's a real treat.

Having only played one of the prequels without even finishing it I don't feel adequate enough to write a review for it, but I will because I think it really deserves one.
For being a flash game, it really does a lot of things very well. It has a bunch of content and the feel of the game and combat offers more replay value than most other games. I'm positive there's some kind of overpowered gear/party setup to be found somewhere/sometime but as far as I have seen there is the complexity where switching equipment to counteract the zones you're currently in will benefit you considerably which is great. It should not be mistaken for an easy game other than being an RPG where you can farm/outlevel zones, because the highest difficulty setting does offer quite a challenge.
There's a whole lot of fun to be had with just the humorous dialogues and references to popular video games and anime culture. If that's not your thing, then you may want to seek elsewhere. The game may run a little bit slower during intense scenes where there's a lot happening on the screen (depending on your graphic settings) but other than that, the only downside I can possibly imagine is feeling a bit disconnected with the story if you haven't played the previous games.. though in my opinion, even that can be nullified because the story is quite bonkers to begin with.
The game can be played for free, but the Steam version does offer a lot more extra content. Whether that's worth the price is subject to personal opinion, but I think the sheer awesomeness of the included soundtrack by the great music artist (and another personal favorite) HalcyonicFalconX definitely makes up for it.

Large variety of items/gear to collect, skills to unlock and chose from, and monsters to encounter. On the higher difficulties, you have to make sure your party make-up is balanced as far as elements, as monsters all have various elements and status conditions that they are either strong or weak against. Combined with the possible synergies between gear and skills, it gives the combat system enough depth to have it not feel stale after a while.
Some minor knocks include lack of widescreen support and lack of built-in controller support. Also obviously, if you dislike JRPGs, this game will not appeal to you.

A well made take on the old classic Atari game Gauntlet, that i can recommend to anyone who wants to enjoy a simple yet deep hack n' slash experience.
The game features fun mechanics, an interesting aesthetic style, as well as having a badass soundtrack, that harkens back to the old preceding Gauntlet games.
Besides the obvious traits of each character (the elf has a bow and the warrior a melee weapon, etc). Each of the characters feature different skills and mechanics that you have to adapt to, in order to maximise your effectiveness. And you can also customize your character with artifacts to suit your style of play.
However when i played this game i didn't do it for the character customization. This game just makes killing feel good. Especially when you get yourself into a trance where everything just clicks and you eviscerate 20 opponents in a matter or seconds.
My only beef with this game is, that compared to the older gauntlet games, the "puzzles" in this game are too easy. It often feels like the game is taking your hand and leading you to where you need to place the dynamite or throwing you an extra key to open one of the locked doors. In the older Gauntlet games, the game would force you to think about managing your keys, and solving the puzzles in the correct order. However in this version this is not the case and takes some of the more cognitive aspects of the game away.
I can't say much about the multiplayer experience, since i've yet to play it with another friend  ( :c ).
But other than that Gauntlet has been a fun experience and i would definately play more of this in the future.

+ Great storyline, with a very nice paced progression.
+ The length of the game is just perfect, and it never feels too slow or too fast.
+ Well developed characters.
+ Great sense of humor, without being too over the top.
+ Nice and suiting music.
+ Easy to get 100% steam achievement ( if you care about that )
- I can't really think of anything bad to say.

Played To the Moon, and cried enough to rival that of my lifetime. Many may have missed the many many nuances of the story, and after completion I suggest reading up on it. This story takes reality by the feet and drags into the realm of Science Fiction. Every element, color choice, and dialogue is carefully placed to further the central focus of this game, the story. This emotional story/journey is the central focus (not gameplay, graphics, or gimmics) and is something so memorable. For me, I felt the tear jerking moment coming... but still caught me completely off guard. Excellent sound track. Bravo. Well done.
Will play again when I actually man up and buy tissues.

Multiplayer would be nice, or at least the ability to meet up and track a friend so you both explore together like co-op play. But in regards to the game overall, well... here we go. Was it "the marketing team that screwed up"? No. Let's be honest... It's a small shop, like REALLY small. Or at least it was at the time of release. There was no marketing "team" like there would be at EA Games, Ubisoft, Sony, or any other large corporation. This was a handful of guys that came together to create and release a video game. So all these claims that it was anyone else's fault is just people grasping at straws trying to ignore the ugly truth. Every video that I watched leading up to the release of this game involved Sean Murray, and Sean Murray ONLY. There was no commercial on TV that showed false gameplay footage, and there were no misleading posters or ads. Sean went on small interviews, talk shows, etc. and discussed the game. "Sean, will I be able to ______" and he answered "yes". That's what truly bothers me. The game was released and we found that all those claims were actually false. I even scheduled time off from work months in advance, just so I could play this when it was released. I was expecting missions/quests, stealing or interacting with freighters, and earning some type of good standing with an alien race, just like Sean said I'd be able to do. But somehow that wasn't possible, the game simply didn't line up with what I was told. By the end of that first day I felt like I was playing a game still in beta. Think about it. Most of us have played games still in Alpha/Beta and that's exactly how it works: you pay full price, play the game as-is, and then you wait for the full content to be added later on down the road. Many times that content completely changes the game in a good way, allowing you to do things that you couldn't before. Well... that's No Man's Sky. The game was released and I could fly around, collect resources and... actually that's it. Now there's a "Foundation Update" where they added content in which you can interact with freighters, build a small base, and a few other things. Great! But... this game came out 4 months ago, why wasn't this in the initial release? That's because the game is in Beta. Wait, it's not? It sure feels like it.
At the end of my first day of playing, I had a moment of reflection. I stopped for a second and thought to myself, I just spent $60 on this. I had also just wasted a perfectly good vacation day. Did I feel enlightened? Did I feel like I had just played the greatest game of 2016? No, no, no, and... no. My only consolation was when I checked the reviews on Steam, just to see if maybe I was missing something. Maybe I just didn't play enough yet, or maybe I was doing something wrong? Boy was I not alone... Not only was I not alone, there were THOUSANDS of others that shared my same frustration and disappointment. Sure, there were a few thumbs up reviews and the "I think the game is great" kind of posts, but they were vastly outnumbered. VASTLY. Even to this day, almost 5 months after, the game is still "Overwhelmingly Negative" on Steam. If you're thinking of buying a game, terms such as "overwhelmingly negative" isn't what you want to see. But that's No Man's Sky. Go ahead, scroll through the other reviews. It's OK. You'll find long rants of dislike, moments of sorrow, and claims of regret from thousands of fellow gamers, much like this one. Click the "buy" button if you dare, and join the community of Beta testers.

Tacopocalypse is a taco delivery game inspired by games like Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, Crazy Taxi, and Jet Set Radio. I was lured into playing this by the fancy graphics in the trailer, but you can get the most out of this game by watching the trailer than actually playing it. The art style is fantastic, and the sounds + punk soundtrack really flow well with it.
My main disappointment was with the lack of content. There's one mode (two if you count the local multiplayer), with only one objective. Your objective is to deliver tacos (within a time limit), and get style points by doing stunts during the process. With the cash you make from delivering tacos you can buy 2 new cars and customize them but that's about it. You can collect hidden songs along the way which I thought was a nice touch, but there's just not enough incentive to play this. It doesn't help that there's no guidance system to tell you where you need to deliver the tacos, which is odd cuz they do point you in the direction of where you can stock back up on tacos after you've run out.
There are 4 levels, which is a small amount but they're big and intricate enough to where you can pull off some neat tricks and grinds while being visually flashy. There aren't enough collectibles or objectives, so this makes them feel a bit too empty. The controls/physics were a little too over the top for my taste, there's too much freedom here with the ability to flip that I end up losing control, but I think this may be personal preference because the game is meant to be over the top and ridiculous. If you can get used them you may have more fun performing sunts than I did. There didn't seem to be much depth to the stunts you can do, you do flips by rotating your car and grind rails but that's all I noticed.
There were some minor bugs I encountered with my short time with the game, including getting a black screen on the first level I played after the tutorial, falling through the ground (not a big deal cuz you can reset your vehicle with ease), and music not playing. I don't know the success rate of the dev fixing bugs, but the dev does respond to bug submissions on the forum.
In its current state, I can't recommend Tacopocalypse. You might be able to get a few minutes of enjoyment out of it, but there's just not enough to do. This comes off more as a tech demo or art project than a game, which is unfortunate because I would love to see this art style, open world level design, and sound/music implemented into a game with a substantial amount of gameplay. I think it's a really cool concept, but not a good execution.

tl;dr This isn't very similar to Minecraft and the game can get stale if you're not in it for building things.
Alright, first off, if you're looking for something similar to Minecraft, you're not going to find it with this game.
This game operates similarly to Minecraft's creative mode, and as far as I can tell there is no way to swap to a different mode. As far as items go, you can find everything within maybe 3-4 hours of gameplay, this includes characters, creatures, vehicles, weapons, and props. Some vehicles are a little weird to drive, and it can get frustrating to play considering that directional movement is based on the angle of your camera (Please fix this devs).
As you've probably heard already, this game relies on procedural generation, so you really can go on forever in any direction, and build a home in a variety of biomes. I really love that a lot of games have been doing this recently as it allows for constant exploration. However, it is very easy to get lost due to a lack of maps or compasses. Also, there is no way to set a marker or anything that can return you to a specific area that you enjoy.
Enemies aren't much of a concern either, they're extremely weak and rarely in groups and the only way you'll die is if you don't fight at all, but that's not a problem because dying doesn't really punish you. It's a bit disappointing that there is no challenging aspect to this game, and yes I know that that isn't the main aspect of this game.
All-in-all though, I love this game and can see myself playing this in the future (Even more if multiplayer is added).

My experience with Skullgirls focuses on the single player story mode and arcade mode only. I will never be good enough to play competitively against people online.
First of all, the artwork and animation are excellent. There is nothing anyone can complain about in that department when speaking of the artwork's technique and implementation. Sure, the designers opted to include some exaggerated and gratuitous breasts, as well as panties shots, but if you can overlook those minor aesthetic flaws, the art in general is very impressive. The backgrounds look good, but what truly shines are character design and character animation. The artists and animators involved in this have accomplished something they should be really proud of. Everything on-screen moves and reacts so smoothly and flawlessly, always at a solid, albeit capped frame rate. From a technical standpoint, Skullgirls should be the example of how to do a fighting game well.
The moves list is extensive, with the blockbuster moves being the highlights of the bunch. In order to perform a character's blockbuster move, you must accumulate a certain amount of power in your meter, so saving them for the best moments is key. You may also perform ensemble attacks, using an additional character selected as part of your optional tag-team, but those can be more difficult to learn. In addition to all of this, there are also some different colors you may choose for your characters if you get bored of the default ones, or just feel like randomizing their looks a bit.
Even though the base roster of fighters is a good one, there are others available for purchase as DLC, with more being added in the future. The developers are constantly patching and updating the game, and there is even a widely used Beta version of Skullgirls available for some major testing.
Overall, you will not be disappointed with Skullgirls and its DLC. It doesn't matter if you're not a fighting game fan, or if you usually don't like the fan service style of the art. There is a good game here for everyone to enjoy.

Playing as one of the two man-eating sharks that stalk the four human divers in each match is definitely the star of the show. Navigating swiftly and silently in third-person perspective, I quickly developed a sense that these oceans were mine to lord over. The sluggish, clumsy humans huddled in groups as they inched their way from treasure stash to to treasure stash, knowing I was out there somewhere, but never sure from what direction I’d attack, or when. Regular sonar pulses showed me outlines of my prey, allowing me to keep tabs on them at great distances. It’s reminiscent of playing as the Infected in Left 4 Dead, or the Alien gameplay in the old Aliens vs Predator 2 multiplayer: speed, stealth, and a superior awareness of the environment were my primary advantages.
The humans brought numbers, hardware, and ranged weaponry to the table in response. Playing from first-person and handicapped by a deliberately-limited sight range, the intrepid landlubbers are forced to use all of these tools to survive. Starting with a basic pistol, divers unlock progressively more potent guns and utility items by gathering and turning in treasure in an interface similar to Counter-Strike’s gear market. Having net guns and fully automatic firepower is nice, but the real key to diver gameplay is making good use of items like sonar beacons and concealed mines that grant an early warning of an approaching maneater and, potentially, blow it up before it gets a chance to take a bite out of anyone’s juicy abdomen.
As the shark, I found myself in a dynamic cat-and-mouse game as the rounds progressed. Successful sharksmanship became a matter of knowing when to strike, using paranoia as a weapon, and getting the hell out of the line of fire with my supper before said supper’s friends could take revenge. As the sharks are always outnumbered and, thankfully for us dirt dwellers, still not immune to bullets, frontal assaults were almost always a one-way ticket to the Belly-Up Ball. As with any horror-movie aquatic menace, the less I was seen, the better. Performing swift passes by windows and cracks in the wall to distract the divers proved very effective, as did planning my attack vector on a straight line between two exits, with my target right in the middle.
When playing for the edible team, I had to trade in my rows of razor-sharp teeth for a SCUBA mask and a more developed prefrontal cortex, which changed the atmosphere completely. I felt slow, exposed, and under-equipped as we escorted our treasure-hauling, mechanical companion S.T.E.V.E. through the oppressive, deep-sea environments. Moving methodically, I found I often had less than a second to react between seeing the first flash of fins and meeting my crunchy demise. Awareness and teamwork were my only insurance policies, and vision-enhancing items like chemlights and tracer rounds (which can stick to a shark and allow it to be tracked at a distance) proved to be the most crucial elements in my arsena

Gauntlet makes for a great reboot of the original and I can easily see it being one of the most popular dungeon crawlers of late 2014-early 2015. It really brings back memories of hours and hours of gameplay and lots of quarters spent in the old arcade days. The graphics did not have to be excellent but adding a "3D" effect and a lot of detail really made the game beautiful. Normally, I would expect it to get boring after a while, having lots of experience with games like this one, but I was wrong - the fun never stopped! Tried both online multiplayer and local and I was definitely not disappointed. The ability to join a lobby twice or 3 times from the same PC for 2 or 3 different people to play was also really good. Overall, that's a game worth its money, even as a "stand-alone" game (that was not a remake of something). The only flaw I can see is in the online multiplayer and it's one hard problem to fix - the ability for hosts to kick in-game players. They not only lose all their progress but there might also not have been a reason to kick them (doing it just for grief or because someone accidentally shot food). Removing that allows for AFKing and other bad behaviors which is why the in-game kicking ability is both a blessing and a curse in Gauntlet and pretty much all online games.

Tacopocalypse:
~~~~~~~~~~~~
Are you looking for a job to get you through your University studies? Maybe you are just looking at an additional income to put food on the table for your family. Have you thought of becoming a delivery person for a Mexican fast food business?  Great, we need drivers to deliver huge numbers of tacos . . . Just think Taco, Taco and only Taco! Tacopocalypse is all you need to know!
Tacopocalypse is a racing / action game where you have to deliver as many Taco orders as possible within three minutes.
As you are a new recruit, it will be a good idea to learn the ropes to become an expert taco delivery person by playing a short an easy-to-follow tutorial. After familiarising yourself with the controls, you will be able to choose to play in one of the four available maps, which are: Golden Bay Burps, Downtown, the Military Airport and the Beachside. You will only be able to carry a maximum of three serves of tacos at any given time. Locate all the taco symbols and make sure you touch them with your state-of-the-art second-hand car to make a delivery. The interesting thing is that some icons will be located on tops of buildings or even in the middle of nowhere. This is where you will need to know how to use ramps as well as your speed booster to be able to reach them. The other interesting point is that your car has a curious suspension system. Yes, your car can jump and even double jump, which can be very helpful at times, especially for avoiding collisions with other vehicles. Each time you successfully deliver an order, you’ll be collecting money which you’ll be able to use to unlock specific upgrades, paints or even for purchasing exciting new delivery cars.  There are other icons to collect, such as tape recorders (which will unlock new songs) and spray paint (which will give you access to additional paint jobs to customize your car). You will definitely run out of stock very quickly (remember, you only carry three meals in your car), so locate the pick-up point to re-stock - you can’t miss it; it’s a big yellow circle with small taco’s flying up towards the sky.
As with all good taco delivery person, stunts are in your veins and the bigger they are the better it is to boost your income.
I like the car customization; nothing too fancy but when you collect enough money, you can purchase new parts such as spoilers, antennas and others.
You can play this game on a local-network too, with three of your friends, which is a lot of fun.
The graphics are nice and the soundtrack is very good too. I would definitely recommend playing with your gamepad as I find it easier to control. I do feel that we need more content (additional icons to pick up and maps) in Tacopocalypse.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Nice artwork
-	Fun and easy to play
-	Good soundtrack
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Definitely need more contents
Tacopocalypse is a fun casual racing game.
