Arcade-style racing games seem to be making a comeback if the 2017 release calendar is any indication. Between Drift Stage, Power Drive 2000, Racing Apex, Distance, and more on the horizon, there's a lot to look forward to racing game wise, and that's not even mentioning any of the more simulation oriented racers. Here we are in March 2017, and the first of these retro driving games has finally been released from Early Access: Tacopocalypse.
Here's how Tacopocalypse works: Imagine a cel-shaded remix of Crazy Taxi with some ramps and grind rails all over the place like a classic Tony Hawk's Pro Skater map. Instead of delivering passengers to their destinations, the objective is to deliver tacos to people's stomachs (figuratively, I guess?) while the world is (literally) falling apart. Sounds like fun? Fortunately, it's quite a lot of fun, albeit a little light.
There are 3 different maps in the game (one of the maps has 2 layouts, making the total number of levels 4) and 3 different vehicles, each with their own handling properties. One carries more tacos but is more clunky to drive, while the faster & lighter car can carry less tacos, and the third is the balanced of the bunch. Each level in the main Delivery Mode starts with 3 minutes on the clock, the goal being to score as much money as possible.
Each time a taco is delivered, payment is received, like in Crazy Taxi, which can be used to buy customizations items in the shop between games. If enough tricks are performed on the way, the style multiplier will increase and each taco will give more money, like Tony Hawk's Pro Skater with its combo system, but only in appearance as the execution here is a bit different. Constant tricks are not required to keep the combo up; here, the current style score (the high score for that round) is what dictates the style multiplier. All this happens while some actually decent indie music plays in the background. The credits list 15 songs which isn't a bad number, but hopefully more will be added along with cars & maps in the future.
Considering how unique this merging of concepts is (and for the most part the execution is really solid), Tacopocalypse stands on its own as something pretty special. Unfortunately, the limited number of maps does limit the replay value a bit and there are some odd bugs and glitches here and there (getting stuck on a black screen, the music glitches out sometimes) but none of these problems are issues that couldn't be rectified with a patch or two.
This is a very original arcade driving game with fun driving, fun tricks & refreshing level design. If any of the above interests you, get it. Hopefully, the developer's plans to add more content post-launch get realized because this recommendation only gets stronger as more maps, cars & music get added.

(Preliminary Review)
Not bad for a discount fighting game. It was rather ironic that this ended up playing better with a keyboard than a PS3 controller. A word of warning: There is a wopping 6 attack buttons. I myself have only experienced fighting games with 4 individual buttons(ie. Tekkan), so this bit me for a while trying to bind controls for the controller.
This game certainly served as a reminder as to why I don't possess a large interest for arcade fighters, however it does well to help bridge the gap. A proper tutorial goes a long way, and I recommend any starting player to go through the first chapter.
I was actually surprised how easy it was to pull off some decent combos after only spending an hour on the game. The combo trees are small (granted, confusing to read) and fairly basic.
Gameplay is what you'd expect. Generic at best, but why change what isn't broken? I was actually surprised to see that there was a story mode. Though, there's very little and unique to each character (stories do not intertwine).
The game looks pretty nice and it runs great. A lot of that is thanks to its 2D approach, something I've seen a lot of fighting games get away from (for better and for worse).
As far as cons are considered, the roster is rather small. 7 characters (9 in you include the 2 DLC characters).
Truth be told, that's all I've been able to discover thus far. Not much of a con considering the game is only 15 bucks.
Overall: Fun time killer, but simply that as far as I can see. It's unique appearance masks what I ultimately see as "another fighting game" - Which it is, so that means it's doing something right.

After spending a good amount of time withing the Tutorial and playing the game in general, I can honestly say that Skullgirls is by far the BEST fighting game I have ever played. I have played Ultra Street Fighter 4, Ultimate Marvel 3 and so on, but, Skullgirls fills some holes those two left me with.
The mechanics are so far similar to Marvel which is great. The game flows very closley to that of Ultimate Marvel vs Capcom 3 as well, which works well! The only difference is there is no combo tagging in/out. Which means a Character soley relys on assists ONLY from their partner if he so chooses to have one. This, in term, make this title feel more like King of Fighters 13, which is also amazing.
The tutorial mode helps newcomers to the fighting game scene explore what the game is capable of, showing them how to play certain characters tuned to said characters styles of play. This actually helped ME out during my playthrough as I often have trouble determining what characters are what and what situations are best for them.
The storyline is different for each character and the online is nearly perfect. The only downside is that you can't play versus a CPU without being in Arcade mode. Its a bit annoying but not a huge deal.
I would also like to add this game doesn't take much to run! Which, on a machine like mine, is a huge plus!
UPDATE:
After sitting with this game as of recently I have some more stellar complaints.
This title is still good at it's core. However, the dwindling base of players made it pretty much a shoe-in for keeping in your backlog, never to be played again. The indie dev's who made this title put a lot of care into the game, which sucks because the game itself is still great!
I would reccomend a more popular title if you are looking for some solid Multiplayer action, something like Street Fighter 5 or Tekken 7 if you are in the market for a fighting game.

Game Dev Tycoon is a fun, simplistic simulation of the interesting game industry and how making games called "Booty Blasters 2: Return of Jaffar" is perfectably acceptable for Young gamers. So is a Typing game with a steering wheel.
:
-Charming, plain graphics that aren't too hard on the eyes.
-Provoking, legitimate strategy when it comes to making a successful game. It isn't just about having correct focuses such as Gameplay or Artifical Intelligence, but also properly using your game's theme in conjunction with the Rating/game console, using specially trained employees to highlight game aspects, research, etc.
-The game's difficulty and complexity growth isn't too sudden, most mechanics are pretty easy to understand when they're introduced.
-Overall charm and dialogue of the game is fun, it's clear the developers were intentional with their easter-eggs and choices.
-Mod support, though modest, is still available and can add to the experience like with many Steam games.
-There are only a couple of soundtracks used, and though they're nice the first time around, it does get a bit tiresome as they loop often.
-Replayability is a mixed bag; it's fun to try different strategies and game-styles you didn't try before, but if you know what you're doing, it can become an easy trip until the later years/consoles. Though going for certain achievements can help spice things up a fair bit.
-This is a personal note, but I find that the only way to get some of the most interesting parts, such as making an online MMO or your very own console, is to play incredibly optimally or to have the year limit higher than default. More of a nitpick than anything.
Overall, I really like Game Dev Tycoon! The price is near perfect for what the game gives you imo, and if you're a fan of tycoons or simple strategy games, this one should be right up your alley.
Just make sure to get all the bugs out of your game and you'll be golden!

Multiplayer would be nice, or at least the ability to meet up and track a friend so you both explore together like co-op play. But in regards to the game overall, well... here we go. Was it "the marketing team that screwed up"? No. Let's be honest... It's a small shop, like REALLY small. Or at least it was at the time of release. There was no marketing "team" like there would be at EA Games, Ubisoft, Sony, or any other large corporation. This was a handful of guys that came together to create and release a video game. So all these claims that it was anyone else's fault is just people grasping at straws trying to ignore the ugly truth. Every video that I watched leading up to the release of this game involved Sean Murray, and Sean Murray ONLY. There was no commercial on TV that showed false gameplay footage, and there were no misleading posters or ads. Sean went on small interviews, talk shows, etc. and discussed the game. "Sean, will I be able to ______" and he answered "yes". That's what truly bothers me. The game was released and we found that all those claims were actually false. I even scheduled time off from work months in advance, just so I could play this when it was released. I was expecting missions/quests, stealing or interacting with freighters, and earning some type of good standing with an alien race, just like Sean said I'd be able to do. But somehow that wasn't possible, the game simply didn't line up with what I was told. By the end of that first day I felt like I was playing a game still in beta. Think about it. Most of us have played games still in Alpha/Beta and that's exactly how it works: you pay full price, play the game as-is, and then you wait for the full content to be added later on down the road. Many times that content completely changes the game in a good way, allowing you to do things that you couldn't before. Well... that's No Man's Sky. The game was released and I could fly around, collect resources and... actually that's it. Now there's a "Foundation Update" where they added content in which you can interact with freighters, build a small base, and a few other things. Great! But... this game came out 4 months ago, why wasn't this in the initial release? That's because the game is in Beta. Wait, it's not? It sure feels like it.
At the end of my first day of playing, I had a moment of reflection. I stopped for a second and thought to myself, I just spent $60 on this. I had also just wasted a perfectly good vacation day. Did I feel enlightened? Did I feel like I had just played the greatest game of 2016? No, no, no, and... no. My only consolation was when I checked the reviews on Steam, just to see if maybe I was missing something. Maybe I just didn't play enough yet, or maybe I was doing something wrong? Boy was I not alone... Not only was I not alone, there were THOUSANDS of others that shared my same frustration and disappointment. Sure, there were a few thumbs up reviews and the "I think the game is great" kind of posts, but they were vastly outnumbered. VASTLY. Even to this day, almost 5 months after, the game is still "Overwhelmingly Negative" on Steam. If you're thinking of buying a game, terms such as "overwhelmingly negative" isn't what you want to see. But that's No Man's Sky. Go ahead, scroll through the other reviews. It's OK. You'll find long rants of dislike, moments of sorrow, and claims of regret from thousands of fellow gamers, much like this one. Click the "buy" button if you dare, and join the community of Beta testers.

I purchased this game during the Steam Winter Sale after the Foundation Update. Seeing all of your comments helped me in my decision. Some of you may remember a game called "starflight" from back in the early 80s - one of the first open space sandbox games created. In that game, you customized your ship, mined minerals, collected (and protected yourself against) rare lifeforms, and looked for planets for colonization - all while trying to find the "Black Egg," an ancient artifact that was triggering supernovae somewhere in the galaxy.  Fast forward to 2016, and now you have a massive galaxy (the Euclid Galaxy) that generated over (supposedly) 100 quadrillion planets and moons and allows you to mine minerals to customize your ship, scan valuable life forms (as well as plants and ores), and encounter various races - but this time instead of the Thrynn and the Velox, you have the Gek, the Vy'keen, and the Korvax.
This game teaches something: patience. You will not find every mineral you need.  You will run out of resources.  You will run out of inventory.  You will not find the last lifeform on a planet for that big bonus for a long time.  I understand - I have gotten very impatient at times, but those are minor problems compared to the larger scope of the game.  The game has improved by leaps and bounds based on what I have read before and after the Foundation Update, although I must admit making my base was almost as difficult as building a settlement in Fallout 4 - damn if I had trouble making things connect!  Nevertheless, this game brings me back to my childhood and really brought one of my favorite games into the 21st century.  I think this game is pretty good given the fact that the public's outcry and the company's response.
Bottom line: I like this game...a lot.  I'm going to play it, I'm going to enjoy it, and I'm going to finally learn that patience that has eluded me for so long.  If and when multiplayer mode comes out, I look forward to exploring the galaxy with you...and pray that I don't get my butt shot out from under me! :)

This game does homage to the Atari classic of running around dungeons, killing baddies, collecting gold, and finding keys to unlock new doors.  But the reboot also adds a bit more depth with semi-robust game mechanics with powers fueled by potions rather than being just a shooter with a "clear screen bomb"  The characters are unique and fun and have balanced strengths and weaknesses.  As someone who does not play dungeon-crawler games like Diablo or the sorts I found it fun without being overly technical staying true to its button-mashing ancestors.  And the game's levels are designed for replayability so you can keep going and upgrade all your characters.  The prologue has you learn the basics of each character.  Then you are able to play through the main game with friends or solo.
There are multiple stages.  Each stage consists of 4 levels and 3 rooms in each level.  This is with the exception of the last level which is one room containing a boss character you must defeat with skill and smarts (simple puzzles).  The room in each level consists of your basic dungeon running and fighting collecting gold and items.  The second part is a dungeon run to stay alive and avoid death's touch.  He will fade in and out throughout the map and you must try and complete it witout getting sucked into death's vortex.  The third part of each level consists of a final larger battle with hordes of adversaries that you must survive in order to complete the level.  The final level as I said is a single boss match where you have to figure out how to beat each one while not being overrun by additional hordes.
You collect coins in the game and those are used to purchase artifacts.  You can equip 2 artifacts at the same time and use them by collecting potions.  For each potion you can use one of your equiped artifacts once.  You can collect up to 5 potions.  Artifacts can be leveled up multiple times for increased effects and abilities.  If you die in mid-combat a timer appears and when it counts down to 0 you can rejoin the fight.  But you can only revive yourself if there are continue coins available.  You get revive/continue coins by killing more and more enemies.  If you run out of coins you cannot revive and as in say Left for Dead, if all players die at the same time, it's GAME OVER for the whole team.
One thing I found surprising as a avid player of the coin-op version, was that not all the characters have ranged attacks.  that is left solely to the elf and wizard.  The warrior and valkyrie are hand to hand fighters with some decent dash and range attacks but do not actually shoot any reasonable distance with primary attacks (special moves aside).
I've got 8 friends that have this game and we enjoy it very much.  It was well worth the $15 each if bought in a Steam 4-Pack and will likely be on sale by December for even less.  If you want to play it though and support the developers.  It's well WORTH the current price.

My review of gauntlet so far.... The game brings something new to the franchise while still keeping the formula that I grew up loving from Gauntlet Legends, and Gauntlet Dark Legacy. Each of the four classes plays different in a dynamic way, along with no option to play the same class when playing multi-player, while some consider it a negative thing, I believe it helps keep the team you have balanced in the dungeons, no redundancy.
** Warning Spoilers Ahead.**
Each level is divided into three Acts.
Act I - Standard, fun mobs, get loot, solve puzzles, the puzzle piece of this is the nice part, it keeps you thinking when you're fighting through hordes of enemies, rather than mindlessly pressing buttons.
Act II - It is a race to the finish, whether it be an erupting volcano, encroaching darkness, or even Death himself. You are forced to keep on your toes.
Act III - It's a hold out. Wave after wave of monsters swarm at you in a varied arena.
Relics - Powerful items that allow you to use pretty sweet abilities. Ranging from super increased attack speed to summoning mirror images of your hero for increased damage and crowd control.
Overall I would give the latest Gauntlet an 8.3/10. The only gripes I have with it, is it was no where near as lengthy that Dark Legacy or Legends. If there is ever any DLC for this game, I'd highly recommend they rebuild Gauntlet Dark Legacy Levels/story.

You've already read the other reviews.  You already know this is supposed to be an updated and modernized verion of the arcade classic.  You already know how they tried to make each character unique, with new elements: twin-stick shooting, MMO tactics, RPG progression, element-mixing magic.  You already know there's both couch and online co-op.
And you know the other reviews aren't answering the one, fundamental question.  One that's hard to vocalize without sounding trivial.  It's about something that can't be measured, can't be analyzed or quantified.  It's about a feeling, a memory.
Is this Gauntlet?  Is this *really* Gauntlet?
And the answer involves a flashback.  Sorry in advance.
1985 --  A group of 15 and 16 year-olds hits the arcade to get their videogame fix.  They were a standard 80s group of teens -- the preppie, the punk, the jock, the girl.  It was a group that didn't outwardly have much in common.  But not long ago, they discovered by accident two shared passions among them: video games, and Dungeons and Dragons.
That day in the arcade, they saw something.  Something new, something different, a game that spoke to both gamers in each of them.  Pixellated swords and sorcery.  Four, count 'em, four players at once.  Four characters, four classes, four roles.  All working towards a common goal: the next level.
These four unlikely friends each took a spot before the grand machine, somehow choosing characters in coordinated silence.  No discussion, just unspoken agreement.  The girl became Warrior, strongest of all.  The punk became Valkyrie, protector of the group.  The preppie became Elf, rogue and rebel.  The jock became Wizard, cerebral and calm.
The next hours were epic.
Fast-forward to 2014.  An old gamer sees an updated Gauntlet.  He sighs, remembering Dark Legacy and other kind-of fun but failed attempts to update and recreate the arcade classic.  But the reviews look positive, and YouTube videos show fun-looking gameplay.  What the heck, there's even a sale on 4-packs.
The next hours were epic ...
The answer is yes.
Yes, this is Gauntlet.

Reus. A great name for a great game. Reus is a sadbox game where you use giants to create and shape the world your way. If you like Minecraft, Terraria, any other Minecraft knockoffs, and any other sandbox game, you're sure to love Reus. 10/10!

I really enjoyed Reus, but I think that it often got a bit too busy, with sustaining all of your villages and completing all your projects at once, as well as not making the village greedy. Other than that, I think this game is well worth what you pay for it.

Reus is far from a bad game, but it is very difficult to actively recommend it. From personal experience during the first four hours of so I had an absolute blast trying out different combinations of powers and land types. It's quite enjoyable to unlock new structures and lands that can then help you achieve further unlocks.
Unfortunately there is a mechanic where towns will actively go to war if they suddenly get too many resources, and if ther aren't any towns to attack they will prey on your titans. At first this was a nice challenge and forced me to try to up danger levels as well put the titans other skills to use. However when building upgrades are on a time limit you're forced into the position of increasing resources and boundaries, but then if the resources you need don't produce danger you have to put up with beating down warring jackasses for the next couple of minutes until they finally simmer down.
It is unbelivably frustrating and it is unfortunate because up until that moment it was a fun game. Perhaps there was some secret method or technique I hadn't discerned to make the game less aggravating in the longer modes? I think it bears repeating that Reus is looks amazing and the general gameplay is interesting and enjoyable - up to a point. You will at least wring a few hours out of it, but if you're a completionist you will have to weather some extremely trying mechanics.

Ori and the Blind Forest is one of the most beautiful indie games you'll ever see! If you are looking for several hours of great atmosphere on a metroidvainia styled map, this is the game you wanna check out.
But there are two things I just can't stand about it:
The cringeworthy intro: In the beginning OatBF kills off a character the player has zero attachment to, in a pseudo dramatic way, which was pretty meh to be honest.
Aside from that, there is this compromise between a hard difficulty and being an absolutely mainstream jump 'n Run for the entire family. You can literally save your game after every jump, every enemy, every small puzzle and you will never run out of save points, ever. For this game to be somewhat challenging, you'd have to "make up" your own rules, limit your save points or go for 100% achievements (which is pretty darn gosh challenging tbh but I couldn't care less).
This whole save where you want mechanic takes away so much of what Ori could have been, that I just cannot recommend it for what it is.
If Ori had a normal and a hard-mode I'd recommend the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game, but with only this few segments with limited save points, there is just no need to learn from mistakes and that's just sad.
/edit: So, I feel like writing some more, so here is another point that was kind of a letdown gameplaywise:
The combat. It works, it's alright, it does it's job and looks freaking gorgeous. But sadly it lacks depth and precision. Just like every single gameplay aspect in Ori, it is a compromise, nothing more, nothing less. And here is how combat in Ori works: Stand near an enemy and mash the attack button. Auto aiming does the rest. Later on you are able to reflect enemy bullets and that is as deep as it gets gameplaywise.
Trying to appeal to every kind of player is just the wrong way to go.

This is one of the most accessible fighting games out there. Its tutorial is thorough, and robust. Not only does it teach you how to play the game, but also the general mechanics and techniques present in all fighting games. The controls are tight and fighting is quick, but not as hyper as something like MvC2.
With mechanics aside, the game looks gorgeous and performs flawlessly. The animation and characters are excellent, and chock full of personality, with references from film, anime, and other videogames. The stories for each characters are short, but are entertaining to watch and learn about.
The voice acting is great, but THE MUSIC is what stands out as the most unique feature of Skullgirls. Michiru Yamane, composer for most notably Castlevania: Symphony of the Night provides a dark, jazzy tone that syncs perfectly with the game's "dark deco" art style. There are some varying genres of music sprinked throughout, but that noir undertone is still present save for Beowulf's and Eliza's themes.
All in all, this is one of the best fighting games ever. The content you get for the price is worth in full or on sale, if you like fighting games, or want to start gittin' gud at fighting games I highly, HIGHLY recommend this game.

Stronghold is like a lot of pay2win/free2play games built on the shoulders of a franchise that used to be great.
The original games were about you building a castle while surviving all sorts of nasty things trying to rip your castle down and harm your villagers.
Kingdoms takes that concept to the next level! Now you have to defend against other humans trying to attack you and you get to attack them too! It's great fun. Yeah that's right, I said
.
Where it falls apart is that as is the norm for games of these types everything takes a very long time to build or  do...Unless you are willing to pay cash money.
Paying gives you an insane advantage over your fellow human players...At first! You see these games are played out in 'seasons' and seasons are about 4 months so if you don't join the choo-choo train immediately at the start of the season then the boundries have been drawn, alliances between players made and attacking anybody will get your castle
!
So the thing you want to do in a PvP game, which is participate in PvP, you can't do because when your castle is destroyed it can take you either lots of months and the season will be over or cost you lots of real life cash so pick your poison.
Outside of the PvP you get to build your kingdom. That's, fun? I guess? You get to pick where a garden goes? And you get to plant some quarries? Yay? Yeah the city building is shallow and boring but you will spend most of your time doing that firstly because you need too since you need the resources to actually build your castle and secondly because you very rarely get to attack players due to them all banding together to rub out anyone who opposes their rulership.
While that is true to history there are plenty of better games that are historically accurate and FUN. The PvP gimmick is fun when you get to partake in it but the rest of the experience is boring or financially costly.

To begin with, I don't like Tower Defence.  That being said, when a friend started playing Bloons Tower Defence 3, I was intrigued by the cute little monkeys and how they interacted with the world around them.  Unlike most tower defene games I've played, the game never ramps up to an 'impossible' level, forcing you to lose.  If you're clever, and you have an understanding of the monkeys you're using, any level is passable, and in fact can be beaten in different ways.
Every version of Bloons Tower Defence was an improvement on the previous version.  When BTD5 came out as a download you could purchase, I bought it.  I'd still be playing it to this day, but Ninja Kiwi informed me that, as a thank you for buying it, they would release a version on Steam, and I could install it for free.  I was actually quite suprised to see that, and quickly went to get my copy.
BTD5 on Steam is an upgrade of the version released on cell phones and tablets.  It's different from the version I was used to - and really, that's the only bad thing I can really say.  It's different.  It still has all the monkeys I'm used to, plus a few new towers I'd never seen before.  It has split up the 'upgrades' you could get between stages, with some costing 'monkey bucks' you earn by beating stages, and coins you earn by beating stages.  There's a variety of upgrades available, some slowed down in progression, while others can be snapped up instantly.  This alters the dynamic of the game, but I don't see it as a negative.
There's a favourite unit of mine (the chipmunk), which doesn't make it into the game.  I can see why - once you have the chipmunk levelled up fully it is quite the overpowered unit.  They've introduced other mercenary units you can buy, and they're interesting - so I'm curious to see what they're like when they've been fully levelled.
There's tons of different levels to play, more so than any version of Bloons I've seen, meaning I'll be at this for weeks and months.  Each stage now has at least four levels of Difficulty, plus never-ending mode, plus reverse mode, plus daily challenges, plus other challenges for you to work through.  There's a lot here to do - meaning it could be quite some time before everything has been finished.
The game allows you to save your progress on the cloud, allowing you to play between computers.  I'm quite happy for this, because the other versions didn't have this feature.  Any installation had to be a new game, and any computer that crashed and needed a fresh install lost any progress.  Now, you can play on any computer you own, and the progress is there for you.
There's also cooperative mode, which I've not tried yet - so I can't comment on this in much detail, but you can play with your friends.  I don't know if it is competitive, or allied play.
This game has a lot to offer - and will give hours upon hours of play.  I highly recommend it.

Coming from a guy who has been playing Trainz since about 2008, it seems clear that Trainz is following the footsteps of everyone else. To sum it up:
-98% of all content full-priced DLC (even if you owned the game BEFORE the DLC was added...)
-(I want to point out that while the series has had DLC in previous games, it was never this much or this pricey...)
-They were all like: "ensure there is just enough content included to allow just enough enjoyment that someone might actually purchase more DLC"
-Most content is unoptimized (in other words: graphics are rendered extremely inefficently, and often visual glitches and problems exist)
-Glitches. We need glitches. LOTS. OF. GLITCHES. (Mostly texture/shadow and sound glitches, but still glitches no less)
-Did you like the Download Station in the previous games? Well ♥♥♥♥ you, we don't like you getting free stuff. (While the DS still exists, it has been downgraded to a system no longer user-friendly and is really just a mess.)
-This game has multiplayer...I can't figure out many people who would want that.
-This game also has Co-op. Again, no clue what that's doing here.
-Variety of trains is down to about a handful of steam engines, no electrics, and six or so diesels. So much for making things fit into the surroundings...hope the Mid-West is fine with seeing Union Pacific slapped on everything.
-The variety of vans and trucks (freight cars) is mild at best. Good luck moving anything, honestly.
-Variety of coaches is even worse. Hope the passengers all enjoy second class cars with identical running numbers.
-You get one route in the UK, one in Australia, one US routes, and one or two "universal" routes. Everything else is DLC. (This includes a single German route, which is the only free DLC avalible. You get no missions with it; literally just the route and the ability to spawn a train. All missions are spammed as Pay-to-Play content)
Overall, a game that promised great potential, but really just derailed the series (pun intended). It is a shame to see that yet another company is taking the DLC route. It's gonna get to the point that years from now, games no longer exist, but rather it's just a bunch of DLC bundled under a single title. (Come to think of it, games are already starting to take that route...)
I liked when the series was so open ended, and allowed one to cram their harddrive if they wanted to with all sorts of stuff they'll use in-game maybe once. At least there was no shortage of content, no lack of things to do, and plenty of hours to be melted and burned into making routes. Now I feel like I can't even do THAT. I can't drive trains, I can't build routes the way I'd like to, and variety is nearly none. I'm sorry to say this game is such a disappointment, but sadly this is the case.

Less content than a game released in 1985. If you're going to do a reboot, at least try to reach parity with the original. Difficulty levels add absolutely nothing to the equation, merely increasing enemy health (which is lazy and definitely not content.) Enemy spawners have inflated health to begin with. Snatching gold and items before the other players is part of the charm of Gauntlet, but some of the masteries and achievements encourage bad play. Like you really want to team up with someone looking to grind their death count. There are no doodads to speak of - no teleport tiles, invisibility, or if you're familiar with the NES port, reflective shot - nothing of the sort. Some of the relics replicate those features, but you've got to grind gold to get them and fuel them with potions. The problem with potions is that they're rare, you have to share and you can't buy them in the shop. So most boss fights see zero relic use. Then there's the length: 12 areas, consisting of 36 levels and 3 bosses. In other words, an indefensible joke. The artists got their palette from a bowl of gumbo. The game looks like one of those souvenir Wild West photos you get at the boardwalk. Enjoy your stay in Brown Town. It's going to be extremely uneventful.

Very fun game. Very Gauntlet feeling. Really brings back the old school arcade action hack n slash fun.
Pros:
- Up to 4 players at once
- Smooth, fast paced combat
- Replayability via harder difficulty modes
- 4 very different classes
- Fun graphics. Easy to look at and enjoy
- Great music
- No crashes (yet)
- Only $20.
- Works amazing well with a controller
Cons:
- Limited replayability based on actual content. This game needs a map maker, or endless levels.
- 4 very different classes that are very poorly balanced with each other. Some are clearly more OP than others, which means the "competitive" aspect results in the same classes coming out on top 99% of the time for the end of level bonus.
- Hackers (hopefully they can fix this soon. At the very least, ban them and remove them from the global scoreboard.)
- Buggy class abilities cause inconsistancy and unreliability when you need them to work as they are intended.
- Obviously designed with paid DLC in mind to keep the game more replayable. (the ending credits even hint at it).
- Works pretty badly with keyboard and mouse. Awkward and limiting.
Over all, despite the cons, the game is very fun. A great game to jump in for a short to mid duration action spree with your friends. If this had been at the arcade, I would have easily spent 20 bucks in quarters just trying to beat it. So yeah, its worth the buy.

The game demands much in terms of strategic placement, as well as planning in character builds. However, the open world exploration (in the old, isometric sense) the rich, vibrant visual style, and the unique, charming sense of humor of the game thoroughly reward the investment. The game can also slow down a bit in its later sections (a desert section comes in mind) and some of the puzzles are forget-it-and-just-check-online hard and the story (though improved in the EE) can feel a bit light sometimes.
However, what sticks with me most is one of THE best character building systems in recent CRPG history (if not just CRPG) history and a game that continually was fun to return to and (after many a tough fight and occasional save scum) one of the most novel approaches to role playing seen in quite some time with the dual protagonist system.
With the sequel now rapidly approaching its likely anyone who would love this game already loves this game, but if you've been on this fence and this is on your steam list, its so very worth the time to check out. One of the greats of the new kickstarter indie area alongside Pillars and (though it has its noticable warts and striking virtues alike) Wasteland 2.

Dvinity Original Sin: EE is one of the nest RPGs made in it's time. I would give it a 9/10.
Not only is it an amazing remodel of it's original counterpart with new imporvements, but it also sticks to what made Original Sin one of the best RPGs to date.
Not only does it give you the absolute freedom a pen and paper RPG would, but it also reacts to your choices  as a real living world would. Want to teleport a chest on top of an enemy? Sure, you'll kill them wish crushing damage. Want to loot a dead man in front of his grieving wife? Sure, as long as you're okay with her attacking you because of it. And not only does it have this incredible freedom, but the story aspect is insanely well polished. There are a million ways to create and customize your character's abilities, and that plays into what type of person they are and how they react to world. Not only is all the dialogue in DOS:EE voice acted, which makes it feel like you're really invested in this real world, but also the mechanics to the story telling are amazing. Choose any nunmber of options from dialogues you wish, create your character to be whoever you see fit. And if some of your party disagrees, they'll let you know and you can argue over how to proceed in the world. All in all, it's a great game that just makes every choice matter and really nails the RPG genre. OVerall, LarianStudios really knocked it out of the park with this one.

Difficult to recommend this game, so I won't. There are a plethora of bugs still within the game, even after several patches. Purchased this game for I believe a 60% discount a long time ago.
This is one of those titles that needlessly has to run on UPlay, even though you can purchase it through steam. So any amount of hours you see on steam, can be less than the total of hours you've played (if that matters to you).
The graphics are not nearly as good as the screenshots or videos you see here on the steam page. Not that it really matters,  as it does not run very well. The game after a 2-3 hours will have a fairly consistent framerate up until that point. Afterwards, the frames just tank and become unacceptably low (20 and below).
Multiplayer is rediculous, as a well rounded character is out classed by someone who opted for damage will simply gun them down. Same thing goes for characters who opted for bonus skill (or tech or something, it's the stat that gives bonuses to skills). It seems damage in multiplayer is superior to defensive and utility stats.
Co-op uses a nice bit of artificial difficulty too. Making enemies have more health and deal more damage. This is okay for FPS games that don't rely heavily on RPG mechanics, especially when you have damage values. It eventually gets to the point where you start running out of ammunition when fighting some enemies, in a full party. Unless of course everyone specialized in damage, but if you do that no one can take point reliably. This really makes snipers useless in coop games, as they can in some cases no longer deal a sufficient amount of damage to make 1 shot kills, even if they opted for high damage.
The game gets very grindy for the end game. Running bulletin board ops (don't remember what they are called, haven't played in a long time.) The game at the end becomes a gear score check, until you hit 256. Then it's trying to grind out a build that you want. Some of  them are useless. If I recall, there is a build that lets you deal more damage to a specific type of NPCS in the game. Not even by a significant amount, I think it's around 25% more damage.
Enemies are very boring in this game. There are not a lot of different voices and some of the voice acting for them is bad. There are not a lot of variations within factions and it is not made up by having 4 factions as enemy. They have lots of creativity for the setting for this game and they didn't go far with it. Especially with some enemies just being colored in different and boom, they're in a different faction.
Navigation can sometimes be a mess. Following the map indicators can be annoying as they had a tendancy to change directions and in some cases, do a complete 180.
This is however the only game I am aware of that allows you suppress enemies. So if you are a fan of tactics, that is something that should make you consider group play.
Close to the last but not least, lets talk about progression. The game starts off great, but slowly grinds to a halt once you hit the level cap. You often can max the level of your base long before you hit max level. Although if you don't, you get a few more resources so you can do it quite quickly.
The repition levels in this game are insane. I was bored of the mission structure with the first 3 hours of the game. Why? There are not a whole lot of varied or interesting mission types. They basically examined horde mode and went, "how can we make this slightly different?" There are missions where you find a scanner and find other scanners. Kill the guy to get the civvies out. Defend against waves of enemies, with the variant of defend the things from a wave(s) of enemy(enemies.) Kill the guys to open up territory (which later will sometimes be populated with enemies, despite the mission stating that you cleaned up the streets). Things like that make missions feel meaningless. There were some missions were I felt betrayed. I recall playing this one mission with my friends, which we died about 4 times and just barely survived the fifth. After this, the area was still full of hostiles 15 minutes later, even though "we cleaned up that part of town." We all got some awful gear drops for it too, despite playing on the hard difficulty, which "guaranteed useful" gear. It was things like this that people don't mention in the reviews. Some of the other reviews I read look like they were paid by Ubisoft to say something nice about the game.
Even after all these problems I have with the game, it was still slightly enjoyable with friends. Don't bother playing this game alone though, as it's more frustrating getting flanked when playing solo. Multiplayer I hear is virtually dead, so that is something to consider when purchasing this title.
Stealth in the game is a joke. Fire one round from a suppressed weapon and you're outta stealth. Doesn't matter if the shot connects. Could be different now, as I have not played this game since mid 2017. This is really disappointing knowing that Ghost Recon Wildlands has the same engine (albeit somewhat tweaked) and the stealth (though very cookie cutter) is marginally better compared to this game.
I sat down for a few days trying to come up with a decent paragraph for the story. I couldn't. The majority of the story happens in the opening cutscene in the game. I almost want to say that the reveal of this game, from several years ago I might add, spoil the "juicy" details. Main "story" missions are side quests. Sure there are bits of dialogue you hear from characters, but the "side" missions give just as much, if not more. It really does not help that they space the game story missions out. You should never have to be locked out of a story mission because of a gear or level check. That is just a failure of game design. Sure you can argue that this game is an RPG, but some of the best RPG's ever made do not do this. If they do, the level requirement can often be reached while playing just the story. If I recall, this is done in the Witcher 3. Which is a game I would have rather played than spending 20 hours on here by myself. All this being said, there is some story in here. Thematically, they do a decent job. It's difficult for a reviewer to give input on something that is basically not there. So the summary for the story is more so for the theme of the game and not the actual story.
I think the game could be worthwhile during  a 75% or higher sale. This would include the DLC's, otherwise I would leave them out. I would not purchase any of the DLC's as some of the game modes provided from them have little to no player base remaining. Not to mention the season pass is quite expensive. Even though this game was released almost 2 years ago, $70 CAD (price as of now says $54.60 in USD from a currency conversion, but I imagine it's probably $55-$60 USD) is still way too much for this game. Ubisoft will never swallow their pride and continue to hope that the "free content" (which is probably why they jusitfy the near release price) will carry the game.
TL;DR
Bugs, grinding, sub-par "story," suppression, mild enjoyment in coop and repitition. A high percentage sale of 75% might be worth your time.

It's like "Clash Royale". A perfect mix between MOBA, TCG and RTS genres, where your hero is your base (every hero is unique) with abilities that you unlock by exping during the match, and your cards are your minions; they differ in attack speed, HP, movement speed, attack range, abilities, stealth, flying or non-flying minions. You are free to unleash them everywhere on your side of the battlefield, but not on the enemy side; choosing good counters against the enemy minions is very important and positioning is important as well. The bridges of the arenas are two control points that generate exp over time.
I find that this game is well done under all aspects: good gameplay, humor and quality.
The devs are friendly and very active.
Is it Pay-to-Win? NO, NO, and NO. Just play.
Golds and cards are earned by exploring in Expeditions mode (which is a large map where you need Supplies to make a step). You are rewarded with Supplies by completing daily quests or by winning PvP matches. Golds are also used to open chests with the tokens that you buy in the shop, and materials are used to craft cards or to buy heroes. You can salvage unused cards to earn materials.
Also, there is a classic hero rotation and a free chest is guaranteed every day.

I don't have a lot of time in with TANE, but here's some early thoughts.
Trainz 12 played ok, but was laggy (I'd get a screen freeze for a few seconds every few minutes.)
Trainz 2016 (TANE) is 100 percent better. No lags at all. And it switches views quickly, including coming in and out of the map. The physics engine (how the trains react) just feels better too.
There are new navigation aids that keep you from being surprised by a station stop when you don't know the route very well. And with the sliders in the default positions the scenery is much better than the previous version and gone seems to be those funny looking wiggling trees. However, now and again when moving the view around with the mouse I'll get a few trees and such popping up out of nowhere, but again not as much, or as bad, as with T-12.
You could easily go broke buying DLC for this sim but there's more than enough right out of the box to keep you busy. And although I haven't tried it much the route builder (Surveyor) works better according to what I've read.
One thing that's gone from the previous T-12 (at least for me) is when looking ahead there's a point (like a horizontal line) where the track's wooden ties are rendered but passed that line they aren't. And I found that really annoying. But that's gone now in TANE.
One thing about sims like this is you have to be really into the subject matter to get the most out of it. I can't tell you how much time and money I've put into flight simming over the last 30 years or so and I know I'll never get that deep with TANE, or any train sim, but it has that kind of depth if you go that route.
I would have liked to see a way to “free move” around the engine cabs like you can in most flight sims, and I think I've heard of a mod for that but haven't taken the time to look into it. However, I've read in the TANE manual there's a way to customize the various view points so that's somewhat of a  improvement.
The passengers on the platforms are still the same lifeless souls (that could have certainly used some improvement.) And while some down-board say there's no new sounds I'm pretty sure I've heard a few new engine and track noises right off the bat.
IMHO, If you put a lot of time into Trainz-12 even with all the lags and flaws you deserve to get TANE!

The story is about two doctors who provide a service to people on their deathbeds. This service they perform is where they go into the person’s memories and change events in their head so that it concludes how they would prefer. The game is focused on one such patient and uncovering pieces of his past. There’s some interesting subjects brought up in the game, about life and death. About the moral and philosophical questions brought up about what these two are doing and the actions with regards to the patient. That being said, I feel like this is a game best experienced by yourself. It's not a story I really want to get into or dissect, as I feel that takes away from the experience. I won't deny that this is a bit of a cop-out but at the same time, that's why I don't usually cover titles like To the Moon all that often. I find them difficult to cover.
The gameplay amounts to you finding certain important items on the level and advancing the story along. There’s not a lot that you, the player, can do when it comes to this game. A lot of the game expects to be watched and read, so there’s not much variance to the experience worth nothing. I get that narrative-driven games are like this, but, it’s getting more and more tiresome.
Settings for this game are extremely lacking. No resolution options (it runs in a 640x480 resolution), v-sync option is hidden away in the game properties menu which is only accessible by pressing F1 in-game (not something that’s made immediately clear I might add). Keybindings can be changed for both controller and mouse + keyboard though. There are separate volume sliders as well.
The graphics are a 2D pixelated affair, with a top-down jRPG-like camera angle. Music is an instrumental affair with a lot of solo piano and strings. It works well to create a morose sort of weight to the game.
Side note: the free DLC story that comes with To the Moon doesn't play on anything but Windows. It's ok, a nice little freebie.
To the Moon is pretty good. The story certainly has its feels and the game is laser focused on telling a tight story. I’ll give them credit that despite being a passive observer for the majority of it, they clearly knew what they wanted to tell. It’s not an entirely passive affair but the most you’ll end up doing is finding items to advance the plot along, moving around rooms and talking with people. There’s some interesting philosophical and ethical questions about death that are brought up as well. Other than that, what’s left to say...

Without spoiling too much, To The Moon tells a short yet captivating story on the work of 2 scientists to fulfil a dying man's wish; a trip to the moon. While being a primarily narrative experience, To The Moon has excellent pacing; balancing legitimately touching moments with intrigue, drama, humor as well as with short gameplay elements that lead to the game being always compelling. The plot is never too complicated without feeling dumbed down to audiences; it requires you to pay attention but is not hard to follow. The highly detailed pixel art is often quite impressive, but is heavily overshadowed by the amazing soundtrack; it very easily ranks as one of the greatest in video game history.
Overall, To the Moon is an experience truly worth checking out; however it is important to note that this is a
moreso then a traditional video game. However; do not let that hold you back from playing To the Moon,  as this is truly one of the best stories presented in the video game medium

(Written from a first impression as a huge fan of Minecraft:) This is a beautiful game visually, but the interface needs a lot of work, in my opinion, as to be expected from a game still in testing.
PROS: Visually amazing. Ability to go anywhere and build anything out of Legos. This is the meat of the game and is why I think it could be a fantastic game.
CONS: This may as well be a wishlist for features!
Interface is not customizable at all.
1. It seems currently designed with the mouse only in mind. I'm left-handed and my WASDs are really JIKLs, but not in this game. One mechanism of moving is the left-click + mouse movement which feels a little awkward. You don't actually need a keyboard to play the game at all by this design.
2. The moving mechanism is not like your typical FPS or Minecraft with the combination of mouse movement at keys.
3. Character is third person and can get in the way of what you'd like to do. Toggling 3rd person vs. 1st person would be great.
Lego placement is rather frustrating
1. As everything it its own shape, getting the Legos in the place you like can take some time. I could not find keyboard controls to nudge placement, which would REALLY help speed things along.
2. The character can get in the way. To get a piece in the correct place, I would try zooming or moving, then the character would fall into lava and die and the screen would keep changing positions.
Again, this game when it's ready for full release seems like it will be amazing. Visually it's practically perfect, but the point of this to to explore and build, not just to admire the scenery, and I feel that aspect needs a lot of work. I'd recommend it, but keep in mind it's still in development.
It's weird, I know the Lego game is trying to distinguish itself from Minecraft, but I kind of wish the interface was more like Minecraft!

I wrote a review months ago and after adding another 100 hours to my time played, I thought I'd re-review it.  Personally, it's not worth $60.  $30 tops.  But if the game was priced at $30, I'd say it was a really cool game, especially with the Pathfinder update.  The land vehicles rock and I can't wait until they are implemented on other planets.  It sucks that they are locked on your home planet, but it does make exploring super fun.  I really like the Pathfinder update.  I still wish other planets were more fleshed out.  It's gets pretty old when you go to another planet only to find it's more like an uninhabited moon.  I'd also like to see more aliens (not animals) inhabiting the planets, and some of them being aggressive.  It would be cool to see tribes who attack players (such as the morloks in HG Wells Time Machine), or civilizations of aliens with towns/cities.  Honestly, the alien interaction in this game sucks.  You find one alien in a small compartment and you either do what he likes and get something or you♥♥♥♥♥♥him off.  Sometimes I just want to blow him up, but you can't do that.  Hello Games, make interesting aliens please.  They suck.  I also wish there were quests on the different planets which would not only flesh them out, but also give you something to do on the planets.  I realize that's probably not possible being an infinitely procedurally generated world, but hey, I guess that just sucks too.  Oh well.  While there is a lot to be done to even make it worth $60, it is a fun game to explore.  I'd wait until there is a deal on it before buying it.  There needs to be much more content before I'd buy it at $60 (Btw, I didn't pay $60.  I waited for a deal).  I will say this, with the updates Hello Games have put out, if they keep these updates with these kinds of changes, this could be a fantastic game, and maybe worth $60, but that's a huge maybe. Right of the bat, let me say this: some people disagree that Reus is categorized as a “God Game”. It is different from the Black and White series (considering by many the gold standard of the genre), or even From Dust, since you don’t control directly a God or Entity.
Instead of controlling a God, you have full control of 4 giants. Each of them have different abilities, weakness and strengths. Working together, they  mold a deserted and inhabited planet by terraforming or creating resources. When resources are laid and combined with several symbiosis, human settlers will appear and so begins the journey to transform the once deserted planet into a beautiful and lustful planet, full of civilized beings.
Because of the way the game works, it is more like a “resource managing, strategic planning and puzzle solver” kind of game. Since humans can become greed, you can’t give them a lot of resources, or they can destroy the other towns around them. In order to grow and become more developed, the villages need to complete project that demand different kind of resources or pre-requisites. This is the main objective of the game: give humans enough resources to complete projects, but don’t let them become greed. Know
Every game run is a 30 min, 1 or 2 hours Era, in which you will need to accomplish several achievements to unlock new resources and new projects. The game is very achievement and objective oriented, although you can “Free Play” it just for fun. The good part is the achievement fits very well with the game mechanic, you don’t have to go out of your way or grind and do repetitive tasks to get them. Your drive to have more resources, more prosperity, more projects is enough to motivate you to keep going. When an Era finishes and you start a new one, a brand new deserted planet will be generated and you and your 4 giants will start form scratch.
The game artwork and soundtrack are both amazing! I do have the soundtrack in my Spotify right now, for example. It is worth to listen to it by itself. The artwork is extremely well done, colorful and beautiful.
I liked this game so much that I dedicated several hours of my free time to translate it from English to Brazilian Portuguese, in a community effort. When I was playing it (now I achieved everything and did everything I wanted to do), it overshadowed several AAA+ games that I have in my Library.
Unfortunately, I don’t think there is a patch, DLC or Expansion on the way. The game is what it is. The Devs said time again that they think it is better to do a brand new Reus game them tweak on it gameplay right now (and I agree with them).
Also several people reported technical difficulties, mostly Mac users. The bright side is that the Devs are present (even on Steam Forums) and always try to solve the problems at hand, with good results sometimes.
Overall, this game is worth it. It is a extremely well made game, fun to play and challenging. If you see it on a Bundle (it is on Humble Bundle sometimes) or a good offer, consider buying it!

Ive played alot of games in my time, though short it has been. some innovative, some revolutionary, some very beautiful and touching. But this game, among many others, tried to do something that has become a trend of indie's lately: It is trying to be "more" than it actually is. I say this because this game has LOADS of content. so many unlockables and achievements and fun things that just look pretty. But thats where the list of good things ends (except maybe the controls, which by the way are flawless IMO). Ive played enough of this game to unlock 90% of everything and found myself wanting more, which is not a good sign. Dont get me wrong, this game is amazing and i WOULD recommend this game... if there wasnt a lack of solid story. The only actual story is the tutorial... yes you read that right. I love games that let you craft your own story and make a new world each time, but this isnt that. This is a game that allows you to build and build and build until you cant build no more (or run out of time). But there is no objectives (except those that are required for a building) and there's no element to this game that truely makes this game stick out other than an interchangable/interlinking environment. Sounds very nice doesnt it? Well it is, for 5 minutes. Then its a hassle to deal with.
So to wrap this up im going to finish with my honest opinion of this game: Its beautiful, its a great time waster, and it can be a good stress-reliever. But that isnt enough for this to be considered a good, long-lasting game. Buy it if you'd like. In the end you'll come to the same conclusion i have.

This game is a must buy for anyone that is a fan of RPGs and one of the best RPGs available for the PC. The art style is very easy to look at and is one of those styles that will never look old. The animation effects during battles are all awesome to look at. The sounds make every hit and effect seem very powerful. It's not something easy to explain, until you experience it for yourself.
As the title of this game says, the main focus is on the epic battles throughout the game. Lots of care and attention to detail has been put into the battle system. Gone are the random encounters from outdated RPGs. You see every enemy on the screen now and can choose whether to fight it or not. As soon as you touch an enemy, the battle instantly loads. No more waiting around for loading times.
The combat system has so much depth. There are *a lot* of different strategies you can use to fight enemies in this game. Different equipment, elemental effects/resistances, skills, crafting and items are all very important in taking down enemies. The boss battles are very epic and will challenge you to see if you have been learning how to play efficiently. You will spend a lot of time figuring out what equipment and skills to use for taking down a boss.
Postgame has the optional Battle Mountain area. Always thought it would be a great idea if RPGs would include a way to fight every enemy in the game during some marathon battles? Welcome to Battle Mountain. Where all normal encounters, minibosses and bosses are thrown into some very difficult battles to test just how good at this game you truely are. Not to mention the extremely difficult new enemies created for that section of the game.
Love collecting achievements in games? This game has over 100 Medals/Achievements waiting to be unlocked. The music is some of the best I have ever heard in a game. You will definately find at least a few songs that you think are amazing. It fits every area and encounter so perfectly. There is also a New Game + mode where you can carry over all your equipment and skills. Enemies will level up and everything will be even more difficult this time around.
There are so many things this game did right for an RPG. You are truely missing out on a great RPG, if you don't give this a try.
You will spend around 50 hours trying to complete it.

by reading that title you're probably gonna assume it's a Final Fantasy knockoff, but don't be so quick to drop this game!
Gameplay:
you explore around the game's map in a zelda/dragon quest style overworld map,
you can use arrow keys/WSAD to move on the maps, but in combat it's mouse only (no gamepad support)
the game is a turn based RPG, battles aren't random, but instead you run into an enemy to engage them in battle,
combat is done with 4 party members, 3 of which are active in battle and one is the backup that you can switch in without wasting a turn, and also recovers their HP/MP while in backup.
you got your nature based archer Anna, your cliche powerful swordsman Matt, the well-endowed mage Natalie, and the crazy gun maniac and tank summoner Lance.
you defeat your enemies using all of your many equipments: weapons, clothes, accessories, Flairs which each have their own resistances/elements (there's a lot!) and they all can be upgraded to increase their effectiveness, not only that but you got skills and magic at your disposal as well!
each enemy has different weaknesses/resistances that you NEED to pay attention to, unless you wanna do 0 damage, or worse, HEAL your enemies by accident, luckily you can "scan" enemies using your summoned scanbot which forever allows you to see their weaknesses/resistances.
each character has their own skills to learn that are unique to each one, but there's also skills that are shared between them, but only ONE can use them so you'll have to plan around this a bit, you can forget skills if you really need to.
there's also "limit breaks" not unlike a FF game you charge your limit guage by taking damage and unleash powerful moves, like a rapid-hit sword slash combo, summoning a space ion-cannon, or fully healing your party
and then you can use summons, which use SP that you gain from defeating enemies, like a dog that throws healing items to you, an Ice elemental that freezes enemies, and a cat with no legs that slashes everyone, and later on even summon boss monsters to your side!
oh and there's quests that require you to grab certain (rare) items and bring them to NPCs, cause they're too lazy to do it themselves!
Music/sound:
this game's soundtrack is what makes it a little more unique, of course it's all original and done by an awesome artist (BTW soundtrack comes with the steam game!) it really sets the mood of the game.
if you've played the flash game, the quality of both sounds and music are a LOT better on this version!
Graphics:
if you're looking for awesome 3D graphical eye-gasms... well you might not enjoy this
but if you like hand-drawn 2D sprites and comical anime-style character designs this game has all of that!
don't worry though the graphics are pretty well done for what they are, with idle animations for both party members and enemies alike, no static combat sprites here! and a lot of the skill/limit break animations are awesome!
I should mention the entire game was originally designed in adobe flash, but personally this has to be one of the best flash graphics I've seen!
again, this version has better graphics quality from the flash game. with resolutions up to 1280x800 and fullscreen!
Difficulty:
this game has an adjustable difficulty from 4 settings, that you can change at ANY TIME.
believe me when I say it makes the difference of a cakewalk 10 hour game, to uber insane Bosses that 1-hit KO the unprepared!!
the games difficulty changes the enemy stats by a percentage, making them have more/less HP and do more/less damage to you
Easy (50%) normal (100%), hard (150%), Epic (200%)
you get the same EXP, money and AP regardless of difficulty, some achievements require you to play on epic that's all.
Replayability:
other than different difficulties, the game has a "second quest" and "third quest" mode which is basically the same game again but with higher level enemies. and also has a new game+ so you can play again and again while still keeping your levels, AP, and equipment.
there's a bonus area called Battle Mountain, that holds extra bosses and challenge battles, including one that puts you against  multiple bosses back to back!
also you can try to finish every quest, learn every skill to max, and forge all your equipment to max, and reach lv99 if you wish to do so.
Summary:
even though it started as a flash browser game, it has to be one of the most AWESOME flash RPGs i've played, and in some ways better than a lot of mainstream RPGs.
this steam version includes  all the "premium" features from the browser version, with better sound and graphics quality, and allows you to transfer saves from the browser game to the steam game! (read in forum how to do this)
it's pretty damn entertaining, the game makes jokes on itself and the dialog, both in battle and out, can be fun to read.
but, damned if your first encounter with "God Cat" won't catch you off guard, and it'll quickly remind you why this game is called EPIC battle fantasy!!

When I saw this game, I thought it was another generic Steam RPG, you know the kind. But my friend convinced me to buy it so we could play co-op and hot damn, was it a good time.
The environments are interesting and varied, with lots of places to explore with lots of side quests.
The addition of voice acting was a huge plus, it would have been such a pain to read all the dialogue.
The combat is especially choice, turn based combat much like Fallout 1 & 2. There are some really challenging areas. However, you can find that beating a high level dungeon can make you overpowered for the next area. Initially I found it a little tedious with a lack of direction in the very early game (within the walls of the first town) but that I think was a lot to do with being new to the genre and not paying attention to the smaller details (rushing through dialogs mostly).  Once I got back to it and got into the story this has been one of the best games I've played, and the only one I've persevered with to 100% of the achievements. I can't stress enough how great this game is. It's a unique title for the RPG genre, in my opinion. The combat has a vaguely similar feel of old style Dragon Age insofar as the bird's eye tactical view, but it's turn based in what reminds me of a Final Fantasy Tactics style, sans the grid. Each unit will act in a specific order (based on an individual character's speed and perception) and you have impeccable control over your environment.
While the awesome combat mechanics are definitely what put this game beyond a lot of others in my eyes, the way you can approach quests, build your characters, employ clever gimmicks to solve puzzles, and generally interact with the game is unlike anything else I've come across in modern RPGs. The co-op is an experience, too, especially if you get a laugh out of screwing each other over in a round or two of combat. That can get really goofy, it's a good time. Oh, I should mention that the soundtrack is excellent, too.
I guess my only "complaint" about this game is that the story was good, but not the best I've ever come across. If not for the variety of ways you can influence your own experience, I might like it less. But really, the premise is good, the build-up is good, the primary cast of characters makes for an interesting introduction and progression. It's helped along a lot by some great voice acting and world-building. I was indifferent to some of the secondary protagonists though, and I ended up foregoing the companions altogether in my solo tactician playthrough. But I wanted a challenge, so it wasn't completely to do with the characters themselves.
Overall, Divinity: Original Sin - Enhanced Edition is a hell of an experience and I'd recommend it to anyone who enjoys RPGs and a more tactical style of combat.

Positives:

Negatives:
FIRST 5-10 HOURS OF THE GAME ARE VERY SLOW! May turn people off but I promise if you can slog through it, the game is well worth it afterwards. The main plotline is mediocre, it is serviceable but nothing to praise, it's really held up by the dialogue of the characters and the world itself just being all around intersting. The difficulty (especially in tactician mode) can feel extremely unbalanced, you can be doing great throughout a section of the map but then run into a boss enemy that seems to have the upper hand on every single aspect of the combat, a GODLY amoung of AP, extremely outnumbered 3 somtimes 4 to 1, hits like a tank, have powers to completely skip your teams turn, etc etc. It can feel down right cheap, especially to new players of the genre. There are some bosses where i felt that if you did not exploit the AI it would just be impossible to beat, even with a strong capable team and a good understanding of the mechanics.
All in all, a great RPG that is barely held back by some minor and 1 annoying set back. IF you are a fan of RPGs and are looking for something juicy to sink your teeth in after playing AAA games like The Witcher 3, this game is most definitley for you, also try Grim Dawn and Pillars of Eternity!
Overall score 8/10. 2 points off the long and slow start through the city of Cyseal which you kind of have to go through since you are not strong enough to venture outside the city in the beginning and the unbalanced difficulty that can feel real cheap at times, even for a veterean Souls player like me. But it is still a great game that any true RPG fan should try!!

-One Year Review-
As of today (4/24/16), it has been one year since I have purchaed T:ANE.
Within this time, I have logged 550 hours + and still adding more. When I had gotten T:ANE, it was in the later state of the Beta builds, when I had gotten it, I find it was pretty well set up, but could use more, or minor tweaks here and there.
I forget exactly how I had the money at the point, but at that time I was looking for a good train sim to get for myself, it was a toss up between TS2016 at $30 and T:ANE Deluxe Edition at $70. I'm glad I chose to get T:ANE.
I have recently gotten a copy of TS2016, and I honestly feel a touch confused with it, to me it doesn't seem to be as user friendly as T:ANE. Maybe I need to do a bit more digging around on TS2016 to find out how it all works, it's editor is weird to me anyways, it doesn't have the nice tabs along the side of the screen for exactly what you want like T:ANE does, it won't let you place custom consists or make custom consists while in editor like T:ANE does.
In my mind the only things TS2016 has going for it is graphics, steam workshop, and the amount of centralized DLC, which costs a fortune. T:ANE may not have a lot of routes, or locomotives, or content in general, but it has one of the biggest things any game can have, user friendliness.
I have seen this game rise and fall with the updates to it, I honestly don't understand the hate towards T:ANE. Granted yes, there are a few things they could do to improve the game. I have seen them starting to centralize the DLC a bit more, give to the public what they want, and doing what they can to keep the game series alive.
To sum it up in quick points of what I feel T:ANE is:
Pros:
- User Friendliness
- Easy to understand route surveyor
- Flexability in what you can do in the game
- "most" models are pretty outstanding in detail and fleshed out (e.g. the SP SD45)
- Staff are helpful
- Tons of free stuff (300,000+) on Download Station
- A test track to test the limitations of your locomotives and see a readout of performance
Cons:
- Some models need to be fleshed out a bit more (e.g Payware DLC TUME BN SD40-2)
- Not a ton of base content
- Needs more centralized DLC, easy to access.
Suggestions:
- Keep centralizing the DLC for ease of access.
- A separate DLC tab on the main screen, rather than going into a route to check it out.
- Put a Visit Test Track button on the launch window.
- Remove 'Connot Edit' lock on DLC routes, We bought the route, I think we should be able to edit it.
DLC Suggestions:
- We need a Union Pacific Dash 9 44CW
- We need Union Pacific's Moffat Tunnel Subdivision.
*hint hint* ;)
Overall review 8/10.
Thank you for the work and keeping this series alive.
-BT

(Written from a first impression as a huge fan of Minecraft:) This is a beautiful game visually, but the interface needs a lot of work, in my opinion, as to be expected from a game still in testing.
PROS: Visually amazing. Ability to go anywhere and build anything out of Legos. This is the meat of the game and is why I think it could be a fantastic game.
CONS: This may as well be a wishlist for features!
Interface is not customizable at all.
1. It seems currently designed with the mouse only in mind. I'm left-handed and my WASDs are really JIKLs, but not in this game. One mechanism of moving is the left-click + mouse movement which feels a little awkward. You don't actually need a keyboard to play the game at all by this design.
2. The moving mechanism is not like your typical FPS or Minecraft with the combination of mouse movement at keys.
3. Character is third person and can get in the way of what you'd like to do. Toggling 3rd person vs. 1st person would be great.
Lego placement is rather frustrating
1. As everything it its own shape, getting the Legos in the place you like can take some time. I could not find keyboard controls to nudge placement, which would REALLY help speed things along.
2. The character can get in the way. To get a piece in the correct place, I would try zooming or moving, then the character would fall into lava and die and the screen would keep changing positions.
Again, this game when it's ready for full release seems like it will be amazing. Visually it's practically perfect, but the point of this to to explore and build, not just to admire the scenery, and I feel that aspect needs a lot of work. I'd recommend it, but keep in mind it's still in development.
It's weird, I know the Lego game is trying to distinguish itself from Minecraft, but I kind of wish the interface was more like Minecraft!
