A really great update to the classic Gauntlet. Each class feels unique with different moves and manuevers.

So 3 of my friends and myself gave the game a go last night. For $15 bucks (each) and based on past Gauntlet games {Legends and Legacy} we figured it was worth a go. Traditional Gauntlet games get a ton of replay value so the $15 should merit that. In either case let me break into the actual review
Gauntlet starts you off by having you play each class; Warrior, Valkyrie, Elf/Archer and Wizard.
Warrior plays like in the typical hack and slash style. Valkyrie feel very Captain America'esc but still hack and slashy. Elf/Archer plays like a character from Smash TV. Lastly Wizard plays like Invoker from Dota 2 (to elaborate you have 9 spells and based on what elements you combine {Lightning, Fire, Ice} you get a different spell with each spell having its own cooldown). With each unique character you sort of get a different button schema. Where Warrior and Valkyrie (I might need clarification on this) smash buttons. The Elf/Archer and Wizard utilize the right analog.
Once you go through the tutorial you have the ability to start a game or begin a lobby. The lobby system is fantastic. There's no shift tabbing into the steam community to select a person's profile to invite them into a game. You simple click the button to open lobby (for me it was 'Y' on the Xbox control or 'X' on the PS3 based on the conversation software). and it brought up a list of friends currently playing Gauntlet who I could invite. The only gief is I wish it only brought up friends who have / are playing Gauntlet. I still get my full list of steam list friends which I think is silly.
Each selection is unique so can't have two Warriors or Valkyries etc. Once your in the game you have worlds to choose from... there's only 3 worlds with 4 levels so that was sort of a let down from the get go.
Also in the lobby you decide on your difficult. Easy is like a light version of Normal so you have more health and monsters are not as strong. Normal you get infinite number of re-spawns. Hard requires that you have tokens to re-spawn other players and Unfair you simply don't re-spawn and food rarely/never(?) exist. We went with Normal for our play-through.
There's also a shop that sells artifacts however to use the artifacts you must use potions you find in the level. So potions are no longer a generic AOE effect but are used in conjunction with artifacts. Shops items can also be upgraded and few items no longer have the 'one time use' feel. This gives potions sort of a customized feel however ultimately make them useless on boss as no potions spawn on those fights.
Another thing that doesn't exist in the shop now is 'stats'. 'Stats' or any sort of character enhancement is gained by spamming a specific character skill (typically bound to a button or in the Wizards case combine two buttons to make a spell). Other character enhancements (which are called Masteries) are gained through eating food, dying and collecting gold provide a passive bonus rather than active.
As to the actually game play...it felt super linear at first and unfortunately stayed that way for most of the game. There was very few 'whoops we went the wrong way' or 'did we miss something'. If such situations occurred it was a result of a bad camera angle hiding a wall that wasn't visible rather than a puzzle to figure out.
There's of course game elements to try to lighten the mood like players can light barrels of TNT on fire and throw it at friends or destroy food that a friend is about to pick up. There's also preset emotes that players can spam at each other. While were on emotes the characters periodically compliment each other when they get a long kill streak...this is 'cute' at first but due to its frequency gets old fast. The last sort interactive element was the crown which when worn gives the player at the end a gold bonus. However if they get hit the crown drops and another player can pick it up.
Level 1 and 2 of each world was typically presenting the theme. Level 3 was typically a small boss battle arena and level 4 was purely focused on the boss. Bosses were a hybrid of spamming the attack key and figuring out puzzles.
So general flow of the game was 'pick a world' -> 'pick a level' -> 'playthrough it' -> 'return to town' -> 'debating on buying artifacts' -> 'pick a world' repeat.
Now with all that said would I recommend picking up the game... probably not at it's current release price or I would definitely split the $15 bucks among several people and play it via Local. Even then not enough bang for the buck for me to recommend it.
As a group of 4 players we beat the game in about 4.3 hours. It really emphasizes on 'party play' and I could see it getting frustrating solo. There's no 'true' leveling system so you don't really feel the progression. You get a new skill to spam or your cool downs on a spell are reduced but your overall power still feels 'fixed'. As I mentioned before there are 'artifacts' that you can buy with gold earned in game but they are nothing game breaking.
Once you complete the game you do unlock cosmetic items however they require that you use in-game gold to buy them... so your reward for completing the game on a certain difficulty is unlocking an item in which you have to grind the levels you just beat to get the gold to buy the cosmetic item....yeah...no.
On a few minor notes there's a few times where death shows up which leads to comical deaths (Death no longer drains he simple kills you) but is quickly forgotten. There's no alternative classes like Tigress, Jester, Minotaur and etc. After we finished playing we expected that they would be DLC or something silly. Pojo (aka EGG911) is not in the game as well as 'X IS NOW IT' system is out as well.
The novelty and hopefully nostalgia you hope to draw out the game is typically gone after the first few hours. At its core it took what made the Gauntlet series unique and made it feel like a generic hack and slash.
Oh one last thing before I close this out...the soundtrack is okay but nothing stellar or to write home about.

A great co-op dungeon crawler experience.  Fans of the classic arcade games (or the re-release of Dark Legacy for the GCN) may find themselves a bit lost, however.  Gone are the days of defending the realms from the demon Skorn, hunting down the traitorous Garm, and the great wizard Summner no longer is even a part of the game.  Instead, players meet Morak, an underdeveloped character with no story whose only purpose is to "summon the gauntlet", be a disembodied voice, and inevitably turn evil for the last boss fight.  A bit underwhelming compared to the expansive and varied play, along with the great non-linear explorable maps, that existed in this game's 1998 arcade counterpart.
Boss fights have also undergone huge changes, some for the better and others for worse, compared to the 1998 classic that everyone playing this game knew and loved.  As mentioned above, levels are extremely linear, with no alternate paths to explore or depth to plunge into using extra keys (stages now have EXACTLY the correct amount for each locked door).  However, this also means that all the puzzles that existed in the first 2 iterations of this game are gone, making levels very repetitive, and more importantly also removing the ability to hunt down items of power to use against bosses.  Instead, boss fights are now broken up by phases, not unlike bosses in WoW or Diablo 3.  While this makes boss fights interesting (and often times very hectic) it doesn't come across as a change that the game needed to undergo, and pulls away even more from the nostalgic value of the game, one of the biggest traits this title had going for it.  Couple this with the fact that not a single boss from the classic Gauntlet titles makes it over to this game, and players will find themselves feeling very confused as to why the developers made so many unnecessary (and sometimes just plain bad) changes to a loved game franchise.
Players will still get to enter into the depths of the "Gauntlet" as one of the four classic characters they remember: The warrior, the valkyrie, the archer (he is NOT the "Elf", he's the damn ARCHER, talk about a fantasy stereotype sellout move), and the wizard.  All of these characters have undergone a number of drastic changes, but the developers did a fantastic job of keeping the core aspects of each class intact while simultaneously removing the outdated (and oftentimes unwieldy) inventory and character statistics (hp, str, def, etc).  The warrior has retained his might cleaving spin, the valkyrie's high defense has carried over into the acquisition of a shield toss and shield block, and the archer is still an archer (and still not an "Elf).  The greatest changes came to the wizard, who now can transmute combinations of 3 different elements in order to access a wide variety of skills (those who enjoy playing Invoker in DotA/Dota2 will recognize these mechanics).
The game is plagued, however, by a very prominent lack of communication and lacks even the most basic of chat features.  While this was also true for the classic 1998 game, all 4 players were at a single machine during those times and could simply speak to each other.  Now, with no form of voice or text chat, you'll find yourself quickly kicking players mid game who don't follow your unspoken, incommunicable  plans so that the group can continue pressing forward.  With players now ALL playing together through online connectivity, this is nothing more than a simple "dropping the ball" moment on the part of the developer, and is hopefully something that will get fixed soon either in a patch or (if they like to scam people as much as EA) in a DLC.
Speaking of DLC, it can't come fast enough.  With only 3 "realms", and each realm only having 3 stages and a boss fight, the game is CONSIDERABLY shorter than the previous games in the gauntlet series.  With the lack of runestones to collect, lack of realms to explore (and lack of depth to the stages), lack of stained glass shards to grab from the bosses, no battlefield at the tower (hiding that last elusive runestone), and no final trip into hell to purge the ultimate evil the only thing we can wonder is... why the hell did our characters even bother coming to this dungeon in the first place?  Hopefully in the near future, this will all be addressed in the form of DLC.  All we can do is hope that the developers truly love the Gauntlet franchise enough to bring back the large, iconic realms and bosses that we all remember and love... even if that means having to pay another $5-$10 for the 4-8 realms (depending on the version of the game you previously played) that were inexplicably left out.
Even with all the awkward changes made, and content that was left out, this is still a GOOD hack & slash co-op experience.  It's not winning any awards in its current state however.  All we as fans of the true Gauntlet can do is hope that WB and Arrowhead love this franchise enough to bring back everything fans remember and loved about the classic games in DLC, changing this into a GREAT hack & slash co-op experience.  Otherwise, this game could likely match Diablo 3 in disappointment as a "finished" product.

Elf - a constant barrage of ranged damage, special skill is a bomb that does AoE damage.

No. Warrior hacks and slashes. What did you expect? His special is even more hacking and slashing.
Valkyria - Less offensive than warrior, seconadary attack is actually a shield block instead, special allows for a more flexible attack.
Wizard - Has a lot of different spells, so it kind of feels like few classes cramed into one. Has supportive spells, variety of offensive spells from long range, medium or close. Is is the most difficult class, but overall can be most usefull as well.

The difficulty raises with more players present. Playing alone can quickly get boring, but playing with a team of 4 randoms usually turns into frantic running.

You can unlock a variety of items and upgrade them up to 3 levels. They give additional skills (up to 2 at a time) but those need potion pickups to be used. In 4 player team, that will be quite rare.
The game can be finished in 3-4 hours, but it is meant to be replayed a lot.
Overall, it can get boring over time, unless more areas (DLCs?) arrive.

by reading that title you're probably gonna assume it's a Final Fantasy knockoff, but don't be so quick to drop this game!
Gameplay:
you explore around the game's map in a zelda/dragon quest style overworld map,
you can use arrow keys/WSAD to move on the maps, but in combat it's mouse only (no gamepad support)
the game is a turn based RPG, battles aren't random, but instead you run into an enemy to engage them in battle,
combat is done with 4 party members, 3 of which are active in battle and one is the backup that you can switch in without wasting a turn, and also recovers their HP/MP while in backup.
you got your nature based archer Anna, your cliche powerful swordsman Matt, the well-endowed mage Natalie, and the crazy gun maniac and tank summoner Lance.
you defeat your enemies using all of your many equipments: weapons, clothes, accessories, Flairs which each have their own resistances/elements (there's a lot!) and they all can be upgraded to increase their effectiveness, not only that but you got skills and magic at your disposal as well!
each enemy has different weaknesses/resistances that you NEED to pay attention to, unless you wanna do 0 damage, or worse, HEAL your enemies by accident, luckily you can "scan" enemies using your summoned scanbot which forever allows you to see their weaknesses/resistances.
each character has their own skills to learn that are unique to each one, but there's also skills that are shared between them, but only ONE can use them so you'll have to plan around this a bit, you can forget skills if you really need to.
there's also "limit breaks" not unlike a FF game you charge your limit guage by taking damage and unleash powerful moves, like a rapid-hit sword slash combo, summoning a space ion-cannon, or fully healing your party
and then you can use summons, which use SP that you gain from defeating enemies, like a dog that throws healing items to you, an Ice elemental that freezes enemies, and a cat with no legs that slashes everyone, and later on even summon boss monsters to your side!
oh and there's quests that require you to grab certain (rare) items and bring them to NPCs, cause they're too lazy to do it themselves!
Music/sound:
this game's soundtrack is what makes it a little more unique, of course it's all original and done by an awesome artist (BTW soundtrack comes with the steam game!) it really sets the mood of the game.
if you've played the flash game, the quality of both sounds and music are a LOT better on this version!
Graphics:
if you're looking for awesome 3D graphical eye-gasms... well you might not enjoy this
but if you like hand-drawn 2D sprites and comical anime-style character designs this game has all of that!
don't worry though the graphics are pretty well done for what they are, with idle animations for both party members and enemies alike, no static combat sprites here! and a lot of the skill/limit break animations are awesome!
I should mention the entire game was originally designed in adobe flash, but personally this has to be one of the best flash graphics I've seen!
again, this version has better graphics quality from the flash game. with resolutions up to 1280x800 and fullscreen!
Difficulty:
this game has an adjustable difficulty from 4 settings, that you can change at ANY TIME.
believe me when I say it makes the difference of a cakewalk 10 hour game, to uber insane Bosses that 1-hit KO the unprepared!!
the games difficulty changes the enemy stats by a percentage, making them have more/less HP and do more/less damage to you
Easy (50%) normal (100%), hard (150%), Epic (200%)
you get the same EXP, money and AP regardless of difficulty, some achievements require you to play on epic that's all.
Replayability:
other than different difficulties, the game has a "second quest" and "third quest" mode which is basically the same game again but with higher level enemies. and also has a new game+ so you can play again and again while still keeping your levels, AP, and equipment.
there's a bonus area called Battle Mountain, that holds extra bosses and challenge battles, including one that puts you against  multiple bosses back to back!
also you can try to finish every quest, learn every skill to max, and forge all your equipment to max, and reach lv99 if you wish to do so.
Summary:
even though it started as a flash browser game, it has to be one of the most AWESOME flash RPGs i've played, and in some ways better than a lot of mainstream RPGs.
this steam version includes  all the "premium" features from the browser version, with better sound and graphics quality, and allows you to transfer saves from the browser game to the steam game! (read in forum how to do this)
it's pretty damn entertaining, the game makes jokes on itself and the dialog, both in battle and out, can be fun to read.
but, damned if your first encounter with "God Cat" won't catch you off guard, and it'll quickly remind you why this game is called EPIC battle fantasy!!

for those wondering why buy the steam game over the free browser one:

If you've talked to me for more than 20 seconds you will no doubt know that my favorite developer goes by the name "Kupo". Matt "Kupo" Rozsak made his debut with a stupid♥♥♥♥♥fighting game where you pressed SPACE before the ai opponent. it had some nice artwork and it was well made for someone working on his own, but it lacked...everything else. Kupo's next game was something far, far better.The first Epic Battle Fantasy game.
5 years or so later he is STILL working on his own and produeced a game of a godlike calibre.  EBF4 was available (as were Matt's other titles) for free on Kongregate, Newgrounds, Armorgame etc for a while, but people where saying EBF3 was so good they'd pay money for it. One installment later, the Epic Battle Fantasy series had a big enough following that 3 or 4 months after the release Kupo decided to put it on steams greenlight, and so it was lit.
Kupo had already programmed an expansion pack for ebf4, so obviously that is included in this version. Some minor changes are the inclusion of grey text that appears when an attack isn't very effective, and putting some new mini-bosses in some places. However, one MASSIVE expansion is that of Battle Mountain. Battle Mountain is a gauntlet, essentially. You fight your way up from the base of the mountain to the top, along the way finding the bosses from the main storyline have returned wit a few...slight twists, aswell as the inclusion of the Dark Players should you get far enough in, which are evil version of the characters you play as, mentioned to be the hardest bosses in the game by Kupo himself.
EBF4 is an rpg, plain and simply. as the ladder part of the name reveals, it's taken inspiration from classics such as Final Fantasy among other popular stratagy games and rpgs. in this game you take control of 4 characters on you mission to smite god herself (yes, herself) before she can do the same to you and all the other living beings on the planet.
The characters you control:
-Matt: Self-inserted pirate-swordsman, Matt Uses almost exclusively physical, single-target attacks which typically don't give enemies statis ailments unless the equipped sword does so.Completely destroys Bosses and has the strongest Limit Break attack in the game (Even stronger than most enemies attacks i'd say) known as "Cleaver", doing 700 Base power(x5) damage without buffs. (The second strongest Limit Break does 550 base power). He also has an ability known as "Revenge" that deals more damage the more total-team health is missing (mostly accounting for his, but if an ally is dead the damage is boosted) making him able to shred through anything aslong as he doesn't die (obviously).
-Natalie: The Healer-mage with huge♥♥♥♥♥♥ Best used as a healer, but can pull her own weight using exclusively ranged-magical attacks, having the widest move pool she's easy to expiremet with and see whether battle-mage or healer is best suited for your stratagy. For Healer, she has the only ability in the game to heal all party members at once, (without summons) and can set up combos by boosting magic attacks of allies and weakening enemies defenses. As a battle-mage, she has the usual fire-ice-electric-boom setup, but also is able to use attacks like "Spectrum" which deals damage and inflicts statuses based on  your currently-equipped staff. Natalie also brings a devestating holy attack know as "Judgement" and it's opposite, a darkness attack "Pulsar" to make quick work of anything of the opposite element.
-Lance: Gun enthusiast and soldier of an unknown army (maybe) -Uses a mixture of Magical and physical attacks, Easily the most powerful against non-boss enemies.He can unload an entire mag of his freakin' awesome gunblade or maybe call in an airstrike, whatever way he takes enemies out, it's always flashy. Lance is able to fire lazers from space, so clearly he is my favorite to play. Easily his most devastating attack is Hyper Beam, where it requires one turn to charge, then, in the the next 3 turns you may fire it, It hits everyone for massive magical damage and reflects the elemental typing of your weapon. Facing five fire enemies at once? Switch to the water cannon and shoop-da-woop their asses out of existence. Awesome.
- Anna: Nature's ♥♥♥♥♥- personally my least favorite, good for inflcting status effects with her Arrow Rain ability, and she also attacks with a mixture of physical and magical damage, leaning more towards physical. She can also learn healing spells so Natalie doesn't have to do all of it, but none of her abilities heal more than one person, to make up for that she gives healed player "Blessed" status, preventing them from being inflicted with status effects. She's the weakest in terms of strength and I find she's only good as a support to set up combos.
The only negative things about this game-
1) It's not kind to the uninformed. Not knowing that you're supposed to summon the ScanBot to get information on your enemies' weaknesses and resistences can be devastating during fights. Also, not knowing which skills to get on whom, how to spread your stat boosting items, and other essential things to survival are not taught to you. I suggest playing EBF1 or 2 before attempting this game.
2) Epic mode is honesty TOO hard. in the older games Epic mode made enemies 40% stronger and gave them new moves. In this game, it makes them 100% harder, and start the battle afflicted with a status they are 200% resistent to (IE- Poison heals instead of damages). This makes the game boring as you are constantly buffing yourself and charging attacks and setting up to do the most damage possible to a level 3 slime because if you don't it will kil you by brushing up against your knees too swiftly.
3) Items essental to the area you're in being given to you 2 areas ahead. This happens surprisingly often. I recall getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked by some ice enemies only to find a staff boosting ice defense and strengthening fire attacks in the next area.
Number 3 is a personal problem, but 1 and 2 should be headed if you are not a veteran to the RPG style of play. Other than that and a few minor complaints I have about the distribution of critical items, I have no real complaints.
If you're not in to RPGs, this game may not be for you, as there is little in the way of minigames. If you do not like to spend time micromanaging every bit of equipment, play on normal, if you are used to RPGs in general, play on hard, if you have played through ebf4 prior, play on epic if you choose. The only reason to play on easy is if the Dark Players are making you rage and you just want to kill them already after your 40th attempt...in other words, easy is too easy

Meaningless and totally bias score: 10/10 as RPGs go. This is easily my favorite of the RPG genre and I encourage anyone to atleast play the free version if you are a cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

The level design still hasn’t strayed all that much from the much-criticized “gray corridors” of the first FEAR – sure, you explore suburban houses, a Costco-like store, a huge bridge, and even a forest, but much of the time you’re still in monochrome corridors.

Went in expecting abject♥♥♥♥♥♥ just based on the Metacritic reviews. First and second one were good, I figured the third couldn't be that bad, and I was right. This is a middling quality modern shooter. You still get the slow-mo mechanics from the first two games, which is always fun, and a variety of weapons strewn about for you to mess around with. The AI is some of the most aggressive I've seen in an FPS in the past few years, and it will really punish you if you try to hide and take potshots. Enemy soldiers will flank and converge on your position, and regularly toss grenades to scare you out. Even with the slow-mo it was a moderate challenge.
The reasons this game scored so poorly I think, were that it's not really a F.E.A.R. game, and it's short. It's about a 6 hour playthrough in full, double that if you play through again as Paxton Fettel, but most people probably won't bother. As for not being a F.E.A.R. game, it comes down to the fact that the game is not scary or even atmospheric. It's not even creepy. Sometimes it'll do the standard "Alma shows up in little girl form to spook you" but she's just there and disappears when you get close. It's like it was a line item on a checklist of things they needed in order to slap the F.E.A.R. brand on it, and has no care put into how it is done.
Excepting the actual gameplay (which is definitely passable), it's easy to see why this was basically the end of the series. It feels like a Modern Warfare clone instead of what the rest of the series was. I can't imagine it was anything but reviled by fans of the series up to this point, even if the shooting was still competent.
It still gets a "Yes" from me because it regularly comes bundled with the other two games, which are certainly worth playing, and overall it's cheap. Being short means it doesn't overstay its welcome. So to anyone wondering if they should get a combo of all three games, or just the first one, pull the trigger on the bundle. They're all worth playing.

Visually and Aurally this game is stunning and almost every review on here (positive or negative) will agree on that.  The story is fairly basic and not overly interesting but I guess it serves it's purpose to drive the game forward.  I'm not going to extol the virtues of the game further than this - there's thousands of reviews here that already do that.  Instead I'm going to talk about some of the problems.
The first issue that you're likely to notice is that there are often lots of very similarly coloured flashing elements on the screen at once.  This makes it extremely difficult to tell the difference between 'good' shiney and 'bad' shiney.  Not a big deal as you progress and collect a few upgrades but early on is definitely an annoyance.  A simliar problem arises further on into the game where you need to navigate multiple glowing teleporters surrounded by dangerous regions in quick succession.  The sequence wouldn't be terribly challenging if not for Ori blending in and being camoflaged by teleporters.  This makes being able to easily tell where Ori is on the screen a nightmare especially when you need to react quickly to avoid yet another death.
The Bash mechanic made me want to rip my hair out with frustration.  The idea itself wasn't bad but the execution.... I'm just going to say the controls didn't feel intuitive at all in the beginning.  I did improve though and by the end I was pretty pro at navigating it... which brings me to the next problem.
The reliance on executing extremely long platforming sequences flawlessly is annoying if not rage inducing (if you've played Nihilumbra think of the Escape the Void parts).  You will die. A lot.  More than once I got frustrated to the point that I had to quit (Ginso Tree I'm looking at you).  It was that or risk throwing my controller through the monitor.  I play games to have fun and to be entertained.  I don't mind being challenged but this style of gameplay goes way beyond that and is decidedly un-fun.  Having said that the sections that followed this were nowhere near as long or as difficult once you'd gotten the hang of using all your abilities together.
Finally, I think the game design is flawed in that certain sections are closed off and/or cannot be revisited once traversed.  So if you miss any items or secrets on the way through and/or inadventantly stumble into an area that triggers an event (without warning I might add) - it's pretty much a case of too bad, so sad.  That's not good enough in my opinion.  I have limited time and very rarely go back to play through a game I've already completed.  So I try to get as much as I can out of one play through (in this case 42/50 achievements) and this is a massive annoyance.  Additionally, some of the achievements appear to be bugged (Airborne doesn't trigger no matter what I do).
Overall, apart from one or two disproportionate difficulty spikes the game is fun to play, and I'd recommend to anyone, especially if you see it on sale.

I enjoy the game in its current build and I look forward to the changes and additions for future versions.

Alright, let me tell you why I'm writing this review at 3:30 am, after I stayed up all night playing this game.
Now, I should note that some may consider this more of an interactive story then a game, as no matter who plays it or how you'll end up with the same story. As well as this, there is pretty much no gameplay to speak of. It is, essentially a story you walk through.
However, I have to say that if you consider this an interactive story, it is in my opinion the best goddamn interactive story out there, and perhaps the best goddamn story period.
Now, as this is a story first and formost, a book or movie reviewer would probably be better suited to this. I can't reallygive you much data on why this is a good story. I can say, though, that it has so many amazing twists and turns in a time span shorter then most modern movies, that I'm seriously thinking this game would make millions if it were a movie.
So, heres the gist of what I can give you;
You play two scientists whose sole job is to grant one final wish to those who are about to die. They can grant nearly any wish, and they do this by manipulateing the patients memories.
The patient you work on in this story is a patient whos final wish is to go to the moon. To truly give you the best experience of the story, that is all I feel willing to tell you.
So then. Are you willing to find out why an old man's final wish is to go to the moon? Or do you, like I once did, think the reason can't possibly be all that remarkable?
I put off playing this game for a while after I bought it. I wish I hadn't- its an amazing story. 'Course, the problem is the description I and the Game Devs can give isnt nearly beffitting enough of how amazing the story is.

Which means they WILL make that sequel. I demand it.
Annnd I guess also because its allready in the works and shows no problems of stopping, but I felt my enthusiasim for this series needed to be expressed.
Anyway, seriously guys. Buy this game. It doesn't matter if this is the most railroded storyline in a game you've ever seen, I garuntee it will also be one of the best storylines in a game you've ever seen, so its worth it.
Oh, and I must say, even though this game looks like it was made in an RPG maker like program (probably because it was), I have to say it really shows such prgrams potential.

Gauntlet is infamous to many old-school gamers. A four-player co-operative/competitive adventure in the dungeons, it's seen it's fair share of versions, from the original on the NES, to Gauntlet Legends on the Dreamcast and even further to Seven Sorrows on PS3 and Xbox 360.  But out of all of them, I respect this version the most. One rule that's vital to adhere to is a half-begrudging friend system. Share your food with your allies to keep them alive (or destroy it when they need it if you REALLY don't like them), but under no circumstances can you share your gold. Trust me, they wouldn't for you. It's a system that even best friends stick to, you CAN'T share gold, so while you're working together with your friends, you may be surprised to realise you're also planning for their demise or the next way you can steal gold from them.
This is a fantastic revamp of a legendary game, Highly recommended.

A blast in co-op in any combination (2, 3 or 4 players) and surprisingly entertaining even played solo. I have been up pretty much every night way too late enjoying its twin-stick shooter-like fun.
For new players, I'd probably recommend Elf (feels at times like you're playing Robotron or Smash TV, a real twin-stick focus with bomb drops and bomb-tipped arrow firing) and Valkyrie (ability to make attackers bounce off via shield, toss shield like Captain America and a charge attack).
Wizard's 9 spells can be a bear to remember unless you jot the combos down. Warrior feels a bit underdeveloped and could maybe use a bit of a re-think, imho.
I do think it's important to both lay out pros and cons, and explain to people what it is and it isn't. If you know what it is, and what its current limitations are, I think you can have a blast with it. If you buy the game based on misconceptions, or mistaken expectations, then you'll likely end up bitterly disappointed or frustrated as per the thousand or so threads at the Steam forums. I always give my friends candid advice and don't try to trick them into getting a game I know they won't like. :)
-Adrenalized, twin-jstick style dungeon shooting/brawling that -- if it's your cup of tea -- may keep you up all night playing. You may have so much fun you won't mind battling through the same areas over and over again.
-Massive hordes of enemies that get crazier and crazier on higher difficulty levels
-Showstopping relic powers, though limited by "potion fuel," and you can only equip 2 at a time.
-No in-game text chat or voice chat, only using cursor keys or gamepad to do a few voice emotes. I suspect they spent so much time demoing the game in local play on one PC, it didn't occur to them anyone might want to communicate in-game a bit.
-Keyboard key bindings aren't currently configurable. Which is, as they say, baffling, ridiculous, unforgivable, etc., ona  PC-only game but they promise it's in the works in a future patch.
-Framerate issues for many players
That said, once I played using my controller I never went back to keys/mouse. It's doable but it was painful and hard on my wrist and elbows, and some of the wizard spell combos feel baffling on keyboard compared to controller. I also felt the key pounding was going to break my keyboard. :)
-Not an action RPG
-Doesn't have loot
-Not a Diablo-style clickfest despite the dungeon setting. No click to move, no click to kill.
-Not a "storyline" game. If you feel like once you've "finished" a game, you have no reason to back through the levels again, then don't get this game. The fun imho is in having different, crazy experiences each time you play any levels in the game with other folks. It's not meant to be a game "you finish." If that doesn't interest you, take a pass on this.
-Other than one type of level, levels are "handcrafted," not randomly generated. Even the "procedurally generated" level type doesn't seem all that different from game to game for me. So if you need to see different mazes and door locations in every level of a game you play, take a pass on this.
*I'll update this review later. Too tired from being up until 3 a.m. playing. :)

If you've played Grotesque Tactics, this game is quite similar but even more simplified, with no leveling up or inventory management. Also, wow, the "humor" is even worse - if you can believe that.
It's not quite as buggy as GT is/was, but there are still some technical problems with it. On the larger maps, the framerate starts to crawl because of the number of units, I suspect because the game isn't quite optimized. There's no music during gameplay, and the sound design leaves a lot to be desired (though I did get a chuckle when I heard the wilhelm scream). Graphics are quite bland, barely passable.
That said, it does scratch the itch a bit just like Grotesque Tactics did. If you've played through Final Fantasy Tactics enough times to really look for something else, you could find worse. If you're a hardcore turn-based tactics fan who likes a lot of depth to their strategy, this game doesn't have it. If you like something light on the tone and challenge, or can get this game really cheap, then give it a look.

Ubisoft is good at creating interesting settings for their sandboxes, whether it is Bolivia for GR: Wildlands or a devastated New York for the division.
Unfortunately this is where Ubisoft's ability seem to stop: Game after game they fail to fill the world with anything memorable or meaningful. I cannot recall a single mission from Wildlands, and I wont be able from the Division in a week. You shoot the men and they die. Rinse and repeat, occasionally get a cutsccene. There is potential here, the setting is interesting and the story sometimes manages to be moderately interesting. But all of that is only remotely connected to gameplay, which is bogstandard shooting with some RPG mechanics.
Ubisoft essentially produces junkfood: throwaway shooters that manage to provide a distraction but leave nothing memorable behind and are probably not good for you (or the industry) in the long run. As a game creator, Ubisoft is an excellent visual designer, but cannot back it up by gameplay or story.
If you don't have sandbox fatigue or want to kill some time, you could do worse than the division. It is definitely not worth full price. Probably not even half the price. But at 70+% off it is not too bad.

Despite all the hate coming from people, F3AR is enjoyable in its own right. Granted, gameplay was streamlined too much compared to the sequels that it feels too much like Cowadoodee (but not completely).
For one, medkits are gone and regenerating health is the new heals BUT unlike COD, regenerating health can bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥also as enemies do like to punish you hard (as in if they're not understrength, they WILL push towards you while trying to regen health). So no medkit abuse to get out of a fight where you're guaranteed dead.
Gunplay is a bit generic, but still enjoyable. You do have a destructible cover system that allows you to shoot from side to side, allowing for limited tactical gameplay. Its not original, but workable enough. The martial arts that the first game had and the second game downplayed, are now gone, however, which is a huge damn shame, because ♥♥♥♥ knives, I wanna punch and kick every person I can find like John Woo from hell.
There's also a unique feature in F3AR in that you can play as the pointman's sociopathic brother: Paxton Fettel. On his own, he can only throw out telekinetic bolts and levitate thiungs and can't use guns. He can, however, posses certain enemy troops for a limited amount of time, allowing you to have your meat puppet wreak havoc on the enemy lines before doing it again. He can also make people's heads explode like in Scanners. If you can find a friend to play Co-Op with, the prospect is quite good.
The atmosphere (after the first level) has to be one of the best features of the game. You do feel like in an apocalyptic wasteland after a psychic/nuclear disaster. It's not "depressingly beautiful" or "adrenalin-pumping beautiful" but just creepy. The more you progress, the more you see how horrifying Fairport has gone down under. People are crazy. Cannibalistic crazy. And the locations you venture through will reveal how high the level of crazy went into this place.
As for difficulty, F3AR does have it. ATC Black Ops and the Replica troops are tough that they usually take a few hits to take down, have a kiiiinda decent set of tactics. Though, the AI does kinda shift from Competent to Call of Duty at times, but most of the time, they remain competent and will give you a run for your money. Cannibal AI is not that far from your everyday zombies from L4D and the likes, but they will try sneak attacks as much as possible.
As for multiplayer. Its pretty much dead. Unless you have friends. Its dead.
Overall, F3AR might be a bit shifty with its price of $10, but is a definite buy if its on sale. It'll give you some decent enjoyment for its price.

Enjoyable core gameplay but ultimately P2W
hours in-game: unknown
Played: World 2 up to Duke rank
Played: Rise of the Wolf (currently playing)
Gameplay 4/10
Building villages is fun, building and sieging castles is fun, collecting stashes is fun, hell even using cards is fun - essentially all the ingredients are there for an entertaining experience - I would give an 8/10 for core gameplay... and then we add the P2W factor. To progress meaningfully in this game(not just be able to login and play around with it) you need premium tokens to use build and research queues, correct mistakes in your village building efforts, etc.. if you want to compete effectively you need to buy cards so I have reduced the gameplay to 5/10.
Example
player A: "mwhahaha i'm gonna kill that guy" *buys and uses 5Xspeed card to send his army to target at lightning speed*
player B: "dammit, that army wrecked my castle defenses. Another attack like that and i'll lose all my hard work*cry*" *buys stone cards, castle construction cards -ding- instantly repaired defenses* [and I do mean literally instantly!]
player A: "hmph, almost had him" *buys mercenary cards to instantly make another army, buys another 5Xspeed card*...
-some time later-
player B: "omgz have i really just spent $200 on 1s and 0s?!, oh god here comes another army..that guy must be a millionaire"
player A: "haha, I win.. razing your village was delicious!"
One other thing that affects gameplay: cheating. You see if you are a F2P player you are not allowed to cheat, the game detects that you are logging into different accounts and stops those accounts from benefiting one another which seems fair right? However, buy a premium token on each of those accounts and Firefly is now happy to let you cheat with multi-accounting! A company that is happy to allow cheating as long as it is receiving $$$...well come to your own conclusions; score reduced to 4/10.
Graphics 4/10
The graphics were just about quaint 4 years ago, and yeah I know we all love shatty graphics as long as we enjoy the gameplay but c'mon.. the pile of poop Stronghold 3 has gorgeous graphics, so why does Stronghold Kingdoms still look like a roadmap? even the freaking trees look like they belong on a roadsign -caution tree ahead- Very little work is done on improving the game that's why, it's just an aging cash cow for a small company that feels like it's going to file bankruptcy in the near future.
Sound 5/10
Pleasant but limited music and sfx will irritate after a few hours, you will turn the music off and listen to your own. Again no additions after 4 years of milking addicted players.
Additional notes
EA kept opening new servers for Lords of Ultima and never closing any, fractured community led to stale worlds with dying populations; EA closed down Lords of Ultima after wondering why they weren't turning enough profit.
FF kept opening new servers for Stronghold Kingdoms and never closing any, fractured community let to stale worlds with dying populations; FF ... ... ... ...
Verdict
Play if you have huge amounts of time to waste or don't mind throwing money at P2W games.

Visually and Aurally this game is stunning and almost every review on here (positive or negative) will agree on that.  The story is fairly basic and not overly interesting but I guess it serves it's purpose to drive the game forward.  I'm not going to extol the virtues of the game further than this - there's thousands of reviews here that already do that.  Instead I'm going to talk about some of the problems.
The first issue that you're likely to notice is that there are often lots of very similarly coloured flashing elements on the screen at once.  This makes it extremely difficult to tell the difference between 'good' shiney and 'bad' shiney.  Not a big deal as you progress and collect a few upgrades but early on is definitely an annoyance.  A simliar problem arises further on into the game where you need to navigate multiple glowing teleporters surrounded by dangerous regions in quick succession.  The sequence wouldn't be terribly challenging if not for Ori blending in and being camoflaged by teleporters.  This makes being able to easily tell where Ori is on the screen a nightmare especially when you need to react quickly to avoid yet another death.
The Bash mechanic made me want to rip my hair out with frustration.  The idea itself wasn't bad but the execution.... I'm just going to say the controls didn't feel intuitive at all in the beginning.  I did improve though and by the end I was pretty pro at navigating it... which brings me to the next problem.
The reliance on executing extremely long platforming sequences flawlessly is annoying if not rage inducing (if you've played Nihilumbra think of the Escape the Void parts).  You will die. A lot.  More than once I got frustrated to the point that I had to quit (Ginso Tree I'm looking at you).  It was that or risk throwing my controller through the monitor.  I play games to have fun and to be entertained.  I don't mind being challenged but this style of gameplay goes way beyond that and is decidedly un-fun.  Having said that the sections that followed this were nowhere near as long or as difficult once you'd gotten the hang of using all your abilities together.
Finally, I think the game design is flawed in that certain sections are closed off and/or cannot be revisited once traversed.  So if you miss any items or secrets on the way through and/or inadventantly stumble into an area that triggers an event (without warning I might add) - it's pretty much a case of too bad, so sad.  That's not good enough in my opinion.  I have limited time and very rarely go back to play through a game I've already completed.  So I try to get as much as I can out of one play through (in this case 42/50 achievements) and this is a massive annoyance.  Additionally, some of the achievements appear to be bugged (Airborne doesn't trigger no matter what I do).
Overall, apart from one or two disproportionate difficulty spikes the game is fun to play, and I'd recommend to anyone, especially if you see it on sale.

Alright, let me tell you why I'm writing this review at 3:30 am, after I stayed up all night playing this game.
Now, I should note that some may consider this more of an interactive story then a game, as no matter who plays it or how you'll end up with the same story. As well as this, there is pretty much no gameplay to speak of. It is, essentially a story you walk through.
However, I have to say that if you consider this an interactive story, it is in my opinion the best goddamn interactive story out there, and perhaps the best goddamn story period.
Now, as this is a story first and formost, a book or movie reviewer would probably be better suited to this. I can't reallygive you much data on why this is a good story. I can say, though, that it has so many amazing twists and turns in a time span shorter then most modern movies, that I'm seriously thinking this game would make millions if it were a movie.
So, heres the gist of what I can give you;
You play two scientists whose sole job is to grant one final wish to those who are about to die. They can grant nearly any wish, and they do this by manipulateing the patients memories.
The patient you work on in this story is a patient whos final wish is to go to the moon. To truly give you the best experience of the story, that is all I feel willing to tell you.
So then. Are you willing to find out why an old man's final wish is to go to the moon? Or do you, like I once did, think the reason can't possibly be all that remarkable?
I put off playing this game for a while after I bought it. I wish I hadn't- its an amazing story. 'Course, the problem is the description I and the Game Devs can give isnt nearly beffitting enough of how amazing the story is.
Oh. And one last thing- this game is part of a series. Now, I know this because this game ends on an insane cliffhanger. Insane enough, that I'm seriously thinking about donateing over 2000 dollars, all the money in my bank account, just to make it happen if for some reason they can't. Which means they WILL make that sequel. I demand it.
Annnd I guess also because its allready in the works and shows no problems of stopping, but I felt my enthusiasim for this series needed to be expressed.
Anyway, seriously guys. Buy this game. It doesn't matter if this is the most railroded storyline in a game you've ever seen, I garuntee it will also be one of the best storylines in a game you've ever seen, so its worth it.
Oh, and I must say, even though this game looks like it was made in an RPG maker like program (probably because it was), I have to say it really shows such prgrams potential.
IN conclusion, please buy this game. Its amazing.

English Review :
"To The Moon is a briliant simple game"
Previously, several game sites rate this game for its beautiful story. And the game won awards for an indie game category. Come with curiosity, I'll tried the game ... and ... To The Moon becomes one of the melancholy and emotional game I've ever played. There is laugh, there is love, there is sad and sacrifice. Sometimes the game make me smile, sometimes make me sad and cry. For a game, To The Moon becomes one of a tearjerker title that ever exist.
This simple game had premise with a sci-fi element become complex & brilliant from the begining. There is a dying old man had a one last wish before he die, he want to go to the moon. So this is a job for Dr. Rosalene & Dr. Watts, they can enter the memory of the patient looking for memory fragment and manipulate it. From the present time to the past until his child era. Reverse driven-story like this, remind me of a french movie directed by Gaspar Noe entitled Irreversible.
For the gameplay, this one made by RPG Maker engine but diffrent. This is not a Fantasy RPG like the other one. But becomes an adventure game with briliant soundtracks and story-driven plot. Characterization in this game is so powerful and can give an emotional impact to player. Maybe, if this one not a game. Plot of this game can be a novel. And I can predict, its become a best seller title. But, if this one become a movie. I can predict, its become a box office movie which won several award if made seriously.

For those of you who are complaining about the graphics... This is an indie game made in RPGMaker, what do you expect?

Pros
+ Can be fun to play (for a few hours anyway) with a group of friends

Cons
-Not fun to play alone.

The original
from 1985 was one of those genre defining games, that was not only one of the first really fun co-op games I ever played, but also was the predecessor to many classic dungeon crawlers we know today like Diablo, Sacred, Path of Exile, Magicka, Baldur's Gate, Dungeon Defenders or even instance dungeons of World of Warcraft. Spawning a classic sequel & several modern remakes on the consoles, Gauntlet has endured the decades, although the modern 3D versions failed to capture the feel from the originals for me. So here we are in 2014 with another remake, one making the bold claim to the title, simply 'Gauntlet', has a lot to live up to!
For those familiar with the original games, first time you start you will be hit with a
. Retro sounds from the original are remixed into the modern music & effects, the logo & look all feels familiar but fresh. Great sound really sets the scene & gets you pumped! I liked the graphics look & the lighting, not super HD but clean and easy to see what is going on. Monster designs were also well done.
, ranging from the 4 well defined character classes, the puzzle like mazing map designs, lotsa gold!, keys, turkeys
, potions, jump platforms, spawners, grim reaper & the awesome narrator telling the classics like
&
. All this feels authentic & refined, honouring the originals faithfully, but there is also many new features & enhancements.
Besides the obvious move into 3D, all the characters have got new moves & upgrades. Each has 3 attack types, plus ability for 2 Relics
, each using unique controller configurations. You can combine your attacks in different ways, & also with other classes based on the situation. Most moves have both strengths & weaknesses so the right selection
is key to survival.

*
is great in mowing down large groups, although weaker against ranged, hard to excel at but tough overall.
*
is good defender with shield, also versatile & powerful offensive moves, but weak destroying spawners.
*
is fast & nimble able to attack from almost any range, good AoE bomb damage for groups but needs space to operate effectively.
*
is the most complex, yet highly adaptable class, with 9 spell combinations both offensive & defensive, it can be seen as over-powered but requires a lot more skill to play.
(There is more to each class but it gives you a rough outline.)
Adapting to the battle is fluid & fun to control though & when mastered, combat can become epic! The combat control system is simple by many modern game standards, but it’s really exceptionally balanced, intuitive & accessible – one of the strongest features of the game!
Each character class independently can gain 72 Mastery Levels
which will unlock perks & upgrades to progress further on the Hard or Unfair difficulty. Each difficulty level needs to be unlocked for each character & higher levels do offer a really intense challenge. This adds a lot of replayability as does the many in-game
achievements you can earn at the end of each level that give you buffs or boosts. There are some cosmetic items you can purchase for the coins you earn in the dungeons, to change the look of your character. There aren’t very many though. Likewise, there are some
Relics, but overall there isn’t a lot of selections for those wanting high level of customisation.
Despite all the positive design choices, the authentic feel & just plain enjoyable co-op gameplay, Gauntlet has one fatal flaw …
.
There is 3 zones each with 4 dungeons, some multiple levels, but overall only 30
levels in total. This includes 3 boss arenas that have no exploration. This will only take 4-5hrs to play through Solo @ Normal. The original Gauntlet I/II had 100s of levels
, practically endless random dungeons to conquer. See how far you could survive with your buddies, but you just don't get that feeling here.
Replaying levels for each character & difficulty level is fine, but with so few levels I have already started to memorise the layouts. I fear this lack of variety will make this a short lived experience with many gamers, when I could have seen it be my go-to favourite game for a while.  I really hope to see lots of new dungeons or at the least support for community workshop maps or a random generated endless mode
to provide a real hardcore on-going challenge to work with your friends towards. More items, perks, customised looks would all be welcome too!
Although I agree with having no chat in the game, having text chat in the lobby &/or hub would be most helpful. Currently, there is
at all with other team mates if not in your friends’ list. Also, it is very limiting in public games when players cannot join in mid-level, you can only join when in a lobby – but who wants to wait in a lobby for that elusive 4th player to drop in, or to go back to lobby every time to find another player when someone drops mid-level? It’s not a smooth experience & comes off as rather basic, along with making it very hard to get a full team together. Matchmaking does seem to work well at least.
Playing with friends is an absolute blast & with so much else done right the limited content can be ignored
along with the online multiplayer limitations I mentioned above. It's a supremely enjoyable experience. Whether you have played the originals or not, this is a solid action dungeon crawler that succeeds in recreating that uniquely
experience.

Short version:
Loving the game, played it for too many hours in a too short timespan.
Long version:
The idea of the game is great, and they pulled it off really well, but there are tiny things that can start to nag at the back of your head.
Cons:
- It's a very short game(but it was advertised as a "small game", so that one can slide)
- The combinations are mostly logical, but many don't make sense, like Casual games on PC being ---. Truck simulator is a casual game along with simulation, this game can be considered casual, Facebook games are the definition of casual. Or Comedy action - Postal 2. Dungeon Adventure is only a +. Really?
- Multi-genre is almost never worth it. Unless you know from the top of your head what are the great combos for multi-genre it's not worth spending money and resources on it, given the short timespan of your game. It's better to just stick to what you know works once you even get far enough for multi-genre.
- MMOs?? The maintenance costs rise so fast that you can maybe push out 2-3 AAA expansions before you'll lose more money than gain. I wanted to make a long lasting MMO, but instead had to drop it once the maintenance costs became ridiculous without much income.
- Consoles. It's pretty much not worth it to make consoles. By the time you can get one out it'll probably have outdated hardware and you'll end up spending way more on it than you actually earn.
- Technology/Design balance. It's not reflected well in the game that it actually matters, and there's not even a hint of what's correct. The only reason I know this is because I started looking solutions to some problems online and fount out it exists.
Looking at that list it doesn't look like the game could be worth much, but other than those points it's a solid game. Micro-manage the game development, assign your team to different tasks, train your team the best for their position.

Highborn is a turn-based strategy game with old-style rules and wacky-stupid kind of humor.  There's a lot of references to the pop culture and the characters break the fourth wall all the time. The rules (and AI) are simple: you attack and then enemy retaliates if not dead or petrified. There are infinite amount of retaliations. Towers shoot any enemy attacking your troops in their area and also help when you attack. Enemy does not remember where you were last round, so you can always hide in the forest (or go invisible as Trillian) without a large chance of discovery, though sometimes enemy somewhat randomly goes there or hits Trillian anyway while moving and "discovers" you.
There are troops and then there are disposable troops that respawn from keeps, mage towers and such. Like expected you are not allowed to lose hero units who are also better than the rest and have a couple of very useful special skills. There are also 6 different spells that both you and your opponent can use, acquired through capturing monoliths scattered within the levels.
AI is not very smart as it is easy to fool someone who doesn't remember enemies going into the forest, but as a snack-type strategy game this one is fine. There's no multiplayer, so don't expect too much replay value. You may complete each level on a higher difficulty level though, meaning more and stronger enemy troops. The level-based special achievements are a nice touch as well.
Do not expect your mind to be blown (except by the puns) but it's a fine game akin to a snack. Do expect to grow to hate some of the characters though because they can be irritating.

Reus has its share of problems.
The game has a high difficulty curve, and its complexity means most players will likely find themselves consulting external resources mid-game to plan their next actions. This is a game in dire need of a "tech tree" interface.
It creates replay value by limiting the gameplay available in any given game until the player's completed tasks, which also constitute the achievements, in a previous game. Players who have no problem with the learning curve may find themselves hitting a glass ceiling of achievement in a given game because they don't yet have access to higher-level resources. This is ironic, because one of the central goals in Reus is for the "giants" to give the humans just enough resources to achieve their goals without becoming greedy: very meta if it was intentional.
Finally, the game is literally incomplete in places: players who get through to higher-level resources may notice grammatical errors or even *placeholders* in the interface text. Many achievements that claim that they "can't be met in Alt Mode", when the player has selected options that make the game slightly easier, are in fact unlocked with "Alt Mode" options active.
All that being said, Reus is a satisfying and engaging puzzle game if you can get past its foibles. I like it. Give it a shot.

Reus is... something that begs a total edit of my original review. Before, I thought it was a "good little time waster", a "frustrating case of something that should have been so much cooler". Quite simply, I had missed the most amazing part of the game and I've since found it, meaning that I can't not change my opinion.
Reus is actually really, really fun once you sink your teeth into it. The only thing I didn't realise was that, where I thought I had got to the marrow of it before, I was still gnawing my way through the bare bones. They were pretty tasty bones to be honest; tasty enough that I thought they would be the main gameplay... well you know what they say about assumptions, this one certainly came back to bite me.
So what actually IS Reus? It's a puzzle-strategy game that looks like a god game. On the surface it looks like a simple progression from the stone age to the space age (or, if your whims are so inclined, maybe they stay in the stone age); and the "god game" elements seemed to just revolve around plonking down resources for the humans to use and then slapping them around with earthquakes and muck bombs if they do something you don't want them to do. You start with a bare and barren planet, and you use four giants with powers over the environment (ocean, mountain, forest and swamp) to create biomes, creatures, plants and minerals; then you grow and evolve those natural resources for the humans to use (or sometimes abuse) while trying to shape the growth of humans so that they unlock the next round of resources. The other thing to note with giants is that, each time you get the humans to complete a project, the humans send you an ambassador and that ambassador will work with one of your giants to unlock further abilities.
However, that's just the SURFACE. In all its glory, Reus is a progressive strategy puzzle game where you have to solve the puzzle theoretically beforehand, then progress through the stages in-game to reach your predetermined solution (dealing with any disasters which you hadn't set in motion; like that mad scientist who wants you to destroy the Bluerock Tribe even though you need them to finish their shrine so you can give the mad scientist his new reptiles to play with...). In other words, you have to think something like a god seemingly would; knowing the details of Your Great Plan and slowly convincing the humans to give you the tools needed to implement it.
That's very abstract, but remember the example of the mad scientist? Well, each time the humans complete a project for the first time, it unlocks a new species you can add to the world. So if you want to get a mad scientist so you can unlock its associated species, then you need to factor in ALL of its requirements - that includes creating a sacrificial village in this case since destroying a village is one of the requirements to complete that project. You might have to give the humans certain resources, impress them with Awe, start wars (and probably end them too to make sure that the chosen village wins), directly interfere with global trade or learning to make sure that a given village takes the lead in that category... there's a lot to consider when you're a god. Each species is used differently by the humans; they all give common resources but different combinations of resources have different results. So in a kind of psuedo-Chaotic (as in Chaos Theory, not dark gods of destruction) algebra, you shape the game world the humans make use of the resources you give them so that you can give them the next lot, and the next lot, and the next lot until you get them to complete that project and unlock that new species (which has been the goal of thousands of years of evolution).
That's a big part of the game. Naturally you only start out wit a RELATIVELY small number of species - but this is where the game tricked me, because you still get a LOT of species to start with. Like, hundreds. And then there's another couple of hundred to unlock... but in that first hundred or so species, there are symbioses and interactions enough to make a thriving world; so I assumed that the unlocks were "endgame" content to polish off the basic systems.
Nope. Not even close. The unlocks build, and build; not just with extra layers of unlocks but also with "tiers" (which you can only unlock with certain combinations of ambassadors). You don't just need to unlock all the species, you also have to create a world that can sustain them and make sure - so if you want the coffea tree to caffeinate your mad scientist in order that he can stay up all night and do astrology; then you have to get certain things happening in the world to be able to make a coffea tree.
In other words, you're eventually going to need a spreadsheet. At the start, Reus looks like it will work if you just add a bit of this and a dash of that and then see what comes out at the end. However, the truth is that if you want to unlock everything, sooner or later you're going to have to really seriously stop and plan the whole pathway to get there. You need to know what the humans need, in what order and in what combination, to make a certain project; and you also need to remember that in order to get some species thriving in the world you'll have to give up on the others that won't help your path.
Yes, that's right, to fully play this game you have to move past the "I want everything in a glorious utopia!" thinking that's immediately obvious to new players; and start thinking about your planet as a means to an end. It's not that species are mutually exclusive - every species will work with every other species - but rather, the requirements for some species will preclude you getting other species because you simply won't have enough room to get both. Whether it's not having enough room on the planet, or not having enough room on your giants, getting to the marrow of this game means coming to terms with the sheer number of possible pathways available, and then figuring out which ones you want to pursue.
That's why I I invoke Chaos Theory to explain Reus. Einstein summed it up pretty well: "Life is like a game of dice - if you know all the variables, your throwing force and the wind and the room's air pressure and the weight of the dice and everything; then you can roll a 6 every time". In Reus, you DO know all the variables - that's why there's an in-game link to the wiki. I missed that bit in the tutorial because I was having too much fun making fish, but if I had paid attention I would have seen how much more complexity there is in Reus.
And then there's in-game challenges - scenarios where you can only use so many of one ambassador type. Scenarios on a strict time-limit (all games are timed, but some of the challenges make it a real race against the clock). Scenarios where whole branches of the "tech tree" are closed and you have to come up with a creative way to replace them... the more you play, the more complexity you find.
And my gosh it's fun to explore that complexity. If you happen to be a completionist, or if you really like problem solving, then Reus gives you a really nice challenge to sink your teeth into. If you don't like complicated maths or grinding, then this probably isn't your kind of game - there is a big chunk of repetition involved, although there are ways to minimise it some missions simply won't work any other way except starting from scratch on a very specific path. That said, if you do have that urge to totally control history and like working with really complex, abstracted challenges; then Reus is still a great hobby - not just a time-waster, but an investment of loads and loads of time into possibly the greatest sense of satisfaction for completing a challenge that you'll eve find in a game.

Fallout 3: Game of the Year Edition is a 2008/09 post-apocalyptic role-playing game that takes place in desolate wasteland of Washington DC. You play as the Lone Wanderer, who travels on a journey to find your Father (voiced by Liam Neeson) in the wasteland. Leaving Vault 101 takes personal risks and responsibility. Would you do the same?
Fallout 3 starts in the year, 2277, 200 years after the Resource War (United States versus China in a fight for remaining sources on Earth) ended suddenly due to atomic weaponry inflicting against the United States and the rest of the world. Washington DC takes the most damage due to its strategic and political significance. The question remains: What was your Father’s intention to leave Vault 101? The main story is good though some people argued that the plot is decent. In my perspective, the plot is typical and good. It’s not the best or have a strong presentation, but it’s good overall. The real reason for playing Fallout 3 has to be exploration and doing major side quests. Exploring the unknown world of post-apocalyptic Washington DC feels so amazing and worrisome at the same time. These two emotions is what makes the game feel so great. The setting is unpredictable. You may find an abandoned settlement that has a mysterious past,  reading journal entries on what caused a location to fall apart, or some batsh*t crazy thing comes to you when you almost finish investigating an area.
The gameplay is primarily first-person or third-person shooter that place strong emphasis on your gameplay type. You can go guns blazing, get a companion and do some killing, conduct stealth and light skirmishes, or just explore alone in the Capital Wasteland. What makes Fallout 3’s gameplay a bit special is the V.A.T.S (Vault-Tec Assisted Targeting System) where you “paused” the game while targeting an enemy’s legs, arms, equipped weapon, and the head. The feature is pretty nice and does help you in dire situations. However, it’s a bit unfortunate that V.A.T.S makes the game paused and not real-time. The stealth mechanic is a mixed bag. You can practically invest a lot of points towards the Stealth skill to make your stealth “level” to what suits you. If your Stealth skill is low then the enemy will “automatically” notice you even when the enemy is not facing you and you are crouch-walking towards an unsuspected enemy. What frustrates me the most was that there is no iron sight or aiming down your equipped weapon. Aiming is mostly useless and “hip-fire” the equipped weapon seems to be what’s best.
Is there criticisms for Fallout 3: Game of the Year Edition? Fallout 3 is definitely not perfect. There are a lot of technical issues and bugs that Bethesda Games Studios neglected. Many PC users now have Windows 7, 8/8.1, and Windows 10 and a high majority will most likely have an major technical issue that can or cannot be fixed. The games does crash to desktop in modern PC architecture due to no support of multi-core processing (when the game came out, it was dual-core). The solution is there to fix it, but it does not fully bandage the problem. The NPCs look stale, but mods do help make it better. The most critical aspect of the game is the karma system. In a post-apocalyptic setting, any person would know that there’s no (or little) black-or-white scenarios. The karma system is a good concept, but heavily flawed since conducting bad “actions” like stealing or pickpocketing is treated like a horrid sin.
The review sounds critical but why does it gives a thumbs up? The answer is simple: It is fun. I remembered when I got the Fallout 3 Collector’s Edition back in October 2008 (where you get the concept art book, featurette DVD, the vault boy bobblehead, and a lunchbox (yes, an actual lunchbox). Fallout 3 crash to desktop so often that I’ve lost count. For some reason, I didn’t too angry about it (even though I should have). Fallout 3 was the first video game that I actually got so immersive to. The setting draws you in and exploration is so much fun. Fallout 3 is one of a very few games that gameplay matters over graphics and “minor” flaws. Does the sequels like Fallout: New Vegas and Fallout 4 improved over Fallout 3? Certainly. Fallout 3’s default price is at $19.99 (for Game of the Year Edition). I’ve strongly recommend (for those who haven’t play Fallout 3) to get it on a steep discount of -75% ($5 USD or regional equivalent) since the game faces technical issues on today’s PC systems. Fallout 3 is certainly not top-tier game (when looking at it today), but the game was a marvelous achievement for a first-person shooter to be in an open-world setting.

I'm going to start off by saying that I loved the first F.E.A.R. and all of its expansions.  Never had I been so scared of a little girl in a red dress or so saddened in a video game by learning what was done to her.  The sci-fi elements were futuristic, but still grounded in the feel of being the kind of thing a military black ops unit would keep hidden from the 21st century public.
F.E.A.R. 2 just didn't have the same punch with either the atmosphere or the gameplay.  I remember the slow motion horror  when the first mechsuit came bursting through a wall at you in F.E.A.R. 1.  Then F.E.A.R. 2 had them shooting down from space.  Just felt like going overboard to me.
Then we have F.E.A.R. 3.  The sense of horror, that fear of the unknown that got triggered whenever the lights flickered.  You just don't feel it anymore once you realize that Alma is pretty much on your side at this point.  This is quite simply a run and gun game.  In addition, the sci-fi elements border on Star Trek with enemies teleporting in via portals.  And changing over to that regenerating health model just makes it feel nothing like the first F.E.A.R.  The only thing that kept me playing was that I've wanted to know how this trilogy would end from the get-go of F.E.A.R. 1.
I wanted to like this game.  I hoped it would undo some of the minor snafus that came up with F.E.A.R. 2 and give us a dark and unsettling finale to one of the best horror games I've played.  Not a total let down, but a let down none the less.

So many divers eaten... So many days ruined. My friends jokingly ask if I'm "hungry" or if I want "a snack" when asking if I'm up to play this game. I always am. Depth is an asymmetrical team-based shooter with sharks vs divers. Essentially, it's what Evolve wishes it could be. There are different sharks, like the tanky great white or the speedy mako. There are various shark upgrades like rapid health regeneration after eating a diver. The sharks don't have it easy, though. Divers protect a robot that opens up deep-sea safes around the map, netting them cash to use on new weapons. gear, and upgrades. Harpoon guns, underwater machine guns, poison rounds, mobile turrets, and a myriad of other tools are at the divers' disposal to fend off the sharks until S.T.E.V.E. is done with the safes. The devs update this game every few months, adding more of everything there is to love. Over more than a year after release, they have changed Depth from a limited-playstyle gimmick to a full fleshed out game with countless hours of fun.

Pros:
* Really immerses you in the underwater world, with the realistic surface textures to the sleek movement of the sharks fins, it just looks gorgeous.
*The asymmetric play style is fluid (no pun intended) and fun to experiment with on both diver and shark mode, gives you a sense of real weightlesness.
*Combat feels great and gritty (the satisfaction from landing a shot on a sneaky shark just feels rewarding in itself!)
Cons:
*Megalodon hunt takes forever to find a match (probably because most people play it in private lobbies with their friends).
*Gametime feels too short and would be a lot more fun if both divers/sharks had more lives or if some power ups/droppables were included scattered around the map.
*No rewards - if you suck at being a diver/shark and had a hard game, you get nothing. For the rest of the game. Game is hard.

This is a bit of a mixed bag.  The basic gameplay is, if you like tactical rpgs, very well done and very enjoyable.  It plays in a manner similar to games like Xcom and Shadowrun Returns.  The addition of co-op, letting you split a 4-man team between two players, makes the game much more fun, and either easier or more difficult, depending on how much you coordinate with your teammate.
On the downside, the game is very slow moving at times, with long stretches where you will not be fighting, but only talking to NPCs, walking back and forth between locations to pick up/deliver things, and running in circles trying to figure out specifically what you need to do next for the numerous side quests, many of which are very vague in their direction.  In this way it is similar to the Witcher games.  However, unlike those games, this one has terrible writing, a terrible story, and terrible voice acting.  Some rpgs manage to create a world and story that interests the player, makes you feel engaged in a dynamic story, leads you to care about the characters and the outcomes, and entertains you so much that you don't notice you haven't really had much to do for hours except talk to NPCs.  This game does not do that.  The writing here reminded me a lot of various JRPGs.  A story that is both cliched and incomprehensible, charracters that are absurd and difficult to care about, and many times more dialog than you want, all of it poorly written and poorly acted.
For the gameplay and co-op, it's worthwhile, but I doubt I'd want to play it a second time just because of how many dull parts you have to sit through, and how little the writers managed to make me care about their story or their world.
