I typically don't play platformers, but I really enjoyed this game.  So much so, it's one of the few (out of the many games I own) that I sat and played all the way through. This game works best with a gamepad, and it plays fine on SteamOS or Big Picture mode, making it perfect for Steam boxes or people that spent the $15 to get a super long HDMI cable and game on their family room TV with their PC.  This might have been a console port, but it doesn't feel like it.  It runs very smoothly.
One thing to note is that this game is pixel-perfect.  The controls are clean, and they are reponsive.  If you die, it's your fault.  The game also follows it's own rules.  If there are spikes on the gorund that thurt you, and you can somehow fling an enemy into them, it will hurt them too.  If what they shoot at you will kill you, and you doge it, it could go on to kill someone else, etc.
...and the game isn't just a game, it's a story telling experience.  It has a bit of an anime vibe, but this is in no way a negative, and feels like it's in the same family as "Spirited Away" or "Howl's Moving Castle", with the same creative art style and characters.  I felt emotionally connected to the story while playing.
If you are very good at platformer games, you could probably beat this game straight through in 6-10 hours. However, you are a completionist (like me) and find the allure of a seemingly impossible to get to treasure teetering on ledge you can't quite yet reach something you can't let go, and are willing to spend extra time figuring it out, you can spend literally hours backtracking with new abilites and finding new ways to negotriate old puzzles. Despite the back tracking, it never gets old as you are finding new ways to traverse your old challenges, with reasonable rewards, even going as far as to unlock new areas, much in the vein of Metroid.
It took me a good 25+ hours to beat this game, but I spent a lot of time wandering around the gorgeous puzzles, and I'm not a platforrmer gamer.  However, this is a creative, well balanced, realtively bug free (I didn't encounter a single bug in my hours of playing), game and story telling experience.  You could do way worse with a platformer title, and I'm certianly glad I snatched this up, and if any of this interests you, you should too! :)

Lego Worlds is a game of two parts.
The first component of the game is exploration. You are dropped (literally) into a procedurally generated world made entirely of Lego bricks. This brings me to a highlight of the game: the aesthetic. Everything, and I mean EVERYTHING in this game is made from Lego, from the buildings, to the trees, to the ground, to the water, to the Moon and clouds; each are made from their own virtual Lego bricks and I, personally, love it.
Many games that have taken the path of the Exploration/Creation genre have “borrowed” the Minecraft block theme, while others have gone the way of simple pixel art or standard Unity Assets. The Lego theme, however, allows for some spectacular worlds, especially when partnered with the biomes currently available. While it is not the most beautiful world ever conceived, I found the "Oriental" and "Mushroom" biomes to be exceptionally pretty.
However, back onto gameplay. The aim of the exploration aspect is simply to explore and collect. Anything you find around the world, from trees to buildings to animals, vehicles and npcs (in the style of Lego Minifigures) can be collected and bought with studs, which you gain from destroying things within the world. These features can then be built (with the minifigures allowing you to customise your character), but I'll go deeper into this during the "creation" section of the review. Vehicles and creatures can be mounted, each being useful in their own way, with some moving on land, water or through the sky. My personal choice of transportation is on dragon-back, although I have recently found a giant drill which can be used to tunnel underground (and confuse the physics engine).
The player is also able to collect "tools"; items that can be carried and used, in the vein of the pickaxes and swords of Minecraft. They are found in large treasure chests within buildings found in the different biomes. I have, so far, collected 9 of these tools, ranging from dynamite and a bazooka (both of which can be used to blow up anything within the game), to a sword (which, as far as I can tell, simply do more damage to enemies than if you attack bare-handed), a blunderbuss (which shoots) and, oddly, a few pieces of food. This brings me to one of my big complaints about the game: very little is explained. While the game gives you instructions on how to move and control the different vehicles (as well as explaining the different abilities in "creative mode"), it doesn't explain what things actually do. In many cases, it’s simple to work things out: blunderbuss shoots, shield reduces damage, ect. However, in other cases, it’s far harder. "Why am I throwing this fish? What does it do?" I ask myself as I launch it at plants. I have still not found a use for the ice cream, fish, or apple that I've found along my journey and, while I am sure that there are many, many more items within the game, the ones I have are not particularly useful. While the dynamite and bazooka are excellent for clearing paths through awkwardly generated foliage, I could easily do without them, and both provide the same job. The weapons are equally needless, with no enemies providing a challenge, especially with the lacklustre combat system (tap left mouse button until the enemy is dead).
In fact, almost all of the "enemies" currently in the game (that I have met) aren't even hostile unless provoked. Although the skeletons and zombies that roam the night seem to have an immense dislike for any passing horses or camels, they ignore you entirely, until you decide to punch one of them. In fact, the npcs as a whole are underwhelming. While it’s nice to see them as they smile and wave at you, that is all they do. Other than that, they only seem to wander endlessly around their islands. The only exception to this rule are the cowboys, who'll occasionally get on a horse or fight one another. This said, the developers have stated that they will be working on the A.I to make them more organic, so hopefully this will be fixed as time goes on.
Now, onto the second part of the game: the creation aspect.
Lego Worlds provides a creative mode, similar to Minecraft's, providing the player with a large number of tools. These are split into three categories:
The first category is "terraforming". The terraforming tools allow the player to add or remove large amounts of land, change the colours of land to match a different biome, raise or lower the terrain and copy and paste large structures.
The second is the "Brick-building" category. This category allows players to use a variety of Lego bricks, from the simple square brick, to the longer, thin ones, to those ones with the flat tops. Bricks can be placed one at a time, moved, or deleted in this mode. There are also an awful lot of colour choices within the mode, including semi-transparent options and light-up options. This brings me to another problem I had, although a more minor one: there was very little indication that the transparent and light blocks were any different from the other colours. While the transparent blocks utilised a different symbol, the light blocks had a perfectly normal appearance. This confused me for a while, as I was searching for these choices, but couldn't find them for a good while.
Finally, the last category is the "Model" choices. This menu is used to summon mounts, change your character and equip tools while exploring, but also allows players to recreate any unique sets seen on the way, and there are a lot, with over 80 collected within my playthrough. After finding these while exploring, they must be unlocked with studs, but can then be placed infinite times. These sets range from pumpkins and Japanese Torii gates to cacti and pump jacks, depending on the biomes.
I feel the creation tools could be more advanced, allowing players to make machines from different parts, such as allowing people to design their own in-game vehicles, in a similar mix-and-match way to the character customisation within the game, as well as allowing the use of features like doors and windows (which are available within real life Lego sets). This would allow for more complex gameplay without forcing it upon the younger targeted audience. Of course, since the game is aimed towards children, it makes sense that it would be kept simple, but it’s still slightly disappointing.
My biggest problem of the game, however, comes from the combination of the two genres. I had been playing for a few hours, exploring and enjoying myself. I decided to stop and try out some of the creative features. 5 hours later, I had made my own island, complete with a stately home, port, secret underground base, tower and all sorts of gadgets and gizmos, enjoying myself in the same way I used to as a kid. Then, foolishly, I decided to explore some more. I haven't seen my island since. The map is so vast (possibly infinite) and the islands so similar that it would be impossible not to get lost without carefully noting your route and returning to your base at regular intervals. To spend 5 hours creating something, only to lose it, really put a damper on my playtime, and it means you must make a choice. While the game allows for both creation and exploration, in reality you can only choose one. If you wish to create Lego designs in-game and not lose them, you can't explore too far, while if you want to explore and collect models and characters, there's no point making anything, as you'll lose it within an hour.
To combat this, I hope the developers add in some sort of map or teleporter function. These functions may already be in there, and I simply haven't found them, but it would be far better to provide them from the start, to allow players to appreciate both parts of the game.
In conclusion, while I certainly would recommend the game, there are definitely things that the developers could, and hopefully will, improve before launch.

This game is a must-buy for any RPG fan!
While its style is distinctly western, in everything but art Epic Battle Fantasy is very much a JRPG. The combat is heavily based on elemental advantage/weaknesses – brute force is rarely an option in harder battles, instead the key to victory is using correct skills and gear.
Speaking of gear, uniquely among RPGs, newer weapons and armor you acquire are not direct improvement of your old equipment. Instead, each weapon and armor has properties that make it good in some situations and mediocre to bad in others. The result is that no equipment becomes useless, and some of early gear may very much be an option for endgame battles.
Instead of acquiring stronger gear, the game features upgrade system for your equipment, allowing you to improve your gear as you progress through the game (most later upgrades require items that are not available until later). And on final note about gear, each item your character wears, from weapons and armor to small badges visibly changes your appearance, which is really a nice touch!
The story doesn’t even pretend to be serious, but it will accomplish what it sets out to: make you laugh from start to finish!
Overall, Epic Battle Fantasy is all kinds of awesome. If you like turn-based RPGs, give it a try and it won’t disappoint!

I think this is actually one of my favourite games of all times.  It's very much focused on the narrative which means there isn't much in terms of gameplay, but this doesn't make it bad.  The story, characters and setting are all so beautiful that it's a pleasure to accompany the characters as they discover new things.
The game focuses on an dieing old man called John, who has requested the services of a company who can alter memories of the dieing so their final moments are pleasing.  You play as two scientists from the company (with great character dynamics) as they traverse his memories in order to learn more about him and to change his memories in the right way so that he goes to the moon.  I won't spoil much more, but you get to see John's journey through life meeting some great characters and gradually learning more and more about him.
The music is also fantastic, accompanying the beautiful, funny and scary parts of the game perfectly.
Apart from a few puzzles (which never become very difficult) and minigame, most of the game consists of searching from objects that will allow you to traverse John's memories.  That might sound tedious, but you often learn things as you explore, so I never really felt annoyed when having to search the level.  If you prefer gameplay over a narrative, then you might want to give this game a skip, but I would prefer it if you gave it a chance.  There's a lot of dialogue, but it's so well written and engaging that you won't minding sitting and reading.
The graphics are done in the 2D RPG style and they are very well suited for this sort of game.  The fact that you grow attached to what are quite blurry 2D characters means the game has done a good job.  Graphics won't blow you away, but they are still good and serve the purpose.

Reus is what I’d call a mix between Populous and Settlers, two of my favorite strategy game series. Your goal is to create an economy eco-system (the Settlers part), but indirectly, by shaping the planet and placing and transmuting different environments and resources (the Populous part). And it’s simply a delight to play.
The basics are quite simple. Our elemental giants can place three environmental object types: animals, minerals, and plants, which in turn give one or more of the three types of resources that humans use: food, wealth and technology. It’s a very basic and simple concept, and the depth comes in combination between the environmental objects and environments themselves (forests, swamps, oceans, deserts and mountains, which our giants also are responsible for creating), symbiotic relationship among nature, settlements, and between each other, and adapting to the situation by transmuting nature as the settlements start expanding and it all suddenly sounds a lot more complex, doesn’t it?
But here’s the thing, Reus is very smartly designed when it comes to expanding depth and not overwhelming the player with it. You start with just the basics, and unlock upgrades (both direct for nature and indirect for humans) as you complete certain number of goals. So this allows you to spend time trying to figure out how to make best of the symbiotic relationships between different plants, animals and minerals (and the way people want to use them depending on what they’re building, we don’t have any controls over the humans) and as you get a better understanding by completing goals – you get access deeper into the systems.
The only thing that I think is missing from the game is a fast-forward function. Even though it’s very enjoyable to listen to the game’s awesome ambiance music as you watch the lush and beautiful graphics, sometimes you just want to speed things up a little bit.
So unless slow pace is something that’s going to push you away, I’d definitely recommend to check it out! I’ve spent hours in the game already, and sense that will spend many more.

A series revived and overall a fantastically fun game; however it's not without it's faults. One, the class selction is limited and because of it you rarely get to play the role you want to play and you'll often see people leave if they don't get the class they want. They should have made two versions of each class like Dark Legacy so people would have more choice and variety for gameplay as the 4 classes get tiring. Two, the items you purchase are merely cosmetic and do nothing, invest your hard earned cash in actives. Three, there is a desperate lack of of levels and variety in the game. This game would thrive off of more unique stages and level creator would be amazing here.  Four, the final and most pressing issue, there's a huge lack of communication. In a cooperative game like this it is very difficult to function properly without proper communication; voice chat, a more fleshed out command system, or even a simple chatbox would makes a world difference in improving the game. The thing Gauntlet does right though is gameplay itself. The actives are brilliant, the gameplay is fantastic, coop is fantastic, and the style is gorgeous. In total I think this game is a step in the right direction for the Gauntlet series and I hope it gets expanded upon in the future or gets a sequel that get's it right.

I feel awful.
Usually, I give games a fair chance, but Divinity is a game which didn't hold my interest at first. I only put a few hours into the game and gave it a 'meh' review. I recently got hooked on its sequel, Divinity 2, and decided to give the first one the fair chance it deserved.
I'm happy that I have. It's an amazing game, with a memorable soundtrack and combat that really feels better than I gave it credit for. I originally thought skill books were going to be a rare commodity, but it turns out they're readily sold at various merchants in town. Oops.
The game is even better with a friend, which causes you to either work together or butt heads to accomplish your goals, occasionally (or often) entering disputes as to what the right choice is. The desputes are handled in game as well through a game of paper rock scissors. It's actually more clever than I gave it credit for originally, and while it does leave persuasion attempts up to chance, really it's no different than dice in that respect. You just enter a furious dramatic paper rock scissors game with the person you're trying to persuade (with advantage or disadvantage depending on your skill).
Honestly I highly encourage anyone interested in trying this game to play it with a friend, as the experience is a lot richer that way. Though the game itself is still easy to appreciate when solo. I originally shut it out due to how 'old school' it was, but when I gave it another try it warmed up to me emmensely.
The combat is turn based and complex. A battle can be won using a variety of tactics, to include creating and manipulating elemental surfaces such as water, fire, oil, and the like. If you don't have the means to create a desired surface there are barrels aplenty full of dangerous substances  ready to sustain your abuse. Come to think of it, why do these barrels exist? Why are there barrels of poison just laying around? Eh, who cares, they're pretty darn useful.
Character creation is also diverse, allowing for many builds. The diversity makes for some fun experimentation as one tries to find that perfect character that suits their personality. It can be either a hardcore tactical experience or a roleplaying experience, or both. The addition of many difficulty levels allow a player to experience the game hwoever they wish, either a casual experience to enjoy the story, up to a difficulty suited for rear clenching tooth grinding massochist driven need to suffer and reload over and over again until the player finally finds a tactic that works for a given situation.
And the soundtrack is a-maaaaaaazing! Honestly, it's one of the things Divinity has over its sequel, the soundtrack is stellar and I wish the composer (Kirill Pokrovsky) was around today to provide his talents to the sequel. Not that the sequel has bad music, it's just nothing like the first.
So, yes, I am awful that I didn't give this game the chance that it deserved. I deleted my previous review and put this one up with both thumbs up to feel at peace with myself. Thanks to Divinity 2 for making me curious enough to revisit this game, and thanks to Larian Studios for their great work.

TL;DR: If you like platformers, and don't mind a challenge, pick this up. If you have ever bought a game just because it looked gorgeous, you won't regret doing that again here.
Visually, this is among the most beautiful games I have ever played. The art is just stunningly good. The music, the controls, and the overall gameplay are also top-notch, adding up to what I can only describe as a brilliant overall experience. The story is fine for what it is--simple, cute, heartwarming--but this is not a story-driven game, so don't expect much of a narrative.
The game is overall pretty tough. It's not "I Wanna Be the Guy" difficulty or anything, but it's a legitimate challenge.
I have one semi-complaint. The game does away with traditional boss fights (a good thing), and instead has extended chase sequences in the place where a boss fight would normally be (also good). The problem is that a good chase sequence is most thrilling when immersion is high--that is, when you're taken off-guard, need to improvise, and just barely squeak through the sudden challenge. But since the chase sequences are basically this game's "boss fights," the designers seemed to feel obligated to make them the most challenging segments. And they are, without question, the most difficult parts of the game. This means unless you are a wizard you will be repeating these chase sequences a number of times before you manage to complete them, which kind of ruins the immersion you get from having a chase sequence in the first place.
This is only a semi-complaint though, because completing these chase sequences after like 20 tries is definitely exhilarating. If you've played Dark Souls, well, it's a little like that. This is a game that is out to kill you, and it feels rewarding to overcome the adversity after many failures.
In my opinion they could have upped the difficulty in other parts of each level, and then made the chase sequences challenging, but still able to be realistically survived on the first go with some skill and improvisation. That would have made these chases much more thrilling and satisfying--like an adrenaline reward at the end of the level, instead of a final obstacle to slam your face against repeatedly.

Skullgirls, no other american studios does fighting games like these guys. The game consist of only a few characters but all of them are different in their own way and none are mere pallet swaps like the Ryu/Ken & Eddie/Christie/Tiger. The game features complex mechanics that make it deeper than most, like Ms. Fortunes ability to throw her head and have it attack independently of its body or Big Bands taunt, that modifies his blockbuster moves or even Valentines ability to apply 3 different type of poisons to her syringe projectile that applies damage over time, increased hit stun, imput lag and all 3 can be enhanced by "upping the dose", its clear that Skullgirls have some unique mechanics. All characters have a upwards to 22 different colors to choose from and most of them are clever references to other media, such as Ms Fortunes Morrigan and She-Hulk colors to Parasouls Jessica Rabbit and Jean Grey colors. You fight on a 2D plain and the game functions on the light, medium and heavy puch and kicks mechanic followed by specials, supers and tags. The games style is also gorgeous, and not because the cast consist of almost all female characters. The sprites are very similar to something you would see off  of something like Scott Pilgrim and each character is beautifully animated, with backgrounds that are Noir-ish in nature. The music, oh my god the music, they are smooooooooooth. Most of the tracks take inspiration from the 1920s-1950s and while they dont get you hyped up to fight one track certainly does. The final boss track, is appropriately epic with creepy choirs that have to be experienced.
But what if Im new to fighting game?
this is the biggest hurdle for all of fighting games and Skullgirls has one of the best tutorials I have ever seem. The games tutorial not only covers the basics, but teaches you fighting game concepts such as mixups, cancelling and ways to use each character. The games training/practice room is also great, giving indicators to hitboxes, frame advantage and recovery as well as simulating various latency lag. Clearly this game is built by those who love the genre is capable of lowering that barrier of entry by a significant margin.

I have to admit, I initially had no plans of ever purchasing this game or playing it in the future, and only have had the opportunity to because of the generosity of a friend. With that being said, I have been surprisingly enthralled by the game. Combat is fast-paced, easy to learn, and the combos aren't ridiculously complex, which are great qualities for a fighting game. While the roster isn't particularly large in size, the difference between playing each character and the variety offered by the mixing and matching of teams has provided more than enough for me thus far. The skins, while not affecting much mechanically, at least let you have a little fun with variety as well.
I will say that the random matches I have played in have been particularly filled with people well beyond my skill as a starter, and so if you don't have friends who own or plan to own the game, it likely won't be as fun. If you do, however, I think this might be a nice time filler for your games library.

It's a fighting game that tells you the basics of how the hell to play fighting games if you ask it to. Also there aren't any 10+ button-press sequences required for any given move. Fast, fun, sombre story-wise, and pretty much all about hitting things.

Reus is a world-building simulation style game, where your god-like interaction with the world is done by way of four giant monoliths with magical powers. You and your four vast minions will help grow small settlements of nomads into bustling village-sized cities, providing the citizens with enough resources to survive, expand and thrive. At first glance Reus seems like a very small and simple god game done a thousand times before, but upon further inspection the game reveals a huge level of complexity that is both shocking and fantastically deep.
Reus only really has one real gameplay mode – Era . The aim of Era is to work towards completing all of the available achievements in the game, and Reus serves up a generous dose of replayability with a staggering 120-odd levels to grapple with. This replayability is thanks in no small part to the curious way in which you control the lives of your nomads.
The mysterious Planet of the Creepy Giants is an artistic 2D slice of barren rock onto which the environments, plants, animals and minerals are spawned from your giant helpers, and the lack of space means efficiency is key. A village might start a project to complete a school or church, and it’s up to you to find the space to squeeze in the mind-numbing amount of food, wealth or technology the project requires. Enter symbiosis,the mechanic where every object your giants summon has the potential to interact with nearly any other object in the game and every base object has about 4 – 6 different ways to evolve.
Reus is a very pretty game to play, if a little repetitive at times. Your 2D slice of planet-pie has a 3D-like surface. The game’s major weakness is the lack of art assets, borne from its small development roots. When every blueberry bush and snake den has the same picture, a row of the same resource breaks the immersion of world-building somewhat, and replaces it with a slightly lesser world-assembly feel instead, and this jarring sensation does hurt the feeling of power and mastery a good god game strives for.
Similarly due to the small team the game was built by, the other major weakness Reus suffers is a poor user interface. The graphics options allow users with poor eyesight to change the resolution to the lowest settings, but even when all the icons and fonts are as large as possible the tutorial text proves impossible to read without 20/20 vision. The few controls the player has on-screen are so minimal and unnoticeable, the tooltips and hotkets are in approximately font size 6. While such a minor graphical issue might go unnoticed by the majority of players, Reus is almost certainly not appropriate for players with less than perfect eyesight.
That said, once the game gets going and the Era progressing, Reus has a huge amount to offer to keep a player engaged. All of the players’ efforts are focussed on pleasing the tiny humans who settle in your lovingly planned environments, and when your forest-dwelling humans plan to open up a world-class mine there are a few options before you, depending on what sort of god you want to be. You could form a large amount of forest-based minerals around the tiny village, terraform a forest into a mountainside landscape or just burn the village down and hope the next squad of settlers aren’t as greedy. A word of warning, however – if a new village settles amongst in a land of plenty, they are much more likely to become greedy and violent.
Weaknesses aside, Reus is a new twist on a god game with a huge amount of gameplay behind it for those who can bear their way through the slightly arduous tutorial. It offers at least 30 hours of entertaining god play, with the ability to command your mountainous workers to bless or crush human villages as you see fit, and that is no bad thing.

After a short while, I began to become engaged in the world the game was painting, and the lack of gameplay mechanics quickly became shadowed by a well-written story and powerful music. Soon, I became dedicated to understanding John's life and helping him get to the moon.
And boy, it was a rollercoaster ride! I was guessing all the way to the end, and the way everything happens was not someting I saw coming. The entire story and it's writing is top notch in a video game. I mean, the concept of the story is great in an of itself! By the end, I was thouroughly invested into the characters, which is something most video game's fail to do I think. And boy, this game is deep! Even though this game, I would say, is family friendly, it is an adult game. Not because of it's content, but because of how deep it goes.  Don't know how to explain it.  There are also a few well placed jokes and references that made me laugh and got the game out of it's emotional train ride when it needed me to.
The music is also amazing! It blends with the game so well! Every moment had the perfect note, I felt. Also, the music literally ties into the story, which just adds so much more emotion into.
However, why I said it's a NEAR masterpiece is because of the gameplay. There honestly isn't to much. Just walking around, finding objects and solving quick little puzzles. The second half get's better forsure, but the gameplay isn't amazing by any means. In that regard, the game lacks. But only in that regard! It may not be mechanically complex, but it still is enough to keep you engaged in the world, and it's good enough to make you want to explore more. And honestly, I don't know how much more complex I would want it to be. Maybe if the gameplay blended with story a little better.
But don't let that stop you from expieriencing this game! This is a game I will play again, it was that good! If you think the gameplay or the art style might stop you from enjoying this work of art, and it may not be worth the $10, let me assure you that it is worth every penny. But if you really are not sure and dont want to take the risk, then follow this game and wait for it to go on sale. I wasn't sure if I was going to like it, and I got it on sale, and I sure am glad I bought it! I would pay 20 dollars for the game now! And seriously, DON'T refund the game. The end is absolutely worth it.
If your looking for a non-combat game, a game that is a little different, then buy this game! This is now one of my favorite games I have ever played. Go right now, add to cart, turn off the lights, and enjoy!

I would definitely recommend this game to anybody looking for a more simplified and more skill based ARPG experience. While it may be tempting at first glance to compare this game to other ARPGs like Torchlight, for most part the only similarities are the top view action.
While I would recommend this to hardcore and softcore players alike, I think the best element of this game is the challenge. While there are some RPG elements, they are somewhat limited in scope and some are purely esthetic. I believe softcore players would not get their money's worth at the moment, so for $20 I can only recommend this to hardcore gamers who are looking to challenge themselves by using teamwork to conquer the game on its hardest difficulties.
The game also rewards players who play a lot, as there are many achievements which grant permanent passive perks such as increased damage, moving speed and decreased cooldown for certain skills, which is very nice and gives the player an incentive to play a lot and perform well. This however is probably only more necessary on harder difficulties, as this is one of those games that relies more on the player's skill rather than gear, equipment, skill tree, etc... You will find none of these elements in this game as this is a remake of an arcade classic.
While you can play this game solo for a while, you will need teammates who know what they're doing on latter difficulties. You can also play up to 4 players locally, so as long as there are enough controllers plugged in the USBs. There is also no in-game chat, which can be a double edged blade in my opinion. On one hand, it prevents needless distraction and conversations (mostly complaining), which helps to keep the focus on the actual game as it's fairly easy to die when not paying attention to the right elements on screen.
There are four playable classes, each of them having their own style, which all feel very unique and contribute in different ways. Only one of these characters may be used at a time, so it may be important to learn how to use every class.
- The Warrior, having high armor and hit points is the natural meatshield of the bunch, deals medium damage in an area of effect or an arc and can bum rush through hordes. However outside of using his skills he can be pretty slow moving. His whirlwind special attack will devastate any enemies standing in his path.
- The Valkyrie, is a hybrid DPS-Tank class with high maneuverability. His main attack pierces through enemy lines and is very effective in taking out cannon fodder units, but may leave him momentarily vulnerable to stronger units. He can also take quite a beating, but not as much as the warrior. However, the ability to block incoming missles gives the Valkyrie a huge advantage in combat, which can be a great for protecting the Elf while he deals ranged damage. Quite an effective combination in my opinion. The Valkyrie's special attack is a devastating chain-damage shield throw that is very effective against hordes, but leaves him unable to block until the shield returns.
- The Elf, is a basic ranged character that can effectively evade anything it comes across, as well as delivering precisie sniper shots to often elusive elite enemies with special abilities that can wreak havoc onto your party. In addition the dealing massive damage to enemies, the Elf is able to drop or attach a bomb onto one of his arrows to deal even bigger damage to radius. The Elf's evade ability can also be key when used offensively in order to reach spawn towers to drop bombs when the action becomes so heavy that no teammates have access to destroy the key units.
- The Wizard, with a staggering 9 spells from which to choose from, is easily one of the most important characters due to his abilities. Each element has 3 spells (fire, ice, lightning) that are all very unique and renders the Wizard one of the most versitile character that can adapt to deal with almost any situation. From shotgun-style ice shards to your face, to mighty exploding orbs that deliver the highest DPS in an area of effect in the game, to chain-lightning and slow aura, the Wizard can quickly dispatch of hordes of enemies while supporting the rest of the party. However, this is the class with the highest learning curve due to his versitality and is by far the most complex character to play in the game.
In the end, this is a great game with a lot of challenge and no drama what's so ever when playing online. I'd recommend to this game to anybody who enjoys and misses the old school arcade-type games.
PROS:
+ Four unique classes, each with their own roles
+ Four player local or online co-op
+ Challenging team-based gameplay
+ No in-game chat, no drama!
+ Pick up and play - Simple interface allows for quickly setting up and starting games
CONS:
- Game balance issues depending on party member play styles and preferences
- Nature of gameplay may sometimes encourage players to be greedy, however this only affects post-game rankings
- A little pricey at $20
VERDICT:
7.2/10 - Highly recommended!

TL;DR: If you like platformers, and don't mind a challenge, pick this up. If you have ever bought a game just because it looked gorgeous, you won't regret doing that again here.
Visually, this is among the most beautiful games I have ever played. The art is just stunningly good. The music, the controls, and the overall gameplay are also top-notch, adding up to what I can only describe as a brilliant overall experience. The story is fine for what it is--simple, cute, heartwarming--but this is not a story-driven game, so don't expect much of a narrative.
The game is overall pretty tough. It's not "I Wanna Be the Guy" difficulty or anything, but it's a legitimate challenge.
I have one semi-complaint. The game does away with traditional boss fights (a good thing), and instead has extended chase sequences in the place where a boss fight would normally be (also good). The problem is that a good chase sequence is most thrilling when immersion is high--that is, when you're taken off-guard, need to improvise, and just barely squeak through the sudden challenge. But since the chase sequences are basically this game's "boss fights," the designers seemed to feel obligated to make them the most challenging segments. And they are, without question, the most difficult parts of the game. This means unless you are a wizard you will be repeating these chase sequences a number of times before you manage to complete them, which kind of ruins the immersion you get from having a chase sequence in the first place.
This is only a semi-complaint though, because completing these chase sequences after like 20 tries is definitely exhilarating. If you've played Dark Souls, well, it's a little like that. This is a game that is out to kill you, and it feels rewarding to overcome the adversity after many failures.
In my opinion they could have upped the difficulty in other parts of each level, and then made the chase sequences challenging, but still able to be realistically survived on the first go with some skill and improvisation. That would have made these chases much more thrilling and satisfying--like an adrenaline reward at the end of the level, instead of a final obstacle to slam your face against repeatedly.

A classic pay-to-win game obtained from the latest PC Gamer magazine.
There's no replayable solo mode, once you're through with that, you won't get any more rewards for playing the same matches. It serves as a testing ground for any new deck concepts you come up with, that's it.
The only way to progress is to battle randomly online and specifically win. Which leads to farming the lower ranks so that you can get the coins to buy a new roulette-spin to get more cards.
You can, however, pay money for rubies, which you can convert directly into these roulette spins, thus neatly skipping the arduous grinding bit of the game.
Daily challenges which also give rewards help to hide these issues, but ultimately this will sit in my 5-minute-game category.

The summary of this game in short can be put like this:
At first it will be entertaining a fun because it is a new game. You will be interested in learning, playing, and even trying to advance your rank. However, after playing for a while and digging deeper into things trying to get better and learning all you can then you will find it incredibly frustrating. The game is very imbalanced. Which if you ever try 'Draft' mode then you will see how random things really are even with good picks.
The long list:
Solo mode - Solo Play is about what you would expect. It is you versus a computer AI. The computer isn't particularly smart though at times it was kind of hard just starting out and having practically nothing or knowing little about the game. Solo is there to give you a basic education though.. nothing special.
"Online" mode - Technically all of it is online...but whatever. first of this is what the game calls 'ranked' mode. you play and as you win or lose your rank is affected. now here is the issue. there is NO 'casual' mode to play against real players in a non-ranked format. so you are always playing with your rank on the line. its not exactly the most relaxing thing. some people would like to just join a casual game and not worry about wins or losses.
Draft mode - This is like 'Arena' format where you get a line up of some random cards and you pick from them one at a time until you have a full deck. As I mentioned before the game is pretty imbalanced and this really comes through when the rng is at its worst...which is here.  In fact I have tried even with really great decks to win as much as possible. the most I have one is 3 out of a possible of 12. It takes 1500 gold to enter after you have grinded it. your reward should you actually win 1-3 is like 1300-1400 gold worth in prizes. you get a power token (1000gold from the store) and around 300-400 gold. i suspect you have to get at least 6+ wins to just break even.
Imbalances - So about those imbalances. Just coming into the game recently I was greeted by the "Call to Arms" meta. Which is that they dont play much except buildings and more buildings. Then they start spamming you with the spell "Call to Arms". Its nearly impossible to beat unless you have a deck specifically dedicated to beating it. Which kind of makes you vulnerable to everything else in the game. It really makes the game a pile of crap at this point in time just by itself.

There is not much that one can say about this title except "If you have not played it yet, what are you waiting for?!". There is a reason that there was Divinity 1 followed by 2, 3,, and now the DOS 2 being released the next month in September.
For those that have not played this beautiful game, you are missing out on an incredible story rich RPG. The story of the game is very deep, has twists and humor in it. The 20ish hours you will spend exploring, questing, and battling will be well worth the time. The graphics is outstanding and the music is spectacular. The artwork will make you appreciate the artistic expressions of the designers of the game. If you have a friend/family member or spouse who likes RPGs, then this title will allow  you to explore the world together.
The main two protagonists of the game have a very close relationship complicated by the forgotten past. You will rediscover your past and either undo or reaffirm the choices made there. It is a story of love, friendship, betrayal and sacrifice. Few game designers choose to explore and try to engage the player in such a way to attempt to clarify what sacrifice, love and lunacy really mean. Larian Studios is another company besides Bioware that delivers stories that have depth. Besides your intelligence, your sense of humor will also be engaged - the game is filled with jokes and humorous situations (quests).

I'm on v1.13 bug fix after foundation patch.  This game still has a number of shortcomings, but since the foundation patch it has become a lot better.  I would say don't get this if you want multiplayer, a shooter, or expect a level of realism in the procedurally generated galaxy.  It is definitely worth a try if you like exploration or survival games with resource gathering and crafting.  They are still not done giving us a fully complete game IMO, but I've certainly enjoyed playing so far, and am glad it appears likely more content is coming.  This game has my attention back with the new foundation release with survival mode, base building, freighters, dog fight improvements, new blueprints, more crafting, farming, and new missions.
My likes:
- Free form travel to any of millions of solar systems, each with their own planets and moons you can land on and explore.
- The exploration is satisfying when checking out new planets.  I still enjoy walkabouts on non-hostile planets.
- The incremental progress that requires you to explore, gather resources, craft tech and base components, and search for ways to upgrade your ship, exosuit, and multitool.
- The ability to "discover" systems and have your name attached to it for other future players to find.
- Freighters, the ability to build bases there, and to call them to you.
- The ability to teleport from home base back and forth to specific space stations anywhere in the galaxy.  This allows you to keep a home base somewhere but be able to continue to advance toward the center of the galaxy at the same time.
- the ability to craft multiple aircraft landing pads
- the ability to craft and place in your planet and freighter base a galactic store interface.
- the ability to farm the resources you regularly need
- the ship varieties are cool.  I enjoy checking out new ones as I travel.  I wish I could control the colors of my own ship.
My dislikes:
- Survival mode launch fuel costs.  I enjoyed survival mode, and I did get through it all the way through the base missions before I installed a mod (if on PC you can mod).  But I thought the plutonium fuel requirements using 100% of your launcher fuel for a single launch was an unnecessary encumbered that discouraged exploration.  I'd rather be encouraged to explore.  Maybe HG should add some new tech upgrade components to the ship that reduce launcher costs for survival mode players that you can search for and discover over time or as you upgrade your ship.  I'm near the end of available content of the foundation patch so I installed a reduced launch costs mod.  Now I can land more often without going on a 40 minute walkabout looking for plutonium, or risk landing on a zero fuel planet.  This leads to frustration with the flight controls being so bad, because the only way to see if a base has a landing boey on it (allowing free launch if you hit it) is to fly in circles around the base as slow and low as you can until hopefully the stupid boey spawns in enough for you to see it.  Which leads to my next dislike:
- Poor flight control.  It's not that the controls are bad, just that the maneuverability of the ship is so limited.  You cannot go slow, low, under things, nor hover.  I have to say that the Low Flight mod I installed has really made this game more fun.  I can now hover over a base long enough to see if a free launch boey exists, and even to let me see resource names without landing.  That automatic height flight thing the game has would be good to toggle on and off.  The mod keeps it off so you can fly right into things.  But you can also fly under the floating islands, or through the loop holes.  Even under water.  So for me the low flying mod and the launch costs mod is making the game more playable. Now I land to see anything I want. I think it would be nice if advanced tech in game could provide these flight improvements, at least toward end game.
- Freighter bases, especially when using the cuboid rooms, become corrupted between game starts.  You can see the rooms stop aligning and you have to rebuild parts.  New walls will automatically add themselves to cuboid rooms walling off your farm plants.  I think this is an artifact of the misalignment that occurs. You can see stars through large cracks into space and they look visibly misaligned.  Also, you can have weather effects hurt while in those rooms, which shouldn't happen.  I end up rebuilding some freighter rooms and hallways every time I play to get rid of the new walls.
- Add variety.  I know this is all proceedurally generated, and that is awesome, but I think Hello Games should continue to add more variety to their existing procedural generation engine.  For example, even though many different variety of animals can spawn, there is a definite SET of types that spawn and the only question is if they have wings, bug heads, or whatever.  Maybe add snakes or some kind of additional variation with the plants and animals.  Kudos for adding barren thamium planets recently and enhancing the terrain.
- Polar variation.  I would like more procedural variety regarding the planets.  The fact that you can land anywhere on the planet and get the exact same environment really limits the value of the exploration.   I would hope to have polar vs equatorial variations added for weather, plants, animals, and terrain.
- Fix the super frustratingly slow interface popups that take over your ability to move...milestones, and trader dialog are the worst.  There should be smaller notices in the corner that don't interrupt your play.
- Crafting interface.  The crafting interface "next screen" blueprint button bug needs to be fixed.  There is something happening that will interfere and prevent the button from registering your click.  Not all the time but enough to make crafting a bunch of Lubricant repeatedly (for an example) frustrating.  But also, if I'm crafting a lot of something repeatedly why should I even have to turn a page to get to my blueprint every single time?  Crafting interface improvements please.  Let me sort by most used and allow me to iniate a batch to be crafted, then let me go explore as it works.
- In a space station when traders are flying in, the audio of the ships lags behind the visual of the ships by a couple seconds.  If you are actively trading with them, it is disconcerting.
Needs a lot of work. Fun for a bit. Overhyped to death.

Consider this a first impression, from someone who has easily spent well over 2000 hours in previous versions of the Trainz franchise (all the way back to 2004).
The usual load times seem to be getting longer and longer.  With my previous version of Train I had the default content, plus about 20 custome routes and about 10,000 extra DLC items I had downloaded using a first class ticket a while back.  I enjoy making my own routes, and so I had a lot of scenery items from which to play with.  Yeah, back then all that extra content sure loaded down the start up of the game.  But I understood it, as there was a lot of content.  Loading up this new version, I thought for sure there would be a lot of content to play with.  Sadly, however, the pickings seemed very slim once I did get in and see what I had available to me.  So imagine if I imported all my old content, it would probably take 3 hours to load :)
So I load up the sessions, and notice that now you have to pay to access some sessions.   $39.99?   Really are they fooling anyone by deducting that one cent?   $40 for a single play session?  WTF.   I would say about half of the sessions that come with the stock routes, you now have to pay extra for.  Here is a question...   If I published a route, could I set a price for sessions too?  And will I get that money as the route publisher?  I somehow doubt it, but damn...  That would be nice.
Anyhow, I loaded up the editor.  I have spent most of my time in the editor, so I can usually throw together something fairly quick.  And alas, nothing has really changed that I noticed throwing together a quick route to test some trains on, in the editor.  I saw that they has a FEC GP9 locomotive.  Oh sweet....   I love GP9's   I have been waiting for an official highly detailed GP9 model.   So I plopped that down on the track.   The outside skin was indeed very sweet.  So I ran the session, and went to drive the GP9 around...
I get into the cab view of the GP9 and...  I can't believe what I am seeing.   No detail at all.  This looks like the stock SD40 interior from 2004.  Nothing has changed!   Seriously?    Very unhappy about this.
Luckily I have been working on a physical real world model railroad, in order to get my train fix as of late.  If I had to rely on Trainz much longer, I imagine I would develop a real bad taste for train simulations.

To the Moon is an experience for all. I get that many people don't find this type of graphics appealing or walking simulators or story rich... Believe me, I had my doubts at first, too. But my friend told me that it was a beautiful game (plus it was on sale).
Playing it at first, I had a passive attitude and I stopped for a while because I was busy. I continued playing it after a month and I think that was my mistake. I didn't stop until I finished it and I'm pretty sure I would've cried if I remembered the beginning full well. It's a great story with an amazing soundtrack. The OST makes up for 70% of the feels in this game.
I tip my imaginary hat off to the storywriters, the composers, all who were involved in the making of To the Moon, and I encourage all those who are having second thoughts on buying and playing this game to give it a shot.
If it helps, this game has boobs. And nekos. And everything you'd want from a game.

This is less a video game, and more of a video story. Despite its pixel art appearnance there's very little about To The Moon that qualifies it as a "game". There are some puzzle solving elements, a "key finding" mechanic that amounts to clicking all over the screen LA-Noire style, and there are some very minor mini-games scattered throughout. I would opine that some of these detract from the experience, and I think most players will find them superfluous at best. Therefore, the reason I recommend To The Moon is not on its strength as a game, but on the strength of its story.
It's a story about loss, about love, and about sacrifice. I can't say that you will feel the same way I did, but I was emotionally affected by To The Moon. I don't think 20-year old me would've appreciated it as much as mid-thirties me does, and I've found myself thinking about the story even after I've finished playing; wrapping up stray plot threads in my mind, and refelcting on how the characters interacted with one another. The soundtrack is also very good as well, tonally setting the scene in many places.
The game does have its weak points. The writing is uneven, with some moments feeling oddly placed, and some falling flat (there is an action beat involving a life-threatening event that seems unnecessary). The interplay between the two doctors is cute at times, even funny at others, but at certain points it gets tiring, Mouse detection can be wonky, which is frustrating at times. The ending is a little saccarrine, and I wonder if the story couldn't have been wrapped up differently without the neat little bow that gets placed on it, but these are just minor quibbles - any game that can make me feel emotions like To the Moon must be doing something right.
I got it during the Summer Sale for $1, and it was worth every penny. I'm hoping the sequel is produced with the same care, quality, and originality as this one.

This game is not a game. It is said. To The Moon is a Visual Novel: a story where you are the main spectator. You will have some riddles to solve, but they are not difficult and allow you diving more profoundly in the story.
To The Moon tells the story of Niel Watts and Eva Rosalene, two doctors working at Sigmund Corp, a firm which developed a way to travel in the memory of their clients. Roughly, Sigmund Corp is contacted by people at the end of their life, wishing to fulfill their dearest dream before death. Sigmund Corp offers them a « second life » by distorting some small elements in the memory, so their clients can achieve their goal before the fateful moment.
So we follow the two doctors at Johnny’s house, whose dearest wish is to go to the moon (you understand now the name of the game). Thanks to the technology of the Sigmund Corp, Watts and Rosalene will travel in Johnny’s memory and go back to his childhood, so they can change the right elements allowing him to fulfill his dream and die as if he had really gone to the moon. This is a beautiful story, very poetic because we experience the different steps of Johnny’s life and his relationship with his wife, the whole punctuated by humor: indeed, Niel Watts is a big troll.
Gameplay and graphism are minimalists. It has its charm. The musics are wonderful, with a lot of piano. About 4 hours are required to see the end of To The Moon.
Conclusion: A beautiful game, poetic, touching. You will shed tears at the end.

Mirrored - Chapter 1 is a 3d point and click, puzzle adventure game.
Rob finds a rather cryptic message from his twin brother Nick and following his brother's suggestion he sets off to explore his office.
This is the basic premise behind the game in what seems like an exciting mystery to solve.
Gameplay:
The game is fairly simple. Your rotate the camera around the room and click on items to examine or collect them.
You have an inventory of sorts where you can examine items, use them on the environment or one with another. The interface works although at times it feels a bit clunky (the inventory/journal part).
The entire chapter 1 evolves inside the office and chapters are separated by 2d cutscenes which are very nicely done.
The puzzles are pretty straightforward. At least to me. Though I have years of experience playing these types of games. I managed to finish the entire chapter in about half an hour.
People not really used to P&C adventure games will probably take much more. That said, this first chapter is somewhat short.
Graphics:
The graphics are nice but nothing too fancy. It is worth mentioning that I did not notice much difference between the quality presets.
Music/Sound Design:
Well done and fitting the atmosphere of the game. I found it very nice that at some part the music track made me feel anxious, as being in danger. It works very good with the setting.
Story:
The story is mysterious and looks very very interesting. This first chapter though leaves you on..let's say a cliffhanger. There are subtle hints on a few things but you really can not figure out where it is actually going by this chapter alone. While it does look very interesting, if it will "deliver" or not, will be seen in the next chapters. By the end of the game you will not know much and will probably have more questions than when you started playing it.
Pros:
-Solid 3d P&C adventure game.
-Atmosphere is mysterious and brooding.
-Presentation is very well done.
-Music works nicely, adding up to the game's atmosphere.
-Puzzles are very logical.
Neutral:
-Story looks very interesting but it doesn't really take off on this first chapter. It feels like an intro to something much bigger.
-Puzzles are very straightforward. Some may like this, others may want to squeeze their brain a bit more on such games.
Cons:
-Chapter 1 is rather short. I finished the game in about half an hour. Less experienced players on such games will probably take about an hour. Maybe a bit more.
Conclusion:
It is a very interesting, although rather short, game and I'm really curious to see where the story will go. Storywise I will rate it 7/10 because the story does not unfold enough for me to have a proper opinion.
Score:
Gameplay: 7/10
Graphics: 8/10
Music/Sound Design: 8/10
Concept/Story: 7/10

And because it was short, I look forward to the next chapter so that I can continue with this particular style of clues to the puzzles.  This style is different than what I am used to as the clues to the puzzles are more obscure and indirect than other point and click games I've played.  I enjoyed the challenge of attempting to shift my approach in this game.  The places where I got stuck, I realized it was both because I was unused to this more obscure and indirect style, and also - mainly in the case of the bookcase - I realized that what was presented to me as the information from pointing and clicking misled me to think that there was nothing more I could do there or see there, and that I had to look or do something elsewhere first (and this turned out to not always be true).  So with the help of the discussion page/forum page, I realized what was going on, and I was happy to get the idea of the 'style' so I could solve the last puzzle with the safe on my own.  And since the only seeming drawback in this game was that it is not that typical, or that it is different in its style, it is this aspect that I so appreciate and look forward to in the next chapter.

Rise of The Wolf update has damaged this game, especially if you are relatively new.
I enjoyed the game when I first started, it was a very slow paced medieval city builder with custom designed castles and such. I spent my days gaining resources and slowly beefing up my stronghold and donating extra resources to my local parish capitol.
Days of doing this was quite relaxing, and the occasional Ai attack spiced things up. Seeing how well my newly made fortifications held up against 30, then 60, then 100, then 130 enemies was quite fun.
I also thought it was very cool getting to view battles between my parish and our enemy Ai, Pig. Large scale battles taking place every day while we fuel the parish with resources was amazing.
Then Rise of The Wolf happened.
All at once we had an enemy Siege camp, wolf dens, bandit camps, Pig and its castle of doom, and all of the associated negative morale. Pig for what ever reason appears to target my town exclusively, on top of daily sieges and bandit raids.
Within 3 days my forces had been reduced to 3 archers and 2 morale resulting in a single peasant every 12 hours, my food consumption was set to max to boost morale with very little effect and my taxes were already starting to drain what little gold reserve I had. Then I realize that no one is attacking Pig, the siege camp, or the bandits.. and it appears most of their aggression is focused towards me. Our parish apparently had been innactive for several days prior so help from them was a long ways off.
After speaking out in global chat, I found out that I am not the only one facing this scenario. The competent players are away or ignoring the enemies, while the weak and defenceless are destroyed by the new enemy spawn rate.
So, unless you know a strong player and can get cozy with them and their army, stay away until Rise of The Wolf is put to rest.

I don't have premium and after not even 30 hours, i got 3 metadecks ready.
This game is a more decision/skill based Hearthstone. Less RNG because it actually matters when you do things and not just in which order you draw and play cards. It actually matters when you do it and where you place certain minions/buildings/spells.
It is still a casual game, but it is fun as hell. Don't take it too serious and ignore some of the bm guys you encounter.
There will always be metadecks that are flat out better than others, sure you can build a deck yourself to counter a specific decktype but then your deck is weak to other decks. And when you more or less fight the same guys, you will only catch them off guard once. Next engagement they either have their deck adjusted to deal with yours or figured out how you play.
But it is all about consistency. There are also idiot proof decks, that you can easily copy and use those to get into the high ranks with, even as a bad player. So there is fun to be had either way.
They are on it to balance it more but it mostly just shifts the meta. But at least they are doing it frequently. So it is really fun to figure out some nice decks.
I wonder why this has so few players. I guess the developers need to step up their game to give their game a bit more exposure.
One thing is for certain, this game will stay on steam and will steadily raise it's numbers.

I was pretty hyped about this game. Never wanted to get it for some reason or another but the incredibly good reviews and such finally made me get it. I am a fan of these kind of games, always throughly enjoyed Neverwinter Nights 1/2, so was ready to have fun. Also plenty able to play difficult games if need be.
Unfortunately, this game is 90% frustration and annoyance. Those elements are common in these types of RPGs, but not to this degree. The in-depth world and fully voiced atmosphere are defintely great and nearly save the game, but unfortunately not enough. This is a after 11 hours of playing. Let me go into why I couldn't stand this game anymore.
The combat has all the makings to be good. Cool systems and all that. Except a major flaw: GROUND EFFECTS EVERYWHERE. Seriously I have never been so outright annoyed at any game this much. 95% of any battlefield I had fought on is littered with ground effects: poison, fire, water-to-be-shocked, its endless. And not just, Oh these are bad, if you accidentally step through them because of crappy pathing BAM you basically get 1HKO'd. Not even fun in the slightest. Oh that super powerful fire boss you have been fighting for 10 minutes and is almost dead? Well he accidentally stepped on some lava while moving toward you, BAM healed for 30k and instantly full health. Just stupid. Seriously, ground effects cover at minimum half the battle environments at all times, it saps the life out of the fighting.
The game has atrocious pacing for combat. I have yet to ever fight an enemy on even level; I am always 1-2 levels below. I have talked to everyone, done every sidequest I can find, explored everything, ALWAYS I am at a huge disadvantage in levels. Level 4 skeletons having AOE poison arrows that they shoot 3 TIMES IN 1 ROUND nearly killing half the party in like your 3rd fight of the game? Yea... that's not cool at all. Also what's with Fire Skeletons using water healing spells (why does a skeleton archer have spells anyway) at each other, jesus I thought this was an immersive RPG. The enemy AI is far too good as well; a roving pack of skeletons and zombies know how to properly target focus, even running through attacks of oppurtunity to finish off 1 of my party? Comeon. It's easy to lose party members 100-0 in a single round with basically nothing you can do, due to enemy AI focusing and generally overwhelming numbers.
Basically the game has a lot going for it, but the unbelievably frustrating and poorly designed combat brings it down so fast. The combat systems in place have so much potential too, but the game just doesn't do them justice. At the end of the day, its just not fun. Difficult isn't the word for it, just annoying. Oh, and I didn't even mention the incredibly frustrating camera, Good luck with that if you get this game.

I don't know what you could want out of a single player video game that Ori doesn't deliver on.
Beautiful art? Check
Engaging gameplay that feels like an exceedingly well done 2D, Metroid-style adventure? Check
Hauntingly beautiful soundtrack? Check
Better story telling in the first 10 minutes without a single spoken word than 90% of AAA titles on the market? Check
Perfect length to tell the story and not drag on, but room to return for achievement completion if you want? Check
The only thing I could remotely think to say is that if you aren't an avid platformer fan, there are a couple parts that will probably challenge you, but it's worth bucking up and overcoming them. Platformer veterans probably won't find Ori extremely challenging, but it has plenty of areas that you can't sleep through and the story and art are so engaging you won't even notice or mind if you're having an easy time with it.
It's an amazing, beautiful game. Worth every penny.

Much like that game made by Studio Ghibli (pronounced Jibbly, I would like to believe) that felt like playing a Studio Jibbly film come to life; Ori and Blind Forest instantly draws you into its weird and wonderful little world populated by Japanese-cute characters being thrown into harrowing ordeals.

If you are not moved towards some kind of salty eye duct discharge after the intro scenes conclude then I suggest calling the nearest butcher that does deliveries, and placing an order for a heart.
After completing your surgery and getting back to playing this game for realz you will discover a very nice, perfectly functioning, platform-run-around-collectathon that provides all the usual suspects present in this genre since the dawn of time.  Including, but not limited to: jumping, wall-climbing, shooting balls of light at the evil, dark, spiky enemies, double-jumping, swimming, some kind of strange catapult-slingshoty manoeuvre that I think is called glamping (?), floor-slamming and towards the end: floating.  The folks who made this game know they’re not re-inventing Mario, but they are fully aware of what decides if a good platform game is good, which is, is it fun to play?  And in this regard (and it should be noted I was playing via a greasy old PS3 pad so I don't know what manner of finger contortion was required for the keyboard) platform fun was achieved!
If you are like me and ever since your first foray into 2D side scrolling you enjoy a game that lets you get by on sheer spheres-to-the-wall luck, then O and the BF will hopefully be a nice step back in time.  You always seem to have a double-jump when you need it, the enemies feel suitably matched to each progression of Ori's abilities and clearing an area feels sufficiently worthwhile.
Of course, the sense of accomplishment from successfully completing a tricky series of fiddly jumps can be lost when, unless you forgot, you can place a save point practically anywhere for little to no detriment.  In fact this is one of my few gripes with not just this game, but most games in general, which is as soon as you allow players to save at will you lose all concept of terror, the terror of failure.  It's an important aspect of video gaming that seems lost on the new generation.  I think I know the reasons for doing it, kids nowadays having attention spans as short as British summers and so on, but after the first few 'areas' of the Blind Forest I felt far too at ease with just diving into certain death to see if that was the right way to go, safe in the knowledge that 5 milliseconds later I could have another try with no harm done.  With this game, though, it's a minor gripe as death is common and that ability to retry a miss-timed leap practically instantly does allow the passage through difficult sequences to flow more smoothly.  Moving on...
The music is really flipping good.
The bit where the giant screeching owl is after you is really flipping good too.
The story was predictable in a good way.
To sum up, I would heartily recommend this game for anyone looking to spend 5-10 blissfully poignant hours in a world ruled by a huge tree with a deep voice and a strong dislike of owls.

I think I postponed this review for far too long. I am torn between pure flattery for the game (just look at my time played) and speaking some "truth" about it. Depth is amazing, the gameplay is fun, intense and challenging, the skill ceiling is really high and the things you can do after you 'get good' are absolutely amazing. You know what they say: being called a hacker is the greatest form of flattery for a gamer - you get this here. Playing as diver is quite different from the usual FPS because you have to learn how to fight against freaking beasts of the sea that will force you to fight them not only horizontally but also vertically. Sharks on the other hand are a blast to play, but they require a lot of planning and skill to get to the divers and survive ... or you can ... you know, go in and hope for the best. Which brings me to the well, not "bad" things per se, but things to be aware.
Now the mentioned truth I would like to share is the fact that this game may not be a very good for casuals as a long term experience. If you don't have a learning curve, you may get outskilled very easily. Due to small community you will encounter pros from time to time and let's be honest, some of them can take average team alone and get called a hacker - that is how ridiculously high the skill ceiling is. That's of course no one's fault, there isn't enough veterans for the matchmaker to make them play only with each other. And remember - it's just from time to time, you won't always get to fight against or with pros. Then again some of the Depth players seems to lack basic understanding of the game despite playing 100+ matches and just forces you to facepalm while playing. Wasting tickets is on the daily basis here, especially if you're already acustomed to the game you will be sometimes forced to carry your teammember(s).
Make no mistake, community is small, but it's very stable, I've been here for almost a year and always can find a game (for divers it's almost instant, but for sharks it takes from 1 to 3 minutes and somethimes it gets down to 4-6 min). Also the community is mostly friendly and active (visit the steam discussions).
So what I want to say is: the game is amazing, the community is amazing, but the difference in skill cap you will feel on many levels, which will put you in all kinds of adventages and disadventages against some setups in teams. One more thing: the game recives a FREE content every 2 months or so that includes maps, new sharks to play, weapons and things like that so that's nice thing to have.

Honestly, people are overreacting when it comes to No Man's Sky. It is a fact that it doesn't reach the original expectations. We all know that, but I feel like somehow, even 4 months after its release, people still think they'll get the game that was originally announced.
If you go into this game with moderate expecations, and if you got it on special (the holliday sales is quite good at 40% off), then I REALLY don't see a reason to complain. The game actually looks good, I don'T know if the performances issues that people had in the beginning was solved by the developpers or if people just had poop rigs, I can run this game with maximum graphics in 1080, I'm still waiting for my new, better screen to try it at higher resolutions. but at 1080 with all settings maxed, I didn't even have a lag spike once. Running this on a 1060 pretty much equivalent to a 980, but cheaper and more recent)

In the beginning I didn't like NMS since it had almost no gameplay content. After the most recent update the whole universe feels more alive and dense. Also building structures adds lots of immersion to the game itself.

I played this game with a good friend before the foundation patch for about 18 hours, and eventually got it, in its patched version, during the Steam Xmas sale. So even though I only have 2 hours playtime on here, I have tried and explored this game quite a bit.
Now, I will try to ignore one of the biggest issues with the game, the insane amount of hype and all the features that were promised yet weren't in the finished product. If those WERE in the game, it might be great, but the way it is right now, even with the update, NMS ends up being a disappointment. Here is why:
- While procedually generated planets sound awesome... they get boring and repetitive very very quickly. The planets all look, or, even more so, FEEL the same. No changes in gravity, just changes in color palette, flora, fauna and some other small things. Almost the same materials on every planet. Sure, you need those same mats to craft stuff and refuel your equipment, but how realistic is it that all those planets are more or less visitable (even though many are more hazardous or unfriendly), and they all have the same materials. TBH, I feel there is more variety between zones in a standard MMO than there is between planets in here.
- The game feels empty while at the same time not making you feel like an explorer. How mysterious, new or unexplored is this universe when you find left behind containers on every planet you visit? The same bases and stations and factories on all of them? In many of these, you will find a lonely alien, sitting there, staring at the wall. What do they do? Do they ever move? Do they sleep somewhere? Eat anything? It just feels so dull, boring and bland... all these places you go to to find yet another generic station with a single alien in it. The sentinels are nothing but an annoyment, appearing on each of the planets you get to.
- The need to CONSTANTLY refill your weapons, suit, and spaceship engines. Sure, it might be more realistic, but mainly, its absolutely annoying.
- Which leads me to inventory management, which is another big time-waster, as the inventory is way too small. You can apparently carry TONS of iron and other things, but only have a limited amount of slots, so eventually, you will have to juggle your items, discard stuff etc just to carry the stuff you need right then (for crafting, refueling etc.)
In the very old days, small inventories might have been a technical thing, but here, it shouldnt be, and to me, you spend WAY too much time juggling your inventory items and refueling all your systems. WAY too much time.
- Again, the universe feels bland, depressing and dead
- The fauna consists of randomly generated animals, some of them aggressive, some passive, all created with the same "building blocks", emitting a very limited range of possible sounds. While at first, this might be interesting, soon it becomes repetitive (same goes for renaming them etc), and eventually, you might just ignore all that stuff.
Verdict:
The idea was interesting, the foundation update might have added some interesting features or little improvements, but: Even with all those procedually generated planets, the game feels incredibly repetitive, bland, dull, empty and lifeless. I didn't expect some kind of crazy action shooter, I do enjoy building, gathering, managing stuff.
However, the amount of silly inventory-juggling, constant need of refilling/refueling your gear while having the low amount of inventory slots taken up by single items you want to sell or stuff like the Atlas cards (why can't those be some permanent buff you get after getting/crafting those keycards instead of taking up an inventory slot??!) is not fun at all, it just feels like wasted time or an annoyance.
The game performs well, no crashes or anything, at least on my system, so at least that works well.
If this was like 9-15 bucks, I might give it a 6-7, but at the prize they ask, ESPECIALLY the non-discounted full prize, this is a 4/10 at best, simply because with all the ambitious promises and inventive ideas, this feels quite empty and very repetitive.
