I cannot, in the game's current form, recommend this title.
It has an intersting premise and a fun art style. The game looked incredibly promising. However, there were a number of issues that prevented me from enjoying it enough to get further than the second tutorial.
The controls are absolutely abysmal. It requires a mouse output to control and activate things. However, rotating and adjusting the view for the game requires the use of the arrow keys. Not WASD, arrows. The abilities have a hotkey function already bound to each one, there's no rearranging or organizing them. The left hand homerow and first row contain the game's shortcut commands.
In order to play the game most optimally, you would need your right hand on the mouse, your left on the quick triggers, and a third hand to control the arrows.
This certainly wouldn't have been any sort of issue if the game developers had allowed you to remap controls, something that is becoming progressively more standard in PC titles. This is not offered here. I would have been happy to continue trying the game if I could map controls to use WASD and the number rows for view-movement and shortcuts.
The game seemed interesting enough to at the least try playing with these confusing controls. However, the game forces you to go through the tutorial in the beginning, there's absolutely no skipping it. so if you're a play-and-learn kinda person, that's not an option. Further, the tutorials are painfully linear. After I planted an ocean and a forest, while I was waiting for fruit to be planted, I had the ocean giant go create another ocean. I soon had two oceans and four forests, though I was primarily using jut one. When the next setting, the desert, came into play, the location I placed it had the forest and desert bordering one another. This either caused some odd interactions, or the game is just that difficult to handle and understand what is gong on. The game wants you to have one ocean, one forest, and a desert far away from them. No room for legitimate learning, just do each command forced upon you. There's also no (at least no easy and readily apparent) way to go back through the dialogue box.
They kindly label each patch with the wealth and food it produces, but that's about it. It makes reference of project patches, but nothing stood out as a "project patch." It also introduced symbiosis and specialization which had almost identical symbols in the text of the dialogue box. Remember how I mentioned there's no way to go back? It would have been great so I could reread the bits about project patches and symbiosis and specialization. Generally speaking, you want the player to be able to review things during the tutorial. Apparently not.
This game might very well be a great and interesting game. However, the tutorial is unhelpful, not all of the UI is clearly labeled and legible at a glance, and the octopus-based control system means that I have to awkwardly use my left hand in a traditionally right hand placement, and just forego the use of shortcuts altogether.
Start with letting us remap controls. Then maybe the tutorial will be easier to bear and pay better attention to, letting us actually get to the game.

Epic Battle Fantasy 4 once again stars the trio of heroic, yet dimwitted adventurers Matt, Natalie and Lance.  This time, however, they're joined by a new character, the ranger Anna, who is easily the smartest of the bunch.  Together, the four this time must travel across the land, searching for crystals and uncovering clues about a new feline menace.
Epic Battle Fantasy has always prided itself on gut busting comedy and intense, over the top action, and this game is no exception.  There are hundreds of weapons, skills and summons to collect and use against literally hundreds of enemies, and the game is full of tongue in cheek moments such as Nat's oftentimes futile efforts to get Matt and Lance to care about the environment, or Anna trying to curb Matt's kleptomaniac tendencies.
Also, is case you're wondering why you should buy this version, well, its because it grants you access to the Premium Pack.  This pack adds a ton of new content to the game, including new weapons, new armor, new summons, new enemies and bosses, and even an entirely new area.
If you're a fan of turn based rpgs, of self-referential comedy, or just plain fun RPGs, then you owe it to yourself to try this out.  Check out the free version on Kongregate, and if you enjoy it, you should definitely considering going Premium by buying the Steam version.

Bee Movie is a 2007 American computer animated family comedy film produced by DreamWorks Animation and distributed by Paramount Pictures.1 Directed by J. Smith and Steve Hickner, the film stars Jerry Seinfeld and Renée Zellweger, with Matthew Broderick, Patrick Warburton, John Goodman and Chris Rock in supporting roles. Its story follows Barry B. Benson (Seinfeld), a honey bee who sues the human race for exploiting bees after learning from his florist friend Vanessa (Zellweger) that humans sell and consume BLEACH
Bee Movie is the first motion-picture script to be written by Seinfeld, who co-wrote the film with Spike Feresten, Barry Marder, and Andy Robin. The film was directed by Simon J. Smith and Steve Hickner and produced by Seinfeld, Christina Steinberg, and Cameron Stevning. The production was designed by Alex McDowell, and Christophe Lautrette was the art director. Nick Fletcher was the supervising editor and music for the film was composed by Rupert Gregson-Williams.
The cast and crew include some veterans of Seinfeld's long-running NBC sitcom Seinfeld, including writer/producers Feresten and Robin, and actors Warburton (Seinfeld character David Puddy), Michael Richards (Seinfeld character Cosmo Kramer), and Larry Miller (who plays the title character on the Seinfeld episode "The Doorman"). Coincidentally, NBC was host to the broadcast television premiere of the film on November 27, 2010.[3]

Plot
A honey bee named Barry B. Benson (Jerry Seinfeld) has recently graduated from college and is about to enter the hive's Honex Industries honey-making workforce alongside his best friend Adam Flayman (Matthew Broderick). Barry is initially excited to join the workforce, but his courageous, non-conformist attitude emerges upon discovering that his choice of job will never change once picked. Later, the two bees run into a group of Pollen Jocks, bees who collect pollen from flowers outside the hive. The Jocks offer to take Barry outside the hive to a flower patch, and he accepts. While on his first pollen-gathering expedition in New York City, Barry gets lost in the rain, and ends up on the balcony of a human florist named Vanessa (Renée Zellweger). Upon noticing Barry, Vanessa's boyfriend Ken (Patrick Warburton) attempts to squash him, but Vanessa gently catches and releases Barry outside the window, saving his life.
Barry later returns to express his gratitude to Vanessa, breaking the sacred rule that bees are not supposed to communicate with humans. Barry and Vanessa develop a close bond, bordering on attraction, and spend time together frequently. Later, while Barry and Vanessa are walking through a grocery store, Barry is terrified to discover that the humans have been stealing and eating the bees' honey for centuries. He decides to journey to Honey Farms, which supplies the grocery store with its honey. Furious at the poor treatment of the bees in the hive, including the use of bee smokers to subdue the colony, Barry decides to sue the human race to put an end to the exploitation of bees.
Barry's mission attracts wide attention from bees and humans alike, and hundreds of people show up to watch the trial. Although Barry is up against tough defense attorney Layton T. Montgomery (John Goodman) the trial's first day goes well. That evening, Barry is having dinner with Vanessa when Ken shows up. Vanessa leaves the room, and Ken expresses to Barry that he hates the pair spending time together. When Barry leaves to use the restroom, Ken ambushes Barry and attempts to kill him, only for Vanessa to intervene and break up with Ken. The next day at the trial, Montgomery taunts the bees, which causes Adam to sting him. Adam's actions jeopardize the bees' credibility and put his life in danger, though he manages to survive. While visiting Adam in the hospital, Barry notices two people smoking outside, and is struck by inspiration. The next day, Barry wins the trial by exposing the jury to the cruel treatment bees are subjected to, particularly the smoker, and humans are banned from stealing honey from bees ever again.
Having lost the trial, Montgomery cryptically warns Barry that a negative shift in the balance of nature is imminent. As it turns out, the sudden, massive stockpile of honey has put every bee out of a job, including the vitally important Pollen Jocks. As a result, without anything to pollinate them, the world's flowers slowly begin to die out. Before long, the only flowers left with healthy pollen are those in a flower parade called "The Tournament of Roses" in Pasadena, California. Barry and Vanessa travel to the parade and steal a parade float, which they load onto a plane to be delivered to the bees so they can re-pollinate the world's flowers. When the plane's pilot and copilot are knocked unconscious, Vanessa is forced to land the plane, with help from Barry and the bees from Barry's hive.
Armed with the pollen of the last flowers, Barry and the Pollen Jocks manage to reverse the damage and save the world's flowers, restarting the bees' honey production. Humans and bees are seen working together, and certain brands of honey are now "bee-approved". Barry becomes a member of the Pollen Jocks, helping to pollinate the world's plants. Barry is also seen running a law firm inside Vanessa's flower shop, titled "Insects at Law", handling disputes between animals and humans. The film ends with Barry flying off to a flower patch with the Pollen Jocks.

Let's get this out of the way, yes, To The Moon is probably the best Free to Play, physics infused, subscription based MMO style dating sim currently on the market. The lack of spoken dialougue made me harken back to the days of reading books where I read what was being spoken but not actually hearing it (except for audiobooks of course). Now what makes this dating sim so unique, well it just does everything so well, but adds a few things in to freshen it up. Ken Gao is probably the best 40 year old Asian video game writer there is, filling the characters with such classic lines like:
"Ken Gao"
"...the..."
"Follow through"
"Name of the Wind"
"Walk"
"Pearl Harbor"
"Dating Sim"
"Frankie Muniz"
etc.
The writing is so spectacular, I needed olive oil to calm myself down. Now my Indonesian roomate by the name of Kareem Abdul Jabaar was watching me play this emotionally charged First Person Shooter, when he turned to me and said, "Are you an angel?"
Confused I turned to him and told him that I was indeed, and we hugged it out for 47 hours. We deficated and urinated together, but it was for the sake of pleasing Kareem, YOU GO GIRL!
The next pro in the never ending list, would be the graphics. Now Ken Gao knows that we haven't had a true story in video games since Tetris, so he intentionally made terrible graphics, in order to give the audience the same wonder when that first Tetris block fell down hard.
The next item, would be the lasting appeal, now it may say that I have eight minutes on this game, but I played in offline mode for a good 2,000 hours because of all of the sweet end game content, that made me both happy and warm. Due to Ken Gao's facsination with antiques and the like, he treated die hard fans, such as myself, to an 40 hour documentary on the breeding habits of chimpanzees living in captivity (with full naration by Steve Irwin himself!). It is incredibly rewatchable. Let's just say Blockbuster better watch out because Ken Gao is gonna suck you dry!
Let me be (Ken Gao) real with you for a second, the music, oh, the music, AHHHHH!!!! As you probably know by now, Elton John and his partner Niel Patrick Harris put in so much effort into this incredibly composed piece of virtual literature. My favorite song in this by far would have to be "Lick my Love Pump" it is gosh darn good.
Now my favorite part about this story driven game, is the lack of gameplay. I turn it on, click start and I'm off to another world. The lack of interactivity allowed me to participate in other activities, such as:
Playing League of Legends
Writing Steam reviews
Buying CS GO keys
Buying hats
Dreaming about Ken Gao
Listening to the soundtrack for the movie Freaky Friday starring Lindsay Lohan
Listening to the soundtrack for the video game To The Moon
Listening to an audio book
Contracting an STD
etc.
Let's just say leaving this game on and then doing something else while the game completed itself has allowed me to buy newer and cleaner oils for bathing, as well as find my soul mate in life. With this game your productivity will go, dare I sat, To The Moon.
Ken Gao.
Alright, alright reviewer, I get it this game is heavenly, but there has to be faults.
Yes, yes there are faults to To The Moon. Even a perfect game is not without cons so I will list them below:
etc.

I think this is one of my all-time favourite games.
The story is gripping and sympathetic unlike any game I've EVER played. The characters are three-dimensional beyond what you would think of a RPG maker -game. I mean the characters are 2 dimensional pixel slabs but you still connect to them more than you could ever do in any triple A -game. When I first played this game, I literally cried 3 hours of my 3,8 hour playthrough.
Yea the game doesn't have much interactivity beyond some puzzles but that just adds to the overall story. Your focus doesn't wonder off to thinking anything else than what happens in the story.
The plot to the game is fairly simple but the way that the story and the characters evolve when the plot goes on is amazing. The basic plot mixes movies like Memento, Eternal Sunshine for the Spottless Mind and Inception. Two doctors from the Sigmund Corporation arrive at their patient Johnny who is at his deathbed. The purpose of Sigmund Corporation is to make your dreams come true right before you die so that you can die happy THINKING that you have acomplished your life dreams. So, what's Johnny's dream? Well he wants to go to the moon. The only problem is that he doesn't know why he wants to go there. And I will stop there because I really don't want to spoil any points of the plot and I despise the people that spoil this game without an warning.
The music in this game is one of the most beautifull soundtracks that you will ever hear. It's got this overarching theme but it still has really good variety of different emotional scales without losing any of it's power. And especially the song "Everything's Allright" sung by Laura Shigihara is just amazing especially when you learn to know the context where the song plays. It's one of the most gripping and emotionally strongest song of any video game by a long run and at the same time it asks a very powerfull ethic question that gets your morality compass directing far away from North.
So, would I recommend "To the Moon"?
Yes, yes and YES! A million times.
It is one of the best indie games you will ever play. It just may be one of the best overall games you will ever play. The games director Kan Gao proves with this game that you don't need a big studio or big sandbox world or a frikkin' symphony orchestra to make a compelling and gripping story that will burn in your brain for the rest of your life.
If you like story rich games this is one you must have played at some point. Better story is still to be found in a video game.

I like point&click adventures. I like escape-the-room games. But this one went just wrong.
First of all, the game is really dark and pixel hunting all those barely visible items was not fun at all. There is a torch to be found but guess what - it's also hidden in the dark so it took me the whole first chapter before I discovered it.
Then there's the password puzzle. You are supposed to guess a laptop password but the clues are so vague they could mean virtually anything. After 20 minutes of clueless staring at the screen I checked a walkthrough and I'm sure I would have never figured that out. Thankfully the safe puzzle is a lot better.
And third, the transitions between chapters make no sense. There are no goals, the game never tells you anything yet it expects you to do a specific set of unrelated actions to move on. So instead of solving a puzzle you desperately click on everything trying to figure out what on earth you are supposed to do.
The game feels more like a tech demo. It's very short, unpolished and the story didn't answer a single question. This is weak even for two euros.

The idea of the game is decent - there's some mystery involving the main character's twin brother, and he's trying to solve it by obtaining clues from his office. I don't like the execution though for several reasons:
- Some parts were too hard to solve, such as the overly cryptic password hint on the computer.
- The interface is awkward; the GUI for the items and journals could be improved to make using/combining items easier.
- The inventory quickly becomes overcrowded; the game should just discard of e.g. used keys.
- At first, the room is very dark, and I had to turn off my lights to even see the room clearly. Which in itself is not really problematic, if not for each time I click something, a VERY BRIGHT line of text appears. My eyes are tired after playing just this one short chapter now.
- The game is very short, even considering the price, with no conclusion in sight.
Sure, the developers want to construct several chapters and combine them into one game, but now they're selling 10% of an unfinished game for much more than 10% of the price that the total game would be worth. I'm going to pass on the next chapters, and if you haven't bought this chapter yet, I recommend you skip this chapter as well.
This is supposed to be a chapter in a game, but as Ive read in another review, it's more of a demo or introduction. It took me about 30 minutes to complete this. For $3, I'm pretty annoyed.

Really quick game that leeaves you feeling unsatisfied. Controls are clunky, and without instruction, it's tough to figure out how to make things work together. On top of all this, some segements go by in 30 seconds, and others take 15 minutes, weird pacing. Lastly, the music looping is really annoying and made me want to look up the solution just so I wouldn't have to hear that segments music anymore. If you like puzzles, the game will go by way too quickly for the price.

Your twin brother seems in trouble, so, you head for his office to find an hidden mask. It's the night, it's raining and you're nearly in the dark. What will you find?
As Mirrored is an episodic game, for now, Chapter 1 is only released. It serves as a teasing given the ending. I can't say anything about the plot: that first taste is generating questions and I would like to see how chapter 2 will answer (or not) these.
It's a point & click game: you look around, you read descriptions about objects, you combine some in your inventory, you use others where it seems to be appropriate and you solve some puzzles. I've just a little complaint to make: the inventory isn't really practical. You need to open it and let it open if you want to use an object around. I'm so used to have the object outside the inventory that I was kinda lost.
Also, I must say that I was already asking myself for 10 minutes about what to do. It was clear that the darkness in the office played a lot in that as I didn't see the only element left and that would be useful for the rest. I would have preferred to use already the flashlight: only the desk lamp was open and wasn't sufficient for the room.
The puzzles, given the fact that they're in English, could be hard for those not speaking it. I couldn't really have found the password for the laptop because despite seeing the hint, I didn't find really the answer. I had some parts of it in the head but the first sentence wasn't clear for me. Another puzzle was finding the code for the safe. It's not really easy to tie it to clues you found. Perhaps a little more subtle guidance could be imagined?
The graphics are good, though you see only the office during the chapter. However, the cutscenes are drawned I must say that the style is enough for the game. It's reminding me of another game, Return:Null, that I'm waiting the third chapter to really review it.
The soundtrack is also good, though limited as you don't really spend a hour to finish the game (and if it takes more, it means either that you were really stuck or that you paused and did something else or that you were idling cards, like I'm currently doing while writing this review).
Because Mirrored - Chapter 1 is short. Very short. Just a tease so that you have to buy the rest if you want to know the ending of the whole arc. True, I'm used to episodic formats - Space Pilgrim, Return:Null, Blues and Bullets, The Walking Dead (both seasons), The Wolf Is Among Us, Tales from the Borderlands... - but it's the first time that I felt a little cheated. Each episode of the games I've mentionned were more consistants than staying in an office and clicking everywhere - you're not even walking, you're turning around on the same spot. I'm probably not seeing Mirrored as a "complete" chapter, more like a prologue or a teasing.
The price is 3 bucks, so, it may explain the shortness too. It's not really expensive.
If I recommend Mirrored? Yeah. It's a polished chapter, a neat one, without encountered bugs. But if you don't like staying in the same spot, in an unique room, you should probably avoid it.

This game is simple yet very gripping. The gameplay itself despite using autonomous minions, still has a lot of intricacies that make it challenging and competitive.
Similar to Clash Royale, this has an added element of bridges that grant experience to your master, giving your more powerful perks that shape the gameplay. This forces a much more dynamic and agressive style where both players are constantly fighting over the important bridges, and creates a nice flow where both players can be attacking and defending simulaneously on different sides of the field.
Already there are enough cards to rival Clash Royale, even in early access, and new cards are coming every week. There's several different winning strategies, some focus on trying to kill the enemy master ASAP, while others try to control the game, deflect enemy attacks, and control the bridges. Even though some decks are "meta" there's still room for deck variations within those strategies, especially since so much of the game is still executing your deck better than the opponent. As your collection fills up you will find a style that fits you.
As of writing this I have not spent a penny yet I have nearly a full collection and am among the top rated players in the game after 200 hrs. Certainly might get a little tougher when more cards are released, but Betadwarf has a strict balance philosophy in that higher rarity cards are more specialized but not really stronger and certainly not necessary to win.
My advice for a new player that loves the game but is having a hard time winning: keep experimenting with new cards, try to identify cards that aren't working out for you, and learn what counters what so you don't waste mana playing minions that will die right away. There's a steep learning curve with a lot of depth to explore and it's not apparent right away, but when you "get it" you'll have a great time. 9/10

Oh wow, what a pleasant and satisfying game!  It's genenrally a safe bet when you see "Overwhelmingly Positive" but never hurts to go in with low expectations.
I generally play RPG/Survival/FPS games, so this was a little off my radar, but it was a blast, even for those with similar taste as mine.
What's great about this game.
1) The intuative nature of the controls.  You'll have some mess ups here and there, but for the most part, little Ori does exactly what you want
2) The story.  It's not some novel idea, but it's genuine, and I felt slight emotional attachments right from the get go.  Has a happy ending too
3) The abilities.  As an Adventure/RPG, you expect new abilities and strengths, and Ori delivers.  It's satisfying to kill a monster in half the time after getting an upgrade.  All upgrades are available during a single play through, and while it's not an extraneous labor to do so, it does require a little extra effort.  A nice balance for me
4) Some very difficult portions that make you sit up in your chair.  You will die during your first playthrough, probably hundreds of times.  Passing some parts elicited a sigh and a "phew" followed by some enjoyable cutscenes
5) Saving games - very easy, you can do it just about anywhere by holding "E".  Usually I'd forget to save costing 10-15 minutes of play time...but it'd only happen once.  Soon as I got back to my previous death, easy save
6) Copy / Paste of saves - There are 3 slots for different playthroughs (mostly for achievements).  In the case of the achievement "IMMORTAL" It helps that you can paste a save point to 2 other spots - holding your progress in the case you do die
What caused a bit (very small) of grief
1) You're required to do a new playthrough once the game ends.  Sure it makes sense, but it's a bummer if you were "planning to come back later".
2) There are parts that, once finished, can not be accessed again.
3)  No fast travel.  Really, not a big deal - but I promise, there will be parts where you are on one side of the map, and there's an ability core on the opposite side that you were JUST at 20 minutes ago.  It happens probably 5-10 times, and in those times I thought "Sure would be nice to travel to places I have explored 100%"
All in all, an excellent game
Graphics/Art  - 10/10.  Simple but beautiful
Challenge       - 8/10.  Most of the game is relatively easy, but some parts made me curse profusely
Story               - 8/10.  Engrossing and a driving part of the game, but nothing jaw dropping
Replay Value  - 8/10.  Depends on whether you want achievements or not.  I've played through twice already
Abilities/Fun   - 10/10.  Nothing quite like being a tiny fox/bunny/squirrel creature who kicks♥♥♥♥♥br>

Possibly the best 10 dollars I've spent on steam. This game has given me more bang for the buck than most AAA 60 dollar titles I have purchased. I think I found this game in my que. While the video on the store page is good, what sold me on the game is a collection of videos by a you tuber named Ohmwrecker. These videos gave me a very clear picture of what the game play was like as a diver and a shark, and he and his friends sounded like they were having a blast. This game usually sells for around 25 dollars, and while I can't recommend it to everyone for that price,  Digital Confectioners have put this game on sale twice since I've purchased it for under 10 dollars. I think anyone who is even remotely interested in what they see in game play videos owe it to themselves to pick this game up. This game does have an intimidating learning curve. As a diver if you are well versed at shooters you will be up to speed in no time. If you aren't, don't sweat it, that is what machine guns are for. I am not the best player, so I steer clear of the spear guns. Also there are ways to play to support your team even if you aren't netting high damage per game. I don't know what to compare playing a shark too, but I love it. There are many very informative guides on steam written by players who have the taken the time to lay the basics and more out to help ease you into the game, I can't recommend enough you read them. I personally figured out diving myself, but was very intimidated by playing as a shark, and used a guide until I got my feet under me. There are always people playing so you don't have to worry about dead servers. The small size of the community is a blessing and a curse. Players are mostly friendly and helpful, and you will run into the same players often. At the same time you will often get matched up with players who far out level you. All said and done I love this game and if it wasn't for bloodborne this would be my game of the year 2015!

I enjoyed FEAR, FEAR Extraction Point and FEAR 2: Project Origin (even if Project Origin was rather short it didn't stop me enjoying the 6 hours of gameplay I went through) so when I started seeing the negative comments and reviews for FEAR 3 I was some what confused as to how bad the game could be. As it turns out, all of these negative reviews have very very good points. I've literally just finished the first interval of this game and I can already see major flaws in gameplay which take away points for this franchise.
NEGATIVE POINTS
-AI are dumber than door nails
At points in the first mission I witnessed at least several cases of incompitant AI. The shotgunners rush your position constantly and won't stop, not even to take cover, until either you drop or they do.
AI seem adamant to hug every damn grenade thrown their way with some AI going as far as to throw grenades at themselves and not give two s*its.
AI seem to like shooting at indestructable objects such as CHAIN LINK FENCES(?) and BULLET PROOF WINDOWS that you are behind. For me this made all enemies which I came accross turn into nothing but moving targets which took away most of the fun in the game for me.
-Jump Scares
Yep...Good ol' jump scares (sarcasm). FEAR and FEAR Extraction point earned their name sake by creating a very tense, suspension filled and dark atmosphere almost all the way throughout the game with minimal jump scares. For me, I prefer the atmosphere in anything to do with horror whether it's a horror movie or a horror game, atmosphere is what I want not some generic sudden appearance of a supernatural force followed by a loud sound effect. I want to feel genuinley scared or on edge during a horror experience. I want adrenaline to be coursing through my body at every interval during this game but that's not going to happen thanks to just five seconds of the screen going dark and Alma walking around with whispers in the background.
-Regenerating Health
Regenerating health is not usually a problem for me as long as health regeneration is balanced for the style of gameplay like after an area is cleared of enemies health can then regenerate at a slow pace and this only applies if regenerating health is in place throught any previous games of the same franchise. In this case however FEAR 3 absolutely ruins the difficulty in this game by having a fast paced regenerating health system during combat.
-XP and Ranking system...in a linear single player Story mode
XP and ranking is fine for online play or in a open world sandbox style game such as TES:5, FALLOUT 3/NV or Borderlands and Mass Effect but having a linear story mode with an XP/Ranking system? Not even the Call of Duty franchise has implemented something that stupid and useless in their campaigns...and their campaigns since after World at War were♥♥♥♥♥♥ You have to unlock abilities with ranking up which the Point Man should already have from the first game...
-Only two weapon slots
Having only two weapon slots is such a disadvantage in a FEAR game as ammo is usually found in very small amounts on corpses and in little supply crates. Not only is ammo an issue but what if you decide to swap out empty heavy weapons for weapons like the pistol and submachine gun which have ammo and you have to fight some big bad Mutha F*cker with heavy armor and weapons which small arms are nothing but a damn tickle to him? You're going to get wrecked because you have only two weapons which do nothing and yet on FEAR and FEAR 2 you could just pull a missile launcher out your a*s and keep those weapons with ammo tucked safely between your butt cheeks whilst you just destroy the guy.
POSITIVE POINTS
-It gave me something to do for 20 or so minutes
Now with all these problems (which are problems that I personally find annoying) that I found in the first damn interval, I have now just completely given up on playing the rest of the game.

In the beginning I didn't like NMS since it had almost no gameplay content. After the most recent update the whole universe feels more alive and dense. Also building structures adds lots of immersion to the game itself.

I played this game with a good friend before the foundation patch for about 18 hours, and eventually got it, in its patched version, during the Steam Xmas sale. So even though I only have 2 hours playtime on here, I have tried and explored this game quite a bit.
Now, I will try to ignore one of the biggest issues with the game, the insane amount of hype and all the features that were promised yet weren't in the finished product. If those WERE in the game, it might be great, but the way it is right now, even with the update, NMS ends up being a disappointment. Here is why:
- While procedually generated planets sound awesome... they get boring and repetitive very very quickly. The planets all look, or, even more so, FEEL the same. No changes in gravity, just changes in color palette, flora, fauna and some other small things. Almost the same materials on every planet. Sure, you need those same mats to craft stuff and refuel your equipment, but how realistic is it that all those planets are more or less visitable (even though many are more hazardous or unfriendly), and they all have the same materials. TBH, I feel there is more variety between zones in a standard MMO than there is between planets in here.
- The game feels empty while at the same time not making you feel like an explorer. How mysterious, new or unexplored is this universe when you find left behind containers on every planet you visit? The same bases and stations and factories on all of them? In many of these, you will find a lonely alien, sitting there, staring at the wall. What do they do? Do they ever move? Do they sleep somewhere? Eat anything? It just feels so dull, boring and bland... all these places you go to to find yet another generic station with a single alien in it. The sentinels are nothing but an annoyment, appearing on each of the planets you get to.
- The need to CONSTANTLY refill your weapons, suit, and spaceship engines. Sure, it might be more realistic, but mainly, its absolutely annoying.
- Which leads me to inventory management, which is another big time-waster, as the inventory is way too small. You can apparently carry TONS of iron and other things, but only have a limited amount of slots, so eventually, you will have to juggle your items, discard stuff etc just to carry the stuff you need right then (for crafting, refueling etc.)
In the very old days, small inventories might have been a technical thing, but here, it shouldnt be, and to me, you spend WAY too much time juggling your inventory items and refueling all your systems. WAY too much time.
- Again, the universe feels bland, depressing and dead
- The fauna consists of randomly generated animals, some of them aggressive, some passive, all created with the same "building blocks", emitting a very limited range of possible sounds. While at first, this might be interesting, soon it becomes repetitive (same goes for renaming them etc), and eventually, you might just ignore all that stuff.
Verdict:
The idea was interesting, the foundation update might have added some interesting features or little improvements, but: Even with all those procedually generated planets, the game feels incredibly repetitive, bland, dull, empty and lifeless. I didn't expect some kind of crazy action shooter, I do enjoy building, gathering, managing stuff.
However, the amount of silly inventory-juggling, constant need of refilling/refueling your gear while having the low amount of inventory slots taken up by single items you want to sell or stuff like the Atlas cards (why can't those be some permanent buff you get after getting/crafting those keycards instead of taking up an inventory slot??!) is not fun at all, it just feels like wasted time or an annoyance.
The game performs well, no crashes or anything, at least on my system, so at least that works well.
If this was like 9-15 bucks, I might give it a 6-7, but at the prize they ask, ESPECIALLY the non-discounted full prize, this is a 4/10 at best, simply because with all the ambitious promises and inventive ideas, this feels quite empty and very repetitive.

Purchased on sale after the 1.1 update without having read the hype and found a fun, survival game. Exploring planets for resources is the core of the game and the planets have a fair degree of variability and there is plenty to build and construct with resources although continually having to find resources for ship engines, guns an life support gets a bit tiring.
While the game is fun it lacks depth and realism. Each system has a single, very simplistic space port and trading is extremely limited. The galaxy to all intents and purposes does not exist because you can only see a handful of stars close to you and navigating large distances is utterly impossible. This would make a base useless but to fix this they added a magical teleporter to allow you to move from whichever spaceport you are at to your base (and your ship teleports too!).
This game is in a similar vein to Astroneer and Kerbal Space program but whereas these make fun of their inconsistencies and cartoon-like nature, No Man's Sky takes it all seriously which unfortunately does not work too well when the game is so unrealistic and inconsistent. Hopefully things will improve in future updates, the game has a lot of promise, but at the moment it is very clearly an early release game which should be priced as such but which may turn out to be something great if it can add more depth and realism.

[Reviewed on 9/26/14]
Gauntlet - the remake of the original 1985 arcade game of the same name.  I imagine most people who grew up in the 80s knew of it quite well.  The age where arcades were still thriving business ventures and kids would come home from school and spend the afternoon sinking token after token into their favorite machines.  Gauntlet was one of those favorite machines for many.  So, the real question is "How does this version stack up?"  Quite well, in my opinion.  The core gameplay is all there.  Despite being a largely cooperative venture, the game still allows for some of your favorite griefing tactics that were ever-so-present in the original.  You can shoot the food and steal other players' gold and you still have the four-player co-op in the form of the Elf, Wizard, Valkyrie, and the Warrior.  The controls are as simple as the original's were.  You've got your movement keys (or sticks, if you're using a gamepad), your basic and strong attacks, a special evasion/speed move, and a special attack.  The game feels fluid.  Everything from the combat and movement, to the seemless transition from room-to-room when you're crawling through the dungeons with your buddies.  The game does allow for solo play, if the player so wishes, but Gauntlet, at its core, is meant to be a cooperative experience.
In that regard, I recommend you find friends to play with, as here comes the negative bit of the review.
For one, there is no built-in communication function in this game.  At all.  No text chat; no voice chat - nothing.  This essentially means that if you and your teammates happen to be getting slaughtered over and over again, there is literally no way for you to attempt to coordinate a strategy.  You will be forced to befriend the individuals on your team, and start communicating through Steam's chat function if you are playing with randoms.  Playing with already established friends can help you sidestep this issue.  The game's difficulty does scale depending on the number of people you're playing with.  Which means that if you're playing with some particularly unskilled individuals, your experience may be arguably harder than simply playing by yourself.  This makes the inability to communicate your thoughts even more frustrating.  Additionally, for whatever reason, the game, which is not especially graphically demanding, seems to heat up my Radeon 7970 much higher than most games.  I'm not the only one to experience this, but turning on v-sync in the game itself and using Afterburner helped mitigate issues.  The only other complaint I have about the game is the fact that keymapping is currently an impossibility.  Sure, the game only has a few controls, but it's a PC-exclusive title and a standard feature amongst PC games was left completely absent (even after two patches at this point).  Regardless, the game is still a ton of fun.  It's addictive.  Hack & slash style gameplay with a stylistic art direction coupled with the ability to get a HUGE challenge from playing the game on its hardest difficulty is what is going to keep you coming back.  The game itself is relatively short.  It only has 12 levels.  Three stages, with four dungeons in each.  Each dungeon has three stages in itself, but it you can't start each dungeon from a checkpoint.  You always start it at the very beginning, unless you die.  In which case, you simply respawn at the beginning of the stage in which you died.
There are bosses at the end of every one of the three sections.  At least two of them will provide you with a significant challenge.  Beyond that, you also have the ability to change your character's appearance with purely cosmetic items.  These items are purchased by a vendor in the hub area with the gold you acquire in the game itself.  Worry not, there are NO microtransactions in the game.  And, as I said, the items you purchase offer only cosmetic incentives.  The game also features a pseudo-leveling system.  In actuality, as you play the game and complete certain challenges - covering everything from destroying props and taking damage, to killing monsters and eating food - your character increases in ability.  He/she will get stronger and faster and luckier (in regards to finding gold) as you continue to play the game.  And then are the potions.  Potions are used to allow you to activate your abilities granted to you by items called 'relics' that you can buy from the vendor.  They offer you the chance to do things like freeze your enemies in place, heal yourself, or even turn your enemies into turkeys.  It's a good bit of fun, and they are certainly game-changers and life-savers on the harder difficulties.
Altogether, Gauntlet is an awesome game.  It's just plain fun.  It's accessible, but it still offers a steep challenge to those looking for it.  If you like the original, I can't guarantee that you'll like this one, but I would be more than willing to imagine that you would.  For a $20 game that has dedicated developers already looking to improve the areas in which it's lacking (evidenced by two patches in a one-day span of time), and is a product that is already very well put together, I have to recommend the game to anyone who enjoyed the original, likes dungeons crawlers, or is just looking for a game that will give them simple enjoyment.  If I had to attach a numerical rating to the game, I would give it a solid 8/10.

Very fun fighter made by fighting game players for fighting game players. It's the best introduction to fighting games I've found since it's super easy to pick up and not do poorly, while at the same time has a very high skill cap to make competitive play very exciting - in this regards it's the perfect fighting game for any skill level. Lighter moves cancel into heavier moves very intuitively, making this game not very hard to pick up.
The characters are all extremely memorable and unique, none of them feel generic at all. The only con I have is that the online play is pretty punishing to beginners, but fortunately the community is very solid and there's lots of people online that are more than willing to help new players improve.  Also, the tutorial is beyond amazing and teaches you the fundamentals to competitive play, which translate to other fighting games as well.
If you've never picked up a fighting game and want to get into them, this is the perfect one for you. If you're not new to fighting games but want to find one with a higher skillcap than you're used to, this is the perfect one for you. I can't think of anyone I wouldn't recommend this to, unless you hate fighting games and are against having fun in general.

I think this is one of my all-time favourite games.
The story is gripping and sympathetic unlike any game I've EVER played. The characters are three-dimensional beyond what you would think of a RPG maker -game. I mean the characters are 2 dimensional pixel slabs but you still connect to them more than you could ever do in any triple A -game. When I first played this game, I literally cried 3 hours of my 3,8 hour playthrough.
Yea the game doesn't have much interactivity beyond some puzzles but that just adds to the overall story. Your focus doesn't wonder off to thinking anything else than what happens in the story.
The plot to the game is fairly simple but the way that the story and the characters evolve when the plot goes on is amazing. The basic plot mixes movies like Memento, Eternal Sunshine for the Spottless Mind and Inception. Two doctors from the Sigmund Corporation arrive at their patient Johnny who is at his deathbed. The purpose of Sigmund Corporation is to make your dreams come true right before you die so that you can die happy THINKING that you have acomplished your life dreams. So, what's Johnny's dream? Well he wants to go to the moon. The only problem is that he doesn't know why he wants to go there. And I will stop there because I really don't want to spoil any points of the plot and I despise the people that spoil this game without an warning.
The music in this game is one of the most beautifull soundtracks that you will ever hear. It's got this overarching theme but it still has really good variety of different emotional scales without losing any of it's power. And especially the song "Everything's Allright" sung by Laura Shigihara is just amazing especially when you learn to know the context where the song plays. It's one of the most gripping and emotionally strongest song of any video game by a long run and at the same time it asks a very powerfull ethic question that gets your morality compass directing far away from North.
So, would I recommend "To the Moon"?
Yes, yes and YES! A million times.
It is one of the best indie games you will ever play. It just may be one of the best overall games you will ever play. The games director Kan Gao proves with this game that you don't need a big studio or big sandbox world or a frikkin' symphony orchestra to make a compelling and gripping story that will burn in your brain for the rest of your life.
If you like story rich games this is one you must have played at some point. Better story is still to be found in a video game.

To The Moon is a story-driven game that has a retro-like apperance that focuses around an elderly man, John, who has the urge to go to the moon, but doesn't know why. So he calls two scientists to enter his memories to find out why he wants he contains this urge and what it means.
This game, as earlier said, is story-driven, meaning that gameplay happens less and plot is more important. Gameplay mainly consists of finding certain elements that have significance during several of John's memories, therefore you can travel backwards (elder to child) and find the reason he want to go to the moon. Aaaaaaand that's basically it. To summarize it up, it's mainly exploration of the environment and finding the "keys" to the "gateway", allowing you to continue. Then, when you get all the "keys", you solve a puzzle that creates a picture by flipping certain rows of square tablets. Not very difficult in the least, to be honest.
However, the story in this game is spectacular. With such a simple concept of trying to find out why a man wants to go to the moon, the story and how going from his elder stage all the way back to his childhood, the story makes you feel all kinds of emotions, especially sadness, joy, anger, and all around deepness that the story goes into. I loved nearly every step of the story. Not many games made me feel actual surprise and gave me a slight intense feeling in the game. Surprisingly, it made me think a little.
Environments and all round art of the game is beautiful. Even in pixelated graphics, this game truly uses pixels in an amazing and stunning way to create colorful and vibrant surroundings and characters. Speaking of characters, I felt like the characters weren't just video game characters on my screen, but instead actually characters that could be in real life, with real emotions and actions a human would have.
The only bad thing about this game is that it's a tad short. With a good 4-5 hour gameplay in all, with most of it being talking, I was kind of expecting it to be a bit longer. All-in-all, I felt the story started and ended on a great note, so I didn't feel like I was being rushed into the story, cause I could go at my own pace in moving around and exploration to my own pace.
In conclusion, To The Moon can be compared to reading a great book. Only visual...and you play as the characters. The beginning, inbetween, and end all were an enjoyment. If you like good stories that take you on a ride of all emotions, try out this game!
(But buy it on sale though :D)

Mirrored is the first of a series of point and click adventure games. However I can't recommend this  game for a number of reasons.
It is common for games to be split into chapters so we don't expect the story to be completed. . With  achievements for completing chapters for this it appears to have more content. In reality this doesn't have enough content to justify it as a chapter. It feels more like a demo or an introduction.
It's nice to have an interactive 3D environment and the artwork is a good standard. Unfortunately as the whole game is set in an office there is no  variety. When you combine a right item you complete a chapter, get a cut scene and you are back in the office again. You have to use and combine all the necessary items to finish the game but only certain items will trigger another chapter.
The inventory menu could also have had a clearer, simpler layout having to swap between sections clunky. It would not be immediately clear for everyone where to combine items due to the dark colours and small buttons . Furthermore this may be a problem for people with poor eyesight.
All the achievements are easy to obtain but the "Thinker" achievement, clicking on all the items, can be tricky to pop up. For a perfect game you may need to do  a second play through which isn't too much hassle for a short game.
The story. about Rob trying to find out what happened to his twin brother, has hints through notes and cut scenes that show potential to be interesting. If this had more going for it this might of been a recommend. I am a little curious about what happens next but I can't recommend this game series as it stands at the time of writing.

I'm a huge fan of adventure games and point 'n' clicks, and I appreciate the devs intentions with this, but the final product leaves a lot to be desired.  While there is some promise to it, it doesn't even play like an opening chapter to a game so much as a prologue.  It's very short, there's not a lot of story there, and there aren't a lot of puzzles.  And one or two of the ones that do exist end up being obscure logic jumps that don't really work, which are paired with everything else being overly simplistic.  Also, one of the achievements is apparently broken.  I've played through the game twice very deliberately, one time even following a guide, and still the glitched Thorough achievemnt would not pop.
I'm fine with having paid a few bucks to support some devs finding their feet, but they really need to concentrate on refining this into a better, more complex, and less buggy experience if they continue to move foward with this project and future installments.  4/10 for me, and a point or two of that is for the game's potential.

Bee Movie is a 2007 American computer animated family comedy film produced by DreamWorks Animation and distributed by Paramount Pictures.1 Directed by J. Smith and Steve Hickner, the film stars Jerry Seinfeld and Renée Zellweger, with Matthew Broderick, Patrick Warburton, John Goodman and Chris Rock in supporting roles. Its story follows Barry B. Benson (Seinfeld), a honey bee who sues the human race for exploiting bees after learning from his florist friend Vanessa (Zellweger) that humans sell and consume BLEACH
Bee Movie is the first motion-picture script to be written by Seinfeld, who co-wrote the film with Spike Feresten, Barry Marder, and Andy Robin. The film was directed by Simon J. Smith and Steve Hickner and produced by Seinfeld, Christina Steinberg, and Cameron Stevning. The production was designed by Alex McDowell, and Christophe Lautrette was the art director. Nick Fletcher was the supervising editor and music for the film was composed by Rupert Gregson-Williams.
The cast and crew include some veterans of Seinfeld's long-running NBC sitcom Seinfeld, including writer/producers Feresten and Robin, and actors Warburton (Seinfeld character David Puddy), Michael Richards (Seinfeld character Cosmo Kramer), and Larry Miller (who plays the title character on the Seinfeld episode "The Doorman"). Coincidentally, NBC was host to the broadcast television premiere of the film on November 27, 2010.[3]

Plot
A honey bee named Barry B. Benson (Jerry Seinfeld) has recently graduated from college and is about to enter the hive's Honex Industries honey-making workforce alongside his best friend Adam Flayman (Matthew Broderick). Barry is initially excited to join the workforce, but his courageous, non-conformist attitude emerges upon discovering that his choice of job will never change once picked. Later, the two bees run into a group of Pollen Jocks, bees who collect pollen from flowers outside the hive. The Jocks offer to take Barry outside the hive to a flower patch, and he accepts. While on his first pollen-gathering expedition in New York City, Barry gets lost in the rain, and ends up on the balcony of a human florist named Vanessa (Renée Zellweger). Upon noticing Barry, Vanessa's boyfriend Ken (Patrick Warburton) attempts to squash him, but Vanessa gently catches and releases Barry outside the window, saving his life.
Barry later returns to express his gratitude to Vanessa, breaking the sacred rule that bees are not supposed to communicate with humans. Barry and Vanessa develop a close bond, bordering on attraction, and spend time together frequently. Later, while Barry and Vanessa are walking through a grocery store, Barry is terrified to discover that the humans have been stealing and eating the bees' honey for centuries. He decides to journey to Honey Farms, which supplies the grocery store with its honey. Furious at the poor treatment of the bees in the hive, including the use of bee smokers to subdue the colony, Barry decides to sue the human race to put an end to the exploitation of bees.
Barry's mission attracts wide attention from bees and humans alike, and hundreds of people show up to watch the trial. Although Barry is up against tough defense attorney Layton T. Montgomery (John Goodman) the trial's first day goes well. That evening, Barry is having dinner with Vanessa when Ken shows up. Vanessa leaves the room, and Ken expresses to Barry that he hates the pair spending time together. When Barry leaves to use the restroom, Ken ambushes Barry and attempts to kill him, only for Vanessa to intervene and break up with Ken. The next day at the trial, Montgomery taunts the bees, which causes Adam to sting him. Adam's actions jeopardize the bees' credibility and put his life in danger, though he manages to survive. While visiting Adam in the hospital, Barry notices two people smoking outside, and is struck by inspiration. The next day, Barry wins the trial by exposing the jury to the cruel treatment bees are subjected to, particularly the smoker, and humans are banned from stealing honey from bees ever again.
Having lost the trial, Montgomery cryptically warns Barry that a negative shift in the balance of nature is imminent. As it turns out, the sudden, massive stockpile of honey has put every bee out of a job, including the vitally important Pollen Jocks. As a result, without anything to pollinate them, the world's flowers slowly begin to die out. Before long, the only flowers left with healthy pollen are those in a flower parade called "The Tournament of Roses" in Pasadena, California. Barry and Vanessa travel to the parade and steal a parade float, which they load onto a plane to be delivered to the bees so they can re-pollinate the world's flowers. When the plane's pilot and copilot are knocked unconscious, Vanessa is forced to land the plane, with help from Barry and the bees from Barry's hive.
Armed with the pollen of the last flowers, Barry and the Pollen Jocks manage to reverse the damage and save the world's flowers, restarting the bees' honey production. Humans and bees are seen working together, and certain brands of honey are now "bee-approved". Barry becomes a member of the Pollen Jocks, helping to pollinate the world's plants. Barry is also seen running a law firm inside Vanessa's flower shop, titled "Insects at Law", handling disputes between animals and humans. The film ends with Barry flying off to a flower patch with the Pollen Jocks.

After Divinity II, I wasn’t really sure what to expect from this game. I mean sure, it looked a lot like the old Divine Divinity games which I really enjoyed, but I was still hesitant to try this one, mainly because of the high price point. After purchasing it together with a friend in the last sale, I quickly realized that I should’ve picked up this game much sooner.
As with all of my reviews, these are my own opinions and experiences; please check out other reviews too!
Let’s begin with the rather annoying rock/paper/scissors minigame during dialogs where you have to win multiple rounds until you get 10 points. While funny at first it quickly becomes a chore where you just save and load if you fail. Your stats simply give a little point boost during the minigame which I feel could’ve been done much better with just using the stats to determine if you are successful or not. Corpses can’t be moved or removed, which lead to one quest being unable to be finished and it thankfully wasn’t a main quest. NPCs will repeat the same sentence over and over again if you’re standing close by which is super annoying if you are sorting your inventory or while selling/buying stuff. A clearer indication as to what is junk and what is used for crafting would’ve been really nice; I bet that half of the stuff in my inventory is just rubbish. You can’t change your race during character creation and the only one available is human.
It all starts with the character creation which is fairly basic; chose your name, your starting class and your desired appearance and you’re ready to go. Eight different skill paths to chose from each with their own distinctive abilities and you can pretty much skill everything if you desire it. Spells are learned through skill books or unlearned if you simply chose to forget about them. You can only have a limited amount of spells at the same time based on the tier of your skill level. There are six different weapon classes that all have different requirements to fit the chosen skills and play style. Pick one of four different difficulties, where the hardest one deletes your savegame once each character in your party dies; there’s something for every type of gamer out there. The game offers an extensive world stretched over four big maps with small and big caves in between and sometimes basements. Various enemies and traps will make you want to quick save often, as it can be game over very fast.
The combat is executed in a turn based manner with action point management where everything has different AP costs; Movement, attacking or using spells and you can even chose to preserve them for next turn to cast even more expensive spells or just do crazy combos. Mix and match dozens of different elements to generate various status changes that can affect your enemies when they walk through it or just blow them up to turn them into a pile of ashes. Ice for example will knock enemies down once they try to run over it but it will melt at some point and leave behind a puddle of water that you can then evaporate with using a fire just to shoot the steam with a thunderbolt to create a thunderstorm which can even stun enemies for several turns. Or burn stuff and get a huge cloud of thick black smoke to block everyone's line of sight so enemies need to run through or around it. However, most fights can even be avoided by having high enough traits and winning the previously mentioned rock/paper/scissors minigame. The game just offers a ton of freedom and even killing most of the NPCs in towns will let you proceed through the main story just fine.
An old-school attribute/ability/talent system is also quiet nice to see in which you spend points earned through level ups in order to shape your characters into what you want them to be. Sneaking lets you steal stuff without anyone noticing as long as they don’t look in your direction. Pick up objects like chairs, crates, and even chests and store them in your inventory or throw them around, if you're strong enough. I was okay with the inventory weight limit since you can increase it and it has infinite space which I really like since I love to pick up everything. Crafting is also very functional since you can pretty much craft anything that you can use; Armor, Weapons, Potions, and even Arrows with elemental tips.
It offers an excellent co-op experience for online and split-screen play. Each player controls up to 2 characters (or even three if one wants to play solo) and fights can even be fought apart from each other resulting in situations where one is in a battle while the other one fights somewhere else. While one of the players is talking to the boss, the other one is not frozen in place and can prepare for battle however he likes or already loot the chests behind it. Important decisions however will be made by both players where they can argue over different outcomes, resulting in rock/paper/scissors to decide or they can simply agree with each other to finish quests more quickly. Additionally, items that are needed to open chests and doors or to advance through the story line are taken right out of the owning player’s inventory and you can easily drag and drop items in other players/characters inventories.
Graphics are reminiscent of old divinity titles but polished for the modern era and are pleasant to look at. Vastly different areas are presented in a believable way and elemental effects are especially beautiful.
While the soundtrack is good to listen to and rather funny sometimes, it fits each of the games situations very well and makes use of a variety of different instruments.

I would’ve loved a more serious story since Divine Divinty is rather humorous but the Divinity series always been like that. The game is very text-heavy with walls of text in dialogs and books to discover, but you can quickly skip them if you’re not interested. A bunch of easter eggs also show the love of the creators and you can tell they enjoyed making this game.
A second game is already on the way, and while I’m really happy about it I still urge you to check out this game first so you see and appreciate the improvements that will be made. I recommend it to anyone who enjoys story-rich RPGs with turn based combat or just fans of the old Divine Divinity and similar games like Baldurs Gate or Shadowrun. Check it out with a friend/girlfriend, it’s a lot more fun!

Not only does this game have serious pacing problems, but it also falls into the same problem that plagued Spore: that is, the game rewards the same types of combinations more than others, making only a few choices worthwhile and the rest redundant.
That being said, this is a very fun and innovative take on the tycoon genre that uses an interesting array of mechanics to keep the player driving towards their own goals as a fictional game developer. The game is also informed by real-life video game history, which gives it an informative edge for a typically straightforward, cartoony genre.
Here is where the pacing problem begins though: most of us are familiar with which consoles came out when, what types of games were played on these consoles, and how they faired against other consoles. The time-ticker in the game moves so fast that the player can't keep up with the fictional technology of the game. For example, by the time you release a single game for the "TES," the "Super TES" is on the market. This demands a very fast pace from the player, which simply clashes with an otherwise casual game.
I recommend this game for players who know they like tycoon games. It's good for its price range, and for a fledgling developer, but if you have never played tycoon games before I wouldn't recommend starting here.

I think a lot of the reviews of this game are judging it unfairly. I've owned this game for over a year now so I'll give you guys the low down.
Is the game good? Yes, it's fantastic and if you can get it on sale for the £5-10 it was over Christmas it's well worth it...
So first to address the typical complaints:
No single player - When I bought this game I was under no illusion about what I was buying, a MP game. This is what it is, just like many other games out there like titanfall or even the Battlefield games, it has a single player but it's mainly to introduce you to the play style.
Not many skins - there are other skins out there to buy and the entire catalogue was on steam for £4 a week or two ago, as standard there are only a couple of skins but you can't see yourself while you play fps games and the sharks will only see an outline of you until you are in their mouth most of the time. I would also like to point out that you can in no way, shape or form pay to win or progress in this game.
Not many weapons - There are plenty enough weapons in my opinion for what the game is, they are always adding more too, over Christmas they made a whole load of new additions including shark sheilds, new skins, a turret and a new shark species alongside a completely new game mode.
Community small and experienced - This is true, in Europe in the evening it usually takes 2-3 minutes to get in a game, this is sped up if you are willing to play as both sharks or divers. The community is very experienced now so getting started will be tricky, but if you are buying the game over a year after release, you've got to expect this. I would say the community are pretty helpful to newbies too.
Gameplay gets old - I disagree with this, but then I play mostly sharks, then again, Battlefront, Battlefield, COD and most other FPS games function on the exact same game modes and have done for years, again, I don't understand how people could have been confused about what they were buying.
This game involves either eating everyone on the map before they escape or making it to the end while collecting gold to increase your chances of doing so while crapping in your pants and shooting at anything that looks even remotely shark-like.
If that sounds appealing to you then get this game when it is on sale, considering titanfall and battlefront were over £50 to get, not including future dlc, I would say this game is reasonably priced, but full price might leave some wanting, if so, wait for it to go on sale. For £5 this game is definitely worth it.
I have played 30 hours of this game so far, it's the kind of game I pick up when I only want to do a couple of games, every time, I have fun and I have no doubt I will still be playing games now and then for years to come.
I think the sharks are the best players, so if you like the idea of swimming around killing people, this will not disappoint.
If you are buying this to play as divers then you must understand that most of the time divers lose, it is a CHALLENGE. With me playing as a shark I win 4 of 5 games, that's simply because the sharks are supposed to be scary and hard to kill, you can't back into a corner and aim straight, the sharks can come from up, down or from any angle.
If you want another generic fps then go buy any of the thousands out there, you'll be more satisfied, if you want to play as a shark or play a challenging fps game that doesn't pretend to be anything but what it is then this is the game for you.
I highly recommend it, almost all of the negative reviews come from people who for whatever reasons must have misunderstood what the game was always meant to be like.

Blackwell Convergence continues the Blackwell series with stronger story, better art and the same disappointing audio. Overall, if you liked the previous installments, you will probably like this one even more.
Production quality has improved a bit. The pixel art has noticeably stepped up its quality. It gives a greater sense of depth with better geometry and shading. Audio quality is still bad, getting to the point where it feels as though they may have actually recorded actors over the phone.  It gets worse though, now the background music has been over compressed.  White noise behind the music pops in and out as the volume of the music changes. Unless you are an audiophile, that particular point will not be a deal breaker.  Voice acting from the main two actors is still pretty strange.  Multiple occasions where Rosangela was supposed to sound awkward, come off as dryly read lines.  It really is unfortunate the actress could not put more into matching her voice to the dialogue.  Joey still sounds like he is talking into a tin can.
The story is speeding up now.  Storylines from the previous two games get tied up nicely while at the same time new plots are teased.  This is a marked improvement over the preceding games that only established the world, this time around the story tests what implications of being in such a world can mean. Moreover, there is now an establishing theme linking alcohol and cigarettes to death. Nothing over stated, this is not propaganda but a simple plot cues that setup for foreshadowing. My review is about the entire Blackwell series, not about a specific episode.
TL;DR - highly recommended if you're looking for good quest games.
Although being quest series, the Blackwell series isn't difficult comparing to other games in that genre as there aren't logic puzzles to solve. However, the games don't suffer from one flaw that exists in many quests, and that is excessive use of items. In some quest games you usually stack up a lot of items and end up trying every combination of item and something clickable on the screen until you find that absurd combination that makes you progress. The Blackwell series doesn't have that flaw as items aren't the main part of the game. Also, when places become irrelevant you can't access them anymore, which also prevents having to go back and try to find something useful in every place that you've been through at the endgame.
The progression in the game is made by combining the abilities of Rosa (or Lauren in Blackwell Unbound) and Joey, which complete each other. Joey can enter locked rooms but cannot interact with anything, and Rosa can do the opposite. Only by combining their abilities you will make progress. There's also a built in search engine inside a game in which you have to use in order to progress, which makes you feel that you're doing detective work and not just trying to figure out how to use your inventory.
The plot becomes "bigger" in each episode and ends with a grand finale in Blackwell Epiphany, so you don't feel like you're doing that same thing in each game.
I really enjoyed the series and I highly recommend it.

You hear a message on your phone from your twin brother, who needs your help. Apparently he is chased and needs to secure an item from these people. So you head to his office and try to find whatever he is hiding first.

I've played the Gauntlet games since I had an NES as a kid.  Between the original and Gauntlet: Dark Legacy I put many many cherished hours into these games.  They were difficult and intricate.  The one thing they lacked was a significant difference between the characters.  This game has that--which I like--I never understood why every character had ranged attacks in previous installments.  That's all it has over the older Gauntlets.  The warrior is purely melee (and the worst class), the Valkyre is primarily melee with limited ranged attacks (and is the second worst class), and the wizard and archer are ranged powerhouses.
It took just a few hours to beat the game solo on normal difficulty.
There's no real leveling system, just gold to be spent on either gear (whose availability is dependant on what levels you've beaten on what difficulty, plus you have to pay for them) or Relics (which are not unique to your character).
It's kind of fun, and I'm still waiting for my friends to install their copies so I can try three or four player mode, but it's not worth the price tag of $15 or $20.

This is something of a Marmite game - you either love it or hate it. There's some very justifiable criticism out there but in some cases at least I think it's down to people's expectations.
For me, this is all about nostalgia for those of us who remember pumping 10p coins into the arcade machine. It'd be a hoot playing with friends too. It reproduces the spirit of the original Gauntlet in an updated game.
That means that the negative points are all correct. Yes, it's simplistic; you shoot stuff and collect gold. No character development, no massive story, it's all in the instant gratification of hurling firepower at suicidal enemies and watching them drop like flies. It's the kind of game you can pick up, blast for ten minutes and put down with a grin.
Other bad points are harder to justify. It's very, very short for starters - only twelve levels which you'll clear in a few hours on the normal difficulty. The writeup claims "randomly generated levels", implying (again, maybe only for those old enough to remember) a massive variety of semi-randomised levels once the twelve designed ones are dispensed with. Sadly, this just isn't true. There are twelve levels, full stop. Some people claim that one or two levels might be partly random but one of those is a "darkness" level, where you can only see a short distance from your character, so it's difficult to tell because most of the screen is just black. And if it's difficult to tell, it might as well not be random. If it is, which I doubt.
At present you can't change the key bindings if you don't have or like the gamepad. And since the best control scheme is "WAXD" and not, as the world seems to incorrectly believe, "WASD", that's a real pain. Maybe I just have unnaturally short thumbs.
Final gripe: un-sodding-skippable chuffing cut scenes! The final level (that's number twelve, in case you missed the "short" comments above) is, not surprisingly, a boss battle. You're gonna die. Lots. And every time you do, you have to sit through the same. God-damn. Cutscene. It's not a five-second intro either, we're talking the best part of a minute to cool your heels after narrowly being smooshed in mid-lunge towards the food. I went postal on the gamepad after the first half-dozen times and after that, the monologuing wizard went silent in all later replays. Maybe he was embarrassed. He still acted the part out though. In full. Every time.
Do I recommend it? Yes - it looks good, controls well (with a gamepad at least), and most importantly of all it recaptures the feel of the original. It desperately needs more places to explore though, at least as randomly-generated maps. Much better would be a Steam Workshop tie-in.

I am also liking that this was not overthought at all and even with the simple adjustment of levers for making a game, there is that complexity of what to put with it from the engine you built to see if it will enhance the game and make it a big hit or not at all. If there was a con to this delightful game, I would say that they did this so well that there really isn't a need for a second version. Allowing mods can extend play, but ultimately it's great as it is. I'm sure someone might think it needs a facelift and might be able to squeeze out another neat take on this, but hands down this is a great game. I thought the interface was different than how I approach keeping track of history, such as how you view your game history and the lack of graphs to see your finances. However, that all seems like splitting hairs and just a different point of view since what is in place is very straightforward and easily accessible.
There is one point, though, that I wonder what the team's thoughts were on: Competition in the game... Yes, it mentions it, but it's as if you're completely independent of compeition. Your efforts are defined by randomness as well as how your company is advancing rather than that AND what the competition is doing. Did it add too much complexity? Based on how you made your game, would it make tasks too stressful? I could see how given what a player has to go through for the game phase and trying to be very progressive with keeping people trained, getting games out fairly back to back, and supplementing income on contracts from time to time or simply farming research points to get more features for your game engines---that that is quite toss about for responsibilities. To add how competitors are progressing and what they are publishing versus what you are can make that feel heavily pinched. So, perhaps right there is another interesting take to the game if a second version was put out and that given what is already there, how can you rightly put in a more challenging aspect to get more out of the game?... (9/10)
