While I am recommending this game, I do so with the caveat that I believe the game, IMO, is seriously flawed. But first, what's GREAT about this game...
Pro's:
- Amazingly beautiful
- Combat Action Points (AP) are spot on and better than I've seen in any other game. Think back to the AP system in the original X-COM (not the crappy new ones) and it's even better than that.
- Environmental and social interactions are very well done. Way better than average.
- Combat is fun, but and challenging. While this is a pro, it's also the biggest con (see below)
- Reistances are done better in this game than nearly any other. Poor resistance to fire increases damage received. Better than 100% resistance to fire heals the target when fire "damage" is recieved. Brilliant!
- AP usage and skill cooldown for magic versus mana pool is interesting; both good and frustrating.
- Character building is flexible but limited. Think in terms of specializations: the more specialized a character, the more powerful they are versus being a generalist which will result in a very poor character build.
Cons:
- Bosses are insanely difficult in many cases. Fights are generally scripted to be won in a very specific way, more or less eliminating the players ability to improvise or adapt the fight to their style. If you don't fight the boss the way the devs planned, you will either not win or will be required to use insane resources to overcome. Play the fight the way the script it and it's a cake walk.
- Environmental interactions (fighting) are required for almost every single fight. The environmental interaction aspect of D:OS was touted (rightly so!) as ground-breaking. Unfortunately, they took this feature way too far and basically made it the keystone of combat. You cannot hack-n-slash or spray-n-pray or nuke your way thru a fight with brute force or standard D&D tactics. Instead, you have to combine your pyromancy skills with that oil barrel over there, and then hit that puddle over there with lightning, but right after you put out all the fires on the screen with a rain spell. It's intriguing and beautiful and, indeed, ground-breaking, but the involement of this feature is so overused that it's actually tedious and that made me sad.
- Environmental interactions (exploring) is fine except that when you use the "highlight items" key only about 95% of the items are actually highlighted. Turns out, some items are actually there and visibile, but as you become reliant upon that left-Alt key to show you with what you need to interact, it turns you you didn't see the key to that uber-chest that wasn't highlighted. I'm not sure if the devs were being cheeky or wanted us to work harder, but if you give me the ability to highlight items with which I may interact or pick up and it works for 95%, making it not work for the other 5% is just really annoying.
I waited a really long time to play this game (I'm cheap and waited for Summer Sale!) and overall, I thinks it's very good. Sadly, the flaws make me crazy to the point that I'm not sure I will complete this game ever. I've not been able to bring myself back to it in nearly a week b/c I really hate the mechanics of the boss fights. It's  not that I can't do them, I just hate doing it they way we're forced to do it.

You know how it's common for people to say "I wish there was a 'mixed' option" for steam reviews? Well, I'm gonna go one step further. I wish there was a 'null' option for steam reviews, as in--I neither reccomend nor wish to stray people away from Divinity.
Because, as I sit here, two steps before the end of the game, I realize that I cannot in good faith reccomend this game to anyone, regardless of their preferences. I very firmly believe that no one could ever make it to the end of Divinity and seriously believe it is a great game. It has so many absolutely unbeliveable flaws--that were apparently never fixed or even got
in this allegedly "Enchanced" edition. But the perverse irony is that I actually did enjoy Divinity. Quite a lot actually. I can safely say that I will
play this game in singleplayer again, but I somehow stepped away from the astonishing mess that is Divinity and came out with a positive experience. Put through rigorously systemic analysis, Divinity is a terrible game, but is a terrible game that I somehow ended up enjoying more than almost every RPG I've played in the past 5 years.
The strength of Divinity, as you'll read in every single positive review, is the combat. It is
. The encounter design, especially during the beginning of the game, is beyond excellent, with enemies (in hard mode) placed in positions that are advantageous for you but appropriate for them, and they usually outnumber you, so you have to use crowd control wisely. Thankfully crowd control is not restricted only to magic classes as it is in other fantasy RPGs, as not only can a warrior-type very easily choose to learn basic crowd-control magic with no fuss, but there are grenades that function as throwable spells. Everything is so well balanced while never feeling homogynous--Fighters get many knockdown effects, Rogues get area control and invisibility, etc. What impressed me most is the difficulty curve, or rather, the linearity of it--almost every fight is decently challenging (on hard mode) as long as you stay within the same levels as your enemies, and yet none of it ever feels excessive, there's no moment where I was ever saying "How am I expected to do this?" because the game makes your options very clear to you. There *are* a few moments towards the end of the game where your super-powered level 20s can effectively end even supposedly difficult encounters in a single round, but by that point the game is pretty much over.
So what are these "unforgivable flaws"? I'll make this simple and list them:
Divinity is way, way, too long, and the pacing is
. Divinity has a serious problem where playing for short periods of time will lead to you making no concievable progress whatsoever, and playing for a long period of time will put you through so much work and combat that it will turn into an unmemorable grind, which is not only bad in and of itself, but also unproductive towards finishing the game because Divinity's quests really do want to make sure you have things memorized and understood.
So much in Divinity leads towards this feeling of endless grind, to the point where I can't even indicate one specific thing as the culprit. One of the biggest problems is that there is too much combat, but it's not only that there's too much combat, it's that the combats themselves are
long and beyond about 50% of the game, many of them are complete repeats of fights you've already done. Then there's the puzzles, the constant save-scumming trap rooms, pixel-hunting puzzles, incredibly long quests with no sense of direction, it just goes on and on.
The scope of the game, both narratively and mechanically, is stretched out as far as it can go. Many RPGs have the classic "Level 1-20" system just because D&D did it, but they won't be insane enough to actually put all 20 levels of difficulty into one game. Not Divinity. You'll immediately start out fighting hordes of slow-but-powerful undead, but in the middle of the game you'll be fighting elementals that can inflict every status imaginable on you, to the point where, by the end of the game, you are fighting enemies that are
for a few rounds at a time.
The most absurd part is that it doesn't even tether enemies to conventional expectations of their levels. You don't fight wolves until level 7. You don't fight goblins until you're level freaking 12. One of the most difficult encounters in the entire game is against a horde of spiders at level 14. So of course they get new, nonsensical abilities appropriate for that level. This leads to insanity like an alpha wolf casting a Mass Disease spell, or a zombie drinking a healing potion. Giant crabs can ♥♥♥♥ing deal Attribute damage to you--in an AOE. It's a bizzaro world.  You know that old image where the caption says "There was a point where we needed to stop and we have clearly passed it--but let’s keep going and see what happens"? That's Divinity encapsulated.
Divinity has traps. Divinity has traps everywhere. Divinity has traps everywhere that are invisible to the naked eye and can kill your entire party if you step on one. So how do you deal with these traps? Well, basically, you don't. There's an Attribute called Perception which grants a slight amount of AP to your first action in combat but otherwise does nothing (not even an acccuracy bonus) except allow you to detect hidden secrets and traps. The way this works is that there's a hidden value for each trap and secret in the game, and you need that much perception to see it. This is dumb enough by itself--Perception is essentially a tax that one of your characters has to pay to even be able to play the game. It's a "you must be this tall to ride" sign, codified as an attribute. Dumb.
But the icing on the cake is that even
Perception, you can't really do jack♥♥♥♥♥♥about traps. The radius in which you can detect traps with a high Perception character is often lower than the effect radius of the trap itself. Therefore the only way you can detect traps is to actually set them off, i.e., get yourself killed. Then you reload (because you WILL be quicksaving every other second in this game, or you WILL lose massive amounts of progress), and either throw a combustion spell over the trap or summon a minion on top of it. To add insult to injury, most of the time your summons can detect things better than your high character. Not that it matters, because even if you have the insane luck to spot a trap before it activates, you still need to disarm it, for which you need to use a consumable item, or shoot it.
In Divinity, there are actually two protagonists. If you play multiplayer, each of you gets to make your own hero. If you play single player, you get to make two heroes, and while you control both, you only control one for each conversation. In 2P, there are points during conversation where the player who is not instigating conversation gets to chime in. In 1P this happens as well, but with an AI controlling the result instead. For some reason, the AI will almost always choose to disagree with every choice you make, which is bad enough by itself. But what's even worse is that the AI can actually
your choices. If you disagree, you have to play RPS with them. Literally.
Whoever wins, wins the "argument" and makes the choice. This means that not only does every single choice force you to play a minigame, but you may not even get to make the choice you wanted to make. The worst part of this is that it can be completely avoided by savescumming; effectively the developers accomplished nothing but wasting the player's time.
So why did I eventually choose to click thumbs up rather than thumbs down? Because honestly, I think this game needs to be played. People need to know just how utterly insane it is.

I picked Divinity: Original Sin up a couple months back to play with one of my friends. Unfortuntely, they got tied up and was unable to dedicate any massive amount of time to an epic RPG.
So I launched it eventually by myself. Played it for about an hour or two and it was... okay. Then you had to speak your partner (The base game has 2 main characters. You control both in single, or one each in coop). I realized that it was expected, or atleast, was enhanced by having a coop partner, so I made one of my other friends buy it and dragged him along.
Both of us has played each day till one of us has to go, every day. I honestly really love it.
A quick game-comparision for RPG-lovers would the classic Baulder's Gate (albeit with less menus, thank god). You're real time while not in combat, fully able to divide the party to do quests seperately, or loot and scout, or talk and shop fully independent from one another. Which is a huge boone if you have two people with different play styles, such as the lore expert who wants to talk to every NPC and read every note, you can have your coop partner continue scouting or lonewolfing through combat while you summarize information to them.
There's a few mechanical issues though, simply down to the UI and core of the game, but thankfully it is just that, a few.
Enemies have an idle animation, which while keeps the game visually exciting, makes a scenerio where you can click to attack an enemy at the wrong moment and they 'dodge' your click, so you instead walk.
There's not much indication on what you're doing wrong, if you're doing something wrong. This is a fine line that games struggle to walk sometimes, but for us we started the game and got a couple hours in. We found out that our build for our characters just weren't sustainable, combat was whiping the floor with us and we weren't getting enough levels. Reroleld our characters and started steamrolling through it though with a bit more knowledge.
But on good notes.
The game is serious enough to be taken.. well, seriously, but it is quirky enough to make you laugh or be caught off guard by something silly. The characters are all well written and the story doesn't feel hamfisted like other RPG's these days. It all falls in place rather naturally.
Combat isn't that bad other than pixel hunting, but it doesn't really innovate anywhere. If you've played Baulder's Gate expect more of the same (But again, with much less menus. Thank the Seven for that). If youve played Dragon Age think of it turned based rather than real time and you know exactly what it's like.
tl;dr
Would I recommend it single player? It's an okay single player game if you just want an RPG like Baulder's Gate.
Would I recommend it coop? If you have another RPG friend, then you'll both have a real good time.

Every time I see FEAR 3 on sale I see people bashing it as the worst in the series, but the meta score is actually not too bad 74/100. Unlike the first 2 FEAR games, FEAR 3 has one of those regenerating health systems where you just hide under cover for a few seconds and you recover back to full health. No need to scrounge for med kits or armor. Also, the game seems built around 2 player co-op, which I like in first person shooter games (when I have someone to play with).
*Spoilers ahead*
FEAR 3 takes place an unspecified amount of time after the events of FEAR 2. Alma is pregnant and getting ready to give birth, as a result her psychic power is tearing up the city (possibly the world). Again the main opposition is the private military contractor Armacham, who seems to have become 100x more powerful than they were in the first games. Even without their clone super soldiers from the first games, Armacham seems capable of overrunning and occupying entire cities with soldiers, aircraft, and power armor. You play the Point Man protagonist from the first FEAR game (the guy you play in FEAR 2 also shows up briefly) but this time you have an “imaginary” friend Paxton Fettel (Bad guy from the first game). Your primary goal this time around is to reach Alma before she gives birth and deal with her once and for all. Unfortunately for you, Alma’s psychic pain has summoned nightmare creatures and twisted the surviving civilian population into crazed psychos.
Unlike the previous FEAR games, FEAR 3 is broken down into missions or “levels” with each mission giving you a point score at the end. You gain points by finding collectables, killing enemies, and completing “challenges.” The challenges are similar to the “Skill shots” in Bulletstorm, where it’s basically just using various methods of killing. For example, 2000 points for killing enemies with a specific weapon, or 1000 points for getting 25 headshots, or 2000 points for getting 3 backstabs. The points aren’t just for show, by the way. You “level up” when you gain enough points and each level gives you some kind of perk, such as +10% health or +bullet capacity. You can replay levels as many times as you want to “grind” for points. This means that the game will get easier over time as you replay it. You might notice that when you first start the game, it seems far more difficult than the previous ones, well this changes as you level up and get stronger. The regenerating health means you can charge groups of enemies and just duck for cover when your screen is almost completely red (near death). Healing is free unlike FEAR 1 and 2 which had limited med kits.
As I mentioned earlier, the game is built with 2 player co-op in mind. At the end of each mission there is a ranking between the 2 players to see who scored highest in several categories. The game’s ending depends on which of the two characters “won” the most missions. Of course if you’re playing single player the character you’re playing (Fettel or Point Man) will “win” every level you complete. Point Man’s gameplay is the same as the previous games (standard shooter with Slow-Mo power), But Fettel is a psychic commander. This means he can possess enemies and use them to fight (he doesn’t have slow-mo). Every time he takes over a new body he gets the weapons of the possessed enemy, so you can’t hoard powerful weapons or grenades the way Point Man does. You can only hold 2 weapons now, unlike 3 weapons in FEAR 1 and 4 weapons in FEAR 2. Possession also means you won’t be able to use the awesome power armors because the possessed body won’t last long enough.
Pros:
+Excellent graphics and visuals. Large variety of weapons available.
+Some cool new enemies, particular the Phase Commander and Phase Caster.
+A lot of replay value. I just finished the game and immediately restarted as Fettel.
+2 player co-op available. Also a bunch of various multiplayer game modes I haven’t tried.
Cons:
-The game is very short, about 6 hours to beat the first time. Replay is strongly encouraged though.
-The story is weaker than the first FEAR games. There’re a lot of unnecessary “dream sequences” that don’t seem to add much. You just walk forward about 15 seconds with someone talking in voice over and it ends.
-I get the feeling that the enemies are much “dumber” than FEAR 1 enemies. They tend to stick behind the same piece of cover and just pop their heads out to shoot from there.
Overall I think the game is well worth playing for fans of First Person Shooters and people who want to see how the FEAR story ends. Once you finish a mission in single player, the Fettel character is unlocked so you can try playing him for that particular level. The way to see the Fettel game ending is by playing through the game a second time (or play the game in co-op and Fettel has the highest score every mission). One thing I noticed is that the game’s Steam achievements seem to be half for multiplayer, and not many people are playing the multiplayer. This isn’t surprising since the game has been out for a few years. I’ll probably only be able to get about 45% completion for the game achievements by myself.

I will say that post "The Foundation Update" No Man's Sky is well worth it's cost. It can never live up to the hype and the lies that were spread about it by it's creator, but in it's current state it is a great game. Sure, if you don't get it on sale (near impossible) it seems expensive. People say you can buy three survival games for the same price. Really though, you can't buy anything that does it it does. It provides you with endless procedurally generated worlds full of weird creatures and interesting landscapes. The lore of the world is deep and interesting. It calls back to the weird cosmic new age philosophies that inspired me as a kid. The visuals are amazing.
I think the problem people have now is they do not know what the game is. They claim they don't like the end. Well the end is the same end that minecraft gave you. It's more of a meta self reflective journey that a lot of people don't like. Neither of these games is made to be beaten though. The genre almost never produces a story or an ending in the first place. Notch only really added the ending of minecraft to quiet down some of it's detractors.
These games are made to be experienced and that is pretty much it. The motivation behind sandbox games belongs to the player. Some people will play the game in order to max out their gear. Some people will try to build the best base, or fully explore a single planet. A few will go on to finish the game and wonder why they feel so unfulfilled. The answer is simple, in a sandbox style game the answer to the question "how do I win?" is "by having the most fun while playing," it is not a race to the finish like most other genres.
It still has a few bugs. On one of the planets I landed it there was really bad texture flickering, you still get annoying milestones every few minutes that seem more like a punishment than a reward, and your ship still auto ejects you when you land which can be deadly if you are not careful.
This is not a run and gun shooter, it's a very chill sandbox exploration and survival game with base building.
TLDR; Strip away the hype and the hate and the current state of the game is amazing. Great visuals, a relaxed world to explore, and amazing music.

LEGO Worlds is a great game for anybody who likes Lego. It is a great new game with a lot of potential, although it is still lacking many things. I highly recommend this game if you want to explore and do many things such as fly a dragon or a plane. Although this game can be entertaining for many hours, whether you want to explore, battle or build, it is still missing many things. I have a list of the things I believe will improve the game and make it even more enjoyable:
-First Person Mode: I think that a great thing about Lego in general, is that kids can imagine that they are whatever they want and LW has the potential to do so. The problem is that if you see your character, it makes it harder to immerse yourself into the Lego World. This is why I think that a 1st Person Mode is necessary, so people who play this game can actually feel like they are looking through the eyes of a minifigure. If you have ever built any building which is small but can fit a few minifigures in LW, you will notice that when your avatar is inside, you cannot see him. This is another reason why 1st Person Mode is necessary: so you can enter the buildings that you created.
-Story: I think that to make this game more interesting, it needs a story. I don't know what kind, but I think that a story gives the game a purpose. I used to play Lego Universe when it was open, and what kept bringing me back to the game was mostly the story, to save the Universe from evil. I believe that the same could be possible with LW, which will make it much more fun and will attract a lerger number of people.
-Building Vehicles: I know that many people have been asking for this, and I am another person who agrees that LW will not be complete until we can create our own vehicles. For a game that is based around building, creating your own vehicles is essential.
-More Enemies: Up until now only skeletons attack you in the game. I think that some other minifigures should be automatically hostile, not just skeletons. I have encountered many warlocks and vampires, but none of them attack. It would be great to have a fight with a wizard that shoots fireballs at you, which I hope will be possible later on. I also think that some animals such as bears, polar bears and dragons should be hostile towards you until you tame them.
-Better Balance In Enemies: Every night a chance arises that skeletons may appear and attack you (and hopefully other different enemies soon!), but there have been many nights that one or two skeletons attacked me and the next night about fifteen swarmed me. I was in the same biome and wasn't doing anything different. There should be more of a balance of being attacked by enemies.
-Better Building: The brick by brick building tool is amazing, but still a little weird. As I have said in the 1st Person Mode section, a player wants to look through the eyes of a minifigure and this is why I believe that building in 1st Person is necessary.
-Better Spawning: The spawning system of LW now is a little wonky. There have been many times that I have found a random, completely healthy looking minifigure in the middle of the desert. This seems a little ridiculous, and while the game is aimed to be funny, I'd rather like to see a weakened, tired minifigure in the desert rather than a young, happy minifigure who looks like he just went to the mall. Same goes for vehicles, as I have found a plane standing on a steep cliff or a helicopter in the middle of a mushroom island. For vehicles like planes, it would be nice to find one at a small airport or landing zone.
-Support For Mods: I know that there is still at least a yeart of development planned for the game, but obviously it is not possible to add everything ever imagined. This is why it would be great to have support for mods so others could help and make the game better.
Overall there are a great many things to be added to the game but it is already very fun to play. There were a few things I haven't mentioned such as the need for multiplayer since I know that it is on it's way. I very highly recommend LEGO Worlds, and I hope that it will be a much improved game soon.

Without question one of the most forward-thinking fighters in the genre right now. While keeping true to its 2D-fighting game roots, LabZero recognizes some of the flaws and annoyances from other fighting games and seeks to correct them.
Faulty netcode? Nope, we've got GGPO.
Unexplained mechanics? Nope, pretty much everything you could want is given to you in the tutorials. More than that, it's done in a way that will challenge newcomers without overwhelming them.
Unblockable setups? Handled.
Unbalanced metagame? Not here. Game design is lead by MikeZ, who has been a part of the fighting game scene for a long while now. In addition to that, balance testing is regularly handled in conjunction with the playerbase itself in the form of the Endless Beta.
The community is currently not too big, so the players you'll find on quick match are generally somewhat skilled and experienced. Because of this, the game might be difficult to get into for a newcomer. But it truly is worthwhile to keep practicing and improve your skills.

Whether you are new to fighting games, or an old vet, THIS is the one you'll want to make sure you have in your collection before any others! It's a modern 2D Fighter that boasts gorgeous visuals, Each character sprite has approximately 1,400 hand-drawn frames of animation, the most amount of frames per character in any fighting game to date, and some of the best hand-drawn character sprites ever used in gaming, it's one of the prettiest With it's very fluid combat,  awesome tutorials and training options, aggressive AI (which have an insane amount of customization) and constant balance tweaks and updates, this is hands down the best fighting game I have ever played, and I recommend it to everyone! Great job guys, great game!

"A DEEP, EMOTIONAL, WELL-WRITTEN STORY."
"IT MADE ME CRY."
"ONE OF THE GREATEST INDIE GAMES EVER MADE."
"A MASTERPIECE."
...And it was with words like these that I dove into 'To The Moon' with very high expectations. I prepared myself for a mind-blowing experience...with all the overwhelming positive reviews, how could it not be? This game was going to OWN, I was convinced. So when I saw this in an attractively priced bundle, I didn't hesitate to snap it up. Unfortunately, the actual game didn't live up to the hype.
GOOD
+ Graphics are decent for this style of game
+ Music is good, though repetitive
+ Interesting concept for the storyline (scientists going back into a dying patient's memories and recreating them to match the patient's one true desire, like granting a wish)
BAD
- Clunky controls. Imagine playing an old school SNES JRPG with a mouse.
- Lack of ENGAGING gameplay. Finding the 'mementos' and completing the ensuing simple flip puzzle got tiresome fast, and having to complete a bunch of them to advance the storyline made me feel like I was slogging through the game after a while. This is pretty much all there is as far as gameplay, other than moving your character around and clicking through dialogue boxes.
- Slow performance. This game wasn't optimized for modern machines. But that's due mostly to the engine it was built on, from what I've read.
- Overrated story. It had its moments, but too much cheese and seemed forced. Characters weren't fleshed out enough. Ending...was typical. And predictable.
- Not enough feels. At least for me. I was really hoping the story and characters were gonna grip me and make me bawl my eyes out, like all the reviews said. My eyes remained dry throughout.
- Zero replay value. No alternate endings. No secrets to find. No extra or hidden characters. No bonuses. You get NOTHING.
Overall...."meh". I finished the game, but it felt like a chore most of the time. With an engaging storyline, which is this game's main selling point, it would have been different. I bought this game in a bundle, and dividing the cost of the bundle with the number of games in it, 'To The Moon' came to about .60 cents; a good deal any way you slice it. Full price = hell no. At $1.99 or less = worth a shot. Still, despite all its positively glowing reviews, I can't give this my full recommendation.

Ok, so I played "A bird story" before "To the moon" and it was a lot shorter and, while equally emotionally stirring and thoughtprovoking, a bit too surreal for my taste. As these two are the first interactive novels I've played, and from the same developer, I will compare them to some extent.
"To the moon" is an interactive novel. It's more interactive than "A bird story" (also from Freebird Games), but it is mostly about telling you the story. Even so, the interaction feels more meaningful in "To the moon".
The setup is a company that works with fulfilling wishes for people who are at life's end. This is done by going through their memories and help them remember a life where their wish was fulfilled. If you've seen the movie "Eternal sunshine of the spotless mind" this game has a similar feel to it.
While the story is told you're provoked to consider things like what memories really are and what they mean. To me the story was also very emotional and had me in tears at times. They manage to bring up the issues in a very serious manner interlaced with some light comedy and breaking the fourth wall, without retracting from the overall experience (apart from one scene that I will not spoil, but that did annoy me somewhat).

Honestly, the game delivers exactly what I expected from it with what I've seen in the trailers and various other gameplay videos.
It is a bit short, having only 27 levels and 3 bosses (3 levels per door, 3 doors per 'world', and 3 worlds.. + 1 door each world that is strictly a boss fight). An endless mode somewhat in vein with the original game that this one is meant to reboot would've been awesome... but for the price, I still think it's a pretty good old-school arcade dungeon crawler that harkens back to a more innocent time in my life.
It might have played it a little safe when compared to the original 1985 arcade game, and I can understand why... but I liked it for what it is.
I'll admit, so far I've only played solo. I imagine it's best played with friends... and I don't mean a PUG. With any luck maybe I can talk my brother and a few others into giving it a spin.
EDIT: As of April 2015 I'm finding it hard to recommend this. I still stand by my claim that the game is really fun for what it is, but the utter lack of content leaves it downright forgettable in the long run. There are only so many times you can play through the same thing before it starts feeling both tedious and monotonous. For me, that ended with about 3 times.. granted, all solo plays, but still.
So yea.. changing my recommendation because I'm not seeing a future for this at all content-wise. And that's a real shame to me.
EDIT 8-12-2015: Well, they released a free update for the PC version of the game to coincide with a PS4 release. I played it for a few hours.. and I can't explain it, but from what I remember before, it feels like it plays much better than it used to. I'm still not used to relics being separate from potions, and having a completely separate potion ability.. but that will probably come in time. I also haven't really tried any of the new weapons and their attacks.
I also don't remember the updated take on the Gauntlet II theme being there in the previous version, so when I first heard that... man, I was taken back a couple decades or more.
However, the big thing for me is that endless mode is now a thing. The stages are a bit simple and linear, and every few of them is a 'Death chase'.. which is a mode I'm not exactly crazy about, but endless is still nice to have.
The stages of the campaign itself have received changes in numerous areas, so it's actually kinda fresh to even play through that again.. which was surprising to me. It's also nice that the 'arena' type levels are optional (at least that first one anyway.. that's as far as I made it really before quitting).
The hub area is gone, however, replaced with a rudimentary map style system. It's nice because it allows you to access stages on their own instead of in sets of three.. but the look and feel of the map system is very basic.
The devs have acknowledged the sort of lackluster camera in this version, so hopefully that will get fixed soon. It's somewhat annoying living on the edge of the screen until you get to one of those 'encounter areas' where it pans out and more or less centers itself.
Anyway, it still plays like a modern arcade game at its core.. and it was pretty much meant to, given the title and game it was meant to reboot. It's a fun hack 'n' slash dungeon crawler, and now that it has an endless mode.. it's very hard to not recommend if you're into that kind of thing.

Divinity: Original Sin is rife with all sorts of interesting features. The character creation system allows you to customize your characters' stats and abilities in a flexible manner. Additionally, in terms of combat, the game provides many interesting skills to use against enemies, along with interactive environments for tactical advantages.
The storyline isn't quite that innovative, but many of the characters that you encounter have enough personality to make the experience feel a little refreshing, especially when it comes to the animals that you can find around the realm. On top of that, several of the quests often provide players different pathways to tackle situations. After reaching a certain point in the plot, it becomes possible to gradually unlock a number of useful tools, including teleportation, storage chests, and recruitable mercenaries.
The only few downsides to Divinity would probably be the scale of difficulty and its argument system. It can be a little challenging to progress if you decide to build your party in a fashion that isn't well-equipped for certain battles. Also, the rock-paper-scissors mechanic for winning arguments can be frustrating at times when playing single player mode. I found myself in a dilemma where I had to make correct choices in order to achieve a certain outcome ,which I had to keep retrying due to A.I. conflicts.
Conclusion:
Other than the two previously mentioned issues, Divinity is a generally fun game that combines turn-based tactics with creative quests and immersive combat that will likely keep any RPG fan occupied for several hours on end.

Highly recommended.

What do you little bobbleheads want from me?
Reus is a resource management god-sim that has you taking on the role of the planet itself, controlling four powerful giants that carry out your will and alter the landscape to your whim. You can create trees and animal life, grow entire plots of fertile swampland, and one of your giants can even punch veins of precious stones directly into the crust.
All of this, to attract the ungrateful little bobbleheads known as man to build great cities upon your surface. The humans create many great works on their own- well, with your help. Your giants can directly influence whether or not they complete their projects (do you really want a mad scientist around? How about a sacrificial altar?) by altering the landscape further, creating new resources that meet the goals of these projects. The more you complete, the more varying projects and resources you unlock, and thus the rabbit hole goes deeper. You can even unlock longer game-times as well, allowing more time to create and build, and allowing more time for the humans to try and rise up against you and your giants.
They do go to war with each other. And they'll attack your god titans too, which is a curious choice. Your giants can slaughter them back, as any good vengeful potential goddess will be happy to know.
The game can get quite complicated as you go on, however, the title screen provides a link to the Reus wiki, which will give a lot of ideas and help.
The graphics themselves are cartoony and relatively simple looking, but always bright and interesting to look at. The game is on a 2D scale, all around the surface of the planet. Your giants traverse the outside of the planet as well, so some of your time will be spent waiting for the big lugs to get to where they're going, but since their abilities have cool-down meters, that isn't too much of a problem. The soundtrack is rather limited, though, so have some of your own music handy for the longer games.
Overall, Reus is a well-designed god game. It'll start off just slow enough to get you hooked, and keep you in for the long haul as you look to see what you can accomplish next.

I was put off for a long while by the negative reviews that this game got. I am so pleased that I took the chance and bought this game. Here are a few reasons why.
Having played Elite, Frontier and First Encounters I always wished that there was more to explore - in this game there is. Every planet that you land on looks like it provided the inspiration for one of those old Sci Fi novels. I have been completely immersed and often just stop to take in the view. I have been impressed with the variety, but then I have only been playing for about 40 hours.
The open nature of the game play means that you can forget the main questline and just explore, then return knowing there is something deeper to investigate. The upgrades and resourcing are reminicent of other crafting games. The interfaces are refreshingly different from other games very easy to use.
My experience has not been without its niggles. I have had random crashes and the reload time is long, but this has forced me to eat and sleep as without these pauses I have found it very difficult to drag myself away. Exploring some of the question markers on planetary surfaces it soon becomes apparent that they are often generated 2 mins flight/walk time away and will disappear even if you revisit the location. It seems that control of thrust disappears during space flight - it is clear that to make the game more accessible there is heavy intervention in the flight controls during battles and near planetary surfaces.
I approached the game with low expectations  but I am really enjoying this game and I recommend it.

LEGO Worlds is a great game for anybody who likes Lego. It is a great new game with a lot of potential, although it is still lacking many things. I highly recommend this game if you want to explore and do many things such as fly a dragon or a plane. Although this game can be entertaining for many hours, whether you want to explore, battle or build, it is still missing many things. I have a list of the things I believe will improve the game and make it even more enjoyable:
-First Person Mode: I think that a great thing about Lego in general, is that kids can imagine that they are whatever they want and LW has the potential to do so. The problem is that if you see your character, it makes it harder to immerse yourself into the Lego World. This is why I think that a 1st Person Mode is necessary, so people who play this game can actually feel like they are looking through the eyes of a minifigure. If you have ever built any building which is small but can fit a few minifigures in LW, you will notice that when your avatar is inside, you cannot see him. This is another reason why 1st Person Mode is necessary: so you can enter the buildings that you created.
-Story: I think that to make this game more interesting, it needs a story. I don't know what kind, but I think that a story gives the game a purpose. I used to play Lego Universe when it was open, and what kept bringing me back to the game was mostly the story, to save the Universe from evil. I believe that the same could be possible with LW, which will make it much more fun and will attract a lerger number of people.
-Building Vehicles: I know that many people have been asking for this, and I am another person who agrees that LW will not be complete until we can create our own vehicles. For a game that is based around building, creating your own vehicles is essential.
-More Enemies: Up until now only skeletons attack you in the game. I think that some other minifigures should be automatically hostile, not just skeletons. I have encountered many warlocks and vampires, but none of them attack. It would be great to have a fight with a wizard that shoots fireballs at you, which I hope will be possible later on. I also think that some animals such as bears, polar bears and dragons should be hostile towards you until you tame them.
-Better Balance In Enemies: Every night a chance arises that skeletons may appear and attack you (and hopefully other different enemies soon!), but there have been many nights that one or two skeletons attacked me and the next night about fifteen swarmed me. I was in the same biome and wasn't doing anything different. There should be more of a balance of being attacked by enemies.
-Better Building: The brick by brick building tool is amazing, but still a little weird. As I have said in the 1st Person Mode section, a player wants to look through the eyes of a minifigure and this is why I believe that building in 1st Person is necessary.
-Better Spawning: The spawning system of LW now is a little wonky. There have been many times that I have found a random, completely healthy looking minifigure in the middle of the desert. This seems a little ridiculous, and while the game is aimed to be funny, I'd rather like to see a weakened, tired minifigure in the desert rather than a young, happy minifigure who looks like he just went to the mall. Same goes for vehicles, as I have found a plane standing on a steep cliff or a helicopter in the middle of a mushroom island. For vehicles like planes, it would be nice to find one at a small airport or landing zone.
-Support For Mods: I know that there is still at least a yeart of development planned for the game, but obviously it is not possible to add everything ever imagined. This is why it would be great to have support for mods so others could help and make the game better.
Overall there are a great many things to be added to the game but it is already very fun to play. There were a few things I haven't mentioned such as the need for multiplayer since I know that it is on it's way. I very highly recommend LEGO Worlds, and I hope that it will be a much improved game soon.

"A DEEP, EMOTIONAL, WELL-WRITTEN STORY."
"IT MADE ME CRY."
"ONE OF THE GREATEST INDIE GAMES EVER MADE."
"A MASTERPIECE."
...And it was with words like these that I dove into 'To The Moon' with very high expectations. I prepared myself for a mind-blowing experience...with all the overwhelming positive reviews, how could it not be? This game was going to OWN, I was convinced. So when I saw this in an attractively priced bundle, I didn't hesitate to snap it up. Unfortunately, the actual game didn't live up to the hype.
GOOD
+ Graphics are decent for this style of game
+ Music is good, though repetitive
+ Interesting concept for the storyline (scientists going back into a dying patient's memories and recreating them to match the patient's one true desire, like granting a wish)
BAD
- Clunky controls. Imagine playing an old school SNES JRPG with a mouse.
- Lack of ENGAGING gameplay. Finding the 'mementos' and completing the ensuing simple flip puzzle got tiresome fast, and having to complete a bunch of them to advance the storyline made me feel like I was slogging through the game after a while. This is pretty much all there is as far as gameplay, other than moving your character around and clicking through dialogue boxes.
- Slow performance. This game wasn't optimized for modern machines. But that's due mostly to the engine it was built on, from what I've read.
- Overrated story. It had its moments, but too much cheese and seemed forced. Characters weren't fleshed out enough. Ending...was typical. And predictable.
- Not enough feels. At least for me. I was really hoping the story and characters were gonna grip me and make me bawl my eyes out, like all the reviews said. My eyes remained dry throughout.
- Zero replay value. No alternate endings. No secrets to find. No extra or hidden characters. No bonuses. You get NOTHING.
Overall...."meh". I finished the game, but it felt like a chore most of the time. With an engaging storyline, which is this game's main selling point, it would have been different. I bought this game in a bundle, and dividing the cost of the bundle with the number of games in it, 'To The Moon' came to about .60 cents; a good deal any way you slice it. Full price = hell no. At $1.99 or less = worth a shot. Still, despite all its positively glowing reviews, I can't give this my full recommendation.

Ok, so I played "A bird story" before "To the moon" and it was a lot shorter and, while equally emotionally stirring and thoughtprovoking, a bit too surreal for my taste. As these two are the first interactive novels I've played, and from the same developer, I will compare them to some extent.
"To the moon" is an interactive novel. It's more interactive than "A bird story" (also from Freebird Games), but it is mostly about telling you the story. Even so, the interaction feels more meaningful in "To the moon".
The setup is a company that works with fulfilling wishes for people who are at life's end. This is done by going through their memories and help them remember a life where their wish was fulfilled. If you've seen the movie "Eternal sunshine of the spotless mind" this game has a similar feel to it.
While the story is told you're provoked to consider things like what memories really are and what they mean. To me the story was also very emotional and had me in tears at times. They manage to bring up the issues in a very serious manner interlaced with some light comedy and breaking the fourth wall, without retracting from the overall experience (apart from one scene that I will not spoil, but that did annoy me somewhat).
Is it worth €8? In my personal opinion this story really touched me, and even though I got it on sale, I would happily have shelled out the 8 had I known how good it was. But if you feel unsure, wait for it to go on sale.
For those who like numbers this was an 8/10 in my opinion.

Looking for a fun, multiplayer arena brawler for friends?  Then move along.  There are far better ones out there.
Gauntlet was about frantically running around a maze, fighting off the oncoming hoard of enemies, and trying to seek an exit.  Gauntlet Legends was about exploring stages, over the top attacks, huge bosses, and playing as a chicken.
New Gauntlet is about walking around muddy-brown areas that all look the same, getting into one locked arena after another until you reach the end.  Occassionally you have to run from Death and his wonky hit box.  Seriously, though.. all previous Gauntlets are bright, gaudy affairs.  This one is all browns and greys.
Most egregious to me, though, is that the game can't detect my PS2 Dual Shock 2 controller.  That's not that it detects it and won't let me remap buttons, but that the game says "is this a 360 controller? No? Then there is no controller".  Which is a load of crap in the modern world of PC gaming.
And while spell slinging as the Wizard can be fun, there's a game out there that can do it better (Magicka).  In fact, any good point I can think of about Gauntlet is done better by another game.

If you PAY for this game, you're in for a disappointment. This game is very unique in how it plays and it is a lot of fun (which I'll get into a moment), but it still boils down to in other aspects this game is just like a million other "free to play" games that you expect to see on mobile (and I think this game does have a mobile version?).
Pros:
-Very addictive, fun battles
-Lots of humor while still being serious about the fights themselves (reminds me of Monday Night Combat)
-Unique PVP gameplay
-Quick rounds, if you or your enemy are bad, the pain will be over quickly. Between 1 and 3 minutes are nornal
-Pleasing graphics
Cons:
-Should be FREE always
-Based around microtransitions (buy premium currency in-game or spend twenty years saving up the scraps you get from leveling, which comes to a screeching halt between levels 15 and 20), exactly like the worst of the Mobile pay-to-advance structures
-Advancing is a lot of fun until you reach Bronze (which is like the third level? Just long enough to get you addicted), suddenly in which each loss actually knocks you down levels. There's a reason almost all players you meet in the Bronze levels are stuck at 5 (the lowest) - even if they are good players
In short, this game is a lot of fun for a couple of hours, then you realize it goes nowhere because each player is meant to advance until they meet others who are even close to their own skill (which isn't hard, as most players are relatively equal in skill and luck/randomness plays a part in such a case). Play this on mobile if you must, where we expect it. I'd pay for this on PC if they got rid of microtransitions and focused on gameplay longevity instead of freezing players in level zones (for the sheer purpose of attempting to frustrate players into paying for premium currency).
I'm not sayng it's pay-to-win (though it sure can help) , it's more like pay-to-(advance once you get to a point where you're kind of just flopping around like a fish and you earn like 10 gold per battle and it takes 1000 to have a chance at winning a new card).
EDIT:: I just heard that this game will be free on full release. The rest of my review still stands as of when this was written. Just a few ins-and-outs of the model of this game, especially for those considering purchasing it before full release.
Pretty interesting, although it has only a few cards and they all are easy to get, it could improve it's variability and become way better than the other games like this.
Dont expect to have a remote chance of getting all the units neccessary to keep up unless you're willing to shell out an obscene ammount of money. Shamefull greed from what was a good developer.

Cons:
- 5 hours long, I was bloody awful at it and my co-op partner carried us, we respawned a LOT and it still only took us about 5 and a half hours.
- Extremely linear, linearity isn't bad but Fear 3's linearity is similar to being on rails
- Co-op gameplay is lopsided. Pointman's gameplay is well worn and honestly sort of boring but much easier, or Paxton, who has gameplay that's more fun yet not nearly as solid, it's much easier to do well in the grading system each mission insists on as Pointman as opposed to Paxton

- MP servers are dead in the water
- Repetitive gameplay
- Questionable AI(at times)
- Just mediocre, neither the graphics, nor the story, nor the non-existent horror help this game stand out.
Now, did I have fun with it? Yeah i did, but more in the vein of it being a fun co-op shooter with a fairly interesting premise instead of it being a Fear game. I'd expected something else and got a fairly fun co-op shooter that's easy to shoot through.
I recommend this to Die-heard FEAR fans, but even then only if it's on steep discount. Otherwise with the amount of other quality games that come out, buying this game for 20 dollars isn't worth it.

:
- Strange AI behavior at times (even on higher difficulty levels)

Combat in D:OS EE, simply put, feels great. It is challenging on higher difficulties and you have many skills and abilities to choose from. Interaction with environment in and out of combat is interesting
, but in my opinion, the game should better communicate whether you will actually step on a surface before you move.
The AI is decent most of the time but (on tactician difficulty) NPCs spend AP to move to the same spot, hit obstacles that are in the way or skip their turn completely after a few seconds standing idle (even though there are many better actions they could take). Nonetheless, the combat is the main reason you will play this game again.
The story, in my opinion, is not bad but nothing special and mediocre at best. On the other hand,
and you have many options - kill anyone, steal anything, sneak past enemies, talk your way out of the problems, be a hero or a villain. The world is interesting and dense and the music is great. There are some puzzles but they are not that difficult to solve. When I got stuck, it was mainly because I overlooked a small switch or hidden lever but that's because my perception was pretty low.
Although I haven't tried neither local nor online co-op yet, many people have enjoyed it and I can definitely see why (less micromanagement, character dialogs etc.).
D:OS EE looks good and works even with older HW on many platforms (great if you travel with a non-gaming laptop for example). There is a completely different UI for controller and keyboard + mouse and it is very well done (something I have never seen in any other game).
Overall, this game is very well polished, replayable even without mods and a must-have for anyone who likes D&D or D&D like RPGs.

My last straw was when I realized a game I bought to play, enjoy, and relax with was giving me some serious hand pain and mental frustration. The relaxtion I'd hoped for? I always ended my gameplay tensed up. Ori is entirely trial and error style game play, but set in a lush visual world. Too repetitive for casual gamers, but not enough of a challenge for super serious gamers either.

Not a bad game; though it has a lot of work left to go.  The naval combat, sailing mechanics, world to explore are all pretty well done.  You can have a great time sailing around and blasting things.
The framework for the greater economy is there, with players gathering the resources and refining them at player-owned facilities around the world.  Not remotely as complex as say, EVE online; but it's in the same vein as far as a player-dependent economy.  That said, there are bugs, balancing issues, and exploits they need to address.
Perhaps the most glaring issue at the moment is the current UI design, which is very clunky at the moment.  Clearly, that will change over time, but if you're looking to play *now*, you can expect some clunkiness.  That's just the state of the game.
Ultimately, if you're willing to roll the dice on this, it's a good game with a lot of potential, especially if you like the genre; just don't happen into this game and expect a finished product just yet.

This game isn't for me anymore.  I joined the early access sea trials before open world and absolutely loved this game, but I've just never taken to the open world or where the devs have taken this game since.  The sea trials were some of the best fun I've had on a game in ages, the way the game was designed back then worked so well and the community was excellent.  What I really liked in sea trials was it was a pure sea battle game both PVP and PVE and it didn't have any of the features like capturing zones, like those in World of Warships, which to me made no sense in a sea game.  Instead we had exciting team based battles with players forming lines of battle, with a nice tactical depth and polite community.  All this changed when it went open world.  The battles were not as fun and the whole premise didn't work for me as you started off as a private captain more like Pirates but you quickly progressed to naval ships.  These sort of ships had professional officers with objectives of protecting or attacking trade  and a command structure, none of which are in this game. The open world did not seem believable to me.
TLDR; The game suffers, in my opinion, in the devs not having a clear idea what kind of game they were creating and it has lost its way.
If they had made a pirate game or a proper naval game or even just a solid battle game without the open world maybe with added scenarios (attack defend the convoy, land troops etc) this could have been a real gem but sadly it's none of these things and instead a mish mash of promisng elements which for me doesn't really work.
The graphics are trully excellent though and the ships look lovely, so I hope eventually they can use the ships and graphics in a new better game.

This is unique sandbox take on the God Game concept.
Rather than the usual God Game where you must indirectly help your followers prosper and defeat their enemies, in Reus you must oversee the whole world.
You get to control 3 giants with the powers of the elements to create various natural resources and environments.
With multiple villages needing your attention, you can chose to help, ignore, or smite each one.    Be careful not to help too much, though, as humans are greedy creatures who, if not faced with challanges, will simply want more and more, until they attack your neighbors, and eventually you!
As more villages prosper and complete projects, you become more powerful, and the more games you play successfully in different ways, the more powers you unlock.

But for the average gamer, this one is a miss.

Scribblenauts Unlimited is a fun, interesting, and innovative game for about 15 minutes. The game concept is engrossing enough; type any word or phrase and it will appear in-game. Y'all already know I was rolling with my posse of George Washington and Napoleon on the reg, sporting a tuxedo and wielding a flamethrower atop my giant flying jaguar. The open nature also makes the options to resolve "quests" interesting (we'll get to that later). I was a vengeful God, and if a person needed, say a bag of money, I would make them blind in return. If they wanted a child, it would be a gargantuan, dying, amphibious baby. And for a while the gimmick was entertaining. However, the gimmick gets old fast. Because that's all the game is; an interesting game concept and gimmick that is stretched into a full-length video game.
The game quests are extremely shallow and repetitive. An NPC says "I need something that can do this/is like this/is this, and you oblige them. This process takes an average of 7 seconds to complete, and is the core of game progression. Like I said, this provides plenty of opportunity for humorous moments. But the game counts on you to make those moments happen. And there's really no incentive to do so; because the game is so repetitive, you want to just blow through it and be done with the quests. As the game progresses I became more and more utilitarian with my answers. I just didn't have the heart to try and make humor out of what felt like work. "I need a friend" - give them a dog. "I want to write" - give them a pencil. THe process became so monotonous and boring it was unbearable.
This is a game that brings the player an interesting but temporarily engaging concept and absolutely drab quests and asks the player to bring the fun. Whereas "make your own fun games" like Just Cause and GTA create diversity in how you can create that fun, Scribblenauts is dull and taxing throughout. Just knowing that this game exists is about as much fun as playing it. Don't buy it, not even on sale.

When you first start Game Dev Tycoon, eager to create masterpieces of software design that blow anything in the actual real world out of the water, you’ll rapidly realise that there’s a big problem ticking away under the surface of the game’s mechanics. That problem is quite simply this; it’s impossible to actually truly gauge whether your decisions are leading towards any sort of positive outcome. Any addition of an untested design element in the creation of each of your games immediately throws everything into obscurity… There’s nothing discernible shown to you from one attempt to the next that lets you know if you are making the right decision in any regard - which, considering information is key to success, is pretty rubbish.

I suppose that’s how it works to an extent in the real world, but of course, that doesn’t really make it into a good mechanic to use here. It IS possible to learn what works and what doesn’t after the fact, but this feels a little pointless and hollow when you’ll potentially be haemorrhaging money by the time you learn your mistake. It’s also annoying when you take the time to read more on how the game works, and learn that there actually is a bunch of complicated and clever algorithms working away under the surface to determine your level of success. It’d be fun if these were presented to you, for you to then try and pick apart and make work to your advantage, but they’re all hidden away never to be seen.

In a sense, this makes everything feel too simple for its own good. A situation rapidly occurs where there’s nothing in the game with any real depth for you to sink your teeth into; Even when you hit the endgame and start bigger projects such as developing your own consoles and research, I found the strategy for this doesn’t really evolve beyond ‘pump money into it’. In fact, that’s an approach that pretty much works across the board – last game didn’t make massive profits? Pump cash into a killer title next time. Need better staff? Pump more cash into your recruitment process and training.

This might all sound overtly cynical, but I don’t really mean it to be that way; in many ways you could see this basic nature as a blessing, rather than a curse. It’s a break away from the endless complexion and confusion that can stem from playing other simulation games – a no frills, easy way to whittle away time. As long as you go into it accepting that, or at least take my approach and enjoy it for what it is, it’s not really an issue – more just something you need to be aware of.

I also haven’t got around to highlighting Game Dev Tycoon's main strength yet - it's a master of non-stop, instant gratification. Start development, and bubbles showing your progress fly all over the screen at a relentless rate; all adding to a grand total highlighting your game’s quality that just keeps shooting up and up as you with each new title. Publish your game, and you’re immediately met with review scores, which (with luck) will shower you with praise that makes you feel warm and fuzzy inside. Immediately after THAT, large chunks of cash from sales roll into your account, and by the time that starts to wane you’ve already started the whole cycle again. Nothing takes long to complete in the slightest, and you’re always moving. Think of it as the simulation genre’s version of fast food – you know there’s more complex and fulfilling meals out there, but sometimes you just want an instant hit of pure satisfaction.

The developer’s love for games in general shines through as well. There’s a nice little (and hilariously copyright avoiding) trip through video game history that - while slightly biased towards certain formats at points - will raise a smile, and there’s a number of similarly themed easter eggs to be spotted both around your development office and elsewhere. I also feel the developer’s comments about piracy, and their approach to preventing it (which, hilariously, sees games made in pirated versions being pirated themselves) are worth noting; again showing a fondness for games in general that should be encouraged in a time where a lot of things feel like soulless attempts to suck as much money out of us as possible.

The key thing to remember with Game Dev Tycoon, then, is to know exactly what you’re getting. This isn’t a game of precise micromanagement and intricate challenges, and if you’re looking for that you’ll be best off going elsewhere. This is a piece of well executed and light-hearted fun, and there isn’t anything wrong with that at all.

If you want to see the end of this sadly reduced series, just get the game.

So, welcome to Naval "no" Action.
This game started out great, beautiful world and ship models.
Then the developers slowly but surely started to push the players towards PVP, by making game-changing decisions on the gameplay level.
Currently, there's an issue with people's ships acting very strange against a few select players, yet the developers continue to hold their stance that their game cannot be hacked.
Well, NEWSFLASH, It's the devs that are using their developer tools to hack their own game.
If you are found in battle against them, prepare yourself that your sails will start to move on their own, and that your crew will brace at the most unconventient times, i.e while you're being boarded, leaving you defenseless.
They got every skillbook and upgrade that's available in the game, in such high quantities that it boggles the mind, and yet they find it necessary to manipulate your ship with fake input so they're being assured a win.
The game in it's current form is rife with:
Gankers
Griefers
Game-Mechanics that force you to do PVP, even if you don't want to (you need PVP currency to be able to build the 1st rate ships)
Basically, if you leave the safezones around the capital, you're setting yourself up to be ganked by 4+ players, of which 1 then still needs to control your ship using dev tools so you can't offer resistance.
Conclusion: The devs are slowly but surely destroying their own game, aiming to get the population so low that Steam won't object too much when they want to pull the plug on the servers. (apparently, the devs find the current cost for the servers too expensive, something that killing the game would surely fix).
TLDR: Don't buy it now, it the game is still alive in 6 months (doubtful), check reviews again to see if any improvement was achieved.

Okay, this game got me by surprise. I got it expecting some primitive city builder and what I got was a very interesting and addictive puzzle game. Basically you use 4 giants, that are aspects of Mother Earth to create a living space for human settlers. These things you create combine and transform as you create other things beside them, giving you access to bigger and better resources, thus reaching higher and higher prosperity (essentially, highscore).
The game also comes with these flavours: A comprehensive tutorial, a 30 minute game, 60 minute game, 120 minute game, complete sandbox game and built-in cheats to make your life easier AND harder, but disabling achievements.
About achievements: in this game, they matter! The more achievements you unlock the better stuff you can place and transmute, you actually HAVE to hunt achievements to reach better tier stuff to place to reach the higher tier resources.
It's a VERY fun little game that often leads me thinking where the past 2 hours went, it's incredibly addicting and YOU decide the pacing and path of each game.
Recommended at full price, it's a gem.

This isn't Gauntlet.
This is a modern version of SmashTV, pretending to be Gauntlet.
This is perfectly fine, if you like SmashTV... which I do.
The path you take through the game is fairly linear. As you go through the game, you will constantly find yourself in self-sealing mini-arena rooms that suddenly spawn monster generators, spamming you with low-level mobs from multiple sides that can be taken out in 1 or 2 hits, and throwing a few medium or high-powered threats in with the swarms of cannon-fodder attackers. The rooms will remain locked tight until all the mobs and generators are destroyed, and only then can you proceed. In between clearing the rooms, you'll pick up treasure, food, and potions which fuel your purchased relic power-ups. The rooms, in any of the three worlds, will all look and feel very similar to each other with little variations. The pattern of kiting around the enemies, using speed to lead them into manageable groupings, and then taking them out when you have the tactical advantage will remain constant throughout the whole game.
Even the cheesy, smarmy dialog between your character and the dungeon controller is similar to SmashTV.
And, its fun... its actually a LOT of fun...
... but its not Gauntlet.
Classic Gauntlet, at its core, has just one simple game mechanic: Control the pacing.
From the second you pressed start, your life force was a timer. Enemies reduced your time. Death drained your time. Traps stole some time and stunned you in place for a few precious seconds. The mazes, shifting walls, and teleporters all disoriented and frustratingly led you down the wrong paths, eating up time. The destrucible walls forced you to spend time to get through them. Hidden objects in plain-looking walls made you trade time for their advantages. Doors that led to only treasure made you spend your time in looting. Being "It" drew the monsters to you, devouring time. Special potions and abilities either assisted or made things more difficult, costing you those few seconds to decide if they were worth the time. Food replenished just a little time.
Every new dungeon level had all of the monster generators in place at the start, pumping out mobs every second, and you had to manipulate the swarms by shooting, hand-to-hand battling, sniping through corners, absorbing the damage, or evading past them if it was advantageous... all to get to the exit with as much time as possible left in your life-force, and then do it again, and again, and again until the game was over in a pile of bones and keys.
... and this new game has absolutely NONE of that in it. There is no sense of urgency, and very little to push your pace faster than you care to go.
Your life bar never drains on its own. You can take 2-5 hits before dying. Food will fill the life bar toward its maximum, but no further.
You can kite and circle your foes for as long as you want, in fact its to your advantage to do so as killing multiple mobs in continual succession gives you a bonus to your Kill-Streak, which helps to build up points toward Skull-Tokens, your Continues.
Exploring is somewhat pointless... there are no secret walls that aren't visibly marked with cracks and nearby convenient barrels for blasting them open.
There is just the somewhat direct path through the dungeon levels with pre-scripted encounters in arena rooms, with just enough keys to make it through the level you are on, and no random encounters to speak of. Major swarms of enemies can't really wander out of their areas because the generators don't appear until you enter the room and trigger the encounter, so your ability to use choke-points and the dungeon layout is limited, at best.
This game is GREAT and a LOT of fun at what it really is... SmashTV dressed up to look and feel like Gauntlet.
... its just not Gauntlet.
(Incidentally, Devs?... SmashTV dressed up to look like SmashTV with this game engine at its core? I'd TOTALLY buy that for a dollar!!)

A really great indie fighter, inspired mostly by Capcom's vs. series (e.g. Marvel vs. Capcom). What this means is that able to pick multiple characters, and give each character an assist ability that you can call out while playing other characters. This adds a ton of variation to the game, despite its relatively small roster (11 characters as of right now).
The art is pretty unique. At first glance, you might think it's a sexy anime girl fighting game, but really the art style is inspired more by old american cartoons (I think at least), with Peacock (a cigar smoking robot girl who throws 50s cartoon items at people) being a prime example of this. It also animates really well, with Double and her transformations being interesting to watch.
It's also the most balanced fighting game on the market right now, probably mostly because of the way assists work, and the fact that the lead designer is a pretty hardcore fighting game player. The netcode is also very good, which is obviously important in a pc fighting game.
Overall, I'd say it's the best fighting game available on the PC. If you are a fighting game enthusiast, or you are looking to get into the genre, I strongly recommend it.

Greetings Everyone!  Minion Masters is an interesting game, sort of reverse tower defense but still tower defense and a bit of MOBA built in.  Let me start by saying this isn't what I'd call a "Primary Game" this is something you pick up when you have a few free minutes to play something, almost like a smart phone game.
Pick it Up, Drop it Off:  One of the qualities I like about this game is that I can start up for 5 minutes or so and immediately drop off when I am done.  Many games are adopting this and I think it is a good thing for ‘secondary games’ (games I play intermittently).  It also helps that it is a free to play game; although there is a paid version and micro transactions (unlike many reviewers I don’t really have too much of a problem with this).
The Few, The Advanced:  One of my biggest complaints about this game is there doesn’t seem to be a variety of people to play with (against), I found myself going up against people much more skilled, equipped or just in a tier above me and I have to admit, this killed the enjoyment for me.  Perhaps if I had started playing earlier this wouldn’t be much of a problem but then it would be someone’s problem and also creates and environment that does not encourage new players.
Forced to Joke:  The humor is a bit puny, where it makes fun of the genre it represents but I feel this fits for the game as otherwise I’d feel that the game is incomplete, the game could really use some additional content though (and lines) as I end up hearing all the one liners and they do tend to teeter off as you play.
Overall, it’s a fun game.  And what it really needs is a larger player base and probably some more balance with some mechanics.  I’d really like to see more to do than just head to head and draft (as well as the challenge enemies AI).  I definitely don’t think that this is a game you dedicate any real time to however; you jump in play a game or two while waiting for friends to log in to something else.  My recommendation?  It’s free, give it a chance and see if you like it!

Ori and the Blind Forest is an action platformer or "metroidvania" game. I'm not very fond of platformers but because of how beautiful the screenshots were, I decided to bite the bullet. My initial thoughts were to blaze through this "just another indie 2D side-scroller" and mainly focus on looking at pretty things on the screen. I'm happy to say that was not the case.
The game surpassed my expectations and was able to excel at everything that makes a game good. It is incredibly rare nowadays for a game that can make me want to keep going and complete it. One thing the game does really well is its rewarding gameplay, there is a great sense of satisfaction from making a difficult jump, solving puzzles and figuring out new mechanics. The game is challenging, but not too difficult as I was still able to complete the game despite not being very good at platformers. (It probably took longer than average at certain portions.) Movement is very smooth and well done, it makes traversing the map very enjoyable. There is a bit of backtracking needed to complete optional requirements which I initially thought would be a chore, but you gain new abilities and certain changes to the map make it so fast and natural to move across the map. Overall, the gameplay experience was just really fun.
In terms of visuals, you can see it for yourself, it is absolutely gorgeous. The world is vibrant and full of life, different areas mesh up very nicely while being unique. There is a lot attention to detail and no assets are used more than once. Sound design and music is also top-notch. Gareth Coker has managed to a craft a beautiful and emotional score that matches up to different areas and sequences in the game, from soothing during peaceful times to intense when escaping death. The story was not hugely impactful for me but it is something very lovely that fits the game.
I am not a fan of platformers but the developers at Moon Studios have created one that is so accessible and welcoming for me. Ori and the Blind Forest is incredible and will be one of the best games have I played.

Ori and the Blind Forest is by far the best platformer I've ever played.
The art style is gorgeous and original. The graphics were highly detailed with stunning colors. It was amazing just to observe the environment of the game as I progressed through the game. I could really tell the considerable amount of effort put into the incredible visuals and animation.
As for gameplay, it is simplistic yet extremely fun. I love the level up system as it offers you choice depending on your personal playstyle. There are numerous abilities to learn as you progress through the game, and its a hell lot of fun to use them in battles, getaways, etc...
I don't usually pay too close attention to the music of a video game, but the soundtrack in this game is definitely one of the best I've ever heard. I loved that each world has its own unique music tracks that reallly do set the mood & atmosphere. The pieces are well written and applied effectively into gameplay.
The storyline was a fantastic component of the game. It is a heavily emotional plot that takes the player on a feels train all throughout the game, also including many unexpected twists and turns.
My only compliant is the fact that some areas are unavailable after you play through them. By this, I mean that you cannot come back to collect items in order to finish the area 100% and unlock achievements.
If you're looking for a platformer game, Ori and the Blind Forest is well worth your money.

To the moon is a story driven indie game developed by
. It is about two scientists who work for a company that goes into a dying persons mind to fufill their last wish by changing their memories . The main thing that sets this game apart from other games is the story. The story is the whole point of the game. It is full of twists and turns and will leave you guessing as you progress through it. It is a very emotional story as I mentioned and it is very original. I dont think iv seen anything like it. After finishing I felt an emty space in my heart and it will for you too. The charecters are very unique and the two main ones that you play as have alot of funny dialogue that made me chuckle. Also I felt like each charecter had their own personalitys which I learnt along the story and it made them all feel individual and unique.

Another thing with gameplay is at a part near the end of the game where they tried to spice it up by making it some sort of platformer/shooter in which you run down a corridor shooting plants. This part was completely broken and everytime I died on it I felt as though it was the games falt because IT WAS.
This game feautures one of the most amazing soundtracks in history. I felt as though without that soundtrack the game wouldnt feel the same. It suits the game and it makes the world feel alive.
