is a truly beautiful game. It's very essence screams with emotion and you find yourself screaming with it. This game is the kind of game you sit down expecting to try for half an hour at 11:00 at night and find yourself still playing sometime the next morning. It's story proves engaging and litterally enthralls you as you become the game's minion. Entrusting you with simple tasks,
requires one to search in reverse chronological order small memories of a dying man in an attempt to convince a younger reflection of himself to follow a certain path in life, motivating him to fulfill his own death wish. As should be plain as daylight, untrained professionals such as us are provided with every opprotunity by Freebird Games to come in conact, learn about, and fall in love with the characters as we travel backwards through a man's most intimate and poignant moments of living. You spend hours caught up in this man's life, almost understanding him as well as he does himself, and that's where you find you've actually spent hours getting caught up in a magnificent and chancy trap: You slowly realize it as the story progresses, I will not reaveal it here, but you do inwardly question this dying man as you roam his thoughts. It even talks about a topic that is not quite well addressed in media and especially in games, and that is commendable in and of itself. Mental illnesses require the attention of close loved ones. This game explores the "whens" and "wheres" of unconditional love and just how significant it is in the lives of others.
The entire time you are investing in a one-way friendship with this man, you are accompanied by a moving, extremely well crafted soundtrack he soundtrack is so fantastic it makes one wish they could either play, pick up again, or practice these songs on the piano. A mix between simplicity and complexity that complements the story line and the artstyle; everything comes together so thoroughly. If one were looking only for music, this game shines as brightly as any lighthouse.
Now, in a sea of drama, the pair of scientists one guides through the memories provide comedic relief and this is where I could see where we lost a portion of the (at the time of writing) 440 out of 16010 people who did not recomend this game and that number could have been cut if there had been the following warning: the characters you play will bicker like siblings and they are present to cut tension. If they were not there, the story would be too heavy to handle. I enjoyed their presence and I laughed out loud a number of times as they allowed the developers over at Freebird to show their humor in a creative way. Actually, I find them reminiscent of certain characters Shakespeare would include in his works (i.e. the Porter in Macbeth) in order to plant some kind of restraint in an otherwise constant flow of deep and taxing storytelling. Please do not let yourself be unwilling to play this game because of them.
My only personal complaint are the controls. I will say that this game is a point and click interactive story that one should use the arrow keys and enter/space bar for. I found the point and click clunky and not always accurate. I lost nothing in using the arrow keys, though, so it does work. The end of my complaints. "Use the arrow keys and I thought they could have cleaned up the programming for the puzzles. Otherwise, job well done. Fantastic story. Fantatstic sound track. Interesting art. 15571/16011 would play again."

Abbey Games is an independent games studio, formed by four computer science students back in 2011. This is also the same year where the concept of REUS came to life. However, their first creation was not REUS but it was the prize-winning Tinytanic. Early 2013 REUS finally landed in our hands and it was the first debut game from Abbey Games that truly left the world in awe. A fun fact that not many know about is that REUS is Dutch for giant and is actually pronounced quite differently than how you would say it out loud.
Imagine yourself as a god, in control of four powerful creatures that can shape the planet to your will. No wait, you don’t have to imagine it anymore. You
a god or a goddess in REUS and you have four mighty giants at your disposal. Each giant has the ability to create nature in its finest: forests, swamps, deserts and oceans. You determine how to shape the perfect world for monads to life in, providing them with the necessary resources such as plants, animal life and minerals in order for them to survive. However, humans are unpredictable and while you do your best to give into their desires, greed may become a possible threat to your once idyllic planet. As the master of these four giants, it is up to you how you react on these threats by adding animal life with danger or minerals that provide awe and much more. You are the creator but you can also be the destructor.
Much like any game, the tutorial is essential if you’ve never played a god game in your life. You start by controlling one giant, then another one and so on. You will also be introduced to giving into the will of mankind that roams your planet and the threats that will arise if greed takes the upper hand.
The rest of the game play is pretty much the same. You start with a planet which you need to shape by creating oceans, forests, swamps and deserts accompanied with mountains. Then you need to decide if you’d rather place plants or animal life, or even minerals for the nomads to settle down. As a god, you need to help them by providing the resources they need in order for them to build the desired projects such as a school, a granary and even a shrine or a temple. You will unlock even more projects, fauna and flora by helping the humans develop differently. Thanks to the complex system of upgrades and synergies, the game provides you with an endless amount of play time and play styles. There are 123 achievements to be unlocked and I would advise you not to focus on these as much since the randomization of the humans needs can slow you down. I tried to hunt these achievements down for three Era’s and then just started playing more strategically, suddenly unlocking five achievements unintended. However, don’t push these achievements to the side completely as you can only level up by completing an X-amount of achievements. By leveling up you will have access to even more projects, plants, animals and resources leaving you completely addicted to the game.
You can say a lot of things about REUS, yet at the same time there isn’t much to say about the game since it completely blows you away. It’s logical and simple but it’s still capable of amazing you in every aspect. A must have for every casual gamer and even every hardcore gamer who wants to slow down every once in a while.
Scoring: 9/10

I played this game for about a year and a half and had a great time in the process. While I did thoughouly enjoy the game, there were, however some draw backs.
THUMBS UP!:
I became (probably quite unhealthily) addicted to this game. The number of elements it brings in to play just hooked me. (mostly the diplomacy and being able to control territory) However, the thing I liked most about Stronghold Kingdoms was the people I played with. I made some good friends while I played and also some truly great memories. It was mostly when a large amount of those friends quit playing that I quit playing as well.
Thumbs down . . . sort of:
(I had to put "sort of" in there because after I wrote it I realized there were some positive things . . . sort of)
This game is just boring to play alone (As I said, I quit when most of my other friends quit)
CARDS: Yes this is essentially a pay to win type of game. However, I found alot of enjoyment without spending much money (only about $15 every couple months) There are those people that spend redicuous amounts of money (one I knew of spent $200 a week), but there are plenty of people that spend a low amount of money like I did, or no money at all, however they don't do as well as the heavy spenders. Just know that those that spend little to no money can still play an import part in a faction and house through sending resources, voting in parishes, counties etc, holding villages, and some fighting.
FAITH POINTS: While I was playing, wars seemed to be decided by who had the most faith points. Here is how it worked: both sides sit under interdiction (protection from attacks) untill one begins to run low on faith points. Then the other begins to get the upper hand because they can protect themselves while the other cannot.
A sideways thumb?
ACTIVITY: The more you play this game the better you will do. This is another thing that got me addicted. There is always something to do in this game. If you are waiting for an army to arrive at it's target, that means there is plenty of time to scout resource stashes and sell stuff. However, this is also another reason that I quit the game. (It's hard to keep track of everything that is going on in game when you are working 77 hours a week, let alone have time to play it at all)
Would I return to Stronghold Kingdoms?
I don't know to be honest. I have tried a few times and had fun for a day or two, but then got bored and quit again. Not playing with the same people I used to just doesn't feel the same. However I do check in on the updates once in a while to see what is going on with the game. If faith points or monking abilities were limited I would definitely consider it. however, if a world was created that does not allow the use of cards I would go back in a heartbeat. Either way, if I ever do go back I will not be spending any more money on this game.

So i have beat this on console and bought it on sale to play some of the co-op with my friend when it was 75% off. The co-op is fun but virtually any game that isn’t flat awful or broken is pretty fun with friends. There are two characters with different game play, the series original Point Man and Paxton Fettel. Here are the pros and cons of the PC version.
Pros
- Paxton Fettel is really fun to play as with unique and fun interesting paranormal abilities like possession.
- Has a Co-op campaign
- A nice achievement and upgrade system
- You have a nice set of customizable controls with secondary bindings for all functions
- Nice sound options with multiple sliders
Cons
- Simple console like FPS cover based shooting. Press Q then arrows to pop out from cover shoot use bullet time to change cover repeat
- Instead of mildly tactical squad based combat you push through a crowed, fight a hoard, push through crowd again.
- Fairly linear with much less alternative routes then the two predecessors
- The bullet time for point man is essentially useless and just thrown in because it is part of the series

In Reus you control four giants who all have their own unique abilites to affect the planet. The goal of the game is to create prosperous villages. Prosperity is gained by having the giants create animals, plants, and minerals for the villages, which in turn give food, tech, and wealth. Sounds simple, right? Wrong. To maximize prosperity, you need to take into account symbioses and transmutations. Both of these concepts take a while to get the hang of and use efficiently (at least for me). And if a village becomes too prosperous, they become greedy and will attack other villages and even the giants. This creates a whole new facet of gameplay, leading you to put the village in danger, take away resources... or even destroy the village. Each giant can create a different biome, meaning each village you create can evolve differently.
What I find interesting about this game, as an avid achievement hunter, is that achievements (developments) must be obtained to progress in the game. Earning achievements unlocks new game modes, resources, projects, etc. If you aren't a fan of achievements, you may find this annoying. Well, earning these achievements actually acclimates you to the game, and gives you the chance to experiment differently every time you play. I find myself planning each game I play in advance in order to maximize achievement gain.
To those who say the game is boring and repetitive, yer doing it wrong. The ability to have villages develop differently every time you play creates massive replay value. My advice: buy the game. If it's too expensive, wait for a sale. But either way, I suggest you give it a try.

Reus is a surprisingly deep strategy game where you indirectly control the growth of villages through the seeding power of four giants. Playing the game multiple times and achieving certain goals unlocks new plants, animals and minerals, that help your villages flourish. There is something particularly satisfying about testing out different combinations and watching it all come together in the form of huge caches of food, wealth and/or tech. But it also requires balance as being over generous to your world can turn villages greedy, resulting in war with other villages or even the giants themselves.

First impressions:
Reus is a god game. You’re given a planet with four giants to help construct said planet and bring life to it. You hold ultimate control over the fate of this barren landscape.
Sure, the game may not look like much out of the box, but its rather complex and has quite the learning curve to it. The game’s tutorial, although long, should suffice, as it did for me. A session in Reus starts you off with four giants and an empty planet. These giants each have their own unique traits and can each create a biome of some sort. There’s an ocean giant, a rock giant, a forest giant, and a swamp giant. Each creates its own specific biome, as you should be able to tell from their name, the rock giant, however, creates deserts and hills.
Life will eventually bloom on the planet in the form of humans. They’ll settle villages, which, being the god of this world, you’re tasked with tending to. You can even destroy these settlements if you wish, which may have to be done if said village poses a problem to all other villages.
The gameplay in Reus gets more complex as you get further into the game and you’re slowly allowed more playtime based on achievements. Once certain achievements are unlocked, you’ll be able to spend more time in a single world than before.
Reus is a a lot of fun, if you can last through the learning curve. The graphics are very simplistic, yet they fit the game well. The gameplay appears simple and fun, but is actually quite complex. Recommended!

Blackwell Convergence is the third game in Blackwell series and it continues at the same pace, still being adventure point-n-click. Another solid title of ghost-helping, albeit with removed Notebook combination feature that was making it more unique.
The game still runs on quite old adventure engine, even if it's updated. It still means that you may encounter small glitches, though... I don't remember any, unlike Blackwell Legacy. The engine still has this anti-aliasing applied to scaled sprites, ruining pixel-art somewhat, but scaling is rarely used in this part. Pressing Shift+Tab, commonly used for Steam Overlay, will make the game to instaskip all the dialogues, you can fix it by just pressing Tab. No real support for widescreen, but at least image isn't stretched.
The game has quite a modern game design to it, as you can't die or get stuck in a dead end because you didn't pick some item hour ago. The game keeps ability to switch between Rosa and Joey (sidekick ghost who can only blow air). Ability to combine clues in notebook is gone completely this time around, which is shame, as it was unique part of it. Notebook is still there though. But it added investigative feature where you can search Internet (and mail), which means that you get to type things that you may figured out, great!
Pixel-art and animations are better than in Legacy, this time even backgrounds look top-notch. Animation for character portrait is missing though. The setting is taking on more of rainy and yellow color this time around and it keeps a bit of jazzy feel in music of Unbound but more modern, relaxing. Though, it feels more forgettable. I still think that soundtrack in Legacy was superior.
And once again the game will start with quite a motion, this time with included short intro case, so you will have easier time starting playing than in Legacy. Then you are off to mostly wandering and chasing a mystery, maybe even saving some ghosts, getting your villian along the way, and a familiar one at that. The scope of a game feels larger and you will even get to explore moer unique locations and character. It does have one loose end that never got properly explained: why certain ghost babbles like another character sometimes. Yea, it's hinted how it got there, but never clearly explained. But yes, it's a little bit more on wandering side. The puzzles make sense by now fully and you getto type your clues in computer.
Also, Rosa trying to act more confidient and doing strange jokes is still cute.
And yes, once again it comes with a commentary mode, great! Well, if forget that once again the focus is on voice acting. Also comes with extra voice acting bloober. Nothing as much of extra content as in Unbound.
Another solid adventure, another solid game which has it's own charm. This and Blackwell Unbound are connected by plot, so try to not play Convergence before that one. Though this one felt as weakest entry for some reason, but technically it's a good game.

As of today I am aware there are 4 parts of the Blackwell game. I was a tad sceptic about playing a game that seemed very outdated due to the low res graphics but boy was I wrong! This game rocks, it has very nice voice acting, a good plot and some nice puzzles. You will not be let down if you like a good story and love to see some humor as well in a game.

This game appeals me much more since the latest Patch/Update.  I would describe my play style as "Deliberate" as opposed to "Hectic". I enjoy the slower paced gameplay which is probably due to my advancing years and lack of a really good twitch reflex. Overall the game is seriously lacking in some departments, but it's not a deal breaker for me.
I like the ability to build, farm & create as this gives the player more to do than the original "Harvest, Kill Sentinals & FInd the next Planet". The Idea of discovering new Tech/Items could be a little less Linear, but I'll take it.  I also like the Freighter idea coupled with onboard storage. A degree of customisation always ticks the box for me.
I don't like the flying experience, this seems repetative and boring for planetary travel, I would have prefered Sustained Jetpack Flight for Planetside exploration. The constant need to refuel the launch booster is at best a PITA. On a planet wide scale the same Biome can be pretty boring. The Inventory Management is a Huge Pain, but it can be done without too many tears. The space stations while working seem unfinished somehow, like a work in progress.
Still as I bought this game without prior expectations I don't find myself experiencing the collosal Butt-Hurt that some people have. I occupies my gaming time without too many negatives, I'll call that a win.

There's a good amount of items of which you can equip your character with 2 at a time, that are activateable and will get you out of a pinch but don't break the game. They're not impossible to get as far as grinding is concerned, and just by playing the game and feeling it out will improve your overall character naturally. The spell selection for the Wizard is a cool idea, forcing you to hit keystrokes/buttons in a specific series to conjure 1 of the 9 different spells available (I guess mimicking hand gestures). The game is really an excellent modernization of the Atari version (which I remember the most, only briefly played any of the others), while it captures much of the same mechanics it really is its own game and holds up against any single player or co-op game I've played over recent years.

TL;DR version: Gauntlet  is good.
The new Gauntlet game on steam is delightfully fun. Each character has a very unique play style. The levels are all well designed, with little to no down time in the action. The game flows pretty smoothly, and the inclusion of local multiplayer means you can have your friends over, pop on some usb controllers and have a great time together.
A few friends and I beat the game last night, after about 6-8 hours of play. At $20, that's about what I was expecting for completion time. There is a decent amount of replay with the challenges, and the unlockables.
The story was very minimalistic, not a lot to it. Which can be expected from a title in the Gauntlet series.
The character customization leaves a lot to yearn for. There are different clothing items and weapons you can wear, that are aesthetics only. There are relics that you can equip to compliment your playstyle, but they aren't game breaking on their own.
Graphics are smooth, run well, and have a few options that allow this to work well on older computers. It also has a 'classic' filter you can apply to the game that puts a layer of pixelization over the game. It's a fun throwback, but makes aiming ranged attacks difficult, and can make it hard to differentiate between certain enemies.
All in all I'd rate this game highly mostly for the nostalgia factor. 7.5/10. Best if played with friends.

Scribblenauts Unlimited takes a diffrent approach to the pats two installments, mostly by making itself an 'open world' game, as opposed to a series of puzzles. This is both a virtue and a vice, because it means there's a lot to see and do, but it reduces the puzzle missions to being the occasional treat, with most of the games collectibles - Starities and Starite Shards, if you're unfamiliar with this series - being obtained through quickfire tasks that build towards Starites - think Heart Containers/Pieces in Zelda, and I suppose that makes a tad more sense.
Still, the game is still very enjoyable and plays pretty nicely, but a few of the puzzles feel like they don't have the potential for multiple outcomes - this as something the past two games emphasised with a lot of Starites coming from having to complete previous missions without repeating previously used words.
What it lacks in depth, Unlimited makes up for in diversity of puzzles.
And besides, any game that lets you create a pink Cthulhu wearing a pair of sunglasses is still a win in my book.

Tom Clancy's The Division is an incredible open world third person cover shooter, with some decent RPG mechanics.  The game takes place in a semi-post apocalyptic mid to lower Manhattan through the middle of winter who's scenery is at times both breath taking and deeply distrubing.  As part of a secret organization know as the Strategic Homeland Division, or just the Division, you attempt to restore order to the city and find a cure for the devestating virus that has wiped out more than three quarters of the population.
Much of what has happened before you begin playing is told through found audio logs, video recordings, or a pirate radio DJ, who can be heard from nearly all radios in game.  The voice acting of the audio logs is well done, and the content is often spine chillingly dark.  The present story is told through the main sequence of missions and the commentary of several NPCs that are located in your base of operations, or the BOO.
Most missions in the game can be done solo, but the main missions are designed to be akin to dungeons and are considerably less risky in a group of 2-4 players.  As you level and complete missions, you gain resources to unlock access to your home base, which grants you new abilities and talents.  The abilities you unlock allow you to customize your play style, and create distinct roles when in groups.  As you reach maximum level, you being to collect set and exotic items, which allow you to specialize and customize your play style even further.  These styles range from being a tank while using a ballistic shield to absorb gunfire, a supporting healer, or a damage dealer.  Even then, there is are varied ways in which to dish out the damage, from being a focused sniper that supports your group by debuffing enemies, to a techno-wizard throwing out a turret, and firing stick bombs on enemies.
Most of the main leveling experience in the world is in your own personal space unless you invite players to join you or join their group. Other players can be seen when you enter safe houses and other collective areas, and at the centre of the map is the Dark Zone.  This place functions more like a traditional MMO, in that you will see and interact with other players, and interact you will, as it's also serves as a PVP area.  The Dark Zone can be a frustrating area at times, especially when a roving gang of players runs by, gunning you down from behind, but it can also offer you a very thrilling experience, due to the increased danger level.
The game certainly has it's share of flaws, but Massive entertainment has put a lot of effort into improving the game, and it has already seen masive changes (see what I did there).   Additional free content, and patches dedicated to fixing mechanics and bugs, and balancing gameplay and items have already been brought to the game, with more free content on the way.  This is in addition to the DLC content which brings new ways to play solo, in groups, and in pvp.  Of the DLC content, it is survival that is perhaps the most interesting addition to the game.  Allowing the player to embark on a mission that changes the solo experience into a desperate struggle to survive even just minutes outside of shelter, while scavenging for anything you can just to stave off an infection, the enviroment, and hostile npcs, who become an much greater threat.
While the game is not perfect, it has improved dramatically from it's inception.  It has to date, the most solid shooting mechanics of any game current and past, a satisfying loot grind, and a healthy dose of end game content to keep you busy.  Unfortunately the player base has dwindled, and remains to be it's larges drawback, as finding players to do missions can be tedious at times.

I highly recommend this game if you have an interest in sailing ships. If you don't, then the game probably isn't for you, because the devs are trying to make it realistic. This means that combat is slow - you need to manage the sails to optimize turning and speed, deal with the wind, select ammunition for cannons (and wait for them to reload, which is a long process), etc. As a representation of how the actual combat was, this game is great, but that will also be a turnoff for many players.
The main downside of the game is that it has a steep learning curve, and there are no in-game tutorials. There are plenty of player created youtube videos, but the best way is to join a clan. Clans need members because territories can shift between nations based on the outocmes of port battles, and so clans will be more than happy to help you learn the game if you're going to help them in port battles.
The trading system is not difficult - you'll want to use the trading tool when you pull up your map. But it is time consuming - you'll often have a long sail between ports, and to be frank it often makes sense to just set your course and then leave the game alone for ten or twenty minutes and do something else. It is possible to be attacked by other players while you're sailing, but it is fairly uncommon if you're in the right areas.
Fun game, needs more players and alot of work but has alot of potential.

I have given this game a psoitive review - i payed £7 for it on sale, if i had payed £30 i would be fuming.  I feel that It is well worth £7, it is not worth £30.  There is no monthly subscription which i like.
You will be happy enough sailing around this world in your boat, but there are glaring weaknesses in the game and therefore the asking price cannot be justified.
Graphics - ships great, excellent detail though id say it is no better aesthetically than something i could have bought in 2010, the world looks pretty, i can only be positive about this,  however the towns do all look the same to me.   In port the user interface screens are abysmal, it just looks like a blue spreadsheet.  I was hoping that when you went into a port, you would be able to see it, the different players production sites, ships in the harbour, click on the silos to see what you have stored in there, go into the tavern and communicate with others, a little along the lines of tropico but with other players.  What you have is a functional interface that performs what it needs to but does not please the senses.
Gameplay - Battle - Excellent, though repetitive in PvE, and in limited experince of pvp it looks excellent.  Balance is not something i have had to worry about yet.
Trading - poor mans eve (you will need a spreadsheet) you build a productions site and transport it to where it sells best.  or you can 'craft' it to something better but the economy is undeveloped.  I will use this example, you can grow sugar cane on a sugar plantation which you build, and then you simply 'craft' it to sugar.  No need for a refinery, then it just stores in a warehouse, there is no wastage or rot which means  you just hang on to it until someone coughs up enough to justify you selling.   different towns sell different things and players can trade between themselves.

The commusnity is pretty helpful and wil generally help where possible, though i see some issues with people using alt accounts which is a nuisance in evey game of this type.  the player base is too low for any real competition to take place on the trading aspect.
A lack of tutorial is a problem, as you have to pester other people for simple reasons, eg how do i fire my cannons?  You can't you're not in battle.  The other bit thing about not having a tutorial is that there are somethings that just are not obvious, like why the guns you just spent all your gold on wont be accepted onto your ship.
In summary - an overpriced but fantasic concept, excellent battle game, poor trading game with huge potential, with terrible user interface.  But i have still enjoyed playing so far.

No Man's Sky isn't for everyone, but it's fast becoming my 2nd place GOTY (sorry NMS--nothing will top Overwatch).  Does that mean it will win anyone of consequence's GOTY?  No.  It's not a perfect game.  Heck, it's not even a well-made or even finished game.  Some people might not even call it a game.
But if you are the type of person who has dreamt of walking on exoplanets his whole life and exploring the vastness of space, then this game might fit you like a glove.
I didn't review the game the first chance I was able, because this really isn't a game you can get a sense of after 10 hours, maybe not even after 100 hours.  That isn't to say that you'll see all this new and exciting stuff 100 hours in, but you will feel a definite sense of progression--you little tiny ship that you started with is now a behemoth anchored with your freighter (an addition in the "foundation" update).  Survival is tough at first in, well, Survival mode, but now you know how to survive on the most unwelcoming heat-scorched or frozen worlds.
Many people have compared No Man's Sky to a puddle that stretches for miles (not deep, but very big), and there's a lot of truth in that.  If you don't like the first few hours, this game might not be for you--don't expect it to suddenly get better, though HG has done a LOT in the "foundations" update.  I think it's no conincidence the update is called "foundations", and you can't help but wonder how rushed the devs must have been to release the product in the state it was in, which is unfortunate.
That said, the update to me holds vast promise and potential, and as I currently like the game as stands, I can only be excited for the future.
No multiplayer?  I don't care.  I wouldn't want any, to be honest, the game doesn't need it--what, are you going to mine Emeril together?--but with the foundations update, we are starting to see the building blocks upon which the game will eventually be built.
This ABSOLUTELY should have been an early-alpha and NOT priced at triple AAA.  It's clearly not finished, but I am enjoying it immensely for what is already there, and look forward to what is to come.

Rating: 5 / 10
(Played this game as a single player so this small review has been based upon that.)
The Gauntlet is an action-rpg primarily focused on co-op party, but going in as a solo player is no problem. The game is a dungeon crawler so that's basically the only environment you encounter which becomes very boring after a while. As this is controller friendly, you loot and pick up items just by walking over them, and don't have to worry about an inventory because there isn't any. Upgrades of your equipment you buy at your local shop for the money you collect while grinding through the levels.
There is no story at all, so you don't have to make choices or encounter npc's. The game focuses 100% on combat and when you're solo in the game this feels a bit lonely. The graphics aren't that great, the rendering distance is a bit too far. What I like is that you can dodge missiles and make use of your class specific skills. Crossing a dangerous floor is easier as a ranger than a warrior, just because you are quicker. Sound logical but in ARPG that isn't always the case.
Fighting is clicking the right buttons. Warrior is the easiest, mage the most difficult as you have to remember button sequences which sounds a bit dated to me. Press this, than this and finally this to cast a spell. Very arcade yes, but hardly modern.
As a solo player I can't recommend this because it is too boring and bland. There are lots of better action rpg's in the world to devote your time to. As a party game I can imagine it can be fun to play. For a while that is as the variety seems a little low.
It's a fun game that I love, but it is very short and unless they bring out free or cheap DLC soon I think the pricetag's a bit much. :|

I'm a picky person when it's about games, just like many people do. There's no such thing like "don't judge a book by its cover" for me, I always judge the cover first so I can tell how good it is inside. I got smitten by this game the very first time I saw the trailer here, and to be honest, I was expecting some disappointment when I play the game, but the only disappointment I get is from my own PC. I'm not actually using a low-spec PC. In fact, it's right in between minimum and recommended requirement. But most of the time I got it all just fine, so it's still fine.
It's not that easy to point out what's so bad in this game. Maybe the fact that you can't teleport to some areas is bad, but I think it's a chance for the players to explore more of the game, since the whole game don't have that big of a 'world'. Since CTDs might be caused by my PC's spec, I'll put that aside and not adding it as a con. Regarding to that, though, the game have no options to reduce graphics quality. I know for something that have such beautiful visuals like that, who would want to reduce the quality? Well, I finished the game, but I didn't get the game complete achievement because it crashed somewhere before the credits. I nearly cried twice in this game, one on the prologue, and the (almost)second is on the epilogue. I keep trying to go and see it all myself on my own copy of the game, but in the end I had to look it up on youtube just to see how it ends.
Key mapping is also an issue. Whether you use keyboard and mouse, or just keyboard, all buttons are available. The "controls" option on the menu is just some kind of manual of what button do what, but there's no key mapping. The only thing that will change your buttons is the QWERTY and AZERTY settings. I mean, sure, all the things you need is right there around your move buttons, but it's so cramped that I ended up holding down a button that's not supposed to be hold at a time, like how I keep pressing shift to climb up but I'm actually tapping space at the same time as well. It's a little bit confusing for me sometimes. I kinda forgot to try to use the arrow buttons to move the direction for your bash, and I've been using keyboard+mouse all the time nearly halfway of the game while I was on full keyboard at the beginning. There's no "new game+" here, so I'll just try it again later.
I don't have anything else to say for the pros, since the huge number of people that really love this game have pointed out most of it. I really don't mind replaying this game over and over again, since it's just THAT beautiful to see and the storytelling is very interesting. You walk right alongside the story as you play through, as if you're experiencing it as well. The replay value of the game might be pretty high in my opinion, but it's diminishing when you keep on playing it because of the small world. I'd still play it for a lot more times to get bored of it. Another best feature of this game is its soundtrack. That "Great Soundtrack" tag is not just for show; it really is great. I've never expected that one theme played in at least three different versions would feel so much different as if that they're completely different theme. A discount is good, but I'm more than willing to pay it full for the OST DLC.

Unshackled from original developer Monolith, FEAR 3 was always going to come up against resistance.  Early impressions seem to justify this – the graphics are terrible (with a poorly optimised PC port),  the story is now more preposterous and impenetrable than ever, and there’s a bizarre focus on co-op that sits poorly with its horror themes. It’s hard not to draw comparisons with Dead Space 3, another horror franchise taken in a direction nobody asked for, that became more and more action orientated in an ill-conceived bid to make the franchise more accessible.
Of course, calling FEAR a horror game is stretching it a bit. Even the excellent original was never truly scary – while it was tense and oppressively atmospheric, being armed with a machine gun and having the ability to slow down time was always going to take the edge off things. However, the horror elements were always fairly subtle – a girlish laugh here, a flitting shadow there. FEAR 2 largely abandoned this sadly, though it did contain the amazing elementary school level – probably the most creepy and sinister level in any FEAR game. FEAR 3, even forgetting the co-op elements, has horror elements so obvious and poorly considered that it is borderline parody. Alma, the series’ resident lank haired J-horror ghost (several years too late to the party even back in 2005) seems like she can barely be bothered even when she does deign to appear. There is a section late on where you’re on an escalator, and the Alma is just going in the opposite direction. You maintain eye contact as you pass, and it’s probably the least scary thing ever – you can just imagine her giving a half hearted shrug or honking a comedy horn.
The core of the game, FEAR’s kinetic slo-mo combat, is thankfully still present and correct. The biggest change is that the game has dispensed with the armour and medpack system of previous game. My initial thoughts were ones of revulsion, but honestly it does work – supplies were so plentiful in the first two that you might as well have had fading health anyway, and your ability to pop medkits like skittles during combat made the normal difficulty a cakewalk – FEAR 2 in particular was almost insultingly easy.
FEAR 3 is significantly harder as a result which is a welcome change, but the difficulty is uneven with some pretty horrible spikes later on. It’s obvious that some of the encounters were built with co-op in mind – there does not appear to be any concessions made to a single player. There’s a bigger variety of enemies compared to previous games too, but unfortunately these enemies are pretty one note compared to human opposition. I’m not sure that FEAR, known to for its excellent AI, really benefits from throwing zombies into the mix.
But when you are fighting human opposition, the game sings – the gunplay is heavy and sharp, and the AI seems to have got its edge back after the lightweights of FEAR 2. The slo-mo gauge both empties faster and charges up more slowly, and though this can be improved with a poorly considered CoD style levelling system (why?), unlike previous games this ability is something you use when you need it rather than just clearing whole rooms. This is mainly down to enemies coming in waves, which adds a welcome level of resource management to every fight.
I should probably cover that co-op mode as well. The game is built from the ground up to support this, which is a bizarre decision in a single player horror themed franchise. There’s a competition element that determines the ending of the game, but psychic ghost Paxton Fettle (still sporting his fetching bullet wound in his head) is so much more powerful (and entertaining) that it makes this part of the game a little trivial. Sadly in the single player you are limited to scowling mute beard-on-a stick Pointman until you have finished the game, and I don’t see this being a favourite to revisit.
So then. Is FEAR 3 worthy of your time? Despite this review being something of a laundry list of complaints, it’s testament to the game’s core appeal that the whole package is still an enjoyable enough diversion. It never strays into greatness, but nor is it the abomination that it is often portrayed as. It’s just a shame that this will be how the series ends – a confused grab at the mass market that dilutes the appeal that made FEAR popular in the first place.

F.E.A.R. 3 is an average, and unremarkable, horror first person shooter.  If you have ever played a fps then you'll be familiar will everything that F.E.A.R. 3 has to offer, if you have never played a fps before... well that kind of odd and remarkable, and you probably shouldn't have your first fps experience with F.E.A.R. 3. This isn't to suggest that F.E.A.R. 3 is a bad game, but more to the fact that the game lacks polish.
It has some nice things going for it, the campaign gameplay varies enough to stay fresh, there is co-op (which I didn't get to experience since none of my friends have this game), and the two playable characters feel slightly different from each other.
However, the game has significant things going against it. For starters, it isn't scary, which is a problem, considering that it is a horror fps. Second, the campaign itself drags on for way too long and often feels like it is stretching things out, just to fully use an environment (a la, if we spent months making a haunted department store, then the player is going to see every freaking room in it). And lastly, the game's story is very narrow and straight to the point, so if you haven't played the previous games in the series, you'll not going to understand everything that is going on, and even if you did, you're still not going to understand everything.
If you play this game under ideal conditions (co-op with a good friend that scares easily) then I would image that this game would be great, however, that isn't going to happen for the vast majority of people, so this game is not worth it.

What do you say about a game that already has nearly 10 thousand positive reviews?
When I was young and naive, I had no idea how to PC game. The first game that changed that was Fallout 1, the iso-RPG predecessor to this game. When Fallout 3 was announced, I admit I was skeptical. A first-person shooter? Trying to catch the imagination, care, precision, and solid (yet challenging) gameplay that the first two games had? Impossible!
I was right. In many ways, more care was put into recreating the mythos in 3D. And by 3D, I don't mean the Van Buren demo ;). No, this game's world was rich! Deep! Intricate, yet approachable. They did a lot of research going into this game and it shows through the environment's rough and rugged textures. Buildings that look nuked is a particularly nice touch.
But I'm sure you could have learned all of this from one of those other ten thousand or so positive reviews!

Reus, the Dutch word for giant. What an appropriate name for a game with such scale. At first glance Abbey Games’ Reus may not look like much, a simple god game with a lack of depth and strategy. But with further examination there is more to Reus than meets the eye. If you can get past the slow start of tutorials there is a surprising amount to learn and discover.
In Reus you are the planet and control 4 giants, the Forest Giant who can create the forest biome as well as basic plant life. The Swamp Giant who can create the swamp biome as well as animals and plants. The Ocean Giant who creates the ocean biome allowing the planet’s soil to support forests and swamps and the Rock Giant who creates the desert biome and raises mountains as well as minerals from the earth’s surface. All these giants are used together to create increasingly advanced forms of life as you progress through the game.
Creating life attracts humans; humans will create villages on your planet in the varying environments provided. These villages will start out as simple towns, but can grow into prospering cities when the right resources have been expanded and advanced. Villages will construct projects requiring certain amounts of food, wealth and technology from resources to be completed. Once completed ambassadors will be asked to join your giants, unlocking new abilities and resources. Reus features many different mechanics including a greed system that can lead to wars with other villages and eventually the giants themselves. Reus is best played when the player is left to discover the game by themselves so I won’t spoil anymore and really, there is too much for me to get into detail about everything.
The way you progress through Reus is rather interesting, and for me the most engaging part of the experience. Progression through the game is made by the collection of achievements, the game is on a timer and when you first start you are given 30 minutes to evolve your planet and complete the goals required to earn achievements. Earn enough and longer time periods are granted.  Achievements also unlock greater and more powerful plants, minerals and animal life so it is certainly necessary, and satisfying to collect them all.
Your level of enjoyment in Reus will be determined by the kind of player you are. For me, Reus really engaged me, and immersed me in its world. It had my interest right from the start and that interest continued to grow as I discovered everything the game had to offer. However, I am the kind of player who loves to collect things, loves to level up my character until it reaches maximum rank. If activities such as achievement collecting or world building does not interest you your opinion on Reus may vary, but even so I have to recommend Reus to everyone. Even if it doesn’t seem like the kind of game you would enjoy I strongly suggest that you give Reus a shot. You could end up having a great time of gigantic proportions!

Reus is strategy build up game where the player controls 4 giants that can set up the ground and resources to start a village. You try to maintain the village progress by building projects. The villages can collect science points, food points, and money points. The four giants will help you choose and shape up the resources for each village, while completing a project will grant you more resources and ambassador that will upgraded the giant ability and their fore, the giant ability to improve the resources of the village.
With those rules, you are limited in the amount of time, where after that, the giants sleep and you see your results and total points number (total= prosperity)
Depending on the results, you progress in the game.
The game is very addictive and has a beautiful art style and beautiful layout. The game will suit any fan of strategy and building managements. I spent many hours and I still can find enjoyments in it.
I recommend this game.

I was going to hold off writing this review until I had more time in the game, but I woke up this morning confused as to why everything wasn't labled with their resource value, so I guess you can say it's made an impression.  Theoretically, Reus is very similar to most civ-strategy games. Resource management is the core mechanic, upgrades are vitally important for continued advancement, great works will occupy a lot of your energy, and warfare is an ever-looming danger. What sets Reus apart is that you're not trying to make one civilization the best in the world; instead, you ARE the world, and you're trying to make ALL civilization succeed.
You exert your will via four semi-elemental Giants - titans, really - each with unique but related powers that alter the landscape of your surface. Humans will automatically settle and then try to form a civilization depending on what resources you give them. You then care for your babies, give them what they need, what they want, and watch as they thrive. But be careful not to give them too much, or they'll grow greedy and war-like; at this point, you either sit back and watch them form an empire, or take action and smite their army - or the entire town.
The game's replay value comes largely from its slew of challenges, which largely boil down to "Be this successful with these limitations." The only way to complete these challenges is by repeatedly playing the game until you understand how resources interact with each other - called Symbiosis because, you know, nature - so that you can maximize resource output with minimal combinations. Completing these challenges unlocks further Transmutations (resource upgrades) that then make it possible to complete even more challenges. So yes, the achievements actually mean something, which means that every time you play, you have to play differently. So if the game gets boring, well, that's your problem.

There's a lot of good things about this game. Clearly it's LEGO's version of Minecraft but with a focus more upon the sandbox aspect as opposed to the survival. There's a lot of people that can find enjoyment or interest in the game and I see where it comes from; however there's still a lot left to be desired.
It's easy to get most of the rewards for exploration, and the building system is very clunky at times. I have good faith in the developers behind that in fixing most of the current issues and adding even more content to an already good looking game.
One feature I hope that they add is the ability to create vehicles and interactable objects. At the moment it's just House Building Simulator 2015 with only a small selection of basic bricks. People want to have dogfights in customized planes and duel with their friends in mechsuits, but at the moment its just wishful thinking.
LEGO has tried their hand at Minecraft, but many of the key traits that made Minecraft so appealing for so many people are currently missing. With Minecraft's mixture of survival and sandbox, a wide audience could find their place in the game. With LEGO Worlds, since most of the game is just building, LEGO has thinned out that audience quite a bit. My suggestion is that LEGO fleshes out the sandbox and focus on that independently (Which is, from the looks of it, what they already seem to be doing).
As it is an Early Access title (and a mighty good one at that!) there is a list of promised features which will make the game much more appealing over time. Good luck to the developers at TT Games and Warner Brothers, I believe this game can make it very far.

Blackwell Convergence is the 3rd game in the Blackwell series, and ties together the story from the first two games. If you need a refresher, in the first game Rosa first meets her spirit guide Joey and begins her adventures as a medium. The second game steps back in time to Rosa's Aunt, and her encounters with the villain The Countess. As of the 3rd game, Rosa and Joey have been working together for some time and have become more accustomed to each other. You continue your adventure as a Medium/Detective, trying to help lost souls move on to the other side.
Blackwell Convergence is a point and click adventure like the previous two games in the series. This game does take a bit of a departure from the notebook mechanic used during interrogations in the other games. While it is still present, it is used very sparingly. I would consider this a much more traditional point and click in that aspect. While I enjoyed the notebook feature as it was before, I wouldn't say that its absence took too much away from Blackwell Convergence. I think the main reason is because this is the tightest story of the three thusfar, with every event building on each other until the conclusion. I really enjoyed the story and dialog, and found myself taking my time more than usual just to hear everything.
The voice acting is on par with the second game, which is in what I would consider the good but not great category. Rosa's is much improved from the first game, and Joey's is on the same level it has been. The graphics have seen an improvement from game to game, and are now reminiscent of mid to late 90's 2D adventure games. The character portraits are very well done, but I would like to see a little more detail in the environments.
Overall, I would recommend Blackwell Convergence for fans of point and click adventure games. It has the best story I have seen in the series so far. It is also probably the easiest, with no puzzles that are real head scratchers. The story leaves the door open for more games in the series, and I am looking forward to giving them a try.

This game is hard to review. At the core this is a great game. The gameplay and mechanics are pretty great. It has a great atmosphere and setting that gets you into the moment. However, I feel the game has almost as many draw backs. The player base is as good as dead, averages only 100 players worldwide at any given time. There is limited content with only 1 gamemode that is played (despite other modes being introduced, nobody plays them and they're just a novelty). The quality of the matches themselves I'd say are pretty poor in terms of matchmaking. 99% of the time its a total landslide and uncompetitive. The third in the Blackwell series of point-and-click supernatural adventures, sequel to the Blackwell Legacy, which draws on the experiences of Lauren and Joey in Blackwell Unbound.
Unlike some other adventure games the mysteries are largely solved by gathering clues and combining pieces of information, so it's less puzzle-based and more like detective work, with a methodical process and moments of insight, which grounds the experience - yes, one of the main characters is a ghost, but the problem-solving is built on real-world logic, not magic.
Another thing I love about the series is the way the relationship between the two main characters develops and matures, and the characters get fleshed out as we learn more about them and their backstories. You can also see the art style and character design mature with each installment.

This is the last game in the series I've bought (so far), and while I know there are two more after, Blackwell Convergence is the best entry! It puts the previous ones to shame in many aspects, including music, storyline and art -- especially the art. It's so lovely and expressive! The music is great and definitely affects the mood of the scenes. Heck, I spooked myself accidentally when one piece started playing.
Even the puzzles/cases are more interesting, with every character playing some important part however tiny it is. (Everyone remember the first minor character in Blackwell Legacy and his not relevant part?) Granted, some of the solutions are harder to find within this point and click game. At least, for me they were. I had to look up a walkthrough for one, because it was hard to figure out what next step to take. This might deter certain people if they can't solve it in a fairly rapid manner, but I promise you, you'll be satisfied once you solve the puzzles/cases. I know I did, and that increased my enjoyment of this game.
The mechanics have also improved, and the animation as well. It's all very fluid. Kudos to the creators for being able to dish out a bit more money for the sake of the game, because it helped. A LOT! The voice-acting's improved too -- in the first game (and possibly the second one), you could literally hear mics crashing against the actors' breath or against something else. Here, there are no audio mistakes. It all sounds professionally done.
I'd recommend to anyone interested in this series to just start with this game...BUT that's a bad move, because unfortunately this game also depends on many plot points that have been brought up in the previous two games. (Also easter eggs will feel juicier when you find them!) Part of the joy in this game is seeing all previously established details come to fruition in Blackwell Convergence. The story (if you care about this more) depends on having played the first two games, in my opinion. It makes it a stronger, and more fun, game to play.
If you just want to have fun and possibly seek out the first two after, then play this first. But it's much more satisfying to play them all in order. THAT's the best suggestion I can give you.

The third game in the series, and first one I played (by accident)! So I know you understand the story without playing the first two, however it does mean spoilers and that you might not get all the references. Fun, sometimes hard, point and click puzzle game.

A great follow-up to Blackwell: Unbound, Convergence has slightly altered graphics and what I would describe as smoother, more fluid mechanics and a more polished overall sound design. That said, it's still a 16-bit game engine, but you can see how Dave Gilbert's dev team have been improving and shoring up a very professional product and I can't wait tsee the next one in the series. SIDE NOTE: I'm pretty sure that Crispin (from Wadjet Eye Games' Primordia, also available on Steam) is voiced by Abe Goldfarb, the voice actor who plays Joey in the Blackwell series. *****

Well, well, well. Another shooter has fallen to the subscriptions of substandard Call-of-Duty-esque gaming.
F.E.A.R. 3 is a game in which you (assuming you play as Point Man, the long-time protagonist of the series.) and your dead, cannibal brother, whom you killed, team up to... Uhmmm. Do something? It involves Alma's baby. That's all that's really made apparent.
Firstly, the "dramatic story-line" they boast about on the store page has little relation to the actual game. The story-line was little more than a rail for you to follow from shooty-segment to shooty-segment. In fact, since Point Man is completely mute, they never really elaborate on why exactly he wants Alma's baby. Maybe it's to shoot it? But that contradicts the ending... I dunno.
Secondly, the game is named FEAR. Shouldn't actual fear be it's main and central focus? Well, it's not. In fact, the FEAR franchise has gotten less and less scary as time's gone on. Sure, there'll be the creepy black figure running across a gate every once in a while, but it all falls flat when you perform a psychic link on a random corpse for "Rank Points" and it gets plastered all over your screen in the middle of the supposed horror that you "HAVE RANKED UP TO LEVEL __"
Lastly, however, the co-op is fun. Not exactly difficult, even in the hardest difficulty, a friend of mine was able to pick the game up and immediately demolish everything. But nonetheless, it was fun. However, it continues to take away from the percieved horror of the game. No matter what game it is, cooperative horror doesn't work. When you have a friend singing "Fireball" on the mic, any horror in the scene tends to be lost.
So, if you played the original F.E.A.R. and are looking for a second dose of the thrilling horror that was in the first game, go buy the original Dead Space. If you're looking for a great story plot with lots of depth and heart-wrenching moments, then go buy The Walking Dead Seasons 1 & 2. If you're looking for a mediocre cooperative experience to share with your friends for about 5 hours of game-time, however, then you've come to the right place.
TL;DR: Not scary, not deep in story, not good single player, not difficult, but a nice little 5 hour time-sink for you and a friend.

Other reviews seem to have focused on the community or the development process as the source of issue here, my problem with this game is far more fundemental.  It just isn't a good naval simulator.  Factoring in the direction of the wind, while it raises it above other age of sail games by a mile or two, does not make it a good simulation.  Why am I magically floating thirty feet above the deck, for instance?  Is that where captains typically sat?  Where is that 'cockpit' view that makes flight simulators so compelling, even with all its limitations.  And I understand that a beta (or alpha even) game does not have a tutorial, but the lack of a simple greeting screen explaining the modes of play, which pvp, pve, asap sob is better for what type of gamer, you know, basic which way is up kind of stuff, just adds to the shoddy feel of the game.  Now I am an intermediate to advanced sailor, an avid fan of Maturin, the Surprise, even Hornblower in a pinch, so this game should have hit home with me.  But I was left uninspired, unimpressed, and somehow less excited about the genre as a whole because of this ugly little game.  I am sure that some real passion went into this game, and to the developers I apologise for slamming your work, but none of that passion shows through, I'm sorry, but it doesn't.

I first watched a You-tube Let's Play of this game about a year ago and immediately added it to my Steam Wishlist.
This is a simulator based in the age of sail and will not appeal to everyone. It's based around captaining and sailing ships of the period in and around the Caribbean and it takes time to sail from point A to point B.
Many folks won't have the patience for this kind of immersion.  It reminds me Of the Silent Hunter submarine simulation series in that way. Though this game is beautifully rendered and nowhere near as buggy as those games.
I'm a fan of the Hornblower books and have been for decades, so I'm steeped in the terminology, lore and mythos of this era. I've played Port Royal 3, Sid Meier's Pirates and this one features most of the likeable aspects of those games (minus the music (and the dancing!))
Plus this is an MMO which you can choose to play on a PvE server (if you prefer playing aginst an AI) or a PvP server (if you enjoy the more challenging intelligence of other players) or you can play on both!
On the down side the learning curve is steep and there's no in-game tutorial yet, but there is a wiki and many many you-tube tutorials, plus the game features well designed, easy to use in-game chat facilities and the user community is very helpful.
As soon as Steam announced their 60% off sale I jumped at it and for me its the best gaming investment I've made in a long long time.
On the other hand if you're one of those folks who needs a LOT of hand-holding and a more dumbed down gaming experience this may not be for you.
I'd advise that you check out any of the many You-tube Let's Plays and decide for yourself. Steam's "buy it and try it and refund it if not satisfied" will not be a good strategy here as the limited play time before being unable to refund the game will not be sufficient for you to make any kind of progress in the game.
Downsides:
Currently no in-game soundtrack
After mastering the basic challenges PvE lacks challenges. Steam Achievements MAY change that when the game goes "live"

The short version:  Rock solid fighting game marred only by garbage boss.
This is a fighting game from the prime years of the streetfighter -- proper, deep combo system, no scrub characters, and excellent total feel.  This is the type of fighting game that people who enjoyed them remember.  Best of all, there's even an option to go team-mode with crossover combos if you so desire.  A fighting game with all the modern conveniences but almost none of the modern garbage design with one exception:  the boss.
The boss has an annoying voice, but its biggest offence is the fact that it uses the same lazy design of bosses like Apocalypse:  No knock-down, no stunning, and no grabs.  Bosses like that defeat the purpose of putting in a deep combat system since what you learn on your previous fights is not applicable there.  Why not just dump the garbage boss and just leave it at a clear-the-board option?  Or better yet -- fix it so it's a PROPER boss and not just using some short-cuts.
Still, one garbage character isn't enough to ruin a great fighting game.  Lots of thought has been put into each and every character, they're beautifully animated and really, really weird -- just how I like my fighters (I'm a big Darkstalkers fan).  The only put-off for some people is the sheer amount of fanservice -- for most of the cast, if they're not given huge, bouncing boobs they're wearing next to nothing.
Well worth the tiny price tag.  Also features the best sexy tutorial ever made.

The game lags a bit for me, even when it's the only program open (aside "Steam", of course); I'm not sure why it wants to lag.  Also, DLC content (such as the PRR T-1 "Fleet Of Modernism") that says it is compatible with T:ANE, and other add-ons I have, do
seem to want to install.  The "Download Station" as I remember it used to be called, now the "Content Manager" does
seem to want to recognize or install the DLC.  I do wish that the routes (when in multiplayer) would allow you to run more than only that region’s trains, and that when advertising the base game, they would not include the payware DLC in images of the base game:  you end up thinking that content is part of what you're buying, and to find it's not; and that you have to pay for that content being shown as part of the base game; it's a real let-down.  Other than that, it's a good game; a lot like the older versions: you have fun, you drive the trains, and all that jazz.  You learn to master every locomotive over time and can enjoy your railroading experience.  The multiplayer is a nice addition as well.
My biggest concerns, and my main concerns, are that
A: DLC from earlier versions of the game that say they are compatible with T:ANE, do not seem to be so, B: not all of the content in the images is in the base/default game--videos can use DLC and add-ons, to show how you can expand, but the stills should be only default content,
& C: the game lags on even the lowest settings (Steam and Trainz being the only open programs), whereas a game like "Railworks", and older versions of "Trainz", I am able to run on their highest settings, with multiple programs open at once.
Once these issues are fixed, I am sure this will be a great game for anyone.  I do miss the "Railyard", and "Favorites" menu/options, but those are just nice to have, but not needed.

I must say again though, even through it's faults, I do like the game, and I do plan on keeping it, and using it; heck, if everything gets sorted out with this game someday, I might end up coming back to Trainz, from "Railworks".

Making a colorful splash in the platformer/metroidvania genre is Ori and the Blind Forest, a game worth playing for its gorgeous aesthetic, but otherwise fairly typical with its story and gameplay.
The early moments of Ori generate powerful emotions, and make for a fantastic entry point. The promise of a great story goes unfulfilled, though, as the narrative becomes predictable and somewhat shallow by the end.  Staying strong throughout, however, are the sharp graphics and stirring soundtrack, which form a very impressive backdrop for the gameplay.
While it took a few hours to warm up to the controls, I found the platforming design to be quite good; standing out in particular was “bash” - the ability to attach to enemies or projectiles, then catapult off of them in any direction I wanted. Unfortunately, the difficulty level is too high; numerous unfair deaths and seemingly endless retries were very off-putting. More shortcuts and a few warp points would have been nice as well, to make exploration a bit more flexible. Ori is at its best when it's most like Metroid: wandering around, searching for health and power expansions, and soaking in the sights and sounds.
All told, Ori is a good game that I'm sure to return to some day, primarily to enjoy the amazing graphics. Just be sure to finish all of your exploration before entering the final dungeon: you can't go back, not even after the ending credits.
(Rating: 7.5/10 “Good”)
Note: I played with an Xbox 360 controller for Windows – recommended for platforming games.

Introduction:
This is my first review and I do it for a game i enjoyed over a long period of time, which kept me awake for 20 hours straight and where I still, after so many hours, find new secrets or ways of solving problems.
It's not a perfect game. There's definetely stuff to improve on. Some bugs are really annoying, some characters are boring and some concepts weren't well thought about. But that doesn't hinder me from absolutely loving this game and I would recommend it to anyone who likes turn-based games with a lovely-created world, interesting lore and endless opportunities.
Keep in mind, that this is the enhanced edition, Larian gave it for free to those who bought divinity: original sin before and they did massive improvements. Everything is voice acted. EVERYTHING.
And start with classic mode. It's hard enough if you don't know anything about the game yet.
Character Creation:
We start with the meh part. You start with 2 main characters. You can choose for gender, different hairs, faces and underwear. That's it about appearence.
You can choose from preset builds like ranger and witch but you can also decide your beginning spells and stats. This is unnecessary for someone being new to the game but it's important for another playthrough and higher difficulty.
You can also give your characters their own KI, which makes them decide on their own in some situation, as long as you don't control them.
Overall, the character creation isn't diversive. At least you can change stats and spells.
4/10.
Beginning:
After a more or less interesting cutscene, you start your adventure. You just got the information that there's a murder to solve. So where to go? At start, the game is somewhat linear but that only counts for the first hour. You realize fast, there's really much to do, in many different ways, and it's just the TUTORIAL. And it's not an ordinary tutorial. You don't read "do this, do that", they are giving you hints you gotta look out for.
The fights are pretty hard for beginners but shouldn't keep you too long busy with a bit brainwork.
It's quite sad, that the beginning doesn't show, what the game has to offer. You see a bit but it's so much more. It breaks my heart that people buy this game, play an hour and stop it because it bores them. The beginning is not bad but it doesn't give away enough information about the beauty of this game.
6/10
Gameplay:
It's a Turn-Action Fantasy Top-down game on the P&P-style and it doesn't take itself too seriously.
Most conversations give you the option to decide if you are peaceful or looking for trouble, if you try to help others or look for own profit. You can basically do whatever you want. Almost any npc is killable, even those who give you quests and seem important to begin with. There are many, many different characters with their own identity and history and there are only 2 you can't kill ... find out yourselves :)
So you can play this game by killing anyone, by killing those you don't like, who are annoying or you can be a nice guy and try to keep as many as possible alive. It's up to you.
Obviously, there are many dialogues and even more books to look up. For those of you who prefer skipping dialogues and just play the game, you will have a hard time because you won't know what to do.
The game doesn't give many information, it's important to listen to people around you, to look for small hints, maybe some animals might help you too. I myself got lost a few time but always managed to get back on track on my own.
Finding your way through the game is a riddle itself but Divinity: Original Sin EE offers more riddles, some of them might seem easy but they are getting more interesting the further you get into the game.
Fighting undeads, discussing with people, solving quests, solving puzzles, discovering towns, dungeons, forests, looting, crafting, making decisions, running into traps, designing your characters and comps, is there anything you don't do in divinity?
- 1 for rock, scissor, paper, 9/10
World:
I wanted to begin with the world design because it's ALMOST perfect. Larian Studios managed to create a beautiful, immersive and diversive world with endless discovers. Everything just feels right. It's all, where it belongs. And so damn good looking. And it makes sense. Monsters, treasures, hills, rivers, caves, their placement makes sense. D:OS has one of the best world designs i have witnessed in my 16 years of playing games.
9.5/10
Music:
Look up at world. Also beautiful, perfect matching, giving a great feeling while playing.
9/10 because I'm missing themed music for boss fights.
Classes: You can skill anything you want. Any combination is possible and most of them are viable, even if they sound weird. The rogue skill tree got left behind which is a shame. The skill mage-skilltrees make up for that. It means, if you wanna play the ordinary mage, rouge or warrior game, one of your main characters HAS TO BE A MAGE! You will be flashed by the combinations. That's my advice for you.
8/10
Battle system:
Basically the best turn-based game you can find. Everyone gets his turn based on his initiative. With action points you receive each turn, you can move, cast spells or do other interactions like taking up an item, using an item, pressing a switch or going into sneak mode.
It offers one of the better KI's compared to other games, though they sometimes have weird interactions with surfaces.
There are several buffs and debuffs. Rain affects enemies and your team as much as a campfire lying next to you.
The surface can change based on the skills you or your enemies cast, into water, poison, fire and many more. These surfaces (and clouds) have special interactions if a spell is casted on or near them. Sometimes, there are oil or poison barrels lying around, which can be manipulated. The environment is your playground, use it to your advantage. Cuz you can. But be careful, or you blow yourself up.
The battles are strategic, hard and don't give room for mistakes, some of them take time but it's definetely fun and rewarding. The Boss fights are epic.
Could've improved on KI and there are too many fights, for my taste.
8/10
Companions:
You can find a small amount of companions, it's enough to change around in your party though. Every class is covered, so you don't need to fear about your main characters. Beside some small presets, the companions can be skilled in every possible way. They also have own dialogues, changing throughout the game, they have special interactions whenever you make a decision (if it bothers them) and they have their own quests.
In general, the characters aren't as "deep" as they could've been, it seems like the developers thought about it and they wanted to give all of them a really deep and well designed storyline but it somehow.. not failed, but not worked out either.
I personally only liked one of these companions, but the conversations, the development of the character, the quest, it was so goooddamn fuc.... good. This companion's design made me forgot about the others while playing.
7/10
Storyline:
I think I'm with many other players when it comes to the main story. It's kind of boring and generic. Not the whole story of course. As you can already imagine, there's much content. But the story, what you are up to, your main goal, it's kind of lame ... And the steps you have to take to get their are well thought about and just made me wonder, why your goal has to be so boring?
Every realm has it's own storypart and they are top.
8/10
Sidequests:
Many. Mostly Good. Decision making. Rarely collection or killing mob quests.
I think there are too many. Making them longer and decreasing the amount wouldve been better.
9 / 10
Overall:  9/10. The combination of world design, music themes and battle system is a masterpiece. And everything is voice acted! The game feels alive itself. It's not about playing the game. You have to feel it.

There's a lot of good things about this game. Clearly it's LEGO's version of Minecraft but with a focus more upon the sandbox aspect as opposed to the survival. There's a lot of people that can find enjoyment or interest in the game and I see where it comes from; however there's still a lot left to be desired.
It's easy to get most of the rewards for exploration, and the building system is very clunky at times. I have good faith in the developers behind that in fixing most of the current issues and adding even more content to an already good looking game.
One feature I hope that they add is the ability to create vehicles and interactable objects. At the moment it's just House Building Simulator 2015 with only a small selection of basic bricks. People want to have dogfights in customized planes and duel with their friends in mechsuits, but at the moment its just wishful thinking.
LEGO has tried their hand at Minecraft, but many of the key traits that made Minecraft so appealing for so many people are currently missing. With Minecraft's mixture of survival and sandbox, a wide audience could find their place in the game. With LEGO Worlds, since most of the game is just building, LEGO has thinned out that audience quite a bit. My suggestion is that LEGO fleshes out the sandbox and focus on that independently (Which is, from the looks of it, what they already seem to be doing).
As it is an Early Access title (and a mighty good one at that!) there is a list of promised features which will make the game much more appealing over time. Good luck to the developers at TT Games and Warner Brothers, I believe this game can make it very far.
