Blackwell Convergence is the third instalment in the Blackwell series. Also this is the first title where you may feel that it had an actual budget, though the improvements are seen mainly in the quality of the background graphics.
Following the footsteps of Unbound, but yet again with the first game’s protagonist, we partake in yet another set of ghost stories where the goal is to learn the spirits’ woes and how to convince them to find peace with their deaths and move on to the afterlife.
Gameplay-wise Convergence is starting to veer back to the classic adventure genre, losing the clue-based puzzles and using item interaction instead. I have to admit, in my opinion it hurts the game’s atmosphere and story, even though the creator was getting better and better in writing character stories for the ghost. This part was always the biggest selling point of the Blackwell series – the ghost and the life stories behind them, which were always more complex than anyone would think from a short indie game – and thankfully the game does not disappoint in this regard.
Also by this time the overall plot of the series is really starting to take form, which is really nice to make you feel you are playing a multi-part epic, but sadly hurts the individual cases somewhat as they all need to be tied into something instead of being completely separate from each other.
Overall the game wasn’t as a big step up from the previous title as Unbound, but it is still exciting enough to keep people interested in Blackwell.

Background: Played episodes 1&2 back to back with Convergence. Love Point and Click games.
Impressions: If episodes 1&2 are Monkey Island 1 in visual style Convergence is certainly Monkey Island 2. The characters are still retro but there's more colour and detail to everything. The 'Randall and Hopkirk (Deceased)' formula continues to be a fun basis for an adventure but for the first time it felt like a pixel hunt and some sections are very wordy. Also it's hint heavy which drives the plot onwards but reduces the challenge.
The Good:
* The upgraded visuals and interface over parts 1&2.
* The plot is ideal and grows the overall story well.
* Save interface is massively improved.
* Voice acting is consistent and good throughout.
* Charming twists and ideas early on but runs out of steam later on.
The Bad:
* Feels a lot shorter and easier than the previous games.
* The great notebook mechanic of 1&2 has been cut back.
* Achievements give away plot points, don't read them.
* Some locations only have plot items clickable.
* Doesn't make use of Joey's ghost skills over the previous games.
* Very few items to collect to further the plot.
* Very heavy-handed hints drive the plot but make it too easy.
* Long sections of speech that go nowhere useful.
Recommended for: Fans of the first 2 games, you need to play them to understand the plot and characters in so sections.
Conclusion.
6.5/10. Not the best in the series but far from unenjoyable and worthy of the Blackwell series.

Ugh.  See my FEAR and FEAR2 reviews for necessary context, but the pros are few and far between here:
1) Even better graphics, but lackluster, repetitive and at times confusing level design.
2) Genuinely bad AI.  It also seemed like there was some fairly cheesy enemy spawning going on, and while it was sometimes hard to tell, there is no doubt that the scary-good AI of the original game is gone for good.
3) Gunplay is definitely a serious regression from FEAR and FEAR2.  Everything has a very arcadey feel to it now, which is only compounded by the braindead AI and level layouts.  Plus, you can only carry two weapons and a small number of grenades, and your health now regenerates.  I play games like this INSTEAD of Call of Duty and the like, since they reduce the difficulty and tension pretty drastically for me.  Walked into an ambush and are on the verge of death?  No problem!  Just crouch behind a box for a few seconds, emerge from cover in slow-mo, and faceroll the AI.
4) Achievements. Why are there achievements unlocking in-game, in real time, as I play a story-driven horror FPS?  Immersion is critical in games like this, and fewer things take me out of that more than random unlocks for "X slow-mo kills" or the like popping up on my screen during firefights or scare moments.  Too much of this felt like priming players to jump into MP, rather than to enjoy the SP mode.
5) Not at all scary.  There are definitely some disturbing and interesting revelations, but many of the plot developments are spoon-fed to the player, rather than being discovered and experienced organically.  Even the things that do come about more naturally still felt forced on some level and certainly weren't frightening.
6) The game's final act is a huge disappointment story-wise.  Again, I don't want to spoil it verbatim here, but I did not feel that the Point Man's "good ending"--which I view as the game's intended ending--really made that much sense.  We never really understand the mind-state of Alma, and nor is her resolution or the implications of the child ever really made clear.  Fettel's "bad" ending certainly followed more logically, so perhaps its more apocalyptic and nihilistic tenor is truer to the nature of the series overall.
Sadly, this game largely self-destructed where it counts, leading to a rather unenjoyable and ignoble end to what could and should have been a great series.  Take a pass and go play the original FEAR again instead.

Before you buy this game keep in mind: THIS IS CLASSIC ARCADE STYLE GAUNTLET. THIS IS NOTHING LIKE GAUNTLET DARK LEGACY.
I have mixed feelings about this one. I am having a lot of fun with it playing it with friends, but I feel like they went so far trying to stay true to the Gauntlet formula that it feels downright unfair and frustrating at times. The biggest problem I have is Death, who pops up every other level, and kills you instantly if you get caught. There is no way to kill him, all you can do is run. I almost rage quit because he popped up directly over a turkey leg and killed me right as I ate it. So not only did I lose a life, but the food was wasted as well.
Having said that, the combat is fun and really thrilling. It feels just like playing gauntlet in the arcade. Because you know you have limited lives and no auto health regen, there is a real feeling of failure and loss if you all die which makes it way more tense than a lot of "modern" games where you know "Meh, if i die I just respawn and keep going".
Overall it is a decent enough time to recommend. If you are on the fence, wait till it goes on sale. It's definitely worth 10$, especially if you can find a couple friends to play with.

I've seen a lot of reviews about this game saying it's really only for hardcore fans of the fighting genre. As someone who enjoys  fighters quite a bit but only plays casually, I have a lot of fun with this game. The art is beautiful, the characters are likeable, the gameplay is smooth and gratifying, and the music is catchy.  The game is community-driven and looks to grow as long as fans support it. There are loads of references to fighting game, cartoon, and anime culture through attacks, phrases, and character palettes.
The single player modes are that of your typical fighting game, and there really isn't much to say about them. The AI may destroy a new player, but it can be adjusted to a laughably easy level, and you'll steadily get better at the game until the AI is only a real challenge at the highest difficulty setting. The final boss is frustratingly hard, however, and you may resort to spamming a cheap move to beat it. Like any fighting game, though, the real fun is playing with friends and/or online.
The controls in this game are responsive, moreso than many fighting games I've tried. It plays very much like Marvel vs. Capcom. You have your usual quarter-circles, dragon punches, and a few charge commands. There are no half-circles or other, more complicated commands. There is one 360 input, but it can be fudged; you don't have to be too precise for most attacks to work.
The roster is small, but the game is constantly growing. It comes with free access to the Endless Beta version, which lets players try new characters or new balancing tweaks as they're being developed. At the time of writing, the game has 11 characters, with at least 3 more scheduled for development, and many more that could be coming.
All in all, I would definitely recommend this for fans of the fighting genre, but I also think it's worth a look for a more casual gamer interested in the art.

It turns out that Ori and the Blind Forest is actually a beautifully animated metroidvania with a great soundtrack (it says all that in the description, but I didn't really believe them at first) that I played for 12 hours in a single sitting. The only point at which I did find something to complain about was very late in the game when I realized that since I had missed a powerup that was in a certain part of the game that you can't return to, I was locked out of 100% completion (though it was mostly my fault, since the powerup is in plain sight and I just assumed I had to come back to it later). That's basically it. I don't even like platformers and I still absolutely loved this game.

I'm talking major graphical issues that make the game unplayable. I'm also not alone in this, many people on AMD hardware seem to be affected, but (once again, just like at first launch) the game makers only seem to be willing to cater to what their own development setup is.

Good RPG

Divinity definitely delivered on combat.  It's a sort of mix between tabletop d20 and tactical RPGs like Fire Emblem.  The environment plays a powerful role, being able to, for example, move nearby barrels of oil to your enemies' location and ignite them, then douse the flames and use a lightning spell on the resulting puddle to induce a stunning shock.  In one area, I was able to use a teleport spell to land enemies directly on top of a pool of lava, instantly killing them.  And by far my favorite tactic was to have my Aerothurge swap the positions of my tank and the nearest enemy; this served the dual purpose of getting my slow-moving tank into the fray without having to waste valuable action points, and getting the enemy directly in front of my archer with a powerful cone attack that's a death sentence at point-blank range.
The point is, while I wish there were more abilities in the game, there is a huge amount of room for strategy and creativity with what's available.  All-around fantastic experience.
Unfortunately, that's pretty much where my positive feelings for this game begin and end.  There are some flaws in the combat--specifically the often-misleading turn indicator at the top (it bugs out fairly commonly)--and the occasional pixel hunting for hitboxes, especially if you don't know that you can use arrow keys to move the camera (I don't remember if this was mentioned in the tutorial but I didn't realize it for many hours).
The story is, unfortunately, very juvenile.  I'm fine with humble beginnings turning into a grand adventure--the "hero's journey" format works--but the plot of the game, especially the primary antagonist, feels like something written by a teenager creating his first D&D campaign, and I say that having been a teenager making mods for Neverwinter Nights in high school.  Also, the Councillor's name is "Jake"?
MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD (almost all of this is in the first few hours)
How do so many people find their way to the Sanctuary hub?  When you get there (very, very early) I think you'll agree that it seems like the type of place that would be extremely difficult to reach, to say the least.  And yet everyone from wizards to imps to just average Joes somehow wind up there with no explanation.  And I have to wonder why the void dragon is...a dragon?  There's no logistical reason other than "it sounds cool", which is what I meant when I said "juvenile" in the last paragraph.  Finally, what is Source magic?  Seriously, it's revered and feared as this abominable super-magic, but it's never explained exactly why or what makes it different from any other magic.  You encounter and even fight several Sourcerers, but they never use any magic that you don't also have access to.  Also, for whatever reason the game makes a point to mention several times that Sourcerers and sorcerers are not the same thing, which is inane when the latter are just "wizards".
END SPOILERS
So combat and story aside, how are the other fundamental mechanics of an RPG?  Dialogue, equipment and items, party management, areas, quests, and general mechanics?  Overall, pretty okay.  The dialogue is incredibly straightforward; if you just press 1 repeatedly you'll exhaust every option for most conversations until a question comes up, in which case you can usually have only two ways to answer.  And NPCs seem to forget they've ever talked to you if you reinitiate dialogue with them, for better or worse.  Quests are usually straightforward, although it's pretty easy to get stuck through no fault of your own, or accidentally trigger fail states for side quests just because you did another quest first or made an NPC mad 3 hours ago.  At one point I was given a main story quest as soon as I zoned into the Phantom Forest, telling me I had to choose one of three directions to a nearby area to secure an objective.  After many, many hours of exploring and completing side quests and other main quests, I finally discovered that this quest was referring to an area in a completely different zone!  Situations like this were common, if not quite to that degree.  After Cyseal, I couldn't go 2 hours without encountering a sequence break or getting redundant journal entries/quest information.  And sometimes, the only way I was sure of what I was supposed to do next was to look at enemy levels in areas until I found one that matched mine.
Items were handled mostly well.  The inventory system works fine and has a lovely sort option, and things can get pretty cluttered with crafting materials.  I've never been one for crafting and thought it was quite tedious, but it's not forced on you in any way and you can unlock recipes and just keep the materials for items you specifically want to craft (for me it was skill books).  The loot is leveled and randomized Diablo-style, which I would have liked more if the game were much more combat-heavy.  As it is, you can never count on bosses to drop anything useful, and I took a level 5 ring to the end of the game simply because I never found anything better.  Thankfully, there are some guaranteed pieces you can count on but I won't spoil that.
Finally, party management: works mostly well although tedious at times.  You can tell the game was definitely meant to be played multiplayer, especially with the frustratingly common forced stealth sections and pyramid usage.  The sneaking in this game is clunky to say the least, but thankfully many of the rogue skills allow you to cheese the sections where it's required.  You can have one party member in a dialogue while the others do something else and there's quite a bit of micromanagement available, which the multiplayer would help with a lot.
With all that being said, I've basically been writing my stream of consciousness and this review is turning into a book.  I'll wrap it up:
Divinity's combat feels fantastic, especially when you gain access to more skills and strategies.  It is by far the game's greatest strength, and I wish it had played to that strength a lot more.  In every other aspect, the game falls short relative to its predecessors.  If you're looking for the next Baldur's Gate or Neverwinter Nights, you won't find it here.  But I see a lot of potential in what the developers can do, and if the sequel makes the right improvements it could shape up to be a masterpiece.

This game is both very enjoyable and very VERY infuriating. And since the cons heavily outweigh the pros, this game gets a thumbs down. I'll explain why; two major reasons.
Reason 1; FALSE ADVERTISING. I'm not sure if the "endless creation" refers to character appearance or class creation, but their both WRONG. the character creater is midly in-depth at best, and the class creation? Well, that's a two-parter on the OTHER reason's side, which I'll cover later.
But, the other false advertisment is the "Overcome any foe" garbage. about three hours into the game there's a forced fight- unless you call playing rock-paper-scissors 5 damn times and losing on the fourth a "solution"- wherein you CANNOT kill this particular sourcerer. You can flank him, sneak attack him, pelt him with arrows of all kinds, poison him, stun him, it DOES NOT MATTER, because after he has only a sliver of health left, HE TURNS INVISIBLE AND SUMMONS AN ANTIRE BATTALION TO KILL YOU. And this sand army is nothing to sneeze at either, they do stupid amounts of damage and spam knockdown attacks like crazy. A stupid fight that could EASILY have been avoided if the game JUST LET ME KILL THAT ♥♥♥♥ING SOURCERER.
Reason 2; YOU ARE LEFT DIRECTIONLESS. Considering this is a game about finding the story path to level up on until you can find that OTHER story path that's much harder, this game does a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor job of showing you which way to go. I've found myself stumbling into high-level areas because I just could NOT find the right path. OH yeah, you remeber that bit about the unkillable sourcerer? WEll, he was guarding a plot-important hole in the ground that I needed to throw myself into. Too bad he and all his stupid minions literally made of sand were all THREE LEVELS HIGHER THAN ME.
This of course leads me to the aformentioned class creation issue; you can only learn new skills by reading skill books of a particular skill. Example; I was playing a knight who found a pyrokinetic skillbook. I couldn't learn the skill because I had no points in pyrokinetics. In my several hours playing the game I only found ONE-♥♥♥♥ing ONE- skillbook pertaining to my chosen skill. It all comes down to the demonic RNG gods if whether or not that basket in the corner of the tavern basement's gonna have a skillbook you can use. The problem with this? THE GAME'S HARD AS BALLS ENOUGH AS IT IS WITHOUT GETTING ANY NEW SKILLS. I had to rely on grenades and scrolls my entire quest because all I had were the three starting skills each of my characters had.
There is a third reason, but it goes without saying in a game like this; the %-to-hit chance is a big fat ♥♥♥♥ing liar. When it shows 80%, it actually means 0%.
Aside from everything above the game is solid. Good story, good graphics, your two characters interacting with one another. But I'm just sick of RNG ruling over games like this, spoiling my fun because my chance to hit or sneak or run over this terrain without incurring a penalty was less than 100% and I failed the roll. OTHER people might like pulling out their hairs because they rolled a 1, that's fine, but I. DON'T.

If you like the idea of a procedurally generated, open world version of the already well established games by the Lego/TT Games partnership, this is a must-buy.  While it certainly has similarities with Minecraft in terms of biomes, animals and zombies and skeletons that spawn at night, this is not a Minecraft copycat.  The game very much continues in the style of the Lego game franchise, with its funny minifigure antics, adventurous music score, and of course the 'studs', the lego 'money' which you gain from beating up vegetation. It takes this into an open world with no set goals and an already large and varied environment where you can adventure, customise your character, collect animals and vehicles dotted around the landscape, spending your studs to unlock them for use at will.
If you love physical Lego and want to build your dream house/castle/pixelart in-game, then keep an eye on the development of this game.  It's currently technically possible, but very rough around the edges and causes a lot of frustration at the moment.  It remains to be seen whether this will be improved upon or whether the adventure gameplay will take precedence, but don't discount it completely just yet.
In short, Lego Worlds is a promising and fun game with a concept long overdue for realisation, but not quite there yet.  I, for one, am excited to see where they take it.

Blackwell Convergence represents the third of five parts in the Blackwell series. While maintaining the style and level of quality that defines the Blackwell games, it feels much more refined than the first two instalments. The focus clearly lies on the strong story and further development of the charming characters.
On the other hand the amount of puzzles and their complexity were reduced. In addition the combining clue feature has been removed, which was a nice option to interact with the different dialogue information.
While the first two Blackwell games had a rather short development cycle of two to three months, the third part took almost two years.
Estimated time for 100% completion: +3 hours
Singleplayer achievements: 12
Multiplayer achievements: none

I want to like this game. I think I do like it, but it reeks of "third in a series"--which has its pros and cons.
Pros: Like the characters? They're back!
Cons: If you haven't played either The Blackwell Legacy or Blackwell Unbound, you'll miss a lot of story-heavy references. [Also, SPOILARZ]
Convergence is definitely an improvement upon Legacy, though for some reason the "upgrade" in graphic quality from Unbound is a little jarring. The puzzles are for the most part straight-forward and logical [no Sierra Syndrome going on], and I've really grown to like the Blackwell universe, even though the idea of ghosts distresses me from a philosophical standpoint. A very well-written game, masterfully executed, that has me eager to play the rest in the series.

All in all, the game does a great job in taking you back to an earlier age of gaming where storyline wasn't always paramount nor required. In terms of being a hack and slash game, it also does a great job. However, it falls short in the category for replay value, variety in level design, and overall balance.
Playing solo is do-able with the Valkyrie or Elf (Played through the first four areas, boss included, as the Elf solo on hard), but the Warrior falls far short of where I believe he should or was intended to be. As above, will withhold judgment on the Wizard due to lack of use.
Unless you're playing with friends with some form of communication (VoIP or third-party chat program) don't expect much from PUG groups. As mentioned above, wound up soloing the first boss on hard when a party of 2-4 failed multiple times due to lack of communication.
Character Balance:
Warrior - Should have been the frontline tank and brawling damage-dealer of the game. However, any time I've tried to pick him up and play the game on hard he feels more like a mobile punching bag for the enemy masses than a fearsome warrior. His rush ability is okay at knocking enemies down, but the overall utility is lacking compared to the Elf and Valkyrie. Perhaps it'll start to shine when I unlock the ability to leap attack with it.
OPINION - Increase health pool and damage dealt, should help to relieve some of his early-game issues.
Valkyrie - Similar role as the Warrior, except with more mobility and utility. Makes me feel like I'm playing some medieval female Captain America character with the shield throw. Tons of fun overall. Possibly the second-best character in the game next to the Elf at the moment.
OPINION - Replace her sword with a spear and give her a mid-ranged thrust attack.
Wizard - Withholding judgment, haven't played the character outside the tutorial. Not my style.
OPINION - Withheld
Elf - Quite possibly the most powerful character in the game, easily solo'd the entire first chapter of the game right through the boss on hard. Very mobile, very versatile, very deadly. Legolas from LotR, 'nuff said. The few times I've had issues using the Elf were due to my own mistake on where to roll, where to place his bomb, and generally running into stupid situations. Otherwise makes hard mode easy mode.
OPINION - Bomb damage should be halved against creature spawners and have its cooldown increased by 20-30%. Should also have a slightly longer delay after finishing a roll to balance the fact it can pass through ANY enemy.

F.E.A.R. 3 is a First Person Horror Shooter.
It continues the story line of F.E.A.R. 1 and 2 but here you are again the protagonist from the first game.
The Point Man, one of Almas childs. And actually you can play 2 characters, the other one being Paxton Fettel, the other son of Alma, but only when you have finished the game once. There are 2 different endings. The first, which is probably the "real" ending is the good one of the Point Man and the other one is the Evil end of Paxton Fettel.
The Story itself is easy explained. You have to reach Alma because she is giving birth to her new child.
But this is a hard and stony way especially because you have to escape from a prison first but because both brothers working together it works. Working together more or less. But beside you are hunted by your bad memories of your childhood which feature Harlan Wade, the "father" of Alma. Saying father is this case is an insult because he is a real ****, well you know what I mean. You have to forget your memories of Harlan Wade.
On your way you pass many levels and especially different ones! No level looks the same and this is actually what was really amazing! Never saw so much variety and nice design in the levels. Pretty much the best from all F.E.A.R. games but this is probably the only aspect thats better compared to other games, sadly.
The game implemented a new Health system what I like to call CoD illness. Really annoying and I missed the Medipacks and armor. It wasnt that bad after all but seriously, why did you have to add this feature to a F.E.A.R. game?
There is also a new level system which I like to call CoD level illness. You get XP for getting Kill rewards or collecting things. Never liked it but to be honest its not that bad implemented here. With "ranking" up you also get new Skills or upgrades. While playing this game I noticed that this game is pretty much build up for Multiplayer or Coop. Annoyed me a bit to be honest, I hate games where Singleplayer campaigns doesnt feel like Singleplayer campaigns.
For me this game was a little bit difficult sometimes, I played on Normal difficulty. But this difficulty was more because of the damn bloodscreen. I hate this and it makes the game hectic.
The scare level is a little bit less I have to say but there were still some nice level parts which scared me. Not as many as before though. You are not hunted by Alma in this game anyway. Alma got nearly friendly, I really like how the developers changed Alma. For me she was never that evil anyway, I even liked her. She had just a bad history.
[SPOILER!] (I try to let them out but in this case I have to say it because its a bad thing for me about the game)
But what really made me sad is the fact that Alma dies in the end anyway, why letting the main character die like this? If you play the game you know what I mean. A really stupid and wasted death for Alma. I hope her child can offer us a similar experience in F.E.A.R. 4, if it will be ever released. Cant tell actually. Maybe this was the final game. Also Becket dies in a poor and questionable way... WHY? This didnt even make any sense. Especially how they made Becket. I mean the 1-2 minutes he actually appears in a cutscene. Yeah, the character was silent in F.E.A.R. 2 but here they just made him like a poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ which wants to end his miserable life. Couldnt they make something more interesting like he teamed up with Alma or something? Its his child after all... Bad decision. They could have made the story so much better.
The graphics of the game are ok but nothing special. Similar to F.E.A.R. 2s graphics.
It has to be said that this game was developed by another studio, not Monolith.
Monolith just provided some help. The main developer was Day 1 Studios.
Noticeable concerning the changes but wasnt that bad for a indie sort of developer.
I had time to play the campaign in coop with my girlfriend.
It was actually a little bit more enjoyable in coop, especially playing with Fettel.
First time I played with him and it was a completely different gameplay.
You can actually move into enemies bodies and control them. This is only for a limited time though. But you can extend it with collecting their souls after they die.
When you are not inside of an enemy you can shoot some sort of projectiles from your hand.
You can also grab your enemies from far away. I actually had quite some fun playing in Coop.
In the end there is a comparison of the statistics of both players and who actually wins the playthrough. This characters ending is played then. I personally felt like Fettel was more powerful than the Pointman. Unbalanced maybe, no clue.
This is where the game actually proper shines in my opinion.

Never the less, Singleplayer is just mediocre.

Blackwell Convergence is a point and click adventure game in which you play Rosa, a clairvoyant detective, and her ghostly sidekick.

Obligatory header to the review: I focus on four primary areas whenever I review a game: gameplay, story, graphics, and sound/audio/general things that go into your earholes. Gameplay and Story get a rating scale from 1 to 10, and the AV stuff gets a rating from 1 to 5. My philosophy on this is that there are some instances in which a game may not necessarily have that much in the way of gameplay (take Amnesia for example), but the story/atmosphere/whatever it may be is reason enough to pick it up. Also, take the cumulative score with a grain of salt; it's just a numerical feeling about the game as a whole. That's part of why I do these subscores. Also, keep in mind that I'm not going off of school grade based rankings. A 5/10 denotes what I feel to be an average game. Likewise, 7/10 is a game that I think is pretty cool, and something that gets a 2/10 is near-abomination level. Pinning scores to an even further obfuscated rating scale is kinda senseless, but for the sake of my backloggery, I'll repeat again that 1.0-2.7 is a one-star game, 3.0-4.7 is a two-star game, 5.0-6.7, 7.0-8.7, and 9.0-10 are three, four, and five stars, respectively.
Additional note: This review will be shorter and will be written in respect to the first and second in the series (Blackwell Legacy and Blackwell Unbound), since this is an episodic sort of series.
Gameplay: We're back to Rosangela for this game. Honestly, this is the kind of improvement I was wanting to see. There weren't any "puzzles" in the traditional sense of adventure games, which made me more than happy. Rather, gameplay took more of a backseat approach in this game. The puzzles that were there didn't require any sort of intense abstraction of logic and generally made a great deal of sense. Definitely a great improvement over the previous two in the series. 8/10.
Story: Oh man, things start getting real this game. With the last two games I felt like I could go for a week without playing the next in the series. This one... I dunno. Maybe a few days at most? Also, this is the game that finally got me to 100% go for Blackwell Epiphany, which is apparently the best. Nevertheless, this game really got the pacing of the story right, with plenty of tense, dramatic moments as well as some much needed comic relief. Things finally came together, and it's oh so good. 9/10.
Graphics: Yet another art style change. Looking at the wikipedia page, I suppose this isn't all that surprising, but it's still kind of jarring seeing the art change so much. Apparently the last two games use the same artist (although yet another different artist), so at least for the review for Epiphany I won't have to bring it up again. Nevertheless, I really liked the comic-y style this iteration in the series presents. All of the art is clean and it just looks good. I just wish they would've kept with a consistant artist throughout the series. 4/5
Sound: At least they kept someone for most of the series in this department. Also, the music is enjoyable as ever, with the soundtrack leading a sort of fusion of the last two game's OSTs' styles. Also, much to my joy, the voice recordings didn't have any glaring errors like popping. Voice acting is still good and still believable, which is the best thing you can say about voice acting (at least as far as I can tell). If you make the character sound believable, you've done your job and done it well. 5/5.
Overall scores are 8/9/4/5; cumulative score of 8.7/10. Very excited for Deception and Epiphany.

F.E.A.R. 3 is a game with an identity crisis. The gunplay is fun, the score attack system is actually pretty engaging, and the asymmetrical co-op is interesting, but it's just not very scary.
It tries to be, doing little spooky bits where Alma just shows up, but there's not too much there. Granted, I'm glad they didn't go "Jump Scare!" constantly, but there never was a feeling of dread when I was going around like a walking armory.
The campaign itself is laughably short. Which is sad because, again, the feel of the guns are fantastic. Fettel's mode of body-hopping kind of calls for a run-and-gun style that is pretty enjoyable. I didn't check multiplayer, but I tried the horde mode on my own. It's fun since it boils it down to strictly the gunplay, but it would sorely require a friend or two.
Comparing to the original FEAR, it's kind of strange. Once again, you're not too worried about ghosts since you're armed to the teeth, but the use of a fantastic lighting engine and robust AI makes this game look really dull.
I don't know if I'd recommend this to fans of the original, or newcomers to the franchise. After every praise I think of for this game, it follows, "but it's just not scary." Certainly don't check this out to get spooked. At the very least I would say if you're looking for an interesting Cooperative game you could do far worse. Otherwise, just go play the first FEAR.

Okay let's be honest: the gameplay of 'To the Moon' is quite boring, it's repetitive and often more annoying than entertaining. It's not the typical 'Fighting & Fantasy'-RPG-Maker game but a strictly linear adventure whichsets its focus on the story about an old man and his dying wish. Sure, there are minigames and some 'better' levels, but after the fifth time collecting some memory links to go on to the next level I just thought 'C'mon just skip this, I don't want to do this agai-... great another memory link level'. But I still recommend this game - without any doubts - to everyone who enjoys a good story.
You ask why? It'S true, for me 'To the Moon' is an 'average' game at best, but at the same time it's a fantastic 'movie' with an interesting story backed up by an amazing soundtrack, well-written dialogues, interesting characters and an atmosphere that makes up for many flaws. I really enjoyed the plot and the great dialogues between the characters and you can definitly see how much time the developers used to make every scene create the right emotional situation. And - at least in my case - they succeeded.

DOSEE remembers my tabletop RPG AD&D childhood. The freedom
is unimaginable for a computer RPG. A locked door can be opened with its key, have its lock picked, can be hammered down by a weapon or blasted with a spell. Only the more architectural surroundings are fixed in place, like walls or big furniture. NPC react in a really good way, but unfortunaly still have the same "problem" of any computer RPG: You can sell them dozens of paintings and they will keep buying if they have the gold/items available, even if they wouldn't need them realistically.
The combat is brutally challenging and aside the level of the enemies you don't have many plot roadblocks: You normally can't advance because of level, not because you need to finish X quest. The environmental effects are great in a way it can became overpowered (for either side) and/or change the battle situation quickly.
The story is good, but start slow. The interaction between the 2 Source Hunters is great for developing each character and only fails to be excellent because the in-game bonus of being (for example) rational or vengeful will be used to min-max the gameplay style, with some options being better than the others for yor style of play.
Character creation is quite good and offer plenty of possibilities, but is also a drawback since you can severily gimp your character in a way only restarting will fix. A look of how Pillars of Eternity dealt with stats/abilities could improve this.
If you like a good, tactical turn based game, this game is for you. It is difficult the way it is meant to be and won't hold your hand: You either learn or die trying.

It has several annoyances that both compound with each other and build up over time which ended up killing all desire to play the game.
First off, *all* enemies in this game are rediculously accurate no matter what type of weapon they're using. You will get hit reliably by enemies with handguns from 30+ meters away. You will get sniped by enemies weilding light machine guns. Shotgunners will do the same as handguns. If your toe is sticking out of cover, it will get shot the hell off.
Second, they operate by different rules than the player (more than is necessary): Shotgunners will kill you in just a couple shots from 20 meters away while your own shotguns hit like a BB gun at that same range. Enemies instantly start firing (accuately, as mentioned previously) after popping up from cover without even "getting set" or taking a moment to aim. Unless you're performing a cover-to-cover move, they have absolutely no issues hitting moving targets.
Third, this game makes every enemy, no matter their "previous life" some sort of tactical and weapons handling savant. Now, there's a faction in the game called LNB, which are mercs and I would expect this from, but the game applies this same level of expertise to your regular old Joe Shmoe who is rioting, and also to Cleaners, a faction that wants to burn the virus out and is seemingly composed mostly of union workers. They all coordinate the same way, attack the same way, are crazy accurate with their grenades in the same way, etc. It's lazy design and actually breaks immersion quite a bit.
Fourth, there are special elite enemies that on level will simply tear you apart in just a few hits (doesn't really matter the range) all the while soaking up every bit of damage you can throw at them and barely taking a dent in their armor for your efforts. You can hit them in the head with some of the highest single-shot damage weapons in the game and it MIGHT take off about half of an armor plate (they have 6).
So yeah, avoid this game unless you like getting frustrated at stupid mechanics.

Ori and the Blind Forest is just... wow.
I have been playing a lot of video games in my life. Many times I have said "This is the most beautiful game I've ever seen." Final Fantasy 6. Ico. Far Cry. Crysis. Oblivion. Skyrim. Dishonored. Mass Effect. X3. Elite. Portal. All very, very pretty games in their own right. Some more art than video game.
But Ori? Ori is something else.
From the very beginning, the game is gorgeous. Literally. The "Moon Studios" intro movie is pretty. The menu is beautiful. Everything from then on just gets better.
At any point in the game, you can hit F12 and get a new screenshot. There simply isn't a single screen that isn't breathtaking. And some of these scenes aren't something you'd think could
pretty. Seriously, one of the zones is basically a bunch of dead brush and bristles. It's one of the scrolling screenshots up there. Another is a frozen wasteland. It's up there, too. A third is a dirty swamp. It's up there, too. They're all amazing.
But I can't sell the beauty of the scenes any more. If those words didn't convince you, and the screenshots didn't, nothing will.
The music is great too. That's kind of an understatement. I love video game music. Ori's is great. At times, it is nice, serene. Peaceful. Then the tempo picks up, the game gets dangerous. It gets your blood pumping. Go YouTube "Up the Spirit Caverns Walls," "Down the Moon Grotto," "The Waters Cleansed," "Restoring the Light, Facing the Dark," and "Escaping the Ruins" to get a taste of it.
The art and the music combine into an experience I can safely call the most beautiful game I've ever played. I don't think anything less than another game from Moon Studios can take that title from Ori.
The storyline isn't groundbreaking, however, to elaborate on it would lead to spoilers. Nonetheless, you'll probably find yourself emotionally invested the game by the end if not right at the beginning.
It's good that the world is amazing. It's great that the gameplay is, too.
Well, amazing might seem an overstatement at first, but I think it describes Ori.
First, the save system. I really like how Ori handles it. Instead of predefined save points (okay, those do exist), Ori has an 'Energy' system. Energy is a resource for an attack, but it's mostly used for saving. At any point you want (assuming you aren't near an enemy or on a moving platform), you can hold down E and save the game. You get to define where you want to respawn and what content you're okay with redoing if you die.
But how often will you die? I guess it really depends on how much platforming experience you have coming into Ori. I consider myself pretty good (not amazing, but I've played a few Metroid titles, one Shantae game), and I finished the game for the first time at roughly 300 deaths. The game isn't very grindy, but some segments you will find yourself dying repeatedly. Dying five times to one complicated jump will account for most of your deaths.
The controls are pretty intuitive, although I personally had to learn them three times. The game supports mouse + keyboard, keyboard only, and controller. It isn't some control scheme you set either, you can set your controller down and change to keyboard/mouse on the fly. I personally started the game keyboard only, then changed to controller, and finally, due to how one power works, changed to mouse + keyboard and stayed there. The controls are good in any configuration, but I'd personally recommend mouse + keyboard.
And the controls are certainly responsive. I never really found myself over- or under-jumping a platform because Ori wouldn't land where I wanted him to. There are some segments where Brambles (thorns? spikes? whatever you want to call them) seem to jut out a bit farther than they maybe should, but that's it.
You also don't really die to dumb reasons either. None of that stupid 'jump across a pit only for a rock to fall from the ceiling and crush you' kind of scenario. Ori doesn't torture you like VVVVVV (which I love, don't get me wrong) and IWTBTG does. There is some quick thinking involved in multi-screen jumps and certainly in four specific segments, but on a whole you can see what might kill you before it kills you.
However, there is some randomness (as far as I know) involved during a rock-fall and icicle-fall segment, which I don't like, however they don't last very long, and only the icicle segment forces you to rush.
Ori is a fairly long game, but again, that depends on how good are you at platformers in general. I personally took just under 7 hours to finish the game the first time; folks who don't try to 100% will likely take less time, and even if you are a completionist, you'll shave off hours on the second run anyways. All-in-all, I have to say length is Ori's weakest point, however, given how memorable they made area, I can't fault the developers for following a traditional "Collect 3 ancient artifacts" approach.
Speaking of replayability, I have to say the game is very replayable. The game's talent system is pretty in-depth but not very gamechanging, but different builds can lead to different playstyles.
Speedrunners will of course find the game enjoyable. Enemy AI is predictable and the general lack of random segments make the game very fun to speedrun. There is only one sequence-break I know of, and no out-of-bounds glitches I'm aware of. Nonetheless, the world record is below an hour; compare that to the 3-hour ingame speedrun achievement.
Overall, I have to say Ori is one of the best games I've ever played. If you care naught for the atmosphere and the music, and heavily prioritize difficulty (I mean VVVVVV difficulty), you may want to skip this. However, I think everyone who has even a minor interest in platformers or videogames as art will enjoy Ori and the Blind Forest.

I played this game when it came out of the beta on one of the first worlds, I just recently came back to see how it developed and whether they worked on anything.
On the bright side, it's a fun MMORTS, it's very slow paced and it takes knowledge to be excellt. Teamwork is huge, and you'll find large houses (aka "guilds") battling over terroity, it can get you hooked for a while, but overall I'd not recommend it, for various reasons:
This another bugger. The game gets very repitive very fast. You'll find yourself doing the same thing over and over and over, and it gets very tedius. Place the same buildings, send out traders evertime you login, scout resources, clearing some AIs.
The only variation you really get in this game is when going at war with other factions, it's pretty much the one thing that can really give excitement, and it's one of the strong points and while the mechanics are awefully similar, you still need to think about what you do in a war situation instead of just mindlessly sending attacks. If you play smart in war,  you will survive.
Overall the concept is really nice, but after seeing how little was done with it, it's a bit say, it could have been a much better game.
It's massively pay 2 win. Premium is cheap, and gives quite the advantage, you can do without, but it also means you don't have to babysit 24/7 just so you can get the next research or building.
This would also be bearable, but the real problem here are cards - while there are ingame systems to obtain cards, such as free cards every 12h (but ONLY after you paid TWICE), and some quests or raids on special AI castles that give you a chance at you card packs, people who just spent TONS of money can buy justwhatever they want.
The more people spend and use cards, the more massive their advantage become; if you bother to look at the maginitude of cards, you can see clearly how advantageous is this - 10x the production, 2x stronger defenses each, lots of instant troops, even instantly building castle defenes.
A good example of this how the most recent world 2 europe just started, and people reached rank 14 within an hour with the use of spamming cards, and the avarage player (even with some cards AND premium), can make it to rank 4 or 5 in the same time; the righer ranks take exceptionally longer to achieve, so the first few are easy, and it would usually take a few days to get to 14.
As I said I've been returning to this game. It was fun for a while, but after 3 years it was shocking to see how little was done to the game. What has changed in such a long time period? They added quests which give you a one time bonus, ears which are mostly just restarting a world with some slight modificiations and 2 new AI castle types.
Oh right, and don't forget that they existed even more pay to win cards. That's the most important part, they added tons and tons of even stronger cards, you can only recieve when you *BUY* card packs (or get really lucky when you find a card pack in game), the weaker card can be bought for card points, but the really strong ones only found.
It shows they only care about the p2w and money aspect of the game.
On the other hand, did anything in the gameplay evolve to make it fairer or improve it? Nope, nothing. Actually, the one change they made it made even worse, i.e. like captains (an extremly expensive unit) that now disappears after attacking other players.

Want to memorize tech trees? This slow, arbitrary game might be for you.
Say your Forest Giant creates a fruit plant. Well by default you get blueberries, for no apparent reason. Using powers ("aspects") from your other giants, you can upgrade those to either strawberries (which produce more food if next to blueberries) or apples (which produce more food if next to animals).
The game is built on these sort of relationships between tiles (which surround your planet in a flat circle). There's never much rhyme or reason as to WHY e.g. armadillos produce slightly more food if there's a mineral nearby, or agate produces 10 more wealth if there are adjacent frogs.
After playing a few rounds I get the strong impression that this game can be mastered by making a giant spreadsheet, or better, just visiting the wiki. There doesn't seem to be much skill beyond memorizing the abritrary numbers on the various convoluted tech trees.

Wrapped this one just now. Lovely game and a massive improvement over the two earlier games, the dev said himself that he spend a 2-3 months on previous games, and this one took almost two year.
You still need to play the earlier games first, else the story won't make any sense, and this is very much a story driven game. Puzzles are almost non-existent, with most of game time being spent either on conversation or cutscenes.
Artwork is still 320x240, but it looks simply stunning, very much on par with late Sierra games (too realistic to compare with LucasArts output). Music is great as well, main motif gets arranged into various, mostly jazzy tunes. Only low point was the ending nu-rock song, which completely didn't fit the rest of the game.
Commentary mode has ~30 minutes of content, but I must say, I'd prefer if it wasn't as much focused on voice acting - roughly half of the entries deal with stories about that.

The third installment of the Blackwell series and better than ever!
The length of this game is a bit longer than Unbound, so there's more content to enjoy without being overwhelmed.
I really enjoy Rosa's character development; she's come out of her shell some and she's bolder, braver and sassier.
And I still enjoy her exchanges with Joey; I can tell they've grown closer since he's now comfortable with taking more personal jabs at Rosa. Even better, the ability to control Joey carries over into this episode.
And, thankfully, this episode allows you to make more than just one save file and you can overwrite them!
It's nice to be able to replay the game over and over and still have the one file that holds the unlocked bonus features.
I do have a couple of complaints but they're rather minor...
For one thing, this is the third episode of the series and not very much has been revealed about Joey.
I don't know how he died, why he became a spirit guide or if he's even related to the Blackwells.
So, I hope something in the fourth (or upcoming fifth) entry will reveal something about his past.
I feel that a couple of deaths in this episode are left unresolved but it doesn't ruin the story or the experience.
Once again, the bonus gallery can only be accessed once you've beaten the game and are given the code to unlock it.
Only this time, you will have to start a new game and go through the prologue portion before you can get home to enter the code on Rosa's computer - and then save your game if you want infinite access to it.
So, this function isn't any better than the last two games.
Overall, I really enjoyed this episode and I'm just about to start playing the fourth!
Also, I hope that in the future there will be a special bundle that will include the series' soundtracks; it's great music and I would like the option of downloading the files and moving them onto my mp3. Maybe one day...

I've only played the player vs environment server of this game. So if you're looking for a player vs player review I'd ask you look somewhere else.

Introduction :
This is a game who is very good at showing the age of the fighting sail in all its glories. Set in the 18th century and in the Napoleonic era. This game features the many naval powers in the Caribbeans.
It has a stunning mechanic in terms of Combat and also a great sense of realism.
Pros:
If you've ever watched Master and Commander the Far Side of the world, and really enjoyed naval history and lore as well as  the combat mechanics of the fighting sail. This would be the game for you.
1. Very realistic naval combat of the fighting sail.
2. No pay to win mentality you have to earn your commission as a naval officer should.
3. Very very good trading system that encourages open world Market trading.
4. High levels of reward for combat actions
5. Gorgeous graphics and scenery in Battle and sometimes out of battle.
6. Wonderful gaming community happy to help junior players.
Cons:
1. Open world sailing takes a very long time
2. Almost no tutorial for players who are starting and must rely on YouTube or other players.
3. Very steep learning curve.
4. Daily one hour server maintenance.
5. Not for casual gamers (which to me is a pro)
Sunmary:
A fantastic game with an excellent combat mechanic, fantastic for history Buffs and those who love the fighting sail era, the lack of microtransactions mean that you have to earn your rank and earn your experience resulting in much better gameplay and much smarter gamers.
Travelling or shall we say sailing takes a serious amount of time that most dislike however for those who enjoy the immersion this would be golden for you.
If I must put a score I would rate this game 8.5 out of 10.
(This is not a game for those casual players who just want to sit back spend about an hour and expect large amount to reward. Having played this game since day 1, I forced to keep myself being quiet about the game unless friends are asking me about it. It's very clear that HG did not deliver the game we all wanted to have and thought we would get after seeing the trailers, presentations etc.
Now, half a year later, we received a big fresh update and I tried as much as possible to mentally restart the game for me. This review is trying to give you a feeling of someone who enjoys video games, exploration and astronomy as the background layer for it.
If you expect competitive gameplay, don't buy it. If you are in for a long, dedicated quest line - don't buy this game.
If you need multiplayer to enjoy a game, please step away. Close this tab and move on.
If you are still here, you probably are a bit like me. I DO enjoy multiplayer, huge quest lines and competitive gameplay, but hell, I don't *need* it to enjoy playing a game.
I expected long evenings in my space ship, freedom of exploring wild and rough planets and a grind-n-craft system to lead me to having a nice ship, base and gear. And this is what no man's sky offers, no more and no less.
The game is far from being perfect and it's still only a good chunk of what we all want this to be, but from my perspective, the game is worth an upvote and will be even more on the future.
Don't let yourself be fooled by earlier votes. If you don't want to to spend your money here, it's perfectly okay.
But if you spend 60$ on a battlefield or doom and play through the campaign in 12 hours to regret your spending, no man's sky offers a better money/time value.

I've been part of stronghold kingdoms since it's early alpha stages, back when there were only a few of us and we all knew each other like neighbors. Therefore I can say that this game is a massive waste of your time.
I see innovation here - a lot of it. I see opportunities to play stronghold like never before, with an MMO idea all taking place on a large map where cooperation and diplomacy are key to victory in the world of thousands of players all with their own individual strongholds they too are building. The game still has all the customization that stronghold offered you as well, placing the walls, towers, gatehouses, moats, spikes, and more all wherever you want to. It also gives you the freedom to train and manually deploy your own troops both defensively in your castle and/or offensively to siege another. In fact, at the time I began testing this game and for some time afterwards, it was unbelievably fun. But since then it's been squashed into a payment-heavy hunk of crap.
"Cards" in the game are used to boost what you can do with no limit to how many you can use, as long as you can afford to spend real world money to get them. On top of that, you require to buy premium subscriptions just to play the game properly, or you'll be logging in every hour to do something when nothing queues up properly. Cards can be earned for free, yes, but they take a long time and are fully randomized. You can earn more for free per week, but that is locked behind not one, but TWO paywalls of buying subscriptions to the game. You must buy TWO subscription tokens in order to unlock the full range of cards. On top of that, cards can still be bought with REAL WORLD MONEY after you ALREADY had to spend REAL WORLD MONEY on buying a PREMIUM SUBSCRIPTION just to play the game properly. This is massively unbalanced and, as is common among MOBILE COW CLICKERS, can take you from the bottom of the pack to #1 on the leaderboard in a matter of minutes should you pay enough money. Nobody will, but the fact that it is a possibility means the game is massively unbalanced. Any game that makes it possible to advance from bottom to top within minutes cannot be considered free to play.
Outside of that, the game itself is barebones. Your castle management becomes minimal, as the tiny map areas and massively limited resources for each "village" means you will not be able to customize the village to look as you please, it's going to have to run for maximum efficiency, followed by waiting through timers and resource walls as you wait for enough resources or an open queue slot to continue. This game also has an issue of expansion, due to the extreme number of players - castles/villages can only be built on predetermined slots, and the number of people in the game makes it very difficult to expand peacefully without spending an absolute fortune of gold and leaving your new towns well outside your support range. Production lines are also removed now, with the only actual production being from wood/iron -> weapons. That's it. All other production chains, no matter how simple, have been ditched. To help slow you down, each time you build something, it raises its own construction cost and also increases the time required to build the next structure. So, don't go too fast - buy our♥♥♥♥♥♥instead!
This game offers so much room for innovation in the stronghold series. It makes me want to see a stronghold game taking place on a large meta-map managing multiple castles against various AI opponents or players doing similar things, but not in this fashion. I want to see it in a microtransaction-free, upfront paid game with no multi-day timers or subsctipitions or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like that. This franchise NEEDS innovation, and the ideas behind stronghold kingdoms if applied to a paid game could provide it. But this just isn't it. All it does is makes you want to go play another stronghold game instead.
Avoid this.

Skullgirls got off to a very rocky start when it initially launched, but since then the content and polish of the game has swollen massively. While the original Skullgirls release was panned for being a very barebones and noticeably unfinished game, the Encore rerelease is without a doubt a complete package now, featuring amazing GGPO netcode integration, one of the most robust training modes in any fighter, excellent beginner tutorials (I could write a whole thing on the overheads tutorial and how good it is) and an obscenely well balanced spread of characters.
There are some issues to nitpick, like the minimal single player options and some higher level features not being mentioned in tutorials, but the overall package is more than worth the €15 price tag.

If only the english language had enough words to describe how amazing this game is.
I've played many games that have been considered by most to be the best of the best, and this is one of them that I can say deserves an 11/10. From its incredibly gorgeous graphics, to its responsive and extremely fun gameplay, once you start playing, you won't want to stop. The story of Ori and the Blind Forest is an astounding and emotional experience, that had me tearing up at times from the connection I had with the characters. The amazing art meshes perfectly with the gameplay, with smooth, fluid animations that make you feel like you're playing the concept art. If you're going to be playing this game, I highly suggest turning up the graphics all the way, and making sure you have an amazing display to view the game in its full beauty. As the game progresses in difficulty, you'll start dying more often. When you die, you go back to your last checkpoint, but you can use energy to create a Soul Link, which acts as a checkpoint. You can't make one anywhere, however, so this system cannot be abused to the point of making the game boring. On the topic of boring, I never once became bored with this game. It kept me in until I had to quit out of the session. Even then, I would close my eyes and see the spike plants. The next thing that this game KICKS♥♥♥♥♥with is the soundtrack. It fits the story and the atmosphere perfectly, and combined with amazing sound effects, you'll want to buy a copy of the soundtrack just to listen to on your own time.
Overall, Ori and the Bline Forest is already on my list of "Best Games Ever Made", and I highly recommend you purchase and play this.

The best things that I have to say about Fallout 3 all have to do with how they handled the atmosphere, backstory and location. Setting FO3 in DC was a great choice, what better place to set a Fallout story? They really captured the Fallout feeling with this game but it's clear they put a different spin on it. It has more of a hopeful feeling instead of the darker, horror like sound that Mark Morgan brought to the first 2, which I liked a lot but I think I like Inon Zur's work better. Fallout 3 does a great job at fleshing out the world too, some of the best stories you'll see in this game are found in the computer terminal logs and random notes you'll find, they did a great job with those and clearly put a lot of work into them.
The main quest is overall hit or miss but will possibly leave you feeling frustrated if you don't have broken steel dlc. I didn't like it, I think the concept is good even though it's pretty clear they took it from Fallout Tactics, it could've been executed a lot better and it definiately felt forced. The DLC is one of my favorite things about this one, Point Lookout is one of my favorite locations in the series so far, the Pitt and Anchorage are also great. My biggest complaint about this game is how they copy pasted a few of the critical story moments from the first 2 games and shamelessly took credit for it from people who never played the first 2. A good example of this would be how you get exiled from vault 101 or how they had a settlement based around and inside a tanker.
Overall, it's a good game, I know it's controversial among some sections of the Fallout community and I was kind of on the Fallout 3 hate bandwagon for a while but I think there is a lot of things this game does right that makes it unique from the other entries. I think Bethesda can make a great Fallout game, they just need to put more emphasis on the main quest and lore next time.

Preface :
I've only played the player vs environment server of this game. So if you're looking for a player vs player review I'd ask you look somewhere else.
With that out of the way, I would 100% recommend this game.
Introduction :
This is a game who is very good at showing the age of the fighting sail in all its glories. Set in the 18th century and in the Napoleonic era. This game features the many naval powers in the Caribbeans.
It has a stunning mechanic in terms of Combat and also a great sense of realism.
Pros:
If you've ever watched Master and Commander the Far Side of the world, and really enjoyed naval history and lore as well as  the combat mechanics of the fighting sail. This would be the game for you.
1. Very realistic naval combat of the fighting sail.
2. No pay to win mentality you have to earn your commission as a naval officer should.
3. Very very good trading system that encourages open world Market trading.
4. High levels of reward for combat actions
5. Gorgeous graphics and scenery in Battle and sometimes out of battle.
6. Wonderful gaming community happy to help junior players.
Cons:
1. Open world sailing takes a very long time
2. Almost no tutorial for players who are starting and must rely on YouTube or other players.
3. Very steep learning curve.
4. Daily one hour server maintenance.
5. Not for casual gamers (which to me is a pro)
Sunmary:
A fantastic game with an excellent combat mechanic, fantastic for history Buffs and those who love the fighting sail era, the lack of microtransactions mean that you have to earn your rank and earn your experience resulting in much better gameplay and much smarter gamers.
Travelling or shall we say sailing takes a serious amount of time that most dislike however for those who enjoy the immersion this would be golden for you.
If I must put a score I would rate this game 8.5 out of 10.
(This is not a game for those casual players who just want to sit back spend about an hour and expect large amount to reward. And honestly if you are that type of gamer, play on your mobile phone.  if you're playing a PC game you should know that the Grind is life. But I assure you it is well worth the grind)

This is a quick review after only using TANE for a couple of days.
My main interest is in building my own layouts and operating trains under a free roam environment.
I purchased TS2015 approx 1 year ago - and though impressed, it didn't seem suitable for free roam.
I reloaded TS2015 again a month or so ago - and tried again. On forums I saw some suggestion as to how one could switch from one train to another - it was cumbersome and didn't work. I asked directly on the TS2015 forum and no-one could give me an answer.
WIth TS2015 - I could only swap "free roam" locos if they were close to each other - and if I did select a second loco, the the first one simply stopped moving.
Went on a TANE forum and asked the same question. Had a same-day answer - that the functionality I wanted was available and easy to use.
Was a little doubtful if it really would work.
Have also seen concerns about frame rate etc with TANE, but decided to give it a go.
Have run through the tutorials - and I'm fine with frame rate and general presentation. I have an NVIDIA 570GTX graphics card - which was deemed good 4 years ago - but if I upgrade, I'm sure I could get better performance now.
The critical issue for me is the ability to develop the equivalent of a large train set,  that I create,  and where I can drive different locos  at the same time, where I want to, and at the speed I choose for each loco.
As indicated it's early days for me - there are numerous tools to learn (as indeed with TS2015 ) but that can come in the weeks ahead.
The key test was yesterday. Without any study of the manual or on-line help etc, I went into surveyor mode - and created 3 separate tracks - one roughly oval with one set of points leading to a side track and the other two were just single curved lines of track.
I put locos and on each track.
I started one loco - at slow speed, selected another from a simple menu - and started that at a quicker speed.
I started a 3rd loco at another speed and moved it in and out of the siding from the oval track.
It all worked - 3 locos running at different speeds that I can control.
From a simple menu I can jump to different parts of my layout - to wherever my locos are present- and I can get control of any one of them without impacting on the other locos which continue to move around at whatever speed I've set for them. Effectively 3 locos in "free roam" that I can control easily and independently.
As indicated above, there is an incredible amount to learn - both TANE and TS2015 are impressive, but the "free roam" functionality is what I wanted. Rather than simply drive up and down long albeit impressive routes created by others, the magic for me comes from creating my own railway.
TANE offers this to me.
I was fortunate to purchase this game on cyber-Monday for £15.
It's worth a lot more.
Over the years I've pondered whether to invest in a model train set. Locos here might be around £100 each. A spend of around £1000 or more might give  me a good layout with a few locos, track, buildings and scenery etc but would seem very restricted to what I can get with a computer program. There is infinite potential if I want to explore it.
The base cost for TANE and TS2015 (now TS2016) is very small - I'd encourage anyone to buy both and see what aspects appeal.
As I said above - for me, the "free roam"  capability is critical. As I understand it, TS2015/6 claim that most users don't want "free roam". That surprises me - but the bottom line is that I do.
HENCE I will be staying with TANE and spending a lot of time on it in the months (and years?) ahead.

I'm happy that TANE can offer what I want - and I'll now invest the time with manual and any other source of learning that I can find.
Subject to anyone checking their computer spec and their graphics card in particular, I'd recommend it to anyone who is interested in trains.

The Division is a romp through a "what-if" scenario if New York had been ravaged by a plague and a bunch of "agents" are activated to go on what is essentially a killing spree against gangsters, looters, and mass murderers. The combat system is exciting and challenging. You can play the game almost entirely by yourself and without ever playing with anybody else, but it really shines when you have a good solid team of players that you're able to romp through downtown New York with and into the Dark Zone.
PvP is also a blast and it's exciting to be stuck deep in the Dark Zone with valuable loot and a sizeable bounty on your head.
One of the major downsides is that it does feel like a grind. You have to continiously complete multiple missions of the same type to level up and get better loot. The enemies are also massive bullet sponges and it feels like you're shooting bullets made out of styrofoam at your enemies while they shoot you back with steel-core rounds that rip through your armour like it's also made of styrofoam. But the end-game of the Dark Zone does make it worth it.
Weapon crafting, upgrades, perks, abilities; it's all there and it's all waiting for you. Give the game a chance with the trial and you'll quickly find yourself wanting to keep going. Sure, the game isn't perfect; but what (besides me) is?
Give it a shot. I'd bet money that you won't regret. Just not much money. Maybe like a quarter or something.

I've been part of stronghold kingdoms since it's early alpha stages, back when there were only a few of us and we all knew each other like neighbors. Therefore I can say that this game is a massive waste of your time.
I see innovation here - a lot of it. I see opportunities to play stronghold like never before, with an MMO idea all taking place on a large map where cooperation and diplomacy are key to victory in the world of thousands of players all with their own individual strongholds they too are building. The game still has all the customization that stronghold offered you as well, placing the walls, towers, gatehouses, moats, spikes, and more all wherever you want to. It also gives you the freedom to train and manually deploy your own troops both defensively in your castle and/or offensively to siege another. In fact, at the time I began testing this game and for some time afterwards, it was unbelievably fun. But since then it's been squashed into a payment-heavy hunk of crap.
"Cards" in the game are used to boost what you can do with no limit to how many you can use, as long as you can afford to spend real world money to get them. On top of that, you require to buy premium subscriptions just to play the game properly, or you'll be logging in every hour to do something when nothing queues up properly. Cards can be earned for free, yes, but they take a long time and are fully randomized. You can earn more for free per week, but that is locked behind not one, but TWO paywalls of buying subscriptions to the game. You must buy TWO subscription tokens in order to unlock the full range of cards. On top of that, cards can still be bought with REAL WORLD MONEY after you ALREADY had to spend REAL WORLD MONEY on buying a PREMIUM SUBSCRIPTION just to play the game properly. This is massively unbalanced and, as is common among MOBILE COW CLICKERS, can take you from the bottom of the pack to #1 on the leaderboard in a matter of minutes should you pay enough money. Nobody will, but the fact that it is a possibility means the game is massively unbalanced. Any game that makes it possible to advance from bottom to top within minutes cannot be considered free to play.
Outside of that, the game itself is barebones. Your castle management becomes minimal, as the tiny map areas and massively limited resources for each "village" means you will not be able to customize the village to look as you please, it's going to have to run for maximum efficiency, followed by waiting through timers and resource walls as you wait for enough resources or an open queue slot to continue. This game also has an issue of expansion, due to the extreme number of players - castles/villages can only be built on predetermined slots, and the number of people in the game makes it very difficult to expand peacefully without spending an absolute fortune of gold and leaving your new towns well outside your support range. Production lines are also removed now, with the only actual production being from wood/iron -> weapons. That's it. All other production chains, no matter how simple, have been ditched. To help slow you down, each time you build something, it raises its own construction cost and also increases the time required to build the next structure. So, don't go too fast - buy our♥♥♥♥♥♥instead!
This game offers so much room for innovation in the stronghold series. It makes me want to see a stronghold game taking place on a large meta-map managing multiple castles against various AI opponents or players doing similar things, but not in this fashion. I want to see it in a microtransaction-free, upfront paid game with no multi-day timers or subsctipitions or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like that. This franchise NEEDS innovation, and the ideas behind stronghold kingdoms if applied to a paid game could provide it. But this just isn't it. All it does is makes you want to go play another stronghold game instead.

I’ve always been a huge fan of so called ‘sim games’, so playing Reus seemed inevitable to me. If You’ve ever heard, or better, played legendary
series, You’ll instantly  notice some similarities between those two titles.  They both may be called “God simulation games”, ‘cause in both of them we take up a role of tremendous beings, with power to shape the world itself, and the humans are only there as some kind of a cattle, growing and expanding their culture thanks to, or despite our actions.
In Reus, we get to control not one, but four godlike beings – The Giants, awoken from their slumber by the power of The Planet itself, in order to reshape it, and make habitable for humans. Each of those cute beings rules over one aspect of the planet – oceans, forests, swamps and mountains/desserts, but in order to restore life, and make it blossom again, they’ll need to use, and combine all of their powers.
One of the main problems Giants will encounter, and an inspiration behind the game itself, will be a growing
of the human race. This feature not only defines gameplay pace, but also may prove crucial in achieving game objectives, required to unlock more complex resources. Basically the more goods You’ll provide to humans, the more they’ll want, and while trying to get them they’ll no compromise, resolving to fighting with each other, launching a full scale war or even attempting an attack on The Giants themselves.
But the best thing about ‘Reus’ is a seemingly endless, and flexible number of possible development strategies. Every resource created has its own unique “symbiosis” making it more potent under certain conditions. For example certain plant may provide more “food” while growing next to a mineral, which may also benefit further from the nearby animal nest. With 108 different types of resources present in total, You’ll need a long time to discover all potentially useful combinations, and craft Your own unique strategy to master the game, and help Your humans complete most challenging projects !
The last thing worth mentioning about this game, are its undoubtedly beautiful visuals. The whole planet, The Giants, and human villages are set in a cute, round and pleasant 2D environment. This concept fits the game perfectly, and in symbiosis (sic.) with a good soundtrack makes a perfectly addicting combination definitely worth it’s price !
-	Extremely high replayability.
-	In-game milestones provide targets for every round.
-	Intense theorycrafting is possible, due to a huge number of possible choices.
-	Lively community, developing its own challenges, and competitions. (
)
-	Cute and enjoyable visuals.
-	Unusual gameplay, may be boring for some players.
-	It takes time to figure out every aspect of the game.

What I loved the most about SG was the audio and visuals. This game is stunning. The anime/60s cartoon style is unique and the animations are dynamic yet fluid. Even if I don't know half the ♥♥♥♥ of what I'm doing with my character, it's incredibly entertaining to watch. The characters are sexy and we get loads of panty shots/ jiggling boobs. Some characters have parasites that act as hair or accessories which highly reminded me of Kill La Kill. Even though this game is action packed, you get some smooth as ♥♥♥♥ jazz during the menus and cinematics. I haven't tried online play yet since it takes forever to find match but I'm sure it must be better than playing against AI's. The game would be better IMO if story mode was more diverse and elaborate. SG sets up an interesting universe but doesn't tell us enough about it. Using voice actors instead of text could be great as well and would feel more like an actual cartoon. I would love to see a SG cartoon series. Overall, I am more than pleased with my purchase.
