Rosangela Blackwell is a struggling author living in New York, and a medium. Enter Joey Mallone, a ghost and spirit guide tied to the female members of the Blackwell family. When Rosa's aunt, Lauren Blackwell, passes after being in a coma for decades, Joey is 'released' from Lauren and enters Rosa's life. Details are revealed throughout the five installments of the Blackwell series regarding the female members of the Blackwell family, how Joey came to be, what happened to Aunt Lauren to trap her in a comatose state, etc. Together, Rosa and Joey seek out and help tormented ghosts trapped in the physical world cross over to "the other side" throughout the series.
In BLACKWELL CONVERGENCE, this installment takes place about six months after the events in Legacy. Rosa's neighbor, Nishanthi Sharma, convinces Rosa to visit an art gallery viewing. There, Rosa and Joey meet a film company director who later reveals that an actor in a recent film died. Murdered is a more accurate statement, they come to find. While working on the mystery, they stumble upon an old murder case whereby the victim's research work was stolen to benefit a rival company. Finally, on the art gallery's opening night, a familiar 'person' makes an appearance and murders the artist. In all three cases, Rosa and Joey learn that the same venture capitalist foundation funded the three separate companies. Rosa and Joey have their work cut out for them to solve the mysteries, help set the tormented ghosts free, and live to tell about it ... well, Rosa, anyway.
Note: CONVERGENCE features two real people included in the cast of characters: writer Joseph Mitchell returns, as well as New York eccentric Joe Gould.
To enjoy the story at it's best, the games should be played in order of creation. 1st 'LEGACY' -- 2nd 'UNBOUND' which explores the events and time that Lauren Blackwell and Joey were working together in the 1970s (while Unbound turned out, unintentionally, to be a prequel to Legacy, it should be played after Legacy to not only help enlighten the player as to what happened in the first installment, but also gives the player clues as to what is coming in future installments) -- 3rd 'CONVERGENCE' which takes place about six months after the events in Legacy -- 4th 'DECEPTION' which takes place some time after Convergence -- and 5th 'EPIPHANY', which is the final installment in the Blackwell game series.

This game really makes me sad. Sad, because it has so much potential that I fear is being wasted by developers of very little vision. Developers who feel that a game (yes, it's a game) should punish its player base to the extent of driving them so far away as to never look back. As many have mentioned, the graphics and combat mechanics are top-notch, but the game pretty much ends there.
The game is designed to be an MMO, but the quests are very limited and redundant. Sailing across open waters is boring and tedious. The map is completely static so there is very little benefit to using it. You are expected to know where you are at all times and find other locations by using landmarks, which only add to the tedium. They are called "landmarks" for a reason, they are on land. You're in the middle of the ocean. There aren't many watermarks to help guide you.
Aside from this, the devs seem to think that all new players should already be experts in the game and offer little in the way of helping you learn things other than by making tragic mistakes. For instance, they will allow you to get a ship and sail out into battle without a crew onboard, which is fine and dandy until you get into a battle (which can take hours) and then you discover that you can't fire your cannons nor even move your ship because stupid you did not hire the crew to operate it. If you say something about it in the chat, veteran players are quick to remind you what an idiot you are and how did you expect to sail a ship without a crew? Well, I sailed it for hours across a boring sea looking for something to fight. How about a popup when you try to leave port suggesting something like "Perhaps you should hire a crew for your ship before sailing"?
I didn't remain long enough to discover the myriad of bad decisions that some other players here have written about. I didn't need to wait that long before realizing my purchase of Naval "Inaction" was a mistake. If the developers want to salvage this game, they should turn it into a match-based tactical game along the lines of World of Warships with both PvP and PvE modes and research trees. With the nice graphics and combat mechanics, the game could really shine in the clipper ship genre, one that has been sorely neglected in the past. As it stands, if you want to play a sailing ship MMO that features a good variety of things usually found in an MMO, you're best to download the free-to-play older game called Pirates of the Burning Sea.

Some work still needs to be done on the PVE content, economy and GUI, but the battles are great. This is still the best ‘age of sail’ game out there (even though its incomplete). If you are considering purchasing this because you want to take part in naval battles, do it! Be warned the learning curve is very steep, but it makes mastering it even more rewarding.

TLDR: Fantastic game with fantastic story line and great enemies to face down. Hands down, a game worthy of praise equal to Baldur's Gate!
Pros:
- Armor & Weapons SHOW on your characters
- You can make powerful gear & upgrade gear
- There are multiple paths to victory, you can outright kill them, you can convince them, or you can cause infighting
- Every character is capable of everything, you can make Jahan the Wizard able o wear Heavy Armor & use Heavy Weapons if you want, and you can have all your characters use Spells too.
- Each Quest is great & very well rewarding, even if some are through the enemy
- You can rob EVERYONE if you wanted
- You can choose to slaughter an entire city if you wanted, an hey, you still gain xp.
- You get to meet Bellegar & Zandalor!
- Death Knights look exactly like the one from Beyond Divinity are fun to fight

- Pickpocket
- Music from other Divinity games in this game & new additions feel awesome
Cons:
- Galvanised Sentinels
- Void Aura
- Every NPC constantly repeats (Example: "Not in the mood for cheese? That excuse has more holes than this fine gormanbare!" imagine hearing that every 10 seconds - you will appreciate the Mute Button)
- Fabulous Five
- Unresolved NPCs like Brassius
- Areas have preset enemy levels so you are forced to play along a specific progression road if you wanna survive
- Mysterious Stranger feels pointless & adds nothing to the game, he's just there because
- Sneaking feels too easy when stealing
- the "Sneak" skill doesn't need to be leveled up to get anywhere
- Attitude can be adjusted positively for NPCs, but not for your companions (if they choose to leave, they are gone FOREVER)
- Jareth & Bairdotr
- Madora's obsession with every superstition imaginable can get really annoying, plus her accent (ugh)
- Autosave only saves in specific points of the game, it does NOT save every couple mins or half hour or whatever, you'll need a mod for that
- The Imps in the End of Time (when you get there, you'll understand)
- Music has a tendency to stop & never come back
Overall rating: 9/10

In short:
-the railsimulation game i have looked for
-good fun, much to explore, scalable difficulty and gameplay
-some issues in performance, sound and game content
-definitely better then the other big railsim (that punishes its players)
My hardware:
-4 year old gaming PC (no SSD drive)
-Nvidia Geforce GTX560 (old)
-16 GB Ram
Game performance:
-purchased: End of November 2015 after HF2 Patch
-time played to review: 20 hrs
-program crashes so far: 0 (zero)
-GFX settings: mostly low detail, visible range: 2500-3000, texture streaming on
-Screenresolution: 1600x900 (performance tip!)
-framerate: acceptable for me, moslty fluid, depends on Route (ofcourse)
-loading times: the first runups took very long (felt like 5 minutes), directly after first launch more content was loaded down, but it was possible to play during that, currently it launches in about 1 minute, some more time to load when entering a session/route, loading times depend on route size (ofcourse).
-loading times are better than on the other big railsim.
Gameplay matchwinner for me:
-easy and realistic driving mode, both fun
-physics simulation very good
-shunting and long hauls, both possible
-Quickdrive Mode in 'Kickstarter county'
-set complete trains onto looped main line and tell the AI driver to drive
-add more trains, they will all follow the speedlimits and signals automatically
-add even more trains, tell the driver to go to a specific point and he will drive there, including direction changing and junction setting, all other trains will wait if that train blocks the track. Awesome!
-plenty of complete trains to set on tracks, my favourite: 'The blue planet' diesel train
-click on a red signal in front of you and the focus jumps th the cause for that.
-switching junctions is straightforward
Not so good details in gameplay:
-questionable price for addon routes, better purchase at bundle with the main game (deluxe version)
-3D-sound is somewhat awkward at some points.
-very good content on one and somewhat old/messed up stuff on the other hand (locos, routes, assets)
-only few missions(2-4) included in every route by default
-some missions surprisingly long (2hrs) with lot risk to mess up on a goal
-map mode feels a little bit chaotic
Documentation:
-about 10 good driving tutorials, 5-20 mins each, good learning curve, good fun
-250 pages manual in english with every topic handled
Building tracks and sessions (Surveyor):
-just tried shortly
-possible to set a track with a train within 20 minutes for basic operation
-easy Interface
-(to be honest:) not real fun because of vastness of possibilities, reading documentation mandatory
NOT tested so far:
-login to developers online service/website
-multiplayer
-downloading free content from 'download station'
Remark:
-everybody writing a Steam review will get free DLC, no matter if it is a good or bad review.

Its minecraft, with usable vehicles, a few items to pickup (rather than craft), and "gold" to loot.
It also has some nice ways to bulk build (such as raise, lower and flatten terrain), which saves on some of the duller aspects of an epic piece of terraforming in Minecraft.
There's a few yeeha moments. Most animals are ridable, not just the horses. So yeeha, I rode a polar bear, and a goat (one of my favourites). I won't spoil it for you by saying the "best" one. Another yeeha was seeing the cowboys jumping on & off horses (neat), and then jumping on a polar bear due to meandering from the neighbouring biome. And some of the vehicles are yeeha. After a few neat vehicles I found the helicopter...oh yes, I am a lego playboy...
The main downside is it's still pretty limited at this stage. In a couple of hours play I have explored most of the biomes, unlocked most of the vehicles and items, so there's not necessarily any motive to play on.
On a personal note, it's very similar to an old design i did for a game (pre-Minecraft), and it reveals some of the issues with my own design. With an open ended game, you need goals, something to aim for.
So far, collectign them all and exploring was my goal, but that's complete. So what next?
Build a castle perhaps? Ah, I can click on the pre-made one and dump it in. Hmm, ok.
What about a defensive structure? Well, the game does have threats, but nothing like the terror of minecraft (death in lego means a respawn in the same location having lost nothing), so that goal is moot.
It needs more layers baby, more layers...
UPDATE: First play it engaged me for a few hours, second play for an hour.
The game is definitely missing the "living world" element of minecraft (where collecting & planting things & watching them grow played a part of the game). Add to that the fact that some vehicles allow you to deform terrain, but terrain deformation is also a free tool. I think the designers need to pick which elements are in sandbox, and which are in survival (or real) mode.
Has potential, but so do a lot of things in early access. Depends how the expand from here.

I like this game. While I realize that it is not perfect, I personally find it to be an enjoyable way to spend my time. I will list what I find to be the Pros and Cons below
-----PROS-----
- It isn't pay to win. You buy the game once, you have access to all the features it offers, and never have to buy anything for it again - there isn't even an option to buy anything with real money - you want something in the game, you work for it.
- Friendly Community I realize that there are a few bad apples, but that is true of any online community. The vast majority of players I have found in Naval Action will do there best to help newbies get acquainted with the game.
- Awesome Graphics I realize that this one is subjective, but I think that the Graphics in this game are amazing. They also can be tailored to fit a wide variety of Computers/Graphics cards. I used to play this game on a AMD radeon HD 6570. I turned all the graphics settings down to minimum and got around 20-30 FPS. I have since gotten a newer gaming rig with a Nvidia GTX 1060 3GB, and I can turn almost all setting up to max. The game looks beautiful now, and I still get like 70 FPS.
- Vast Open World. You can sail all the way from the Bermudas to panama if you want - and if you have the time (see cons below) and are free to visit as few or as many ports along the way as you like. In each port, you can trade goods, and buy different ships. You can also establish bases and trading depots in ports. There are no time limits or quests or anything like that, (though you can take on specific missions if you want to get more XP to level up faster).
- Many different types of ships, all with beautifully rendered 3D Ships. Ever dreamed of sailing an Indiaman through the Carribean, (or even a fleet of them) and role-playing a merchant in the late 1700s and early 1800s? what about re-enacting Pirates of the Carribean as a pirate, preying on merchant ships full of loot, and fighting other pirates? now, with this game, you can live out those dreams in a giant open world online game.
-----CONS-----
- Game is still in early access. This means that there are bugs, and some of them are fairly severe when they occur. Most of them can be fixed by rebooting the game though.
- Steep learning curve. This one may actually be a PRO for some people, and a CON for others. If you are the type of person who likes arcade-style ship games (Think World of Warships in this case) this isn't the game for you. On the other hand, if you are a fan of simulation naval games (Think Silent Hunter 3 in this case) you will probably enjoy this game. It is fairly accurate in its physics, decently accurate in its map placement (Though this varies on server population), and very accurate in its ship models.
- Devs that, while friendly and helpful, seem to reset the servers/conduct server wipes more frequently than they probably should. This one is the biggest CON for me. I don't like working to get a nice ship, and a good amount of game money and XP, only to lose it all on a reset. While the devs do provide redeemables to get XP back, and Full-Scale XP and gold wipes are fairly rare, they are still more common than they should be in my opinion, and rather annoying.
- No system in place to protect new players from experienced ones. This one is a problem, and while most of the community is friendly, some ofit is not, and these players team together to steal things from new players who can't adequately fight back. As of now, these players are not punished, and there is no system in place to prevent them from doing the same thing again in the future. Fortunately, these types of players are rare.
- Some in-game nations have a language barrier. Want to sail for Spain? learn spanish first, as many of the spanish players are actually spaniards who speak little to no English. This means that Spain tends to lose out on the game map, since they have fewer players and fewer new players join them, since few of them speak spanish. This same problem also applies to the French Faction. Want to sail for France? You guessed it, learn French first, and many of the French players won't speak English to you even if they are able to.
- No Time compression for long voyages. This one tends to put off a lot of people. The fact that sailing from, say the bermudas to Panama actually would take you days is modeled in this game. While there is a very limited type of time compression (your ships go faster in the open world than they do in battle) it is very limited, and not really adequate. While you can log out after sailing a certain distance, and log back in later and continue your voyage, it is likely to be boring, as for most of that time you will see nothing but water, sky and the occasional seabird.
All in all though, I like this game, and reccomend it to anyone who likes History, Naval Warfare, or just simulation games in General.

Blackwell Convergence, third game in the Blackwell series, is a bit surprising: new features are being added, the graphics have been updated, and even the character portraits got a make-over. What has not changed, however, is the basic gameplay (point and click like the rest of the series) and the ever-excellent writing. The metaplot, if you will, is getting darker and more complex, yet the characters retain their sense of humor and quirkiness. Not to be ignored is the music, which like the other games is haunting and lovely.

The third part in the Blackwell series, Convergence returns with even better graphics and more lost souls to put to rest. Once again taking place in the modern world with Rosangela Blackwell, it's up to you to figure out the common thread(s) that bind these tragedies together, all with the help of your ever present guide, Joey.
As can be expected from the Blackwell series, the stories are beautifully developed and are interwoven with the history and culture of New York. As a point-and-click adventure, the challenge is in figuring out where to look for clues and for whom those clues are relevant. The result is a rather slow pace that can at times be slower yet due to minor discrepancies between the logic of the player and the creator. Nonetheless, a relaxing and engrossing way to spend a few hours.

Here are some downsides:
-Sometimes there are graphical glitches but nothing gamebreaking
-I got stuck on a rock during the campaign and since there is no way to jump....

Some good stuff:
-The campaign is quite solid and I enjoyed it. It does not have that horrendous cheese like the rest of Warhammer. I'm not a big Warhammer person but when I pick this game up it feels inviting, and I feel that any person who picks this game will be able to enjoy it without having to know anything about the Warhammer 40k universe.

-Even though multiplayer is dead, the customization it offers is great. You can make a skittles marine or an edgelord and anything in between and bring your OC space marine or chaos chapter to life.
-You feel and sound like you're a space marine in power armor
-The guns are fun and I found it challenging (in a fun way) to learn which one worked best against which situation and enemy
Overall, I give the game an 8.5/10. The annoying spam parts and that annoying pause in between actions has caused me frustration and not joyus challenge.
I can't speak for Warhammer fans but I can speak for my fellow gamers. If you want another great action game to play to either get drawn into another universe or to just tickle the itch, then I reccomend this game.

I got Reus from the Humble Bundle and did not expect too much after reading some of the reviews. I was surprised that this was the first title in some time costing me sleep.
First things first, to advertise this as a god game is maybe a bit ambitious. When considering a god game, I expect to have more options, and in the end maybe more things which are random, events I have to respond to. This reminds me more of city-building, like you do in the Anno-series.
However, setting up your world, making the best landscape possible for the humans, trying to finish their projects ("challenges") is all very motivating and satisfying. With the limited game length (30 min to 2 hrs per game, which can be set at the beginning), you can finish a session in one evening, which is quite a nice contrast to "proper" god games and building games like the aforementioned Anno. The replayability comes from two aspects mostly, first the game has a roguelike (eventhoug this word is hugely overused) concept, as you can unlock new upgrades when you finish a game with certain requirements met. Second, the way you are able to shape the world differs, depending on how you upgrade your four giants, which are used to set and upgrade ressoureces.
It's beautifully made, the graphics style is a bit rough, yet very detailed. For me a huge plus is the interface, I see how this could have gone wrong in many ways, but I think the interface allows you a really good overview and usability. Also, it's possible to pause at any given time and still give commands, which is something I really appreciate in strategy games.
Maybe some issues I have with it: I see how this game may lose its appeal quite fast over time, in contrast to full budget building titles. There are a lot of options for the setup of your world, but the things the player can do are limited (after all, basically it is a 1-d game). Also, I wonder if the implementation of the giants was really necessary. They are surely a great idea, fit nicely into the setting and help the player identifying with something, but ultimately for the gameplay one would not need them - the ressources and upgrades could just be placed via a menu. I really like them, but I think they missed some possibilities there.
I can recommend this game to anybody who likes strategy titles which have some depth, but are not too time consuming. It is an enjoyable game. Also, it is cheap, and turns up at sales every now and again, give it a try!

So my child and I are pretty big Lego fans. We buy a lot of the Lego sets every year, and when I saw this game, it was an instant purchase. We own many of the other Lego games, and in a world where so many releases contain content that is questionable for children, Lego does a great job of making fun games that you can trust to stay clean and kid-friendly. That said, do not expect the ease and simplicity of other building type of games like Minecraft.

In its current state, this game's building mode is frustrating. Sometimes, bricks are placed in different colors even though you know you are selecting the same color. The drag and select tool is an absolute disaster. I spent half the day crafting a very detailed house only to have the drag and select tool wipe out half of the house while trying to simply copy a tiny section. The third person in building mode is terrible. The minifigure is constantly in the way of your view when building in tight spaces.  And when the minifigure is not in the way, the camera has a way of suddenly zooming out or down or simply going off elsewhere.  Also the menu could use a lot of work. Scrolling through the menu sometimes actually scrolls the menu and sometimes it makes the camera zoom out or in, even though you're only moving the wheel. Sometimes when you click something in the menu, the game thinks you're trying to do something else like place bricks, so expect to erase a lot of misplaced bricks unless you're exceptionally careful with every single click of the mouse.  Making things more frustrating, the undo function does not seem to work at all. Also, this game needs an eye dropper  tool for quick color selection.
Further, do not expect to build things in this game the way you would with actual Legos. There are no Technic pieces. There are no curved slopes. There are no bricks with studs on the sides. Do not expect wheels, doors, windows, or any of the other mutitude of strange pieces Lego produces. These are the basic bricks, tiles, and slopes with a few fancier bricks such as masonary bricks, grill bricks, and log bricks.
You're probably wondering how I managed to give this a thumnbs up despite all of the negative criticism. It's because I know Lego does not release garbage. For what it is, it's still decent in its current state. My son absolutely loves it. And I love the potential that it has. $15 is a little steep in its current form, but if you like building games, Lego, or if you just like a sandbox to mess around in, it's still worth a purchase. I have very high hopes out of this early access. Unlike other early access, I can't imagine Lego letting us down. More types of bricks, a more refined building mode, and simply more variety will make the building mode better. A survival mode, crafting mode, story mode and so on would really round out the single player. I'm looking forward to what this game brings us.

There are these ancient stones littered on some of the planets that teach you how to converse with the different alients. I had made it a point to search them out until I learned that its not really necessary, You can pretty much figure out what each alien wants just by viewing the choices that the alien gives you.
This is supposed to be an exploration game and so you want to land your spaceship near every building you find, but you then realize you will have to hunt for fuel each time you do that as it is very expensive to take off again after you land. You cant have more than one ship and you cant sell your existing ship when you purcahse a new one. You just have to pay the price whithout any sort of discount for what your ship is currently equipped with. Hence why its better to just go out and find new ones.
The foundation update that just came out seems interesting as you will need to go out and hunt for various resources to build your base. Unfortunately, you can only have one base. This game is a metroidvania. I like that a lot. I've been looking for a good metroidvania for a while now. This absolutely delivers. It has the wide open map, the secrets placed in every nook and cranny, the procedural power-ups and definitely the backtracking. It does it really well.
This game also has some RPG elements. You start with only 3 life and 1 energy, but you can bolster that up enough. Maybe too much. More on that later. You also get ability points that you can use to add new character features. These include stronger attacks, better power up visibility, and better mobility, though the mobility thing is weird because most of the power-ups that you need to get are also mobility upgrades.
The wide open map is great. It's laid out really well by the in game map and there are mapstones that let you increase your visibility of an area before you explore it so that you know what you're getting yourself into. You can also ignore these mapstones if you want the experience to be more surprising. I wouldn't worry about using them though because they don't reveal any of the secrets so you'll still have some exploring to do.
The secrets are everywhere and range from a few experience points to life cells and full ability points. They're well hidden and fun to find. These make a huge difference in the difficulty of the game. Here, I want to mention a con. Once you have a lot of life you don't have to care about getting hurt. But then the game starts to introduce more instant death obstacles. I got to a point where I didn't care about any of the obstacles that weren't instant death. They felt more like a chore than fun. They posed no threat, but they impeded my progess. This wasn't too much of a problem because many times they integrated with the instant death scenarios, but it still got frustrating to get hurt when I could never die from getting hurt.
Then there's the rush sequences. You know the part at the end of Super Metroid? This game does that a couple times. I liked them. It varied the pace of the game. But the rest of the game teaches you that if you see danger you soul link (checkpoint). These sections don't let you. And with all the instant death scenarios, having to start this sequence over for the 15th time can be really annoying. Especially so when you just know that you were right next to the end and you would've soul linked if you could've.
The power-ups and the backtracking need to be addressed together. The power-ups increase how you can move about the world. You get things like wall climb, double jump, and charge blast. These greatly increase where you can move around the map. It also opened up secrets in locations that you had been to previously. Thankfully, some of these secrets were shortcuts. These were really useful for getting to previous locations to get those secrets that were just asking to be gotten. However, the shortcuts don't make traversing from the top left corner to the bottom right corner any less annoying. They have these spirit wells. Why don't they let you fast travel between them? It's something really small that could've made a huge difference in whether or not I wanted to go back to get those secrets. They even put the spirit wells on the map. Why?
All in all, it's a great game. There's a lot here for fans of great art, fans of the super nintendo generation games, and fans of fun. My complaints are mostly nitpicks, but they're easy to change, and I'm kinda sad that this 8/10 could've easily been a 10/10.
**SPOILERS**
I also want to talk about the story a bit. This was my least favorite part of the game. And I think the worst part is that this surprises me. I went into the game and loved the story at the beginning. The first half of the game was very endearing. It had a very strong UP component. You'll see what I'm talking about. But as the story got near the end, it seemed like the story writers got cold feet. This ended made me mad. They just flipped on all the character development they built throughout the story. I don't wanna get too specific, but they didn't want a grey ending so they made it hyper happy. It bothered me.
Okay, this is the heavy spoiler section. I want to complain about specific parts of the story. They tried to make us care for the big bad. They tried to make us believe that a mother would choose your love over her child. They brought back to life a dead guy. Everyone still alive at the end are presented as friends. That kind of thing made me not care about the fact that my friend died. That made me not care about the children of the mother. By trying to bring us back to happy, they made me not care about the sad they tried to inflict. This frustrated me more than any gameplay decisions. They actively made the story less impactful.
**END OF SPOILER**

Ori and the Blind Forest is a fantastic platformer which takes level traversal mechanics to the next level.
The controls and animations in this game make Mario feel stiff in comparison. The weight and speed of the main character are pretty much perfect. This attention to detail of controls also carries on to every skill you can learn in the game, meaning they are all fun to use and none of them feel forced. I won't spoil what the skills are but I can say that some are staples in the genre and others are either entirely new or inspired by recent games ( e.g. Guacamelee ).
As you can probably tell from the screenshots, this game is not a tile based platformer and instead uses natural looking environments as the playing field. You can probably also tell that the art is beautiful - on par with games like Rayman Origins and Muramasa with bonus points for great use of particle effects. I was skeptical at first and thought the game would end up sacrificing level design for the sake of flashy art assets, but that is not the case at all. In fact the free form shapes can make some sections feel special to play ( for example spikes aligned to fit the arc of of a well timed jump).
Something I wasn't expecting was that save points and special attacks are both tied to an energy system. This essentially lets players tailor the difficulty to their liking. If you like getting punished for dying you can save less often and instead use your energy to clear enemies quickly.  If you want something more like quick saves from Oddworld you can do that as well.  Energy is usually found in areas where you would need it most but can also be refilled for free in some locations on the map.
On top of skills there is an optional ability tree that lets you improve your character in a variety of ways. For a game of this length, the depth of customization is good enough.
Unfortunately this game is not without some flaws. None of these were a deal breaker for me, but they can hold the game back from becoming a classic in some people's opinions.
- Although you are free to explore the world to the extent that your current abilities allow, you can't revisit 3 special areas in the game once you beat them, so keep that in mind if getting 100% is on your radar.
-The art style makes it so that some enemy attacks may be hard to react to if there's a lot of action on screen. The developers did their best to mitigate this by adding a glow effect to almost everything that comes out of an enemy.
- Combat is not as satisfying as games like Symphony of the Night or Cave Story. However, a more combat driven game would have probably been very different and might have suffered in other areas.
- The story can be hit or miss. It made sense for the game but wasn't anything innovative.
Obviously I really enjoyed this game and would recommend it to fans of all kinds of platformers.

I haven't played a lot of third person shooters but this game seemed to offer an unique post apocalyptic themed open world setting along with a focus on co op content which was something I was looking for.
Therefore compared to any of the not so recent Tom Clancy games I remember playing I had some more expectations from this modern title not like I didn't enjoy the stealth based mechanics of the previous games but this is more of a cover and shoot based game here. Lets proceed!
First lets talk about the equipment you will be utilizing on the streets of New York!
As a division agent you have access to some of the most lethal and technologically advanced equipment available within the US arsenal which translates to 'skill objects' like turrets, seeker mines to something more common like a ballistic shield but with additional capabilities which comes in the form of modifications for all the basic skills. You can equip upto two of these basic skills and one 'master skill' which simply is like an ultimate ability giving you a considerable health/damage/shield bonus for a short time.
But you probably don't want to fight with just these skills alone (you can if you want though!) so talking about the weapons or guns you have a pretty decent selection of sniper rifles, assault rifles, SMG's, LMG's for primary and pistols for secondary. You can further modify most of the weapons with attachments which boost its statistics like damage, range, magazine size, stability and accuracy.
All of the guns are useable but some guns are just more efficient than the others so yes some specific guns are more desired than the others. The weapon attachments on the other hand are decently balanced except a few. You can carry two primary guns and one secondary gun at any given time.
Besides these your knee pads, vest, gloves, backpack, holster and mask can also boost some major and minor statistics. Some of these equipment also support addition of further modifications which can further increase some major and minor statistics.
Until you hit level 30 the combination of your guns and skills along with strategy and coordination if you are playing with other people, is what will matter the most. Once you hit character level 30 you get access to the game changing named gear set equipments, high end equipments and weapons and exotic equipments and weapons.
Recently classified gear sets were added which can provide upto six different bonuses for equipping six pieces of equipment from the same named gear set. I know I'm probably not helping much but confusing more at this point but honestly I'm just trying the detail the depth of the gameplay customization you can have.
This is definitely one of the best looking open world setting currently available. I have not been to New York personally but the level design is very good and consistent. While you can't enter each and every building or more specifically all the floors and rooftops which would be epic but still the areas you can access are very well detailed.
User Interface is also very well done in my opinion especially the fully customizable HUD though they could have used a little more colors in the main map window but that is not a major problem.
Whether you are playing alone or with other people you will need to complete about a dozen of main missions and several dozens of smaller side missions both of which add to the storytelling and setting the theme.
Regarding the story itself I personally enjoyed doing all the main missions and learning about the different factions especially from the audio logs you can collect on the map. As you complete more of these missions you will be upgrading your 'personal' base of operations which unlocks the previously mentioned skills as you progress and also passive statistical boosts along with more possible interactions with NPC's in your base which is a main part of the story as well.
PvE content is definitely one of the biggest drawing factor of this game however it is more similar to RPG's than realistic shooters or simulators due to all the statistics and calculations of equipped item combination involved so this is something to keep in mind.
Regarding the missions themselves there are a lot of options for PvE content even in the base game (without the DLCs). You can do them solo or with a group, the choice is yours but the harder the difficulty the more tougher the enemy and their AI is. Enemies on the highest difficulties have much more armour than players so the shoot and cover mechanics are important for PvE.
In the base game as of update 1.8 there are two areas of New York where you can engage in PvP, one is the new 4 vs 4 dedicated PvP only Skirmish mode in West Piers and the other area is the Dark Zone which also has a significantly higher density of NPC's along with timed Dark Zone specific mini events so it is both an alternative for PvE and PvP. Also if you want to engage in PvP in the Dark Zone you can now voluntarily turn on 'Rogue' mode so no more accidental and friendly fire however cutting other players rope during item extraction still makes you 'Rogue'.
Since there are conflicting reports of whether there is any third or first party anti cheat implemented or not, from my experience all I will say is that determining whether someone is cheating or not is a little difficult many times as the time to kill is not very high especially for 1 vs 1 battles. Therefore if you primarily want a PvP experience you might want to look at other third person shooters of which I have played very few.
There are three DLC's available for the game, which add three different games modes and two of them also unlock an incursion (PvE mission) each on the base map. Underground is good for those looking for procedurally generated PvE challenges. Survival has separate PvE and PvP modes but its major appealing factor is the significantly different mechanics, it offers a good experience to those looking for more realistic challenges. Last Stand is for 8 vs 8 capture point based PvPvE game mode set on Dark Zone levels.
I have played a little bit of Last Stand and Survival and the experience has been quite good so far except for some encounters with some obvious cheaters in the Last Stand PvP.
Overall 'The Division' is one of the better third person shooters available especially for a good co op PvE experience. Nothing technically wrong with the PvP aspect but the implementation has not been smooth due to the constant changes to the game for PvP balance but that also tends to affect the PvE mechanics which often results in a divided community based on opinions as many people (including myself) mostly prefer keeping themselves restricted to the PvE activities which is not a negative thing in anyway in my opinion as everyone should have a decent level of freedom in an open world game.
The playerbase is still 'healthy' in my opinion considering that it is more than 1.5 years old (at the time of writing this), you can find people up for matchmaking for most base game content within few minutes but just like any decently popular multiplayer game your experience with strangers will vary as communication and team work is quite vital if you are attempting some of the toughest missions in a group.
At the end all I will say is whether you are playing with close friends or the new people you meet in the game you will have a lot of fun on the streets of New York, goodluck agent!

A good value in the Humble Indie Bundle, or for a couple bucks on its own.

Not only a great game, but one of the best games, period.
Don't let my playtime fool you, I have 700 hours in this game on Xbox 360 that I accrued before building my first PC, I bought this version mostly to play Tale of Two Wastelands, a mod that combines Fallout 3 and New Vegas into a seamless experience, and is in my opinion the optimal way to experience both games.
Fallout 3 (along with Oblivion) defined roleplaying games for me in my teens, and turned them into an obsession. Fallout 3, although at times clunky and dated, retains all of the charm and wonder it had when I first played it.
The appeal of this game, at least for me, isn't great characters or an interesting plot, but the freedom this game gives you to just go out into the wastes and tell your own story. Every burned out building or cave can hold a mystery, seeing some structure on the horizon and trying to reach it out of nothing more than curiosity often supplants questlines and story missions, encountering some enemy faction and having an unscripted running battle in some ruined street can happen around any corner, and you'll come out of it with a hundred stories to tell that are all your own.
The game is backed up by an alternate history of the Cold War that is genuinely interesting, and I found myself scouring computer terminals and museums desperate for snippets of lore to flesh out the world.
You don't play Fallout 3, you experience it, immerse yourself in the world and just explore it. Pick a direction and start walking, you can't predict where you'll end up or who you'll meet.

Fun game with fast-paced, short games that offers plenty of possibilities for tactical manouvers to beat your opponent.
Things that I found really appealing were that there is no excesive grinding required to be competitive in top tier (there will always be some grinding required to get the content of a F2P game, but it's much lower compared to other F2P games that involve collecting cards) due to most expensive units having solutions to deal with that are really cheap, even for new players, and frequent updates (of which many are based on the discussions with the community) that include new content and/or balance changes.
Balance wise the game is looking pretty good in my opinion. It offers plenty of possibilities of building different decks that are viable, and there aren't that many cards that I consider a really bad choice. It still needs some work, but it feels much less meta dependant that other games I have played.
The game charges 20€ for a premium version which in return offers much less grinding needed to get most of the things in the game, but the game is playable even with the free (being given away by streamers or various giveaway sites), basic version. It will require a bit more time invested to get some basic things, but with that more time invested you can be on par with premium users in terms of competitiveness.

I've never been an fan of Warhammer 40k, not to say I dislike it, in fact I've tried numerous times to get into it. But I don't think I've succeeded up until now.
Warhammer 40k: Space Marine is a linear campaign based third person shooter, with some extra PvP and Co-op if one feels so inclined as to do so. This game doesn't try anything too new, but it shows great strengths in the features it uses.
Combat:
The combat is extremely enjoyable and well designed. It's designed so that you'll be using your melee for a large portion of the time, sometimes even as much as your ranged weapon(s). It contains absolutely no health packs; instead, the player is required to activate executions to regain health (think DOOM 2016 if you ONLY got health from glory-kills). Though the mechanic is fun and can be interesting at times, there are times, especially towards the end of the game, where you will hardly ever be able to activate this because enemies can still damage you while you execute someone. This flaw, however, is borderline canceled out by the 'Fury' ability. Working almost like an ultimate, the Fury ability gives the player increased damage and a few other stats, but, most importantly, regenerating health for it's entire duration. The combat is also balanced very well; I played through it on Normal and never once felt like the encounters I was going against were anything harder than Normal. Overall, the combat is 9/10.
Level Design:
Though the game never had any apparent level designs, there were a decent number of times throughout the campaign, especially in the ending segment, where there were enemies who were in parts of the map unreachable to the player. At first, this creates very little problem, however as there start to become more and more of them it becomes quite an annoyance, especially if a player goes in with a shotgun and LMG, like myself. Beyond that, however, and sometimes a lack of cover in areas where cover was almost mandatory, the level design is extremely well done. It isn't groundbreakingly amazing, nor is it bland, repetitive, or unbearable. Overall, the level design is 8/10.
Variety:
There two primary factions who you fight throughout the game (who I will not say for spoiler reasons). The first, that you fight since the beginning, have eight enemies, and the other, which is encountered from about %66 of the way into the game and onward, has about 5 enemies.
Location-wise, there isn't too much variety; hallways and doors are almost always the same no matter where you are. This isn't a flaw with the game, mind you, in fact I honestly think the cathedral-based design of some of the levels, especially the city ones, is absolutely beautiful.
Weapon variety is somewhat decent. The primary bolter stays with you throughout the game, though at one point you do upgrade it, and the secondary weapons and melees can be switched out all the time, which is useful, as you'll probably be wanting different gear for different encounters. Also, well on the topic, there is the jetpack, which leads to some of the most fun encounters in the game. In theory, it adds very little; it gives the player the ability to jump and flyand to do a ground pound. Though it isn't the most original, it certainly is extremely fun.
Overall the variety is 7/10.
Story:
You don't need to be a fan of the Warhammer franchise to enjoy Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine. The game does a good enough job at explaining it's simplistic story, and most lore needed to understand the game can be looked up and read or watched quite simply.
The story of the game itself is, well, it's a thing. It's nothing insane, it's not going to make you laugh and cry, but it's a legitimate story where characters develop throughout it, and in a legitimately well done way. It doesn't bring forward anything totally unexpected, but it does a legitimately good job at telling the simple story it has to tell.
Overall, the story is 7/10.
Overall review: 7.75/10, I would recommend it to anyone who is interested in trying out a new franchise and who enjoys third person, on the ground shooters, or any fans of the Warhammer 40,000 franchise as a whole.

This game is awesome!
Overview (TL;DR): A great game, especially on sale. Gives you the feeling of being a space marine perfectly. The combat feels awesome, and is incredibly brutal. Besides some minor game play things (and the touch of matt ward) the game is by far worth the purchase. The only major downside is that the multiplayer is dead, but it's not the best anyway. Easily in my top ten games.
Positives:
The games art design is amazing, The backgrounds have a tendency to fall in the trap of the gray-brown cholor scheme typical of the time which is a drawback but it's actually very appropiate. The enemy designs are actually very colorful, along with your own troops, so it balances out and imo is how it's optimal as the orcs are very easy to spot and engage. Also they nail that blend of gothic, latin and sci-fi art design perfectly so it should appeal to veteren fans.
The combat in this game is great. It's very much a hack and slash all the way to the end, but it never stops being visceral and engaging with new enemy types being fed at a decent pace. They also feel different, and are usually easy to distinguish (the rokkit boyz look almost excatly like their basic ♥♥♥♥♥ counterparts idk why). The missions are not always the same and the variation is typically welcome and well placed. They also don't take very long so if you're not into a particular mix-up then you'll move on relatively quickly. If you are into that mix-up then don't worry either, because they recycle some of them. There are also very visually appealing boss fights and they tend to differ from each enough to be enjoyable (although none particularly memorable as they aren't very inspired boss ideas).
Although captain ♥♥♥♥♥ is a mary sue, he still manages to feel like an actual marine. That's my favorite part of the game, for I AM THE EMPORERS INSTRUMENT, THE ENFORCER OF HIS WILL, ANGEL OF DEATH, I WILL PURGE THE HERETIC...
If you can find a match, definitely check out the multiplayer. It's not the best but it is fun to pick up every now and then. I bought this on 360 back at launch, and I probably got another 30-40 hours over the years I had that console out of the multiplayer.
All the melee weapons feel pretty different and fun. (The ranged ones not so much but it's forgivable.)
Negatives:
If you're looking for a gripping 40k story then look elsewhere. This is beyond stock standard for 40k tropes, so much so that before I knew anything about 40k lore I had already predicted the games ending. None of the characters are that great or memorable but the orcs voice acting will keep you going. (my favorite is when they scream AROOGA as you dismember them FOR THE EMPORER). Also, you play as the ultramarines and IDK if matt ward had his hands on this script but it feels like it. Captain ♥♥♥♥♥ and his merry band of stereotypes are all ultramarines and they fit the bill, sadly. (mary sues whooooo).
The game has horrible pacing outside of enemy types. I know I also said the mix up's aren't bad but one of them in particular felt like the whole game got derailed. (a weird psuedo-stealth cover based mission against turrents that feels way too long.) You'll go from one mission where there's virtually no dialogue and just nonstop blood shed into a mission where all just talk, and talk, and talk. Normally I'm not against heavy-handed story telling but if your games story is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥it probably doesn't deserve to slow down the amazing game play. Also, the bosses are kind of weak and weird until the end. They are fun, but usually they kind of halt the flow of the game and generally aren't that cool until the fourth act.
The game is dead online for the most part.
This game isn't hard at all. I remember struggling with it as a kid, which makes me feel pretty embarresed because I picked this up now on hard mode with absolutely no difficulty. Typically when I play a game on hard, I want it to force me to really take in the game. Learn its mechanics, enemy types, etc. Thats really not the case with this, you're pretty much an ultrawoodchipper regardless. The only time I ever felt the game was 'hard' was in areas of little to no cover and lots of aoe enemies. The rockets generally get you in two - three hits, so if anything it's more cheese difficulty then actually making the game feel 'harder'.

Really addictive little strategy game. You control God-like creatures around a rotating globe, creating oceans, mountains, deserts, swamps and forests and managing a surprisingly complex system of resources to grow your villages. Lovely art style, smooth intuitive controls and deep gameplay.

It's a pretty decent game, worth more than the $2.50 I paid for it.  While my initial impression was that the game was overly restrictive in its lack of a second dimension, the layout actually plays into the strategy.  I won't get too into the details of the mechanics, but the idea is to be thoughtful in your placement of natural resources, which gain different bonuses depending on the resources that surround it.  Upgrades to the basic improvements get pretty extensive as you unlock more and more, and more and more strategy is required.  To this end I find that the game paces itself pretty well.  You don't have control over humans in this game, so trying to manage them into developing further while not letting them mess up everything is the name of the game.  Perhaps there is not much replay value after you unlock everything, but overall it was pretty entertaining.

The synopsis of this game speaks strongly when it mentions of the fact that while you can control everything, you can never control humans. Give them too little and they will stay stagnant in time. Give them too much and they will turn into greedy devils. You control 4 elemental giants to shape the world to an ecology of your choice and while you can allow the world to prosper, there's a strong chance for the world to crumble and shatter.
Do you want to create a mountain in a swamp village with blueberries beside a nest of poisonous frogs? Go ahead. Do you want to add sharks to the pier to force the people into a state of isolated fear? Up to you. Do you want to control your rock giant and level a whole village with two seismic punches? Sure.
These are all posibilities and the best part is, there is no right and wrong. It's a simulation game that relies on unlocking its unlockables to unlock (phew) more content in the game itself. For example, you can't exacly breed sharks if you have not completed, say, the challenge to win 5 wars. On the other hand, you can't unlock mango trees if you even had a war in a single session in the first place.
The game also introduces a mechanic known as the symbiosis system. It adds a lot more depth to the gameplay while still making it simple enough to follow from the get-go. It's a system that makes use of the the ecology within your village and how you link them all up together. The giants each possess a number of skills which are used to help produce and maintain the symbiosis of the village(s). Mastery over the system and the skills would ensure global prosperity and ultimately, that is the true main goal of the game.
Its art style, music and atmosphere come together sweetly and makes for an enjoyable experience. If you're a fan of the genre, then by all means, give it a go. I highly doubt you will regret the decision.

There is planned DLC for two more characters, with Elise in development now and Robo-fortune later.  These will be FREE upon release so make sure you pick them up!
For gameplay, this is one of my favorite fighters.  It is very similar to Guilty Gear and Marval vs Capcom in playstyle, but without the cheap brokenness of Marval series and the unique character design of the GG series.  This game is constantly being updated by Mike Z who is a former pro FGC player.
The most important part of the game is to PLAY THROUGH THE TUTORIAL!  This game has one of the most comprehensive tutorials in the game going from basics like movment and jumping to kara throws, anamation cancelling, and buffering.  Playing through the tutorial gives you a very good foundation of playing the game.
I can't recommend this game enough.

Ori and the Blind forest is a MetroidVania Rpg Platformer where you play as the child of a tree, raised by a sparrow. When all hope is lost in the wake of a wrathful owl, you are ignited with renewed furvor, given the task to bring the forest back to harmoy.
The look of the game is wonderful, I praise all the hard work these artist put into it, and the music. I find the story to be short and thin, but it never overstayed it's welcome despite it.
Where I feel it lacks in polish, and when, is around and after the 2nd dungeon and into the late game. You can easily explore and obtain what this place has to give you if you're peristant in doing so, leaving little after when you make the march for the final dungeon. I virtually had everything picked clean and had all the skills at the ready for when I entered inside.
When reaching the goal then, you are given the final escape, which I found to be rough on the edges. The instant death marks that you have to avoid are a little mired in the haste and confusion that the game sets for you in that moment, leaving me befuddled during the final stretch when I forgot a certain mechanic the game notifies you upon in the previous area, when you had to obtain the 3rd dungeon's enterance key.
Once beating the game, I'm left with the question of whether or not I was satisfied. My time with it was spent in a sort of up and down rollercoaster with my own life and physical health. I feel like Ori himself, as a character, hadn't had much chance to really develop, or express that development through his travel through the forest. I'm left to wonder, if at all, that it could've been enhanced by a mechanic where you find pieces of story you could sit down and read, about the world, the races within, the tree itself, whether it's in a text or possibly slide show esque sort. I would've enjoyed on top of the fact if I could enter in my save game, and just roam around the world when it's all healed, have like no monsters to bother me with and just let the platforming side of things take me wherever.
With all that said, I'm happy I bought the game. I enjoyed myself for the experience the game had to offer. I can wish for this and that all I please, but the game is nice for what it is.

Superbrothers; Swords and Sworcery is
a bad game.  However, in Steam's binary recommend/don't recommend system, I feel like I'm leaning much closer to "not recommended" versus the alternative.
+Fantastic soundtrack that is smartly integrated into the gameplay
+Great pixel-art
+Relatively novel gameplay and story
-"Puzzles" seem to be less sleuthing/cerebral, and more trial-and-error with (what seems to be) missing information.  For example, if I have to click on a series of environmental objects in a specific order, I often don't seem to have access to
that order should be beyond trial-and-error.  Considering that there's really only one kind of puzzle in the game--and it constitutes a bulk of the gameplay--hopefully you like playing the same "what objects and in which order should I click on them?" puzzle over and over again.
-The game's iPad/touchscreen-based roots are showing; You're frequently instructed to tap/swipe/drag on objects, and KB&M controls generally feel unresponsive and clunky (sometmes inputs seem to have a moderate delay; other times it feels like you need to tell the character to do something more than once before s/he moves).    The gameplay mechanics are
basic, so it's bizarre that they didn't properly adapt the game for conventional KB&M controls.
-The narrative is interspersed with really dumb dialogue.  For example,
I can't help but feel like the writers are constantly elbowing us and asking, "Huh?  HUH?  Isn't that zany?"
-The game's persistent attempts to integrate social media into the game (i.e. constantly getting prompts about whether or not I want to upload a character's quote or event to Twitter, even if you don't provide social media information) is obnoxious, and while I don't think it's the case, it feels like the sort of design decision an out-of-touch executive would force developers to add to a game to better connect with millenials and people who compulsively take pictures of their food.
Again, is this a bad game?  No, not at all.  In fact, it's obvious that it was made with love, and I can always respect a developer for that.  However, while I found the storyline relatively unique and compelling, the gameplay (primarily comprised of navigating from one puzzle to another, awakening sprites) was repetitive and dull, the controls unpleasant, and too many minor annoying aspects to file this as a strong recommendation, even for adventure-game types.

One of the most amazing and outstanding games I have ever played. It is not so much of the gaming and interaction aspect, but the story and comprehension that makes it so.
The story is about two doctors who traverse back in time through a man, Johnny's, memory to fulfill his wish to go to the moon. They learn of his unstable past of his first love, the horific accident of his childhood, and a meaningless life filled with regret and guilt.
The story brought me to tears. Literally. It was so moving and so complex. The doctors take big risks to make fulfill the dying man's wish. It is so reminiscient of the past, and it makes me wonder what my own life will bring.
The music also amazed me. It's all instrumental, except for one bit at the end, which has lyrics. The music made everything better. And I don't think that just because I'm a classical musician.
Despite minimal physical gameplay, and more dialogue, the story was very moving and a very fun game to play. I normally hate dialogue and reading and clicking, but this time it really didn't matter. The gameplay was also very clever, how you have to find meaningful memories and travel between time peroids in Johnny's life through mementos. Very clever and very simple.
There are a few cons, however. The movement and controls were a little goofy, but it didn't matter. The dialogue between Rosalene and Watts (the two memory doctors) was also very childish. It catered too much to an immature, younger crowd, rather than an adult/teenage crowd. The references made me feel like Niel Watts is a comic relief to the story. While every story needs a comic relief (Shakespeare devloped that very well), I feel like Watts was a little off the deep end. It was childish humour and references and all around useless and meaningless and long dialogue. For once, swearing bothered me. There wasn't too much, but just enough to know that the story doesn't need it.
But all cons aside, it's definitely an amazing game with a touching story that will make you so upset you don't want to play anymore, but it all resolves in a bittersweet ending.

Ori and the Blind Forest review: "a challenging and beautiful journey"
At first sight you may think that something so beautiful couldn’t possibly have substance. Ori and the Blind Forest is so lovingly drawn, so full of light and colour, so deeply layered with scenic detail, that you suspect the developers will want to take you by the hand to ensure you see it all.
To the credit of Moon Studios, the opposite is true. This game may be beautiful, but it is also deadly.
Mixing interactive sequences and memory vignettes, the Ghibli-inspired opening sequence introduces us to the eponymous forest spirit Ori and her bear-like caregiver before tearing them apart. The rich artistic style conspires against the player: hazards are not exaggerated and obvious but blend in like natural features, and you’ll likely end up stumbling into a cluster of deadly spiky growths as you stumble into a nettle patch in the garden of your childhood home.
From the start precision and attention to detail are demanded. A lazy jump won’t automatically reach its target; you have to perfect the timing and learn the arc of the motion. Also, your limitations aren’t immediately obvious – you might not realise right away that some areas are supposed to be out of reach until Ori has learned a new skill.

Warhammer 40K: Space Marine is one of the better Warhammer games out there because of a couple of reasons:
First: Games Workshop sometimes is very generous to whom they give the license to make games, because of this, there's a lot of Warhammer games that are either forgettable or don't have good quality.
Second: Warhammer 40K has a long history with games, PC specifically like the Space Hulk franchise, but most games were designed with the idea of also letting you play with other races besides the space marines so they have to balance the factions to not feel as overpowered or they just ramped the difficulty making your units feel like they were made of paper, like early Space Hulk games.
Space Marine not only has the quality of a Triple A game in all the right places made by a studio that actually cared for the product but also lets you play a complete campaing as a space marine so you can really go all out and its one of the most accurate representations of what a space marine can do.
The soundtrack is orchestra, very well composed but it makes you miss some of the chants other games have for the space marine chapters.
The story is also a good selling point if you dont't know much about the warhammer universe or if this is your first contact with the franchise, the lore is massive with a great amount of backstory, worlds, space marine chapters and alien races but they're not required in order to enjoy this game, the story is straightforward and easy to follow with characters just mentioning lore from the side, a good entry point for the Warhammer universe.
The gameplay as I said before, its the strongest point of the game, not being tied to any other race to balance for the single player story lets you have full control of a captain space marine, the weapons in the warhammer universe range from brutal to overpowered, and this game does them great justice, all of them feeling incredible to handle. The game gives you the option to play ranged or melee, some guns are more powerful than others but all of them are viable to finish the game. There is no cover system in the game which is good, you're a space marine, you don't need one, but I do recommend to play the game in a moderate difficult, higher difficulties will limit you from the melee aspect of the game the closer you are to the endgame because of how accurate the enemies are and some levels will become a spamfest, making you try to take cover when the game wasn't designed for it.
The game also has 2 multiplayer modes, a 8v8 that is dead for the most part so don't count on it, and a horde mode that still works since you can use P2P to play with your friends, but if you want to play co-op warhammer games with your friends there are better options like Eternal Crusade or the most recent Space Hulk games, so you'll want to get this game for its most important aspect, the single player campaing, best option would be to wait for a sale to get it.
One of the weak aspects of the game is the scenary and the backgrounds, the explanation for this is that the world the story takes place is a forge world (basically the planet being an entire military factory) but this doesn't stop the game's locations from looking the same, the good thing about this is that by making the backgrounds empty for the most part it enhances the performance, so this game can easily reach 60fps as long as your hardware is close to this current decade.
One more thing, this game belongs to the last generation of consoles so there will be quick time events in some moments of the game, nothing too serious.

This is good Ork-slaying fun brought down by clunky controls and poor AI implementation. If you have any interest whatsoever in the 40k universe and action games, this is a good pick.
The $60 release price was absurb and justifiable only by the 40k branding. This was NEVER a $60 game. It's current normal price of $20 is a bit steep considering the game's age, but if you don't have it yet put it on your wishlist and wait for a sale. If you feel like it was worth more after playing, there's always DLC.
Pros:
-Good job of portraying the Orks as a giant swarming horde
-Although you are constrained to certain areas of the environment, the game maintains an expansive feel when it should, e.g. when outdoors or inside massive buildings
-Excellent job of maintaining the look and feel of 40k; the units (and wrecks of vehicles) look like they came straight from the tabletop
-Co-op is surprisingly fun. Wholesale slaughter of Orks.
Cons:
-The AI is awful, both for your fellow Ultramarines in the single-player campaign and for enemies. Ultramarines survive by being invincible (except for that one time) and enemies succeed by swarming and sometimes being OP.
-Some fights feel poorly balanced, specifically up against Chaos. I understand that Chaos is powerful, but Tainted Psykers...come on. Not only are they strong, but if they post up in front of their warp rift you straight up can't see them. The rift obscures not only them, but your targeting reticle so you can't be sure you're locked on. This forces you to find a new angle not for tactical reasons, but because of an unfortunate aesthetic flaw. Aside from that, it's just a matter of making sure your most OP gun has enough ammo to dispatch tough enemies.
-And finally, the clunky controls. If the intent was to feel like your hands were inside giant gloves, good work. This isn't helped by the number of obstacles you can get stuck on.

Unfortunetly you won't find many good action games in Warhammer 40000 (yeah, I'm looking at you Eternal Crusade). This game almost 8 years old, but people still play it. Because this is THE best Spacemarine experience. When you're done with campaign, come join us in Exterminatus (Horde) mode for some brutal ork murderfest.

Despite of all the cons listed above, I really loved this game ! The only bad part that I still hate a lot is that you need to farm for a while after beating the game to get the last 2 achievements. And the farming part isn't optimized.

In spite of the little pixelated animation at the beginning and at the end of the game, graphics are great. Every thing is well animated and the level design is colorful.
The only real thing is that the game is lack of worlds : you have only 2 kind of patterns/worlds : the castle one with grey walls and tiles and the library with wooden flooring and book shelves.

You only have 2 music for the game. One played at the beginning (and maybe that one at the end too) and one for most of the game. So, adding to the same world patterns, it can make you bored.

You can only play the game with a mouse and or a keyboard. (Controller not supported)
Despite using the mouse may seems easier : you just need to click and your hero will choose the fastest way to go there, that trick won't works sometimes : your hero may sometimes take the longest path because a monster or closed door (even if you get the key) is blocking the way.
In addition, when you click on a tile which have an item, you need to take it. (Unless your inventory is full.) OR you can use the keyboard to move on that tile without taking it. ( I think you need to press the spacebar to take items.) But most of the case it can work with a mouse by clicking before or after the said tile.

The gameplay is always improving by adding new features which make every new level more and more challenging to beat with a 3-star rating. Obviously (or not) when they had a new feature into the game, you get a tutorial level which is obvious and simple to beat.
To beat a level you need to reach the exit door with a limited number of steps. If you reach the exit with 12 steps or above, you get a 3-star rating which grants you a treasure. Otherwise you will get a lower star rating or you will need to restart again if you have no more steps left.
So the game progressively adds new gameplay mechanisms up to 24 features. That includes : new items, new monsters, new traps and new NPCs. And this makes the game very challenging and interesting.
You will also unlock 3 features :
your inventory where you will see your in-game currency, treasures and others
the goblin with nasty business where you can donate all your treasures in exchange of a few items
the in-game tracking where you can check your progress for your achievements

You will get most of them by beating the first 100 levels. Only 3 are farming related achievements and they only count after you've unlocked the in-game quests tracking. So yes, unless you've beaten every level with 3 stars and got to the bonus level every 5 levels, you will need to farm them for a while.
WHY ? Because of a goblin with nasty business. Yes, everyone knows that buying things from a goblin is always too expensive. But that one ? Well its prices always extremely increase every time you buy something.
If you are like me, you will need to play 5 levels to get nothing but a bonus room appearing in the levels overview. If you are unlucky you will get a room with secret walls (17% of chance) which you mostly can beat it again on the first try. Obviously the bonus room disappears if you run out of steps. And then you need to have another 5 levels to beat to get a new bonus room.

I've really enjoyed Naval Action so far, and have had the pleasure of meeting some great people through the game.
The best thing that I can say about the game is that it offers great combat mechanics.  In my view, this is the most important aspect to focus on--a fancy UI, while nice to have, is not nearly as important. Winning a battle depends to a great extent on pilot skill (crew allocation, cannon aiming, ship handling, positioning relative to the enemy); and having a tremendously powerful ship is no guarantee of a win.  In PvP, often several smaller ships will devour lone lineships.  Sail with a group as this is a multiplayer game and is not easily played solo.  This also goes for production--it's not easy to produce a lineship by yourself using only resources you've personally harvested, nor should it be.  Trade with other players to get what you're looking for.
Recent development changes have trended towards making the game more difficult, which I agree with, though beginners can still get a feel for the combat without risk, as the beginner ship type and it's repairs are free--sinking or taking damage doesn't entail a cost until you buy a larger ship.  Though once you've bought a larger vessel, it does not respawn after being sunk/captured--don't sail what you cannot afford to lose.
Given that the game is still in development, you can expect there to be changes.  I'm inclined to believe that a lot of the recent negative reviews are motivated by an asset rebalance/reset that occured a few months back, and a number of players that had accumulated (and thereby lost) many items were sufficiently disappointed to lose interest.  I can understand this, though in my view this was necessary to achieve a better sense of balance, as powerful items acquired in early alpha would have given older players an overwhelming advantage.
On the whole, you're going to have a lot more fun if you play the game with other people.  Joining up with an existing clan, or starting off with a few friends makes it worthwhile.  Make use of the extensive third party resources--guides to ship building, trading, and combat can be easily found online and help to give you an idea of where to start.

I more or less automatically downvote any review that dismisses casual games with the throwaway insult of "mobile game". And while Tiles & Tales is a mobile game I don't hold this against it as such. What I do hold against it is that it's a BAD mobile game in the style of the piles of forgettable three star dross clogging up the various app stores.
Tiles & Tales offers a variation on fairly straight forward casual tile matching. Unlike much better games in the style such as You Must Build A Boat and Gems of War, however, I'm struggling to find much skill here. Matching consists of dragging every tile on the board simultaneously in one of four directions (left, right, up and down). All tiles therefore end up bunching up on the side you have dragged them to with matches merging together to create larger stacks. Larger and larger stacks are required to progress.
Because you only have four options each turn (left, right, up or down), strategy is minimal and inevitably you find the board clogging up with tiles that, counterintuitively for a game of this style, become harder and harder to match until the game grinds to a gridlock and you die. Often you find that well before the end of a round you're just pushing the same tiles back and forward to run down the timer because there's literally nothing else you are able to do.
Every time you "die" due to lost health from creating too small stacks in the correct suite you get a cheery popup asking you to use "gems" to reset your health and continue.
More or less that's it. Other than a very, very light RPG skin (basically, just a generic animated fighter character who whacks something every few turns) there are no "Tales" here at all.
Graphically the game sits in a standard mobile-sized vertical frame in the centre of the screen, with the edge bars filled with a static, generic screen filler image. Overall, things look attractive enough for what they are.
But seriously, this is a poor game that largely seems to exist to be simple enough to pass a couple of hours in before you notice, and annoying enough to provide a little bit of incentive to cough up a couple spare bucks to push through the tedium in the hope that something interesting eventually opens up. Sadly, I can't see any evidence that handing over money is going to result in anything other than more of the same.

This is a game where you will die. Oh you will die. And no that is not a threat from the game, it is almost a welcomed fact!
