It was tough to choose between recommending this game or not; I'd give it a thumbs up for being an experience that you won't forget, but a thumbs down for numerous other reasons that I'll explain.
It has interesting (but drab) pixel art that's somewhat reminiscent of the older Sierra/King's Quest series. If you're looking for action and excitement, this is NOT for you...but, if you're looking for an interesting experience of a game with retro early 90s graphics, you'll probably want to give it a shot.
Game play is mundane - a LOT of senseless walking, with a "double click to move" interface. Combat is literally non-existent except for certain checkpoint scenarios where you have to enter combat mode...which consists of clicking the shield or sword at the right moment, and nothing more. It's strictly a methodical game with moderately difficult puzzles to solve.
This game is the definition of "linear." There is one path and one path only, and when you've finished this game, there is no purpose in ever playing through it again. Unfortunately, the only way to get the final achievement, and 100%, is to play through the game in its entirety twice, which is nothing short of a cruel joke and complete torture.
Expect to finish the game in about 4-5 hours. With that being said - get "Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP" when it's at a deep discount only.

I don't like the phrase "form over substance", since form already IS a part of a substance. However, playing (trying to play) Superbrothers on PC in 2017 was a very unpleasent experience for me. Oh, "experience" indeed. The puzzles are mostly silly ("click a couple of object in a correct order, if you make a mistake - repeat"), the majority of game is waiting for your character to walk from one area to another and infamous "wait 11 days or cheat with your OS clock to proceed" mechanism is, in my opinion, a failed experiment.
There are, of course, great pros to Sword & Sworcery, such as one of the most impressive pieces of pixel art made in the gaming history, great 80's-inspired sythwave music and clever writing. However, annoying attempts of adding some humor and teen-like quality to the dialogues (or rather - subjective pieces of narration) can be absolutely immerse-shattering for some.
My probably most hated feature was the constant reminder that I totally can and should twitt about my in-game progress. These suggestions were popping off in both dialogues and HUD. I should be able to decline once, not have this meta-garbage visible all the time whenever I play. I hated it.
For many people these issues are completely irrelevent and if you're one of those people, you may have a blast reaching for this piece of art. I'm glad I played it since I like pixel art a lot, but I wouldn\t recommend it to anyone. Watching a playthrough may be a better choice.

This game is clearly made for mobile devices, a fact that is often apparent by the recurring "Tap to Continue" text, the Quest menu that requires you to click and hold to view all quests but doesn't show a scroll bar, and the incessant need to click and drag in order to navigate the map.  However, the obvious lack of effort to properly port this game to computers really is not a major problem.
This game holds up very well as a non-abstract maze puzzle game.  The game contains 120 puzzles for you to solve.  New game mechanics are steadily added throughout the course of the game rather than all at once, ensuring that the game is constantly offering a fresh experience.  Additionally, the game periodically opens a path to the Treasure Room, which requires you to resolve an earlier level in one attempt in order to access the Treasure Room to claim the artifacts and gems that lie within.  I was surprised to find that there were some levels that I couldn't remember exactly how to solve on my first try, so I missed a few opportunities for bonus loot.
Levels require you to navigate to the exit in a limited number of moves.  The more moves you have remaining when you finish the level, the more experience you will receive.  Experience levels up your hero and grants you additional gems.  You also get one artifact when you score 3-stars on a level.  Artifacts can be sold to the trader at any time to give you more gems or scrolls (more on gems and scrolls later).
There are 24 different maze elements for you to encounter, varying among items, monsters, and maze elements.  Some monsters cause more damage than others, some poison you, and others can be killed with items to avoid damage.  Health potions will automatically heal you one hit point when needed if you have them in your inventory, but Elixirs require manual consumption to regain full health.  Spider webs will cause you to drop the first object in your inventory, but torches can burn spider webs away and allow you to reclaim your dropped items.  Keys can be used to unlock doors or chests of gold.  The list goes on...
The only maze element that I did not enjoy is the secret passageway aspect.  The secret passageways allow you to walk through walls that appear solid, but the only way to know if you can walk through a wall is to click on each and every wall in the level.  This is time consuming and requires you to play the level two or three times just to be able to check every wall and find where the passages are before you can correctly solve the puzzle.  Thankfully the levels prompt you if they have secret passageways so you don't need to worry about always checking for secrets that may not exist.
Should you ever encounter a puzzle that is just too difficult for you to solve, fear not!  The game offers a few avenues to ease your puzzle-solving woes.  Those gems you acquired by leveling up your hero and trading in artifacts can be used to give your hero additional moves if you take too many steps reaching the exit, or you can use gems to revive your hero if you happen to die before finishing the level.  The game also provides scrolls that you can use to make the puzzle a little easier.  The scrolls allow you to unlock a random door, add a coin to a level, give you an extra hit point, or kill a random monster.  Gems can be used to purchase additional scrolls if you ever run out.
I enjoyed the game and certainly recommend it to any puzzle fans.  I did not find any of the puzzles terribly difficult.  I was able to get a 3-star rating on every level without using any guides, many of them on my first attempt (but I admit I used scrolls for a few of them).  The learning curve is perfect, starting off easy and ramping up difficulty at an appropriate pace as you progress through the 120 levels.  It's fun, it's cheap, and it offers several hours of enjoyment.
Note: you can play this game for free online if you'd rather not buy it on Steam.  Just google it.

Imagine being able to create whatever you wanted just by writing it in a book. Now, instead of using this book to give yourself a flying rainbow llama, you use it to help people in need. This is Scribblenauts Unlimited, the third game in the Scribblenauts series.
You play as Maxwell, a young boy who has been given the gift of a magic notebook from his parents. Maxwell then uses the notebook to give a rotten apple to a hungry man, and angers him. The man puts a curse on Lily, his sister, who now slowly turns to stone. To stop this, Maxwell has to make up for his trickery by collecting Starites from people, to free his sister from the curse.
The gameplay in Scribblenauts Unlimited is basic, but it is obtained and used well. I was never confused by the controls or wandered around pressing buttons. The notebook feature is easy to use, and writing something with multiple meanings (say, 'bat') will bring up a menu to select which type of object you would like. There is also a backpack feature that allows you to save your favourite creations for easier access later, but I rarely used this feature as I created new and different things all of the time.
While Scribblenauts Unlimited is simple, its charming art style is colourful, playful and different to a lot of other games that I am used to. Playing the first two games on the Nintendo DS, Scribblenauts Unlimited combines the series-defining mechanics of the first game with the creativity and art style of Super Scribblenauts, building a game that is definitely one of the best puzzle games available on PC. While this game is definitely directed towards a younger audience, I couldn't help but pick up the third instalment of this amazing franchise.
There are no borders in Scribblenauts Unlimited. Unlike the first two games, Scribblenauts Unlimited is set it over 20 different locations, which when unlocked are accessible all the time, creating an open world to explore and invent wonderful contraptions and experiments. Never in any other game have I seen so much creative freedom.
To conclude, Scribblenauts Unlimited is a flawless addition to the series, and definitely a game that will consume a fair amount of play time.

One of the most amazing and outstanding games I have ever played. It is not so much of the gaming and interaction aspect, but the story and comprehension that makes it so.
The story is about two doctors who traverse back in time through a man, Johnny's, memory to fulfill his wish to go to the moon. They learn of his unstable past of his first love, the horific accident of his childhood, and a meaningless life filled with regret and guilt.
The story brought me to tears. Literally. It was so moving and so complex. The doctors take big risks to make fulfill the dying man's wish. It is so reminiscient of the past, and it makes me wonder what my own life will bring.
The music also amazed me. It's all instrumental, except for one bit at the end, which has lyrics. The music made everything better. And I don't think that just because I'm a classical musician.
Despite minimal physical gameplay, and more dialogue, the story was very moving and a very fun game to play. I normally hate dialogue and reading and clicking, but this time it really didn't matter. The gameplay was also very clever, how you have to find meaningful memories and travel between time peroids in Johnny's life through mementos. Very clever and very simple.
There are a few cons, however. The movement and controls were a little goofy, but it didn't matter. The dialogue between Rosalene and Watts (the two memory doctors) was also very childish. It catered too much to an immature, younger crowd, rather than an adult/teenage crowd. The references made me feel like Niel Watts is a comic relief to the story. While every story needs a comic relief (Shakespeare devloped that very well), I feel like Watts was a little off the deep end. It was childish humour and references and all around useless and meaningless and long dialogue. For once, swearing bothered me. There wasn't too much, but just enough to know that the story doesn't need it.
But all cons aside, it's definitely an amazing game with a touching story that will make you so upset you don't want to play anymore, but it all resolves in a bittersweet ending.

There's a lot of complaints about the game's need for some kind of "twitch" or ethereal platforming skill.
This game is inherently a Metroidvania platformer, and requires a more skilled mixture of techniques the farther you go in. You will die often and you should take your time getting through these hurdles.
The game is appropriately challenging in a very integrated way, adding to the tension at some points of the story. There is a lot of intentional backpedaling through the world, and you'll do it often on accident, but that's part of the game's intent to make the player solve puzzles. You will sigh, whine, and huff repeatedly in some areas. This game is all about muscle memory and being able to scale through the world efficiently and effectively.
For anyone that's an amateur or a veteran of platformers, I highly recommend and urge anyone remotely interested in Ori and the Blind Forest to buy it.

I don't know why it took me so long to crack this one open since buying it on a Steam sale, but it's a fantastic game. Tips here:
If you slide 3 or more tiles of the same type together, the resulting tile will be double the sum of the tiles
If you slide 4 or more tiles of the same type together, every tile in the row or column the new tile rests in gets doubled(including the new tile)
If you beat an enemy/chest by more than 2x it's number, the highest portal/treasure value gets doubled.
If you beat an enemy/chest by more than 4x it's number, the highest two portals/gold get added  together and then doubled.
If you beat an enemy/chest by more than 8x it's number, the highest two portals/gold get added  together and then every tile gets doubled.
Priortize getting the 3's and 4's early, and do everything you can to beat the enemy/chest by 8x, as that makes it a lot easier to beat later challenges in the level

The game comprises many levels, and the objective is to work your way to the exit on every level. You are given a fixed number of moves to do so; if you exceed the given number of moves, you die. After completing a level, you are awarded either 1, 2 or 3 stars based on how many moves you used. To get 3 stars, you must complete that level in the smallest number of moves possible. There is usually only 1 solution.
The levels get progressively more difficult, and the obstacles and solutions require increasingly more thought. You also have a small inventory of "treasures" picked up along the way that you can sell for in-game boosters. (Though I failed to see why those boosters were needed in the first place.)
The game supports both keyboard and mouse, but there are minor bugs using both, especially with item pick-ups.
All in all though, this is still a fun title to try. It's a relaxing way to de-stress after a long day and you can just sit back, think about your next move (there are no time limits), and click to get there.

7.5/10.

Well, It's not for the faint of heart.
I'm 30h in, and only about 1/2 of the abilities unlocked. I played an 120 minute era, that took me 7h to complete (you can pause the game and move it around, and sent the next commands whlist paused).
There are 150 give or take,  different resources, and each one has a unique upgrage path - you need this type of rock, with this type of ambassador on this giant, plus you need to get the 'rare' version of the ability (about 30% chance) to unlock the mines you need to finish your objective. (an objective might give you +100 money per marlin within 2 tiles of it - and a marlin is makeral+ lesser hert aspect=seabass. Seabass + Greater hunt aspect (2x desert ambassadors on the forest giant)).
The reason for the unlock system is so that you can begin to grasp the wide depth of this game. Trust me, you're going to need it.
I like this game. It is micromanagement, resource management, time management. and it's key game mechanic: synergies. That's what truely makes this game special. For eg; rabbits give 3xfood. foxes give 5. every rabbit you put together gives an extra +2 food over 5 tiles. every rabbit inside a foxes range gives +4 food.put 2rabbits, a fox, 2rabbits, and you get something huge like 100 food. Then add a hunt apsect to the foxes to gain a money bonus of +2 gold for evey food on the foxes' tile. so you get about 50 gold, as well. Oh, and a blueberry in range of the rabbits for more food, and a bit of natura (some things give bonuses if the natura is high enough under it's tile)
or maybe by puttingferrits next to a mineral they gain a +14 gold bonus, and putting quartz next to quartz gives each one a +10 gold bonus. and you ned to figure out how to maximise a villages resources, inside it's borders, so that you maximise their potential BASED ON THE CURRENT PROGECT (eg a project might give you +35 tech for every pair of apple trees).
If you expand a village too fast, it gets greeedy and will soon be destroying other villages (meaning less resources and no ambassadors coming from that city or land type), or killing your giants (game over).
Add to this the fact that there is no real manual, only a short tutorial, and no clear documentation showing the upgrade paths (so how do I build silver again?) There is a lot of too and fro trying to find the information on the wiki - what you need to build to get the resources you want for later. and the "access the wiki on the ingame browser" seems to be broken for me as well. The wiki is not great - it says iron is transmuted from salt. then you need to find salt transmutes from agate. then you need to find out what is required in each resourse to make it transmute. agate becomes salt when you put lesser siesmic on it, which comes from the rock giant if he has a swamp ambassador. salt becomes iron once you have a greater siesmic, which requires two ambassadors. and then it only occurs 30% of the time.

Reus is a fun "little" game.
Little an understatement. the amout of depth this game has may not seen my all and certainly at first glance.
The premise of the game is you have the control over four giants. Sea, Nature, Rock and swamp (for some reason). Each giant has his own unique abilities. combining these abilities is essential as combining certain elements provides you with better prosperity that humanity uses to complete building projects. completing these projects brings ambasadors. these ambasadors provide new skills for your giants or upgrades it's current depending on which ambasador you wish to give to which giant.
May people overlook the potential of this game and the tutorial barely even gives you slightly less information than you need to know to really understand what you're doing the first "real" game you play.
At the start of the game itself you're forced to play the tutorial itself, these are about basic navigation, how to complete building projects and what to do when a town gets too greedy.
after the tutorial you unlock the half hour game. when you've completed enouth in-game (and steam) achievements you unlock one hour games and after some more achievements the two hour games. Many achievements are achieved rather easily, although some of the harder ones really test your skills as the controller of the giants. thus making this game one of those easy to learn hard to master games.
all in all i would say that this game is worth the money and certainly the time. the game has beautiful and clean graphics, an easy interface that is quite inviting and gameplay that keeps challenging you.

Obviously this game is not for every buyer, but anyone who did a little bit of research beforehand should have known that going in. Yes, it was overhyped. Yes, it seemed far grander in the trailers than the player's first impression. Yes, the PC-port fiasco was a fiasco. But all of the 'lies' and 'broken promises' can really be tied to angry customers who shouldn't have purchased the game to begin with, and all of the supposed shotcomings of the game were well-stated pre-launch. I'm not mad at Hello Games for this game. I'm not even disappointed. I'm just incredulous at the general opinion of this game. All the anger and uproar really was not well-founded. I bought this game fully aware of what I was buying, and for the folks who can't say the same and pointed the finger of blame at HG, shame on you. If you're not responsible enough to manage your own expectations, you're setting yourself up for disappointment again and again. I'm relieved you got your money back.
Now, if you are easily immersed in a nonspecific, nonlinear storyline, enjoy casual, nondemanding gameplay, and enjoy working for occasionally really very rewarding exploration situations, look into this game. Don't buy it expecting visceral combat or endless excitement or a highly polished experience. This is a small-studio game with definite limitations. Occasionally, though, you find something truly breathtaking. And along the way you're bound to discover new and exciting situations. I wish it had broader appeal, but a game like this just can't possibly satisfy everybody's expectations.

This is a game about the perils of civil engineering. Tasked with improving civic infrastructure and equipped only with slow, clumsy bureaucratic giants, you soon learn what a сlustеr♥♥♥♥♥ it really is. Reus is the perfect example of a game that may not introduce new mechanics or concepts to its genre, but shines in the execution and variety of its parts. Reus is an strategy game based on resource generation, you play the role of 4 giants in a wasteland with different abilities of creation, you may use these abilities to terraform the wasteland into habitable land, like forests, swamps or even deserts. You may then create resources in the land, like plants or animals, to attract human settlers, whom will start projects that require certain amonts of different resources within their territory, like food or wealth. You may boost the resources you create for them by procuring synergy beween them, like putting domestic animals near fruit for example; this is essential since human territory is limited and you need to take advantage of every tile. To this the game adds other concepts like humans getting too greedy with their resources, or blocked abilities that may only be obtained by procuring human ambassadors from different kinds of civilizations by completing projects. Reus is a basic strategy game on the surface, with great complexity hidden to those who are not seeking it, making it ideal for all audiences, from casual to hardcore. If you are familiar with this kind of game, Reus doesn't shine with new ideas, it does, however, shine with perfect execution and design.

Depth is a Multiplayer asymmetric PVP game, a fight to the death between Sharks and Divers. Each match is short, engaging, and surprisingly not repetitive. Within this game, the Divers will accompany there friend S.T.E.V.E the robot down into the ocean in search of the riches, only to disturb the very ocean the Sharks live in, who react (very) aggressively.
The PVP System is very fluid, the servers optimal, with 11+ maps spread over 3 game modes. In the base Blood and Gold Game, Divers go down into a wreck of a city or ship and attempt to find treasures and protect S.T.E.V.E whilst the Sharks try to hinder and kill the Divers. Each game starts with 2 Sharks against 4 Divers, each side having a shared 24 life pool. The game is terribly balanced, with an average life expectancy of a shark being one kill for one death, and as the game drags on, the Divers have the option of purchasing new gear, weapons and consumables in their fight against the Sharks. Meanwhile, the Sharks have the ability to upgrade their genetics, evolving and adapting to the scenario.
In terms of content, the player unlocks more and more weapons, upgrades for weapons and shark evolutions throughout playing, with each level up giving new options for the players. The common humor and comedy within the game adds to the chilled yet intense and thrilling atmosphere, and the only available In-Game Purchases are skins for sharks or weapons, making it entirely skill-based. There are currently 6 sharks available(each with its own active ability) and around 8 weapons available. The choice within the game of picking this weapon or this one depends entirely on the ability of the Sharks, which makes each weapon equal and useful in their own way, either dealing with pesky and fast sharks or a single shot high damage weapon for slower more tough sharks. The sharks themselves have expansive evolution trees, and could base their decisions off of the divers placing too many mines, or putting too many attachments to their weapons.
The game has a great skill learning curve, with Sharks being slightly harder to use than humans. The player base is pretty good, with an average of 10 seconds to 30 seconds if you are a diver and around 1 min to 2 min if you want to be a shark(At least, in my regions). In summary, this game is great, definitely buy it, and its humor, whether in the form of the speeches the captain makes, the updates to the game or its in-game chat potential make it a one-of-a-kind deathmatch arena.

SPOILER FREE REVIEW
As a gamer who loves the lore of the 40k universe, I was not sure what to expect when I first started playing Space Marine. In my experience Warhammer games of any type have been very hit or miss (with most unfortunately being a miss). Thankfully, despite some shortcomings, Space Marine manages to avoid this stigma AND also manages to be a game worth owning.
Pros
+Rich visuals. Models, environments are on point with 40k.
+Combat is fun and engaging while remaining deceptively simple.
+Campaign is solid with fair pacing.
+Multiplayer co-op "horde" mode is a blast complete with fair unlockable progression.
+Voice acting is on point.
Cons
-Environments, while rich, have fairly basic level design throughout most of the game. This leads to an almost constant claustrophobic feeling of being hand held and funneled to your objective.
-Connection issues GALORE with multiplayer. I have come back and played this game many times over the years for the co-op since it is so fun however no matter where I have lived at the time and no matter how good my internet is there is moderate to severe latency issues. Not sure if this is from terrible servers or terrible location for mainland US players.
-Campaign, while solid, is straight forward and most objectives are bland.
-Sound could have been better across the board.
Overall, my experience with Space Marine is one I will always look back on fondly. You really feel like a powerful Space Marine more than almost any other 40K game I have played. This game deserves a WELL MADE sequel. Even riddled with connection issues and a dwindling playerbase Space Marine gets a 7/10 would gladly battle heresy again.

I'm used to playing games like Age of Empires, Starcraft, Supreme Commander and the like, where playing too slow gets you booted, so when I'm forced to go immensely slow just to see my fifth or sixth pig farm get built to feed my many cities, I got a bit batsh-erhem...I go a bit wonky.

My house was unlucky enough to be one of the lesser houses on the winning side, and knowing my luck another house would not pick up me or my faction due to the low priority of both my parish and my region.  So, I bade my party farewell and offed my castles, and have lived the better for it.  Too bad I'm not going to be getting all those hours back I should have spent studying for college.

We entitled PC gamers are fast to circle jerk any F2P mobile port that graces our Master Race platform Steam, but it is rare when a really good, really well done mobile puzzle RPG dares to and it totally deserves a positive review.
Tiles & Tales is a puzzle RPG based around the board-sliding mechanics of cult hit among bored developers, 2048. It swaps the exponential difficulty for multiple color tiles, regular board-cleanup through attacks, opening treasure, healing and whatnot. You need to collect enough Mana to open a portal to win the level, and better you are at stacking numbers, the faster you can beat the level before you're exhausted by taken damage. It's much easier than 2048 but that opens it up to a broader audience.
Tiles & Tales has relatively engaging game loop - there're multiple upgrades, daily and weekly quests, and very generous free hard currency (a.k.a. gems) gifts every 4 hours. Given that first respawn in a failed level costs only 1 gem, and a 4-hour free chest contains 3-7 gems, this is a very generous, soft-paywall game. There are premium characters, but even the most expensive takes 15-20 days play for free (only running game to get your free gems). I hope authors have enough revenue to cover for the Steam port, but the game as it is too generous, maybe unsustainingly so.
Some people complain that it costs LOTS of coins to upgrade, forcing you to pay, but the game actually rewards skill (or luck?) by stacking coin tiles up to 9,999. I was able to achieve such a luck run around Level 14. It shot me 5-6 upgrades further in the game, making it very easy. It definitely is not "PAY or GTFO" game.
PROS
* Great visuals for mobile title, at par with Zynga and King.
* Engaging, addictive puzzle RPG mechanic.
* Okay upgrade system.
* Daily, weekly quests, timed gifts reward retention well.
CONS
* Very few uses for hard currency (a.k.a. gems)
* Very few permanent purchases for hard currency

In Tiles & Tales you have to slide the different block types into each other to grow the number inside the block. This can be used to accomplish the tasks in combat from healing to attacking, and even unlocking loot crates. Its simple gameplay but I havent seen anything like this on Steam yet, and I enjoy it enough so I am recommending it. Tiles & Tales  plays similar to some other games you can find on Mobile.

Tiles and Tales is a mix between 2048 and Match 3. The objective of the game is to go through each level collecting a specified number of Blue Crystals. You use the arrow keys or WASD keys to move the blocks in a similar pattern in 2048. Blocks of the same colour combine with one another and go up in value. At the end of the round, the required coloured block with the highest value is broken and used.
Red blocks deal attack damage to enemies at the end of round, green blocks heal you at shrines, purple blocks unlock chests, coin blocks give you coins and so on. You can use coins to buy passive skills that can aid you in game. You can also buy potions that give you temporary buffs.
Conclusion, I think this game should not be on Steam. It's better suited for Facebook or a mobile platform and I don't think it's a good idea to encourage more of these games to port over to Steam. The Pay To Win system is also a major no-no. The cash currency in this game is called Diamonds. Best price was 7000 Diamonds for $140.

Before I start this review, I just want to say that is pretty hard to choose between thumbs up or down. In my opinion Naval Action has a lot to offer for hardcore gamers. It's not a game you can play for 5 hours and get a feel for it. Even at the time I'm writing this review I only put 21 hours in it so far.
When you first start the game you can choose between several nations. It doesn't matter which nation you pick, they're basically all the same. After that you spawn at your nearest (main) port in a Basic Cutter (default ship). After that you're on your own. there are no tutorials at all and thus it can be quite demotivating. don't let this get to you however.
Now the real game starts. A lot of these reviews say it is a grindy game. I agree, however it doesn't take long to get your first (new) ship. If you play solo you get a minimum of 9000 gold and 120xp per mission (the lowest mission that is). You only have to do this a mere 4 or 5 times to buy a new ship. Even 5th rate ships aren't that grindy to get. After that however, I must agree It wil get pretty grindy. (note: I'm not at this level yet, but I couldn't find a 4th rate ship yet) From this point onwards you will just have to fight harder ships, join clans and participait in big fights. before I sum up some of the pros and cons, I advise you to play it with a friend. Note that you will earn less rewards, but is way more fun.
So now on to the pros and cons.
Pros:
- Ships look incredible
- Sailing mechanics are very real
- Lots of ships to choose from
- Gigantic map
- Very immersive
Cons:
- After a certen point it gets grindy
- It's early access so expect some bugs here and there
- If you loose a ship it's gone (except the Cutter)
- Quite pricey
So in the end, do I recommend this game? I would, but only if you love sailing and if you are determined to play this game  a lot. If this is not the case and you are debating whether you should buy this game, I think you shouldn't. If you're not completely sure this game is in my opinion to expensive.

This game has serious RPG wall in the first town. My best friend and I got this game a few yaers back and we played it for a little bit, but we ultimately quit playing it in the first town because the pace slowed down a lot. After a year or two of collecting dust, we picked it back up. This time we were determined to get through the first city in order to play this awesome strategy game.
Holy crap that was one of the best decisions we made. See, we restarted the game on tactition mode when we came back to it. It's like the difficulty setting below the hardest, so we wanted to goof around and see how hard it would be. Now we know that it's the only way to play the game. The challenge, and how fair it felt made my friend and I fall in love with the game so fast. I had to ignore my girlfriend for days so that my buddy and I could just get through like 5 fights because EVERY SINGLE FIGHT was hard and it felt rewarding to come up with creative ways to win. Every single encounter involved critical thinking and other sorts of shenanigans.
To be transparent, we still never beat the game and that's because around level 16 or so, our characters became too powerful. Fights weren't a challenge anymore. One time there was this boss who we walked up to, just out of its range, and I had my spell caster use her most powerful spell to initiate the fight with it (the boss was our level keep that in mind). A fun game, decent compromise between old school turn-based RPGs and more modern RPG concepts, but a few shortcomings bar it from reaching its full potential. 7.5 / 10
Disclaimer: I only played in Tactician Mode.
It's refreshing to find a proper turn-based game like this, which present a decent tactical challenge. The important thing in the game worked: combat and character progression is fun. There is a good quantity of content as well, and I personally liked the art, finding D:OS overall a pleasant game to the eye as well.
In particular, I love the interaction with elements like oil barrels, water, snow, etc., which make each fight feel unique.
Thorough the game you always feel vulnerable to attacks, even when you become powerful. Plus enemies will often use special items and spells like "charm" on you, forcing you to be ready for all kind of contingencies.
Itemization is a bit chaotic, but I liked it, and overall the time/effort required to get new gear felt right through the progression.
Now, my criticisms.
The game has some serious pacing issues. 3 fights in the first 4-5 hours, in which you are presented with a large town and plenty of talking & fetch quests which I didn't find particularly inspired, but were ok. The "murder mystery" which is in itself a great idea and had me motivated, is actually never satisfactory resolved by the player, you just get to know what happened but that's about it; the rest of the town quests and encounters are somewhat original, a few genuinely fun, but many others truly felt as "filler", and I found myself wanting to do some fighting instead. but of course those orcs out there would annihilate me if I tried, sigh.
As you keep progressing and more areas open up, the game apparent open-world design is actually proved as linear with a little optional branching. I would have enjoyed more real choices out there on where to go, right now the choices are there but if you enter the wrong area, you die, so in the end there's an "order to do things" which simply allows a few variations.
Combat animations need an option to be sped up, seriously. After 20-25 hours some fights begin to feel like a chore because of this (goblins, mine). You'll find yourself spending 20 minutes on a battle with 4 goblins that you know you're going to win easily. Animation easily takes 70% of that time.
Finally, a minor gripe: too much junk in the game, especially all the crafting items, and inventory management is quite cumbersome.
Now don't let the negatives discourage you, if you are a fan of TB-RPGs this game is a must-play.

If you♥♥♥♥♥♥off a certain country, you won't be allowed into their cities and ports anymore. Then you can sneak in.

The choice of playing style is great. You don't even have to be a pirate. If you'd rather make your fortune by trading, you can. It won't be as fun, but it's a valid choice. You can side with a country or just attack any ships that come by. You can sail with 40 pirates or 150. You can treat your crew well or take them to the point of desertion.
Controls are slightly akward. As I've mentioned before, you're meant to use the number pad. I'm left handed and I would prefer to use, say, the WASD keys. If you have a laptop or a keyboard without a number pad you'll have some difficulties, which is unfortunate since even a non-gaming laptop could run this game easily. I haven't played many games that force you to use the number pad. It's difficult and frustrating, but I wouldn't miss out on the game due to this minor issue.
An interesting feature of this game is the ability to wander around on land for days at a time. I ancored my ship and went aboard with a few crew members. We ran in one direction for a few months, all the time making pirate noises and walking through trees. This aspect is obviously flawed. I was trying to walk to Panama and couldn't find it since terrain is identical and repeating and your party of pirates won't appear on the map. I appreciate the effort of actually being able to go on land, although there isn't really a good reason to.
The map itself is a bit poorly designed. It's hard to find destinations since they all look the same and I don't think you can zoom out all the way. I liked that the gameworld itself is really large. However, cities are all basically the same with a few minor differences.
I could go on for hours about this game and how pleased I am with it. It's great and it deserves to be played even 13 years after its release.

There's a lot of work that went into the making of this game from what I can tell but I sure as hell wish more developers put that extra time into a single game that churning out multiple 'mediocre' games.

The biggest downfall of the game is that it is short. The developpers get around this by using "real world" time and the lunar cycle to control the game enviroment to stretch what is about four hours into one month of content. This mechanic reminded me of Boktai in a way as it forces you to play at certian times unless you cheated by tapering with the clock.
Overall it was a fun game, neat visuals, amazing sound, and unique game mechanics.

Really fun game, honestly. Neither side feels too OP, although I'd say the fairness varies widely depending on the map. Some shark types feel a little on the weak side, not because other sharks are inherently better, but because some sharks have their stats excessively nerfed because of their unique ability. Divers have a wide range of tools available to them, and the they all seem pretty balanced. Any weapon that does tons of damage is approriately tougher to land hits with. The only complaint I'd have about the diver equipment is that some of the rifles are just larger versions of the sidearms, and cost far too much for seemingly meager improvements.
My primary gripe with Deptjh, far beyond and above all, is that the matchmaking system realllllly needs work. Or rather, it needs one to begin with. My first 30 games were very fair and even, and everyone was on a level playing field.
The very moment I hit level 30 and achieved the final unlock, I began regularly seeing an incredible disparity between player experience. I'd play shark one game, and win 27 tickets to 0, against a diver team of all newbies, and then my next match would be against 2 divers with together  more than 4,000 games, and THEY would chase ME around the map, and I'd lose the match 25 to nothing. This wild gap between player experience is present in at least one player per game. While the majority of players I've been recently matched with fall in somewhere betwee 25-60 matches total, there is at least one player with 500+ matches at a minimum.
This has made recent playtime really frustrating, and while I would still reccomend this game to everyone except the easily frustrated, I would urge the development team to work on a matchmaking system that would at least place players within 200 games or so, so that every game is not an absolute stomp by one team or the other.
Even with this glaring issue, I would recommend Depth. The maps are gorgeous and interesting (except Quarry, f*** quarry), the sharks are fun to play, and the divers likewise, and I look forward to anything more the team might add to the game. As soon as a system is developed to pair equally experienced players against each other, my 6/10 will transform into a 8/10 for sure.

In a nutshell - good game for a good price. Devs are dedicated and not greedy. In the modern gamedev world it's probaby as awesome as one can get.
Was really hesitant to buy it, because earlier Divinities looked to me like Diablo clones. But this game is definitely right step into the world of real RPG. Not even close to the masterpieces of Black Isle and Bioware, but still, really good change comparing to earlier games of the franchise.
Cons first:
1) No lore worth mentioning whatsoever.
2) Bad immersion - protagonists don't feel like heroes in predicament, more like bystanders who make comments on what's goin around. Most NPC feel like stunts. Also some jokes and  pop references are from our world not from theirs. Some like it  - I call em immersion breakers.
3) Main story is... erm.... vague.
4) The world is too small. Only 3 locations and they are so small that characters could have croseed it in 30 sec. Fact that to feel it bigger devs had us run through folded firehose (all the way to the left - up - allthe way to the right - up - to the left...) doesn't make it feel better.
5) Combat is both con and pro - so read below.
6) Loot management... probably worst I've seen in my 30 year gaming career. So many items with no way to know if you gonna need em or not later....
7) Class balance - no classes, but the game is severely unfair to melee characters in combat.
Pros:
1) Music. It's fantastic. 10/10. Dunno how many hours I've spent just standing near frozen Icara just listening to her theme. Don't know who is the composer but his place is on Olympus among titans like Morgan, Hoenig, Zur...
2) Char development is really interesting and worth to play around. Buildcraft revived. Choices are meaningful and important. Pretty much all skills are usefull on many occasions. 9/10 Only because no races or classes, otherwise would be 10/10.
3) Gear  - endless field for creativity. 10/10.
4) Combat - mixed feelings. Too much randomacity which turns some fights into "load button abuse". One and the same fight, in the same place, same gear, using one and the same strategy can result in:
-Both heroes dead before their first turn.
- Hard  interesting fight that you've won.
- Enemy obliterated - heroes haven't lost a single HP.
Boss fights are... strange. While trash mobs look kinda intelligent and in case of bowmen and crossbowmen I'd even say  devious. Bosses just keep running around selfbaffing casting random abilities effectively... sabotaging themselves.
Also elements of arcade - barrels, vents, puddles... I personally don't like it cause it's once again an immersion breakers. But it creates additional field for creativity in combat. More stuff to avoid more stuff you can combo and use. All in all - good.
To wrap it up...
Money well pent - I had fun for 2 months.

Bought this game on a super-sale type deal because I had heard lots of good things and finally wanted to give it a try.  I enjoyed it well enough at first, roaming about the beaches, getting gently intoduced to the story and mechanics by getting an entire starter-dungeon type thing to explore.  It was nice.
Then I got to Cyseal, the main area of the game you'll be stuck in for a while.  I say "stuck" because there's a lot to do/see, and while I initially enjoyed the 'theme park'-esque ye olde dialogue, I found it to get quite repeatative (and a bit tiring even) after hearing so much of it without a break inbetween.  It was made especially worse by having my voice volume still on, hearing all of the merchants shout the same repetative lines about their wares over and over with very little respite.
I had to eventually turn the voices off, and while it certainly made going about the town a little easier I still would've liked to have seen the ammount of things to do there broken up a little bit.  As a video game player who wants to explore every inch of a location before leaving, the value of everything I was learning felt lessened because of how much there was to see in the town.  If I could've left and came back after a while, and walk in on some new event or strange happening going on, I likely would've felt much more engaged with all of the different little side-stories.
That said though, the turn-based combat was solid.  I enjoy when I can accidentally cause something bad to happen to my allies by getting them caught in a fireball or not realizing the surface they were stood on was a puddle of water and shooting lightning at their nearest foe.  The skills felt varied and impactful, and I always enjoy talent-based systems that let me make my character what I imagine rather than just straight up 'class' systems where the only ones who can heal or shoot magic are cloth-wearing squishies.
...I think the worst thing Divinity: Original Sin did, however, was introduce me to its main plot way too early.  I don't mean the first couple encounters before you come into town.  I don't mean the things you learn from Arhu upon talking to him for the first time.  I mean the whole mcguffins that happens when you first encounter a Star Stone in the game.  I *hated* learning about the "End of Time" and the true mystery behind the game.  To avoid specifics as much as I can, i'll simply say that a plot-line based around you being the 'fated hero' who is the only possible one who can save the universe was the true travesty the game committed (especially when it happens so fricken' early on!).
I was sold on the idea of being a Source Hunter running around cleaning up magic hoo-hah and making the world a better place or whatever.  I didn't *need* some impish little butt-head coming along to tell me all about grand design and that I'm some mystical, foreign element in it all.  I tried *so damned hard* to stay as far away from all that crap as I possibly could and continue through the game pretending it didn't exist, but the game keeps pulling you back to it to remind you of its existence.  "Found another star stone?  Well go back to the End of Time!", "Major plot-point just occured?  Better go back to the hub and talk about it with your pals!"  Gah!  No!   ...I eventually stopped playing, just before the end of the game, my enthusiasm having fully been eroded away.  As a person who loves stories and with that being such an important part of this game, I cannot recommend this one.  Hopefully Divinity Original Sin 2 will do better in this respect.

With a charmingly touching narrative and awe inspiring artwork that'll have you lost in the scenery alone, Ori is a true gem of the 2D Platformer genre that combines the challenging elements of skill, quick reflexes, and puzzle solving into what I can only describe as the best game of it's genre that I've played in a long time, with obvious inspirations from other great titles such as  Meatboy and Metroid.

Ori has something for everyone - it offers a reasonably fair learning curve for those new (or returning) players to the genre; and has a few tricks up its sleeves for the more devoted platformer fan - the "save anywhere" idea is perhaps more interesting in concept than execution, but once you've got the basics down there's great enjoyment to be had from the free-flowing movement, most notably in several truly memorable set-pieces.
The story has its mis-steps (personally I found it a little too minimalist in places) but there's no arguing with the gorgeous art throughout the title. In short, this title is an above-average platformer wrapped in a truly superior aesthetic. Well worth playing.

Beautiful artwork, atmosphere, and feelings fill this platformer with peace of mind even as you're struggling to get through the most difficult gameplay areas, but the self-fullfillment and emotional attachment makes even the difficulty curve relaxing.
I am not typically a fan of platformer games, though I do play a few of them. What past games have been exceedingly frustrating to overcome obstacles, leaving me putting the game away for an undefined period of time, Ori has managed to pull the game together in such a way that the experience is enjoyable even when you're faced with a difficulty you can't seem to overcome.
The people who put this game together are geniuses, to say the least. I would recommend this to anyone who asks about it, as it was an experience that makes me feel compelled to play it again even after completing it, which is not something I can often say for a linear game.

Reus is such a well-designed game! There are three tutorials which go by quickly, teach you everything you need to know about the game without being heavy handed, and are quite fun. Then you're launched into the real game. At first, you can only play 30-minute sessions, but as you play, you unlock the ability to play 60-minute, then 120-minute sessions. Even after the tutorials, there are loads of things to unlock (which you unlock by trying different styles of play) and tons of things to learn. The game is very good about encouraging experimentation. Even the tutorials will say things like, "Experiment with X," so you learn without losing any sense of exploration or control.
The in-game achievements each correspond to a Steam achievement, and they all encourage different play styles. One might be, "End an era with only one village," and another might be, "End the game with six co-existant villages." If you get both of these achievements, you have played two very different games.
It's hard to explain what makes the game so fun. However, I know half the fun is in learning the game for yourself, so I won't try to spoil that for you. If you're looking for a short-ish game with infinite replay value, Reus is for you.

Update:
since my first review, I have upgraded my video card to a single EVGA Nvidia GTX Titan X super clocked GPU and now I get decent FPS with all settings on High or Ultra.
Note that I updated the video drivers and did a complete fresh reinstallation of the latest from the manufactures website.  I wanted to make sure there were no bugs from my original GPU drivers, so a fresh install was performed.  It is an option when performing a custom install.
The first few times I ran this with the new video card caused the system to load the game slow enough to make me think the computer had locked up, and I prematurely used Task Manage to shut down the program.
Then out of frustration, I just let the system to load the game without intervention from me.  I just walked away from it thinking I would come back later to see if anything changed?  Although I was expecting it to still appear stalled; Sure enough, the system was up and running as if there was nothing abnormal.
I thought if it is going to take that long every time I want to play, then I would just dump the game and chalk it up to "Live and Learn".
Turns out, the system started loading the game in a reasonable time of less than a minute.
Now I enjoy the game with an average Frame Rate of 25-35 FPS with the occasional dip to the low 20's and peaks as high as 48 FPS.  Wow -  What a difference.  The game is what I was hoping for.  Is it perfect - NO, but the frustration of constantly searching for a tweak or Over Clock that would work is in the past.  Now I enjoy the experience and am exploring new things all the time.
My one complaint now is that I can't get the HotFix-2 to install which I think is more a problem with STEAM than T:ANE.

Trainz: A New Era is definitely a next generation Train Simulation that takes advantage of current CPU technology and can challenge even high end Gaming Systems when visual settings are pushed towards their maximum - It brings whole new capabilities and exciting feature with one significant drawback in the Graphics department, even high end Graphics Cards will produce slow FPS often less than 10-30 (Frame Rates per Second) when visual settings are adjusted towards their maximum settings.
The fix is to adjust the settings down until you get an acceptable Frame Rate for your system.

This can be a huge disappointment to a majority of end-users who upgrade from previous versions hoping the visual presentation will be everything the software developer says it will be only to be forced to reduce visual effect settings to prevent poor performance or system crashes.
It is unfortunate that the developers produce videos promising stunning visual performance, but have not put more effort into solving these well-known and long standing visual performance issues for the majority of users.  Eventually, I believe they will solve these issues, because it is a major selling point that Trainz: A New ERA  is a true enthusiast’s next generation simulation software taking advantage of newer more powerful computers with what could be Outstanding Graphics and Realism once they resolve these performance issues that prevent users from getting the best experience possible.
As enthusiasts we understand the possibilities, and sometimes catch glimpses now and then before the software crashes the system, but for now, I recommend those with older systems stick with previous versions until they can deliver on their promise to give us a true Next Generation Simulation as promised in their video’s.
Obviously there is a wide variety of systems out there, and not everyone is going to have the same experience.  As for me, I have a high end system, and thus far I have been spending a lot of time trying to tweak the settings to get reasonable FPS and visual experience – but that shouldn’t be happening based on their promises deliver a stunningly realistic experience.  Perhaps someone out there has a system that just knocks it out of the park, but they are the exception and not the rule.
Please comment to the developer’s about not delivering the experience they advertise and perhaps it will motivate them to solve these issues sooner rather than later.

Maze Lord is a fantasy and dungeon themed puzzle game. There is no true combat, so if you're looking at this thinking it plays like a board game, it does not.
The puzzles in Maze Lord are fun and simple. It is a very casual experience. Each puzzle has a set number of moves in which you must complete it. The more moves left over when the puzzle is finished, the higher your star rating (out of 3). Each star is worth 10 experience.
Experience points let you gain account levels. There are certain break points where you need a specific account level or higher to access later game levels. You can always replay the levels to achieve a better star rank and thus more experience.
As you complete levels and earn 3 stars, you'll open trinkets. Trinkets can be turned in for rubies. Rubies can be spent to purchase power ups for those tougher puzzles. You can purchase a number of items with rubies (no real money purchases in the game. There is no cash shop...whew!), such as fire to kill a random enemy at the start of the puzzle, a key to unlock a random door at the beginning of the puzzle, a coin to purchase items on the ground, or an extra life point.
There are 120 puzzles in Maze Lord. I would say it's well worth the $2.99 price tag, though it has been mentioned in the community hub that the game is free elsewhere. For me, $2.99 ($4.99 after the sale, still worth it) was well worth giving the developer for a game that killed me a bit of time and gave me some fun doing it!

So I’ve owned this on the PSP for a while and decided to pick it up over this Autumn Sale. Because of this I will be talking about it from a ported perspective.
This is a game with some varied, mix and matched gameplay. You have real time naval combat and land exploration, turn based land warfare, and the dreaded dancing mini game. It is very open ended, reminding me of Mount and Blade. You can be anything from a pirate raiding anything in sight, a merchant sailing for profit, or a admiral of one of the nations in the game. Despite being an older game, it instill rather complicated. Ship variations, upgrades and managing your food supplies and crew morale, as well as the fame system which determines where you end up end game.
I should probably talk about the fat system. You gain fame through various deeds, such as defeating one of the villains of the game, defeating pirates, finding treasure or family members, and more. These all add up to a counter that decides where you’ll go at the end of the game after you retire from pirating. These roles go from a beggar who is quickly forgotten, to a governor who’s exploits are recorded and immortalized in the annals of history. Additional factors include your age and health, the land you’re granted by governors, personal wealth, and whether you were married or not. I remember one game on the PSP I got the “best ending” where I was extremely wealthy, the most famous person alive, married, and had saved all my family and avenged them.
Coming from the port, there are a number of things different. The interface is much more point and click style, and the graphics and information on ships are expanded on. A menu glossary detail everything from Shrunken Heads to Frigates. And land exploration is much more intuitive. Combat remains relatively the same, though much easier to navigate instead of the crust of buttons needed to be used on the PSP. Seeing your entire fleet at sail is also fun to see, and makes maintaining all of them much more pressing.
EDIT: This game also has a pretty nice soundtrack and I appreciate that in games, there;'s variety but you can still hear similar notes in each track.
I would recommend picking this game up if you’re interested in this sort of thing, though do save often as it can crash like most of these old games.

One of the more memorable D&D type games that I've played in many years. It has an amazing amount of lore, a well crafted story and superb voice acting, leading up to a pretty immersive and unforgettable storytelling-RPG experience. The difficulty setting is high enough (on normal) that the game provided a good challenge along the way and the use of environmental effects combined with teleportation skills in combat was highly creative and often led to very satisfactory results.
One of the things I didn't like was the difficulty of the puzzles - some were pretty straight-forward in nature, but some were a real pain. It didn't help that there weren't many hints along the way (or very vague ones) on how to progress and I found myself backtracking, wasting a lot of time doing random stuff like inspecting every painting on the walls, talking to every person and animal I met, scouring every book in the library and getting frustrated trying to solve some of puzzles along the way. A very good game if you have a lot of patience but not if you don't.
I also found myself spending a lot of time on inventory management, partly due to the massive amounts of loot I picked up along the way and an individual inventory for each party member rather than a shared one. There is no way to select multiple items at the same time for transfer between one party member to the next, again a time-issue rather than a real game flaw.
Overall, I like it enough to buy the next game in the series but I really hope they do something about the puzzles and improve inventory management.

Noticed when it was published but bought it from the summer sale. I was looking for "cheap" full controller couch platformer, and boy did this deliver.
I admit nothing of tears for first 10 or so minutes of getting into the game. After that I spent a good while just jumping around trying to break animations - never managed. Instead level of detail in minor things like timing your jumps right makes your glowy fox thing spin off to next jump.. Yeah, details.
Game world, background, foreground.. Gorgeus. Foreground shadows moving gave me shivers.. Style reminds me of Trines' except slightly less colourful - bright, (mostly) easy to recognize enviromental hazards and enemies with proper contrast on dark 'ground', atmosphere in tons. One of the better soundtracks I've heard in games for very long time, guess previous
And this game really doesn't hold your hand through it. Only very few checkpoints with autosave - otherwise you'll have to pick a spot to save and use your energy for it. Wander too far without another save and swear when you've got to do it all again. Jumping puzzles are unforgiving. Miss a jump - you're dead. Don't move fast enough - you're dead. Try to move faster and miss the jump - you're very dead. Becomes a con at a part where you have to escape from water up the level. That's few minutes jumping, no pauses, no places to save on the way. Missing last jump is a rage worthy.
But same mechanics are used so well; after acquiring the skill you can pause time briefly to jump off enemy projectiles, or even enemies, bouncing them to opposite direction. Sometimes you're required to do it, sometimes it gets you up to secret spots - both cases you'll feel very proud of yourself for managing 10+ jump combo without killing the monsters required to keep jumping. Good timing and aim you can kill nasty strong monsters by kicking them into water or spikes.
So looking for something pretty to play on couch with a controller? Grab this one. Sit back, maybe have a drink, and enjoy.

What I love about the game is (you guessed it!) the planets and the animals. I’m constantly running into things that have me going “That’s so awesome!”. Everything looks so un-real and it does remind me of a classic Si-Fi a bit. And to me that is the whole point of the game. If someone bought this for any reason other than to explore planets and see new things: they shouldn’t have bought it.
There are some things that could be better. I wish there was more than 3 races (I guess 4 sentinels included). And I wish we had some quests where a faction would hire you to do something (maybe cargo run, ship defense, taking care of an enemy land base). This would work really well if there were all kinds of groups who all controlled their own part of the universe and had their own agendas.
Also, I wish all the buildings and space stations didn’t look the same.
Finally, there’s almost too much story for me. I know a lot of other people have the opposite problem (even though Sean Murray said there wouldn’t be too much of a story) but I just feel like the game tries to make you start heading to the center of the universe as that is the only way to unlock certain things (the atlas pass for example). You don’t have to, but there is a push in that direction that I don’t like. The only kind of story/quests I want are star-gate style ones where you come into a new area and there’s some kind of situation there for you to have fun with.
None of these things make the game worth a thumbs down or not worth playing. It is still incredibly fun. There’s a sense of progression as you upgrade your gear/ship, a nice amount of combat, and compelling worlds to explore; what else do you people want? And they’re still working on it to make it better despite all the negative reviews.
I think some people don’t like this but, even though the inventory is unrealistically big, it’s not so big that you can just horde stuff (at least at first) until you get a freighter so you have to decide what’s worth carrying and what isn’t. It’s awesome because it encourages players to find what they need (which is probably available in abundance) instead of just stockpiling it.
To a certain (large) extent I question the intelligence of
who gave this game a negative review. Normally it is ok for people to buy a game and, not liking it, give it. a negative review. However, in this case the (right now) 70% of people who gave this game a thumbs down are all pretty much wrong.
Now, I have read through some of the negative review and mostly they're written by people who either had unrealistic expectations about the game (in some cases expecting what Sean Murray said would not be included), people who are butt-hurt for no reason, and trolls who think they're funny (but aren’t). Some people are upset that certain of what was promised (apparently) didn’t make it into the game. I don’t, myself, know what all they're talking about specifically. I did not really follow the development of the game too closely but pretty much everything I saw promised made it. Or at least, everything that I was excited enough about to remember. And besides, even if we didn’t get everything that was promised, it is still an awesome game and deserves a big-ol’ thumbs up for that reason.
By the way the community guidelines say to not mean so I want to point out that this is my opinion so take it for what you will but I don't mean it in a mean or unkind way. Even if you disliked the game you *may* still be a good person in other ways :).
I don’t write reviews that often, but I had to write this one to show some support to the game. And besides, with all those negative reviews, if I didn’t write a positive review I’d be part of the problem. There are probably other points I could have touched on but this review is long enough and the main point is this: the game is awesome so buy it.

My introduction to PC gaming was when I was a kid and played Lego World. I remember the "free flow" gameplay and it set me up for life to enjoy gaming and Legos. So I own and have played every Lego game including those crappy ones. But when I heard that Lego was going to make a game that basicly ran like Minecraft I was sceptical about it because Minecraft is great at what it is. So how does Lego Worlds "STACK UP" (EEEHH EEEHHH :D )
It does a great job; now there is a long list of complaints about the gameplay and game features, but heres the thing I have to remember, this is an early alpha lego game, something not played before, so yeah things might suck at first but it will get better.
Pros:
-It is open world. Lego games have always been games about exploring the levels even, and so it's no supprise that this game does a great job.
- terra form tool. Where Minecraft you have to place every block individualy; unless you have a world edit mod installed, Lego Worlds has an entire tool menu that is just about terra forming the land, there are vehicals that help terra form as well.
-Vast number of different posibilities to build. As you explor the world you will find characters, structures, and different items that you will discover and they will unlock in your building menu. You can then spawn those items with the Lego Coins you collect.
- MY FAVORITE PART. BRICK PLACING. That is right you can actualy just place brick by brick and build your own structures, you have a lot of colors and every type of brick that has ever been created by Lego to use for your builds, it takes me back to being a kid building a brick house, the only difference is not I can make the house one color instead of having to throw yellow in certain places because I don't have enough red bricks.
Cons:
- Bugs. I will just state it, I'm not going to go into detail, because it is an early stages game so bugs are a given, and truth is there isn't that many that I have seen that go beyond a sound clip glitching for a few seconds.
- Targeting. Now in a 3rd person game targeting is a key mechanic and the issue is that there isn't really any kind of crosshair system, items just glow when it thinks you've aimed at them. can make for some frustration.
- The brick building feature could use a little work. It is fun my only complaint is there is a lot of button clicking to switch between deleting a misplaced brick and getting back to placing bricks, the camera isn't the smoothes so you will spend a little time working to get the right angle for your build.
In its current stage I give the game a solid 7 out of 10. But I see the potential of being a game that is a 9 out of 10, and again my complaints are really just the minor bugs and lack of features, but again its an early alpha game so its all a givin.

Sword & Sworcery is a highly experimental and artistic game, often too experimental for it's own good.
: Side scrolling & Exploration, with occasional Action & Puzzle elements.
: Fantasy
: Minimalism, Magic, Mythology
: Passing resemblance to Oxenfree and Kentucky Route Zero gameplay.
Given that it was quite an influential game (now the better part of a decade old), and given it's self-depreciating humour, it's odd that recent reviews have labelled Sword & Sworcery pretentious. I suppose it is quite grandiose at times, but in a way which I feel is engaging and works. It may be that it's bold, experimental nature combined with some lackluster design decisions has made it retrospectively appear pretentious, especially as much of the artistic novelty which offsets it's weaknesses has since been incorporated into other games.
In summary, it's artistically rich and design poor, yet I just have to recommend Sword & Sworcery because it's still a tonally unique, special experience to me.

The tacky pop-up buttons that look totally out of place? Gtradiant omn mouse clicks? The weird health stars that aren't pixel-art at all? If you're going for a style, by all means do so, but if your game is mostly just the look, sound, and aesthetic, well.. you gotta hammer that home.
The controls being entirely mouse-click based just felt kinda needlessly sluggish, and I was feeling punished for trying to explore around a bit. Nothing about the world immediately pulled me in, and while I may come back to it when I'm feeling in a more to play a game one-handed while my other hand props up my chin from almost-boredom, I'll giave it another shot. Maybe there's more to it, but nobody wants to find the "more to it" if there's not "something to it" from the get go. :(

I received Naval Action as a gift almost a year ago and have been playing it almost every day since (almost 1,000 hours in total). The graphics are great and, for the most part, the mechanics of sailing and battle well-implemented. However, the latest "update" turned an enjoyable game into a very frustrating experience. Here are some examples.
In the latest update, the logic for determining how many ships are docked in a port is greatly flawed. In short, if you buy a ship in one of your ports, that ship is counted as a docked ship in that port even though it is sailed to another port or sunk in enemy action. As a result, the number of ships you can actually dock in a port decreases over time as you buy ships in that port. I've seen it get as low as only one ship. (The logic in the previous version worked perfectly. I don't know why they changed it.)
In the previous version, friendly forts would fire on enemy ships when you were in battle mode. In the latest update, forts are useless in normal battles. Even if you lure an enemy ship within range of a friendly fort, the fort will not fire on the enemy ship.
Who can attack who is a total puzzle. Theoretically, you can attack any enemy ship or any ship carrying contraband. This seems to be true for ships controlled by artificial intelligence (NPCs or non-player characters). When confronting ships controlled by other players, it is not true. As far as I can tell, you can't attack another player's ship when it is carrying contraband even on the PVP (player vs player) servers.
Curiously, when selling goods, the dialog box sometimes tells you how much you will be getting and sometimes it doesn't.
Occasionally, the dialog for managing the crew throws you for a loop. Even though the dialog box indicates that your allocation of crew adds up to the number of crew currently available, when you click OK, an error dialog appears telling you that you don't have enough crew. When this happens, I cancel the dialog. When I reopen it, it tells me I have one less crew member than it told me that I had before.
Currently, there are two PVP servers and one PVE (player vs environment) server. The PVP servers are geared mostly to players who gather into clans so they can wreak havoc on other players or clans. On the PVE server, you can only fight NPC ships. What I would like to see is a PVP server without clans. I don't mind fighting other players but it is no fun to get ambushed by an armada of clan ships.
The previous version of the game provided your current coordinates when viewing the map. I realize that there is some controversy over this feature, but even in the age of sail, mariners had a least some idea of where they were. This is gone in the new version. As a result, you have no way of knowing even approximately where you are on a long open-sea voyage or when you are stuck in a fog-bound storm (as I once was for 3 solid days of game time). The complete absence of information regarding your present position is not accurate even for a sailing simulator and totally inappropriate for a game.
Even the trading aspect of the game is seriously flawed. For example, even after paying for an oak forest, the cost of just harvesting the logs was higher than the amount for which I could sell the harvested logs anywhere on the map.

Story 10/10
Gameplay 10/10
Music 11/10
Art 10/10
Challenge 10/10

Storyline is heartwrenching in parts, and just beautiful in others. Without spoilers hard to go too deep into it, but it's well told and doesn't interrupt the gameplay, which keeps it immersive. I'm  not sure how other games I play from now on will stack up. Seriously.
Gameplay mechanics get progressively deeper as the game goes on. Zelda-esque in the way some objectives are blocked off until you get the necessary skills to get to it. Agile fingers are required! Keeps you guessing too... one section, you get gravity changes, and it's sorta out of left field and only for that one section, but introduced in such a way that it's just another challenge and not super frustrating.
This music, though... pretty much inspired. Buy the soundtrack. Seriously. If you like game OSTs, this one will treat you very well.
The art speaks for itself. The crazy bit is, it's throughout the game. The cutscenes and the gameplay all use the same, deep, beautiful art. Usually in a game you just focus on the foreground art, and you -maybe- get some textures for the background. This game, though, sometimes you need to pause and look at the background art, because the scenery is amazing. The level of detail is breathtaking.
And it's challenging. Not so challenging that you get frustrated. If you die, there is NO LOAD SCREEN. You end up at your last save point, immediately, and get to keep going. You can save (nearly) freely, and the skills (can) help you out there. However, there are places you can't save, of course, and some platform parts are instant death if you mess up even once. Learning how enemies act when you're forced to drop in on them because of the terrain can be interesting. Anyway, the overall experience is great, because when you get past a challenge, you feel satisfied, sometimes relieved. And then you save.
The combat system was very decent, but if I had to pick a weak point it would have to be here. After you get bash, all enemies are laughable, and they pretty quickly turn into just another way of getting around faster. Still, early on there is a bit of a challenge, and they do provide an obstacle. The rollers are especially annoying before you get bash. It doesn't matter though, as an addition to the platforming challenge it functions exceptionally well.
Overall 10/10 Zero regrets buying this game (and on the summer sale too!) If I were you, I'd start throwing my money at the screen until good things happen.

Don't expect a masterpiece, but expect a bit of fun.
The story is not deep and well-developed but ends on an interesting cliffhanger, albeit one that has not been acted on after 6 years. The characters are similarly not deep and don't undergo an awful lot of development.
However, the gameplay is quite a lot of fun. Your weapons improve over time and you can select a variety of armaments, either going full smash squish hammer explosions or preferring long distance precision marksmanship squishing. The melee executions are absolute overkill, and on the higher difficulties it really does get quite challenging facing swarms of Orks and Chaos Marines.
For a 6-year-old game the graphics are pretty good maxed out, but aren't the best in optimisation. Before I upgraded to a 1060 6GB, my old 750ti 2GB got about 50-60 fps roaming, 40-50 in intense fight sequences when on max settings.
The multiplayer, as is to be expected with a 6-year-old game that was never particularly huge in the first place, is pretty dead. Don't expect to get much, if anything, out of it.
As I said before, the game isn't a masterpiece, but it's certainly pretty darn fun, and on easy, pulverising those squishy Orks really is a great way to vent out your anger.
In concurrence with RPS, I rate it a solid 7/10.

Man this game is good. Real good. It's got great music, and the visuals are stunning. It's a platformer that tells a story you can actually kind of give a crap about. That's because it takes the smart path of telling you just enough. It doesn't try to beat you over the head with some obtuse tales; instead it introduces you to a few characters that you'll care about by the end of the game as you see them change.
Even after all the artsy fartsy stuff, this game is a solid platformer. In a game about a rabbit thingy that you think would be a cake-walk, there were numerous intense platforming sections that I failed at over and over. Not because of bad design. Actually the opposite: the levels are very well designed, they just expect a lot from the player. For a game that looks casual, I can imagine some casual gamers, or at least those not into platformers, might feel it a bit too difficult.
The one thing that made me nervous was the auto-aim. I was afriad at first that it would make killing enemies too easy. However, the game makes up for this because enemies have EXTREMELY GOOD aim. If you're next to an enemy that can shoot and you sit still for even a second or two, you're going to be dead. Beacuse of this and the auto-aim, areas with multiple enemies can feel a bit like mini bullet-hell levels, where you momentarily focus only on projectiles and dogding them while continuing to mash the fire button.
All in all, this game is super solid. I'd say the only people who shouldn't play it are people who completely hate platforming games or are exceptionally bad at them. I took about 8 hours to finish, but if you really speed through, you could probably finish it in 6ish hours.
