I bought No Man's Sky just after its first major update, and have been playing it - a lot - while recovering from major surgery.  I'm really bored, but compelled, too. I'm compelled partly because I'm a game dev major and it's fascinating trying to figure out what went right, and what went wrong (so far) with this game.
There's so much potential to this game. It could be epic. But it's not because, at its core, the game is out of balance. The content provided by the devs in no way matches the vastness of the game universe and the potential for discovery. What is the point, I wonder, of providing a seemingly endless galaxy to explore, if you only provide enough unique dialogue, equipment upgrade, etc., for a much more limited game? In a word, this game lacks an overall story arc; it lacks game design. It's fun to be lost or aimless in space for a little while; but it's more fun when you get your bearings. By that time, though, boredom will have begun creeping in.
Positives:
*  It's a beautiful game a lot of the time. Kudos to the color theory expert on the team.
* The sound is good, although I find the Gek alien voices annoying.
* Scanning life forms on planets is a cool and fun idea. The game is not based soley on survival and crafting. Exploration has a purpose. That said, it's more of an inferred purpose; there seems to be no concrete objective related to it other than impressing Polo and getting units for everything you scan.
*  Being able to fly through space and land directly on planets is a lot of fun.
* Base building is fun, but why can we have only one base? Why are the base sizes so limited?
* Being able to explore endless planets is a lot of fun, but just try getting back to a planet you like once you've strayed too far from it.
* Building up your vocabulary for the alien races you encounter is a very unique idea, but again, it's out of balance. By the time you build up even a small vocabulary, the game will have started repeating itself in every respect, so you'll be bored, and there's no real purpose that one can ascertain.
* The little number sequence puzzles are nice; sometimes overly simple, but that's okay.
* The animal life is sometimes quite enchanting. Sometimes it seems as if Hieronymous Bosch meets Keith Haring
Negatives:
* There is no story whatsoever. There's no sense of what you're doing in this universe, who you are, why you're there, what you want. You play as an inferior being, apparently. One gets the sense, slowly, that he/she is chosen to fullfil some electro-spiritual quest for oneness in a sea of unbridled capitalism...
* On every planet, regardless of the star system, everything is the same. The flora and fauna may be different, but the buildings, the dialogues, et al, all the same. There are no cities to encounter, which is really weird, and a huge oversight as far as I'm concerned. Cities or other gathering places (besides space stations) would add a whole new layer of depth to the game. Cities with people who might need help performing tasks. Give me a reason to seek out specific planets. Maybe this notion wouldn't work with the procedurally generated monotony.
* The Foundation update provided some goals for the player. But alas, these end all too soon. Your hirelings will, one by one, announce they've got nothing left to teach you. At this point the game becomes purely economic in scope. It's a really good start, though. It's hard to imagine playing this game without at least that.
* My status with the various races is endlessly increasing, but to no apparent end. Once I reached certain levels, there seems to be no higher I can go, and there are few, if any, benefits to my increasing status. The sad thing about this is that it remains one of the few goals left in the game after you've acquired all the blue prints and all of the formulas, and once you've exhausted all of the unique dialogue. The thing is, you get all of this stuff before you've even gotten to the blue or violet star systems, probably. You can look forward to those systems, but if they are anything like th Red and Green and Yellow star systems, they will only offer more identical experiences. The ships with Theta warp drives installed are really expensive if they have a reasonable number of storage slots. Even with a prettye big farming operation, it will take a while to raise the many millions one will need to buy a good ship.
* The Atlas passes are too damn hard to find, and no clue is provided in the game as to how one might locate them.
*Once you get the Atlas passes, after way, way too much effort, the reward is...voila!...more of the same stuff you find everywhere. The Atlas passes do not unlock any mysteries, any levels, any extra cool gear, or whatever else might be worthy of such a tedious and mysterious route to gaining the passes in the first place.
* The UI is seriously slow and intrusive. It takes over the screen, and removes player control while the cinematic UI scenes are unfolding. However, drones can still attack you while you're trapped in a UI vortex from which there is no fast escape. Also, what is with the blinding white screen everytime we save a new location? Are we not doing enough damage to our vision by staring at the game screen so long in the first place? Everything UI and HUD needs to happen a lot faster.
BUGS:
* When I teleport to my base, game play drags for several minutes. Same can happen if I load a former save from any location. My PC is a fairly powerful MSI gaming device wtih an i7 and lots of RAM, so it's hard to imagine that it's my machine causing the problem.
* When I return to my home planet and base, one of the ladders I placed to reach a second floor is always closed at the top. The only way I can deal with it is to delete and rebuild the ladder. Every time.
All of the above notwithstanding, this is a really GREAT foundation for an epic game. I hope the developers will continue crafting this. They need to expand content and get a few quest lines in the game pronto. Adding these features will only enhance one's rambling and haphazard journey toward convergence. I haven't reached the end yet. Maybe it all becomes clear by that time. But there's a great danger I'll simply get too bored with the monotony of the game to ever get that far.

Sometimes, second impressions are more important than the first...
I picked this game up last year, not long after finally playing "Divine Divinity", which quickly became a favorite of mine, due to the off-kilter writing, challenging and free-form battles, and stellar atmosphere and audio. With all the buzz around the latest Divinity and overwhelmingly positive reviews, I finally plunked down the premium price for the game, and entered a world of initial disappointment: The complex mechanics, challenging difficulty , and voice acting that comes out of all corners, on top of convoluted quests seemed to be a bit too much for me at the time. I put several hours into the game and then shelved it, rather disappointed. I couldn't see how the game received such overwhelming reviews with what a mess it seemed to be at the time. Fast forward about a year later, and I give it another whirl, just on a hunch...that maybe, just maybe I'd be able to find it more palatable this time. I'm sure glad I gave it another go. After reading up a bit more on the game's mechanics and stats, I started with an open mind and a brand new character. I decided to devote a good four or five hours into my first session back and really get a good undertstanding of what's going on, and that's when it just *clicked* for me. The attention to every detail, every line in conversation, every battle, every creature, scroll, skill book, ingredient and object you can interact with is unparalleled. This game gives me the same feeling I got when playing Ultima VI and Wizardry V back in the day...you want to keep exploring, learning, experimenting, and not stop playing. I'm 40 years old and have many responsibilities in life, yet I've found "Divinity: Original Sin" keeping me up until the wee hours of the morning, going to work exhausted, telling myself "I'll take a break from it tonight", but going back to play again and again. I've put about 30 hours into this play through so far and I feel I'm just scratching the surface. The writing takes some of the fantasy stereotypes and rewrites them in such a way that makes them unpredictable. Once you understand the battle mechanics and the different ways you can win a fight, it becomes very rewarding. Plenty of loot in the game, even the seemingly useless items can obtain value by crafting or sellling for a few extra gold pieces. Speaking of selling: most random NPC's you can trade with, which is a great touch: just like in real life, most people will have some sort of currency or item you'd want. Digging graves, making traps explode, talking with animals, setting random things on fire, breaking into inn rooms, the list of things to do goes on and on...and unlike a lot of RPG's, none of it feels like "filler" or busy work. I'm very much looking forward to checking out the sequel when it's officially released in later 2017. For now, I see "Divinity: OSEE" keeping me plenty of busy, and rewarded, until that time.

I have been playing Divinity: Original Sin - Enhanced edition (D:OS) with a friend, so the review is solely on the perspective of co-op gaming. Also, we have *not* played the game in hardcore (permanent death of a party) mode. The option exists though, and as much as I love roguelikes, sinking tens of hours to a story which does not really change just to erase the progress due a stupid mistake of blowing yourself up or accidentally picking a fight with a wrong NPC is not fun -I've done it before.
We have not completed the game yet, but we've had a blast playing through so far. I've been playing with a controller (Playstation 3 (PS3) controller) and my friend is using keyboard + mouse (kb+m), so keep that in mind.
Playing with the controller takes a little bit of getting used to, but it works pretty well. I'm used to see x-box controls in every game which supports controllers, but in D:OS you can swap the controller layout to use playstation controller. You can't use mouse on-the-fly to hover over buffs and debuffs or for precision which is a small setback. You can do pretty much everything with controller (and, actually, a bit more) than with kb+m. For example, a small item on the ground is next to impossible to target with a controller. This has been accounted for and thus there is an area-loot command (when using controller, apparently there isn't with kb+m). This lets you to interact with items and objects around your character in an set area without meticulously trying to target the object or item with the controller.
We've not encountered any crashes or glitches, the performance is great and solid, so nothing to nitpick about that.
The game is real fun! There is a lot of choises to make along your adventure, and playing with a friend brings another layer of choises you need to respect and think about. We don't reload the game even if we do a stupid, wrong or immoral choise so they might bite your ankle, as they should. Most of the non-player-controlled (NPC) characters feels alive, and they have a personality. You can read the NPC characters traits pretty well just how they talk to you and what -more importantly how- they're speaking to your character. You can burn bridges, form bonds and be mischievous if that is what you wish.
Every level up feels powerful so far. My character is a two-handed weapon wielding dude, my friend is playing a summoner mage. Smacking enemies faces in with huge critical hits feels really satisfying and missing a clear swing is a real frustration every time and certainly can swing the battle out of your favour pretty quickly. The types of enemies are consistent (for example, you learn that zombie is a zombie and has zombies traits and zombies to come does have the same traits). The visualization of enemies and monsters is clear, most of the enemies look just like they are. You can tell with a glimpse if the enemy is a human, orc, zombie or whatever it happens to be.
Pacing of the game gets tedious at times, but overall it's quite balanced. When you just are getting bored of the dialogues and running from a to b, the story does progress in a way which gives you something entirely different to do -be it sneaking, combat or whatever.
All in all, I heartily do recommend Divinity Original Sin. I can't speak for the single player experience, but if you have a friend to play with the game is really fun!

A fun indie god/creator style game that is refreshingly new in the way of gameplay and graphics, inspired by the likes of Civilization but also by the Binding of Isaac in some retrospects. Playing as up to four diffrent god-like beings, to create a new world for humanity to settle, it makes for a refreshing and relaxing game, occasioanlly stressful if you've bitten off more that you can chew as humanity develops out of control.
An enjoyable and fun game to sink many hours of your life.

Note: This game, though thoroughly enjoyable, is not a god game in the sense most gamers are used to. While you do play a godlike being in charge of building a world, little of the game involves direct interaction with the population. You will seldom use attacks on cities or armies.
Recommendation: If you like puzzles involving synergy, this game is for you. Each resource has a certain bonus effect that occurs when conditions are right, and the vast majority of gameplay is spent figuring out how to maximize synergistic outputs. For some projects, these synergies must be very precisely managed indeed. Often success comes down to a single configuration of resources boosted precisely by aspects.
When you start play, most of the resources will not be available, along with the 60 minute and 120 minute game modes. Completing a variety of objectives unlocks the resources you will need to complete the hardest projects. Objectives can only be completed during the regular game modes, but you are free to experiment at any time in the 'Alt' mode, where a number of conditions will make the game easier to mess around with.
I found this game very fun and entirely worth the $5 or so I spent on it when it was on sale. It took me about 50 hours to unlock every resource, and I may still go back to complete the 60 minute challenge achievements at a later time. There are a few errors in the printed synergies. For instance, a Snow Leopard will gain the listed gold and danger boosted for each zinc or silver in range, not just once. (Exploit this if you want a gigantic amount of gold and danger from one Snow Leopard.)
Greed can be frustratingly hard to combat. However, with careful play, greed is usually completely avoidable. Keep danger high, or keep the resource gain under the awe. Never let greed go above 3 if you can help it.

But in this game you don’t control a giant benevolent hand, able to squish your people between thumb and forefinger. I’m going to call them titans since every time I play the game, I imagine the guys from Hercules.
Reus is very fun and by setting a strict time limit on each game, you don’t get carried away spending hours trying to perfect your planetoid, or trying to perfect a single village… which never happens since they inevitably get too greedy and turn on your, despite the generations of aid you have provided them.

Sid Meier's Pirates is still really immersive to this day. I owned it on PC for years, and also on the PlayStation Portable. If you let yourself get immersed in it, it is a really fun experience. Even with how simple the game is, you have a different experience every single game. You can do anything you want at the start. You wanna defeat pirates? Go ahead! Date an Emperor's daughter? Do it! There is no limitations, but the game progresses very well no matter what you do! The greatest part is that the gameplay is very satisfying. Sid Meier's games are usually very proficient on that front. You can spam stuff for combat on easier modes, but on the harder modes you have to try to guess your opponents moves. The difficulty can be grueling for some players on higher levels. So you have a great challenge if you really want it. If you wish to do everything without hassle, you can always play on an easy difficulty and still have an entertaining game.
I learned the controls of this game so easily. The only thing I can really say is if your keyboard does not have a number pad, this game will control much more difficultly, and the dancing minigame will be borderline-unplayable since you have to use the mouse for it. Though it is avoidable, as you do not have to do it. The graphics might seem a bit dated to some, but I never had any immersion lost because of them. They are good enough for what the game is.
This game is hardly demanding of your PC. I could almost imagine any PC could run it, unless your PC is a really old Windows 98 one or something. If you don't have a gaming computer to game on, this is a perfect game for your computer. Very fun, looks great for what it is, and you are getting a game with a ton of replay value. There is way more to do in this game than it feels like. Most of the time I feel like I have done everything, I retire, and realized I missed a couple of things. For a game that is 13 years old and counting, it has aged like fine cheese and wine. Alike cheese and wine, this game lets you lose yourself and enjoy being the pirate of legends.

I bought No Man's Sky just after its first major update, and have been playing it - a lot - while recovering from major surgery.  I'm really bored, but compelled, too. I'm compelled partly because I'm a game dev major and it's fascinating trying to figure out what went right, and what went wrong (so far) with this game.
There's so much potential to this game. It could be epic. But it's not because, at its core, the game is out of balance. The content provided by the devs in no way matches the vastness of the game universe and the potential for discovery. What is the point, I wonder, of providing a seemingly endless galaxy to explore, if you only provide enough unique dialogue, equipment upgrade, etc., for a much more limited game? In a word, this game lacks an overall story arc; it lacks game design. It's fun to be lost or aimless in space for a little while; but it's more fun when you get your bearings. By that time, though, boredom will have begun creeping in.
Positives:
*  It's a beautiful game a lot of the time. Kudos to the color theory expert on the team.
* The sound is good, although I find the Gek alien voices annoying.
* Scanning life forms on planets is a cool and fun idea. The game is not based soley on survival and crafting. Exploration has a purpose. That said, it's more of an inferred purpose; there seems to be no concrete objective related to it other than impressing Polo and getting units for everything you scan.
*  Being able to fly through space and land directly on planets is a lot of fun.
* Base building is fun, but why can we have only one base? Why are the base sizes so limited?
* Being able to explore endless planets is a lot of fun, but just try getting back to a planet you like once you've strayed too far from it.
* Building up your vocabulary for the alien races you encounter is a very unique idea, but again, it's out of balance. By the time you build up even a small vocabulary, the game will have started repeating itself in every respect, so you'll be bored, and there's no real purpose that one can ascertain.
* The little number sequence puzzles are nice; sometimes overly simple, but that's okay.
* The animal life is sometimes quite enchanting. Sometimes it seems as if Hieronymous Bosch meets Keith Haring
Negatives:
* There is no story whatsoever. There's no sense of what you're doing in this universe, who you are, why you're there, what you want. You play as an inferior being, apparently. One gets the sense, slowly, that he/she is chosen to fullfil some electro-spiritual quest for oneness in a sea of unbridled capitalism...
* On every planet, regardless of the star system, everything is the same. The flora and fauna may be different, but the buildings, the dialogues, et al, all the same. There are no cities to encounter, which is really weird, and a huge oversight as far as I'm concerned. Cities or other gathering places (besides space stations) would add a whole new layer of depth to the game. Cities with people who might need help performing tasks. Give me a reason to seek out specific planets. Maybe this notion wouldn't work with the procedurally generated monotony.
* The Foundation update provided some goals for the player. But alas, these end all too soon. Your hirelings will, one by one, announce they've got nothing left to teach you. At this point the game becomes purely economic in scope. It's a really good start, though. It's hard to imagine playing this game without at least that.
* My status with the various races is endlessly increasing, but to no apparent end. Once I reached certain levels, there seems to be no higher I can go, and there are few, if any, benefits to my increasing status. The sad thing about this is that it remains one of the few goals left in the game after you've acquired all the blue prints and all of the formulas, and once you've exhausted all of the unique dialogue. The thing is, you get all of this stuff before you've even gotten to the blue or violet star systems, probably. You can look forward to those systems, but if they are anything like th Red and Green and Yellow star systems, they will only offer more identical experiences. The ships with Theta warp drives installed are really expensive if they have a reasonable number of storage slots. Even with a prettye big farming operation, it will take a while to raise the many millions one will need to buy a good ship.
* The Atlas passes are too damn hard to find, and no clue is provided in the game as to how one might locate them.
*Once you get the Atlas passes, after way, way too much effort, the reward is...voila!...more of the same stuff you find everywhere. The Atlas passes do not unlock any mysteries, any levels, any extra cool gear, or whatever else might be worthy of such a tedious and mysterious route to gaining the passes in the first place.
* The UI is seriously slow and intrusive. It takes over the screen, and removes player control while the cinematic UI scenes are unfolding. However, drones can still attack you while you're trapped in a UI vortex from which there is no fast escape. Also, what is with the blinding white screen everytime we save a new location? Are we not doing enough damage to our vision by staring at the game screen so long in the first place? Everything UI and HUD needs to happen a lot faster.
BUGS:
* When I teleport to my base, game play drags for several minutes. Same can happen if I load a former save from any location. My PC is a fairly powerful MSI gaming device wtih an i7 and lots of RAM, so it's hard to imagine that it's my machine causing the problem.
* When I return to my home planet and base, one of the ladders I placed to reach a second floor is always closed at the top. The only way I can deal with it is to delete and rebuild the ladder. Every time.
All of the above notwithstanding, this is a really GREAT foundation for an epic game. I hope the developers will continue crafting this. They need to expand content and get a few quest lines in the game pronto. Adding these features will only enhance one's rambling and haphazard journey toward convergence. I haven't reached the end yet. Maybe it all becomes clear by that time. But there's a great danger I'll simply get too bored with the monotony of the game to ever get that far.

I HATE PLATFORMERS. I HAAAATTEEEEE THEM.
These days, there's a LOT of ridiculous games on steam...and especially a lot of lame platformers. It's gotten so bad until even beautiful visuals are no promise either; far from it in fact. For some reason, iOS devs think as long as the game looks good, then boring, dunce-like gameplay is fine. The lame part is how people constantly fall for this garbage.
Enter Ori & The Blind Forest:
This is hands-down THE MOST beautiful hand-drawn platformer in existance. Trust me...I've done the research. The only game perhaps coming close is Odin Sphere or King's Crown. Dust: An Elysian Tale are close, but clearly second to the level of polish this game has. Pretend Meat Boy & Portal had a kid who decided to go off to college to do his own thing, but still kinda listens to his parents while he's away -- that's EXACTLY this game. The controls are fluid/soft, yet tight & the platforming has some instances where you need to think a bit more laterally than you otherwise would. Nothing as crazy as portal (despite having a fun portal section), but certainly some very refreshing mechanics to take note of.
This game isn't a pushover, but it's not hard either. It's moreso a moderate mini-puzzle platformer. A great game to relax with and unwind, while still getting the same pleasure you would from a "more complicated" game. Further complimented by an INCREDIBLE move called "bash," you can burst around the screen at great speeds slingshotting off projectiles and enemies -- or sometimes both. Think dishonored's blink that Daud had or Mark of the Ninja's Grappling hook...but on MASSIVE CRACK. Essentially a speedrunners wet dream. I had oodles of fun with it & it never got old. When you play, there's gonna be this one part you'll never forget in terms of gaming experiences, trust me. You'll love it.
The only real big qualm I had with it gameplay-wise was that it had no boss fights...and oddly enough I hate bosses in games. Contrary to my normal MO...I wanted more, but sadly just got grunt enemies. Didn't cut down satisfaction too much, but I would've really enjoyed that. I'd liken it to a Fitting dinner...but would've been made better by a sublime dessert after
While I absolutely LOVEEEEEEDDD this game and will play it again at least 2 more times back to back...I still don't feel like it's worth $20 entry. A couple features are lacking to substantiate such a thing. You're not allowed to re-enter your completed game and 100% it...which was done purposefully, but they could easily make the completed save a "memory" that Ori dives back into to fit the lore. Also aside from the game being fun, there's no incentive to replay. Also, a number of areas are super fun to do over & over...but there's no way to do them outside of an actual save/campaign. I could go on & on about things missed, but that'll be another video.
If you've a choice of a gift or can get this discounted around $15 or $10, definitely get it. If you've got money burning in your pocket & nothing to do, then for sure nab this. We NEED A SEQUEL MOON STUDIOS. PLEASE.
There are a number of things with this game that urk me, but none of them truly detract from the whole experience. When you play, be sure to get some good headphones. You'll need them ;)

TL;DR This is a frail attempt at a "2deep4u" sound-art based exploration adventure game complete with horrid combat, inconsistent visuals, and an entirely unremarkable soundtrack. Your time is legitimately better spent on another game.  2/10
To get into why without examining every little detail of the game, let me break this down into the main components and try to keep it short.
This game starts off immediately making references to the Zelda franchise to the point of directly using the phrase "skyward sword" and having the main objective of power be the "trigon trifecta" which is literally just the Triforce. You didn't even try. Also of note are the very direct and out of place fourth wall breaks where the player is directly addressed and at some point even complimented for playing. Modern lingo and objects makes the player all too aware that the writer (I'm assuming Jim Guthrie, the singer-songwriter behind this) thought he was being very cool and unique, using terms like "dude", calling the female character "Girl", and even having a pixel version of himself playing a rock show in game complete with huge modern speaker systems surrounded by people who live in log huts. Social media is forced down the players throat at the very beginning of the game encouraging them to tweet some of these awful "this is so deep" quotes out to the world and while optional, put a huge stain on any game even having these buttons present.
Since this is a big selling point the game tries to stand on, it ought to be quite beautiful, and in some areas it actually is decent. The starting meadow is quite peaceful and beatiful and with the soothing soundtrack playing I thought I was in for something good. Shapes were recognizable enough despite being very blocky, people looked simply like abstracted people and that's perfectly ok. I noticed very early on however that the inconsistencies with the art are not limited to UI elements. The trigons (just triangles) the game seems so very focused on were very obviously out of place with no pixelation to have them settle into the motif. And this was even worse with these ugly gradiants on many of the entities such as the sprites and the evil spirit, and even all over many of the effects in the game. The record with the Triforce on it is a very poor quality image complimented by the awful MSPaint star effect that it rests on when activated. Let me do a small sin and compare this to another recent pixel art game, Hyper Light Drifter. Whereas character animations in HLD move fluidly, with intent but natural, SSSEP is slow, clunky, very uninventive, and (as dumb as it may sound) blocky. The same  can be said of some of the effects animations as well, those that were'nt gradiants at least. Overall the sort of soothing and calm atmosphere it tries to build is lost by the lack of technical ability to make a pixelated world really spring to life.
The other main selling point of the game is of course the soundtrack as this is some sort of experimental hybrid EP and video game. Some of the soundscapes were quite pretty and added an enjoyable element to the scenery. The little blurb the sprites make when you click to make them ascend I found to be quite pleasing. The main body of the music however is entirely lackluster. Simple patterns are made up of alright guitar and very poor synth sections, sometimes broken up by simple drum loops. The EP (actually a 27 song, just over an hour long
) adds essentially nothing to the music you've already heard playing the game, just that there's slightly less looping of the same sections. The sound effects themselves are pretty much alright alone but again suffer from massive inconsistency where a bitcrushed fight engaging sound takes place right next to an enemy dog growling that seems like it's just some stock recording. Some sounds even seem like a post production element was added to make them sound like they were bitcrushed. One of the worst offenses in this category though is that at one point the relatively silent Logfella just starts giving this awfully acted monologue rattling off about being boring or something, and it shocked the hell out of me, I could not believe it was that poorly done and out of place. Other than that dialogue is restricted to grunts, humming, and the occasional "Hey" which is brief enough not to be silly.
Whoo boy. This is some of the worst mechanical and gameplay design I've ever seen in a game. I understand this was made also with tablet/phone gaming in mind but oh god. Every combat section in the game is very literally just a QTE. Controls are just point and click, this isn't bad in itself but some things are painful. Movement is very unintuitive but there's so little of it since paths are just straight lines most of the time. You can't open your item menu without stopping your character's movement, and every menu in the game is slow. Opening the book takes ages, complimented only by the poor design where messages are chronologically recorded backwards but only in breif periods. You move so slowly across the screen even when "fast" moving to an exit. And this is made even worse by the fact that some areas have scripted cutscenes that must play as you enter, every time. One of the worst things out of all of the mechanics is that you have the option to "play the game as it was meant to be played" and wait for the literal phases of Earth's moon to change the phase of the in game moon to progress. You can access a room in game to change it luckily or this review would be very short. You can also change the clock on your PC or device, but the game will record change and give you only 99% completion when finished.
I definitely failed to keep this review short but it's relatively short compared to all that I thought about writing. Also whoever drew and animated a bear-man's twig-n-berries, you know that was unnecessary.

A very average, if not slightly below average action game. However, this game is set in one of the most extensive and engaging universes I have ever come across, known as Warhammer: 40,000. As a fan of Warhammer 40k, this game does some very good justice to the franchise, but all while being just an average action game. It has a decent story, with some twists. Ultimately, this is an awesome Warhammer 40k game, and an average action game. There are some very entertaining and cool sequences, in between long stretching and bland areas. Overall, I recommend this game to Warhammer 40k fans, and encourage anyone who does not know about Warhammer 40k to look into it, and then come back and play this another time :) 7/10
Just some closing remarks: I do wish that the orks has been presented a little bit better and more varied, you will kill probably 500 ork boyz that all look exactly the same and have the 3 same voice lines. Now there are other "specialty" ork enemies for you to fight. Also, the kinda goofy humorous side of orks was not really shown. The best part about Orks in 40k for me is that while they are serious fighters and a brutal threat, they also are goofy. There is a way to incorporate both, but they decided to only show off the "bloodthirsty monster" side of orks. A bit of a bummer, but not a deal breaker. The second "faction" of enemies you encounter fight you much differently (ranged), and makes for a very nice change of pace after killing hundreds of orks. Not to mention they look very cool :) The final boss is a QTE event, which by itself is not a deal breaker for me, but on the hardest difficulty this QTE event was bland, easy, and not even visually interesting. Dissapointing ending fight.

Don't expect a masterpiece, but expect a bit of fun.
The story is not deep and well-developed but ends on an interesting cliffhanger, albeit one that has not been acted on after 6 years. The characters are similarly not deep and don't undergo an awful lot of development.
However, the gameplay is quite a lot of fun. Your weapons improve over time and you can select a variety of armaments, either going full smash squish hammer explosions or preferring long distance precision marksmanship squishing. The melee executions are absolute overkill, and on the higher difficulties it really does get quite challenging facing swarms of Orks and Chaos Marines.
For a 6-year-old game the graphics are pretty good maxed out, but aren't the best in optimisation. Before I upgraded to a 1060 6GB, my old 750ti 2GB got about 50-60 fps roaming, 40-50 in intense fight sequences when on max settings.
The multiplayer, as is to be expected with a 6-year-old game that was never particularly huge in the first place, is pretty dead. Don't expect to get much, if anything, out of it.
As I said before, the game isn't a masterpiece, but it's certainly pretty darn fun, and on easy, pulverising those squishy Orks really is a great way to vent out your anger.
In concurrence with RPS, I rate it a solid 7/10.

This is by far the greatest Dawn of War game I've ever encountered.
It has everything that a Warhammer 40000 fan needs:
1) Outstanding story line
2) Perfect graphic design solutions
3) All necessary slasher game mechanics, including spectacular (and extremely brutal) execution of low hp enemies
4) Incredible multiplayer with Co-op mode "Extreminatus", where you massacre hundreds of orks (literally) and can feel how it is like to be a true Emperor's Angel of Death
5) Challenging (but not extreme) hard mode in single player Campaign
6) Multiplayer character visual customization, where you can set any chapter and apply any type of armor you want (but armor should be unlocked through multiplayer achievements)
7) And of course... rivers of CRIMSON RED BLOOD
But even though it is an outstanding game, it definitely could use some changes:
- Lack of people in multiplayer due to a poor advertisement campaign
- No killing blows or executions in multiplayer
- No extreme difficulty in single player campaign
- Could use some new game regimes as for example Co-op seige of an Adeptus Mechanicus fortress including a party of 4 players with a group of AI Imperial Guard on their side (just my personal suggestion)
- The price of the game has grown TOO high (when it was released it had less than half a cost it has now).
To sum all things up, I would say that if you are a DoW fan and you have 2-3 friends who share your interest, this game is 100% recommended for purchase.

I bought this game years ago and only put a few hours on it simply because I didn't have any time at the time I purchased it.  So after a recent playthough with fresh eyes I have to say this game is still good. I will compare the good with the bad below.
The Good
The gameplay is somewhat arcade style shoot em up, and hack and slash... but it is awesome at it, and it does do exactly what you want it to do. The game gives you the perspective of being one of the baddest military soldiers in the universe. One that has waged countless wars in ever ongoing combat and still just thinks it is just another day. The space marine allows you to play as a ranged combat specialist if you so choose, but that is not where I would say the game excels. For you to get the real feel of the rage, the aggressiveness, and brutality that is the satirical world of Warhammer, you have to wade into the melee combat of the game and get your hands dirty with the blood of a thousand Orks.
Nothing makes you change your perspective on your days playing wow, starcraft, or other warhammer titles like when you stun and ork, then grab him one armed pick him up then body slam him and finally for the finisher step on his head which explodes like watermelon on an old Gallagher comedy night. THAT RIGHT THERE IS HOW YOU KILL AN ORK! I heard myself saying. No other game that I have played gave that absolute sense of well done, as when you make it through a huge onslaught of orks, and finally execute the last one.
So for pure action, and gameplay fun, I give it a 10/10.
The musical score is epic and fully orchestral so it sounds great, the voice acting is top notch, with major Hollywood actors doing the voiceovers and the game plays perfectly without flaw.
The Bad
The storyline is good lets say 6/10, and extraordinarily linear almost like a COD game. This is not entirely bad, but you cannot focus on the story to make you want to replay the game since by the 6 or 7th playthough, you can speak the lines yourself. The game features a very consolish style of saving content. You know what I mean, it auto save's every so often and then tells you you will lose progress if you quit playing... and honestly, you will want to keep playing this game, but because it has an 8 hour story or so, you can no life through the content rather quickly, and after playing for 6 or 7 hours straight feel a bit fatigued, not by the game, but by the repetition that a space marine must feel after killing thousands of orks and seeing no end in sight.
So on that front, I would say the game designers could have given the player a bit more dialog, and even side quest or something to prevent that feeling from becoming prominent. The way I see it, I can play for around 4 or 5 hours, and not feel fatigued, so I should manage my own experience and keep it positive.
So overall I would recommend this game. It does exactly what it is supposed to do. The small exception that I can see is that you must manage your own expectations and not overdo the game too much or it will become boring or disappointing when it is not the game, it is you.

Ori and the Blind Forest proves video games can be art. The graphics have touches of genre classics like Metroid and Rayman, but also of animation giants like Gibli, Disney and Dreamworks. Ori is a typical Metroidvania platformer at its core, but it's the presentation that sets it apart. Not only is it the most visually stunning 2D platformer I have ever played, it also knows how to tell a simple yet moving story through short cut-scenes. The story isn't very complex, but the way it is told makes the player emotionally invested in Ori's quest. The soundtrack is equally fantastic. The forest of Nibel feels like it once was alive, but now in decay. What still lives is mean and tries to kill you. The art direction is phenomenal !
You play as Ori, a forest creature that looks like a cross between a squirrel and a monkey and is accompanied by Sein, a spirit obviously inspired by Zelda's Navi. While the gameplay is fairly standard Metroidvania fare - you explore a side-scrolling 2D world, collecting new powers to open up new areas - there's some original concepts as well. One of the most vital parts of exploring the forest of Nibel comes in the form of Bash, a move that allows Ori to launch himself along falling objects, enemies and their projectiles or lanterns hanging from the ceiling. It takes some getting used to but once you figure it out, you'll have a blast using blobs of slime hurled at you by enemies as stepping stones to safety, Another cool feature comes in the form of Ability Points. Basically these are like XP, allowing you to upgrade your powers once you collect enough of them.
While exploration is as important as in other games of this type, it's also very much about tricky platforming sections. You will die very often. Ori features tight controls that are absolutely needed for the many carefully designed platforming sections. Thankfully, you can create a save point almost everywhere. This costs energy, though, forcing you to think carefully where to create them. Guiding Ori through Nibel's deadlier parts will challenge even seasoned genre fans, but the save system prevents it from becoming frustrating. The balance between challenge and convenience is great.
It's not all perfect, though. There's a lack of boss battles, and the ones that are there usually aren't very complex. The three dungeons can't be re-entered, forcing you to replay the whole game if did not do a 100% run the first time. This is a major omission in an exploration-based game like Ori. Also, controller support isn't perfect at the moment. I strongly recommend an Xbox controller as the game was made for Xbox One control schemes. Other controllers may not be fully recognized, with some buttons not working. You can play with the keyboard or with a keyboard/mouse combo, but neither offer the level of comfort and precision that Ori's complex platforming sections require. For optimal control, the Xbox controller is the way to go.
For purists there's still the usual speed runs or completionist playthroughs you can do, adding up to Ori's 10-15 hour quest, All in all, this is simply one of the best side-scrolling platformers in years. Still upset about not getting that proper Metroid game at 2015's E3? Stop whining and start playing the next best thing. Ori and the Blind Forest is simply fantastic. A true work of art !

With its enchanting pixel design and beautiful music by Jim Guthrie and scntfc, Sword & Sworcery piqued my curiosity and I was really impatient to play it. Quickly you sense a poetry, a peculiar, peaceful yet heavy atmosphere, like every pixelated element of this quiet place is telling you that trouble is coming.
However, I'm not sensitive to the story it's trying to tell, the way it's telling it and the way we have to navigate through it. S&S feels like venturing in a weird dream. You can tell there's much more behind it, a bigger universe with its own mythology, yet you feel stuck, like everything is slow paced and possibilities are restricted. And maybe that's what the game creators wanted it to feel like - dreams play a big part in this game after all. Yet from the beginning to the end I haven't felt fully satisfied with what it had to offer, often getting bored, sometimes annoyed, almost feeling glad it's over.
Despite all that, recommending people not to play S&S wouldn't feel right, because I truly admire the passion and the boldness it takes to make a game that can't be defined by any genre and creates its own instead, hence contributing to the broadening of the definition of video game.

The six different sharks each have their own strategy, tactics and skill, which varies depending on your shark buddy.  Eating divers is satisfying.

The business model is very fair. No DLC, and lots of content has been added for free. Real world money only buys you skins, no special advantages. Still getting updates a year after release.

This game is absolutely stunning for strategy and intelligent quick thinking. Large scale wars, faction vs faction, House vs House. Downs: You're prone to destruction at a low level if you don't find yourself protected by a high standing Liege Lord. My Liege Lord is my grandfather, who currently holds a high position, in the top 500 players globally, with over 14 villages, he's a Crown Prince. I chose a small island community, which may have it's ups as far as being seclusive and peaceful goes, but the resources can be a bit slim until you are able to go over-seas.

A very fun game I played a lot as a kid. Now playing again and I'm still discovering parts of the gameplay that I didn't get back then.
The game looks cartoony and friendly not unlike the Sims games but still challenging and really great fun. There is a lot to do like capturing ships, trading, building reputation with the factions, hunting famous pirates and finding their hidden treasures, ballroom dancing with the governor's daughters, collecting special items, messing with the diplomacy and economy to turn things in your favor, blasting other ships with your cannons, entering and fighting the captain on the deck, or even capturing whole towns...
The "pirate simulation" is detailed enough to be interesting but not too realistic so it doesn't take away from the fun. You can get all kinds of upgrades for your ships and you must think about the wind direction and the kind of cannon ammunition you use when fighting. There are a lot of ships each with their own specifications like speed, manoeuvrability cargo and crew capacity, amount of cannons, ... and you can customize and name your ships. If you are defeated you may be left on an island or imprisoned until your crew finds you. You will loose your flagship, and loosing your flagship hurts, believe me. I lost my Ship of the Line, twice... now I row in a canoe.
You also need to keep your crew happy and divide the treasue after every couple of months, to keep them from mutineering. Every time you do this you age up and after a while you will retire and the game will be over, so it's really a sandbox game where you can choose what to do with your time as a pirate, and then maybe take another road in the next playthrough.
One negative point is there is not a lot of variation in the main quest. You are basically always tracking down a ship somewhere to fight the same captain over and over and recover a piece of a puzzle each time. You will be chasing a lot of Evil Baron Raymundo's.
That's why I think it's an ideal game for casual players. If you let some time in between the missions, you will not be so annoyed. There are lots of hours to enjoy with this game, if you can look past the minor defects and dated graphics.
I think it's totally worth it. It feels great to be able to cruise through the beautiful blue waters of the caribbean, at first cautiously but in the end as a big powerful pirate destroying every ship in your path. It really makes you feel like the pirate you always wanted to be as a kid.

While the game can be fun once you get up to a high level, it is almost impossible to progress through the ranks without help from more senior players or a clan. Because the game has no tutorial or any sort of introduction to new people, it can be extremly hard to learn. Fortunally I had a more expierenced player teach me the basics. I do love the concept of the game and how you can have massive battles for dominance over ports, the game is 99% grind.
The combat missions need to be looked into because you fight a 30 minute battle against a supporier enemy for a handful of xp and a few thousand gold (Do twenty of these missions and you might just have enough gold to advance to the next level ship after the starter ship). Once you finally complete enough of those missions, outfit your next ship with whatever it needs, you'll begin to get harder combat missions for more xp and gold. However, if you lose your ship due to some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t (Internet cutting out so the enemy ships sink you) Then you're back to square one. Or another example: If you light a ship on fire with your last volley and are sitting next to it waiting for it to officially die so you can loot it's hold, the ship can explode and kill your ship. So there goes another 5 hours of work to RNG.
The game can be enjoyable in the future, it has a long way to go before it reaches those stages. In addition, I understand this game is sopposed to be "hardcore" but at what point does the hardcore-ness of the game begin to drive away your player base.
Pros
-Good ship combat
-Good way to learn the basics of sailing
Cons
-Very hard on new people
-Port UI looks like it was made in MS paint
-Open world terrain looks terrible
-Too hardcore
-Too much RNG (Boarding, random ship explosions)
-Confusing market
-Poor navigation system

Naval Action is an great open world / age of sail / combat simulation game at its core.  It does have some rough edges though.  Its greatess weakness is the reliance upon a community to build its numbers to make the game more fun. For me in this game more players = more fun.
Ive read tons of criticism and negative review, much of which is very acurate. The problem is then saying oh this game is not worth X or will never be Y. What game in thi genre and era comes anywhere close to this in terms of scope and strength of core game elements?  Combat is very well done, and feels very realistic. It may take a long time in battles, 30 minutes for a 1v1 battle,  larger fleet encounters of 5-20 players per side can take anywhere from 30mins - 3 hours.   But it should, sailings ships weren't fast and neither were their engagements.
Diplomacy has been taken out for a short time to be worked on i believe, however the old system seemed like a step in the right direciton.  You are part of a nation English, Danes, France ect.  There was a diplomacy tab where you could click and cast votes to go to war or make an alliance with the other nations.  It didnt operate perfectly but i believe that system would play very well.  The players of any given nation decide their own path.  I would hope to see a return to a system similar to this.
The economy  has elements of greatness with being able to craft, buy and sell or produce goods.  There are some problems but its nearly a player driven economy so i feel like it is what the player base makes it.  A lot of people have complained about the new patch making ships only have one life, and not being able to capture ai ships.  I think it is certainly the right direction for the game and ship economy.  Before this patch ships had 5-3 lifes, ships didnt matter, there were to many to cheap.  Now ships are valuable, it makes for better balance and the game being played the way it was intended to.  Your ship should matter, you shouldnt want to die.
If you are a potential buyer of this game i would say.....

Do you like age of sail open world/sandbox style games that are focused on realism? If yes this game is for you.
This is not your typical game and does not play like one, it may become something great though.
In closing and what I would say to the developer, I bought in early and this game has been one of my dream games for many years.  Making this game more casual is not the direction to go.  DO NOT listen to and cater to people who want you to change what your game is at its heart, stay true to what you have built at the core of your game, do not dumb it down for whiny un-satisfiable gamers. Work on making your game more informative and user friendly for new players and victory is yours.

Wow. Just, wow. I had fairly high expectations for this game, and my expectations were exceeded 100%. It had me in tears within the first 10 minutes. Not just "boohoo, that was sad" tears either: full on, choking on my tears, ugly-crying-face, "why is life so awful?" tears.
The story is as moving as it is light-hearted, and aesthetically the game is superb. The music complements everything perfectly, tying it all together (possibly one of the most beautiful soundtracks for a game ever?), and adds to the fantasy-feel of the game. The controls and new abilities are easy to master, but not so easy as to make you feel like you're playing a kid's game either. I initially bought this game thinking, "Well, this should be relaxing to play" - and it was! ...except for the parts where I died about 100 times trying to do one thing. One particular escape-scene left me with a stomach ache and shaking hands when I'd finally managed it (I only died 170 times trying, so no biggie).
I suppose the only thing that bugged me a little at the end is that you can't go back and try to collect all the items you missed along the way, but that's just a small quibble.
Overall: a beautiful, well-made, immersive and amazing game, that will have you wanting to play it again and again. 12 out of 10 - just astounding.

Cute, fun, gorgeous, sentimental platformer.
The price is a bit higher than your regular indie game, but the quality is also superior. The animation is top-notch, the levels are genuinely atmospheric and although they use many familiar mechanics the level designers never rely too long on any one trick, never letting you get bored. Very few parts feel redundant or unbalanced and consequently the pacing is great throughout the 8-10 hours you'll spend playing it.
There are a few very difficult passages where you're not allowed to save until you complete the whole obstacle course, and they will require patience and training to get through, which could be annoying for some players (harder than Limbo, easier than the regular levels of Super Meat Boy). Another downside is that the game has little replaybility value, and you can't go back to explore and complete parts of levels you may have missed after you finish the main quest without starting a fresh save. I also encountered a minor video bug in the cutscenes, where the video is repeadedly flipped upside down fast for short periods of time.
On the whole this is a very well-crafted game, absolutely worth it if you grab it on sale. At full price I'd say it lacks the replayability to make it a solid purchace.

Superbrothers: Sword and Sworcery is a little indie marvel created by less than a handful of guys that was originally released for the iPad in 2011 but then ported over to PC a year later. And for the most part, this is a good port, but for the whole part, this is an amazing game.
In Superbrothers, you play as the unsuspecting Scythian who you must use to complete a mysterious "woeful errand" involving three pieces of a Trigon (an obvious call back to the Triforce from the Zelda series). The game appears has a very medieval-fantasy look at first, but as time goes on, you'll start to realize how many ties it has to the modern world and how quirky the world is actually designed.
Characters speak with a mix of Shakespearian speech with modern hipster lingo thrown in. A giant vinyl record hovers suspicious in a grove. And a strange naked bear dances inside your dreams. But surrounding all this quirky world, is the meta-narrative framework.
To quote Carolyn's apt review from GameSpot, "Sword and Sworcery doesn't so much break the fourth wall as it never built it in the first place." You fully interact with the world as an unseen entity that can tap bushes, read minds, and forcibly control the character of the Scythian. The game recognizes this and the illusive character known as the Archetpye casually remarks at your actions as commonplace, and with humor will remind you of the social features within the game (as well as how necessary they are to completing the game).
The story is a interactive and aesthetic masterpiece. The world of Superbrothers is both beautiful to look and astounding to listen to. I was drawn into this game purely from Jim Guthrie's fantastic score in "Indie Game: The Movie", so I wanted to see his earlier work and this might be one of the best soundtracks I've ever heard in a game. He blends instrumental music with synthetic hums and beats to showcase the tender, casual, and powerful moments the game has to show. I'll never forget releasing the Sylvian sprites or being chased by the chilling demonic monster from Mingi Taw.
The massive world constructed in Superbrothers is designed with 8-bit pixels, but also contains objects that are obviously not pixelated (like the vinyl record and the Trigon pieces), and doesn't really animate like traditional 8-bit video games from the past do. It's much more smooth and it makes the atmosphere of the places you visit all the more gorgeous to explore. Superbrothers is a treat, both visually and audibly.
However, with so much praise, I must note my problems with the game. The plot is sort of short and after so much build-up to the climax... the ending isn't particularly that great, in my opinion. Not every loose end is tied, and I'm not sure if that was the intention of the designers or not, but I played the game and beat it the honest way so I feel somewhat disappointed with the climax.
Along with that, the combat is a little basic. And fighting the Trigons in the game can be a massive chore if you die and have to start all over again, because their animations between attacks while effectively ominous during my first attempts, become tiring after trying to fight them the second and third time. On top of all that, the Scythian isn't the fastest walker and some of the more obtuse puzzles might have you slowly backtracking which can sometimes be a bit of a pain.
Don't be dismayed by my criticisms, though. For what problems I had with this game, I loved all the other things within it so much more. It's not so much of a masterful story that reveals something about humanity that has never been shown before, as it is more of an interactive journey that you can undertake within a few hours, and get swept away with. Between the charm and excellent crafting of this game, it's really hard to hate on Superbrothers: Sword and Sworcery. I'm giving it an 8/10 and a high recommendation.

Before I begin, I would like to point out the major problem I have with most "free to play" games, Well, two.
1. They suck
2. They seem to all be based of the "Farmvile Forumla"
Do not get me wrong, there are plenty of Free to Play games that do not do that, like Tribes Ascend, Star Trek Online after the F2P conversion, and a few others that operate on the concept of "Pay because you're having fun and want to support it." not "Pay because you have to." Those games are fine. Hell, I enjoy playing STO still, even after the F2P change.
Stronghold Kingdoms, on the other hand..is a medival reincarnation of Farmvile, but even more hands off! I came into the game expecting a cut-down version of Stronghold, but what I got out of it was pretty much like the fabled "Age of Empires Online".
When you're put into the game, you're given a basic tutorial, and some things to help. Sadly, it's not much (unless you preordered Crusader 2, or bought the starter pack for some reason), and even if you manage to make do, it's only a matter of time before you run into some barrier, like lack of resources or even not having enough gold. When that happens, you either have to bug your friends, making them hate your guts forevermore, or get your credit card and pay up, which, again, seem very much like the Facebook games we're all spammed with.
So then, would I reccomend this game? Are you joking?!  It makes me worry for the future of a decent series, being all pay to win and such.

I'm only saying no, because I'm on the fence. If you've got the real-life money to support the in-game upgrades, then you're fine and you'll really enjoy the game, without, you're kinda ♥♥♥♥ed. For a 'free' game, it's not so free.
The whole game is in real-time, and that's ok. However, with every building you place, and every thing you research, it bumps up the time. No matter the type of building, or research option. Just adds minutes to the time. And that's not so bad, until it hits over 30 minutes and you haven't got the tokens to have a building and research queue.
So with this, it takes a long time to build up a decent, protected base with enough peasants to train a competent army to defend your stronghold. Problem with that is, you're a new player, and this is an online world. A lot of players will ignore rule 7 - don't be a♥♥♥♥♥♥ and just attack you for the sake of attacking. For me, who is a slow learner, that just makes the game even harder and unfair. the 2 days worth of protection at the beginning is great, but I think that needs to be a week. In a week you an have a decent wooden defence line and a good-ish sized army (depending on how happy you keep the peasants) to protect your stronghold after the timer goes out.
Other than that, the user friendly-ness of the game is great, and I love the option that you get to keep the tutorial pages near by, in case you forget anything, then you an just turn it off when you're ready, and that's awesome. I also like having the different tabs at the top, keeping everything seperated out and neat really helps you get to grips with the game.
So overall, I like the game and won't stop playing it, but I wouldn't recommend it. I'm just stubborn and miss being able to play the old Stronghold games.(Saving the money up for the complete pack though)

The problem I have with this game is that it's shallow. It's a bunch of different genres in one, meaning that there are a lot of things to do, but it's spread very thin. The main selling point of the game is sailing around, battling with other ships, and visiting ports. All of that feels good enough, but takes some getting used to, because the control scheme is a bit strange (you use the numpad for most things). Everything else though is represented through various minigames which range from turn-based strategy to rhythm action. It has that "Spore" problem of trying to do too much at once instead of focusing on something specific it can do well, but this game didn't seem to get criticised in the same way. Maybe people love it for the atmosphere and the pirate theme (still rare in gaming), and I can respect that. But while the minigames are varied, none of them are particularly complex or refined, and they're basically the same every single time, just progressively more difficult.
I can totally see the appeal, it's a very unique game, and it's fun for a few hours, but it just became repetitive after a short while and I lost interest. If you're looking for a pirate game you can play casually, it might be the game for you. But if you're looking for something with more depth to it, it won't be.

Naval Action is a naval war game set in the era where sail ships was all we had, setting the stage for one of the most reckless, but visually stunning eras of warfare to ever exist. The intricate detail that was put into the design of the ships paid off, and they look perfect. The game looks and feels smooth when played, as well as feeling very realistic. Naval Action takes the depth of command a step further than games such as World of Warships, Napoleon: Total War and Empire: Total War - with reference to their Naval battles, making players take into account windspeed, positioning, damage, gun crews etc. There are a lot of factors that you must keep an eye on. You don’t get any voice over or warning to tell you that your hull is breached like you do in other games, or that your crew is dead. You have to look out for this, as well as navigate your ship and fight the enemy. It sounds like a lot, but it is not impossible, and I like the challenge. For me, the battles are the only enjoyable part of the game though, and I can’t help but feel the developers have wasted their time with everything else that they did.
In Naval Action, you spend a lot of time in the open world, where you must assume command of your ship and navigate it from your whereabouts to your desired location. This is done by using a map with grid coordinates on it. However, you must deduct your location on the map yourself (using nearby ports or coastal outlines), and monitor it carefully, because there is no marker displaying your location. Neither can you set a waypoint to the place you’re going. This is much more realistic in its approach to navigation, but for someone like me who is bad at maths and map reading, it makes the game too much like hard work, and takes a way a lot of the enjoyment.
You can spend a long time sailing around looking for battles or missions in which you hope you might be able to use your ship and progress in the game, which all seems such as waste of time. The game would do well to remove that and just implement a matchmaking system, obviously keeping the battles as they are. I just don’t see there is any need for the open world. The ports that you can travel to are all models on the map, and to enter them you must go through a loading screen which takes you to the interface, so it is not like, say, Assassins Creed Black Flag, where you could actually explore the ports. I would much prefer it if they did something like implement this open world map into single player, but let you explore it and even take over other nations ports/settlements, almost like Total War or Warband, but just…better.
The open world has a different perspective with the camera than the battle does. The only way I can describe it is the open world, in terms of controlling and viewing, feels like Mount and Blade campaigns, and the battles, in terms of controlling and viewing, feel like World of Warships. The game does a better job on both counts, but uses it badly. If they’d give us the open world in single player and let us explore it from the second perspective I described, it would be fun. If you look at the images of the game on the Steam Store, the close-up shots are taken from battles (HUD removed) and the distant shots (Also distinguishable by the worse graphical quality) are taken from the open world, again, without HUD. I hope this clears up my point a little.
My next point is the interface. I do not know what they were thinking with this. I had to watch a surprising number of videos to just learn the basics of this game – it is too open ended and hard to understand. There are no tutorials in the game, and nothing is obvious. The interface looks messy, and lacks any form of professionalism. It is just confusing. I was clicking on random things and trying to drag random things and…ugh. It was just annoying.
Overall, I can’t give this game more than a 3/10. I do like the concept, but it didn’t turn out like the trailers and teasers would have you believe. If it had…it would have been perfect. It is really a shame, because it was a beautiful idea, and one of the best eras to set a game in. This sort of game is rare, and the developers didn’t do a very good job with bringing it to the spotlight. I paid full price for this, like an idiot. Please, take my advice and don’t do that. In no way can they demand £30 for this. World of Warships is free, and Napoleon + Empire: Total War can be purchased for about £30. If you want terrible Naval gameplay, get those. Otherwise, get World of Warships. Just don’t get this. Trust me.

Titular Ori looks like a cutie with his appearance reminding of similarly titular Stitch with a more thin physique. It doesn’t stop him however from getting rather devious and mean to the player right off the start. The trial and error approach which the game is based upon overwhelms you at first. A new character death happens faster than you would’ve expected from a game which desperately tries to look like a Disney animated feature with a touch of Studio Ghibli’s design and mystique. Everything is dangerous and kills our hero instantly with one attack punishing for a single mistake. Sharp spikes, flying aggressive thingies, crawling aggressive thingies, thingies spewing glowing bombs  will kill you mercilessly and send you to the most recent checkpoint which you created yourself with the same energy that can also be spent on you most powerful and helping in “oh♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation attack.

And this creates an interesting resource management dynamic for a while. Should you keep it and see a little more or should you spend it right here right now so you won’t have to respawn far behind and re-do all that painstakingly hard jumps again? Of course you should do it now like any sensible person would! Problem is, that it stops being a problem after a while, as you progress through the story guided by glowing arrow on the world map pointing to where you should go next for things to happen: like gaining a new ability from the list which inevitably includes a double jump. Curiously enough you can turn that into a triple jump with leveling up of one of ability trees, though it won’t be really necessary. Otherwise how you would be able to get all those items hidden in the backgrounds or placed in previously inaccessible areas. “So many secrets” the game tells you through its achievement notification. Sadly that it doesn’t mention all of them containing only three types of glowing orbs, which you don’t really need after some initial leveling up. The main difficulty that persists throughout the game is a challenge of speed jumping puzzles which are using your newly acquired mechanic.
Going back to the previous locations as the side activity can’t really compete with going on with the story; you run back to the already visited area to just use that recently got ability in a challenge that is fairly trivial compared to the ones you just did during one of those this-is-it-run-or-die-sections, and, well, while it doesn’t hurt you’ve already lost count of your energy glowing balls and you probably don’t really need that another one; it would’ve just unnecessarily lengthened the already not that compact experience which this game wants to be at heart. This unnecessary increase affects the story which in compensation tries to be more vague than it should be, making the narrator speak in an artificial language and immediately translating all his lines through subtitles with a fairly generic lines of not that inventive a story.
What I’m saying is not that cheesy stories with cheesy endings don’t work, because otherwise I wouldn’t love Pixar movies. Maybe they aren’t that stretchable to 12-hour-long format even if they are so beautifully looking, and sounding, and being adorable.

Whenever I find a game that lets me connect with the characters, makes me cheer on the characters, makes me emotionally invested in the world, I always seem to want to tell all of my friends to play it. Usually, when I tell them of the adventure that I went through, they just shake it off as just another good game. But when they finally sit down with the game, they realise that they missed out on an amazing game that just get them right where it hurts. I allowed my friend to play this game in front of me, and in the first 10 minutes, he cried.
This game is barely touched by anyone, and it truly amazes me that not many people have played it. This game is underated, but honestly, this game has been one of the most exhilarating, exciting, heart pumping and emotional games I have ever played.
This game barely has any dialogue, but it doesn't need any. You can see how the characters act and see how they get affected by the events that happen to them. It is masterful, and sure, the story isn't complex, but the simplicity makes it fantastic.
Oh, and the art design and graphics both work together and make it a joy to the eyes. It is the most beautiful games I have ever seen in the graphics department. And I bet this game (visually) will not date.
Of course, the game is a "Game", so it needs good gameplay. And the gameplay is really fun both because:
1. The metroidvania mechanics are built it very well,
2. It is fun to explore,
3. The platforming was challenging, but not frustrating.
The soundtrack is also some of the best I have ever heard. Even better than some of the classics like Zelda and Halo imo. It is emotional, powerful and beautiful.
This game has become one of my favorite games of all time. It has everything. Simple story, great gameplay that is challanging, beautiful graphics, powerful music and memorable characters.
