Fallout 3, surprisingly, is a game that was actually developed and made by Bethesda, and not a fan made mod. This is surprising because from just playing it, it can be hard to tell at times. I know I'm late to writing this review, but I wanted to remind both myself and anyone who reads this of how Fallout 3 was in case Fallout 4 doesn't seem as good as it looks when it comes out. (It may not look like it with the 90 minutes I have tracked, but I have completed the game twice; once from a retail copy and more recently through New Vegas using the Tale of Two Wastelands mod.)
Fallout 3 is set in the Capital Wasteland, a new location set on the opposite side of the US from the traditional west coasts of Fallout 1, 2, and later New Vegas. By doing this, they allowed themselves to have a clean slate of sorts, and have more creative freedom in writing the story. So naturally, being skilled writers as they are, they just copied a bunch of stuff from the old games and rewrote it to be worse. The Brotherhood of Steel is back, only this time they're a splinter faction that's a bunch of goodie two-shoes that go from shunning you to thanking you for letting them bask in your presence over the course of one quest (the "real" brotherhood is still technically there in the form of the Outcasts, but they barely have any presence in the game). The Enclave is back for no real reason at all, considering they were pretty much ended in 2. They made up their own east coast brand of super mutant just so they could flood the game with them. Even things like caps don't really make sense, since the only reason caps were used as currency in the west coast games is because they were backed by the Hub. The whole game just feels like they went through a picture book of Fallout and saw cool things and went "hey that looks cool, let's put it in our game too!" without really thinking that much about why they would actually be there.
Gameplay-wise, the game is a mixed bag. The exploration can be pretty fun, especially with mods like DC Interiors (which opens up a bunch of the boarded up buildings that Bethesda was too lazy to furnish), but the shooting is fairly subpar, and you can tell that the engine wasn't really built for shooting games at that stage of its development. Of course, you can always use VATS if you'd rather watch the game play itself instead, since it's effectively been turned into an easy button that lets you have 5 turns to blow an enemy to pieces and then gives the enemy one. The whole stat system is a joke, and between the rate you get perks, the perks added by DLCs, and the bobbleheads scattered throughout the world, it's almost impossible to not end up with 10 in every SPECIAL stat and 100 in every skill by the time you finish the game.
Because it's basically impossible to specialize in any particular ability due to inevitably having to specialize in all of them, and the fact that the game doesn't really give you any major choices that have actual consequences, it can be difficult to feel like you're actually roleplaying in Fallout 3. But that's fine, because it's pretty much impossible with the dialogue anyways. The dialogue options are, as best as I can describe them, schizophrenically written. You can blow up an entire settlement and laugh it off, then five minutes later meet a group of people you believe to be cannibals and have no dialogue option to say anything other than something negative towards them. At one point early in the game you meet a ghoul bartender, and your only options are two choices of mocking him and the last option, "Let me think about it for a moment, my good man.", which is so cringey that I can only assume that if Bethesda's animators had any talent it would be accompanied by an animation of the player character tipping an imaginary top hat and taking a puff from a wooden pipe. Most of the intelligence choices are just repeating what someone just said to you back to them in a summarized form written in an overly wordy way, and a lot of the speech checks go beyond ridiculousness in terms of convincing people or things to do things they would never realistically do in a single sentence. The game has a karma system, but I don't know if it's even possible to keep a negative karma level because of how much of it you get dumped onto you just for things like killing ghouls or raiders (which are impossible to allign with because Fallout 3 has no faction system), but it doesn't really matter because it's not even that much fun to play evil. There are no real meaningful evil choices, just a bunch of "for the laughs" things. There are one or two noteworthy evil moments and then the rest of it is just "ahaha i shoot you in the face" options in dialogue that just aren't really fulfilling, and some of them are just plain nonsensical and make no sense for the player to do, like the one at the end of the Broken Steel DLC. The game also has two factions that hunt you down depending on whether your karma is too high or low, but while the evil karma version is a group of lawbringers who are hunting you down because you're a known criminal, the good varient just gets Talon Company, a mercenary unit that Bethesda just made up and gave no backstory aside from "they're bad guys and so they want to kill good guys because they're really bad people!" and set them loose on you.
The DLC is about what you would expect so far. Operation Anchorage is essentially just a 3 hour crappy military corridor FPS with a few good rewards, Mothership Zeta is a crappy space corridor shooter with a few good rewards, and Broken Steel is only worth playing because of the fact that it basically forces you to after the end of the base game. The Pitt and Point Lookout are basically the only ones that I would consider "good", with the former being a brief but interesting quest line and a relatively fun collectathon with some good rewards and the latter being the only dlc to give a more open experience in a new map with new side quests and things to explore. If it wasn't for the fact that the GOTY edition costs the same as buying regular fallout 3 + point lookout + the pitt I'd just tell you to buy those, but oh well.
Fallout 3 is what I would consider a "popcorn RPG". It's the kind of game where you can spend 100 hours just exploring the wasteland and looting buildings and doing side quests and then remember that there's a boring main storyline for you to do, but it's not a game where you have to make choices or develop a character or anything associated with more in-depth RPGs, and while to an extent I feel that way about all of Bethesda's post-Morrowind RPGs, Fallout 3 in particular exemplifies the concept. If you're new to the Fallout series you may love it, or if you've played them all you can probably still just forget that it's a Fallout game and have fun exploring, but it's both a terrible RPG and a terrible Fallout game. It's extremely unstable on its own, so either modding it to high heaven or playing it through New Vegas in the A Tale of Two Wastelands mod (which requires both games and all of their DLC) is basically required. If you have time to kill and just want to relax in the wasteland for a little while, there's no reason not to buy Fallout 3 if it's on sale and you've got nothing else to play, but there just isn't anything exceptional that would prompt me to actively recommend the game. Hopefully Bethesda will have learned from New Vegas when we get to play Fallout 4.

The sad fact is, this game places far, far too much focus on melee combat than is necessary, especially when your opposition is both stronger than you in melee combat, more numerous and features vastly superior ranged support than your ranged weapons can reliably dish out. The low-and-slow means of melee damage and inability to simply push through injuries results in every fight quickly turning into an uncomfortable meat grinder.
This is a significant flaw of the game; an inflexible concentration on melee weapons and combat, yet melee combat is punishing and tedious to engage in... and then, at the same time, it restricts your method of regaining health to melee executions! Executions themselves seem to have been advertised as magnificent and epic means of finishing off an enemy, yet it rapidly becomes a boring and even tiresome affair, especially since enemies can counteract your attempts to execute them. The function itself is largely unexplained, leading new and uncomfortable players ot blindly fumble at an "elite" melee opponent and receive a faceful of alien knuckle sandwich for their efforts.
Evidently, the designers wanted players to approach each level as though it were a river, constantly moving forward with little deviation from progress, yet the level design itself does not reflect this sentiment properly; the levels all have the one true path, obviously, but they go back and forth between being linear corridors and branching paths and sometimes arena zones and proper fortified staging areas, eliminating any concept of consistent level layout and causing no small amount of confusion and flow disruption.
The story, from what little of it I could grind my teeth through, came across as unimaginitive and stale, with very little genuine character from anybody and no clear long-term intent, seemingly just fabricating a big, empty pit to throw sword-swinging "Space Marines" into and then flood them with uninspired orkish clumps. The only Imperial Guard character who seemed to exist beyond the background was a woman, so I have an uncomfortable suspicion that the story would attempt to hamfist some kind of romantic subplot to thrust upon the player's mind, which on its own isn't typically an all too impressive move, but in the setting of the grim darkness of the 41st millenium just seems outright foolish, and all but flies directly in the face of the spirit of Warhammer 40,000. Make war, not love. (I would also like to make the "all's fair in love and war, and this ain't love" joke.)
For the designs of the marines themselves... maybe put some helmets on before you launch yourselves into an open aerial combat zone.
Speaking of which, the utterly flagrant disregard for the teachings of the Codex Astartes just to make your special helmet-less Space Marines seem like bad-*** mavericks and loose cannons who don't abide the rules because it gets in the way of how much booty they kick and how many names they take... is nothing short of shallow writing, and the kind of empty aggrandizement I would expect only from common fanfiction and Hollywood.
Which, in retrospect, is sort of how the game felt; like a bad Hollywood film. Flat characters, unclear goals, cookie cutter enemies and supporting cast, ferociously illogical tactics (you start out with a pistol and a large knife, for the record) and a great big bombastic 10,000ft high air battle with plenty of Michael Bay brand explosions and fast-moving objects.
As a final critique, I want to quickly address the orks themselves, as they're the ONLY enemies I wasted time fighting and never made it to the daemons I've been told are later on in the story. Their voices are painfully bad, and their lines repeat over and over and over again. It's not just pathetic; it's disgusting.
Which is sort of how I'd summarize the game. Less than pathetic. As someone who can enjoy getting their face kicked in as a Chaos Sorcerer in Eternal Crusade simply because of the setting logic (no matter who wins, I will be revived later by the dark gods and blood will have been spilled to please them, so I technically win), I feel confident in my judgement when I say that this game does NOT feel like a Warhammer 40,000 game. It feels like a really, really bad attempt to make a parody of Gears Of War... which, ironically enough, WAS a good franchise. Had their ups and downs, but each game had redeemable features.

Stronghold Kingdoms is as much a game of politics as it is a game of Medieval warfare or simulation. The articulate politician will find himself advancing far more quicker than the warrior and it is not at all uncommon to find House Marshalls who have only razed a handful of players.
First I'd like to address the two foremost complaints about Stronghold kingdoms; Pay to Win and Multi Accounters
Mulits - Players controlling 2 or more accounts per game world.
The problem here is twofold and blame falls equally on both the players and Firefly. All too often I see a user on the forums calling for heads to roll after he reports a player suspected of cheating and nothing happens. The paranoid player would do well to remember that suspicious does not equal guilty and that Firefly will not disclose the outcome of any investigation to the player who filed the report.
If it appears nothing has been done it's likely because the investigation turned up nothing illicit and remember the more information you include in your report the more likely the accusation is to be investigated.
The other half of blame sits squarely upon Firefly's shoulders in my opinion due to the sheer ambiguity of the game rules. Time and time again I've had players coming to me with multiple accounts firm in their insistence that they weren't breaking any rules because they "had premium tokens in play on both accounts".
Despite what anyone might say to convince you otherwise the above allegation is flat out untrue. Regardless of premium tokens, players are only allotted one account per game world. All Firefly here has to do is update the game rules page to be less ambiguous in regards to the IP restrictions and premium players clause but they will not and this apathy towards one of the top complaints about Stronghold Kingdoms promotes the continued perpetuation of the myth that Firefly doesn't care and that they don't investigate informed allegations against suspected cheaters.
Pay To Win - The belief that to succeed at any level in Stronghold Kingdoms the player must spend liberal amounts of money to obtain their own virtual crown.
Pay to Win (or P2W) is a hotly debated topic in many 'Free to play' games and the same applies to Stronghold Kingdoms and there is no doubt that in this case it's a grey area for sure. But to answer whether or not the game is p2w one must first define what winning means to them and what winning means to Firefly.
For many players 'to win' is to beat another player in a one on one mano a mano fight. Providing both players are of the same skill level and neither receive any outside help there is no doubt that whichever of the two players spends more on the game will ultimately be the winner. There are just too many cards in the Stronghold Kingdoms deck that artificially boost combat stats such as army speed or the strength of castle structures and Firefly doesn't help the matter by continuing to introduce more powerful combat cards all the time.
Sure, the only players who use those aces are probably the top 0.5% but in worlds with dwindling playerbases those players hold the entire server at their collective whim.
In contrast, many experienced players realize that winning is actually more than a one on one fight and that loosing one battle doesn't mean the war is lost and that there are dozens, if not hundreds, of players participating on both sides of the conflict, carder and non carder alike. This means that while you are going up against a house with spending players your house will likely have spending players of it's own which levels the playing field.
Firefly's definition is similar to the above, Houses compete against one another to gain glory, ultimately eliminating all others houses to be the last one standing. That final House is considered the winner of that age and inducted into the hall of fame while their members all share in on the spoils of the victory which mostly consists of a few quest wheel spins, card packs, and new charges for their coat of arms.
This means that to 'win' Stronghold Kingdoms all one has to actually do is be a member of whichever house is left standing when the dust settles.
As you can now see the definition of winning in stronghold Kingdoms is actually quite subjective and by paying attention to ongoing house politics virtually anyone can achieve victory regardless of their financial status.
## Now that that's cleared up.... ##
Although my Steam time doesn't show it, I have played Stronghold Kingdoms via the Standalone client for almost 3 years now and in that time I have been active in many roles. I'm currently on a sort of hiatus with Stronghold Crusader 2 gearing up for release.
Anyways, here's what I liked:
+ First and foremost is the community, a game that pretty much coerces you into logging in every day lends itself to the establishment of long distance relationships that can become something like a second family to you.
+ 2D graphics invoke a nostalgic feeling in fans who have been with the Stronghold franchise from it's inception.
+ Freedom to design my castle as I please, there is no generic 'castle' building that is placed with one click. You have to determine where each wall segment and Stone Tower will be built.
+ Village building can be as simple or as intricate as you want, village buildings fit together much like a puzzle and those who take the time to optimize their village layout will enjoy increased production.
What I felt could be improved on:
- Battles aren't fought in real time, you play puzzle games by setting up your troops and letting the AI resolve it. The AI is quite predictable and stupid at times.
- The ingame chat system is so unintuitive it actually drives players away from the game.
- The entire card system requires too much micromanagement. For a game that requires more and more of your time as you grow having to juggle cards daily to stay competitive gets pretty old pretty quick.
- The formula used to generate AI castles needs to take the number of players in that parish into account, not only the rank of the players. It's a real kick in the head to get the strongest wolf castle in your parish every week when the only 3 villages there are yours.
What I'd like to see added in the future:
> Castles and villages merged into one design, this would mean that defensively strong players would have weaker economies and the inverse for economically strong players. This would encourage greater diversity in playstyle.
> Actual RTS battles that allow direct player control of the attacking armies and the defending garrison if the player so wished.
> More units, especially siege units. Even the original Stronghold had twice as many units as there are currently in Stronghold Kingdoms.
In short, yes, I strongly recommend this game. It's probably the best free to play RTS on Steam at this moment, and while the graphics hail from a previous decade they still retain the charm of the original Stronghold.
- IGN DavidSpy

Alright here is where I will probably get a lot of flack from people based on the hours I have recorded in game, but I think that is actually somewhat of a testament to some issues I can bring up.

First off, I'd like to make it clear, I'm not a rookie rpg player. I have thousands of hours across many rpgs including Diablos, Path of Exile, Titan Quest, and even Dungeons and Dragons and other pen and papers. So as a real rpg lover, this game does a great job skratching that customization itch. There are numerous paths to take a character, with interesting skills and class combination that allow for interesting gameplay. The tactical aspect of the pen and paper rpg made a great transition in the game. As well there is a very vast world that makes me feel like the game has an actual life to it.

But there are some gripes. The first issue is the quests, on a good day they can be cryptic, other times quests will have you walking in circles until you stumble upon just the right thing for the quest. This can realistically be overlooked as the game pitches a challenging story telling game. Second, there is little to no measure of how difficult or when an encounter is going to occur. As such there is a good chance, that you might face check into an encounter you can't beat. Again this could be forgiven as the game is supposed to be challenging, but the fact that if the AI auto pathing sets your characters in the wrong place, you're stuck in that combat until your party dies, and you are forced to reload. Now this wouldn't be that much of an issue if it weren't for the third issue, the severe lack of autosaving. Now if your party dies, and you just completed three combats and four quests, but forgot to save, well nuts to you, and happy three hour setback bud. And that is the crux of what has killed both of my playthroughs of this game. I don't mind redoing a combat I failed or grinding and coming back, that's what it means to play an rpg. What I do mind is grinding forward and realizing that by losing this combat I effectively lost every combat and action for the hours preceding this. That is what it means to have frustrating game play. Someone could compare this issue to something like the Dark Souls franchise that pitches the ‘beat the head against the wall’ game play, but even that game has a well rounded save system that doesn’t force hour long retreks of content.

Am I a bit salty? Yeah that should be obvious, but that doesn’t change the point being made. There needs to be a line between having a challenging game and helping the player enjoy the the challenge of the game. Hard and punishing combat are great ways to make this work. Hard and punishing combat paired with hours of having to redo content over a single mistake, is not.

Now, considering I’ve levied some harsh words against Divinity, I don’t want this to scare the errant buyer away. Divinity is a great game, it just has some very irritating tics that can be more punishing than originally intended.

Naval Action is a game where you become a Captian of your vessel or own little fleet in the Caribbean during the Napoleanic Era. You can either join a PVE server, where you capture and battle ships controlled by the AI, or the PVP server, where you are thrown into an open world with other players. From your humble beginnings you have various options to work yourself through the ranks: you can start out as a trader, join a clan or do solo combat missions. All with the aim to either buying larger ships or investing your money into producing them and the ressources consumed by other players, like repairs upgrades, etc.
The graphics are stunning and very well made. The sky and the sea are just beautiful. The ships look gorgeous. The battle mechanics all work excellent and I found all of the trade mechanics to work as well.
Well, if you know anything about the Age Of Sail, then you should probably take heed that is was an era during which everything took time. So will the game, especially so in the beginning. You will probably have to play a couple of missions against AI ships until you build some sort of capital to invest in more expensive tradegoods to expand your margins. Sailin gacross the Caribbean also takes its time, because the open world is huge.
Be warned, you will experience frustration. Because there are other players that have larger ships, know the map and their trade well. You will lose your ship, you will lose your cargo and depending on the nation you play, you will witness one of your outposts an its buildings getting lost after a city flips ownership after a port battle.
Remember that this game is in Early Access, so you will be considered to be a testing player. The developers are making a lot of changes and are trying out a lot of variants for the gameplay. If you are adverse to changing environments, this may cause frustration to you too.
I really like this game, exactly because of all the challenges it provides to the players. The open world is not just a cozy place, but there are risks involved when you set your sails to go to battle or deliver your goods to another port. There is no save game so every bad decision on your side will have consequences. I like to carve out my own career. There is a worth to it when you begin figuring out your strategy and when you start to build your own support structure. I love how the weather changes and the sun and moon rise while I am sailing out into the unknown. Most of the people I have met so far are really invested into this game and friendly. Beware though, it is a multiplayer open world and just like in real life, you are going to meet uncomfortable persons.
All in all, if you love the Age Of Sail, if you bring patience and you can tolerate some frustration, if you are willing to make the game yours by carving out your own career and accept the very nature of an multiplayer open world, if for now you can accept that development on this is not yet closed and finished -  this game is for you!

I really love this game. The open world design of being able to sail anywhere in the Caribbean and fight for whoever you want, makes this game fresh every time you start a new campaign.
You start as an enforcer of one of 4 major expansionist powers, each giving you a unique ship exclusive to that nation. Once you hit the open waters, it’s open season! You can attack any ship you want, including your own country. There are native war canoes that can attack, or you attack them, take their boat, and have a small and very quick raiding party to attack those huge Spanish treasure ships! You also have other pirates to attack to bolster your reputation.
Controls can be tricky, as the game uses the 10 key almost exclusively. The different aspects of the game: sailing, attacking, sword fighting, raiding, and (gasp) dancing, make this a fun game to play, but challenging to master! There are many opportunities to woo different governor’s daughters, and if you can master the different elaborate dances, you will inherit a treasure trove of maps, special items, and information from these women.
The storyline is always a loose path you weave while playing this game. While there are explicit instructions on how to move the story along, you do not need to adhere to it to find enjoyment out of this game. You can search for your missing family, and revenge them, or you can enjoy the simple life of running spices and sugar to the different ports.
Most ports have a governor (with a daughter to woo), a shipbuilder to repair, sell, or upgrade your fleet, a merchant, and a tavern to recruit more crew and gather information pertinent to finding your family.
I highly recommend this game! I would love to see an updated version and a Mac port. I found out too late there was an iPad version. If the developers are listening, please bring a fresh version of this to modern systems!!!

I originally played this back in summer 2012 and returned summer 2014 to see what had improved. But like all free to play games it just has too many limitations and timers to recommend on a long term basis.
What's good - Watching your village becoming fully operational, scouting, trading, researching and seeing the occasional level up process, watching the battles from bandit camps, wolf lairs or your castle keep
What's bad - timeframe limits, the only thing that stops this is Maths but ultimately everything just takes too much time unless you play an insta-build card or time speed card and even then it only lasts a few hours. Castle building takes days, village building takes hours, raising your own military requires several researches and buildings which you "must" have unless you like being attacked regularly by the AI and having no means of defending yourself thus losing resources. The card system is a mess and you have to click through them until you find what you wanted at the time. 7 day premium tokens and cards are where they want you to pay but really unless you can fully use a 7 or 30 day token dont even bother. If you want me paying £3 a throw I expect a 30 day token, not a 7 day one, I think the 7 day ones should be scrapped entirely. But back to my point, you need merchants+speed, scouts+speed, max housing capacity and military to fully get your moneys worth from the tokens, all of which takes time. The biggest thing that kills the game however is research, once you run out of RP you either need to level up or spend gold to get more, Philosophy helps with this but like Maths it's a temporary fix at best.
Conclusion - when I first played I was around a few weeks and then left, there were several things I never got to experience like trading for gold or helping a house/faction take an area while watching big all out battles occur, never raided a vilage, never done parish heals, and it goes on and on because the game is basically a giant timesink even with a premium token. Does the token speed everything up? No! Does the token provide you with extra research points? No! And guess what...when you use a token it ONLY applies to the world you were in instead of applying to ALL worlds, sorry but I want my 7 or 30 days to cover all worlds that I play instead of just the 1, forcing you to buy several tokens for the worlds you do play in assuming you can get any fun or enjoyment out of this game. Sorry Stronghold Kingdoms but ultimately you dont offer enough benefits to justify the time spent in the game and you don't do things you SHOULD be doing. Personally I dont have the time to stay up and wait for a timer to end just so I can see the end result. Which means I wont spend the money for cards and/or tokens unless I felt like I was getting proper value for money. You can do better and you can implement changes like what you did for banner creation or the recent avatar update. Give us players more options, more choices, scrap the 7 day token and make the 30 day one viable for 3 pounds a throw, give somebody like me enough of a reason to play and it's a very viable F2P game. But until you do these things I cannot recommend the game long term. This ends my review.

Fallout 3, surprisingly, is a game that was actually developed and made by Bethesda, and not a fan made mod. This is surprising because from just playing it, it can be hard to tell at times. I know I'm late to writing this review, but I wanted to remind both myself and anyone who reads this of how Fallout 3 was in case Fallout 4 doesn't seem as good as it looks when it comes out. (It may not look like it with the 90 minutes I have tracked, but I have completed the game twice; once from a retail copy and more recently through New Vegas using the Tale of Two Wastelands mod.)
Fallout 3 is set in the Capital Wasteland, a new location set on the opposite side of the US from the traditional west coasts of Fallout 1, 2, and later New Vegas. By doing this, they allowed themselves to have a clean slate of sorts, and have more creative freedom in writing the story. So naturally, being skilled writers as they are, they just copied a bunch of stuff from the old games and rewrote it to be worse. The Brotherhood of Steel is back, only this time they're a splinter faction that's a bunch of goodie two-shoes that go from shunning you to thanking you for letting them bask in your presence over the course of one quest (the "real" brotherhood is still technically there in the form of the Outcasts, but they barely have any presence in the game). The Enclave is back for no real reason at all, considering they were pretty much ended in 2. They made up their own east coast brand of super mutant just so they could flood the game with them. Even things like caps don't really make sense, since the only reason caps were used as currency in the west coast games is because they were backed by the Hub. The whole game just feels like they went through a picture book of Fallout and saw cool things and went "hey that looks cool, let's put it in our game too!" without really thinking that much about why they would actually be there.
Gameplay-wise, the game is a mixed bag. The exploration can be pretty fun, especially with mods like DC Interiors (which opens up a bunch of the boarded up buildings that Bethesda was too lazy to furnish), but the shooting is fairly subpar, and you can tell that the engine wasn't really built for shooting games at that stage of its development. Of course, you can always use VATS if you'd rather watch the game play itself instead, since it's effectively been turned into an easy button that lets you have 5 turns to blow an enemy to pieces and then gives the enemy one. The whole stat system is a joke, and between the rate you get perks, the perks added by DLCs, and the bobbleheads scattered throughout the world, it's almost impossible to not end up with 10 in every SPECIAL stat and 100 in every skill by the time you finish the game.
Because it's basically impossible to specialize in any particular ability due to inevitably having to specialize in all of them, and the fact that the game doesn't really give you any major choices that have actual consequences, it can be difficult to feel like you're actually roleplaying in Fallout 3. But that's fine, because it's pretty much impossible with the dialogue anyways. The dialogue options are, as best as I can describe them, schizophrenically written. You can blow up an entire settlement and laugh it off, then five minutes later meet a group of people you believe to be cannibals and have no dialogue option to say anything other than something negative towards them. At one point early in the game you meet a ghoul bartender, and your only options are two choices of mocking him and the last option, "Let me think about it for a moment, my good man.", which is so cringey that I can only assume that if Bethesda's animators had any talent it would be accompanied by an animation of the player character tipping an imaginary top hat and taking a puff from a wooden pipe. Most of the intelligence choices are just repeating what someone just said to you back to them in a summarized form written in an overly wordy way, and a lot of the speech checks go beyond ridiculousness in terms of convincing people or things to do things they would never realistically do in a single sentence. The game has a karma system, but I don't know if it's even possible to keep a negative karma level because of how much of it you get dumped onto you just for things like killing ghouls or raiders (which are impossible to allign with because Fallout 3 has no faction system), but it doesn't really matter because it's not even that much fun to play evil. There are no real meaningful evil choices, just a bunch of "for the laughs" things. There are one or two noteworthy evil moments and then the rest of it is just "ahaha i shoot you in the face" options in dialogue that just aren't really fulfilling, and some of them are just plain nonsensical and make no sense for the player to do, like the one at the end of the Broken Steel DLC. The game also has two factions that hunt you down depending on whether your karma is too high or low, but while the evil karma version is a group of lawbringers who are hunting you down because you're a known criminal, the good varient just gets Talon Company, a mercenary unit that Bethesda just made up and gave no backstory aside from "they're bad guys and so they want to kill good guys because they're really bad people!" and set them loose on you.
The DLC is about what you would expect so far. Operation Anchorage is essentially just a 3 hour crappy military corridor FPS with a few good rewards, Mothership Zeta is a crappy space corridor shooter with a few good rewards, and Broken Steel is only worth playing because of the fact that it basically forces you to after the end of the base game. The Pitt and Point Lookout are basically the only ones that I would consider "good", with the former being a brief but interesting quest line and a relatively fun collectathon with some good rewards and the latter being the only dlc to give a more open experience in a new map with new side quests and things to explore. If it wasn't for the fact that the GOTY edition costs the same as buying regular fallout 3 + point lookout + the pitt I'd just tell you to buy those, but oh well.
Fallout 3 is what I would consider a "popcorn RPG". It's the kind of game where you can spend 100 hours just exploring the wasteland and looting buildings and doing side quests and then remember that there's a boring main storyline for you to do, but it's not a game where you have to make choices or develop a character or anything associated with more in-depth RPGs, and while to an extent I feel that way about all of Bethesda's post-Morrowind RPGs, Fallout 3 in particular exemplifies the concept. If you're new to the Fallout series you may love it, or if you've played them all you can probably still just forget that it's a Fallout game and have fun exploring, but it's both a terrible RPG and a terrible Fallout game. It's extremely unstable on its own, so either modding it to high heaven or playing it through New Vegas in the A Tale of Two Wastelands mod (which requires both games and all of their DLC) is basically required. If you have time to kill and just want to relax in the wasteland for a little while, there's no reason not to buy Fallout 3 if it's on sale and you've got nothing else to play, but there just isn't anything exceptional that would prompt me to actively recommend the game. Hopefully Bethesda will have learned from New Vegas when we get to play Fallout 4.

After playing this game for just over a year, and somehow managing to clock up around 1500 hours game time total across both the Steam and Standalone clients, I think it's safe to say I have an addiction to this game. I would like to say the whole game is unique, but it's really not. It's a generic place a building in your city and wait X amount of hours for it to build, and you can pay to use some sort of bonus to speed it up, theres 1000 other games like that, so why is this one so good? For me, it's the sense of freedom. Firefly has set us up with the base game, and left everything else to the player. The politics, how the world progresses, the choice of how you want to play, is all down to the players. Each player can join a faction of allies, and that faction can join a House, a group of factions that vow to work together, these Houses can then become allies with other houses, or wage war in an attempt to gain more land, or to defend the land they already own. The only real problem with this game is how easily it is to think "I'll buy some crowns, it's only £10" and then another £10... and another.. and before you know it, you've spent far more than you intended. But Firefly has to make money some way :)

Confession time: I'm a die-hard Warhammer 40K nerd. Bought most of the Horus Heresy books, built, painted and played three different armies in the tabletop game, and spent hours upon hours browsing Warhammer wiki, BOLS, and 1d♥♥♥♥♥.

One of the few games that actually does asymetrical multiplayer well and pretty much the only multiplayer only game I could recommend for the following reasons:
1: it is well paced. While other games with the same concept like "Evolve" ended up as a gloryfied hide and seek mission, this one has really good pacing. The 4 Divers defend a robot digging for treasure, setting up defenses, while the 2 sharks try to simply murder them efficently.
Several changes of location reset the status quo several times, and also give the shark-side moments to pick of single divers while they are trying to move to another location.
2: Both side feels unique, mostly the shark-side does, but since everything plays under the sea(insert little mermaid song here) you have to fight in a 3D environment, which in itself is not done all that often in Shooter games. Yes, most of the time you are in a literal 3D environment, but giving you free movement in every way constantly is something not done to often and opens up many new styles of gameplay.
It also has a little bit of horror in there, since it can actually be quite terryfing as a diver. For the sharks? Not so much, it is rather tactical, since you are outnumberd 2:1, therefore, can't simply go in and eat every diver alive. No you have to coordinate your attacks with one another, need to think of ways to get out again before your targets can retaliate and even open up new paths by crashing walls open and attacking from angles your opponents didn't expect.
Sure, the game is far from perfect, but it is still one of the best asymetrical multiplayergames out there and probably everything "Evolve" tried to be, just better, without beeing a fullprice release.

Scribblenauts Unlimited pertains to the latter. Don't get me wrong, it's a fun game, at least for the first couple of levels, after that, well it just becomes repetitive. I could see this being a great for the fam-fam if everyone sat down in front of the tele and played the Wii U port together.

Trainz offers so much to train fans that I really can’t call it simply a “game.”  It can be a full-fledged hobby if that’s what you’re interested in, and I am.
Not only can you learn to drive realistically modeled rail vehicles on beautiful developer-created routes; additionally, choosing from a vast supply of built-in asset-content (and from a treasure-trove of free user-created downloadable content), you can design and literally build your own virtual 3D-world of colorful, seasonal, and environmental real-world sights and bring it all to life with railroad sound and motion. You can populate your world with interactive industries and task your rail creation to meet their needs.  As engineer, you can yourself perform these tasks, or you may build and set AI Trains to handle the job, or—with multiple trains running simultaneously—you can schedule both AI’s and personal tasking.  And, of course, with AI’s you can sit back and watch all the fun you’ve created in the world you’ve created. You can even become your own director and set cameras along the routes to capture the action from all angles.
The more I experience Trainz, the more I see it’s incredible range and potential.  Driving detailed locomotives and rolling stock on working and lovingly created routes in simulation, learning all about railroad life and tasks is only the start. But it’s a great start that has obviously benefitted from it’s 15 years of evolution. When you watch the You Tube fan-based videos and tutorials of previous offerings and compare them with today’s T:ANE (“Trainz: A New Era”—the latest offering in that evolution), you can clearly see the continuous dedication involved.  As the graphics and computer capabilities have improved, Trainz has taken advantage of that by improving the game’s qualities of realism. I find that growth exciting and something to continue looking forward to.
But Trainz is about more than a software developer’s product, their ongoing refinements, and your individual creativeness.  Indeed, it’s about a worldwide community of enthusiastic players and knowledgeable hobbyists who are online and only a button-click away. Whether you’re ruling the single-player rails or playing in multiplayer, push that chat-button and you can interact with others from all over who have discovered and are enjoying Trainz.  Also, from the help button, you have immediate access to n3v’s Internet Wiki.  From there you’ll find all kinds of developer-information and can ask questions from other hobby/game enthusiasts who can and do respond with valuable information to help you.  I have personally found the response to be really helpful, timely, and truly there from other train enthusiasts!
There is so much to talk about.  If you think you’d like to rule the rails, become a Trainzer and watch a whole new world open up to you.

Alright, I'm seventeen hours into this game and have half the achievements in the bag, so for $2.50 (steam sale price) this was unquestionably worth it.
Is it a God game? Civ building? Puzzler? RTS? It's hard to categorize the game. Briefly, you command 4 giants clockwise and counter- around a flat "globe", creating features such as animals, minerals or vegetables in segments or terraforming into mountains/deserts, oceans, swamps or forests. Villagers move in. They'll randomly decide on "projects" which you complete by having your giants create resources in the village. But take care -- if the villagers grow too fast they get greedy, and either attack other villages or even the giants themselves!
Games are timed, and you're given rudimentary tools to start. You can't do everything that's possible in the game without "unlocks": achieving some goals each game. This may turn some off but it really works on multiple levels: limits the complexity to start and gives you different goals for each game so that you won't want to find the One Winning Strategy. 60 to 120 minutes is a big time sink (especially if you're pausing), but you can knock out a half dozen "unlocks" in a given game, especially at the beginning.
In a game where everything works together well, it only makes sense that the core mechanism of the game is "symbiosis". Some features work better next to others (e.g., bonus food for having this animal near this plant), and then you can embue features with different aspects and then transmute them into higher-level items which likely have different symbioses. This is crucial because there's simply not enough land within the border of each village to accomplish the goals as they get harder and harder.
And I didn't even mention ambassadors. Or having to have your giants "put down" advancing armies (or let them through -- Hammerville was looking a little snobby).
Really, everything in this game works together so well, and it's very unique. Definitely buy this if you like puzzle or sim games.

“Quests in games can actually provide an interesting type of bridge between game rules and game fiction,” Jeff Howard claims in his book, Quests.  Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery is an independent quest game unlike any other I have played.  I would like to initially say that I am pleasantly suspired, unsettlingly frustrated, and utterly confused.  I am surprised because I appreciate and enjoy the game.  Frustrated because the game feels like the one friend you have, but don’t know why you still hang out with them because they’re pretty lame most of the time, but occasionally awesome.  However, I feel the story was very well presented and overall enjoyable with amount of closure I felt satisfied with.
Mechanics
Sword and Sworcery has interesting mechanics, as far as a heads up display goes, there is not really any aside from a triangle to press in the top right hand corner of the screen. This will drop down your inventory which contains at different times, a key, the megatome, and mushrooms. On the topic of victory, there is a auditory response associated with defeating foes which is quite rewarding (all the sounds in the game are absolutely amazing!) Combat mechanics include right clicking the mouse (on computer) to draw your sword, then you click either a sword icon or shield icon in the bottom right part of the screen.  If you hold your shield up for a long enough time you can regenerate health points, which are displayed as stars in your inventory.  Something quite unique about this game is its negative progression.  As the story progresses, you loose your stars of health and eventually our brave protagonist dies.
Dynamics
The dynamic in the game are quite interesting and I enjoyed them.  You use the mouse to walk around, you double click to go places, or you can hold the mouse button.  You can use W, A, S, D or the arrow keys to move the camera around, you can zoom in or zoom out the camera with the scroll wheel.  I did enjoy this because it seemed like a more relaxed way to play sometimes. I don’t think the game would have been as good if you walked the character with buttons. The game puts you in the position of a god.  It says that the finger of a god is leading the Sythian (our protagonist).
Aesthetics
The overall effect of this game was quite incredible.  I feel that sensation, fantasy, narrative, challenge, fellowship, discovery, and expression. Sensation mostly because of the audio.  The soundtrack in this game is just so enchanting, it’s really what ties the mystical bow on this gem of a game.  This game would not work without it’s music. Fantasy applies because this game is very much make believe, there are things that would not make sense at all in the real world. Narrative because, as we’ve learned, the Archetype is our narrator who appears inside and outside of the game. Challenge this game was quite challenging at this times, mostly the trigon battles.  You would make a few mistakes and then die and have to start is all over again, they were just very annoying. Fellowship because we have the Archetype, Logfella, Dogfella, and Girl all on your side somewhat helping you or at least provide aid on your quest. This game is also most definitely Discovery.  We are expected to go around this game and discover the secrets of the land. Expression, this was one of my favorite parts of the game. The player fights this grizzled boar.  At the end of the fight you are given the option of sparing his life or taking it.  Each choice has the same outcome, aside from a note from the Archetype in the megatome. Lastly, submission, this game most definitely an outcome of this. I was able to sit down and just enjoy the game for a few minutes.
I enjoyed the game quite a bit and would actually recommend it to other, it’s witty, it’s sad, it’s got lots of humor too.

This is an excellent PvP and RvR sailing game, more simulation-style rather than arcade-style.  This isn't a fast game, expect to play for at least an hour or two per session.  Sailing speeds in the open world are accelerated, but it still takes a couple of real-life hours to sail all the way across the map.  This also isn't a game for the risk-averse: if your ship gets sunk you lose it permanently along with all its cargo (but starter ships can be obtained in any port for free so you will never be stranded without any ship at all).  For those willing to take risks, there is plenty of reward!
There are a number of bad reviews from players who are mad because they got banned; take these with a large grain of salt.  This is a game about sailing ship combat, not a meta-game about bending the rules to maximize personal gain for minimum risk.  If somebody played for 300+ hours and left a bad review, keep in mind that they enjoyed the game enough to play for 300+ hours.

Three days after I installed the game I was making my first big trade run, running my small trader's ship from a city a stone's throw from my nation's capital back to the big city, my hold packed with iron ore from a local mine.  Just as I left the cover of the smaller town's fort, I spotted sails on the horizon, 45 degrees off my bow.  Using my looking-glass, I determined that it was a player controlled pirate brig, waiting halfway between the city and town for unsuspecting prey.  Me.  I checked my speed and the wind direction as he pulled his ship around, and realized he would have me before I reached the safety of Port Royal's guns.  I swung my own ship around, pulling close against the wind, knowing my fore-and-aft rigged trader would be faster against the wind than his square-rigged brig.  I gained speed, and he pulled in behind me as I passed him.  But I was too fast for him, and he pulled off back the way he came, to wait for the next catch.  I entered the bay of Port Royal safely, calling out the pirate's location and last seen trajectory in national chat.  After selling the hard earned iron to a local crafter, I had enough coin to outfit my own brig, and was pirate hunting ten minutes later.
So this game has a lot of undeserved bad reviews.  The most important thing to know about this game is it is still in ALPHA.  What you get is a beautifully modeled world filled with gorgeous ships, all supplemented with the best pvp naval combat that exists right now.  This game is really good, for a game in ALPHA.  The bad reviews are a result of people expecting a fully developed MMO on purchase.  The devs are still learning how to create good, EVE-like MMO mechanics in the world, while keeping said mechanics faithful to the time period.  They are making good progress, and since the 10.0 patch in May 2017, have been improving the game in leaps and bounds.  This will be an excellent MMO one day.  But do not buy this game and expect a finished product.  There are no tutorials excepting the ones in the forums, and you need to set aside a minimum of an hour and a half per session, because this is not a fast paced game.  However, the payoff is worth it to me, and if it isn't to you yet, then it will be soon.  It's definitely worth a shot.

I play this game since the steam release of the early acces.
The game is great, combats are very intense and beautifull.
It not really an hardcore game, but i understand that right now it's not easy for lone beginners. There is no tutorial yet. User interface is still the fonctional but dull work in progress blue UI.
Naval action is a sandbox where you can pick a faction and sail everywhere in the huge carribean. Visit ports, attack any enemy ships (bot or players), ask for PvE missions, build production buildings, produce, loot, craft stuff, material, trading goods, cannons & ships, participate in conquests, trade .
All of this you can do, but you can't do all of this easily if you don't organise with other players from your faction.
So you better buy a microphone and install teamspeak then join your faction teamspeak server, even if you don't join a guild from the start.
Other players will help you in your first steps, they will give you advices, usefull links, maybe even gold or ships.
Because if everything can sometimes seems very difficult to get and easy to loose when you play alone, the game is build around cooperation, and most factions have well organized guilds looking for you even if you are not hardcore.
About combat:
Ship handling is a good mix between realism and arcade. You will have to use wind to your advantage and the more you progress in square-rigged ships, the more it will be important. You will have to use rudder, but also your masts manually to turn or stop faster.
Waves will make you ship roll & pitch. Depending on wich wood your ship is build on, it will be faster or balanced, or very resistant. Crew can be lost by cannon ball or spall and are vulnerable to grape shots if not protected. In short: damage model is very detailled: holes, leaks, fire, demasting, damaged sails, critical explosions, boarding (fonctional but wip) are well represented and you will really be able to feel like a real age of sails captain.
But being an age of sail captain is not an easy career, and battle instance are only a small aspect of Naval action.
Open sea:
If sailing in the open world is faster than real sailing, and wind is not modeled like on Virtual regatta or other sim games,  sailing time can still be important if you choose to sail somewhere far with a bad wind, it can take very long.
Speed and wind is what keeps you alive so you still need to watch for enemy ships & wind or you will be sunk by superior forces before you know it. So sail in group or sail fast, ask others about enemy spotted, no place is sure on the map.
Economy:

This deceptive little gem keeps me playing hours after I intended to stop.  The goal is simple: take your game development studio from a one-(wo)man garage band to a AAA team by making hit games.  Game development is done by naming your game, selecting a topic, a project size (small, medium, large, AAA), a target rating (Y, E, M), a genre (or two), the game engine you want to use, and the gaming system(s) you want to release on.  You also get to choose what features you want your game to have based on the options afforded you by the engine you chose.  This is all good and well, but not what hooks you in.
The hook comes from taking the feedback from your game's release to try and figure out how to make the next blockbuster.  Every time you release a game you are given review scores which have an impact on how well the game sells.  The score also includes a small blurb from the reviewer that can give you some insight into why you earned that score.  You can also generate a post development report that will provide you with critical information regarding how well your choices (topic, rating, genre, systems) worked (or didn't work) for you.  Being able to use this feedback to craft better games is vital to your company, because a string of bad games could easily crumble your empire.  This is especially evident in the early stages where any game could very well be your last.  I was on the very edge of bankruptcy after a streak of bad games, but was able to turn everything around with a last ditch effort into a Fantasy RPG.
Unnecessarily long story short: this is a great example of a game that has a simple premise that lures you in and hooks you with the desire to keep pushing yourself to reach a higher goal long into the night.
Addictive time killer. Wasn't long before I had a multi-billion dollar company.

Have to edit my review here. For nearly five months, I was completely unable to even launch the game because of some unknown issue. I had the game on PS4, too, so I knew the gameplay was subpar, but I still wanted to see if there was any chance it would be better on PC.

You could say, "Oh, well just explore all the planets, surely there's something interesting to do somewhere." but sadly, that turns into a chore. Everything is the exact same on every planet as far as things to do are concerned.
Overall, dreadfully boring. Plenty of other exploration games that are worth buying, so go play those instead.

The game looks really good, but plays ever so poorly. It's a stylish 3rd person shooter that's undermined by uninspired or bad mechanics.
The main problem with the combat in the game is the way it manages health. You have almost no way of avoiding damage so health regeneration is the key to your survivability. The problem is that recovering health requires you to engage in lengthy melee execution animations during which you are still 100% vulnerable. And the real stupidity of it? You don't even get your health back until the animation FINISHES. The game also includes a shield that acts as a second health bar, but insufficient cover and a multitude of ranged enemies ensure your shield only gets a chance to regenerate once the fight is over.
My frustration is further amplified by a dodge roll that's nearly useless, wonky melee targeting, getting stuck on terrain and enemies, and occasions where my character stopped responding to input.
I forced my way through the game hoping it'd get better (it didn't), but it only took me 10 hours to beat the game on the hardest difficulty. Even if I'd found the game enjoyable, the value isn't there. You might be able to get some mileage out of the multiplayer stuff if people still play it. It didn't interest me so I didn't look into it.
I think the game would have been much improved if they had gone one of two ways with it: make it a brawler with shooting elements, or make it a cover shooter a la gears of war. Instead, all we've got here is a pretty Warhammer 40k veneer plastered on top of a bland 3rd person shooter.

Fallout 3. My gosh, this game is near to perfection. This game is my favorite RPG at the moment, I mean, every RPG fan needs to play this game. NEEDS TO. Especially GOTY Edition, it's only $20 such a good deal. Lets sum up the story.
You and your Dad lived in a vault, your Dad (played by Liam Neeson) leaves the vault, to find a water purifier called the 'G.E.C.K.' You also leave the vault, in search of your father. Now, let me tell you the pros and the cons of this game +DLC
Pros
+Unlike Oblivion, Fo3 is a very immersive game
+Lots of interesting characters as you progress through the game.
+Most of the DLC (Except Mothership Zeta) is actually pretty good, my personal favorite is The Pitt
+Lots of weapons and guns, lasers, and plasma rifles are awesome, and the Fat Man
+The Soundtrack in this game is superb, I love the oldies music in this game.
+ Interesting antagonist (The Enclave)
+ The Power Armor (Whether BOS or Enclave) is freaking sweet
+ Most of the Companions are interesting,and fun to use
+ Lots of places to explore
+ THe Perk System is great, makes the game more fun
+ V.A.T.S. just makes this game morew fun than ever
+ You can put a lot of hours into this game, and not get bored (I know at the moment it says i put 52 hours, but i put much more on the ps3.)
Cons
- Comanions die if they lose all of their health, luckily for the dog comapnion there's a perk to have him have another dog, but you can't get that perk until much later in the game.
- The ending without the Broken Steel DLC, Sucks, once you complete the story, without the dlc, it doesnt let you go back
- The DLC Mothership Zeta was a HUGE disappointment for me, you're not missing out if you dont play it. (except for the new guns)
- Poorly optimized for Windows 7 and up, and Bethesda refused to patch it, you can get an unofficial patch that will fix this problem.
So... Despite some of the Minor flaws this game has, it is still a fantastic RPG that must be played by anyone that calls themselves an RPG fan
Final Verdit: 9.5/10 MUST BUY

Short review:
Good: Well-varied cast of characters, great visuals, fast-paced fighting action, includes most variances in fighting games, best tutorial for any fighting game that I have ever played, astonishingly-amazing online play, decent-looking stages, possibly balanced metagame, great training mode.
Bad: Music is generic and forgettable, gameplay although fun is not all too different or unique, plot of the game needs some more work.
Ugly: No time attack, score attack, etc. modes.
Long review:
I am in a dangerous position right now. Either I get mauled to death by the people who love this game, or I get called a baka hentai weeboo or whatever other insult there is from those who want to shun the game for what it is. Oh well, here I go.
Skullgirls is a 2D fighting game, involving an all-female cast, minus two characters which are DLC male characters, which borrows a lot of elements from several fighting games which made those games fun. The story involves a Skull heart which can grant any wish for the female user, but in order to reach the Skull heart, one must first defeat the previous Skullgirl. The rest of the story is just character backstory, with character interaction between only a select few characters, so yes, the story is weak here, although probably better than the likes of Tekken 6 and other fighting games which tend to disregard plotlines. When the game started out, there were eight characters, with Fukua now being added as the ninth character. There are currently two DLC characters in the game, with three more on their way. The game was first released in 2012 on consoles, and was ported to PC on Steam a year later, which was a smart move since there is little variety in 2D fighters on the PC, and I do mean the ones which are still active enough, so ASW games, Melty Blood, and the last two Netherrealm Studios fighters do not count. The game includes a cartoonish theatre aesthetic, which I personally do enjoy a lot.
So to start, is this game original? No. Like I said, it does borrow a lot of elements from various fighting games, although the counter-argument is that we are well beyond the point for improvement that is too noticable to exist, as most of the ideas have been taken and implemented already. Is it fun? Yes. Pretty fun. While I am not an avid player of Skullgirls, the time that I have spent on it has been pretty enjoyable.
The game is more fast-paced than your average fighter, more along the lines of Marvel vs Capcom 2, and it also includes the option of either choosing to play as one, two, or three characters. The game also includes being able to pick your traditional round-based system, or the one where you have more than one health bar and winners of rounds do not replenish their bars, which is present in games such as Mortal Kombat and Killer Instinct. The characters have unique designs, and tend to stand out by having the same amount of uniqueness in their gameplay as well, although not on the same level as games such as Guilty Gear and BlazBlue. Still, the game does have some extremely high-quality hand-drawn sprites for their characters, with a large frame-per-second to boot too. Some people, however, may believe that Skullgirls has a little too few fighters to use, but I believe that 8-9 varied characters for a fighting game that just started out, and at $15 in contrast to your usual $50 or $60, is pretty good. Also, the stages look pretty neat.
And let me tell you about the tutorial mode. This game has one which covers not only the mechanics for Skullgirls, but for fighting games in general. I am not kidding; there are lessons here which helped me a great deal in BlazBlue which that game failed to clearly convey to me, and that game used to have the best tutorial mode until I got my hands on this game. This is perfect for beginners and experts alike to hone their skills, and learn new techniques. And if that isn't enough, the game even goes as far as to lay out special tutorial modes for each individual character too.
Now I have not played enough of Skullgirls to get a grasp of the metagame, but from what I have been told, the metagame is fair and decent - or was, until Big Band showed up. Hopefully, he will be patched soon in the future. One thing I do want to point out is the gorgeous online play. If you dislike playing online because of the lag, Skullgirls uses the GGPO system, which involves the use of reducing the amount of frames for a better and more sustained connection. It works like a charm, and honestly, I have played with a friends from Jordan and Asia with little to no lag. Heck, I even played with people from Korea without experiencing game-breaking lag.
So what are the disadvantages to Skullgirls? Well, aside from the story, I didn't enjoy the game's BGM, except for the one made for the cathedral stage. Most of the other songs are, well, not bad, however they still do not stand out enough to be considered a strong point of the game. Again, the gameplay is nothing too different from things that have been done before, so if you come in here expecting the same level of potency of Arc System Works games, you will not find it here.
My only major complaint is the lack of any special mode, such as time attack, score attack, challenge mode, survival mode, and so on. I understand that it would have set the developers back when the game first came out, but it still is disappointing that such modes were not later included in the game. Maybe I just expect too much from this game, but this is still a point that should be made.
Skullgirls is still an amazing fighting game. It has a very large and active community, an extremely talented developer close to its players, and not to mention that the game in itself is still very fun. I would very much recommend it, especially if you are a new fighting gamer because you should not miss out on the tutorial mode this game has. People who probably do not enjoy the cartoonish nature of the game (again, I love its aesthetic) may stay away from this, and while I would argue that one should never judge a game due to its design choice, it is still their opinion. Buy Skullgirls.
---------------------------------------
Now that I finished the review, some of you may be interested in what I have to say about this game's fanservice. Personally, I dislike fanservice, but if the game is good enough and if the fanservice is not extreme (Senran Kagura and Dragon's Crown levels of extreme), I will simply ignore it. I also bought this game without knowing that it included fanservice, why? I don't know, I must have been pretty naive back then. Oh well. Great game though.
Still, I think the fanservice is not too distracting, nor is it a major part of the game as most claim to be. The only character whom is probably a little too fanservicey is Valentine, but aside from her, things do not get crazy enough to raise a flag. You will get jiggling breasts and panty shots, but the fighting is fast enough for you not to stop and notice.
I didn't want to include this in the review, for as I mentioned before, you should not judge a game based on aesthetics. Even if I were to review a game like Senran Kagura, I would not mention it in my review, but only as a warning after the review for people who may find this kind of content offensive.

Reus is a game that sits in a very particular niche. Though I do enjoy this game, and am recommending it, it's usually only fun in short bursts. The game involves controlling different giants (such as an ocean giant and a forest giant), using their abilities to help villages of humans settle and grow. In the regular game mode, you are given a certain amount of time (the first mode is 30 minutes) to see how far you can develop the human cultures.
The game is enjoyable overall, but the giants move very slow, sometimes have long cooldowns on abilities, and, ultimately, don't do very much. The core game mechanic seems to be helping the humans build and upgrade special building, which usually just involves spamming the same resources in the area surrounding their village. The game gets repetitive very fast, has very little to offer in the long run, but is actually pretty charming and decent.
As a gamer, this game gets a little boring. As a graduate student who dabbles in video game studies, this game offers some interesting mechanics to the civilization building genre, offers some interesting ideas about religion and the environment, and serves as a good experiment in different forms of game design. I wouldn't spend too much on this, and would do a good deal of research on it first.

I don't think I would have enjoyed the game if I didn't have a friend to coop with, but I did, and over the course of many small and medium dose sessions we got through it and for the most part enjoyed ourselves. My impression overall is mixed.
Divinity OS is ambitious, and when the designers, my friend and myself were all on point it is fantastic, but there is a bloat and annoyance throughout also. I personally hated the crafting system and all the elder scrolls garbage items that brought into the mix. Having to heal up every party member after combat seemed like a pointless annoyance (it literally costs nothing but time to cast whatever healing spells you doubtless will know). There's no real balance between different skills and traits, some of them are just trash, and the skills you can raise with items are generally not worth putting as many points into because of how costs scale. These skills also seem generally less useful, for example lockpicking won't do much of anything after the first few hours as lock levels start going into NO YOU NEED THE KEY territory, and other skills like Charisma etc come up less often as the game goes on. I feel like secondary skills should've been in a seperate category or something.  In the long run of the game there are basically three classes, Strength, Dexterity and Intelligence, because those are the casting stats and what you build around. There are some incredibly♥♥♥♥♥♥ways to build a character in theory, and while to an extent that's unavoidable it also just seems like poor design, wasted space. Oh god and the traits. Being able to argue with my friend about a course of action or an event was pretty fun at first, and then getting a bonus based on what we chose? Cool! Then we quickly started to realize that certain bonuses were♥♥♥♥♥♥compared to others and instead of trying to roleplay it became "What traits do you think this one is highlighting?" because being a caster and getting a bonus to backstabbing sucks, or missing out on immunity to fear because you're not into spiritual woo♥♥♥♥♥♥
I think that's most of my gripes out of the way? Electrifying pools of blood was a giant pain in the♥♥♥♥♥in the early game, and ice is sometimes stupid hard to see for something that will cause you to lose a turn. I could go on, I have gone on, but let's try to get past the horde of petty annoyances. The story is not impressive, but not terrible. The combat is rich, at times in certain really combat heavy sections it can get a tad stale, but for the most part (in pansy normal) it was challenging with a solid amount of scenarios to mix things up. The puzzles were one of my favorite parts, also cheesing the puzzles with teleport, although there were definitely a number of times where I found myself wondering what the hell Divinity wanted from me. Solving Councilor Jake's murder was easily the high point of the game, and actually felt like playing a decent table top thing, which impressed me at the time, unfortunately it never quite got back to that after the first act, and started to feel more like a generic fantasy RPG as it went on.
Anyway it's worth trying if you're willing to push through all the baggage it carries from its predecessors. Oh and make sure to quick save a lot if you're the Host, because god damn.

I would recommend T:ANE for train sim fans but with a few caveats. I probably have had more enjoyment with this version of Trainz than I have had with previous versions, partly because I am semi-retired now and have had  more time with it. I have seen steady improvement in the sim from the early betas through HotFix 1 and 2 (beta) and expect it will continue to get better.
That's not to say that the game has been without its problems. Along the way I have upgraded my video card to an NVidia 750. which made a big difference in frame rates and the level of detail I can use. Shadows remain problematic. On some routes, I can use them; on others shadows really bog down performance.
Finding T:ANE compatible content can be a problem. I spent a lot of time floundering about on the Download Station until I discovered the freeware routes uploaded by Bob, msgsapper. His routes and sessions all work well in T:ANE and are all available on the Download Station.
Since I don't have the ability to create my own routes or rolling stock, I'm looking forward to more T:ANE payware and freeware that take advantage of T:ANE's advanced graphics.
Overall, if you love trains and have the time and patience to work through T:ANE's quirk, I think the average user can have a lot of fun.

So far, I've had a lot of fun playing this game.  However, like all Sid Meier games, I expect that it will get exponentially harder on the higher difficulty levels.  That's OK, cuz it's worth it, even at regular price.
The game is suitable for most ages, and would probably get a PG rating if it were a movie.  It's relatively tame, in terms of violence and destruction--milder than the LEGO games, and maybe on par with what you'd see in old Looney Tunes or Popeye cartoons.  There has yet to be any blood and guts, which is fine.  Villains are pretty easy to identify and figure out once enough clues are gathered to allow them to be found.  You can court governors' daughters, but the interaction is mostly dancing, with some mild kissing.  I've seen worse things in Disney movies.
There are several minigames that can be played, depending on the situation.  The duel and dancing scenes are such.  The ship and land battles play out differently as well, and are pretty decent in their own right.  Things can get a little repetitive, so if you play the game the same way twice--that is, after starting over with a new character--you might get a little bored.  That said, there are many ways to actually play the game, and enough randomization has been implemented to keep things just this side of interesting.  Truth is, even the pirate's life had its share of routines and dull moments.  I can't say that encountering such moments put me off very much at all.  Just keep moving around, and you'll be fine.
My one complaint about this, is that the criminals and villains mostly have the same last names, as if there were 23 brothers named Shawshank that managed to♥♥♥♥♥♥off the Spaniards, 13 brothers named Connery that managed to♥♥♥♥♥♥off the English, etc.  The same two pirates are always the ones to hunt down when someone's daughter gets kidnapped, or when a new clue to the main quest is to be discovered.  I can't imagine it would be hard to fix this.  In any case, it's an amusing issue, and while it doesn't significantly detract from the game, it is kinda strange to encounter it in the face of the other good game elements.
I'd like a game like this with additional side quests, such as intrigue or other villains or treasures to hunt down.  Also, since the Civilization games play on customizable worlds, it would be cool to see this game get some procedurally-generated maps.  Aside from these requested features, though, there is enough in this game to warrant plenty of replays.  This is the beauty of the better Sid Meier games.  Even if I were to get tired and go to something else, I always end up going back to Civ3 or Alpha Centauri, and Pirates will be on my list as well.
